Many bugs come from a set of true-or-false flags, like is_paid and is_shipped. Four flags give 16 mixes, and some make no sense: shipped but not paid. Use one state value instead. Then the impossible mixes cannot even be written.

Patterns that solve problems

Divide and conquer

Find a name in a phone book. Open it in the middle. The name comes later, so throw away the first half. Do it again with the half that is left. Here it is with one million numbers.

// Look for target in a sorted slice. Count the steps.
fn search(xs: &[u32], target: u32) -> (String, u32) {
    let (mut lo, mut hi) = (0, xs.len());   // the answer is in xs[lo..hi]
    let mut steps = 0;
    while lo < hi {
        steps += 1;
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;       // the middle
        if xs[mid] == target {
            return (format!("index {mid}"), steps);
        }
        if xs[mid] < target { lo = mid + 1; } else { hi = mid; }  // drop one half
    }
    (String::from("not found"), steps)
}

fn main() {
    let xs: Vec<u32> = (1..=1_000_000).collect();   // sorted numbers
    for t in [765_432, 1, 0] {
        let (answer, steps) = search(&xs, t);
        println!("{t}: {answer} after {steps} steps");
    }
}
# Look for target in a sorted list. Count the steps.
def search(xs, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(xs)              # the answer is in xs[lo:hi]
    steps = 0
    while lo < hi:
        steps += 1
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2         # the middle
        if xs[mid] == target:
            return f"index {mid}", steps
        if xs[mid] < target:         # drop one half
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return "not found", steps

xs = list(range(1, 1_000_001))       # sorted numbers
for t in [765_432, 1, 0]:
    answer, steps = search(xs, t)
    print(f"{t}: {answer} after {steps} steps")
765432: index 765431 after 18 steps
1: index 0 after 20 steps
0: not found after 20 steps

Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller parts of the same kind. It solves each part and joins the answers. Binary search is the simplest case: one part is thrown away each time. One million items need at most 20 steps, because 2^{20} is just over one million. In general it takes about \log_2 n steps.

Merge sort uses the same idea. Split the list in two, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves. The chapter Sorting, searching, divide and conquer shows why this takes about n \log_2 n steps.

Binary search works only on sorted data. On an unsorted list it gives wrong answers with no error. Also, in languages with fixed-size integers, (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow on huge arrays. The Rust code uses lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to stay safe.

Recursion

How big is a folder? It is the size of its files, plus the size of each folder inside it. To answer, you ask the same question again on a smaller folder.

Recursion solves a problem with a smaller copy of the same problem. It needs a base case that stops. Divide and conquer is usually written with recursion. Trees are recursive too: each child is the root of a smaller tree. The full story, with the call stack, is in Programming foundations.

Recursion that solves the same small problem many times can be very slow. The next two patterns, greedy choice and dynamic programming, are two answers to that.

Greedy choice and dynamic programming

You must give change with as few coins as possible. A simple plan: always take the biggest coin that still fits. Does it always work?

// Greedy: always take the biggest coin that still fits.
fn greedy(coins: &[usize], mut amount: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut used = Vec::new();
    for &c in coins {                       // coins from big to small
        while amount >= c {
            amount -= c;
            used.push(c);
        }
    }
    used
}

// Dynamic programming: best[a] is the fewest coins that make a.
fn min_coins(coins: &[usize], amount: usize) -> usize {
    let mut best = vec![usize::MAX; amount + 1];
    best[0] = 0;
    for a in 1..=amount {
        for &c in coins {
            if c <= a && best[a - c] != usize::MAX {
                best[a] = best[a].min(best[a - c] + 1);   // reuse a smaller answer
            }
        }
    }
    best[amount]
}

fn main() {
    for (coins, amount) in [(vec![25, 10, 5, 1], 63), (vec![4, 3, 1], 6)] {
        let g = greedy(&coins, amount);
        println!("coins {coins:?}, amount {amount}");
        println!("  greedy: {g:?} = {} coins", g.len());
        println!("  best:   {} coins", min_coins(&coins, amount));
    }
}
# Greedy: always take the biggest coin that still fits.
def greedy(coins, amount):
    used = []
    for c in coins:                         # coins from big to small
        while amount >= c:
            amount -= c
            used.append(c)
    return used

# Dynamic programming: best[a] is the fewest coins that make a.
def min_coins(coins, amount):
    best = [float("inf")] * (amount + 1)
    best[0] = 0
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:
                best[a] = min(best[a], best[a - c] + 1)   # reuse a smaller answer
    return best[amount]

for coins, amount in [([25, 10, 5, 1], 63), ([4, 3, 1], 6)]:
    g = greedy(coins, amount)
    print(f"coins {coins}, amount {amount}")
    print(f"  greedy: {g} = {len(g)} coins")
    print(f"  best:   {min_coins(coins, amount)} coins")
coins [25, 10, 5, 1], amount 63
  greedy: [25, 25, 10, 1, 1, 1] = 6 coins
  best:   6 coins
coins [4, 3, 1], amount 6
  greedy: [4, 1, 1] = 3 coins
  best:   2 coins

With US coins, greedy gives the best answer. With coins 4, 3 and 1, it fails. It takes 4 first and then needs two 1s. The best answer is 3 + 3, only two coins.

A greedy algorithm makes the best local choice and never changes it. It is fast and simple. But it is correct only for some problems, and you need a proof. The usual proof is an exchange argument.

Dynamic programming tries every choice, but it never solves the same small problem twice. best[a] holds the answer for each smaller amount. Each new answer reuses old ones. It needs two things. Small answers must combine into big ones. And the same small problems must come up again and again.

Do not trust a greedy plan because it works on two examples. Look for a small example that breaks it, like coins 4, 3 and 1. If you cannot prove it, use dynamic programming. Both are in Dynamic programming and greedy algorithms.

Randomisation

Quicksort picks one item, the pivot, and splits the list around it. A bad pivot on sorted data makes it very slow. A random pivot makes that bad case very unlikely, whatever the input is.

Randomisation uses chance on purpose. It has three common uses. It avoids a worst case that an attacker or bad luck could cause. It estimates a big answer from a small sample, as in polls and A/B tests. And it breaks ties, as in random waits before a retry. A Las Vegas algorithm is always right, and only its time is random. A Monte Carlo algorithm has a fixed time but can be wrong with a small chance.

"Random" is not the same as "secret". Python's random module is fine for games and tests. Its numbers can be predicted, so never use it for passwords or tokens. Use the secrets module. See Cryptography.

Patterns that organise data

Hashing

A cloakroom gives you ticket number 42 for your coat. Later, the worker goes straight to hook 42. Nobody searches all the coats.

A hash function turns a key, like a word, into a number. The number picks a place in a table. So you can find the key in about one step. Python dict and set, and Rust HashMap and HashSet, all work this way. When two keys get the same place, we have a collision. Every hash table must handle collisions.

Hashing also uses randomisation. Python gives each run a random seed for the hash of text. Watch the same word get a new hash in each run:

python3.14 -c "print(hash('cat'))"                   # run 1
python3.14 -c "print(hash('cat'))"                   # run 2
PYTHONHASHSEED=0 python3.14 -c "print(hash('cat'))"  # seed fixed
976145891017134162
-7664392394897802033
692052486964499043

Why? An attacker who knows the hash function can send many keys with the same hash. Then each lookup becomes a slow scan, and the server stops. This attack is called HashDoS. A secret random seed stops it. Rust does the same. Its HashMap uses SipHash 1-3 with a random seed by default. The Rust docs say the exact algorithm can change.

Never save Python's hash() to a file or send it to another machine. It changes on the next run. For a stable fingerprint, use a fixed hash like SHA-256 from hashlib. Also, never change a key while it is inside a dict or set.

Indexing

A search engine cannot read every page each time you search. Instead it builds a list in advance: for each word, the pages that contain it.

use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BTreeSet};

fn main() {
    let docs = ["the cat sat", "the dog ran", "a cat ran"];
    // The index: word -> the set of documents that hold it.
    let mut index: BTreeMap<&str, BTreeSet<usize>> = BTreeMap::new();
    for (id, text) in docs.iter().enumerate() {
        for word in text.split_whitespace() {
            index.entry(word).or_default().insert(id);
        }
    }
    println!("cat -> {:?}", index["cat"]);
    println!("ran -> {:?}", index["ran"]);
    let both: Vec<_> = index["cat"].intersection(&index["ran"]).collect();
    println!("cat AND ran -> {:?}", both);
}
docs = ["the cat sat", "the dog ran", "a cat ran"]
# The index: word -> the set of documents that hold it.
index = {}
for doc_id, text in enumerate(docs):
    for word in text.split():
        index.setdefault(word, set()).add(doc_id)

print("cat ->", index["cat"])
print("ran ->", index["ran"])
print("cat AND ran ->", sorted(index["cat"] & index["ran"]))
cat -> {0, 2}
ran -> {1, 2}
cat AND ran -> [2]

An index is extra data that points into the main data. This one is an inverted index. Databases use indexes too. In PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX makes a B-tree index unless you ask for another kind. Vector databases use special indexes to find similar meanings.

An index is not free. Every insert and update must change the index too, and it uses disk space. Do not index every column. Index the columns your slow queries really search.

Trees

Open the folders on your computer. One root folder holds folders, which hold more folders and files. A web page, a company chart and a program's grammar have the same shape.

A tree has one root. Each node has one parent, except the root, and any number of children. There are no loops. A balanced search tree finds a key in about \log_2 n steps. The B-tree is a wide, short tree. It fits disks well, so databases and file systems use it. A compiler turns your code into a syntax tree before anything else.

Insert sorted keys into a simple search tree, and every new node goes to the right. The tree becomes a long line, and search costs n steps. Balanced trees fix this by turning parts of the tree as it grows. See Data structures.

Graphs

Cities and roads. People and friendships. Packages and their dependencies. Each has things, and links between things.

A graph is a set of nodes and edges. Edges can have a direction, like a one-way street. They can have a weight, like a distance. A tree is a graph with no loops. With graphs you ask: Is there a path? Which path is the shortest? What must come first? The figure in the next section is itself a graph.

Two graph questions can look the same and still be very different. A shortest path is fast to find. The shortest tour that visits every city once is the travelling salesman problem. No fast method is known for it. See Complexity theory.

Patterns that move and keep data

Caching

You keep your keys by the door, not in the cellar. Things you use often should be close. A cache is that place by the door.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

// A tiny least-recently-used cache. Front = used longest ago.
fn run(size: usize, requests: &[u32]) -> (u32, u32) {
    let mut cache: VecDeque<(u32, u32)> = VecDeque::new();
    let (mut hits, mut misses) = (0, 0);
    for &id in requests {
        if let Some(pos) = cache.iter().position(|&(k, _)| k == id) {
            hits += 1;
            let entry = cache.remove(pos).unwrap();
            cache.push_back(entry);              // now the most recent
        } else {
            misses += 1;
            if cache.len() == size {
                cache.pop_front();               // evict the least recent
            }
            cache.push_back((id, id * 10));      // the slow lookup goes here
        }
    }
    (hits, misses)
}

fn main() {
    let requests = [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1];
    for size in [2, 3] {
        let (h, m) = run(size, &requests);
        println!("size {size}: hits={h} misses={m}");
    }
}
from functools import lru_cache

def run(size, requests):
    @lru_cache(maxsize=size)          # keep the most recent answers
    def price(item_id):
        return item_id * 10           # the slow lookup goes here
    for i in requests:
        price(i)
    info = price.cache_info()
    return info.hits, info.misses

requests = [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1]
for size in [2, 3]:
    h, m = run(size, requests)
    print(f"size {size}: hits={h} misses={m}")
size 2: hits=1 misses=5
size 3: hits=3 misses=3

A cache keeps copies of recent answers in a small, fast place. A hit means the answer was there. A miss means we must do the slow work. When the cache is full, it must evict something. LRU throws out the item that was used longest ago. Python's lru_cache does this, and its default size is 128.

  1. A hit takes 1 ms. A miss takes 100 ms. 90% of requests are hits.
  2. Average time = hit share × hit time + miss share × miss time.
  3. 0.9 \times 1 + 0.1 \times 100 = 0.9 + 10 = 10.9 ms.
  4. With no cache, every request takes 100 ms. The cache makes the average about 9 times faster.
  5. Notice: the 10% of misses cause almost all the time. Raising the hit rate to 99% gives 0.99 + 1 = 1.99 ms.

A cache can serve old data. A price changes, but the cache still shows the old price. You must decide when a copy is too old. This is called cache invalidation, and it is a classic source of bugs. Also, a size of 2 in the example gave only one hit. A cache that is too small barely helps.

Queues and buffering

A coffee shop takes orders faster than it makes coffee. The orders wait in a line. The cashier does not stop, and the barista does not rush.

A queue is a line: first in, first out. A buffer is a queue of bytes between two parts. It lets a fast part and a slow part each work at their own speed. It also smooths out bursts. Keyboards, network cards, video players and message systems between services all use buffers.

A simple law links the numbers. It is called Little's law. Suppose 50 requests arrive each second, and each one stays 0.2 seconds. Then on average 50 \times 0.2 = 10 requests are inside the system. See Cloud and system design.

If items arrive faster than they leave, a queue grows forever. A buffer cannot fix a slow worker. It only hides the problem until memory runs out. Give each queue a limit. When it is full, tell the sender to slow down. This is called back-pressure.

Replication with trade-offs

You keep an important file on your laptop, on a USB stick and in the cloud. One copy can break. The file is still safe.

Replication keeps copies of data on several machines. It gives safety, and more machines to answer reads. But the copies must agree. Raft is a well-known method for this. Its site says a cluster of 5 servers keeps working when 2 of them fail. A majority, 3 of 5, must agree on each change.

Quorums with 3 copies (N = 3)
Write waits for W copiesRead asks R copiesR + WDoes a read see the last write?
112Not always. Fast but can be old.
224Yes. 4 is more than 3, so the groups overlap.
314Yes, but one broken copy stops all writes.

The rule behind the table: if R + W > N, every read group shares at least one copy with every write group. That copy has the newest value. The proof is in Distributed systems.

Replication is not a backup. If you delete a file by mistake, every copy deletes it too, in a few milliseconds. Keep real backups as well. And remember the trade-off: when the network splits, a system must choose. It can stop answering, or it can answer with data that may be old.

How the patterns connect

The patterns are not separate. Most real designs mix three or four of them. The graph shows some links. Drag the nodes to read it.

When you meet a new problem, ask short questions. Each answer points to a pattern.

Is the same work done many times?

Save the answers. Use a cache for repeated requests. Use dynamic programming for repeated small problems inside one calculation.

Is finding things slow?

Use hashing for exact keys. Do you also need ranges, like "all orders from May"? Then use a sorted index or a tree. Use binary search on sorted data.

Is the problem too big to think about at once?

Split it. Use divide and conquer for data. Use abstraction layers for a system. Use recursion when the parts look like the whole.

Does a thing move, or might it change later?

Add one level of indirection: a name, a pointer or a config entry. Only one place then needs to change.

Does the object have steps, like "paid" and "shipped"?

Write a state machine. List the states, the events and the allowed moves.

Does work arrive in bursts, or faster than it can be done?

Put a queue between the parts. Give it a limit, and add back-pressure.

Can one machine break?

Replicate the data. Then decide what to do when the copies disagree.

Could bad luck or an attacker cause the worst case?

Add randomisation: a random pivot, a random hash seed, or random waits before a retry.

Design interviews and system design exams test these patterns by name. A good answer names the pattern, says why it fits, and states its cost. For example: "I add a cache. It cuts reads to the database. The cost is old data, so each entry expires after 60 seconds."

Butler Lampson, a Turing Award winner, wrote a famous paper of design hints in 1983. He published a long new version in 2020, with more updates in 2021. Many of its hints are the patterns of this chapter: caching, indirection, divide and conquer, and doing work in the background.

Patterns to remember

The 15 patterns of computing
PatternPurposeModelNote
Abstraction layersBuild big systems from simple levelsapp → library → operating system → hardwareA layer hides cost but does not remove it.
IndirectionLet a thing move without breaking usersa domain name points to a server addressEach level adds one more lookup.
State machinesAllow only legal stepsmatch (state, event) for an orderUse one state value, not many flags.
Divide and conquerSplit a big problem into partsbinary search: 20 steps for 1,000,000 itemsSplit and join must be cheap.
RecursionSolve with a smaller copy of the problemfolder size = files + inner folder sizesNeeds a base case. Deep calls fill the stack.
Greedy choiceTake the best step nowbiggest coin first: 63 = 25+25+10+1+1+1Fails for coins 4, 3, 1. Prove it first.
Dynamic programmingSolve each small problem oncebest[a] = min(best[a - c] + 1)Needs repeated subproblems that combine.
RandomisationAvoid the worst case, or estimate fastrandom pivot in quicksortrandom is not for secrets. Use secrets.
HashingFind a key in about one stepdict, HashMapCollisions happen. Python's hash() changes per run.
IndexingFind data without reading all of itword → documents, or a B-tree in PostgreSQLEvery index slows writes and uses space.
TreesStore parents and childrenfolders, syntax trees, B-treesUnbalanced trees become slow lists.
GraphsStore things and their linksroads, web links, dependenciesSimilar-looking graph problems can differ hugely in cost.
CachingKeep recent answers close@lru_cache(maxsize=128)Copies get old. Plan the invalidation.
Queues and bufferingJoin fast and slow parts50 per second × 0.2 s = 10 waitingSet a limit and use back-pressure.
Replication with trade-offsSurvive the loss of a machine5 Raft servers survive 2 failuresNot a backup. Choose speed or agreement.

Practice

A web shop shows the same top-10 list to every visitor. The list changes once an hour. Which pattern helps most?

  • Replication
  • Caching
  • Greedy choice

The same answer is asked for many times. Compute it once, keep the copy, and refresh it every hour.

How many steps does binary search need, at most, for a sorted list of 1,000 items?

  • 1,000
  • 100
  • 10

Each step halves the range. 2^{10} = 1024, which is just over 1,000.

An order has the flags is_paid, is_shipped and is_cancelled. Bugs show orders that are cancelled and shipped. What is the best fix?

  • Add a fourth flag.
  • Replace the flags with one state value and a table of allowed moves.
  • Put the orders in a queue.

A state machine allows only legal states. The impossible mix cannot be stored any more.

A system keeps 5 copies (N = 5). Writes wait for 3 copies (W = 3). What is the smallest read size R that always sees the last write?

  • 1
  • 2
  • 3

We need R + W > N, so R + 3 > 5 and R > 2. The smallest R is 3.

Which statement about Python's hash("cat") is true?

  • It is the same on every computer, forever.
  • It usually changes between runs, because the seed is random.
  • It is safe to use as a password hash.

Python seeds text hashes at random in each run, unless you set PYTHONHASHSEED. For stable or secure hashes, use hashlib.

A cache with 90% hits, 1 ms per hit and 100 ms per miss has an average time of ? ms.

By Little's law, 20 requests per second that each stay 0.5 seconds give ? requests in the system on average.

  1. Name the patterns in this sentence: "The phone app saves your last 50 messages, so it opens fast. New messages wait in a list until the network is back."
    Answer

    Saving the last 50 messages close by is caching. New messages waiting in a list until the network returns is a queue, or buffering.

  2. Find coins and an amount where greedy fails, different from 4, 3 and 1.
    Answer

    One example: coins 6, 4 and 1, amount 8. Greedy takes 6, then 1 and 1: three coins. The best is 4 + 4: two coins. Many other examples work too.

  3. A team adds an index to every column of a table "to make it fast". Writes become slow. Explain why.
    Answer

    Each insert or update must also change every index. With ten indexes, one write becomes eleven writes. Indexes help reads, but they cost writes and disk space. Keep only the indexes that real queries use.

  4. Why does a server that writes log lines to a buffer still crash if the disk is slower than the log lines arrive?
    Answer

    A buffer only smooths bursts. If the arrival rate stays above the write rate, the buffer grows without end. Memory runs out. The fix is a limit plus back-pressure, or dropping or sampling log lines.

  5. Expert. Explain why a hash table needs a random seed on a public web server.
    Answer

    Suppose the hash function is known and fixed. Then an attacker can make many keys with the same hash. All keys fall into one place, so each lookup scans a long chain. Building a table of n such keys costs about n^2 steps, and the server stops. A secret random seed makes these keys impossible to plan.

  6. Expert. Pick a system you know, like a chat app. Name four of the 15 patterns it uses and say where.
    Answer

    One possible answer. Queues: messages wait for offline users. Replication: messages are stored on several servers. Caching: recent chats are kept on the phone. State machines: a message is sent, delivered, then read. Indexing also fits: search over old messages uses an index.

Key takeaways

  • A pattern is a reusable solution shape, not a piece of code. Fifteen of them return in every course.
  • Shape a system with abstraction layers, indirection and state machines.
  • Solve problems with divide and conquer, recursion, greedy choice, dynamic programming and randomisation.
  • Organise data with hashing, indexing, trees and graphs.
  • Move and keep data with caching, queues and replication.
  • Every pattern has a cost: a lookup, memory, old data, slower writes or a hard choice.
  • Real designs mix patterns. Name the pattern, say why it fits, and state its cost.

Sources

  • Butler Lampson: Hints and Principles for Computer System Design (arXiv). The long 2020 version of the classic paper on system design hints.
  • The Raft Consensus Algorithm. Replicated state machines, logs, and how a 5-server cluster survives 2 failures.
  • Python docs: functools. lru_cache, its default size of 128, and cache_info().
  • Rust standard library: HashMap. SipHash 1-3, the random seed and protection against HashDoS.
  • Python docs: Command line and environment. PYTHONHASHSEED and why text hashes are randomised.
  • PostgreSQL documentation: Index Types. The index kinds, and B-tree as the default.

Discrete maths for computer science

Computers work with whole things: bits, keys, nodes and steps. The maths of whole things is called discrete maths. It gives you the tools to prove that code is correct and to say how fast it is.

  • Read and write logical statements, and choose a proof method for a claim.
  • Use sets, relations and functions to describe data and keys.
  • Prove a loop correct with induction and a loop invariant.
  • Count choices and use the pigeonhole principle to find collisions.
  • Compare growth with big-O, big-Omega and big-Theta, solve recurrences, and use expectation and the union bound.

Logic: statements and proofs

Start with a true sentence. "If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even." Now turn it around. "If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4." This is false. The number 6 is even, but 6 is not divisible by 4.

A proposition is a sentence that is true or false. "7 is prime" is a proposition. "Close the door" is not. We join propositions with connectives. The main ones are and \land, or \lor, not \lnot and implies \to.

An implication p \to q says "if p, then q". It is false in only one case: p is true and q is false. A truth table shows all the cases. The program below builds one and checks two famous claims.

fn implies(p: bool, q: bool) -> bool {
    !p || q                       // false only when p is true and q is false
}

fn tf(b: bool) -> char {
    if b { 'T' } else { 'F' }
}

fn main() {
    let vals = [false, true];
    let (mut contra_ok, mut converse_ok) = (true, true);
    println!("p q | p->q  q->p  !q->!p");
    for &p in &vals {
        for &q in &vals {
            let (a, b, c) = (implies(p, q), implies(q, p), implies(!q, !p));
            println!("{} {} |  {}     {}     {}", tf(p), tf(q), tf(a), tf(b), tf(c));
            if a != c { contra_ok = false; }    // contrapositive
            if a != b { converse_ok = false; }  // converse
        }
    }
    println!("same as contrapositive: {contra_ok}");
    println!("same as converse: {converse_ok}");
}
def implies(p, q):
    return (not p) or q           # false only when p is true and q is false

def tf(b):
    return "T" if b else "F"

contra_ok, converse_ok = True, True
print("p q | p->q  q->p  !q->!p")
for p in [False, True]:
    for q in [False, True]:
        a, b, c = implies(p, q), implies(q, p), implies(not q, not p)
        print(f"{tf(p)} {tf(q)} |  {tf(a)}     {tf(b)}     {tf(c)}")
        if a != c: contra_ok = False      # contrapositive
        if a != b: converse_ok = False    # converse
print(f"same as contrapositive: {str(contra_ok).lower()}")
print(f"same as converse: {str(converse_ok).lower()}")
p q | p->q  q->p  !q->!p
F F |  T     T     T
F T |  T     F     T
T F |  F     T     F
T T |  T     T     T
same as contrapositive: true
same as converse: false

The converse of p \to q is q \to p. It is a different claim. The contrapositive is \lnot q \to \lnot p. It always has the same truth value as p \to q. The table proves this for every case.

Many claims talk about all items or some items. A quantifier says how many. \forall x means "for all x". \exists x means "there exists an x". To negate a quantifier, flip it and negate the inside. "Not every test passes" means "some test fails". This is De Morgan's law for quantifiers. The version for and and or is in How computers compute.

Five proof methods
MethodIdeaShort example
Direct proofAssume p. Use known facts until you reach q.n even means n = 2k, so n^2 = 4k^2 is even.
ContrapositiveProve \lnot q \to \lnot p instead."If n^2 is even, n is even." Prove: if n is odd, n^2 is odd.
ContradictionAssume the claim is false. Reach something impossible.Assume finitely many primes. Multiply them all and add 1. No prime divides the result.
CasesSplit into cases that cover everything. Prove each one.n^2 + n is even. Case n even, case n odd.
CounterexampleOne example kills a "for all" claim."Every odd number is prime" is false: 9.

Proving the converse by accident. You want "if the input is sorted, the search works". You test a case where the search works and the input is sorted. That only fits the converse. Also, examples never prove a "for all" claim. One counterexample is enough to break it.

Sets, relations and functions

A small app has users with roles. Ann and Bo are admins. Bo and Cy are editors. Who has any role? Who has both? Sets answer this at once.

A set is a collection of items with no order and no repeats. Each item is an element. We write x \in A for "x is in A". A \subseteq B means every element of A is also in B. Then A is a subset of B.

Set operations with admins A = {ann, bo} and editors E = {bo, cy}
NameMathsPythonRust (HashSet)Result
union: in eitherA \cup EA | Ea.union(&e)ann, bo, cy
intersection: in bothA \cap EA & Ea.intersection(&e)bo
difference: in A, not in EA \setminus EA - Ea.difference(&e)ann
membershipx \in Ax in Aa.contains(&x)true or false

The Cartesian product A \times B is the set of all pairs (a, b). If A has 3 elements and B has 4, there are 12 pairs. The power set of A holds every subset of A. A set with n elements has 2^n subsets. Each element is either in or out.

Relations

A relation on a set is a set of pairs. "a divides b" is a relation. The pair (3, 6) is in it. The pair (4, 6) is not. Four properties matter most:

  • Reflexive: every a is related to itself.
  • Symmetric: if a \sim b, then b \sim a.
  • Antisymmetric: if a \sim b and b \sim a, then a = b.
  • Transitive: if a \sim b and b \sim c, then a \sim c.

The program tests the first three properties on the set {1, ..., 6}. It tries every pair and every triple.

// Test three properties of a relation on the set {1, ..., 6}.
fn yn(b: bool) -> &'static str { if b { "yes" } else { "no" } }

fn check(name: &str, r: fn(u32, u32) -> bool) {
    let s: Vec<u32> = (1..=6).collect();
    let refl = s.iter().all(|&a| r(a, a));
    let sym = s.iter().all(|&a| s.iter().all(|&b| !r(a, b) || r(b, a)));
    let trans = s.iter().all(|&a| s.iter().all(|&b| s.iter().all(|&c| {
        !(r(a, b) && r(b, c)) || r(a, c)   // a~b and b~c must give a~c
    })));
    println!("{name:<12} reflexive: {:<4} symmetric: {:<4} transitive: {}",
             yn(refl), yn(sym), yn(trans));
}

fn main() {
    check("same mod 3", |a, b| a % 3 == b % 3);
    check("divides", |a, b| b % a == 0);
    check("less than", |a, b| a < b);
    check("differ by 1", |a, b| a.abs_diff(b) == 1);
}
# Test three properties of a relation on the set {1, ..., 6}.
def yn(b):
    return "yes" if b else "no"

def check(name, r):
    s = range(1, 7)
    refl = all(r(a, a) for a in s)
    sym = all(r(b, a) for a in s for b in s if r(a, b))
    trans = all(r(a, c) for a in s for b in s for c in s
                if r(a, b) and r(b, c))   # a~b and b~c must give a~c
    print(f"{name:<12} reflexive: {yn(refl):<4} symmetric: {yn(sym):<4} "
          f"transitive: {yn(trans)}")

check("same mod 3", lambda a, b: a % 3 == b % 3)
check("divides", lambda a, b: b % a == 0)
check("less than", lambda a, b: a < b)
check("differ by 1", lambda a, b: abs(a - b) == 1)
same mod 3   reflexive: yes  symmetric: yes  transitive: yes
divides      reflexive: yes  symmetric: no   transitive: yes
less than    reflexive: no   symmetric: no   transitive: yes
differ by 1  reflexive: no   symmetric: yes  transitive: no

"Same remainder mod 3" has all three properties. Such a relation is an equivalence relation. It cuts the set into groups called equivalence classes. Here they are {3, 6}, {1, 4} and {2, 5}. A hash table does the same thing. Keys with the same bucket number form one class.

"Divides" is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. That makes it a partial order. Some pairs are not comparable: 4 does not divide 6, and 6 does not divide 4. Task dependencies in a build tool form a partial order too. A topological sort turns it into one line, see Graph algorithms.

Functions

A function f: A \to B gives every input in A exactly one output in B. A is the domain. B is the codomain.

  • Injective (one-to-one): no two inputs share an output. A good user id map is injective.
  • Surjective (onto): every element of B is hit. A hash into 8 buckets should hit every bucket.
  • Bijective: both. It pairs the two sets perfectly. Then |A| = |B|.

A hash function maps all strings to 64-bit numbers. There are far more strings than numbers. So a hash function can never be injective. Collisions must exist. The pigeonhole principle below makes this exact.

Mixing up \in and \subseteq. The number 2 is an element of {1, 2}. The set {2} is a subset of {1, 2}. Also, {1, 2} and {2, 1} are the same set. The pairs (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different, because pairs have order.

Induction and loop invariants

Add the first odd numbers and look at the totals. 1 = 1. 1 + 3 = 4. 1 + 3 + 5 = 9. 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. The totals are 1, 4, 9, 16. They look like n^2. But four examples are not a proof. Induction gives a proof for every n.

Let P(n) be a claim about a whole number n. Suppose P(1) is true. Suppose also that P(k) implies P(k+1) for every k \ge 1. Then P(n) is true for every n \ge 1.

Think of a line of dominoes. The first one falls. Each falling domino knocks over the next one. So all of them fall. The first part is the base case. The second part is the inductive step. Inside the step you may use P(k). That assumption is the induction hypothesis.

Proof idea

Assume some n fails. Take the smallest one that fails. It is not 1, because P(1) is true. So n - 1 works. The step then gives P(n). That is a contradiction. Every set of positive whole numbers has a smallest element, so this argument is safe.

  1. Claim P(n): 1 + 3 + \dots + (2n - 1) = n^2.
  2. Base case. For n = 1 the left side is 1 and 1^2 = 1. True.
  3. Induction hypothesis. Assume 1 + 3 + \dots + (2k - 1) = k^2.
  4. Inductive step. Add the next odd number, 2k + 1, to both sides.
  5. The new total is k^2 + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)^2. This is P(k+1).
  6. By the principle of induction, P(n) holds for every n \ge 1.

Two stronger forms are common. In strong induction, the step may use all of P(1), \dots, P(k). Example: every number from 2 up is a product of primes. If n is not prime, then n = a \cdot b with smaller a and b. In structural induction, you prove a claim for small trees, then for a tree built from smaller trees.

Loop invariants

A loop is induction in disguise. A loop invariant is a fact that is true at the start of every turn. You prove three things:

  1. Start: the invariant is true before the first turn.
  2. Keep: if it is true before a turn, it is true after the turn.
  3. End: the loop stops, and the invariant then gives the answer.

Here is an integer square root by binary search. The invariant is lo^2 \le n \lt hi^2. The code checks it with an assertion on every turn.

// Integer square root: the biggest r with r * r <= n.
fn isqrt(n: u64) -> u64 {
    let (mut lo, mut hi) = (0u64, n + 1);
    // Invariant: lo * lo <= n < hi * hi
    while hi - lo > 1 {
        assert!(lo * lo <= n && n < hi * hi);   // check the invariant
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if mid * mid <= n { lo = mid; } else { hi = mid; }
    }
    // Now hi = lo + 1, so lo * lo <= n < (lo + 1) * (lo + 1)
    lo
}

fn main() {
    for n in [0, 1, 15, 16, 17, 1_000_000, 999_999_999] {
        println!("isqrt({n}) = {}", isqrt(n));
    }
}
# Integer square root: the biggest r with r * r <= n.
def isqrt(n):
    lo, hi = 0, n + 1
    # Invariant: lo * lo <= n < hi * hi
    while hi - lo > 1:
        assert lo * lo <= n < hi * hi        # check the invariant
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if mid * mid <= n:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    # Now hi = lo + 1, so lo * lo <= n < (lo + 1) * (lo + 1)
    return lo

for n in [0, 1, 15, 16, 17, 1_000_000, 999_999_999]:
    print(f"isqrt({n}) = {isqrt(n)}")
isqrt(0) = 0
isqrt(1) = 1
isqrt(15) = 3
isqrt(16) = 4
isqrt(17) = 4
isqrt(1000000) = 1000
isqrt(999999999) = 31622

Start: 0^2 \le n \lt (n+1)^2 is always true. Keep: each branch moves one end to mid and keeps the inequality. End: the gap hi - lo gets smaller on every turn, so the loop stops. Then hi = lo + 1, and the invariant says lo is the answer. The shrinking gap is called a variant.

Forgetting the base case. Try the false claim n + 1 \lt n. The step works: if k + 1 \lt k, add 1 to both sides and get k + 2 \lt k + 1. But the base case 2 \lt 1 is false, so nothing is proved. Another mistake is a weak invariant. "lo is a number" is always true, but it gives no answer at the end. A good invariant plus the stop condition must give exactly the result you want.

Counting

A password has 4 lowercase letters. How many passwords exist? There are 26 choices for each place. So there are 26 \cdot 26 \cdot 26 \cdot 26 = 26^4 = 456{,}976. A computer can try them all in well under a second.

That was the product rule. Independent choices multiply. The sum rule says: if the options split into separate groups, add the groups. Most counting problems ask two questions. Does order matter? Are repeats allowed?

Choose k items from n kinds
Repeats allowedNo repeats
Order mattersn^k (passwords)\frac{n!}{(n-k)!} (race places)
Order does not matter\binom{n+k-1}{k} (scoops of ice cream)\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} (teams)

An ordered list without repeats is a permutation. An unordered group is a combination. \binom{n}{k} is read "n choose k". Each team of 3 appears as 3! = 6 ordered lists. So we divide the ordered count by 6. The code counts both ways, by brute force and by formula.

fn fact(n: u64) -> u64 { (1..=n).product() }
fn choose(n: u64, k: u64) -> u64 { fact(n) / (fact(k) * fact(n - k)) }

fn main() {
    // Ordered picks of 3 from 5 people, no repeats: count by brute force.
    let mut ordered = 0;
    for a in 0..5 { for b in 0..5 { for c in 0..5 {
        if a != b && b != c && a != c { ordered += 1; }
    }}}
    // Teams of 3 from 5 people: order does not matter, so a < b < c.
    let mut teams = 0;
    for a in 0..5 { for b in (a + 1)..5 { for _c in (b + 1)..5 {
        teams += 1;
    }}}
    println!("ordered: {ordered}  formula 5!/2! = {}", fact(5) / fact(2));
    println!("teams:   {teams}  formula C(5,3) = {}", choose(5, 3));
    // Numbers 1..=100 divisible by 2 or by 3.
    let both = (1..=100).filter(|n| n % 2 == 0 || n % 3 == 0).count();
    println!("2 or 3:  {both}  formula 50 + 33 - 16 = {}", 50 + 33 - 16);
    // Pigeonhole: 11 keys, 10 buckets. Find two keys in one bucket.
    let mut first = [None; 10];
    for key in [12u64, 47, 85, 3, 61, 29, 90, 74, 38, 56, 21] {
        let b = (key * 7 % 10) as usize;            // a toy hash function
        if let Some(old) = first[b] {
            println!("collision: {old} and {key} both go to bucket {b}");
            break;
        }
        first[b] = Some(key);
    }
}
from itertools import combinations, permutations
from math import comb, factorial

people = range(5)
ordered = len(list(permutations(people, 3)))   # order matters
teams = len(list(combinations(people, 3)))     # order does not matter
print(f"ordered: {ordered}  formula 5!/2! = {factorial(5) // factorial(2)}")
print(f"teams:   {teams}  formula C(5,3) = {comb(5, 3)}")
# Numbers 1..100 divisible by 2 or by 3.
both = sum(1 for n in range(1, 101) if n % 2 == 0 or n % 3 == 0)
print(f"2 or 3:  {both}  formula 50 + 33 - 16 = {50 + 33 - 16}")
# Pigeonhole: 11 keys, 10 buckets. Find two keys in one bucket.
first = {}
for key in [12, 47, 85, 3, 61, 29, 90, 74, 38, 56, 21]:
    b = key * 7 % 10                           # a toy hash function
    if b in first:
        print(f"collision: {first[b]} and {key} both go to bucket {b}")
        break
    first[b] = key
ordered: 60  formula 5!/2! = 60
teams:   10  formula C(5,3) = 10
2 or 3:  67  formula 50 + 33 - 16 = 67
collision: 61 and 21 both go to bucket 7

The third line uses inclusion-exclusion. 50 numbers are even. 33 are divisible by 3. But 16 numbers are divisible by 6, so we counted them twice. In symbols, |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|.

Look at the last line. The first ten keys landed in ten different buckets. The eleventh key had no free bucket left. This is not luck. It must happen.

If n items go into m boxes and n \gt m, then some box holds at least two items. More generally, some box holds at least \lceil n/m \rceil items.

Proof

Assume every box holds fewer than \lceil n/m \rceil items. Then every box holds at most \lceil n/m \rceil - 1 items, and that is less than n/m. So all boxes together hold less than m \cdot n/m = n items. But there are n items. This contradiction proves the claim.

In simple words: too many pigeons, too few holes. Two of them must share. Example: 367 people always include two with the same birthday, because there are at most 366 days. With 1000 keys in 300 buckets, some bucket has at least \lceil 1000/300 \rceil = 4 keys.

No compressor can make every file shorter. There are 2^n files of exactly n bits. There are only 2^n - 1 files shorter than n bits. So two files would get the same short output, and you could not get both back. The pigeonhole principle forbids it. See Information and coding theory.

Using a permutation when order does not matter. "Choose 3 people for a team" is \binom{5}{3} = 10, not 60. Ask yourself: would swapping two choices give a new answer? If not, divide out the orders.

Growth of functions: O, Omega and Theta

Four programs do \log_2 n, n \log_2 n, n^2 and 2^n steps. A computer does about a billion simple steps per second. Look at what happens as n grows.

Number of steps for each growth rate
n\log_2 nn \log_2 nn^22^n
103.3331001,024
1006.666410,000about 1.3 \times 10^{30}
1,00010.09,9661,000,000about 1.1 \times 10^{301}
1,000,00019.9about 20 million10^{12}a number with 301,030 digits

At n = 10^6, the n^2 program takes about 17 minutes. The n \log_2 n program takes 0.02 seconds. The 2^n program never finishes. Even at n = 100 it needs about 4 \times 10^{13} years. The growth rate matters more than the speed of the machine.

We want to compare growth and ignore small details. Machines differ by constant factors. Small inputs are fast anyway. So we look at large n and allow a constant factor. This is asymptotic notation.

Let f and g be functions from whole numbers to positive numbers.

  • f = O(g) if there are constants c \gt 0 and n_0 with f(n) \le c \cdot g(n) for all n \ge n_0. This is an upper bound.
  • f = \Omega(g) if there are constants c \gt 0 and n_0 with f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n) for all n \ge n_0. This is a lower bound.
  • f = \Theta(g) if f = O(g) and f = \Omega(g). This is a tight bound.

Big-O says "grows no faster than". Big-Omega says "grows at least as fast as". Big-Theta says "grows at the same rate".

  1. Pick c = 4. We need 3n^2 + 10n + 5 \le 4n^2.
  2. Subtract 3n^2. We need 10n + 5 \le n^2.
  3. Test n = 10: 105 \le 100 is false. Test n = 11: 115 \le 121 is true.
  4. For bigger n, n^2 grows faster than 10n + 5. So n_0 = 11 works.
  5. Also 3n^2 + 10n + 5 \ge 3n^2 for all n. So it is \Omega(n^2) too, and therefore \Theta(n^2).

You rarely need the constants. These rules do the work:

  • Drop constant factors. 5n^3 = \Theta(n^3).
  • Keep the biggest term. n^2 + 100n + 7 = \Theta(n^2).
  • Log bases do not matter. \log_2 n = \log_{10} n / \log_{10} 2, only a constant factor.
  • The limit test. If f(n)/g(n) goes to a positive constant, then f = \Theta(g). If it goes to 0, then f = O(g) but not \Theta(g).
  • The usual order: 1 \lt \log n \lt \sqrt{n} \lt n \lt n \log n \lt n^2 \lt n^3 \lt 2^n \lt n!.

Polynomials and exponentials cross. For small n, n^2 can be bigger than 2^n. After n = 4, 2^n wins forever.

Big-O is not "the worst case". Worst, average and best case pick which inputs you look at. O, Omega and Theta describe how a function grows. You can say "the worst case of quicksort is \Theta(n^2)" and "its average case is \Theta(n \log n)". Also, "binary search is O(n)" is true but weak. Give the tight bound when you know it: \Theta(\log n).

Recurrences and the master theorem

Merge sort splits a list into two halves, sorts each half, then merges in n steps. Its cost T(n) satisfies T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. A recurrence like this defines a cost through smaller costs. Algorithms are in Sorting, searching, divide and conquer. Here we learn to solve the equations.

Draw the recursion tree. The top does n work. The next level has two calls of size n/2, so again n work. Every level does n work. There are \log_2 n levels. So T(n) = n \log_2 n. To be sure, you can prove a guess by induction. This is the substitution method.

Many recursion trees add up a geometric series. So we need one formula first.

For a ratio r \ne 1: 1 + r + r^2 + \dots + r^k = \frac{r^{k+1} - 1}{r - 1}.

Two facts follow. If r \lt 1, the sum stays below \frac{1}{1-r}, a constant. The first term wins. If r \gt 1, the sum is less than \frac{r}{r-1} times the last term. The last term wins. Example: 1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + 2^k = 2^{k+1} - 1. That is less than twice the last term.

Let T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + \Theta(n^d) with constants a \ge 1, b \gt 1 and d \ge 0. Then:

  • if d \gt \log_b a, then T(n) = \Theta(n^d). The top level wins.
  • if d = \log_b a, then T(n) = \Theta(n^d \log n). All levels are equal.
  • if d \lt \log_b a, then T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a}). The leaves win.

In simple words: compare the work at the top, n^d, with the number of leaves, n^{\log_b a}. The bigger one decides. If they are equal, you pay one extra \log n factor for the levels. Rounding n/b up or down does not change the answer.

Proof idea

Level i of the tree has a^i calls. Each call has size n/b^i and does about (n/b^i)^d work. So level i does n^d \cdot (a/b^d)^i work. The total is n^d times a geometric series with ratio r = a/b^d and \log_b n terms. If r \lt 1, the first term wins: \Theta(n^d). If r = 1, all \log_b n + 1 terms are equal: \Theta(n^d \log n). If r \gt 1, the last term wins. The last level has a^{\log_b n} = n^{\log_b a} leaves. Note that r \lt 1 is the same as d \gt \log_b a.

Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1

a = 1, b = 2, d = 0. \log_2 1 = 0 = d. Equal case.

T(n) = \Theta(n^0 \log n) = \Theta(\log n).

Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n

a = 2, b = 2, d = 1. \log_2 2 = 1 = d. Equal case.

T(n) = \Theta(n \log n).

Karatsuba: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n

\log_2 3 \approx 1.585 \gt 1 = d. The leaves win.

T(n) = \Theta(n^{1.585}), faster than the school method n^2.

Top heavy: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²

d = 2 \gt \log_2 2 = 1. The top wins.

T(n) = \Theta(n^2). The recursion adds only a constant factor.

Let us check the theorem with real numbers. The program computes four recurrences exactly, with T(1) = 0. Then it divides by the answer the theory predicts. A ratio near a constant means the prediction is right.

// Solve T(n) = a * T(n / 2) + f(n), with T(1) = 0, for n a power of 2.
fn t(n: u64, a: u64, f: fn(u64) -> u64) -> u64 {
    if n == 1 { 0 } else { a * t(n / 2, a, f) + f(n) }
}

fn lg(n: u64) -> u64 { 63 - n.leading_zeros() as u64 }   // log2 of a power of 2

fn main() {
    for k in [10u32, 20] {
        let n = 1u64 << k;                              // n = 2^k
        let nf = n as f64;
        let l = lg(n) as f64;
        let a = t(n, 1, |n| n) as f64 / nf;             // T(n/2) + n
        let b = t(n, 2, |n| n) as f64 / (nf * l);       // 2T(n/2) + n
        let c = t(n, 4, |n| n) as f64 / (nf * nf);      // 4T(n/2) + n
        let d = t(n, 2, |n| n * lg(n)) as f64 / (nf * l * l);  // 2T(n/2) + n log n
        println!("n=2^{k}: {a:.3} {b:.3} {c:.3} {d:.3}");
    }
}
# Solve T(n) = a * T(n / 2) + f(n), with T(1) = 0, for n a power of 2.
def t(n, a, f):
    return 0 if n == 1 else a * t(n // 2, a, f) + f(n)

def lg(n):
    return n.bit_length() - 1                     # log2 of a power of 2

for k in [10, 20]:
    n = 2 ** k
    l = lg(n)
    a = t(n, 1, lambda n: n) / n                  # T(n/2) + n
    b = t(n, 2, lambda n: n) / (n * l)            # 2T(n/2) + n
    c = t(n, 4, lambda n: n) / (n * n)            # 4T(n/2) + n
    d = t(n, 2, lambda n: n * lg(n)) / (n * l * l)  # 2T(n/2) + n log n
    print(f"n=2^{k}: {a:.3f} {b:.3f} {c:.3f} {d:.3f}")
n=2^10: 1.998 1.000 0.999 0.550
n=2^20: 2.000 1.000 1.000 0.525

The first three columns divide by n, n \log_2 n and n^2. All three ratios settle at a constant, as the theorem says. The last column is special. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n \log n does not fit any case. The top work n \log n is bigger than n, but only by a log factor. The recursion tree still works: level i costs about n \log(n/2^i). The sum is \Theta(n \log^2 n), and the ratio goes to \frac{1}{2}.

Expert: recurrences the master theorem cannot solve
  • T(n) = T(n-1) + n. The size drops by 1, not by a factor. Unroll it: n + (n-1) + \dots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2). This is insertion sort on bad input.
  • T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, the Towers of Hanoi. The tree has n levels and doubles each time. T(n) = 2^n - 1.
  • T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n. The parts have different sizes. Each level costs at most n. The longest path has \log_{3/2} n levels. So T(n) = O(n \log n), and in fact \Theta(n \log n). A general tool for unequal parts is the Akra-Bazzi method.
  • The full master theorem compares any f(n) with n^{\log_b a}, not only n^d. In the unequal cases, the gap must be a power n^{\varepsilon}. The top-heavy case also needs a f(n/b) \le c f(n) for some c \lt 1.

Using the master theorem on T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1. It needs n/b, a division. Another mistake: confusing a and b. a is the number of calls. b is how much smaller each call is. For merge sort both are 2. For binary search a = 1 and b = 2.

Probability for algorithms

Shuffle 10 cards at random. How many cards stay in their old place, on average? Most people guess a small fraction. The true answer is exactly 1. It is also 1 for 52 cards, and for a million cards. Let us see why.

A sample space lists all possible results. An event is a set of results. A random variable gives each result a number. Its expectation is the average, weighted by probability: E[X] = \sum_x x \cdot \Pr[X = x].

For any random variables X_1, \dots, X_n: E[X_1 + \dots + X_n] = E[X_1] + \dots + E[X_n]. The variables do not need to be independent.

Proof

Take two variables. E[X + Y] is the sum over all results \omega of (X(\omega) + Y(\omega)) \cdot \Pr[\omega]. Split the sum into two sums. The first is E[X]. The second is E[Y]. Independence was never used. Repeat for more variables.

The trick is an indicator variable. Let X_i = 1 if card i stays in place, else 0. Then E[X_i] = \Pr[\text{card } i \text{ stays}] = \frac{1}{n}. The count of fixed cards is X = X_1 + \dots + X_n. So E[X] = n \cdot \frac{1}{n} = 1. The X_i depend on each other, but linearity does not care.

The same trick counts hash collisions. Put n keys into m buckets at random. Each pair of keys collides with probability \frac{1}{m}. There are \binom{n}{2} pairs. So the expected number of colliding pairs is \binom{n}{2} / m. For 10 keys and 100 buckets, that is 45/100 = 0.45.

For any events A_1, \dots, A_k: \Pr[A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_k] \le \Pr[A_1] + \dots + \Pr[A_k].

In simple words: the chance that something bad happens is at most the sum of the single chances. Results in an overlap are counted twice on the right side, so the right side can only be bigger. Let A_{ij} be "keys i and j collide". The union bound gives \Pr[\text{any collision}] \le 45 \cdot \frac{1}{100} = 0.45. The program below tests both numbers. It uses the same small random generator in both languages, so the outputs match.

// A tiny random number generator (xorshift64). Same numbers in Python.
struct Rng(u64);
impl Rng {
    fn below(&mut self, m: u64) -> u64 {
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13;
        self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7;
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 17;
        self.0 % m                       // a number from 0 to m - 1
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng = Rng(2026);
    let trials = 100_000;
    let (mut fixed, mut pairs, mut any) = (0u64, 0u64, 0u64);
    for _ in 0..trials {
        // 1. Shuffle 10 cards. Count cards that stay in their place.
        let mut p: Vec<u64> = (0..10).collect();
        for i in (1..10).rev() {
            let j = rng.below(i as u64 + 1) as usize;
            p.swap(i, j);
        }
        fixed += (0..10).filter(|&i| p[i] == i as u64).count() as u64;
        // 2. Hash 10 keys into 100 buckets. Count pairs in the same bucket.
        let keys: Vec<u64> = (0..10).map(|_| rng.below(100)).collect();
        let mut c = 0;
        for i in 0..10 { for j in (i + 1)..10 { if keys[i] == keys[j] { c += 1; } } }
        pairs += c;
        if c > 0 { any += 1; }
    }
    let t = trials as f64;
    println!("average fixed cards: {:.3}", fixed as f64 / t);
    println!("average colliding pairs: {:.3}", pairs as f64 / t);
    println!("share of runs with a collision: {:.3}", any as f64 / t);
}
# A tiny random number generator (xorshift64). Same numbers in Rust.
class Rng:
    def __init__(self, seed):
        self.x = seed
    def below(self, m):
        M = (1 << 64) - 1                 # keep 64 bits, like a Rust u64
        self.x ^= (self.x << 13) & M
        self.x ^= self.x >> 7
        self.x ^= (self.x << 17) & M
        return self.x % m                 # a number from 0 to m - 1

rng = Rng(2026)
trials = 100_000
fixed = pairs = anyc = 0
for _ in range(trials):
    # 1. Shuffle 10 cards. Count cards that stay in their place.
    p = list(range(10))
    for i in range(9, 0, -1):
        j = rng.below(i + 1)
        p[i], p[j] = p[j], p[i]
    fixed += sum(1 for i in range(10) if p[i] == i)
    # 2. Hash 10 keys into 100 buckets. Count pairs in the same bucket.
    keys = [rng.below(100) for _ in range(10)]
    c = sum(1 for i in range(10) for j in range(i + 1, 10) if keys[i] == keys[j])
    pairs += c
    anyc += c > 0
print(f"average fixed cards: {fixed / trials:.3f}")
print(f"average colliding pairs: {pairs / trials:.3f}")
print(f"share of runs with a collision: {anyc / trials:.3f}")
average fixed cards: 1.001
average colliding pairs: 0.452
share of runs with a collision: 0.374

The first two lines match linearity: 1 and 0.45. The exact chance of at least one collision is 1 - \frac{100}{100} \cdot \frac{99}{100} \cdots \frac{91}{100} \approx 0.372. The simulation gives 0.374. The union bound said "at most 0.45". It is true, but not tight, because collisions overlap.

How algorithms use these tools

  • Expected running time. Write the cost as a sum of small indicator costs. Randomised quicksort is analysed this way in Sorting, searching, divide and conquer.
  • With high probability. Show that each of n bad events has chance at most 1/n^2. The union bound says no bad event happens, except with chance at most 1/n.
  • Waiting for success. If each try succeeds with chance p, the expected number of tries is 1/p. A fair coin needs 2 flips on average to show heads. Skip lists in Data structures use this.
  • Markov's inequality. For a variable X \ge 0, \Pr[X \ge t] \le E[X]/t. A program with expected time 1 second runs 10 seconds or more at most 10% of the time.

Linearity works for sums, not for products. E[XY] = E[X]\,E[Y] needs independence. Also, the union bound can give a number above 1. With 50 keys in 100 buckets it gives 1225/100 = 12.25. That is true but useless. Then you need a better tool, like the exact product above.

When a question says "expected number of ...", write the count as a sum of indicator variables. Then add their probabilities. You almost never need the full distribution. For "the chance that any ... fails", try the union bound first.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for discrete maths in computer science
PatternPurposeModelNote
Prove the contrapositiveTurn a hard implication into an easy one"n^2 even means n even": show "n odd means n^2 odd"The converse is a different claim.
One counterexampleBreak a "for all" claim"All odd numbers are prime": 9Examples never prove a "for all" claim.
Negate a quantifierSay exactly what failure meansnot (all tests pass) = some test failsFlip \forall and \exists, then negate the inside.
Equivalence relation, then classesGroup items that act the samekeys with the same bucket numberCheck reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
Base case plus stepProve a claim for every n1 + 3 + \dots + (2n-1) = n^2Without the base case, the proof is empty.
Start, keep, endProve a loop correctinvariant lo^2 \le n \lt hi^2Also show a variant that shrinks, so the loop stops.
Order? Repeats?Pick the right counting formulateam of 3 from 5: \binom{5}{3} = 10Divide out orders that give the same answer.
Too many pigeonsProve a collision must exist11 keys in 10 bucketsIt says a collision exists, not where.
Keep the biggest termSimplify a cost3n^2 + 10n + 5 = \Theta(n^2)O is an upper bound only. Use \Theta when you can.
Top versus leavesSolve a divide and conquer recurrence2T(n/2) + n = \Theta(n \log n)Needs n/b. Not for T(n-1).
Sum of indicatorsFind an expected countexpected fixed cards = n \cdot \frac{1}{n} = 1Works without independence. Products do not.
Union boundBound the chance that anything fails\Pr[\text{collision}] \le \binom{n}{2}/mUseless when the sum is above 1.

Practice

"If the build passes, the tests ran." Which sentence means the same?

  • If the tests ran, the build passes.
  • If the tests did not run, the build did not pass.
  • If the build did not pass, the tests did not run.

The contrapositive \lnot q \to \lnot p has the same meaning. The first option is the converse. The third is the inverse, which equals the converse.

Is "has the same first letter" an equivalence relation on words?

  • Yes. It is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
  • No. It is not symmetric.
  • No. It is not transitive.

Every word has its own first letter. If A matches B, then B matches A. If A matches B and B matches C, all three share one letter. The classes are "words that start with a", "words that start with b", and so on.

How many people must you pick to be sure that two share a birth month?

  • 12
  • 13
  • 24

There are 12 months, the boxes. With 13 people, the pigeonhole principle forces a shared month. 12 people could all have different months.

Which statement is false?

  • n^2 = O(n^3)
  • 2^{n+1} = O(2^n)
  • 4^n = O(2^n)

2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n, only a constant factor. But 4^n / 2^n = 2^n grows without limit. No constant c works.

Solve T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n^2.

  • \Theta(n^2)
  • \Theta(n^2 \log n)
  • \Theta(n^3)

\log_2 8 = 3 \gt d = 2. The leaves win: \Theta(n^{\log_2 8}) = \Theta(n^3). This is the simple recursive matrix product.

A set with 4 elements has ? subsets.

\binom{6}{2} = ?

The expected sum of two fair dice is ?.

  1. Prove by induction that 1 + 2 + \dots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
    Answer

    Base case: for n = 1, both sides are 1. Step: assume the formula for k. Add k + 1 to both sides. The right side becomes \frac{k(k+1)}{2} + (k+1) = \frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}. This is the formula for k + 1. So it holds for all n \ge 1.

  2. A loop finds the largest item of a list: best = xs[0], then for i from 1 to n - 1, if xs[i] > best then best = xs[i]. Give the loop invariant and the three proof parts.
    Answer

    Invariant: before the turn with index i, best is the largest of xs[0..i]. Start: for i = 1, best = xs[0] is the largest of one item. Keep: the turn compares xs[i] with the old largest and keeps the bigger one. End: the loop stops at i = n. Then best is the largest of the whole list.

  3. Show that n \log_2 n = O(n^2) but not \Omega(n^2).
    Answer

    For n \ge 1, \log_2 n \le n, so n \log_2 n \le n^2. Take c = 1 and n_0 = 1. For the second part, \frac{n \log_2 n}{n^2} = \frac{\log_2 n}{n} goes to 0. So no constant c \gt 0 can give n \log_2 n \ge c n^2 for all large n.

  4. Put n keys into n buckets at random. What is the expected number of empty buckets? Give the number for n = 100.
    Answer

    Let X_j = 1 if bucket j is empty. Each key misses bucket j with chance 1 - \frac{1}{n}. So E[X_j] = (1 - \frac{1}{n})^n. By linearity, the expected count is n (1 - \frac{1}{n})^n. For n = 100 this is about 36.6. For large n it is close to n/e, about 37% of the buckets.

  5. Expert. A service gives each of one million objects a random 64-bit id. Bound the chance that two objects get the same id.
    Answer

    There are \binom{10^6}{2} \approx 5 \times 10^{11} pairs. Each pair collides with chance 2^{-64} \approx 5.4 \times 10^{-20}. The union bound gives at most about 2.7 \times 10^{-8}. That is very small. With 2^{32} objects, the bound grows to about \frac{1}{2}. This is the birthday effect, see Cryptography.

  6. Expert. Solve T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n and T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n^2. Then explain why the second one does not get a log factor.
    Answer

    First: \log_3 3 = 1 = d, the equal case, so \Theta(n \log n). Second: d = 2 \gt 1, the top wins, so \Theta(n^2). The level work is n^2 \cdot (3/9)^i = n^2 \cdot (1/3)^i. It shrinks by a factor of 3 per level. A geometric series with ratio \frac{1}{3} adds up to at most \frac{3}{2} of its first term. So the levels add only a constant factor, not \log n.

Key takeaways

  • An implication equals its contrapositive, not its converse. One counterexample breaks a "for all" claim.
  • Sets have no order and no repeats. An equivalence relation splits a set into classes. A partial order allows items that are not comparable.
  • A function with a smaller codomain cannot be injective. So every hash function has collisions.
  • Induction needs a base case and a step. A loop invariant is induction over the turns of a loop.
  • For counting, ask: does order matter, and are repeats allowed? The pigeonhole principle proves that a collision must exist.
  • O is an upper bound, Omega a lower bound, Theta both. Keep the biggest term and drop constants.
  • The master theorem compares the top work n^d with the leaves n^{\log_b a}. Equal means an extra \log n.
  • Linearity of expectation needs no independence. Write counts as sums of indicators. The union bound limits the chance that anything fails.
