Data structures

A data structure is a way to store data so that some operations are fast. No structure is fast at everything. This chapter shows the classic structures, what each one costs, and how to choose.

  • Explain why a growing array has amortised constant-time append, and prove it.
  • Use stacks, queues, hash tables, heaps, tries and union-find in Rust and Python.
  • Say why search trees must stay balanced, and how AVL, red-black and B-trees do it.
  • Use skip lists and Bloom filters, and compute a Bloom filter's error rate.
  • Pick a structure for a task with a decision tree and a cost table.

Arrays and dynamic arrays

A list grows one item at a time. When its memory block is full, it moves to a bigger block. How should it grow? The program compares two rules. Rule one doubles the size. Rule two adds 100 slots. It counts how many items get copied.

// Count how many items get copied when an array grows.
fn copies(n: u64, double: bool) -> u64 {
    let (mut cap, mut len, mut copied) = (1u64, 0u64, 0u64);
    for _ in 0..n {
        if len == cap {
            copied += len;                       // move every item to the new block
            cap = if double { cap * 2 } else { cap + 100 };
        }
        len += 1;                                // write the new item
    }
    copied
}

fn main() {
    for n in [1_000u64, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000] {
        let d = copies(n, true) as f64 / n as f64;
        let a = copies(n, false) as f64 / n as f64;
        println!("n={n:>7}: double {d:.2} copies per item, add 100: {a:.1}");
    }
}
# Count how many items get copied when an array grows.
def copies(n, double):
    cap, length, copied = 1, 0, 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if length == cap:
            copied += length                     # move every item to the new block
            cap = cap * 2 if double else cap + 100
        length += 1                              # write the new item
    return copied

for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:
    d = copies(n, True) / n
    a = copies(n, False) / n
    print(f"n={n:>7}: double {d:.2f} copies per item, add 100: {a:.1f}")
n=   1000: double 1.02 copies per item, add 100: 4.5
n=  10000: double 1.64 copies per item, add 100: 49.5
n= 100000: double 1.31 copies per item, add 100: 499.5
n=1000000: double 1.05 copies per item, add 100: 4999.5

With doubling, each item is copied less than twice on average, for any n. With "add 100", the copies per item grow with n. At a million items, each item is copied about 5,000 times.

An array keeps its items side by side in one block of memory. Item i lives at address \text{start} + i \cdot \text{size}. So reading any item is one calculation: O(1). A dynamic array also keeps a capacity. When the length reaches the capacity, it gets a new, bigger block and copies every item. Rust's Vec and Python's list are dynamic arrays.

Start with capacity 1. Double the capacity each time the array is full. Then any sequence of n appends does fewer than 3n item writes in total. So one append costs O(1) amortised time.

Proof

The array grows when its length is 1, 2, 4, ..., 2^k, where 2^k \lt n. Each growth copies all current items. The copies add up to 1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + 2^k = 2^{k+1} - 1 by the geometric series. Since 2^k \lt n, this is less than 2n. Each append also writes its own new item: n writes. In total there are fewer than 2n + n = 3n writes.

In simple words: a slow copy happens rarely, and each copy is paid for by the cheap appends before it. Amortised is not the same as average over random inputs. It is a promise about every sequence of operations. Any growth factor bigger than 1 works. A factor g gives about \frac{1}{g-1} copies per item. Adding a fixed number of slots does not work. It gives \Theta(n^2) copies in total.

What do real libraries do? Here is what Rust 1.99 and Python 3.14 did on this machine.

fn main() {
    let mut v: Vec<u64> = Vec::new();
    let mut last = usize::MAX;
    let mut caps = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..200u64 {
        v.push(i);
        if v.capacity() != last {               // the vector moved to a bigger block
            last = v.capacity();
            caps.push(last);
        }
    }
    println!("{caps:?}");
}
[4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]
import sys

xs = []
last = -1
caps = []
for i in range(200):
    xs.append(i)
    size = sys.getsizeof(xs)                    # bytes used by the list object
    if size != last:                            # the list moved to a bigger block
        last = size
        caps.append((size - sys.getsizeof([])) // 8)  # 8 bytes per slot
print(caps)
[4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76, 92, 108, 128, 148, 172, 200]

Rust doubled. CPython grows by about one eighth plus a few slots. Its source code gives the same pattern: 0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76. Both are geometric, so both give O(1) amortised append. The Rust documentation does not promise a growth factor. It only promises amortised O(1) push. These numbers can change between versions.

Expert: the potential method, and shrinking

Another proof uses a potential \Phi = 2 \cdot \text{len} - \text{cap}. A cheap append raises \Phi by 2. A growth at \text{len} = \text{cap} = c copies c items, but \Phi drops from c to about 0. The saved potential pays for the copy. So every append costs at most 3 units.

Shrinking needs care. If you halve the array when it is half full, one push and one pop at the boundary can force a copy every time. That is O(n) per operation. Shrink to half when the array is only a quarter full. Then a slow copy again follows many cheap operations.

Inserting at the front of an array. v.insert(0, x) and xs.insert(0, x) shift every item, so they cost O(n). Also, a push can move the whole block. Old pointers into the array then point to freed memory. In C++ this is a classic bug. Rust's borrow checker refuses a push while a reference into the vector is alive.

Linked lists, stacks and queues

An editor checks that brackets match. A print server serves jobs in arrival order. The first task needs a stack. The second needs a queue.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

// A stack checks that brackets are balanced.
fn balanced(s: &str) -> bool {
    let mut stack = Vec::new();
    for ch in s.chars() {
        match ch {
            '(' | '[' | '{' => stack.push(ch),          // push an opener
            ')' | ']' | '}' => {
                let want = match ch { ')' => '(', ']' => '[', _ => '{' };
                if stack.pop() != Some(want) { return false; }  // pop must match
            }
            _ => {}
        }
    }
    stack.is_empty()                                    // nothing left open
}

fn main() {
    for s in ["f(a[i], {b})", "(]", "((x)"] {
        println!("{s:<14} {}", balanced(s));
    }
    // A queue serves jobs in arrival order.
    let mut q: VecDeque<&str> = VecDeque::new();
    q.push_back("job1");
    q.push_back("job2");
    q.push_back("job3");
    let first = q.pop_front().unwrap();                 // O(1) at the front
    let rest: Vec<&str> = q.iter().copied().collect();
    println!("served {first}, waiting {}", rest.join(" "));
}
from collections import deque

# A stack checks that brackets are balanced.
def balanced(s):
    stack = []
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    for ch in s:
        if ch in "([{":
            stack.append(ch)                            # push an opener
        elif ch in pairs:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:   # pop must match
                return False
    return not stack                                    # nothing left open

for s in ["f(a[i], {b})", "(]", "((x)"]:
    print(f"{s:<14} {str(balanced(s)).lower()}")
# A queue serves jobs in arrival order.
q = deque()
q.append("job1")
q.append("job2")
q.append("job3")
first = q.popleft()                                     # O(1) at the front
print(f"served {first}, waiting {' '.join(q)}")
f(a[i], {b})   true
(]             false
((x)           false
served job1, waiting job2 job3

A stack is last in, first out. You push on top and pop from the top. A queue is first in, first out. You add at the back and take from the front. Both are interfaces. Many structures can implement them.

  • A stack fits a dynamic array perfectly. Push and pop at the end are O(1) amortised. The call stack, undo history and depth-first search all use stacks.
  • A queue fits a ring buffer. Two indexes mark the front and the back, and both wrap around. Rust's VecDeque is a growable ring buffer. Breadth-first search and job systems use queues.

A linked list stores each item in its own node. Each node points to the next node. In a doubly linked list it also points back. If you already hold a node, you can insert or remove next to it in O(1). But finding the item at place i means walking i steps: O(n).

Linked lists look good on paper. In practice they are often slow. The nodes are spread over the heap. Each step may be a cache miss. The Rust documentation advises Vec or VecDeque unless you are sure you need a linked list. A good real use is an LRU cache. A hash map finds a node, and a doubly linked list keeps the use order.

Using a Python list as a queue. xs.pop(0) shifts every item, so it costs O(n). A loop that empties a queue this way costs O(n^2). Use collections.deque with popleft(). In Rust, use VecDeque, not Vec::remove(0).

Hash tables

You store a million users and look them up by email. A sorted array needs about 20 comparisons per lookup. A hash table needs about one or two steps. The trick is to compute where a key lives.

A hash function turns a key into a number. Take it modulo the table size m. That gives a bucket index. Two keys can get the same bucket. This is a collision. By the pigeonhole principle, collisions cannot be avoided. There are two main ways to handle them.

Chaining

Each bucket holds a small list. Colliding keys share the list. A search hashes the key, then walks that one list.

Open addressing

All keys live in the table itself. If a slot is taken, try another slot by a fixed rule. Linear probing tries the next slot, then the next.

The load factor is \alpha = n/m. It says how full the table is. The program fills a table of 65,536 slots to three load factors. It counts the slots a search reads.

struct Rng(u64);
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 {             // xorshift64, as in the maths chapter
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13; self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7; self.0 ^= self.0 << 17; self.0
    }
}

fn main() {
    let m = 1usize << 16;                   // 65,536 slots
    for alpha in [0.5, 0.75, 0.9] {
        let n = (alpha * m as f64) as usize;
        let mut rng = Rng(7);
        let mut slots = vec![false; m];     // linear probing: is the slot used?
        let mut chains = vec![0usize; m];   // chaining: length of each list
        let (mut lp, mut ch) = (0usize, 0usize);
        for _ in 0..n {
            let h = (rng.next() % m as u64) as usize;
            let mut i = h;
            lp += 1;
            while slots[i] { i = (i + 1) % m; lp += 1; }  // step to the next slot
            slots[i] = true;
            chains[h] += 1;
            ch += chains[h];                // a search walks the list to this key
        }
        // Miss: from each start slot, count slots read until an empty one.
        let e = slots.iter().position(|&u| !u).unwrap();
        let (mut d, mut miss) = (0usize, 0usize);
        for k in 0..m {
            let i = (e + m - k) % m;        // walk backwards around the table
            d = if slots[i] { d + 1 } else { 1 };
            miss += d;
        }
        println!("load {alpha:.2}: linear hit {:.2}, miss {:.2} | chaining hit {:.2}",
            lp as f64 / n as f64, miss as f64 / m as f64, ch as f64 / n as f64);
    }
}
class Rng:
    def __init__(self, seed):
        self.x = seed
    def next(self):                         # xorshift64, as in the maths chapter
        M = (1 << 64) - 1
        self.x ^= (self.x << 13) & M; self.x ^= self.x >> 7; self.x ^= (self.x << 17) & M
        return self.x

m = 1 << 16                                 # 65,536 slots
for alpha in [0.5, 0.75, 0.9]:
    n = int(alpha * m)
    rng = Rng(7)
    slots = [False] * m                     # linear probing: is the slot used?
    chains = [0] * m                        # chaining: length of each list
    lp = ch = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        h = rng.next() % m
        i = h
        lp += 1
        while slots[i]:                     # step to the next slot
            i = (i + 1) % m
            lp += 1
        slots[i] = True
        chains[h] += 1
        ch += chains[h]                     # a search walks the list to this key
    # Miss: from each start slot, count slots read until an empty one.
    e = slots.index(False)
    d = miss = 0
    for k in range(m):
        i = (e - k) % m                     # walk backwards around the table
        d = d + 1 if slots[i] else 1
        miss += d
    print(f"load {alpha:.2f}: linear hit {lp / n:.2f}, miss {miss / m:.2f} "
          f"| chaining hit {ch / n:.2f}")
load 0.50: linear hit 1.51, miss 2.52 | chaining hit 1.25
load 0.75: linear hit 2.48, miss 8.48 | chaining hit 1.37
load 0.90: linear hit 5.67, miss 54.82 | chaining hit 1.45

The numbers match the classic estimates. With chaining, a successful search reads about 1 + \alpha/2 items. With linear probing, a hit reads about \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\right) slots. A miss reads about \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{(1-\alpha)^2}\right). At \alpha = 0.9 that is 50.5. Keys pile up in long runs called clusters, and each run makes the next one longer.

So a hash table must resize. When \alpha passes a limit, make a table twice as big and insert every key again. By the same argument as for arrays, this costs O(1) amortised per insert. Real tables differ in the details:

  • CPython's dict uses open addressing. It resizes when the table is two thirds full. Its probe order mixes in the high bits of the hash, so it is not plain linear probing.
  • Rust's HashMap is a port of Google's SwissTable. It uses quadratic probing and SIMD instructions to check many slots at once.
  • Rust's default hash is SipHash 1-3 with a random seed. This protects against HashDoS. The documentation says the algorithm may change.

Deleting from an open-addressing table needs care. If you just empty a slot, a later search may stop there too early. So deleted slots get a mark called a tombstone. A search skips over it. The next resize removes it.

Changing a key after you insert it. Its hash changes, so the table looks in the wrong bucket. That is why Python refuses a list as a dict key. In Rust, keep Hash and Eq consistent. Equal keys must give equal hashes. Also remember that O(1) is expected, not guaranteed. With a bad hash or an attacker, every key can land in one bucket. Then each operation costs O(n). Universal hashing gives the formal promise, see Randomised, approximate, streaming and string algorithms.

Search trees: BST, AVL, red-black and B-trees

A hash table cannot answer "which keys are between 100 and 200?". A search tree can, because it keeps keys in order. But a search tree can also go badly wrong. The program inserts 1000 keys into a plain search tree. First in sorted order, then in random order.

const NONE: usize = usize::MAX;
// A plain binary search tree in a vector. Returns the height (levels).
fn height_after_inserts(keys: &[u64]) -> usize {
    let mut nodes: Vec<(u64, usize, usize)> = Vec::new();  // (key, left, right)
    let mut height = 0;
    for &k in keys {
        let mut depth = 1;
        if !nodes.is_empty() {
            let mut cur = 0;
            loop {
                depth += 1;
                let (key, l, r) = nodes[cur];
                let next = if k < key { l } else { r };   // smaller keys go left
                if next == NONE {
                    let id = nodes.len();
                    if k < key { nodes[cur].1 = id } else { nodes[cur].2 = id }
                    break;
                }
                cur = next;
            }
        }
        nodes.push((k, NONE, NONE));
        height = height.max(depth);
    }
    height
}

fn main() {
    let sorted: Vec<u64> = (0..1000).collect();
    let mut shuffled = sorted.clone();
    let mut x: u64 = 7;                                   // xorshift64 seed
    for i in (1..1000usize).rev() {
        x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17;
        shuffled.swap(i, (x % (i as u64 + 1)) as usize);  // Fisher-Yates shuffle
    }
    println!("sorted order: height {}", height_after_inserts(&sorted));
    println!("random order: height {}", height_after_inserts(&shuffled));
}
# A plain binary search tree in lists. Returns the height (levels).
def height_after_inserts(keys):
    key, left, right = [], [], []
    height = 0
    for k in keys:
        depth = 1
        if key:
            cur = 0
            while True:
                depth += 1
                side = left if k < key[cur] else right   # smaller keys go left
                if side[cur] is None:
                    side[cur] = len(key)
                    break
                cur = side[cur]
        key.append(k); left.append(None); right.append(None)
        height = max(height, depth)
    return height

n = 1000
shuffled = list(range(n))
x, M = 7, (1 << 64) - 1                                 # xorshift64 seed
for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
    x ^= (x << 13) & M; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= (x << 17) & M
    j = x % (i + 1)
    shuffled[i], shuffled[j] = shuffled[j], shuffled[i]  # Fisher-Yates shuffle
print(f"sorted order: height {height_after_inserts(range(n))}")
print(f"random order: height {height_after_inserts(shuffled)}")
sorted order: height 1000
random order: height 22

A binary search tree (BST) keeps one rule at every node. Keys in the left subtree are smaller. Keys in the right subtree are bigger. A search starts at the root and goes left or right. It costs one step per level, so all operations cost O(h). Here h is the height. An in-order walk (left, node, right) visits the keys in sorted order.

Sorted input turned the tree into a line of 1000 nodes. Every new key went to the right. Random input gave height 22. The best possible height for 1000 keys is 10. Real data is often sorted or nearly sorted, so we cannot trust luck. A balanced tree fixes its shape after each change.

An AVL tree with n nodes has height less than 1.45 \log_2(n + 2). A red-black tree with n nodes has height at most 2 \log_2(n + 1). So search, insert and delete in these trees take O(\log n) time.

Proof idea

AVL. Let N(h) be the fewest nodes an AVL tree of height h can have. Its two subtrees have heights at least h-1 and h-2. So N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1, with N(1) = 1 and N(2) = 2. By induction, N(h) + 1 is a Fibonacci number. Fibonacci numbers grow like 1.618^h. So n \ge 1.618^h roughly, which gives h \le 1.44 \log_2 n plus a small constant.

Red-black. Let b be the number of black nodes on every path from the root down. By induction, the tree has at least 2^b - 1 nodes. Red nodes never touch, so a path has at most 2b nodes. So n \ge 2^{h/2} - 1, which gives h \le 2 \log_2(n+1).

For 1000 keys: an AVL tree has at most 14 levels, and a red-black tree at most 19. The plain tree above had 1000.

Rotations: how trees rebalance

A rotation changes the shape but keeps the order. It lifts a child above its parent. The middle subtree B changes sides. In-order, the keys still read A, x, B, y, C. A rotation touches only three links, so it costs O(1).

  • AVL trees (1962) store a balance factor at each node. It must stay -1, 0 or 1. After an insert, one or two rotations fix any node that breaks the rule. AVL trees are strictly balanced, so lookups are fast.
  • Red-black trees colour each node red or black. The root is black. A red node has no red child. Every path down has the same number of black nodes. The rules are looser, so inserts and deletes need fewer rotations. Java's TreeMap and the Linux kernel use red-black trees.

B-trees: trees for disks

A database has a billion rows on disk. A binary tree would need about 30 levels. Each level can be one disk read. A B-tree puts hundreds of keys in one node. One node fills one disk page. With 500 children per node, a billion keys fit in at most 4 levels. The top levels stay in memory, so a lookup reads only one or two pages from disk.

  • Every leaf is at the same depth. The tree grows at the root, not at the leaves.
  • A full node splits into two half-full nodes. The middle key moves up to the parent.
  • A B+ tree keeps all data in the leaves and links the leaves in order. A range scan finds the first key, then walks along the leaves.

PostgreSQL creates B-tree indexes by default. SQLite stores tables and indexes as B-trees. Rust's BTreeMap is a B-tree in memory. Each node holds between B-1 and 2B-1 keys in a small array. That means fewer heap allocations and fewer cache misses than a binary tree. See Relational databases for indexes in depth.

Writing your own plain BST and feeding it sorted ids. The tree becomes a list, and every operation is O(n). Use the library tree: BTreeMap in Rust. Python's standard library has no balanced tree. Use bisect on a sorted list for small data, or a third-party package such as sortedcontainers.

Heaps and priority queues

An on-call system must always handle the most urgent task first. New tasks arrive all the time. Sorting the whole list after each arrival is wasteful. A heap does it in O(\log n) per task.

use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

fn main() {
    // Rust's BinaryHeap is a max-heap. Reverse turns it into a min-heap.
    let mut tasks = BinaryHeap::new();
    tasks.push(Reverse((3, "write report")));   // (priority, name), 1 = urgent
    tasks.push(Reverse((1, "fix outage")));
    tasks.push(Reverse((2, "review PR")));
    while let Some(Reverse((p, name))) = tasks.pop() {
        println!("priority {p}: {name}");
    }
    // Keep the 3 largest values of a stream in a min-heap of size 3.
    let stream = [42, 7, 93, 18, 77, 5, 64, 88];
    let mut top = BinaryHeap::new();
    for x in stream {
        top.push(Reverse(x));
        if top.len() > 3 { top.pop(); }          // drop the smallest of the 4
    }
    let mut best: Vec<i32> = top.into_iter().map(|Reverse(x)| x).collect();
    best.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));
    println!("top 3: {best:?}");
}
import heapq

# Python's heapq is a min-heap on a plain list.
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "write report"))     # (priority, name), 1 = urgent
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "fix outage"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "review PR"))
while tasks:
    p, name = heapq.heappop(tasks)
    print(f"priority {p}: {name}")
# Keep the 3 largest values of a stream in a min-heap of size 3.
stream = [42, 7, 93, 18, 77, 5, 64, 88]
top = []
for x in stream:
    heapq.heappush(top, x)
    if len(top) > 3:
        heapq.heappop(top)                     # drop the smallest of the 4
print(f"top 3: {sorted(top, reverse=True)}")
priority 1: fix outage
priority 2: review PR
priority 3: write report
top 3: [93, 88, 77]

A priority queue lets you add items and remove the smallest (or largest). A binary min-heap is the usual way to build one. Every parent is smaller than or equal to its children. So the smallest item is at the root.

The tree is always complete: every level is full except the last, which fills from the left. So it fits in an array with no pointers. The children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The parent of index i is \lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor.

Start

Array [2, 5, 3, 9, 6, 8]. Root 2 has children 5 and 3. Node 5 has children 9 and 6. Node 3 has child 8. Every parent is smaller than its children.

Push 1 at the end

1 goes to index 6: [2, 5, 3, 9, 6, 8, 1]. Its parent is index 2, the value 3. Now the rule is broken, because 1 is smaller than 3.

Sift up

Swap 1 with 3: [2, 5, 1, 9, 6, 8, 3]. The new parent is the root 2. 1 is smaller, so swap again: [1, 5, 2, 9, 6, 8, 3]. 1 is the root. Stop.

Pop: take the root

Remove 1. Move the last item, 3, to the root: [3, 5, 2, 9, 6, 8]. The rule is broken at the root.

Sift down

The children of 3 are 5 and 2. Swap with the smaller child, 2: [2, 5, 3, 9, 6, 8]. 3 now has only the child 8. 3 is smaller. Stop.

Cost

Each swap moves one level. A complete tree has about \log_2 n levels. So push and pop cost O(\log n). Reading the minimum costs O(1).

Building a heap from n items one by one costs O(n \log n). There is a faster way called heapify. Sift down every node, from the last parent back to the root. It costs only O(n). Half of the nodes are leaves and need no work. A quarter move at most one level, an eighth at most two, and so on. The sum \sum_h \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} \cdot h is less than n. Python has heapq.heapify. Rust's BinaryHeap::from(vec) builds a heap from a vector in linear time.

Heaps appear everywhere. Dijkstra's shortest paths take the closest node next, see Graph algorithms. Schedulers take the earliest deadline. Heap sort is in Sorting, searching, divide and conquer. Merging k sorted files keeps one item per file in a heap.

A heap is not sorted. Print a Python heap list and you see a jumble, for example [2, 5, 3, 9, 6, 8]. Only the first item is special. Finding any other value costs O(n). Also, Rust's BinaryHeap gives the largest item first, while Python's heapq gives the smallest.

Tries

A search box suggests words as you type "te". It needs every stored word that starts with those letters. A hash table cannot do this. A trie can.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
#[derive(Default)]
struct Node {
    kids: BTreeMap<char, Node>,   // one child per next letter, kept sorted
    end: bool,                    // a word ends here
}

impl Node {
    fn insert(&mut self, word: &str) {
        let mut cur = self;
        for ch in word.chars() {
            cur = cur.kids.entry(ch).or_default();   // walk or create
        }
        cur.end = true;
    }
    fn collect(&self, prefix: String, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        if self.end { out.push(prefix.clone()); }
        for (ch, kid) in &self.kids {
            kid.collect(format!("{prefix}{ch}"), out);
        }
    }
    fn complete(&self, prefix: &str) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut cur = self;
        for ch in prefix.chars() {
            match cur.kids.get(&ch) { Some(k) => cur = k, None => return vec![] }
        }
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        cur.collect(prefix.to_string(), &mut out);
        out
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut root = Node::default();
    for w in ["tea", "ten", "to", "in", "inn", "team", "tree"] { root.insert(w); }
    for p in ["te", "i", "x"] {
        println!("{p:<2} -> [{}]", root.complete(p).join(", "));
    }
}
class Node:
    def __init__(self):
        self.kids = {}            # one child per next letter
        self.end = False          # a word ends here

    def insert(self, word):
        cur = self
        for ch in word:
            cur = cur.kids.setdefault(ch, Node())   # walk or create
        cur.end = True

    def collect(self, prefix, out):
        if self.end:
            out.append(prefix)
        for ch in sorted(self.kids):
            self.kids[ch].collect(prefix + ch, out)

    def complete(self, prefix):
        cur = self
        for ch in prefix:
            if ch not in cur.kids:
                return []
            cur = cur.kids[ch]
        out = []
        cur.collect(prefix, out)
        return out

root = Node()
for w in ["tea", "ten", "to", "in", "inn", "team", "tree"]:
    root.insert(w)
for p in ["te", "i", "x"]:
    print(f"{p:<2} -> [{', '.join(root.complete(p))}]")
te -> [tea, team, ten]
i  -> [in, inn]
x  -> []

A trie (say "try") stores strings letter by letter. Each edge is one letter. A path from the root spells a prefix. A flag marks nodes where a whole word ends. All words with the same prefix share the same path.

A lookup costs O(L), where L is the length of the word. It does not depend on how many words are stored. Prefix queries are natural: walk to the prefix, then collect everything below it.

  • Autocomplete and spell checking use tries.
  • Routers find the longest matching address prefix with a binary trie over the bits of the IP address. See Computer networks.
  • A radix tree joins long chains into one edge. "tree" would need one edge "ree" below "t". This saves a lot of memory.

Giving each node a fixed array of 26 or 256 child slots. Most slots stay empty, so memory explodes. Use a small map per node, like the code above, or compress chains into a radix tree.

Union-find

Ten computers get network cables one by one. After each cable you want to know: are computers 0 and 3 connected now? How many separate networks are there? Union-find answers both, almost instantly.

struct UnionFind { parent: Vec<usize>, rank: Vec<u8>, groups: usize }

impl UnionFind {
    fn new(n: usize) -> Self {
        UnionFind { parent: (0..n).collect(), rank: vec![0; n], groups: n }
    }
    fn find(&mut self, x: usize) -> usize {
        if self.parent[x] != x {
            let root = self.find(self.parent[x]);
            self.parent[x] = root;               // path compression
        }
        self.parent[x]
    }
    fn union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) {
        let (ra, rb) = (self.find(a), self.find(b));
        if ra == rb { return; }                  // already in one group
        // union by rank: hang the lower tree under the higher one
        let (lo, hi) = if self.rank[ra] < self.rank[rb] { (ra, rb) } else { (rb, ra) };
        self.parent[lo] = hi;
        if self.rank[lo] == self.rank[hi] { self.rank[hi] += 1; }
        self.groups -= 1;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut uf = UnionFind::new(10);             // 10 computers, no cables yet
    for (a, b) in [(0, 1), (2, 3), (1, 2), (5, 6), (7, 8), (8, 9), (6, 9)] {
        uf.union(a, b);                          // add a cable
    }
    println!("groups: {}", uf.groups);
    println!("0 and 3 connected: {}", uf.find(0) == uf.find(3));
    println!("3 and 5 connected: {}", uf.find(3) == uf.find(5));
}
class UnionFind:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank = [0] * n
        self.groups = n

    def find(self, x):
        if self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x])   # path compression
        return self.parent[x]

    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return                                       # already in one group
        # union by rank: hang the lower tree under the higher one
        lo, hi = (ra, rb) if self.rank[ra] < self.rank[rb] else (rb, ra)
        self.parent[lo] = hi
        if self.rank[lo] == self.rank[hi]:
            self.rank[hi] += 1
        self.groups -= 1

uf = UnionFind(10)                                       # 10 computers, no cables yet
for a, b in [(0, 1), (2, 3), (1, 2), (5, 6), (7, 8), (8, 9), (6, 9)]:
    uf.union(a, b)                                       # add a cable
print(f"groups: {uf.groups}")
print(f"0 and 3 connected: {str(uf.find(0) == uf.find(3)).lower()}")
print(f"3 and 5 connected: {str(uf.find(3) == uf.find(5)).lower()}")
groups: 3
0 and 3 connected: true
3 and 5 connected: false

Union-find, also called a disjoint-set forest, keeps items in groups that never overlap. Each group is a tree. Each item points to a parent. The root names the group. find(x) follows parents to the root. union(a, b) links one root under the other. Two items are in the same group when they have the same root.

Simple linking can build a long chain, and then find costs O(n). Two small ideas fix this:

  • Union by rank. Each root keeps a rank, an upper bound on its tree height. Always hang the lower tree under the higher one.
  • Path compression. After a find, point every node on the path straight at the root. The next find from those nodes takes one step.

Use union by rank and path compression together. Then any sequence of m union and find operations on n items takes O(m\,\alpha(n)) time. Here \alpha is the inverse Ackermann function. It grows so slowly that \alpha(n) \le 4 for any n a real computer can hold.

Proof idea

First, union by rank alone. A rank grows only when two trees of equal rank r join. By induction, a root of rank r has at least 2^r nodes. So no rank is above \log_2 n, and each find costs O(\log n). Path compression makes paths much shorter over time. Tarjan proved in 1975 that the total cost is O(m\,\alpha(n)). The proof sorts nodes by rank into very fast-growing groups. It is long, so we skip it. Fredman and Saks proved in 1989 that no structure of this kind can do better.

In simple words: each operation costs at most a handful of steps, for any real input. Kruskal's minimum spanning tree uses union-find to skip edges that would close a cycle, see Graph algorithms. Other uses: connected parts of an image, and grouping accounts that share an email.

Linking the items instead of their roots: parent[a] = b. This can cut a tree apart and break other groups. Always link find(a) to find(b). Union-find also cannot split a group again. If cables can be removed, you need a different structure.

Randomised structures: skip lists and Bloom filters

Balanced trees work, but rotations are tricky to code. Some structures use coin flips instead. They are simple, and they are fast with very high probability. The probability tools from the maths chapter explain why.

Skip lists

Start with a sorted linked list. Now add an "express lane" above it that skips about half the nodes. Above that, another lane skips half again. A search runs along the top lane until the next key is too big. Then it drops one lane and continues.

A skip list (Pugh, 1990) builds the lanes by chance. Each new key flips a coin. Heads: it also joins the next lane up, and it flips again. Tails: it stops. No rotations, no rebalancing. The program gives levels to many keys and looks at the result.

// Give each of n keys a random level: flip a coin until it shows tails.
fn main() {
    let mut x: u64 = 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15;            // xorshift64 seed (many 1 bits)
    for n in [1_000u64, 1_000_000] {
        let (mut total, mut highest) = (0u64, 0u32);
        for _ in 0..n {
            x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17;
            let level = 1 + x.leading_ones();       // each 1 bit is one "heads"
            total += level as u64;
            highest = highest.max(level);
        }
        println!("n={n}: average level {:.3}, highest level {highest}, log2(n) = {:.1}",
                 total as f64 / n as f64, (n as f64).log2());
    }
}
import math

# Give each of n keys a random level: flip a coin until it shows tails.
x, M = 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15, (1 << 64) - 1            # xorshift64 seed (many 1 bits)
for n in [1_000, 1_000_000]:
    total = highest = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        x ^= (x << 13) & M; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= (x << 17) & M
        level = 1 + 64 - (x ^ M).bit_length()       # count the leading 1 bits
        total += level
        highest = max(highest, level)
    print(f"n={n}: average level {total / n:.3f}, highest level {highest}, "
          f"log2(n) = {math.log2(n):.1f}")
n=1000: average level 1.952, highest level 9, log2(n) = 10.0
n=1000000: average level 1.999, highest level 21, log2(n) = 19.9

Each key has 2 levels on average. A coin needs 2 flips on average to show tails. By linearity of expectation, n keys use about 2n nodes. The highest level stays close to \log_2 n. The next result makes that exact.

Build a skip list on n keys with fair coins. The chance that any key rises above level 3 \log_2 n is at most 1/n^2. The expected number of nodes is 2n, and a search takes O(\log n) expected steps.

Proof

A key rises above level L only if its first L flips are all heads. That has chance 2^{-L}. With L = 3 \log_2 n, the chance is n^{-3}. There are n keys, so by the union bound the chance that any key rises that high is at most n \cdot n^{-3} = n^{-2}. For the search: walk the path backwards, from the found key up and to the left. Each step goes up with chance \frac{1}{2}. So about 2 steps happen per level, over O(\log n) levels.

Skip lists are easy to make concurrent, because an insert changes only a few local links. The in-memory table of LevelDB uses a skip list. Redis uses one for large sorted sets.

Bloom filters

A web crawler has seen a billion URLs. Before it fetches a page, it asks "have I seen this URL?". Storing every URL takes many gigabytes. A Bloom filter answers with about 10 bits per URL. The price: it sometimes says "yes" by mistake.

A Bloom filter (Bloom, 1970) is an array of m bits, all 0 at the start. It uses k hash functions. To add a key, set its k bits to 1. To test a key, check its k bits. If any bit is 0, the key was surely never added. If all are 1, the key was probably added. A wrong "yes" is a false positive.

fn mix(mut z: u64) -> u64 {                      // splitmix64: scramble the bits
    z = z.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
    z ^ (z >> 31)
}

struct Bloom { bits: Vec<bool>, k: u64 }

impl Bloom {
    fn spots(&self, key: u64) -> Vec<usize> {    // k bit positions for one key
        let (h1, h2) = (mix(key), mix(mix(key)) | 1);
        let m = self.bits.len() as u64;
        (0..self.k).map(|i| (h1.wrapping_add(i.wrapping_mul(h2)) % m) as usize).collect()
    }
    fn add(&mut self, key: u64) {
        for s in self.spots(key) { self.bits[s] = true; }
    }
    fn maybe_has(&self, key: u64) -> bool {      // false means "surely not there"
        self.spots(key).iter().all(|&s| self.bits[s])
    }
}

fn main() {
    let n = 1000u64;
    for (bits_per_key, k) in [(10u64, 7u64), (5, 3)] {
        let mut b = Bloom { bits: vec![false; (n * bits_per_key) as usize], k };
        for key in 0..n { b.add(key); }
        let missed = (0..n).filter(|&key| !b.maybe_has(key)).count();
        let tests = 100_000u64;
        let fp = (1_000_000..1_000_000 + tests).filter(|&key| b.maybe_has(key)).count();
        let formula = (1.0 - (-(k as f64) / bits_per_key as f64).exp()).powi(k as i32);
        println!("{bits_per_key} bits/key, k={k}: false negatives {missed}, \
                  false positives {:.4} (formula {:.4})", fp as f64 / tests as f64, formula);
    }
}
import math

M64 = (1 << 64) - 1
def mix(z):                                      # splitmix64: scramble the bits
    z = (z + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M64
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M64
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M64
    return z ^ (z >> 31)

class Bloom:
    def __init__(self, m, k):
        self.bits = [False] * m
        self.k = k
    def spots(self, key):                        # k bit positions for one key
        h1, h2 = mix(key), mix(mix(key)) | 1
        m = len(self.bits)
        return [((h1 + i * h2) & M64) % m for i in range(self.k)]
    def add(self, key):
        for s in self.spots(key):
            self.bits[s] = True
    def maybe_has(self, key):                    # False means "surely not there"
        return all(self.bits[s] for s in self.spots(key))

n = 1000
for bits_per_key, k in [(10, 7), (5, 3)]:
    b = Bloom(n * bits_per_key, k)
    for key in range(n):
        b.add(key)
    missed = sum(1 for key in range(n) if not b.maybe_has(key))
    tests = 100_000
    fp = sum(1 for key in range(1_000_000, 1_000_000 + tests) if b.maybe_has(key))
    formula = (1 - math.exp(-k / bits_per_key)) ** k
    print(f"{bits_per_key} bits/key, k={k}: false negatives {missed}, "
          f"false positives {fp / tests:.4f} (formula {formula:.4f})")
10 bits/key, k=7: false negatives 0, false positives 0.0078 (formula 0.0082)
5 bits/key, k=3: false negatives 0, false positives 0.0930 (formula 0.0918)

The code makes k positions from two hashes: h_1 + i \cdot h_2. This trick is called double hashing. It saves work and works well in practice. There were no false negatives, as promised. The false positive rate matched the formula below.

After n keys go into m bits with k hash functions, the false positive rate is about \left(1 - e^{-kn/m}\right)^k. It is smallest when k \approx \frac{m}{n} \ln 2. Then the rate is about 0.6185^{m/n}.

Where the formula comes from

One hash write misses a given bit with chance 1 - \frac{1}{m}. After kn writes, the bit is still 0 with chance (1 - \frac{1}{m})^{kn} \approx e^{-kn/m}. A new key is a false positive when all its k bits are 1. If the bits were independent, that chance would be (1 - e^{-kn/m})^k. They are not quite independent, so this is a close estimate, not an exact value. The best k makes about half of the bits 1.

With 10 bits per key, the best k is 10 \ln 2 \approx 6.9, so 7. The rate is about 0.82%. Each extra 4.8 bits per key divides the rate by about 10. Databases built on log-structured merge trees, like LevelDB, RocksDB and Cassandra, keep a Bloom filter for each data file. A "no" saves a disk read.

Treating "maybe yes" as "yes". Always check the real data after a positive answer. Also, you cannot delete from a plain Bloom filter. Clearing a bit could erase other keys too. A counting Bloom filter stores small counters instead of bits, so it supports deletes. A Bloom filter also cannot list its keys.

Choosing a structure

Start from the operations you need, not from the structure you like. Ask which operation runs most often. Then ask if you need order, and if the data fits in memory.

The cost of the main operations
StructureSearchInsertDeleteSmallestKeeps order?
Dynamic arrayO(n), by index O(1)O(1) amortised at endO(n)O(n)insert order
Sorted arrayO(\log n)O(n)O(n)O(1)yes
Linked listO(n)O(1) at a known nodeO(1) at a known nodeO(n)insert order
Hash tableO(1) expectedO(1) expected, amortisedO(1) expectedO(n)no
Balanced tree (AVL, red-black)O(\log n)O(\log n)O(\log n)O(\log n)yes, with ranges
B-treeO(\log n), few disk readsO(\log n)O(\log n)O(\log n)yes, with ranges
Binary heapO(n)O(\log n)O(\log n) for the rootO(1)no
TrieO(L)O(L)O(L)O(L)yes, by prefix
Skip listO(\log n) expectedO(\log n) expectedO(\log n) expectedO(1)yes
Union-findfind and union: O(\alpha(n)) amortisednot supportedno
Bloom filterO(k), may say yes by mistakeO(k)not supportednot supportedno

Big-O is not the whole story. Arrays use memory in one block, so the CPU cache helps them a lot. A linear scan of 50 items in an array often beats a hash lookup. Measure with real data before you switch.

  1. 1962 AVL trees. Adelson-Velsky and Landis publish the first self-balancing search tree.
  2. 1970 Bloom filters. Burton Bloom trades a small error rate for much less memory.
  3. 1972 B-trees. Bayer and McCreight design a tree for large indexes on disk.
  4. 1975 Union-find analysis. Tarjan proves the inverse Ackermann bound.
  5. 1978 Red-black trees. Guibas and Sedgewick describe the red and black colour rules.
  6. 1990 Skip lists. Pugh offers coin flips as a simple alternative to balanced trees.

Exams and interviews often ask you to design a structure with two fast operations. Combine two structures. An LRU cache is a hash map plus a doubly linked list. A "median so far" is a max-heap for the lower half plus a min-heap for the upper half. A leaderboard with ranks is a balanced tree that also stores subtree sizes.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for data structures
PatternPurposeModelNote
Grow by a factorCheap appends on averagecapacity 4, 8, 16, 32A fixed step like +100 gives O(n^2) in total.

Keep the load factor lowShort probe sequencesresize at \alpha = 2/3Linear probing misses explode near \alpha = 1.

Practice

Which operation costs O(n) on a dynamic array of n items?

  • Read the item at index 500
  • Append at the end
  • Insert at the front

Inserting at the front shifts every item one place. Reading by index is one address calculation. Appending is O(1) amortised.

Your Python program processes a queue of a million jobs. Which call should take the next job?

  • jobs.pop(0) on a list
  • jobs.popleft() on a collections.deque
  • jobs.pop() on a list

popleft() is O(1). pop(0) shifts all items, so the whole loop would cost O(n^2). pop() takes the newest job, which makes a stack, not a queue.

You insert the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in this order into a plain BST. What is its height?

  • 3
  • 4
  • 7

Each key is bigger than all earlier keys, so it goes to the right every time. The tree is a line of 7 nodes. A balanced tree would have height 3.

A Bloom filter says "no" for a key. What do you know?

  • The key was never added.
  • The key was probably not added.
  • The key was added and then deleted.

An added key sets all its bits to 1, and bits never go back to 0. So a 0 bit proves the key was never added. Only "yes" can be wrong.

A server must always give the job with the earliest deadline, while new jobs keep arriving. Which structure fits best?

  • Hash table
  • Min-heap
  • Stack

A min-heap gives the smallest deadline in O(1), and push and pop cost O(\log n). A hash table has no order, and a stack gives the newest job.

In an array heap, the parent of index 9 is index ?.

A table has 600 keys in 1000 slots. Its load factor is ?.

An array starts at capacity 1 and doubles. After 33 appends its capacity is ?.

  1. Pop the minimum from the min-heap [1, 4, 2, 7, 5, 3]. Show each step and the final array.
    Answer

    Remove 1. Move the last item, 3, to the root: [3, 4, 2, 7, 5]. The children of 3 are 4 and 2. Swap with the smaller, 2: [2, 4, 3, 7, 5]. Index 2 now has no children. Stop. The final heap is [2, 4, 3, 7, 5].

  2. Explain why "add 100 slots when full" makes n appends cost \Theta(n^2).
    Answer

    The array grows at lengths 100, 200, 300, and so on. Growth number j copies about 100j items. There are about n/100 growths. The copies add up to 100(1 + 2 + \dots + n/100), which is about \frac{n^2}{200}. The simulation showed 4999.5 copies per item at n = 10^6, which is n/200.

  3. Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. When it is full, it removes the least recently used key.
    Answer

    Use a hash map from key to a node in a doubly linked list. The list holds the keys in use order, newest at the front. get finds the node by the map and moves it to the front in O(1). put adds a node at the front. If the cache is full, remove the node at the back and delete its key from the map. Every step is O(1).

  4. Why does Rust's BTreeMap use nodes with many keys, even in memory, where there is no disk?
    Answer

    Memory also has a speed gap: the CPU cache is much faster than main memory. A binary tree node is a separate heap allocation, and each step down is a likely cache miss. A B-tree node keeps several keys in one small array. One cache load brings many keys. There are fewer levels and fewer allocations. It does a few more comparisons, but they are cheap.

  5. Expert. You want a Bloom filter for one million URLs with a 1% false positive rate. How many bits and how many hash functions do you need?
    Answer

    At the best k, the rate is about 0.6185^{m/n}. Solve 0.6185^{m/n} = 0.01: m/n = \frac{-\ln 0.01}{(\ln 2)^2} \approx 9.6 bits per key. So m \approx 9.6 million bits, about 1.2 MB. The best k is 9.6 \cdot \ln 2 \approx 6.6, so use 7. Storing the URLs themselves would take tens of megabytes.

  6. Expert. An attacker sends a web server many JSON keys that all land in one hash bucket. What happens, and how does Rust's default HashMap defend against it?
    Answer

    Every insert must walk past all earlier colliding keys. So n keys cost \Theta(n^2) time, and the server slows to a crawl. This is HashDoS. Rust's default hasher is SipHash with a random seed for each map. The attacker does not know the seed, so they cannot compute which keys collide. A faster hasher without a secret seed would give up this protection.

Key takeaways

  • Arrays give O(1) access by index. Growing by a constant factor gives O(1) amortised append. Growing by a fixed step does not.
  • Stacks are last in, first out. Queues are first in, first out. Use a ring buffer for queues, not list.pop(0).
  • Hash tables give expected O(1) lookups if the load factor stays low and the hash is good. Collisions always exist.
  • Search trees keep order and support ranges. They must stay balanced. AVL and red-black trees guarantee O(\log n) height. B-trees use wide nodes to save disk and cache reads.
  • A binary heap is a complete tree in an array. It gives the minimum in O(1) and push and pop in O(\log n).
  • Tries answer prefix questions in time that depends on the word length, not on the number of words.
  • Union-find with union by rank and path compression costs almost constant time per operation.
  • Skip lists use coin flips for balance. Bloom filters use a few bits per key and allow false positives, never false negatives.
  • Choose a structure from the operations you need most. Then check memory, order and cache behaviour, and measure.

Sorting, searching, divide and conquer

Sorting puts items in order. Searching finds one item fast. Both are old problems, but every database, search engine and AI system uses them every second. This chapter also teaches divide and conquer, a method that solves big problems by splitting them into small ones.

  • Write and analyse insertion sort, merge sort, quicksort and heap sort.
  • Explain why comparison sorting needs about n \log_2 n comparisons, and how radix sort avoids it.
  • Write a correct binary search and use it to search for an answer.
  • Find the median or the top k items in linear time.
  • Use divide and conquer to multiply numbers, matrices and polynomials faster.

Sorting by hand: insertion sort

Think of playing cards. You pick up one card at a time. You put each new card in the right place in your hand. The cards in your hand are always in order.

That is insertion sort. We use one list in the whole chapter: [38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21]. An algorithm is a list of exact steps. Here are the steps in code.

// Sort in place. Return how many shifts we made.
fn insertion_sort(a: &mut [i32]) -> usize {
    let mut shifts = 0;
    for i in 1..a.len() {
        let key = a[i]; // the next item to place
        let mut j = i;
        while j > 0 && a[j - 1] > key {
            a[j] = a[j - 1]; // move the bigger item one step right
            j -= 1;
            shifts += 1;
        }
        a[j] = key; // the hole is the right place
    }
    shifts
}

fn main() {
    let mut a = [38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21];
    let shifts = insertion_sort(&mut a);
    println!("{a:?} shifts = {shifts}");
}
def insertion_sort(a: list[int]) -> int:
    """Sort in place. Return how many shifts we made."""
    shifts = 0
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]                  # the next item to place
        j = i
        while j > 0 and a[j - 1] > key:
            a[j] = a[j - 1]         # move the bigger item one step right
            j -= 1
            shifts += 1
        a[j] = key                  # the hole is the right place
    return shifts

a = [38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21]
shifts = insertion_sort(a)
print(a, "shifts =", shifts)
[3, 7, 12, 16, 21, 29, 38, 45] shifts = 18

Why is the code correct? Use a loop invariant. Before step i, the part a[0..i] is sorted. One step puts a[i] into that sorted part. So the sorted part grows by one. At the end the whole list is sorted.

The cost depends on the input. Each shift fixes one inversion. Our list has 18 inversions, so it needs 18 shifts.

  • Best case: the list is already sorted. We make n - 1 comparisons. That is linear time.
  • Worst case: the list is in reverse order. We make n(n-1)/2 comparisons. That is O(n^2).
  • Average case: about n^2/4 comparisons. For 1,000 random numbers we measured 251,312.

Insertion sort is in place. It is also stable. Equal items never jump over each other.

Do not call insertion sort useless because it is O(n^2). On short or nearly sorted lists it is the fastest choice. Python's own sort uses binary insertion sort for short pieces of the list.

Divide and conquer: merge sort

Here is a different plan. Cut the list in two halves. Sort each half. Then merge the two sorted halves into one sorted list. How do we sort each half? With the same plan. We stop when a piece has one item.

  1. Look at the first item of each half: 7 and 3. Take the smaller one, 3.
  2. Now compare 7 and 16. Take 7. Then compare 12 and 16. Take 12.
  3. Compare 38 and 16. Take 16. Then take 21, then 29.
  4. The right half is empty. Copy the rest of the left half: 38, 45.
  5. Result: 3, 7, 12, 16, 21, 29, 38, 45. Each step does one comparison and moves one item.

This plan is divide and conquer. It always has three steps.

  1. Divide. Split the problem into smaller problems of the same kind.
  2. Conquer. Solve each small problem with recursion.
  3. Combine. Join the small answers into the big answer.
// Return a new sorted vector. The input is not changed.
fn merge_sort(a: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32> {
    if a.len() <= 1 {
        return a.to_vec(); // base case: already sorted
    }
    let (left, right) = a.split_at(a.len() / 2);
    let (left, right) = (merge_sort(left), merge_sort(right));
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(a.len());
    let (mut i, mut j) = (0, 0);
    while i < left.len() && j < right.len() {
        if left[i] <= right[j] {
            out.push(left[i]); // "<=" takes the left item first: stable
            i += 1;
        } else {
            out.push(right[j]);
            j += 1;
        }
    }
    out.extend_from_slice(&left[i..]); // one side still has items
    out.extend_from_slice(&right[j..]);
    out
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", merge_sort(&[38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21]));
}
def merge_sort(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """Return a new sorted list. The input is not changed."""
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a[:]                 # base case: already sorted
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i])     # "<=" takes the left item first: stable
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    out.extend(left[i:])            # one side still has items
    out.extend(right[j:])
    return out

print(merge_sort([38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21]))
[3, 7, 12, 16, 21, 29, 38, 45]

Now count the work. Let T(n) be the time for n items. We make two calls on n/2 items, and the merge costs about n. This gives a recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. The picture shows why the answer is n \log_2 n.

Many divide and conquer recurrences have the shape T(n) = aT(n/b) + n^d. The master theorem from Discrete maths for computer science solves them. Compare d with \log_b a.

The master theorem on the algorithms of this chapter
AlgorithmRecurrenceCaseTime
Binary searchT(n/2) + 1d = 0 = \log_2 1\log n
Merge sort2T(n/2) + nd = 1 = \log_2 2n \log n
Karatsuba3T(n/2) + nd = 1 \lt \log_2 3n^{1.585}
Strassen7T(n/2) + n^2d = 2 \lt \log_2 7n^{2.807}

Merge sort is stable because of the <= sign. On a tie it takes the left item first. But merge sort is not in place. It needs extra memory for about n items.

Writing < instead of <= in the merge. The list is still sorted. But equal items can swap places, so the sort is no longer stable.

Quicksort and random pivots

Quicksort also divides and conquers. But the hard work comes first. Pick one item, the pivot. Move smaller items to its left and bigger items to its right. This step is a partition. Then the pivot is in its final place. Sort the left part and the right part.

Set up

For this trace the pivot is the last item, 21. A marker called store starts at place 0. Items left of store are smaller than 21.

38, then 12

38 is not smaller than 21. Do nothing. 12 is smaller. Swap it to place 0. store becomes 1.

[12, 38, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21]

45, then 7

45 is bigger. Do nothing. 7 is smaller. Swap it to place 1. store becomes 2.

[12, 7, 45, 38, 29, 16, 3, 21]

29, then 16

29 is bigger. 16 is smaller. Swap it to place 2. store becomes 3.

[12, 7, 16, 38, 29, 45, 3, 21]

3

3 is smaller. Swap it to place 3. store becomes 4.

[12, 7, 16, 3, 29, 45, 38, 21]

Put the pivot in place

Swap the pivot with the item at store. Now 21 is at place 4 for ever.

[12, 7, 16, 3, 21, 45, 38, 29]

Recurse

Sort [12, 7, 16, 3] and [45, 38, 29] the same way. We used 7 comparisons for this partition.

A fixed pivot is dangerous. Take the last item of a list that is already sorted. Every partition then removes only one item. The cost becomes n + (n-1) + \dots + 1, which is O(n^2). The fix is simple: choose the pivot at random.

struct Rng(u64); // a tiny xorshift random number maker
impl Rng {
    fn below(&mut self, n: usize) -> usize {
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13;
        self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7;
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 17;
        (self.0 % n as u64) as usize
    }
}
// Put a random pivot in its final place. Return that place.
fn partition(a: &mut [i32], rng: &mut Rng, cmps: &mut u64) -> usize {
    let last = a.len() - 1;
    a.swap(rng.below(a.len()), last); // the pivot waits at the end
    let mut store = 0; // a[..store] holds the items below the pivot
    for i in 0..last {
        *cmps += 1;
        if a[i] < a[last] {
            a.swap(i, store);
            store += 1;
        }
    }
    a.swap(store, last);
    store
}
fn quicksort(a: &mut [i32], rng: &mut Rng, cmps: &mut u64) {
    if a.len() <= 1 { return; }
    let p = partition(a, rng, cmps);
    let (left, right) = a.split_at_mut(p);
    quicksort(left, rng, cmps);
    quicksort(&mut right[1..], rng, cmps); // right[0] is the pivot: done
}
fn main() {
    let (mut rng, mut cmps) = (Rng(2026), 0);
    for _ in 0..100_000 {
        let mut a = [38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21];
        quicksort(&mut a, &mut rng, &mut cmps);
        assert!(a.is_sorted());
    }
    println!("average comparisons: {:.1}", cmps as f64 / 100_000.0);
}
import random

def partition(a: list[int], lo: int, hi: int, cmps: list[int]) -> int:
    """Put a random pivot in its final place. Return that place."""
    r = random.randint(lo, hi)
    a[r], a[hi] = a[hi], a[r]           # the pivot waits at the end
    store = lo                          # a[lo:store] holds the items below the pivot
    for i in range(lo, hi):
        cmps[0] += 1
        if a[i] < a[hi]:
            a[i], a[store] = a[store], a[i]
            store += 1
    a[store], a[hi] = a[hi], a[store]
    return store

def quicksort(a: list[int], lo: int, hi: int, cmps: list[int]) -> None:
    if lo < hi:
        p = partition(a, lo, hi, cmps)
        quicksort(a, lo, p - 1, cmps)
        quicksort(a, p + 1, hi, cmps)   # a[p] is the pivot: done

random.seed(2026)
cmps = [0]
for _ in range(100_000):
    a = [38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21]
    quicksort(a, 0, len(a) - 1, cmps)
    assert a == sorted(a)
print(f"average comparisons: {cmps[0] / 100_000:.1f}")
average comparisons: 16.9

Pick every pivot uniformly at random. Then on any input of n different items, the expected number of comparisons is 2(n+1)H_n - 4n, where H_n = 1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac1n. This is about 1.39\, n \log_2 n.

Proof

Name the items in sorted order z_1 \lt z_2 \lt \dots \lt z_n. Two items are compared at most once, and only when one of them is the pivot.

Look at the group z_i, \dots, z_j. While no pivot comes from this group, the group stays together. The first pivot from the group decides. If it is z_i or z_j, the two are compared. If it is an item between them, they go to different sides and never meet. Each item of the group is equally likely to be first. So the chance of a comparison is \frac{2}{j - i + 1}.

By linearity of expectation, add these chances over all pairs: \sum_{i \lt j} \frac{2}{j-i+1}. Group the pairs by the gap k = j - i + 1. This sum is less than 2n H_n, and H_n \approx \ln n. Working it out exactly gives the formula above.

Check it with numbers. For n = 8, H_8 \approx 2.718. So 2 \cdot 9 \cdot 2.718 - 32 \approx 16.92. Our programs measured 16.9 over 100,000 runs. The word "expected" matters. The random choice gives the speed, so no bad input exists. Only bad luck exists, and it is very rare.

Quicksort is in place, but not stable. It is often faster than merge sort because it reads memory in order and moves few items. Lists with many equal keys need a three-way partition: smaller, equal, bigger.

Heap sort: a sort with a guarantee

A max-heap is a tree stored in an array. The children of place i are at places 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The biggest item is always at place 0. The Data structures chapter builds heaps in detail.

Heap sort has two phases. First, turn the array into a max-heap. Our list becomes [45, 29, 38, 21, 12, 16, 3, 7]. Second, swap the top item to the end and repair the heap. Repeat until the heap is empty.

// Move a[i] down until it is bigger than its children. The heap is a[..n].
fn sift_down(a: &mut [i32], mut i: usize, n: usize) {
    loop {
        let (left, right) = (2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2);
        let mut big = i;
        if left < n && a[left] > a[big] { big = left; }
        if right < n && a[right] > a[big] { big = right; }
        if big == i { return; }
        a.swap(i, big);
        i = big;
    }
}

fn heap_sort(a: &mut [i32]) {
    let n = a.len();
    for i in (0..n / 2).rev() {
        sift_down(a, i, n); // build a max-heap from the bottom up
    }
    for end in (1..n).rev() {
        a.swap(0, end); // the biggest item goes to its final place
        sift_down(a, 0, end); // repair the heap that is left
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut a = [38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21];
    heap_sort(&mut a);
    println!("{a:?}");
}
def sift_down(a: list[int], i: int, n: int) -> None:
    """Move a[i] down until it is bigger than its children. The heap is a[:n]."""
    while True:
        left, right, big = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2, i
        if left < n and a[left] > a[big]:
            big = left
        if right < n and a[right] > a[big]:
            big = right
        if big == i:
            return
        a[i], a[big] = a[big], a[i]
        i = big

def heap_sort(a: list[int]) -> None:
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        sift_down(a, i, n)              # build a max-heap from the bottom up
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        a[0], a[end] = a[end], a[0]     # the biggest item goes to its final place
        sift_down(a, 0, end)            # repair the heap that is left

a = [38, 12, 45, 7, 29, 16, 3, 21]
heap_sort(a)
print(a)
[3, 7, 12, 16, 21, 29, 38, 45]

Building the heap costs only O(n). Most nodes sit near the bottom and move very little. Each of the n - 1 repairs costs at most the height, \log_2 n. So heap sort is O(n \log n) even in the worst case. It is also in place. But it is not stable, and it jumps around in memory. On real machines it is slower than quicksort.

Real libraries mix the two. Rust's sort_unstable uses a quicksort called ipnsort. Its documentation says it falls back to heap sort for a guaranteed worst case. This mix is called introsort.

How fast can sorting be?

Merge sort and heap sort need about n \log_2 n comparisons. Can a smarter idea do better? Not if it learns only by comparing items. To see why, draw every possible run of the algorithm as a tree. Here is a best possible tree for three items a, b and c.

A decision tree must have one end for every possible order. Three items have 6 orders. A tree of height 2 has at most 4 ends. So some run needs 3 comparisons.

Any sorting algorithm that learns about the items only by comparing them needs at least \lceil \log_2 n! \rceil comparisons in the worst case. This is n \log_2 n - 1.44\,n + O(\log n), so it is \Omega(n \log n).

Proof

Fix n. Run the algorithm on all n! orders of n different items. Each comparison has two answers, so the runs form a binary tree. Two different orders must reach different ends, or the algorithm would sort one of them wrong. So the tree has at least n! ends.

A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h ends. So 2^h \ge n!, and h \ge \log_2 n!. The height is the worst-case number of comparisons.

For the size, note that n! has at least n/2 factors that are n/2 or more. So \log_2 n! \ge \frac{n}{2} \log_2 \frac{n}{2}, which is \Omega(n \log n). Stirling's formula gives the exact form above.

We tested merge sort on all 40,320 orders of 8 items. Its worst case is 17 comparisons, only one above the bound. Then we sorted 1,000 random numbers 200 times and counted comparisons.

The bound is about comparisons only. An algorithm that looks inside the keys, for example at their digits, is not covered. The next section shows such algorithms.

Beating the bound: counting sort and radix sort

Suppose you sort 10,000 exam scores from 0 to 100. Make 101 counters. Read each score once and add one to its counter. Then write the scores out in counter order. You never compare two scores. This is counting sort. It costs O(n + k) for k possible keys.

Big keys need too many counters. Radix sort fixes this. It sorts by the lowest digit first, then by the next digit, and so on. Each pass is a stable counting sort. In the code below one digit is one byte, so a 32-bit key needs 4 passes.

// Sort by one byte of the key. This is a stable counting sort.
fn sort_by_byte(a: &[u32], shift: u32) -> Vec<u32> {
    let mut count = [0usize; 257];
    for &x in a {
        count[((x >> shift) & 0xFF) as usize + 1] += 1;
    }
    for d in 0..256 {
        count[d + 1] += count[d]; // now count[d] is the first slot for byte d
    }
    let mut out = vec![0; a.len()];
    for &x in a {
        let d = ((x >> shift) & 0xFF) as usize;
        out[count[d]] = x; // left to right: equal bytes keep their order
        count[d] += 1;
    }
    out
}

// Four stable passes, from the lowest byte to the highest byte.
fn radix_sort(a: &[u32]) -> Vec<u32> {
    (0..4).fold(a.to_vec(), |v, pass| sort_by_byte(&v, 8 * pass))
}

fn main() {
    let a = [70_000, 329, 4_000_000_000, 457, 65_536, 329, 12];
    println!("{:?}", radix_sort(&a));
}
def sort_by_byte(a: list[int], shift: int) -> list[int]:
    """Sort by one byte of the key. This is a stable counting sort."""
    count = [0] * 257
    for x in a:
        count[((x >> shift) & 0xFF) + 1] += 1
    for d in range(256):
        count[d + 1] += count[d]        # now count[d] is the first slot for byte d
    out = [0] * len(a)
    for x in a:
        d = (x >> shift) & 0xFF
        out[count[d]] = x               # left to right: equal bytes keep their order
        count[d] += 1
    return out

def radix_sort(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """Four stable passes, from the lowest byte to the highest byte."""
    for p in range(4):
        a = sort_by_byte(a, 8 * p)
    return a

print(radix_sort([70_000, 329, 4_000_000_000, 457, 65_536, 329, 12]))
[12, 329, 329, 457, 65536, 70000, 4000000000]

Radix sort costs O(d(n + k)) for d digits with k values each. For fixed-size keys this is linear in n. Why must each pass be stable? After the pass on byte 2, items with the same byte 2 must keep the order from byte 1. Otherwise the earlier work is lost.

In practice you call the library sort. Stability is useful when you sort by one field after another. This example sorts staff by team only. Inside a team, the old order stays.

fn main() {
    // (name, team). We sort by team only.
    let mut staff = vec![("Mia", "ops"), ("Leo", "dev"), ("Ana", "ops"), ("Sam", "dev")];
    staff.sort_by_key(|&(_, team)| team); // stable: Mia stays before Ana
    let names: Vec<&str> = staff.iter().map(|&(name, _)| name).collect();
    println!("{}", names.join(" "));

    let mut scores: Vec<f64> = vec![0.7, 0.1, 0.9, 0.4];
    scores.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.total_cmp(a)); // b first: biggest first
    println!("{scores:?}");
}
# (name, team). We sort by team only.
staff = [("Mia", "ops"), ("Leo", "dev"), ("Ana", "ops"), ("Sam", "dev")]
staff.sort(key=lambda person: person[1])    # stable: Mia stays before Ana
print(" ".join(name for name, _ in staff))

scores = [0.7, 0.1, 0.9, 0.4]
scores.sort(reverse=True)                   # biggest first
print(scores)
Leo Sam Mia Ana
[0.9, 0.7, 0.4, 0.1]
Which algorithm does Python use?

Timsort, a stable merge sort. It finds runs that are already sorted and merges them. Short runs are grown with binary insertion sort. The CPython notes say the merge order now follows the powersort rule of Munro and Wild.

Which algorithm does Rust use?

Since Rust 1.81 (September 2024), sort is driftsort and sort_unstable is ipnsort. Both are linear on fully sorted input. The documentation says sort allocates up to len / 2 items for long slices.

Why can't I sort floats with sort() in Rust?

Floats have NaN, which is not equal to itself. So floats have no total order. Use sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b)), as in the code above.

Binary search and its variants

You look for a word in a paper dictionary. You open it in the middle. The word comes later, so you throw away the first half. Each look halves the pages. This is binary search.

The safest form finds the first place where the item is at least the target. People call it the lower bound. The invariant is simple: the answer is always between lo and hi.

// First index i where a[i] >= target. Returns a.len() when there is none.
fn lower_bound(a: &[i32], target: i32) -> usize {
    let (mut lo, mut hi) = (0, a.len()); // the answer is always in lo..=hi
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; // this form cannot overflow
        if a[mid] < target {
            lo = mid + 1; // the answer is to the right of mid
        } else {
            hi = mid; // mid itself can be the answer
        }
    }
    lo
}

fn main() {
    let a = [3, 7, 12, 16, 16, 16, 29, 38, 45];
    println!("{}", lower_bound(&a, 16));
    println!("{}", a.partition_point(|&x| x <= 16)); // one past the last 16
    println!("{:?} {:?}", a.binary_search(&29), a.binary_search(&30));
}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

def lower_bound(a: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    """First index i where a[i] >= target. Returns len(a) when there is none."""
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)              # the answer is always in lo..hi
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2        # Python integers cannot overflow
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1            # the answer is to the right of mid
        else:
            hi = mid                # mid itself can be the answer
    return lo

a = [3, 7, 12, 16, 16, 16, 29, 38, 45]
print(lower_bound(a, 16), bisect_left(a, 16))
print(bisect_right(a, 16))          # one past the last 16
print(bisect_left(a, 29), bisect_left(a, 30))
Rust:            Python:
3                3 3
6                6
Ok(6) Err(7)     6 7

Each loop halves the range, so the loop runs at most \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1 times. For one billion items that is only 30 looks. The loop always ends, because the range hi - lo gets smaller in both branches.
