Binary search works on more than lists. It works on any yes or no question that changes only once, from "no" to "yes". Here is an AI example. You have 8 documents with these token counts: 700, 300, 900, 400, 600, 200, 800 and 500. You must send them in order in at most 3 prompts. What is the smallest prompt size that works? If a size works, every bigger size also works. So we can search for the answer.

// Can we split the documents, in order, into at most k prompts of size limit?
fn fits(tokens: &[u32], k: u32, limit: u32) -> bool {
    let (mut used, mut parts) = (0, 1);
    for &t in tokens {
        if t > limit {
            return false; // one document is too big alone
        }
        if used + t > limit {
            parts += 1; // start a new prompt
            used = 0;
        }
        used += t;
    }
    parts <= k
}

fn main() {
    let tokens = [700, 300, 900, 400, 600, 200, 800, 500];
    let (mut lo, mut hi) = (*tokens.iter().max().unwrap(), tokens.iter().sum::<u32>());
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if fits(&tokens, 3, mid) {
            hi = mid; // mid works: try smaller
        } else {
            lo = mid + 1; // mid fails: the answer is bigger
        }
    }
    println!("smallest limit for 3 prompts: {lo}");
}
def fits(tokens: list[int], k: int, limit: int) -> bool:
    """Can we split the documents, in order, into at most k prompts of size limit?"""
    used, parts = 0, 1
    for t in tokens:
        if t > limit:
            return False            # one document is too big alone
        if used + t > limit:
            parts += 1              # start a new prompt
            used = 0
        used += t
    return parts <= k

tokens = [700, 300, 900, 400, 600, 200, 800, 500]
lo, hi = max(tokens), sum(tokens)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if fits(tokens, 3, mid):
        hi = mid                    # mid works: try smaller
    else:
        lo = mid + 1                # mid fails: the answer is bigger
print("smallest limit for 3 prompts:", lo)
smallest limit for 3 prompts: 1900

Two bugs are famous. First, (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow with fixed-size integers. Joshua Bloch reported this bug in the Java library in 2006. Write lo + (hi - lo) / 2. Second, the update lo = mid can loop for ever when hi = lo + 1. Every branch must make the range smaller.

Selection in linear time

A search engine finds 1,000,000 matching documents. It shows only the top 10. Sorting all of them wastes work. We need selection: the item at place k in sorted order. The median is the case k = n/2.

Quickselect reuses the quicksort partition. After one partition the pivot sits at its final place p. If k = p, we are done. If k \lt p, we go left. Otherwise we go right. We follow only one side, never both.

The expected cost is linear. One random pivot cuts the list to about three quarters or less, often enough. So the work is about n + \tfrac34 n + (\tfrac34)^2 n + \dots \le 4n. For the median of 1,001 items we measured about 3,325 comparisons. A full quicksort used about 10,992.

  1. Cut the list into groups of 5. Find the median of each group.
  2. Find the median of those n/5 medians with a recursive call. Use it as the pivot.
  3. Partition. Recurse into the one side that holds place k.

This pivot is always good. At least 3n/10 items are smaller than it, and at least 3n/10 are bigger. So the next call gets at most 7n/10 items. The recurrence is T(n) \le T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + cn. Since \tfrac15 + \tfrac{7}{10} = \tfrac{9}{10} \lt 1, the total is at most 10cn. This is linear even in the worst case. Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan published it in 1973.

fn main() {
    // Similarity scores of 8 documents. We want the top 3.
    let mut scores: Vec<f64> = vec![0.31, 0.92, 0.15, 0.77, 0.58, 0.84, 0.42, 0.66];
    scores.select_nth_unstable_by(2, |a, b| b.total_cmp(a)); // linear time
    let mut top = scores[..3].to_vec(); // the 3 best, in any order
    top.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.total_cmp(a)); // sort only these 3
    println!("{top:?}");
}
import heapq

# Similarity scores of 8 documents. We want the top 3.
scores = [0.31, 0.92, 0.15, 0.77, 0.58, 0.84, 0.42, 0.66]
print(heapq.nlargest(3, scores))    # a heap of size 3: O(n log k)
[0.92, 0.84, 0.77]

Rust's documentation says select_nth_unstable is an introselect. Its fallback is median of medians, which guarantees linear time. Python's heapq.nlargest keeps a small heap of size k. It costs O(n \log k), which is close to linear for small k.

Groups of 3 do not work. The recurrence becomes T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + cn. The parts add up to 1, so the total is n \log n, not linear. Groups of 5 or more keep the sum below 1.

Faster multiplication: Karatsuba, Strassen and the FFT

School multiplication of two n-digit numbers uses n^2 digit products. In 1960, Anatoly Karatsuba found a way with fewer products. Split each number in two halves. Normally you need 4 half-size products. Karatsuba needs only 3.

  1. Split: 12 = 1 \cdot 10 + 2 and 34 = 3 \cdot 10 + 4.
  2. Product 1, the high parts: 1 \times 3 = 3.
  3. Product 2, the low parts: 2 \times 4 = 8.
  4. Product 3, the sums: (1 + 2)(3 + 4) = 21. The middle part is 21 - 3 - 8 = 10.
  5. Join: 3 \cdot 100 + 10 \cdot 10 + 8 = 408. Check: 12 \times 34 = 408.

The trick works for polynomials too. A number is a polynomial in x = 10. The code multiplies 1234 by 5678. The digits are stored lowest first.

// Multiply two polynomials. a[i] is the number in front of x^i.
// Both inputs have the same length, and it is a power of two.
fn karatsuba(a: &[i64], b: &[i64]) -> Vec<i64> {
    let n = a.len();
    if n == 1 {
        return vec![a[0] * b[0]];
    }
    let h = n / 2;
    let (a_lo, a_hi) = a.split_at(h);
    let (b_lo, b_hi) = b.split_at(h);
    let a_sum: Vec<i64> = a_lo.iter().zip(a_hi).map(|(x, y)| x + y).collect();
    let b_sum: Vec<i64> = b_lo.iter().zip(b_hi).map(|(x, y)| x + y).collect();
    let low = karatsuba(a_lo, b_lo); // product 1
    let high = karatsuba(a_hi, b_hi); // product 2
    let mid = karatsuba(&a_sum, &b_sum); // product 3. There is no product 4.
    let mut out = vec![0; 2 * n - 1];
    for i in 0..low.len() {
        out[i] += low[i];
        out[i + n] += high[i];
        out[i + h] += mid[i] - low[i] - high[i];
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    // 1234 is 4 + 3x + 2x^2 + 1x^3 at x = 10. The lowest digit comes first.
    let c = karatsuba(&[4, 3, 2, 1], &[8, 7, 6, 5]);
    println!("{c:?}");
    println!("{}", c.iter().rev().fold(0, |acc, d| acc * 10 + d));
}
def karatsuba(a: list[int], b: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """Multiply two polynomials. a[i] is the number in front of x^i.
    Both inputs have the same length, and it is a power of two."""
    n = len(a)
    if n == 1:
        return [a[0] * b[0]]
    h = n // 2
    a_sum = [x + y for x, y in zip(a[:h], a[h:])]
    b_sum = [x + y for x, y in zip(b[:h], b[h:])]
    low = karatsuba(a[:h], b[:h])       # product 1
    high = karatsuba(a[h:], b[h:])      # product 2
    mid = karatsuba(a_sum, b_sum)       # product 3. There is no product 4.
    out = [0] * (2 * n - 1)
    for i in range(len(low)):
        out[i] += low[i]
        out[i + n] += high[i]
        out[i + h] += mid[i] - low[i] - high[i]
    return out

# 1234 is 4 + 3x + 2x^2 + 1x^3 at x = 10. The lowest digit comes first.
c = karatsuba([4, 3, 2, 1], [8, 7, 6, 5])
print(c)
print(sum(d * 10**i for i, d in enumerate(c)))
[32, 52, 61, 60, 34, 16, 5]
7006652

The recurrence is T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n), so the time is n^{\log_2 3} \approx n^{1.585}. This is real code in real tools. CPython's integer code uses Karatsuba once both numbers have more than 70 internal digits.

Strassen used the same idea for matrices in 1969. Cut each matrix into four blocks. The normal method needs 8 block products. Strassen found clever sums that need only 7. We checked his 7 formulas on thousands of random matrices. For 8 \times 8 matrices they use 343 number products instead of 512. The time is n^{\log_2 7} \approx n^{2.807}.

The best known exponent for matrix multiplication keeps going down. A 2024 paper by Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou showed \omega \lt 2.371339. In August 2026 a preprint by a Google DeepMind team and academic co-authors reported \omega \lt 2.371177. It was not peer reviewed when we checked. These methods are far too slow for real matrices. Fast libraries use the normal method, tuned for the cache.

The fast Fourier transform (FFT) goes further. It multiplies polynomials in O(n \log n). The idea has three steps.

  1. Evaluate. A polynomial of degree below n is fixed by its values at n points. Compute both polynomials at the same points.
  2. Multiply. Multiply the values point by point. This costs only n products.
  3. Interpolate. Turn the values back into coefficients.

With any points, steps 1 and 3 cost n^2. The trick is to choose the n complex roots of unity. Write A(x) = A_{\text{even}}(x^2) + x \, A_{\text{odd}}(x^2). The squares of the n roots are only n/2 points. So one problem of size n becomes two problems of size n/2, plus linear work. That is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), the merge sort recurrence again.

type C = (f64, f64); // a complex number: (real part, imaginary part)

fn mul(a: C, b: C) -> C {
    (a.0 * b.0 - a.1 * b.1, a.0 * b.1 + a.1 * b.0)
}

// Values of the polynomial at the n complex roots of 1. n is a power of two.
fn fft(a: &[C], sign: f64) -> Vec<C> {
    let n = a.len();
    if n == 1 {
        return a.to_vec();
    }
    let even: Vec<C> = a.iter().step_by(2).copied().collect();
    let odd: Vec<C> = a.iter().skip(1).step_by(2).copied().collect();
    let (even, odd) = (fft(&even, sign), fft(&odd, sign)); // two half-size problems
    let mut out = vec![(0.0, 0.0); n];
    for k in 0..n / 2 {
        let w = sign * 2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI * k as f64 / n as f64;
        let t = mul((w.cos(), w.sin()), odd[k]);
        out[k] = (even[k].0 + t.0, even[k].1 + t.1);
        out[k + n / 2] = (even[k].0 - t.0, even[k].1 - t.1);
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    let (p, q) = ([4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0], [8.0, 7.0, 6.0, 5.0]);
    let pad = |v: &[f64]| (0..8).map(|i| (*v.get(i).unwrap_or(&0.0), 0.0)).collect::<Vec<C>>();
    let (fp, fq) = (fft(&pad(&p), 1.0), fft(&pad(&q), 1.0));
    let values: Vec<C> = fp.iter().zip(&fq).map(|(&x, &y)| mul(x, y)).collect();
    let back = fft(&values, -1.0); // the inverse transform
    let c: Vec<i64> = back[..7].iter().map(|z| (z.0 / 8.0).round() as i64).collect();
    println!("{c:?}");
}
import cmath

def fft(a: list[complex], sign: int = 1) -> list[complex]:
    """Values of the polynomial at the n complex roots of 1. n is a power of two."""
    n = len(a)
    if n == 1:
        return a
    even, odd = fft(a[0::2], sign), fft(a[1::2], sign)   # two half-size problems
    out = [0j] * n
    for k in range(n // 2):
        t = cmath.exp(sign * 2j * cmath.pi * k / n) * odd[k]
        out[k] = even[k] + t
        out[k + n // 2] = even[k] - t
    return out

def multiply(p: list[int], q: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    size = len(p) + len(q) - 1
    n = 1
    while n < size:
        n *= 2                                  # room for every coefficient
    fp = fft(p + [0] * (n - len(p)))
    fq = fft(q + [0] * (n - len(q)))
    values = [x * y for x, y in zip(fp, fq)]    # multiply point by point
    back = fft(values, sign=-1)                 # the inverse transform
    return [round((c / n).real) for c in back[:size]]

print(multiply([4, 3, 2, 1], [8, 7, 6, 5]))
[32, 52, 61, 60, 34, 16, 5]

Cooley and Tukey made the FFT famous in 1965. Today it is everywhere: audio, images, radio and big-number maths. The Whisper speech model is one AI example. It cuts 16,000 samples per second into windows of 400 samples and runs an FFT on each window. The hop is 160 samples, so it makes one frame every 10 ms. In 2019 Harvey and van der Hoeven used FFT ideas to multiply n-bit integers in O(n \log n). Their paper appeared in 2021.

Floating-point FFTs give answers like 59.99999. You must round them. For very long inputs the error can grow too big. Exact libraries then use a number-theoretic transform, which works with whole numbers modulo a prime.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for sorting, searching and divide and conquer

Practice

Which of these sorts is stable?

  • Heap sort
  • Merge sort with <= in the merge
  • Quicksort with a random pivot

On a tie, merge sort takes the left item first. Heap sort and quicksort move items over long distances.

Quicksort always takes the last item as pivot. The input is already sorted. What is the running time?

  • O(n)
  • O(n \log n)
  • O(n^2)

Every partition removes only the pivot. The costs are n - 1, n - 2, \dots, which add up to about n^2/2.

Why can radix sort beat the n \log n lower bound?

  • It uses more memory.
  • It looks at the digits of the keys instead of comparing them.
  • It is only fast on sorted data.

The lower bound covers algorithms that only compare. Radix sort reads parts of the keys.

Sorting 8 items by comparisons needs at least ? comparisons in the worst case.

Karatsuba replaces 4 half-size products with ? products.

In [3, 7, 12, 16, 16, 16, 29, 38, 45] the lower bound of 16 is place ? and the upper bound is place ?.

  1. How many shifts does insertion sort make on [3, 1, 2]? Why?
    Answer

    2 shifts. The list has two inversions: (3, 1) and (3, 2). Each shift fixes exactly one inversion.

  2. Solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n with the master theorem.
    Answer

    Here a = 4, b = 2, d = 1. Since \log_2 4 = 2 \gt 1, the leaves win. T(n) = \Theta(n^2). This is the school method with 4 products, so Karatsuba's third product really matters.

  3. You need the 10 best of 1,000,000 search results. Compare a full sort, a heap of size 10, and quickselect.
    Answer

    A full sort needs about n \log_2 n \approx 20 million comparisons. A heap of size 10 needs about n \log_2 10, so a few million in the worst case and fewer on average. Quickselect needs about 2n to 4n expected, then sorts only the 10 winners. Both of the last two beat the full sort.

  4. Show that the loop in lower_bound always ends.
    Answer

    While lo < hi, we have lo ≤ mid < hi. The branch lo = mid + 1 raises lo. The branch hi = mid lowers hi. Either way hi - lo shrinks by at least 1. A whole number that keeps shrinking reaches 0.

  5. Why must the passes of radix sort go from the lowest digit to the highest, with stable passes?
    Answer

    The last pass decides the main order, so it must use the most important digit. Stability keeps the order of the earlier, less important digits inside each group. Without stability, 329 and 457 could swap after the hundreds pass is done, and the list would break.

  6. Expert: prove that in median of medians at least 3n/10 items are smaller than the pivot (ignore rounding).
    Answer

    There are n/5 groups. Half of the group medians, so n/10 of them, are at most the pivot. Each such median has 2 more items in its group below it. So at least 3 \cdot n/10 items are at most the pivot. The same count works for the bigger side.

Key takeaways

  • Insertion sort is O(n^2) but fast on short or nearly sorted lists. Libraries still use it for small pieces.
  • Divide and conquer has three steps: divide, conquer, combine. Its time comes from a recurrence.
  • Merge sort is stable and n \log n but needs extra memory. Heap sort is in place with a worst-case guarantee.
  • Random pivots make quicksort O(n \log n) in expectation on every input.
  • Comparison sorts need \lceil \log_2 n! \rceil comparisons. Counting and radix sort escape the bound by reading keys.
  • Binary search halves the range each step. It can also search for the smallest answer that works.
  • Selection finds the median or top k in linear time. Do not sort just to pick a few items.
  • Karatsuba, Strassen and the FFT use clever splits to multiply faster than the school method.

Graph algorithms

A graph is a set of things and the links between them. Roads, web pages, friends, package dependencies and agent workflows are all graphs. This chapter teaches the classic graph algorithms, why they are correct, and when to use each one.

  • Store a graph as an adjacency list or a matrix and know the cost of each.
  • Use breadth-first and depth-first search, and prove that BFS finds shortest paths.
  • Order tasks with a topological sort and find strongly connected components.
  • Choose and run Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall or A* for a shortest-path problem.
  • Build a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal or Prim, and explain the cut property.

Graphs and how to store them

Seven people use a chat app. Ana talks with Ben and Cai. Ben talks with Dev, and so on. Draw each person as a dot and each friendship as a line. You get a graph.

A graph has vertices and edges. We write n for the number of vertices and m for the number of edges. Some graphs have a direction on each edge, like links between web pages. They are directed. Some edges carry a number, like the length of a road. That number is a weight.

There are two main ways to store a graph in memory.

Adjacency list. For each vertex, keep a list of its neighbours. Ana: [Ben, Cai]. Ben: [Ana, Dev]. The memory is O(n + m). Visiting all neighbours of u costs only its degree.

Adjacency matrix. Keep an n \times n table. The cell in row u and column v says whether an edge exists. The memory is O(n^2). Testing one edge costs O(1).

The cost of each way to store a graph
OperationAdjacency listAdjacency matrixEdge list
Memoryn + mn^2m
Is u–v an edge?degree of u1m
All neighbours of udegree of unm
Good formost real graphssmall or dense graphsKruskal, file formats

Most real graphs are sparse. Take one million vertices with ten million edges. A matrix needs 10^{12} cells, which is 125 GB even at one bit per cell. An adjacency list needs about eleven million entries. Big graph libraries often pack the lists into one array, a form called CSR (compressed sparse row).

In an undirected graph, store each edge twice: u \to v and v \to u. If you store it once, a search can reach Dev from Ben but never Ben from Dev.

Breadth-first search

Ana wants to send a message to Gus through friends. What is the smallest number of steps? Look at Ana's friends first. Then look at their friends. Then at the next ring. This search by rings is breadth-first search (BFS).

BFS uses a queue. Take a vertex from the front. Put each new neighbour at the back. Give each new neighbour the distance of its parent plus one.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

// Fewest edges from start to every vertex. Also the parent on a shortest path.
fn bfs(adj: &[Vec<usize>], start: usize) -> (Vec<Option<usize>>, Vec<Option<usize>>) {
    let n = adj.len();
    let (mut dist, mut parent) = (vec![None; n], vec![None; n]);
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([start]);
    dist[start] = Some(0);
    while let Some(u) = queue.pop_front() {
        for &v in &adj[u] {
            if dist[v].is_none() {
                dist[v] = Some(dist[u].unwrap() + 1); // the first visit is the shortest
                parent[v] = Some(u);
                queue.push_back(v);
            }
        }
    }
    (dist, parent)
}

fn main() {
    let names = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cai", "Dev", "Eva", "Fay", "Gus"];
    let edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 5), (5, 6)];
    let mut adj = vec![Vec::new(); names.len()];
    for &(a, b) in &edges {
        adj[a].push(b); // undirected: store both directions
        adj[b].push(a);
    }
    let (dist, parent) = bfs(&adj, 0);
    let line: Vec<String> = names.iter().zip(&dist).map(|(n, d)| format!("{n}={}", d.unwrap())).collect();
    println!("{}", line.join(" "));
    let mut path = vec![6];
    while let Some(p) = parent[*path.last().unwrap()] {
        path.push(p); // walk back to the start
    }
    let path: Vec<&str> = path.iter().rev().map(|&v| names[v]).collect();
    println!("{}", path.join(" -> "));
}
from collections import deque

def bfs(adj: list[list[int]], start: int) -> tuple[list, list]:
    """Fewest edges from start to every vertex. Also the parent on a shortest path."""
    dist = [None] * len(adj)
    parent = [None] * len(adj)
    dist[start] = 0
    queue = deque([start])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] is None:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1       # the first visit is the shortest
                parent[v] = u
                queue.append(v)
    return dist, parent

names = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cai", "Dev", "Eva", "Fay", "Gus"]
edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 5), (5, 6)]
adj = [[] for _ in names]
for a, b in edges:
    adj[a].append(b)                        # undirected: store both directions
    adj[b].append(a)
dist, parent = bfs(adj, 0)
print(" ".join(f"{n}={d}" for n, d in zip(names, dist)))
path = [6]
while parent[path[-1]] is not None:
    path.append(parent[path[-1]])           # walk back to the start
print(" -> ".join(names[v] for v in reversed(path)))
Ana=0 Ben=1 Cai=1 Dev=2 Eva=2 Fay=3 Gus=4
Ana -> Ben -> Dev -> Fay -> Gus

Each vertex enters the queue once, and each edge is checked once from each end. So BFS costs O(n + m). The parent links form a search tree. Follow them back to get one shortest path.

Run BFS from s. For every vertex v that s can reach, the label \text{dist}[v] equals \delta(s, v), the smallest number of edges on a path from s to v.

Proof

First, the queue always holds labels in order, and they differ by at most one. At any time it looks like k, k, \dots, k, k+1, \dots, k+1. Taking a k from the front only adds k+1 at the back. So BFS removes all vertices with label k before any vertex with label k + 1.

Now use induction on d = \delta(s, v). For d = 0, only s has label 0. Take v with \delta(s, v) = d + 1. Some neighbour u of v has \delta(s, u) = d, and by induction its label is d. The label of v cannot be d or less. That would mean a parent with label d - 1 or less, so a path of length d or less to v. When u leaves the queue, v is either new and gets d + 1, or it already got a label from an earlier vertex. That earlier vertex has label at most d. So the label of v is exactly d + 1.

Mark a vertex as seen when you put it in the queue, not when you take it out. If you mark it late, the same vertex can enter the queue many times. The answer stays right, but the cost can grow far beyond O(n + m).

Depth-first search

You explore a cave. You follow one tunnel as far as you can. At a dead end you walk back to the last fork and try the next tunnel. That is depth-first search (DFS). Recursion does the walking back for us.

DFS gives each vertex one of three colours. White means not seen yet. Gray means we are inside it right now: it is on the current path. Black means finished. These colours tell us a lot about the edges.

  • A tree edge leads to a white vertex. DFS walks along it.
  • A back edge leads to a gray vertex. It points back up the current path. So it closes a cycle.
  • Edges to black vertices are forward or cross edges. They never close a cycle in a directed graph.

Here is the key fact: a directed graph has a cycle exactly when DFS finds a back edge. A second fact gives us an order. A vertex finishes only after everything it can reach has finished. So in a graph with no cycle, the reverse of the finish order puts every edge forwards.

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum Color { White, Gray, Black } // not seen, on the current path, finished

// Depth-first search. Returns Err(edge) for a back edge, else the finish order.
fn visit(u: usize, adj: &[Vec<usize>], color: &mut [Color], order: &mut Vec<usize>)
    -> Result<(), (usize, usize)> {
    color[u] = Color::Gray;
    for &v in &adj[u] {
        match color[v] {
            Color::White => visit(v, adj, color, order)?,
            Color::Gray => return Err((u, v)), // v is still open: a cycle
            Color::Black => {}                 // already finished: no problem
        }
    }
    color[u] = Color::Black;
    order.push(u); // u finishes after everything it can reach
    Ok(())
}

fn topo_order(adj: &[Vec<usize>]) -> Result<Vec<usize>, (usize, usize)> {
    let mut color = vec![Color::White; adj.len()];
    let mut order = Vec::new();
    for u in 0..adj.len() {
        if color[u] == Color::White {
            visit(u, adj, &mut color, &mut order)?;
        }
    }
    order.reverse(); // reverse finish order is a topological order
    Ok(order)
}

fn main() {
    let mut adj = vec![vec![1], vec![2, 5], vec![3], vec![4], vec![6], vec![6], vec![]];
    println!("{:?}", topo_order(&adj));
    adj[6].push(1); // add the edge report -> clean
    println!("{:?}", topo_order(&adj));
}
WHITE, GRAY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2    # not seen, on the current path, finished

def topo_order(adj: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    """Depth-first search. Raise on a back edge, else return a topological order."""
    color = [WHITE] * len(adj)
    order = []

    def visit(u: int) -> None:
        color[u] = GRAY
        for v in adj[u]:
            if color[v] == WHITE:
                visit(v)
            elif color[v] == GRAY:      # v is still open: a cycle
                raise ValueError(f"back edge {u} -> {v}")
        color[u] = BLACK
        order.append(u)                 # u finishes after everything it can reach

    for u in range(len(adj)):
        if color[u] == WHITE:
            visit(u)
    return order[::-1]                  # reverse finish order is a topological order

adj = [[1], [2, 5], [3], [4], [6], [6], []]
print(topo_order(adj))
adj[6].append(1)                        # add the edge report -> clean
try:
    topo_order(adj)
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
Rust:  Ok([0, 1, 5, 2, 3, 4, 6])  then  Err((6, 1))
Python: [0, 1, 5, 2, 3, 4, 6]  then  back edge 6 -> 1

The vertices are numbered in the order download, clean, chunk, embed, index, summarize, report. So the first answer reads: download, clean, summarize, chunk, embed, index, report. Every arrow points forwards. DFS also costs O(n + m).

Recursive DFS can run out of stack on a long path. Python stops at a recursion limit, which is 1,000 by default. Rust can overflow its thread stack and crash. For graphs with millions of vertices, write DFS with your own stack in a loop.

Topological sort

A DAG is a directed acyclic graph: arrows, but no cycle. A topological order lists its vertices so that every arrow points forwards. Build tools, package managers, spreadsheets and agent workflows all need one. The agent orchestration chapter proves that such an order exists exactly when the graph has no cycle.

DFS gives one method. Kahn's algorithm gives another, and it shows which tasks can run at the same time.

  1. Count the arrows into each task. Only download has 0. It is ready.
  2. Run download. Remove its arrows. Now clean has 0 inputs left.
  3. Run clean. Now both chunk and summarize are ready. They can run in parallel.
  4. Continue: embed, then index. report waits for both index and summarize. It runs last.
  5. If tasks are left but none is ready, the graph has a cycle.
// Kahn's algorithm. Returns the tasks in rounds that can run in parallel.
fn kahn_rounds(adj: &[Vec<usize>]) -> Option<Vec<Vec<usize>>> {
    let mut indeg = vec![0; adj.len()];
    for list in adj {
        for &v in list {
            indeg[v] += 1; // count the arrows into v
        }
    }
    let mut ready: Vec<usize> = (0..adj.len()).filter(|&u| indeg[u] == 0).collect();
    let (mut rounds, mut done) = (Vec::new(), 0);
    while !ready.is_empty() {
        let mut next = Vec::new();
        for &u in &ready {
            for &v in &adj[u] {
                indeg[v] -= 1;
                if indeg[v] == 0 {
                    next.push(v); // all inputs of v are finished
                }
            }
        }
        done += ready.len();
        rounds.push(std::mem::replace(&mut ready, next));
    }
    (done == adj.len()).then_some(rounds) // tasks left over: a cycle
}

fn main() {
    let names = ["download", "clean", "chunk", "embed", "index", "summarize", "report"];
    let adj = vec![vec![1], vec![2, 5], vec![3], vec![4], vec![6], vec![6], vec![]];
    for (i, round) in kahn_rounds(&adj).unwrap().iter().enumerate() {
        let r: Vec<&str> = round.iter().map(|&u| names[u]).collect();
        println!("round {}: {}", i + 1, r.join(", "));
    }
}
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter

def kahn_rounds(adj: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]] | None:
    """Kahn's algorithm. Returns the tasks in rounds that can run in parallel."""
    indeg = [0] * len(adj)
    for vs in adj:
        for v in vs:
            indeg[v] += 1                   # count the arrows into v
    ready = [u for u in range(len(adj)) if indeg[u] == 0]
    rounds, done = [], 0
    while ready:
        nxt = []
        for u in ready:
            for v in adj[u]:
                indeg[v] -= 1
                if indeg[v] == 0:
                    nxt.append(v)           # all inputs of v are finished
        done += len(ready)
        rounds.append(ready)
        ready = nxt
    return rounds if done == len(adj) else None   # tasks left over: a cycle

names = ["download", "clean", "chunk", "embed", "index", "summarize", "report"]
adj = [[1], [2, 5], [3], [4], [6], [6], []]
for i, r in enumerate(kahn_rounds(adj), 1):
    print(f"round {i}:", ", ".join(names[u] for u in r))
# The standard library does the same. It wants the inputs of each task.
needs = {"clean": {"download"}, "chunk": {"clean"}, "embed": {"chunk"},
         "index": {"embed"}, "summarize": {"clean"}, "report": {"index", "summarize"}}
print(list(TopologicalSorter(needs).static_order()))
round 1: download
round 2: clean
round 3: chunk, summarize
round 4: embed
round 5: index
round 6: report
['download', 'clean', 'chunk', 'summarize', 'embed', 'index', 'report']

The last line comes only from the Python version. Python has had graphlib.TopologicalSorter in the standard library since version 3.9. It raises CycleError when it finds a cycle. Its get_ready and done methods let you run ready tasks in parallel, round by round.

The number of rounds is the length of the longest chain of tasks. With unlimited workers, it is the best possible time. Here it is 6 rounds for 7 tasks, so parallel workers save only one step. The chain download, clean, chunk, embed, index, report is the critical path.

A topological order is usually not unique. Exams ask for "a" topological order. Any order where every arrow points forwards is correct.

Strongly connected components

In a directed graph, two vertices are strongly connected when each can reach the other. The graph splits into groups, called strongly connected components (SCCs). Inside a group, every vertex reaches every other one.

Shrink each component to one dot. The result is always a DAG, called the condensation. Why? If two components could reach each other, they would be one component. This turns any directed graph into a DAG, and DAGs are easy.

Kosaraju's algorithm finds the components in two passes. First, run DFS and record when each vertex finishes. Second, flip every arrow. Run DFS again, starting from the latest finisher. Each search in the second pass collects exactly one component.

// Kosaraju: DFS on the graph, then DFS on the reversed graph.
fn finish(u: usize, adj: &[Vec<usize>], seen: &mut [bool], order: &mut Vec<usize>) {
    seen[u] = true;
    for &v in &adj[u] {
        if !seen[v] { finish(v, adj, seen, order); }
    }
    order.push(u); // record u when it finishes
}

fn collect(u: usize, radj: &[Vec<usize>], comp: &mut [Option<usize>], id: usize) {
    comp[u] = Some(id);
    for &v in &radj[u] {
        if comp[v].is_none() { collect(v, radj, comp, id); }
    }
}

fn scc(adj: &[Vec<usize>]) -> Vec<Option<usize>> {
    let n = adj.len();
    let (mut seen, mut order) = (vec![false; n], Vec::new());
    for u in 0..n {
        if !seen[u] { finish(u, adj, &mut seen, &mut order); }
    }
    let mut radj = vec![Vec::new(); n];
    for u in 0..n {
        for &v in &adj[u] { radj[v].push(u); } // flip every arrow
    }
    let (mut comp, mut id) = (vec![None; n], 0);
    for &u in order.iter().rev() { // latest finish first
        if comp[u].is_none() { collect(u, &radj, &mut comp, id); id += 1; }
    }
    comp
}

fn main() {
    let adj = vec![vec![1], vec![2], vec![0, 3], vec![4], vec![5], vec![3], vec![5, 7], vec![6]];
    let comp: Vec<usize> = scc(&adj).into_iter().map(Option::unwrap).collect();
    println!("{comp:?}");
}
def scc(adj: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    """Kosaraju: DFS on the graph, then DFS on the reversed graph."""
    n = len(adj)
    seen, order = [False] * n, []

    def finish(u: int) -> None:
        seen[u] = True
        for v in adj[u]:
            if not seen[v]:
                finish(v)
        order.append(u)                 # record u when it finishes

    for u in range(n):
        if not seen[u]:
            finish(u)
    radj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u in range(n):
        for v in adj[u]:
            radj[v].append(u)           # flip every arrow
    comp = [None] * n

    def collect(u: int, cid: int) -> None:
        comp[u] = cid
        for v in radj[u]:
            if comp[v] is None:
                collect(v, cid)

    cid = 0
    for u in reversed(order):           # latest finish first
        if comp[u] is None:
            collect(u, cid)
            cid += 1
    return comp

adj = [[1], [2], [0, 3], [4], [5], [3], [5, 7], [6]]
print(scc(adj))
[1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0]

Vertices 6 and 7 got component 0, vertices 0 to 2 got 1, and vertices 3 to 5 got 2. The numbers come out in a topological order of the condensation: arrows go from 0 and 1 into 2. The cost is two searches, so O(n + m).

Why does the second pass work?

The vertex that finishes last lies in a "source" component: no arrow enters that component from outside. After we flip the arrows, that component has no arrow leaving it. So the second search from that vertex cannot escape. It collects exactly its own component. Remove it and repeat the same argument. Tarjan's algorithm finds the same components in one pass, with a stack and "low-link" numbers.

SCCs find groups of packages that depend on each other in a loop. Compilers use them to find groups of functions that call each other. The 2-SAT problem, a simple kind of logic puzzle, is solved with SCCs in linear time.

Shortest paths with weights: Dijkstra

Now the edges have weights, such as minutes of travel. BFS counts edges, so it gives the wrong answer here. A path with many short edges can beat a path with one long edge. We need a new idea.

The basic step of every shortest-path algorithm is to relax an edge. For the edge u \to v with weight w: if \text{dist}[u] + w \lt \text{dist}[v], set \text{dist}[v] = \text{dist}[u] + w. Dijkstra's algorithm relaxes edges in a clever order. It always settles the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance. It finds that vertex with a priority queue.

Only S is known

dist: S = 0. All others are ∞. The queue holds (0, S).

Settle S at 0

Relax S→A: A = 4. Relax S→B: B = 1. Queue: (1, B), (4, A).

Settle B at 1

B→A gives 1 + 2 = 3, better than 4. So A = 3. B→C gives C = 6. Queue: (3, A), (4, A old), (6, C).

Settle A at 3

A→C gives 4, better than 6. A→D gives D = 8. The old entry (4, A) comes out next. We skip it, because A is already settled at 3.

Settle C at 4

C→D gives 7, better than 8. C→E gives E = 10. The old (6, C) comes out later and is skipped.

Settle D at 7

D→E gives 8, better than 10. So E = 8.

Settle E at 8: done

Final: S 0, B 1, A 3, C 4, D 7, E 8. The path is S → B → A → C → D → E. It has 5 edges, but it is the cheapest.

use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

// Shortest distances from start. adj[u] holds (v, weight). Weights must be >= 0.
fn dijkstra(adj: &[Vec<(usize, u64)>], start: usize) -> (Vec<u64>, Vec<usize>) {
    let n = adj.len();
    let (mut dist, mut parent) = (vec![u64::MAX; n], vec![usize::MAX; n]);
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::new(); // a max-heap, so we wrap items in Reverse
    dist[start] = 0;
    heap.push(Reverse((0, start)));
    while let Some(Reverse((d, u))) = heap.pop() {
        if d > dist[u] { continue; } // an old entry: u was settled with a smaller d
        for &(v, w) in &adj[u] {
            if d + w < dist[v] {
                dist[v] = d + w; // relax the edge u -> v
                parent[v] = u;
                heap.push(Reverse((dist[v], v)));
            }
        }
    }
    (dist, parent)
}

fn main() {
    let names = ["S", "A", "B", "C", "D", "E"];
    let edges = [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1), (2, 1, 2), (2, 3, 5), (1, 3, 1),
                 (1, 4, 5), (3, 4, 3), (3, 5, 6), (4, 5, 1)];
    let mut adj = vec![Vec::new(); names.len()];
    for &(u, v, w) in &edges { adj[u].push((v, w)); }
    let (dist, parent) = dijkstra(&adj, 0);
    println!("{dist:?}");
    let mut path = vec![5];
    while *path.last().unwrap() != 0 {
        path.push(parent[*path.last().unwrap()]);
    }
    println!("{}", path.iter().rev().map(|&v| names[v]).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(" -> "));
}
import heapq

def dijkstra(adj: list[list[tuple[int, int]]], start: int) -> tuple[list, list]:
    """Shortest distances from start. adj[u] holds (v, weight). Weights must be >= 0."""
    dist = [float("inf")] * len(adj)
    parent = [None] * len(adj)
    dist[start] = 0
    heap = [(0, start)]                 # heapq is a min-heap
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                    # an old entry: u was already settled
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if d + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = d + w         # relax the edge u -> v
                parent[v] = u
                heapq.heappush(heap, (dist[v], v))
    return dist, parent

names = ["S", "A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]
edges = [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1), (2, 1, 2), (2, 3, 5), (1, 3, 1),
         (1, 4, 5), (3, 4, 3), (3, 5, 6), (4, 5, 1)]
adj = [[] for _ in names]
for u, v, w in edges:
    adj[u].append((v, w))
dist, parent = dijkstra(adj, 0)
print(dist)
path = [5]
while path[-1] != 0:
    path.append(parent[path[-1]])
print(" -> ".join(names[v] for v in reversed(path)))
[0, 3, 1, 4, 7, 8]
S -> B -> A -> C -> D -> E

Neither library heap can lower the key of an item. So we push a new entry and skip old ones when they come out. The Python heapq documentation suggests the same trick. With a binary heap the cost is O((n + m) \log n). A Fibonacci heap gives O(m + n \log n) in theory.

If every edge weight is zero or more, then each vertex u has \text{dist}[u] = \delta(s, u), the true shortest distance, at the moment Dijkstra settles it.

Proof

Suppose the claim fails. Let u be the first vertex settled with a wrong value, so \text{dist}[u] \gt \delta(s, u). Look at a true shortest path from s to u. Walk along it. Let y be the first vertex on it that is not yet settled, and x the vertex just before y.

The vertex x was settled earlier, so its value was right. When we settled x, we relaxed x \to y. So \text{dist}[y] \le \delta(s, y). The rest of the path from y to u has weight zero or more. So \delta(s, y) \le \delta(s, u) \lt \text{dist}[u].

Together: \text{dist}[y] \lt \text{dist}[u]. But Dijkstra picked u because it had the smallest value. This is a contradiction. The step "the rest of the path is not negative" is exactly where we need non-negative weights.

Do not use Dijkstra with negative weights. Take S→A = 2, S→B = 3, B→A = −2. Dijkstra settles A at 2 first. But S→B→A costs 1. Our skip-old-entries code repairs this tiny case by settling A again, but on other graphs it can take exponential time. Use Bellman-Ford instead.

For decades, Dijkstra's m + n \log n looked like a wall for directed graphs. In 2025, Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu and Yin gave a deterministic O(m \log^{2/3} n) algorithm for real non-negative weights. It won a best paper award at STOC 2025. Earlier, a FOCS 2024 paper looked at a related task: list the vertices in order of distance. It showed that Dijkstra with a special heap is "universally optimal" for it. On every fixed graph shape, with the worst weights, no algorithm beats it by more than a constant factor.

Negative weights, all pairs and A*

Negative weights do happen. Take currency exchange. Suppose 1 dollar buys 0.9 euro, 1 euro buys 0.8 pound, and 1 pound buys 1.4 dollars. These rates are made up. The round trip gives 0.9 \times 0.8 \times 1.4 = 1.008 dollars: free money. Give each edge the weight -\ln(\text{rate}). A product above 1 becomes a sum below 0: 0.1054 + 0.2231 - 0.3365 = -0.008. So free money is a negative cycle.

The Bellman-Ford algorithm is simple. Relax every edge, and repeat this n - 1 times. After round k, every shortest path with at most k edges is correct. A shortest path without a cycle has at most n - 1 edges, so then we are done. If one more round still improves something, there is a negative cycle.

// Bellman-Ford. Edges are (u, v, weight). Weights may be negative.
// Returns None when a negative cycle can be reached from start.
fn bellman_ford(n: usize, edges: &[(usize, usize, i64)], start: usize) -> Option<Vec<i64>> {
    const INF: i64 = i64::MAX / 4; // big, but adding a weight cannot overflow
    let mut dist = vec![INF; n];
    dist[start] = 0;
    for _ in 0..n - 1 {
        // after round k, paths with up to k edges are right
        for &(u, v, w) in edges {
            if dist[u] < INF && dist[u] + w < dist[v] {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w;
            }
        }
    }
    for &(u, v, w) in edges {
        if dist[u] < INF && dist[u] + w < dist[v] {
            return None; // still improving after n - 1 rounds: a negative cycle
        }
    }
    Some(dist)
}

fn main() {
    // S=0, A=1, B=2, C=3
    let mut edges = vec![(0, 1, 2), (0, 2, 3), (2, 1, -2), (1, 3, 2)];
    println!("{:?}", bellman_ford(4, &edges, 0));
    edges.push((3, 2, -1)); // B -> A -> C -> B now costs -2 + 2 - 1 = -1
    println!("{:?}", bellman_ford(4, &edges, 0));
}
def bellman_ford(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int, int]], start: int) -> list | None:
    """Bellman-Ford. Weights may be negative.
    Returns None when a negative cycle can be reached from start."""
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[start] = 0
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        # after round k, paths with up to k edges are right
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
    for u, v, w in edges:
        if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            return None             # still improving after n - 1 rounds: a negative cycle
    return dist

# S=0, A=1, B=2, C=3
edges = [(0, 1, 2), (0, 2, 3), (2, 1, -2), (1, 3, 2)]
print(bellman_ford(4, edges, 0))
edges.append((3, 2, -1))            # B -> A -> C -> B now costs -2 + 2 - 1 = -1
print(bellman_ford(4, edges, 0))
Rust:   Some([0, 1, 3, 3])  then  None
Python: [0, 1, 3, 3]  then  None

Bellman-Ford costs O(nm), much slower than Dijkstra. Distance-vector routing on the internet grew from the same idea. Each router keeps relaxing with the distances its neighbours report.

Sometimes we want the distance between every pair of vertices. The Floyd-Warshall algorithm does it in three nested loops. In round k, paths may also pass through vertex k. The update is d[i][j] = \min(d[i][j],\ d[i][k] + d[k][j]). This is dynamic programming, and the next chapter explains that method.

const INF: u32 = u32::MAX / 2; // "no path yet"; INF + INF still fits

// All-pairs shortest paths. d[i][j] starts as the edge weight (or INF).
fn floyd_warshall(d: &mut Vec<Vec<u32>>) {
    let n = d.len();
    for k in 0..n {
        // now paths may also pass through vertex k
        for i in 0..n {
            for j in 0..n {
                d[i][j] = d[i][j].min(d[i][k] + d[k][j]);
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut d = vec![
        vec![0, 3, INF, 7],
        vec![8, 0, 2, INF],
        vec![5, INF, 0, 1],
        vec![2, INF, INF, 0],
    ];
    floyd_warshall(&mut d);
    for row in &d {
        println!("{row:?}");
    }
}
INF = float("inf")

def floyd_warshall(d: list[list[float]]) -> None:
    """All-pairs shortest paths. d[i][j] starts as the edge weight (or INF)."""
    n = len(d)
    for k in range(n):
        # now paths may also pass through vertex k
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j])

d = [[0, 3, INF, 7],
     [8, 0, 2, INF],
     [5, INF, 0, 1],
     [2, INF, INF, 0]]
floyd_warshall(d)
for row in d:
    print(row)
[0, 3, 5, 6]
[5, 0, 2, 3]
[3, 6, 0, 1]
[2, 5, 7, 0]

Floyd-Warshall costs O(n^3) time and O(n^2) memory. It is fine for a few thousand vertices. It also works with negative edges. A negative number on the diagonal at the end means a negative cycle. For big sparse graphs, Johnson's algorithm is better. It runs Bellman-Ford once to remove negative weights, then Dijkstra from every vertex.

A* search is Dijkstra with a sense of direction. It orders the queue by f(v) = g(v) + h(v). Here g(v) is the distance found so far and h(v) is a guess of the distance left. On a map, the straight-line distance is a good guess. With h = 0, A* is exactly Dijkstra. If h never overestimates, A* still finds a shortest path. The classical AI chapter proves this.

We tested both on a 30 × 30 grid with a long wall. Both found the same path of 52 steps. Dijkstra settled 860 cells. A* with Manhattan distance settled 404. Without the wall, A* settled only 51 cells.

Minimum spanning trees

A company has six offices, A to F. It wants to connect them all with cables. Each possible cable has a cost. What is the cheapest network that connects everyone?

The cheapest network never has a cycle. You could remove one cable of the cycle and stay connected. So the answer is a tree that touches every vertex: a spanning tree. The cheapest one is a minimum spanning tree (MST). With n vertices it has n - 1 edges.

Both classic MST algorithms are greedy. They rest on one theorem. A cut splits the vertices into two groups. An edge crosses the cut when its ends are in different groups.

Take any cut of a connected weighted graph. Let e be a cheapest edge that crosses the cut. Then some minimum spanning tree contains e. If all weights are different, every minimum spanning tree contains e.

Proof (an exchange argument)

Take any MST T. If it contains e, we are done. If not, add e to T. Now there is exactly one cycle. The edge e crosses the cut, and the cycle must come back across it. So the cycle has another crossing edge f.

Remove f. The result T' = T + e - f is again a spanning tree. Since e is a cheapest crossing edge, w(e) \le w(f). So T' costs no more than T. It is also an MST, and it contains e. With all weights different, w(e) \lt w(f) and T' would be cheaper than T. That is impossible, so T must contain e.

Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges by cost. It takes each edge unless it closes a cycle. To test for a cycle fast, it uses union-find from the Data structures chapter. Each taken edge is a cheapest edge leaving its group, so the cut property says it is safe.

// Union-find with path halving and union by size.
struct Dsu { parent: Vec<usize>, size: Vec<usize> }
impl Dsu {
    fn new(n: usize) -> Self { Dsu { parent: (0..n).collect(), size: vec![1; n] } }
    fn find(&mut self, mut x: usize) -> usize {
        while self.parent[x] != x {
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]; // skip one level
            x = self.parent[x];
        }
        x
    }
    fn union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) -> bool {
        let (mut a, mut b) = (self.find(a), self.find(b));
        if a == b { return false; } // same tree already: the edge makes a cycle
        if self.size[a] < self.size[b] { std::mem::swap(&mut a, &mut b); }
        self.parent[b] = a; // hang the small tree under the big one
        self.size[a] += self.size[b];
        true
    }
}

fn main() {
    let names = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"];
    let mut edges = vec![(4, 0, 1), (1, 0, 2), (2, 1, 2), (5, 1, 3), (8, 2, 3),
                         (10, 2, 4), (2, 3, 4), (6, 3, 5), (3, 4, 5)]; // (cost, u, v)
    edges.sort(); // cheapest first
    let (mut dsu, mut total) = (Dsu::new(names.len()), 0);
    for (w, u, v) in edges {
        if dsu.union(u, v) {
            println!("take {}-{} cost {w}", names[u], names[v]);
            total += w;
        }
    }
    println!("total {total}");
}
def kruskal(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int, int]]) -> list[tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """Minimum spanning tree. edges are (cost, u, v). Uses union-find."""
    parent, size = list(range(n)), [1] * n

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]   # path halving: skip one level
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    tree = []
    for w, u, v in sorted(edges):           # cheapest first
        a, b = find(u), find(v)
        if a == b:
            continue                        # same tree already: the edge makes a cycle
        if size[a] < size[b]:
            a, b = b, a
        parent[b] = a                       # hang the small tree under the big one
        size[a] += size[b]
        tree.append((w, u, v))
    return tree

names = "ABCDEF"
edges = [(4, 0, 1), (1, 0, 2), (2, 1, 2), (5, 1, 3), (8, 2, 3),
         (10, 2, 4), (2, 3, 4), (6, 3, 5), (3, 4, 5)]
tree = kruskal(len(names), edges)
for w, u, v in tree:
    print(f"take {names[u]}-{names[v]} cost {w}")
print("total", sum(w for w, _, _ in tree))
take A-C cost 1
take B-C cost 2
take D-E cost 2
take E-F cost 3
take B-D cost 5
total 13

The edge A–B (cost 4) was skipped. A and B were already joined through C. Sorting costs O(m \log m), and the union-find work is almost linear. So Kruskal runs in O(m \log m).

Prim's algorithm grows one tree from a start vertex instead. The cut is "inside the tree" against "outside". Each step adds the cheapest crossing edge.

  1. Tree {A}. Crossing edges: A–C 1, A–B 4. Take A–C.
  2. Tree {A, C}. Cheapest crossing edge: B–C 2. Take it.
  3. Tree {A, B, C}. Crossing: B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10. Take B–D.
  4. Tree {A, B, C, D}. Crossing: D–E 2, D–F 6, C–E 10. Take D–E.
  5. Tree {A, B, C, D, E}. Crossing: E–F 3, D–F 6. Take E–F. Total 1 + 2 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 13, the same as Kruskal.

Prim with a heap looks almost like Dijkstra. The only change is the key. Dijkstra uses the distance from the start. Prim uses the weight of the single edge into the tree. It costs O(m \log n) with a binary heap.

An MST is not a shortest-path tree. Take a triangle X, Y, Z with X–Y = 2, Y–Z = 2 and X–Z = 3. The MST takes the two edges of cost 2. In the tree, X to Z costs 4. The direct edge costs only 3. The MST makes the total cost small, not each path. Also, the MST is for undirected graphs. Directed graphs need a different algorithm (Chu-Liu and Edmonds).

Patterns to remember

Patterns for graph algorithms
PatternPurposeModelNote
Adjacency listStore a sparse graphadj[u] = list of neighboursUndirected: store each edge twice.
BFS with a queueFewest edges from one sourceAna to Gus in 4 stepsMark a vertex when it enters the queue.
DFS with three coloursFind cycles and finish orderA gray neighbour means a back edgeDeep graphs need an explicit stack.
Reverse finish orderTopological order of a DAGdownload, clean, summarize, ...Only works when there is no cycle.
Kahn's roundsRun tasks in parallel in a safe orderRound 3: chunk and summarizeTasks left over mean a cycle.
Two DFS passesStrongly connected componentsKosaraju on the reversed graphComponents shrink to a DAG.
Relax an edgeThe step inside every shortest-path method\text{dist}[v] = \min(\text{dist}[v], \text{dist}[u] + w)The order of relaxing is the whole difference.
Dijkstra with lazy deletionShortest paths, weights zero or morePush new entries, skip old onesWrong with negative weights.
n - 1 rounds of relaxingNegative weights, find negative cyclesBellman-Ford, O(nm)An extra round that improves means a negative cycle.
Allow one more middle vertexAll-pairs shortest pathsFloyd-Warshall, O(n^3)The k loop must be the outer loop.
f = g + hPoint-to-point search with a guessA* with straight-line distanceThe guess must never overestimate.
Cheapest edge across a cutBuild a minimum spanning treeKruskal with union-find, Prim with a heapAn MST is not a shortest-path tree.

Practice

Which structure does BFS use to decide which vertex to visit next?

  • A stack
  • A queue
  • A priority queue

A queue gives "first in, first out". So vertices leave in the order of their distance.

DFS on a directed graph finds an edge to a gray vertex. What does that mean?

  • The graph is not connected.
  • The graph has a cycle.
  • The vertex was visited twice by mistake.

A gray vertex is on the current path. An edge back to it closes a cycle.

A graph has one negative edge but no negative cycle. You need distances from one source. What do you use?

  • Dijkstra
  • BFS
  • Bellman-Ford

Dijkstra's proof needs non-negative weights. Bellman-Ford works with any weights when no negative cycle exists.

A minimum spanning tree of a connected graph with 10 vertices has ? edges.

BFS on a graph with n vertices and m edges costs O(?).

Floyd-Warshall on 100 vertices runs the inner update 100^3 = ? times.

  1. In the Dijkstra example, which distances got better after they were first set?
    Answer

    A went from 4 to 3 (through B). C went from 6 to 4 (through A). D went from 8 to 7 (through C). E went from 10 to 8 (through D).

  2. Give a topological order of the pipeline that is different from both orders in this chapter.
    Answer

    For example: download, clean, chunk, embed, summarize, index, report. Check: every arrow still points forwards. Summarize only needs clean, and report comes last.

  3. Why does Bellman-Ford need exactly n - 1 rounds and not fewer?
    Answer

    A shortest path without a cycle can have up to n - 1 edges. Round k fixes all shortest paths with up to k edges. In the worst case, edges are relaxed in a bad order, and each round moves the right value only one edge further. A path on a line of n vertices, with edges listed backwards, needs all n - 1 rounds.

  4. Use the cut property to show that the cheapest edge of the whole graph is in some MST.
    Answer

    Let the cheapest edge be u–v. Take the cut {u} against all other vertices. The edge u–v crosses it, and no edge is cheaper. By the cut property, some MST contains it.

  5. Expert: a company has 1,000 servers in a cluster. You need the round-trip delay between every pair, and delays are positive. Compare Floyd-Warshall with running Dijkstra from every server, if each server links to about 10 others.
    Answer

    Floyd-Warshall costs n^3 = 10^9 simple steps. Dijkstra from every source costs about n \cdot m \log n. Here m \approx 10{,}000 and \log_2 n \approx 10, so 1{,}000 \times 10{,}000 \times 10 = 10^8 heap steps. Dijkstra from every vertex is better for this sparse graph. Floyd-Warshall wins on dense graphs and is simpler to write.

Key takeaways

  • Store sparse graphs as adjacency lists: memory O(n + m). Use a matrix only for small or dense graphs.
  • BFS finds the fewest-edge paths in O(n + m). The queue keeps vertices in order of distance.
  • DFS finds cycles (back edges) and gives a topological order by reverse finish time.
  • Kahn's algorithm orders a DAG in rounds. The number of rounds is the critical path.
  • Any directed graph shrinks to a DAG of strongly connected components.
  • Dijkstra is correct only for non-negative weights. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and finds negative cycles.
  • Floyd-Warshall gives all pairs in O(n^3). A* adds a guess to reach one goal faster.
  • The cut property makes greedy MST algorithms correct: Kruskal by edges, Prim by growing a tree.

Sources

  • Jeff Erickson, Algorithms. Free textbook with chapters on graph search, DFS, shortest paths and minimum spanning trees.
  • Rust std::collections::binary_heap. The module documentation includes a Dijkstra example with a max-heap.
  • Python heapq. The min-heap and the notes on marking old entries as removed.
  • Python graphlib. TopologicalSorter, static_order, get_ready, done and CycleError.
  • Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu and Yin: Breaking the Sorting Barrier for Directed Single-Source Shortest Paths. The 2025 result.
  • Haeupler, Hladík, Rozhoň, Tarjan and Tětek: Universal Optimality of Dijkstra via Beyond-Worst-Case Heaps. FOCS 2024.

Dynamic programming and greedy algorithms

Many problems ask for the best choice: the shortest path, the cheapest plan, the smallest file. Dynamic programming finds the best answer by solving each small problem once and saving it. Greedy algorithms take the best-looking step now and never look back. This chapter shows how both work, how to prove them, and when greedy fails.

  • Spot overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure in a problem.
  • Write a dynamic program top-down with memoization and bottom-up with a table.
  • Solve knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance and matrix chain problems.
  • Prove a greedy algorithm correct with an exchange argument, and build Huffman codes.
  • Recognise problems where greedy gives a wrong answer.

Overlapping subproblems and memoization

The Fibonacci numbers start 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Each one is the sum of the two before it. The plain recursive code is short. But look at what it does for fib(5).

The same small problems appear again and again. We call them overlapping subproblems. The fix is simple: save each answer the first time and reuse it later. Saving answers this way is memoization.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// Plain recursion: the same subproblems are solved again and again.
fn fib_naive(n: u64, calls: &mut u64) -> u64 {
    *calls += 1;
    if n < 2 { n } else { fib_naive(n - 1, calls) + fib_naive(n - 2, calls) }
}

// Top-down: the same recursion, but remember every answer (memoization).
fn fib_memo(n: u64, memo: &mut HashMap<u64, u64>, calls: &mut u64) -> u64 {
    *calls += 1;
    if n < 2 { return n; }
    if let Some(&v) = memo.get(&n) { return v; } // solved before: reuse it
    let v = fib_memo(n - 1, memo, calls) + fib_memo(n - 2, memo, calls);
    memo.insert(n, v);
    v
}

// Bottom-up: solve the small problems first, keep only what we still need.
fn fib_table(n: u64) -> u64 {
    let (mut a, mut b) = (0, 1); // fib(0), fib(1)
    for _ in 0..n {
        (a, b) = (b, a + b);
    }
    a
}

fn main() {
    let (mut c1, mut c2) = (0, 0);
    let x = fib_naive(30, &mut c1);
    let y = fib_memo(30, &mut HashMap::new(), &mut c2);
    println!("naive: {x} with {c1} calls");
    println!("memo:  {y} with {c2} calls");
    println!("table: {}", fib_table(90));
}
from functools import cache

calls = 0
def fib_naive(n: int) -> int:
    """Plain recursion: the same subproblems are solved again and again."""
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return n if n < 2 else fib_naive(n - 1) + fib_naive(n - 2)

@cache                                  # top-down: remember every answer
def fib_memo(n: int) -> int:
    return n if n < 2 else fib_memo(n - 1) + fib_memo(n - 2)

def fib_table(n: int) -> int:
    """Bottom-up: solve the small problems first, keep only what we still need."""
    a, b = 0, 1                         # fib(0), fib(1)
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a

x = fib_naive(30)
print(f"naive: {x} with {calls} calls")
y = fib_memo(30)
print(f"memo:  {y} with {fib_memo.cache_info().misses} different subproblems")
print("table:", fib_table(90))
Rust:
naive: 832040 with 2692537 calls
memo:  832040 with 59 calls
table: 2880067194370816120
Python:
naive: 832040 with 2692537 calls
memo:  832040 with 31 different subproblems
table: 2880067194370816120

Plain recursion made 2,692,537 calls for fib(30). The number of calls grows like the Fibonacci numbers themselves, so it is exponential. With memoization there are only 31 different subproblems, fib(0) to fib(30). Python's functools.cache, added in version 3.9, does the saving for you.

Memoization helps only when subproblems repeat. Merge sort splits a list into halves that never overlap. Saving its results gains nothing. That is divide and conquer, not dynamic programming.

Optimal substructure and Bellman's principle

The fastest way from Tokyo to Osaka passes through Nagoya. Then its part from Nagoya to Osaka must also be the fastest way from Nagoya to Osaka. If a faster way existed, you could swap it in and beat the "fastest" route. This is optimal substructure.

Dynamic programming (DP) needs two things. The problem must have optimal substructure. And it should have overlapping subproblems, or DP gives no speed-up. Richard Bellman named the method in the 1950s and stated its main idea.

In an optimal sequence of decisions, the first decision can be anything. But the decisions after it must form an optimal sequence for the state that the first decision leads to.

Proof (cut and paste)

Let the total cost be the cost of the first step plus the cost of the rest. Suppose an optimal plan makes its first step into state x, and the rest is not optimal from x. Then a cheaper plan from x exists. Keep the first step and paste in the cheaper rest. The new plan is valid and costs less than the "optimal" one. That is impossible. So the rest was optimal from x.

The principle turns into an equation. For shortest paths, let d_k(v) be the shortest distance to v using at most k edges. Then d_k(v) = \min\big(d_{k-1}(v),\ \min_{u \to v} d_{k-1}(u) + w(u, v)\big). This is exactly Bellman-Ford from the graph algorithms chapter. Floyd-Warshall is a DP too: its subproblems are "paths that use only the first k vertices in the middle".

Every DP is a shortest or longest path in a DAG. The vertices are subproblems. An edge says "this answer uses that answer". We solve the subproblems in a topological order, so each one is ready when we need it.

Not every problem has optimal substructure. Take the longest simple path, which never repeats a vertex. A longest simple path from a to c through b may use a part that is not the longest simple path from a to b. The best part from a to b could take vertices the rest of the path needs. The pieces interfere, so the principle fails. This problem is NP-hard.

Top-down and bottom-up

There are two ways to write a DP. Top-down keeps the recursion and adds a memo. It solves only the subproblems that it really needs. Bottom-up fills a table from small to large with loops. It has no recursion, so it cannot overflow the stack, and it is often faster.

Name the subproblem

Write one sentence: "best[i][c] is the best score using the first i items with c tokens of room." Most of the work is here.

Write the recurrence

Look at the last choice. For one item: skip it or take it. Then best[i][c] is the larger of the two results.

Set the base cases

With no items or no room, the score is 0. Base cases stop the recursion.

Choose the order

Each cell must come after the cells it uses. Here row i uses only row i - 1. So fill the rows from top to bottom.

Get the answer and the choices

The answer is in one cell. To learn which items to take, walk back through the table. Then count the cost: number of cells times work per cell.

Top-down or bottom-up?
QuestionTop-down (memo)Bottom-up (table)
Easy to write from the recurrence?yes, add a cacheyou must find a fill order
Solves only needed subproblems?yesno, it fills every cell
Risk of stack overflow?yes, on deep recursionno
Can save memory by keeping only recent rows?hardoften easy

Knapsack: packing a context window

A retrieval system found four documents for a question. The model's context window has room for 1,000 tokens. Each document has a size and a relevance score. Which documents should go in to get the highest total score?

Four documents and a 1,000-token budget
DocumentTokensScoreScore per token
A20060.030
B400100.025
C600120.020
D30050.017

This is the 0/1 knapsack problem. "0/1" means each item is taken whole or not at all. A greedy idea takes the best score per token first: A, then B, then D, because C no longer fits. That uses 900 tokens for a score of 21. Dynamic programming finds a better answer.

// 0/1 knapsack: pick documents for a context window of `cap` tokens.
// best[i][c] = the best score in c tokens, using the first i items.
fn knapsack<'a>(items: &[(&'a str, usize, u32)], cap: usize) -> (u32, Vec<&'a str>) {
    let n = items.len();
    let mut best = vec![vec![0u32; cap + 1]; n + 1]; // row i: first i items
    for (i, &(_, tokens, score)) in items.iter().enumerate() {
        for c in 0..=cap {
            best[i + 1][c] = best[i][c]; // choice 1: skip item i
            if tokens <= c {
                let take = best[i][c - tokens] + score; // choice 2: take it
                best[i + 1][c] = best[i + 1][c].max(take);
            }
        }
    }
    let (mut c, mut chosen) = (cap, Vec::new());
    for i in (0..n).rev() {
        if best[i + 1][c] != best[i][c] { // the value changed: item i was taken
            chosen.push(items[i].0);
            c -= items[i].1;
        }
    }
    chosen.reverse();
    (best[n][cap], chosen)
}

fn main() {
    let docs = [("A", 200, 6), ("B", 400, 10), ("C", 600, 12), ("D", 300, 5)];
    println!("{:?}", knapsack(&docs, 1000));
}
def knapsack(items: list[tuple[str, int, int]], cap: int) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    """0/1 knapsack: pick documents for a context window of cap tokens.
    best[i][c] = the best score in c tokens, using the first i items."""
    n = len(items)
    best = [[0] * (cap + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i, (_, tokens, score) in enumerate(items):
        for c in range(cap + 1):
            best[i + 1][c] = best[i][c]                 # choice 1: skip item i
            if tokens <= c:                             # choice 2: take it
                best[i + 1][c] = max(best[i + 1][c], best[i][c - tokens] + score)
    c, chosen = cap, []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        if best[i + 1][c] != best[i][c]:                # the value changed: taken
            chosen.append(items[i][0])
            c -= items[i][1]
    return best[n][cap], chosen[::-1]

docs = [("A", 200, 6), ("B", 400, 10), ("C", 600, 12), ("D", 300, 5)]
print(knapsack(docs, 1000))
(22, ["B", "C"])

The best choice is B and C: exactly 1,000 tokens and a score of 22. The table has (n + 1)(W + 1) cells for n items and capacity W. So the cost is O(nW). If the sizes are in tokens, that is fine. But W is a number in the input, not a count of items. Its size in bits is only \log_2 W. So O(nW) is exponential in the input size. Such a time is called pseudo-polynomial. The 0/1 knapsack problem is NP-hard, as the complexity theory chapter explains.

If you may take part of an item, the problem is the fractional knapsack. Then greedy by score per token is optimal. Take A, B, then 400 of C's 600 tokens for 6 + 10 + 8 = 24. Small changes to a problem can change which method works.

Sequences: LCS and edit distance

A subsequence keeps some letters in their order, with gaps allowed. "GRP" is a subsequence of both GRAPH and GROUP. The longest common subsequence (LCS) is the longest such shared sequence.

Let L[i][j] be the LCS length of the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b. Look at the last two letters.

  • If they are equal, use the letter: L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1.
  • If not, one of them is not in the LCS. Drop it: L[i][j] = \max(L[i-1][j],\ L[i][j-1]).
The LCS table for GRAPH (rows) and GROUP (columns)
–GROUP
–000000
G011111
R012222
A012222
P012223
H012223
 
// Longest common subsequence. L[i][j] = LCS length of a[..i] and b[..j].
fn lcs(a: &str, b: &str) -> String {
    let (a, b): (Vec<char>, Vec<char>) = (a.chars().collect(), b.chars().collect());
    let mut l = vec![vec![0usize; b.len() + 1]; a.len() + 1];
    for i in 1..=a.len() {
        for j in 1..=b.len() {
            l[i][j] = if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] {
                l[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 // same letter: use it
            } else {
                l[i - 1][j].max(l[i][j - 1]) // drop a letter from one side
            };
        }
    }
    let (mut i, mut j, mut out) = (a.len(), b.len(), Vec::new());
    while i > 0 && j > 0 { // walk back through the table
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] {
            out.push(a[i - 1]);
            i -= 1;
            j -= 1;
        } else if l[i - 1][j] >= l[i][j - 1] {
            i -= 1;
        } else {
            j -= 1;
        }
    }
    out.iter().rev().collect()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", lcs("GRAPH", "GROUP"));
    println!("{}", lcs("ALGORITHM", "LOGARITHM"));
}
def lcs(a: str, b: str) -> str:
    """Longest common subsequence. L[i][j] = LCS length of a[:i] and b[:j]."""
    L = [[0] * (len(b) + 1) for _ in range(len(a) + 1)]
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                L[i][j] = L[i - 1][j - 1] + 1           # same letter: use it
            else:
                L[i][j] = max(L[i - 1][j], L[i][j - 1]) # drop a letter from one side
    i, j, out = len(a), len(b), []
    while i > 0 and j > 0:                              # walk back through the table
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
            out.append(a[i - 1])
            i, j = i - 1, j - 1
        elif L[i - 1][j] >= L[i][j - 1]:
            i -= 1
        else:
            j -= 1
    return "".join(reversed(out))

print(lcs("GRAPH", "GROUP"))
print(lcs("ALGORITHM", "LOGARITHM"))
GRP
LGRITHM

Edit distance, also called Levenshtein distance, is a close cousin. It counts the fewest single edits that turn one sequence into another. An edit is an insert, a delete or a substitution. The table has the same shape. Each cell takes the minimum of three moves: from above (delete), from the left (insert), or from the diagonal (keep or substitute).

The function below works on any sequence. So we can use it on letters and on words. Word error rate (WER), the usual score for speech recognition, is the word-level edit distance divided by the number of words in the correct text.

// Levenshtein distance between two sequences of any comparable items.
// d[i][j] = fewest edits that turn a[..i] into b[..j].
fn edit_distance<T: PartialEq>(a: &[T], b: &[T]) -> usize {
    let mut d = vec![vec![0; b.len() + 1]; a.len() + 1];
    for i in 0..=a.len() { d[i][0] = i; } // delete everything
    for j in 0..=b.len() { d[0][j] = j; } // insert everything
    for i in 1..=a.len() {
        for j in 1..=b.len() {
            let swap = if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] { 0 } else { 1 };
            d[i][j] = (d[i - 1][j] + 1)          // delete a[i-1]
                .min(d[i][j - 1] + 1)            // insert b[j-1]
                .min(d[i - 1][j - 1] + swap);    // keep or substitute
        }
    }
    d[a.len()][b.len()]
}

fn main() {
    let (x, y): (Vec<char>, Vec<char>) = ("monday".chars().collect(), "money".chars().collect());
    println!("letters: {}", edit_distance(&x, &y));
    // Word error rate of a speech model: word edits / words in the reference.
    let reference: Vec<&str> = "the cat sat on the mat".split(' ').collect();
    let heard: Vec<&str> = "the cat sit on mat".split(' ').collect();
    let e = edit_distance(&reference, &heard);
    println!("word edits: {e}, WER = {:.1}%", 100.0 * e as f64 / reference.len() as f64);
}
from typing import Sequence

def edit_distance(a: Sequence, b: Sequence) -> int:
    """Levenshtein distance between two sequences of any comparable items.
    d[i][j] = fewest edits that turn a[:i] into b[:j]."""
    d = [[0] * (len(b) + 1) for _ in range(len(a) + 1)]
    for i in range(len(a) + 1):
        d[i][0] = i                             # delete everything
    for j in range(len(b) + 1):
        d[0][j] = j                             # insert everything
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            swap = 0 if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] else 1
            d[i][j] = min(d[i - 1][j] + 1,      # delete a[i-1]
                          d[i][j - 1] + 1,      # insert b[j-1]
                          d[i - 1][j - 1] + swap)   # keep or substitute
    return d[len(a)][len(b)]

print("letters:", edit_distance("monday", "money"))
# Word error rate of a speech model: word edits / words in the reference.
reference = "the cat sat on the mat".split()
heard = "the cat sit on mat".split()
e = edit_distance(reference, heard)
print(f"word edits: {e}, WER = {100 * e / len(reference):.1f}%")
letters: 2
word edits: 2, WER = 33.3%

"monday" becomes "money" with two edits: change d to e, and delete a. The speech example has one substitution (sat to sit) and one deletion (the second "the"). Both tables cost O(nm) time. Each row uses only the row above, so two rows are enough. That cuts memory to O(m).

Real diff tools use faster special methods. Git's default diff algorithm is Myers. Git's documentation calls it the basic greedy diff algorithm. A separate --minimal option spends extra time to find the smallest diff. Python's difflib uses a different matching idea and does not promise a minimal diff. Its documentation says that minimal diffs often look strange to people.

Matrix chain: the best order of products

Multiply three matrices: A is 10 \times 30, B is 30 \times 5, C is 5 \times 60. The answer does not depend on the order. The work does. Multiplying a p \times q matrix by a q \times r matrix costs pqr number products.

  • (AB)C: 10 \cdot 30 \cdot 5 + 10 \cdot 5 \cdot 60 = 1{,}500 + 3{,}000 = 4{,}500.
  • A(BC): 30 \cdot 5 \cdot 60 + 10 \cdot 30 \cdot 60 = 9{,}000 + 18{,}000 = 27{,}000.

The bad order costs six times more. With n matrices the number of orders grows very fast. So we use DP over intervals. Let \text{cost}[i][j] be the best cost for matrices i to j. The last product splits the chain at some k: \text{cost}[i][j] = \min_k \big(\text{cost}[i][k] + \text{cost}[k+1][j] + p_i \, p_{k+1} \, p_{j+1}\big). Short chains come first.

// Matrix chain order. Matrix i has size dims[i] x dims[i+1].
// cost[i][j] = fewest number products to compute matrices i..=j.
fn chain(dims: &[u64]) -> (u64, String) {
    let n = dims.len() - 1;
    let mut cost = vec![vec![0u64; n]; n];
    let mut split = vec![vec![0usize; n]; n];
    for len in 2..=n { // short chains first
        for i in 0..=n - len {
            let j = i + len - 1;
            cost[i][j] = u64::MAX;
            for k in i..j { // the last product joins i..=k and k+1..=j
                let c = cost[i][k] + cost[k + 1][j] + dims[i] * dims[k + 1] * dims[j + 1];
                if c < cost[i][j] { cost[i][j] = c; split[i][j] = k; }
            }
        }
    }
    fn show(s: &Vec<Vec<usize>>, i: usize, j: usize) -> String {
        if i == j { return ((b'A' + i as u8) as char).to_string(); }
        format!("({}{})", show(s, i, s[i][j]), show(s, s[i][j] + 1, j))
    }
    (cost[0][n - 1], show(&split, 0, n - 1))
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", chain(&[10, 30, 5, 60]));
    println!("{:?}", chain(&[10, 30, 5, 60, 10]));
}
def chain(dims: list[int]) -> tuple[int, str]:
    """Matrix chain order. Matrix i has size dims[i] x dims[i+1].
    cost[i][j] = fewest number products to compute matrices i..j."""
    n = len(dims) - 1
    cost = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    split = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for length in range(2, n + 1):              # short chains first
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1
            cost[i][j] = float("inf")
            for k in range(i, j):               # the last product joins i..k and k+1..j
                c = cost[i][k] + cost[k + 1][j] + dims[i] * dims[k + 1] * dims[j + 1]
                if c < cost[i][j]:
                    cost[i][j], split[i][j] = c, k

    def show(i: int, j: int) -> str:
        if i == j:
            return "ABCDEFGH"[i]
        return f"({show(i, split[i][j])}{show(split[i][j] + 1, j)})"

    return cost[0][n - 1], show(0, n - 1)

print(chain([10, 30, 5, 60]))
print(chain([10, 30, 5, 60, 10]))
(4500, "((AB)C)")
(5000, "((AB)(CD))")

There are O(n^2) cells and each tries O(n) splits, so the time is O(n^3). The same problem appears in deep learning tools. A chain of tensor products can be done in many orders, and a good order can save a lot of work.

Greedy algorithms and the exchange argument

One GPU can run one job at a time. Eight jobs want it, each with a start and an end time. How many jobs can we run without overlap? Try this rule: always pick the job that finishes first, then repeat with the jobs that start after it.

A greedy algorithm makes one local choice at each step and never changes it. It is fast and simple. But it is correct only for some problems, so we must prove it. The usual tool is the exchange argument.

Choosing the compatible job with the earliest finish time, again and again, gives the largest possible number of jobs without overlap.

Proof (exchange argument)

Let g be the job that finishes first overall. Take any optimal schedule O, and let o be its first job. Replace o by g. Since g finishes no later than o, it cannot overlap the other jobs of O. The new schedule is valid and has the same size, so it is also optimal. It starts with the greedy choice.

Now remove g and every job that overlaps it. What is left is a smaller problem of the same kind. The rest of the optimal schedule is optimal for it, by the cut-and-paste idea. By induction, greedy solves the smaller problem optimally too.

Now give each job a value and maximise the total value. Greedy breaks: it picks a, d and h for a value of 9. The best is c and g for 12. The fix is DP. Sort the jobs by end time. For job i, either skip it, or take it plus the best answer for the jobs that end before it starts. Binary search finds those jobs, as in the sorting and searching chapter.

// Jobs are (start, end, value). A job uses the time [start, end).
fn most_jobs(jobs: &[(u32, u32, u32)]) -> Vec<(u32, u32, u32)> {
    let mut by_end = jobs.to_vec();
    by_end.sort_by_key(|j| j.1); // greedy: earliest finish first
    let (mut free_at, mut chosen) = (0, Vec::new());
    for job in by_end {
        if job.0 >= free_at { // it starts after the last chosen job ends
            free_at = job.1;
            chosen.push(job);
        }
    }
    chosen
}

// Weighted version: greedy fails, dynamic programming works.
fn best_value(jobs: &[(u32, u32, u32)]) -> u32 {
    let mut by_end = jobs.to_vec();
    by_end.sort_by_key(|j| j.1);
    let ends: Vec<u32> = by_end.iter().map(|j| j.1).collect();
    let mut best = vec![0; by_end.len() + 1]; // best[i] = best value of the first i jobs
    for (i, &(start, _, value)) in by_end.iter().enumerate() {
        let p = ends.partition_point(|&e| e <= start); // jobs that end before this start
        best[i + 1] = best[i].max(best[p] + value); // skip job i, or take it
    }
    best[by_end.len()]
}

fn main() {
    let jobs = [(1, 4, 3), (3, 5, 2), (0, 6, 8), (4, 7, 3),
                (3, 9, 6), (5, 9, 2), (6, 10, 4), (8, 11, 3)];
    println!("{:?}", most_jobs(&jobs));
    println!("best total value: {}", best_value(&jobs));
}
from bisect import bisect_right

# Jobs are (start, end, value). A job uses the time [start, end).
def most_jobs(jobs: list[tuple[int, int, int]]) -> list[tuple[int, int, int]]:
    free_at, chosen = 0, []
    for job in sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1]):    # greedy: earliest finish first
        if job[0] >= free_at:           # it starts after the last chosen job ends
            free_at = job[1]
            chosen.append(job)
    return chosen

def best_value(jobs: list[tuple[int, int, int]]) -> int:
    """Weighted version: greedy fails, dynamic programming works."""
