    by_end = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1])
    ends = [j[1] for j in by_end]
    best = [0] * (len(by_end) + 1)      # best[i] = best value of the first i jobs
    for i, (start, _, value) in enumerate(by_end):
        p = bisect_right(ends, start)   # jobs that end before this start
        best[i + 1] = max(best[i], best[p] + value)     # skip job i, or take it
    return best[-1]

jobs = [(1, 4, 3), (3, 5, 2), (0, 6, 8), (4, 7, 3),
        (3, 9, 6), (5, 9, 2), (6, 10, 4), (8, 11, 3)]
print(most_jobs(jobs))
print("best total value:", best_value(jobs))
[(1, 4, 3), (4, 7, 3), (8, 11, 3)]
best total value: 12

"Shortest job first" and "earliest start first" sound good for interval scheduling. Both are wrong. A job from 0 to 10 starts first but blocks everything. A short job from 4 to 6 can block two long jobs, 0 to 5 and 5 to 10. Only "earliest finish first" survives the exchange argument.

Huffman codes

Store the text "banana bandana" with as few bits as possible. ASCII uses 8 bits for each of the 14 characters: 112 bits. Only 5 different symbols appear, so a fixed 3-bit code needs 42 bits. Frequent letters should get short codes. The letter a appears 6 times, n 4 times, b twice, d and the space once each.

The code must be a prefix code, so we can decode without separators. A prefix code is a binary tree: each symbol is a leaf, left means 0 and right means 1. Huffman's algorithm, from 1952, builds the best tree greedily.

  1. Start with one small tree per symbol: a 6, n 4, b 2, d 1, space 1.
  2. Join the two lightest trees: space 1 and d 1 make a tree of weight 2.
  3. The lightest are now b 2 and that new tree 2. Join them into weight 4.
  4. Now n 4 and the tree of 4 are lightest. Join them into weight 8.
  5. Join a 6 and the tree of 8 into the root, weight 14. Done.
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BinaryHeap};

enum Node { Leaf(char), Join(usize, usize) } // Join holds two child ids

// Give each code word to its leaf: left adds '0', right adds '1'.
fn walk(nodes: &[Node], id: usize, code: String, out: &mut BTreeMap<char, String>) {
    match nodes[id] {
        Node::Leaf(ch) => { out.insert(ch, code); }
        Node::Join(a, b) => {
            walk(nodes, a, code.clone() + "0", out);
            walk(nodes, b, code + "1", out);
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let text = "banana bandana";
    let mut freq = BTreeMap::new();
    for ch in text.chars() { *freq.entry(ch).or_insert(0u32) += 1; }
    let (mut nodes, mut heap) = (Vec::new(), BinaryHeap::new());
    for (&ch, &f) in &freq {
        heap.push(Reverse((f, nodes.len()))); // (weight, node id), smallest first
        nodes.push(Node::Leaf(ch));
    }
    while heap.len() > 1 {
        let Reverse((fa, a)) = heap.pop().unwrap(); // the two lightest trees
        let Reverse((fb, b)) = heap.pop().unwrap();
        heap.push(Reverse((fa + fb, nodes.len())));
        nodes.push(Node::Join(a, b));
    }
    let mut codes = BTreeMap::new();
    walk(&nodes, nodes.len() - 1, String::new(), &mut codes);
    let bits: usize = text.chars().map(|ch| codes[&ch].len()).sum();
    println!("{codes:?}");
    println!("{bits} bits instead of {} with 8-bit ASCII", 8 * text.len());
}
import heapq
from collections import Counter
from itertools import count

def huffman(text: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Build a Huffman code. Each heap item is (weight, tie_breaker, tree)."""
    ids = count()                               # equal weights: older tree first
    heap = [(f, next(ids), ch) for ch, f in sorted(Counter(text).items())]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    while len(heap) > 1:
        fa, _, a = heapq.heappop(heap)          # the two lightest trees
        fb, _, b = heapq.heappop(heap)
        heapq.heappush(heap, (fa + fb, next(ids), (a, b)))
    codes = {}

    def walk(tree, code: str) -> None:          # left adds "0", right adds "1"
        if isinstance(tree, str):
            codes[tree] = code
        else:
            walk(tree[0], code + "0")
            walk(tree[1], code + "1")

    walk(heap[0][2], "")
    return codes

text = "banana bandana"
codes = huffman(text)
print(dict(sorted(codes.items())))
bits = sum(len(codes[ch]) for ch in text)
print(bits, "bits instead of", 8 * len(text), "with 8-bit ASCII")
{' ': "1110", 'a': "0", 'b': "110", 'd': "1111", 'n': "10"}
28 bits instead of 112 with 8-bit ASCII

Check the total: 6 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 4 = 28 bits. That is 2.0 bits per symbol. The entropy of these frequencies is about 1.985 bits per symbol, the lower limit for any symbol code. The information and coding theory chapter proves that limit.

Given symbol frequencies, Huffman's algorithm builds a prefix code with the smallest possible total length \sum_x f(x) \cdot \text{len}(x) among all prefix codes.

Proof

Step 1 (exchange). Let x and y be the two least frequent symbols. Some optimal tree has x and y as sibling leaves at the deepest level. Why? In an optimal tree, the deepest level has two sibling leaves. Swap x and y into those places. A rare symbol moves down and a more frequent one moves up, so the cost does not grow.

Step 2 (merge). Replace x and y by one new symbol z with f(z) = f(x) + f(y). A tree for the new alphabet becomes a tree for the old one if we hang x and y below z. This adds exactly f(x) + f(y) to the cost. So the old problem's best cost is the new problem's best cost plus f(x) + f(y).

Step 3 (induction). Huffman joins x and y first, then solves the smaller problem. By induction on the number of symbols, it solves the smaller problem optimally. By steps 1 and 2, adding back x and y gives an optimal tree for the whole problem.

Huffman coding is still everywhere. The DEFLATE format inside gzip, zlib and PNG uses Huffman codes for its symbols, as RFC 1951 describes. JPEG and many other formats use it too.

When greedy fails

Greedy feels natural, so it is easy to trust it too much. Here are classic traps.

Problems where a natural greedy rule gives a wrong answer
ProblemGreedy ruleGreedy answerBest answerCorrect method
Coins {1, 3, 4}, make 6biggest coin first4 + 1 + 1: 3 coins3 + 3: 2 coinsDP over amounts
0/1 knapsack (our documents)best score per tokenA, B, D: score 21B, C: score 22DP over capacity
Weighted intervals (our jobs)earliest finisha, d, h: value 9c, g: value 12DP with binary search
Shortest path, negative edgessettle nearest vertex (Dijkstra)can be wrongsee graph chapterBellman-Ford

For coins, DP is short. Let \text{best}[x] be the fewest coins for amount x. Then \text{best}[x] = 1 + \min_c \text{best}[x - c] over the coins c \le x. For amounts 0 to 6 the table is 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2. Greedy is fine for some coin systems, such as 1, 5, 10 and 25 cents. But you must prove it for each system.

How do I know if greedy will work?

Try to write the exchange argument. If you cannot swap a best answer's first choice for the greedy choice without loss, be careful. Then test the rule on small cases by brute force. A program that checks all answers for 5 to 8 items finds most counterexamples in seconds.

Is there a general theory?

Yes. Greedy works exactly on structures called matroids, for every choice of weights. The spanning trees of a graph form one. That is why Kruskal's algorithm is correct. Sets of non-overlapping intervals do not form a matroid. Huffman codes are not a problem of choosing a set at all. So both need their own exchange proofs.

Greedy is wrong but fast. Is it still useful?

Often, yes. For many hard problems, greedy gives a guaranteed approximation. Greedy set cover is within a log factor of the best, as the advanced algorithms chapter shows. In practice, greedy is also a good starting point for local search.

Exams often give a problem and ask "greedy or DP?". Give a small counterexample to reject greedy. To accept greedy, write the exchange argument. For DP, always state the subproblem in one sentence, the recurrence, the base cases, the fill order and the running time.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for dynamic programming and greedy algorithms
PatternPurposeModelNote
Memoize a recursionStop repeated work@cache on fib: 31 subproblemsHelps only if subproblems repeat.
Name the subproblem in one sentenceStart any DPbest[i][c]: first i items, c tokensA vague subproblem gives a wrong recurrence.
Last choice recurrenceWrite the DP ruleSkip item i or take itList every possible last choice.
Fill in topological orderBottom-up tablesShort chains before long chainsA cell must come after the cells it uses.
Walk back through the tableRecover the choices, not only the valueKnapsack: B and CKeep the full table, or store the choices.
Two-sequence tableCompare strings or listsLCS, edit distance, WERTwo rows are enough for the value.
Interval DPBest way to split a rangeMatrix chain, O(n^3)Loop over the length of the range first.
Pseudo-polynomial checkJudge a DP's real costKnapsack O(nW)Big W makes it slow: W is a value, not a size.
Exchange argumentProve a greedy ruleEarliest finish firstSwap the first choice of a best answer.
Join the two lightestOptimal prefix codeHuffman: 28 bits for "banana bandana"Break ties in a fixed way to get the same codes.
Brute-force small casesFind where greedy failsCoins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6One counterexample is enough to reject greedy.

Practice

Which two properties make dynamic programming useful?

  • Sorted input and small numbers
  • Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
  • A greedy choice and a heap

Optimal substructure makes the recurrence correct. Overlapping subproblems make saving answers pay off.

Why is the O(nW) knapsack algorithm not polynomial time?

  • Because it uses a table.
  • Because W is a number whose input size is only about \log_2 W bits.
  • Because it is recursive.

Doubling the number of bits of W can square its value. So the running time is exponential in the input length.

For unweighted interval scheduling, which greedy rule is always optimal?

  • Earliest start first
  • Shortest job first
  • Earliest finish first

The exchange argument works only for earliest finish: the greedy job never ends later than the job it replaces.

The edit distance between "monday" and "money" is ?.

With coins {1, 3, 4}, the fewest coins that make 6 is ?.

In a Huffman code for frequencies 6, 4, 2, 1, 1, the total length is ? bits.

  1. Write the recurrence for the number of ways to climb n stairs, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
    Answer

    W(n) = W(n-1) + W(n-2) with W(0) = 1 and W(1) = 1. The last move is 1 step or 2 steps. It is the Fibonacci recurrence, shifted by one.

  2. Compute the cost of A(BC) and (AB)C for A: 2 \times 10, B: 10 \times 3, C: 3 \times 8.
    Answer

    (AB)C = 2 \cdot 10 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 8 = 60 + 48 = 108. A(BC) = 10 \cdot 3 \cdot 8 + 2 \cdot 10 \cdot 8 = 240 + 160 = 400. So (AB)C is better.

  3. Find the LCS length of "DYNAMIC" and "PYTHONIC".
    Answer

    4, for example "YNIC". Y, N, I and C appear in this order in both words. No common subsequence of length 5 exists, which the table confirms.

  4. Show that "take the biggest coin first" is wrong for coins {1, 5, 6, 9} and amount 11.
    Answer

    Greedy takes 9, then 1 and 1: three coins. But 5 + 6 = 11 uses two coins.

  5. The text "aaaa bb" has frequencies a 4, b 2, space 1. Build the Huffman code and count the bits.
    Answer

    Join space 1 and b 2 into 3. Join 3 and a 4 into the root. One possible code: a = 0, b = 11, space = 10. Total: 4 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 2 = 10 bits. A fixed 2-bit code needs 14.

  6. Expert: a speech model hears 1,000 words of a 1,200-word reference. The word-level edit distance is 300. What is the WER? Can WER be above 100%?
    Answer

    WER = 300 / 1,200 = 25%. Yes, WER can pass 100%. The denominator is the reference length, but insertions have no limit. A model that adds many extra words can make more edits than the reference has words.

Key takeaways

  • Dynamic programming needs optimal substructure. It pays off when subproblems overlap.
  • Bellman's principle: after the first decision, the rest of an optimal plan is optimal for the new state.
  • Top-down adds a memo to a recursion. Bottom-up fills a table in a topological order.
  • Design a DP in five steps: subproblem, recurrence, base cases, order, answer and cost.
  • Knapsack is O(nW), which is pseudo-polynomial. LCS and edit distance are O(nm). Matrix chain is O(n^3).
  • A greedy algorithm needs a proof. The exchange argument is the usual one.
  • Huffman's greedy merges give an optimal prefix code. DEFLATE, gzip and PNG still use it.
  • Coins, 0/1 knapsack and weighted intervals show how greedy fails. One small counterexample is enough to reject it.

Sources

  • Jeff Erickson, Algorithms. Free textbook with chapters on dynamic programming and greedy algorithms.
  • Python functools. The cache and lru_cache decorators and cache_info.
  • RFC 1951: DEFLATE Compressed Data Format. How DEFLATE uses Huffman codes.
  • git diff documentation. The diff algorithms; Myers is the default.
  • Python difflib. SequenceMatcher and its note on minimal diffs.

Network flow and linear programming

How much data can a network carry from one server to another? How many cakes should a bakery bake for the most profit? Both questions are about the best use of limited resources. This chapter gives you two strong tools for them: network flow and linear programming.

  • Find a maximum flow with augmenting paths, and read a minimum cut from the result.
  • Explain why the max-flow min-cut theorem is true, and why integer capacities give integer flows.
  • Turn matching and shipping problems into flow problems.
  • Write a linear program, solve it with the simplex idea, and write its dual.
  • Say when a problem needs integer programming, and why that is much harder.

Flow networks

Look at the picture first. Data goes from a server s to a server t. On the way it passes four routers: a, b, c and d. Each link has a limit in gigabits per second. On each arrow you see two numbers: the amount we send, then the limit.

A flow network is a directed graph with two special nodes. The source s produces the flow. The sink t takes it in. Each edge e has a capacity c(e) \ge 0.

A flow gives each edge an amount f(e). It must obey two rules.

  • Capacity rule. 0 \le f(e) \le c(e). No pipe carries more than its limit.
  • Conservation rule. At every node except s and t, flow in equals flow out. Routers do not store or create data.

The value of a flow, written |f|, is the net amount that leaves s. In the picture, 7 + 8 = 15 leaves s. Check node b: 8 + 1 = 9 comes in, and 9 goes out to d. The rules hold.

The maximum flow problem asks for a flow with the largest value. Flow models more than data. It models water in pipes, cars on roads, goods on trucks and work given to people.

Do not forget conservation. A flow where node c gets 6 but sends out 7 is not a flow at all. When you check an answer, check every inner node, not only the edges.

Augmenting paths: the Ford-Fulkerson method

Here is a natural first idea. Find a path from s to t with room on every edge. Send as much as the smallest room allows. Repeat. This idea almost works. The slides show where it breaks, and the fix.

A small network

Edges s→a, s→b, a→b, a→t and b→t. Each has capacity 1. The best flow is clearly 2: one unit on s→a→t and one on s→b→t.

A bad first choice

We pick the path s→a→b→t and send 1 unit. Now s→a, a→b and b→t are full.

Stuck?

From s, only s→b has room. From b, the edge b→t is full. With forward edges only, we stop at a flow of 1. That is wrong.

Add back edges

For each unit on a→b, we add a back edge b→a with room 1. Using it means "take back the unit on a→b".

A new path

Now s→b→a→t is a path with room 1. We send 1 unit. The unit on a→b is cancelled.

Done

The flow is s→a→t plus s→b→t, value 2. No path from s has room left. This is the maximum.

The graph of rooms, with the back edges, is the residual graph. For an edge u→v with flow f and capacity c, it has two edges. The forward edge u→v has room c - f. The back edge v→u has room f.

A path from s to t in the residual graph is an augmenting path. Its smallest room is the bottleneck. We push the bottleneck amount along the path.

Start with zero flow. While the residual graph has a path from s to t, push its bottleneck along it. Then update the forward and back rooms. Stop when no path is left.

The method does not say which path to take. The code below uses breadth-first search. It always finds a path with the fewest edges. That choice has a name, Edmonds-Karp, and we study it later. The code keeps only the rooms, in a matrix r.

use std::collections::VecDeque;
const NAMES: &[u8] = b"sabcdt";

// r[u][v] is the residual capacity: how much more can go from u to v.
fn max_flow(r: &mut Vec<Vec<i64>>, s: usize, t: usize) -> i64 {
    let n = r.len();
    let mut total = 0;
    loop {
        let mut parent = vec![usize::MAX; n];  // BFS finds a shortest path
        parent[s] = s;
        let mut q = VecDeque::from([s]);
        while let Some(u) = q.pop_front() {
            for v in 0..n {
                if parent[v] == usize::MAX && r[u][v] > 0 {
                    parent[v] = u;
                    q.push_back(v);
                }
            }
        }
        if parent[t] == usize::MAX {           // no path: the flow is maximum
            let side: String = (0..n).filter(|&v| parent[v] != usize::MAX)
                .map(|v| NAMES[v] as char).collect();
            println!("source side of a min cut: {side}");
            return total;
        }
        let mut path = vec![t];
        while path[path.len() - 1] != s { path.push(parent[path[path.len() - 1]]); }
        path.reverse();
        let push = path.windows(2).map(|w| r[w[0]][w[1]]).min().unwrap();
        for w in path.windows(2) {
            r[w[0]][w[1]] -= push;
            r[w[1]][w[0]] += push;              // back edge: we may undo later
        }
        total += push;
        let p: String = path.iter().map(|&x| NAMES[x] as char).collect();
        println!("path {p} adds {push}");
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut r = vec![vec![0i64; 6]; 6];
    for (u, v, c) in [(0, 1, 10), (0, 2, 8), (1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 6),
                      (2, 4, 9), (3, 4, 2), (3, 5, 7), (4, 5, 10)] {
        r[u][v] = c;
    }
    println!("max flow = {}", max_flow(&mut r, 0, 5));
}
from collections import deque
NAMES = "sabcdt"

# r[u][v] is the residual capacity: how much more can go from u to v.
def max_flow(r, s, t):
    n = len(r)
    total = 0
    while True:
        parent = [-1] * n               # BFS finds a shortest path
        parent[s] = s
        q = deque([s])
        while q:
            u = q.popleft()
            for v in range(n):
                if parent[v] == -1 and r[u][v] > 0:
                    parent[v] = u
                    q.append(v)
        if parent[t] == -1:             # no path: the flow is maximum
            side = "".join(NAMES[v] for v in range(n) if parent[v] != -1)
            print("source side of a min cut:", side)
            return total
        path = [t]
        while path[-1] != s:
            path.append(parent[path[-1]])
        path.reverse()
        push = min(r[u][v] for u, v in zip(path, path[1:]))
        for u, v in zip(path, path[1:]):
            r[u][v] -= push
            r[v][u] += push             # back edge: we may undo later
        total += push
        print("path", "".join(NAMES[x] for x in path), "adds", push)

r = [[0] * 6 for _ in range(6)]
for u, v, c in [(0, 1, 10), (0, 2, 8), (1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 6),
                (2, 4, 9), (3, 4, 2), (3, 5, 7), (4, 5, 10)]:
    r[u][v] = c
print("max flow =", max_flow(r, 0, 5))
path sact adds 6
path sbdt adds 8
path sabdt adds 1
source side of a min cut: sab
max flow = 15

Three paths add 6, 8 and 1. The total is 15, as in the picture. The last search from s reaches only s, a and b. Keep that set in mind. It is the key to the next section.

Do not leave out the back edges. Without them the method can stop too early, as in the slides. Also, do not use floating-point capacities in this simple method. With irrational capacities the method can loop forever. It may even move towards a wrong value. Erickson's notes give such an example.

Cuts and the max-flow min-cut theorem

In the picture, draw the dashed line. On the left are s, a and b. On the right are c, d and t. Every unit from s to t must cross this line. Only two edges cross it from left to right: a→c with capacity 6 and b→d with capacity 9. So no flow can ever be bigger than 6 + 9 = 15.

An s-t cut splits the nodes into two sets. The set S holds s. The set T holds t. The capacity of the cut is the sum of capacities of edges from S to T. Edges from T back to S do not count.

For any flow f and any s-t cut (S, T): |f| = f(S \to T) - f(T \to S) \le c(S, T).

Proof

Add up "flow out minus flow in" over all nodes of S. For s this gives |f|. For the other nodes of S it gives 0, by conservation. An edge inside S is counted once as out and once as in, so it cancels. What is left is the flow on edges leaving S minus the flow on edges entering S. The first part is at most c(S,T). The second part is at least 0.

So every cut gives an upper limit. The smallest such limit is the minimum cut. The great surprise is that the limit is always reached.

In every flow network, the value of a maximum flow equals the capacity of a minimum s-t cut. Also, these three facts about a flow f are equal:

  1. f is a maximum flow.
  2. The residual graph has no augmenting path.
  3. |f| = c(S, T) for some cut (S, T).
Proof

(1) gives (2): if an augmenting path existed, we could push more. (3) gives (1): by the lemma, no flow beats c(S,T), and f reaches it. The real work is (2) gives (3). Let S be the nodes that s can reach in the residual graph. t is not in S, because there is no augmenting path. Take an edge u→v from S to T. It must be full, or v would be reachable. Take an edge v→u from T to S. It must carry 0, or its back edge u→v would make v reachable. So |f| = c(S,T) - 0.

In simple words: when you are stuck, the stuck place is a bottleneck. Its size is exactly the flow you have. In our run the last search reached {s, a, b}. The cut from {s, a, b} has capacity 15, and the flow is 15. Both are proved best at the same time.

Ford and Fulkerson published this in 1956. Elias, Feinstein and Shannon proved it the same year, for communication networks. Ford and Fulkerson later wrote that T. E. Harris gave them the question in 1955.

A minimum cut is often the answer you really want. In image segmentation, pixels are nodes. The cheapest cut splits the object from the background. In network design, the minimum cut is the weakest part of your network.

Do not count the edges that go back from T to S. In our picture, no edge goes back, but in other networks they do. The cut capacity counts only edges from the s side to the t side.

Integer flows, Edmonds-Karp and Dinic

Look again at the run. The capacities were whole numbers. Every bottleneck was a whole number, so every flow stayed a whole number. This simple fact is very useful.

If every capacity is an integer, then there is a maximum flow in which every edge carries an integer. The Ford-Fulkerson method finds one.

Proof

Use induction on the steps. At the start all flows are 0. If all flows and capacities are integers, all rooms are integers. So the bottleneck is an integer, and after the push all flows are still integers. Each push adds at least 1 to the value. The value cannot pass the cut capacity, so the method stops. When it stops, the flow is maximum by the theorem.

Integrality lets us count things with flow. "One unit of flow" can mean "one person" or "one task". The answer will never say "half a person".

How fast is the method? Each search costs O(E), where E is the number of edges. With integer capacities there are at most |f^*| pushes, so the time is O(E\,|f^*|). That can be very slow. Take edges of capacity X = 1{,}000{,}000 around a middle edge of capacity 1. Bad path choices use the middle edge every time, so the method needs two million pushes.

Edmonds-Karp fixes this. It always pushes along a shortest path, found by breadth-first search. Yefim Dinitz, whose name is often spelled Dinic, published it in 1970. Edmonds and Karp published it on their own in 1972. The time is O(V E^2), with V nodes. It does not depend on the capacities at all.

Why is it O(V E^2)?

Two facts. First, the distance from s to every node never goes down after a push. Second, each push fills at least one edge on the path, the critical edge. One edge can be critical only about V/2 times, because its distance must grow by 2 between two times. So there are O(VE) pushes. Each costs O(E) for the search.

Dinic's algorithm goes one step further. It works in phases.

  1. Run breadth-first search from s. Give each node its distance, or level.
  2. Keep only residual edges that go from level k to level k + 1. This is the level graph.
  3. Push flow with depth-first search until every s-t path in the level graph has a full edge. This is a blocking flow.
  4. Repeat. The distance from s to t grows in every phase, so there are at most V phases.

Dinic runs in O(V^2 E). On bipartite matching networks, where all capacities are 1, it runs in O(E \sqrt{V}). SciPy's maximum_flow uses Dinic by default and also offers Edmonds-Karp.

  1. 1956 Ford and Fulkerson. Augmenting paths and the max-flow min-cut theorem.
  2. 1970 Dinitz. Shortest paths and blocking flows.
  3. 1972 Edmonds and Karp. Shortest augmenting paths give O(VE^2).
  4. 1986 Goldberg and Tarjan. Push-relabel, a different method that moves extra flow node by node.
  5. 2013 Orlin. Maximum flow in O(VE) time.
  6. 2022 Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg and Sachdeva. Almost-linear time, E^{1+o(1)}, even for min-cost flow.

O(E\,|f^*|) is not polynomial time. The capacity X takes only about \log_2 X bits to write. A running time that grows with X itself grows exponentially in the input size. Always choose paths with a rule, such as the shortest path.

Matching by flow

Four people and four tasks. Ana can do the API or the database. Ben can do only the API. Cho can do the database or the UI. Dev can do the UI or the ML model. Can every person get a different task?

A bipartite graph has two groups of nodes, here people and tasks. A matching is a set of edges with no shared node. Each person gets at most one task, and each task gets at most one person.

The model has four parts. Add a source s with an edge to each person. Add an edge from each person to each task they can do. Add an edge from each task to a sink t. Give every edge capacity 1. By the integrality theorem, a maximum flow uses only 0 and 1. The edges with flow 1 in the middle form a maximum matching.

On unit capacities, an augmenting path has a simple meaning. Give a person a free task. If no task is free, move another person to a different task. The code below is that idea, with depth-first search. It is the Ford-Fulkerson method written for matching.

const PEOPLE: [&str; 4] = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cho", "Dev"];
const TASKS: [&str; 4] = ["api", "db", "ui", "ml"];

// Look for an augmenting path that starts at person p.
fn try_person(p: usize, can: &[Vec<usize>], seen: &mut [bool], owner: &mut [Option<usize>]) -> bool {
    for &task in &can[p] {
        if seen[task] { continue; }
        seen[task] = true;
        // The task is free, or its owner can move to another task.
        let free = match owner[task] {
            None => true,
            Some(q) => try_person(q, can, seen, owner),
        };
        if free {
            owner[task] = Some(p);
            return true;
        }
    }
    false
}

fn main() {
    let can = vec![vec![0, 1], vec![0], vec![1, 2], vec![2, 3]]; // who can do which task
    let mut owner = vec![None; TASKS.len()];
    for p in 0..PEOPLE.len() {
        let mut seen = vec![false; TASKS.len()];
        let found = try_person(p, &can, &mut seen, &mut owner);
        println!("{}: {}", PEOPLE[p], if found { "matched" } else { "no task" });
    }
    for (task, p) in owner.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("{} -> {}", TASKS[task], PEOPLE[p.unwrap()]);
    }
}
PEOPLE = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cho", "Dev"]
TASKS = ["api", "db", "ui", "ml"]
CAN = {0: [0, 1], 1: [0], 2: [1, 2], 3: [2, 3]}   # who can do which task

def try_person(p, seen, owner):
    # Look for an augmenting path that starts at person p.
    for task in CAN[p]:
        if task in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(task)
        # The task is free, or its owner can move to another task.
        if owner[task] is None or try_person(owner[task], seen, owner):
            owner[task] = p
            return True
    return False

owner = [None] * len(TASKS)
for p in range(len(PEOPLE)):
    found = try_person(p, set(), owner)
    print(f"{PEOPLE[p]}: {'matched' if found else 'no task'}")
for task, p in enumerate(owner):
    print(f"{TASKS[task]} -> {PEOPLE[p]}")
Ana: matched
Ben: matched
Cho: matched
Dev: matched
api -> Ben
db -> Ana
ui -> Cho
ml -> Dev

Ana took the API first. Then Ben needed the API, so the path moved Ana to the database. This is a back edge in action. The method costs O(VE). The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm (1973) finds many short paths at once and costs O(E\sqrt{V}). SciPy offers it as maximum_bipartite_matching.

A vertex cover is a set of nodes that touches every edge. Every matching edge needs its own cover node, so a matching is never larger than a cover. In bipartite graphs, the two are equal.

In a bipartite graph, the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover.

Proof idea

Use the flow model, but give the middle edges a huge capacity. A finite minimum cut then never cuts a middle edge. It cuts some s→person edges and some task→t edges. The people on the t side and the tasks on the s side form a vertex cover of the same size. By the max-flow min-cut theorem, that size equals the maximum matching.

Matching appears in AI systems too. The DETR object detector (2020) must pair each predicted box with a true box during training. It solves this assignment problem with the Hungarian method. In Python you can call scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment.

Do not use greedy matching and stop. "Give each person the first free task" can block later people. Ben would get nothing if Ana kept the API. Only an augmenting path search proves that the matching is maximum.

The min-cost flow idea

A shop must send 4 boxes from s to t. Each edge has a capacity and a cost per box. The cheap route is small. The big route is expensive. How do we send all 4 boxes at the lowest total cost?

The shipping network
EdgeCapacityCost per box
s→a31
s→b34
a→t22
a→b21
b→t41

In min-cost flow, each edge also has a cost per unit. We must send a fixed amount, and we want the smallest total cost. One classic method is successive shortest paths. It is Ford-Fulkerson where "shortest" means "cheapest".

  1. The cheapest path is s→a→t with cost 1 + 2 = 3. Its bottleneck is 2. Send 2 boxes. Cost so far: 6.
  2. Now a→t is full. The cheapest path is s→a→b→t with cost 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. s→a has 1 room left. Send 1 box. Cost so far: 9.
  3. Now s→a is full. The cheapest path is s→b→t with cost 4 + 1 = 5. Send the last box. Total cost: 14.

A back edge gets the cost -c. Pushing along it gives the money back, because it undoes a unit. So the residual graph can have negative edges. The search needs Bellman-Ford, or Dijkstra with node prices called potentials. See Graph algorithms. Here is a library check of our answer.

import networkx as nx

G = nx.DiGraph()
G.add_node("s", demand=-4)          # s sends 4 units
G.add_node("t", demand=4)           # t receives 4 units
for u, v, cap, cost in [("s", "a", 3, 1), ("s", "b", 3, 4), ("a", "t", 2, 2),
                        ("a", "b", 2, 1), ("b", "t", 4, 1)]:
    G.add_edge(u, v, capacity=cap, weight=cost)

flow = nx.min_cost_flow(G)
for u in flow:
    for v, f in flow[u].items():
        if f:
            print(f"{u}->{v}: {f}")
print("total cost:", nx.cost_of_flow(G, flow))
s->a: 3
s->b: 1
a->t: 2
a->b: 1
b->t: 2
total cost: 14

I ran this with networkx 3.7. A flow is a min-cost flow exactly when its residual graph has no negative cycle. If one exists, sending flow around it saves money. Min-cost flow includes maximum flow, shortest paths and the assignment problem as special cases.

Do not run plain Dijkstra on the residual graph. Back edges have negative costs, and Dijkstra is wrong with negative weights. Use Bellman-Ford, or keep potentials so that all reduced costs stay non-negative.

Linear programs and the simplex idea

A small bakery bakes trays of bread and trays of cake. A bread tray needs 1 kg of flour and 1 oven hour. A cake tray needs 1 kg of flour and 3 oven hours. There are 4 kg of flour and 6 oven hours. Bread earns 3 euros a tray. Cake earns 5 euros a tray. What should it bake?

Let x be the bread trays and y the cake trays. Then the problem is:

\begin{aligned} \text{maximise } & 3x + 5y \\ \text{subject to } & x + y \le 4 \quad \text{(flour)} \\ & x + 3y \le 6 \quad \text{(oven)} \\ & x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0 \end{aligned}

This is a linear program, or LP. It has decision variables, here x and y. It has a linear objective and linear constraints. A point that obeys all the constraints is feasible.

The feasible points form a shape with straight sides, a polyhedron. Its corners are its vertices. Here they are (0, 0), (4, 0), (3, 1) and (0, 2). Their profits are 0, 12, 14 and 10. The best is 14 at (3, 1). Move the profit line up. The last feasible point it touches is always a corner, or a whole side.

If an LP has an optimal solution and its region has a vertex, then some vertex is optimal.

The simplex method, by George Dantzig in 1947, uses this fact. It starts at a vertex. It moves along an edge of the shape to a better neighbour vertex. It stops when no neighbour is better. Because the region is convex, a local best is the global best.

In the computer, one move is a pivot. We add a slack variable to each constraint, such as spare flour. A pivot picks a variable with a negative cost to enter. The ratio test picks which variable leaves, so no value goes below zero.

const NAMES: [&str; 4] = ["bread", "cake", "spare flour", "spare oven"];

// Maximise c.x with A x <= b, x >= 0, and b >= 0 (so x = 0 is a start).
fn simplex(c: &[f64], a: &[Vec<f64>], b: &[f64]) -> (Vec<f64>, f64, Vec<f64>) {
    let (m, n) = (a.len(), c.len());
    // One row per constraint: [A | slack columns | b]. Last row: objective.
    let mut t: Vec<Vec<f64>> = (0..m).map(|i| {
        let mut row = a[i].clone();
        row.extend((0..m).map(|j| if i == j { 1.0 } else { 0.0 }));
        row.push(b[i]);
        row
    }).collect();
    let mut obj: Vec<f64> = c.iter().map(|v| -v).collect();
    obj.extend(vec![0.0; m + 1]);
    t.push(obj);
    let mut basis: Vec<usize> = (n..n + m).collect(); // the slacks start in the basis
    loop {
        let col = (0..n + m).min_by(|&i, &j| t[m][i].total_cmp(&t[m][j])).unwrap();
        if t[m][col] >= -1e-9 { break; }              // no negative cost left: optimal
        let row = (0..m).filter(|&i| t[i][col] > 1e-9)  // ratio test
            .min_by(|&i, &j| (t[i][n + m] / t[i][col]).total_cmp(&(t[j][n + m] / t[j][col])))
            .expect("unbounded");
        println!("pivot: {} enters, {} leaves", NAMES[col], NAMES[basis[row]]);
        let p = t[row][col];
        for v in t[row].iter_mut() { *v /= p; }
        let pivot_row = t[row].clone();
        for i in (0..=m).filter(|&i| i != row) {
            let f = t[i][col];
            for (v, r) in t[i].iter_mut().zip(&pivot_row) { *v -= f * r; }
        }
        basis[row] = col;
    }
    let mut x = vec![0.0; n + m];
    for (i, &j) in basis.iter().enumerate() { x[j] = t[i][n + m]; }
    (x[..n].to_vec(), t[m][n + m], t[m][n..n + m].to_vec()) // point, value, dual prices
}

fn main() {
    let (x, value, y) = simplex(&[3.0, 5.0], &[vec![1.0, 1.0], vec![1.0, 3.0]], &[4.0, 6.0]);
    println!("bread = {:.2}, cake = {:.2}, profit = {:.2}", x[0], x[1], value);
    println!("price of flour = {:.2}, price of oven hour = {:.2}", y[0], y[1]);
}
NAMES = ["bread", "cake", "spare flour", "spare oven"]

# Maximise c.x with A x <= b, x >= 0, and b >= 0 (so x = 0 is a start).
def simplex(c, A, b):
    m, n = len(A), len(c)
    # One row per constraint: [A | slack columns | b]. Last row: objective.
    T = [A[i] + [1.0 if j == i else 0.0 for j in range(m)] + [b[i]] for i in range(m)]
    T.append([-v for v in c] + [0.0] * (m + 1))
    basis = [n + i for i in range(m)]           # the slacks start in the basis
    while True:
        col = min(range(n + m), key=lambda j: T[m][j])
        if T[m][col] >= -1e-9:                  # no negative cost left: optimal
            break
        rows = [i for i in range(m) if T[i][col] > 1e-9]
        if not rows:
            raise ValueError("unbounded")
        row = min(rows, key=lambda i: T[i][-1] / T[i][col])   # ratio test
        print(f"pivot: {NAMES[col]} enters, {NAMES[basis[row]]} leaves")
        p = T[row][col]
        T[row] = [v / p for v in T[row]]
        for i in range(m + 1):
            if i != row:
                f = T[i][col]
                T[i] = [a - f * r for a, r in zip(T[i], T[row])]
        basis[row] = col
    x = [0.0] * (n + m)
    for i, j in enumerate(basis):
        x[j] = T[i][-1]
    return x[:n], T[m][-1], T[m][n:n + m]       # point, value, dual prices

x, value, y = simplex([3.0, 5.0], [[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]], [4.0, 6.0])
print(f"bread = {x[0]:.2f}, cake = {x[1]:.2f}, profit = {value:.2f}")
print(f"price of flour = {y[0]:.2f}, price of oven hour = {y[1]:.2f}")
pivot: cake enters, spare oven leaves
pivot: bread enters, spare flour leaves
bread = 3.00, cake = 1.00, profit = 14.00
price of flour = 2.00, price of oven hour = 1.00

The walk went (0, 0) → (0, 2) → (3, 1). Each pivot is one move to a neighbour corner. The last line prints two "prices". They come from the next section, duality.

Is simplex fast? In practice, yes. In theory, not always. Klee and Minty (1972) built LPs where Dantzig's rule visits exponentially many corners. Khachiyan's ellipsoid method (1979) was the first polynomial-time method for LP, but it is slow in practice. Karmarkar's interior-point method (1984) is polynomial and fast. Spielman and Teng's smoothed analysis helps explain why simplex is quick on real inputs.

Simplex can cycle when many constraints meet at one corner. Bland's rule stops this. Among the candidates to enter or leave, always pick the one with the smallest index. Also, our small code needs b \ge 0, so that (0, 0) is a start. Real solvers first run a "phase one" to find a feasible start, or report that none exists.

Duality

A miller wants to buy all the bakery's flour and oven hours. She offers u euros per kg of flour and v euros per oven hour. The bakery sells only if the offer beats baking. One bread tray uses 1 kg and 1 hour, and earns 3. So we need u + v \ge 3. One cake tray needs u + 3v \ge 5. The miller wants to pay as little as possible: 4u + 6v.

\begin{aligned} \text{minimise } & 4u + 6v \\ \text{subject to } & u + v \ge 3, \quad u + 3v \ge 5, \quad u, v \ge 0 \end{aligned}

This is the dual of the bakery LP. The bakery LP is the primal. In general, the primal "maximise c^{\top}x with Ax \le b, x \ge 0" has the dual "minimise b^{\top}y with A^{\top}y \ge c, y \ge 0". Each primal constraint gets one dual variable. Each primal variable gets one dual constraint.

If x is feasible for the primal and y is feasible for the dual, then c^{\top}x \le b^{\top}y.

Proof

c^{\top}x \le (A^{\top}y)^{\top}x = y^{\top}(Ax) \le y^{\top}b. The first step uses A^{\top}y \ge c and x \ge 0. The last step uses Ax \le b and y \ge 0.

So every miller offer is an upper limit on the bakery's profit. The offer u = 3, v = 3 costs 30, so profit is at most 30. Better offers give tighter limits. The best limit meets the profit exactly.

If the primal LP has an optimal solution x^*, then the dual LP also has an optimal solution y^*, and c^{\top}x^* = b^{\top}y^*.

Proof idea

Run simplex until it stops. In the final table, the objective row has no negative entry. Read the entries under the slack columns as y^*. "No negative entry" says exactly that y^* is dual feasible. The table also shows that b^{\top}y^* equals the primal value. Weak duality then makes both optimal. A second proof uses Farkas' lemma, a fact about separating a point from a convex set.

Check it on the bakery. Our simplex code printed u = 2, v = 1. The dual cost is 4 \cdot 2 + 6 \cdot 1 = 14. The best profit was also 14. These dual values are shadow prices. One more kg of flour would raise the profit by about 2 euros. One more oven hour would raise it by about 1 euro.

Optimal x^* and y^* fit together. If a constraint has spare room, its dual price is 0. If a dual price is positive, its constraint is tight. The same holds the other way round, for primal variables and dual constraints.

A library solver gives the same numbers. SciPy's linprog always minimises, so we give it -3x - 5y. I ran this with SciPy 1.18.1.

from scipy.optimize import linprog

# linprog minimises, so we minimise -3x - 5y to maximise 3x + 5y.
primal = linprog(c=[-3, -5], A_ub=[[1, 1], [1, 3]], b_ub=[4, 6])
print("primal:", primal.x, -primal.fun)
print("marginals:", primal.ineqlin.marginals)   # minus the dual prices

# The dual: minimise 4u + 6v with u + v >= 3 and u + 3v >= 5.
# Turn each >= into <= by multiplying by -1.
dual = linprog(c=[4, 6], A_ub=[[-1, -1], [-1, -3]], b_ub=[-3, -5])
print("dual:  ", dual.x, dual.fun)
primal: [3. 1.] 14.0
marginals: [-2. -1.]
dual:   [2. 1.] 14.0

Duality also explains the flow section. Write maximum flow as an LP. Its dual is a "fractional cut" LP, and it has an optimal solution that is a real cut. So the max-flow min-cut theorem is one case of strong duality.

The four cases of an LP and its dual
PrimalDual
has an optimumhas an optimum with the same value
unbounded (profit grows without end)infeasible (no point at all)
infeasibleunbounded, or also infeasible

Watch the signs of solver output. SciPy reports marginals for the minimisation it solved, so the bakery prices come out as −2 and −1. Also, a shadow price holds only for small changes. Add 10 kg of flour and the best corner changes, and so does the price.

Modelling, and why integer programming is hard

A good model is half the work. Many real problems become flows or LPs after a few standard tricks.

Common modelling tricks
Problem shapeTrick
many sources or many sinksadd a super source with edges to all sources, and a super sink
a node has a limitsplit it into "in" and "out" nodes, joined by an edge with that limit
an undirected linkuse two arcs, one in each direction
how many paths share no edge?capacity 1 on every edge, then max flow (Menger's theorem)
choose projects that need toolsmin cut in a project-and-tool network (project selection)
a "≥" constraint in an LPmultiply both sides by −1 to get "≤"
minimise the largest of several costsadd a new variable z, require z \ge each cost, and minimise z

Now change the bakery a little. You can only bake whole trays. The variables must be integers. This is an integer program, or IP. It sounds like a small change. It is a huge one.

from scipy.optimize import linprog

c = [-5, -8]                       # maximise 5x + 8y
A = [[1, 1], [5, 9]]
b = [6, 45]
lp = linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b)                     # x, y may be fractions
ip = linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b, integrality=[1, 1]) # x, y must be whole
print("LP relaxation:", lp.x, -lp.fun)
print("integer program:", [int(round(v)) for v in ip.x], -ip.fun)
LP relaxation: [2.25 3.75] 41.25
integer program: [0, 5] 40.0

Look at the two answers. The LP gives (2.25, 3.75). Rounding to (2, 4) breaks the second constraint: 5 \cdot 2 + 9 \cdot 4 = 46. Rounding down to (2, 3) earns only 34. The true best is (0, 5), far from the LP point. Dropping the integer rule gives the LP relaxation. It is a limit, not an answer.

Deciding whether a 0-1 integer program has a feasible point is NP-complete. It is one of Karp's 21 NP-complete problems (1972). So no polynomial-time algorithm is known for IP, and none exists unless P = NP.

See Complexity theory for what NP-complete means. In practice, IP solvers still solve large models. They use branch and bound. Solve the LP relaxation. If x = 2.25, make two cases: x \le 2 and x \ge 3. The LP value of a case limits everything inside it. Skip a case whose limit is worse than the best whole answer so far. Cutting planes make the relaxation tighter.

Why are flows easy, then? Their constraint matrices are totally unimodular. For such a matrix and integer limits, every vertex of the LP is an integer point. So the LP relaxation of a flow or a bipartite matching is already integral. This is the integrality theorem again, seen through LP.

A common exam task says: "model this as a flow". Name the nodes, the edges, the capacities, s and t. Then say what one unit of flow means. Finally say which theorem makes the answer correct, usually integrality and max-flow min-cut.

Do not solve an IP by rounding its LP. The rounded point may be infeasible, or far from the best. Use an IP solver, such as linprog with integrality, which calls HiGHS.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for flows and linear programs
PatternPurposeModelNote
Residual graph with back edgesLet later paths undo earlier choicesr[u][v] -= push; r[v][u] += push;Without back edges the method stops too early.
Push the bottleneckGrow the flow along one pathpath s-a-b-d-t, rooms 4, 3, 1, 2: push 1At least one edge on the path becomes full.
Shortest augmenting pathPolynomial timeBFS in Edmonds-Karp, O(VE^2)Any-path Ford-Fulkerson can take O(E\,|f^*|).
Reachable set gives the cutProve the flow is maximumlast BFS reaches {s, a, b}: cut 6 + 9 = 15Count only edges from the s side to the t side.
Unit capacities for countingModel matching and disjoint pathss → person → task → t, all capacity 1Integrality makes every flow 0 or 1.
Cheapest path firstMin-cost flowsuccessive shortest paths, cost 14Back edges have negative cost: no plain Dijkstra.
Variables, objective, constraintsWrite an LPmax 3x + 5y, x + y \le 4, x + 3y \le 6Check that every part is linear.
Best answer at a cornerSolve small LPs by handcorners (0,0), (4,0), (3,1), (0,2)A whole side can be optimal too.
One dual variable per constraintWrite the dualmin 4u + 6v, u + v \ge 3, u + 3v \ge 5Max with ≤ becomes min with ≥.
Dual values as pricesKnow what a resource is worthflour 2 euros, oven hour 1 euroValid only for small changes.
Relax, then branchSolve integer programsLP gives 2.25: try x \le 2 and x \ge 3Never just round the LP answer.

Practice

In the residual graph, an edge u→v carries 3 units and has capacity 5. Which rooms does the residual graph show?

  • u→v with room 5 only
  • u→v with room 2 and v→u with room 3
  • u→v with room 3 and v→u with room 2

The forward room is 5 − 3 = 2. The back edge lets us undo the 3 units that already flow.

Ford-Fulkerson stops. The last search from s reaches the set S. What is true?

  • Some edge from S to T still has room.
  • Every edge from S to T is full, and the flow equals the capacity of this cut.
  • The flow could still grow if we searched again from t.

This is the heart of the max-flow min-cut proof. Full edges out and empty edges in make the flow equal the cut.

Which augmenting path does Edmonds-Karp choose?

  • The path with the largest bottleneck
  • A path with the fewest edges, found by BFS
  • Any path found by DFS

Shortest paths make the distances grow, which bounds the number of pushes by O(VE).

An LP is unbounded. What do you know about its dual?

  • It is also unbounded.
  • It has an optimum with value 0.
  • It is infeasible.

By weak duality, any dual feasible point would be an upper limit on the primal. An unbounded primal has no such limit.

If every capacity is an integer, some maximum flow uses only ? values on its edges.

The value of every flow is at most the capacity of every s-t ?.

The dual of a maximisation LP with ≤ constraints is a ? LP with ≥ constraints.

  1. Network: s→a 4, s→b 2, a→b 3, a→t 1, b→t 5. Find the maximum flow and a minimum cut.
    Answer

    Push 1 on s→a→t, 2 on s→b→t and 3 on s→a→b→t. The value is 6. Now s→a (4) and s→b (2) are full, so the last search reaches only s. The cut from {s} has capacity 4 + 2 = 6. Flow equals cut, so both are optimal.

  2. Three reviewers must read five papers. Each paper needs two reviewers. Each reviewer reads at most four papers. Each reviewer has a list of papers they may read. Model this as a flow.
    Answer

    Edges s→reviewer with capacity 4. Edges reviewer→paper with capacity 1, only when allowed. Edges paper→t with capacity 2. A valid plan exists exactly when the maximum flow is 5 × 2 = 10. By integrality the flow is 0 or 1 on each middle edge, so it reads as a plan.

  3. Write the dual of: maximise 2x + 3y with x + 2y \le 8, 3x + y \le 9, x, y \ge 0.
    Answer

    Minimise 8u + 9v with u + 3v \ge 2, 2u + v \ge 3, u, v \ge 0. The primal optimum is at x = 2, y = 3 with value 13. The dual optimum is u = 1.4, v = 0.2 with value 11.2 + 1.8 = 13. They are equal, as strong duality says.

  4. A person says: "IP is easy. Solve the LP and round." Give a reply with numbers.
    Answer

    Maximise 5x + 8y with x + y \le 6 and 5x + 9y \le 45. The LP point is (2.25, 3.75). Rounding to (2, 4) is infeasible. Rounding down gives 34. The real best is (0, 5) with 40. Also, 0-1 IP is NP-complete, so no fast exact method is known.

  5. Expert. Why is the running time O(E\,|f^*|) of plain Ford-Fulkerson not polynomial?
    Answer

    Input size counts bits. A capacity X uses about \log_2 X bits. The time grows with X, which is exponential in \log_2 X. On the network with four big edges X and a middle edge 1, bad choices need 2X pushes.

  6. Expert. A company has projects with profits and tools with costs. Each project needs some tools. How do you choose the most profitable set with one min cut?
    Answer

    Edges s→project with capacity equal to its profit. Edges tool→t with capacity equal to its cost. Edges project→tool with infinite capacity when the project needs the tool. Take a minimum cut. Choose the projects and tools on the s side. The best net profit is the sum of all profits minus the cut capacity. The infinite edges make sure a chosen project never misses a tool.

Key takeaways

  • A flow obeys capacities and conservation. Its value is the net flow out of the source.
  • Augmenting paths in the residual graph grow the flow. Back edges let later paths undo earlier ones.
  • Max-flow min-cut: the largest flow equals the smallest cut. The last search shows the cut.
  • Integer capacities give an integer maximum flow, so flows can count people, tasks and paths.
  • Edmonds-Karp takes shortest paths for O(VE^2). Dinic uses level graphs and blocking flows for O(V^2E).
  • An LP has a linear objective and linear constraints. Its optimum sits at a corner, and simplex walks between corners.
  • Every LP has a dual. Weak duality gives limits. Strong duality says the best values are equal. Dual values are prices.
  • Integer programming is NP-hard. Use branch and bound, and never trust a rounded LP answer.

Sources

  • Jeff Erickson, Algorithms: Maximum Flows and Minimum Cuts (Illinois CS 473 notes). Residual graphs, the theorem and its proof, integrality, slow and looping examples.
  • Maximum flow problem. Overview of algorithms and their running times, from 1956 to the 2022 almost-linear result.
  • Max-flow min-cut theorem. History, the LP view of the theorem, and applications such as project selection.
  • SciPy: scipy.optimize.linprog. The HiGHS solver, the integrality option and the dual marginals.
  • SciPy: scipy.sparse.csgraph.maximum_flow. Dinic and Edmonds-Karp in a library, and matching by flow.
  • Dual linear program. Weak and strong duality, the four cases, and shadow prices.

Randomised, approximate, streaming and string algorithms

Some problems are too hard, too big or too fast for a perfect, exact algorithm. Then we give up one small thing to win a lot. We accept a tiny chance of error, an answer close to the best, or a summary instead of all the data. This chapter shows when that trade is safe, and how to prove it.

  • Tell Las Vegas from Monte Carlo algorithms, and make an error chance as small as you want.
  • Prove that universal hashing gives short chains, and find a minimum cut with Karger's algorithm.
  • Use and prove approximation algorithms for vertex cover, set cover and metric TSP.
  • Measure online algorithms with the competitive ratio, and prove that LRU paging is k-competitive.
  • Build streaming sketches, fast string search and simple parallel algorithms, and give their costs.

Randomness as a tool: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo

Someone says: "I multiplied two big matrices, A times B, and got C." Checking by doing the product again costs O(n^3). Here is a much cheaper check. Pick a random vector r of 0s and 1s. Compare A(Br) with Cr. Each side is two matrix-vector products, so it costs only O(n^2).

  1. A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{pmatrix}. The claim is C = \begin{pmatrix} 19 & 22 \\ 43 & 51 \end{pmatrix}. The true last entry is 50, so the claim is wrong.
  2. Try r = (1, 1). Br = (11, 15), so A(Br) = (41, 93). But Cr = (41, 94). They differ, so the check says "wrong". Caught.
  3. Try r = (1, 0). A(Br) = (19, 43) and Cr = (19, 43). They agree. This r misses the error.
  4. Of the four 0/1 vectors, two catch the error. That matches the theory: one random try catches a wrong C with chance at least 1/2.

This is Freivalds' algorithm. It is a Monte Carlo algorithm. Its time is fixed, but it can be wrong. When it says "wrong", it is surely right. When it says "correct", it may be fooled, with chance at most 1/2.

Randomised quicksort is different. It always sorts correctly. Only its running time is random. This is a Las Vegas algorithm. Its expected time is O(n \log n) for every input. See Sorting, searching, divide and conquer.

Two kinds of randomised algorithm
Las VegasMonte Carlo
Answeralways correctcorrect with high probability
Running timerandom, with an expected boundfixed bound
Examplesrandomised quicksort, quickselectFreivalds, Miller-Rabin primality test, Karger's min cut
How to improvenothing to fixrepeat and combine the answers

A Monte Carlo error shrinks very fast with repeats. Run Freivalds' check 30 times with fresh vectors. A wrong C survives all 30 tries with chance at most 2^{-30}, less than one in a billion. This is amplification.

You can also turn one kind into the other. Stop a Las Vegas algorithm at twice its expected time. By Markov's inequality it has finished with chance at least 1/2. Now it is Monte Carlo. In the other direction, if you can check an answer quickly, repeat a Monte Carlo algorithm until the check passes.

"Randomised" does not mean "the input is random". The chance comes from the algorithm's own coin flips. The promise holds for every input, even one chosen by an enemy. Also, our code uses a fixed seed so that you see the same output. For security, use randomness from the operating system.

Hashing with guarantees

A hash table with chaining is fast when its chains are short. Look what happens when the keys have a pattern that the hash function does not like. Here 1000 keys are all multiples of 1024, and the table has 1024 buckets.

const P: u64 = (1 << 61) - 1;              // a prime, bigger than every key

struct Rng(u64);                           // splitmix64: small, fast, repeatable
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
        let mut z = self.0;
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
        z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

fn longest_chain(keys: &[u64], m: usize, h: impl Fn(u64) -> usize) -> usize {
    let mut sizes = vec![0; m];
    for &x in keys { sizes[h(x)] += 1; }
    *sizes.iter().max().unwrap()
}

fn main() {
    let m = 1024;
    let keys: Vec<u64> = (0..1000).map(|i| 1024 * i).collect(); // bad for "x mod m"
    println!("x mod m:   longest chain = {}", longest_chain(&keys, m, |x| (x % m as u64) as usize));
    let mut rng = Rng(42);
    for trial in 0..3 {
        let a = 1 + rng.next() % (P - 1);  // pick h at random from the family
        let b = rng.next() % P;
        let h = |x: u64| (((a as u128 * x as u128 + b as u128) % P as u128) % m as u128) as usize;
        println!("universal {trial}: longest chain = {}", longest_chain(&keys, m, h));
    }
}
P = (1 << 61) - 1                       # a prime, bigger than every key
M64 = (1 << 64) - 1

class Rng:                              # splitmix64: small, fast, repeatable
    def __init__(self, seed): self.s = seed
    def next(self):
        self.s = (self.s + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M64
        z = self.s
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M64
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M64
        return z ^ (z >> 31)

def longest_chain(keys, m, h):
    sizes = [0] * m
    for x in keys:
        sizes[h(x)] += 1
    return max(sizes)

m = 1024
keys = [1024 * i for i in range(1000)]  # a bad input for "x mod m"
print("x mod m:   longest chain =", longest_chain(keys, m, lambda x: x % m))
rng = Rng(42)
for trial in range(3):
    a = 1 + rng.next() % (P - 1)        # pick h at random from the family
    b = rng.next() % P
    h = lambda x: ((a * x + b) % P) % m
    print(f"universal {trial}: longest chain =", longest_chain(keys, m, h))
x mod m:   longest chain = 1000
universal 0: longest chain = 2
universal 1: longest chain = 2
universal 2: longest chain = 2

With "x mod 1024", every key lands in bucket 0. One chain holds all 1000 keys, so a lookup costs O(n). With a randomly chosen function, the longest chain has 2 keys. Both programs use the same small generator, splitmix64, so Rust and Python print the same numbers.

The trick is to choose the hash function at random, from a good family, when the table is made. An enemy who does not know our choice cannot build bad keys.

A family H of functions from keys to \{0, \dots, m-1\} is universal if, for every two different keys x \ne y, \Pr_{h \in H}[\,h(x) = h(y)\,] \le \frac{1}{m}.

Carter and Wegman (1979) gave a simple universal family. Take a prime p larger than every key. Use h_{a,b}(x) = ((a x + b) \bmod p) \bmod m, with random a \in \{1, \dots, p-1\} and b \in \{0, \dots, p-1\}. That is the family in the code.

Store n keys with chaining in m buckets, with h chosen at random from a universal family. For any key x, the expected number of other stored keys in the bucket of x is at most n/m. So with m \ge n, the expected chain length seen by any lookup is at most 2, which is O(1).

Proof

For each stored key y \ne x, let X_y = 1 if h(y) = h(x), else 0. By universality, E[X_y] = \Pr[h(y) = h(x)] \le 1/m. The number of other keys in the bucket is \sum_y X_y. By linearity of expectation, its mean is \sum_y E[X_y] \le n/m. Linearity needs no independence, so pairwise collision chances are enough.

In simple words: on average, a key shares its bucket with about n/m other keys. With 1000 keys and 1024 buckets that is less than one key. The average is over our random choice of h, not over the keys.

The danger is real. In a hash flooding attack, an attacker sends many keys with the same hash to a web server. Each insert becomes slow, and the server stops. So languages now use a secret random key in their string hash.

  • Rust. HashMap uses SipHash 1-3 with a random seed by default. The documentation says the algorithm may change.
  • Python. str and bytes use SipHash with a random seed per process. On my Python 3.14.3, sys.hash_info.algorithm prints siphash13. You can fix the seed with PYTHONHASHSEED.

Python's int hash is not random. On 64-bit builds, for a non-negative n, hash(n) is n \bmod (2^{61} - 1). So hash(5) is 5 in every run. Keys from users can still collide on purpose. Also, a keyed hash like SipHash is not a universal family in the exact maths sense. It acts like one only while the key stays secret.

Karger's minimum cut

A global minimum cut splits the nodes of an undirected graph into two non-empty groups. It cuts as few edges as possible. It shows the weakest place in a network. Here is a graph with two tight groups of 5 nodes, joined by only 2 edges.

struct Rng(u64);                         // the same splitmix64 as before
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
        let mut z = self.0;
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
        z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

fn find(parent: &[usize], mut x: usize) -> usize { // which super-node is x in?
    while parent[x] != x { x = parent[x]; }
    x
}

fn karger_once(n: usize, edges: &[(usize, usize)], rng: &mut Rng) -> usize {
    let mut order = edges.to_vec();
    for i in (1..order.len()).rev() {    // random shuffle of the edges
        let j = (rng.next() % (i as u64 + 1)) as usize;
        order.swap(i, j);
    }
    let (mut parent, mut groups): (Vec<usize>, usize) = ((0..n).collect(), n);
    for &(u, v) in &order {              // contract edges in random order
        let (ru, rv) = (find(&parent, u), find(&parent, v));
        if ru != rv && groups > 2 { parent[ru] = rv; groups -= 1; }
    }
    edges.iter().filter(|&&(u, v)| find(&parent, u) != find(&parent, v)).count()
}

fn main() {
    // Two groups of 5 nodes, each fully linked, plus 2 bridge edges.
    let mut edges = vec![];
    for g in [0, 5] {
        for u in g..g + 5 { for v in u + 1..g + 5 { edges.push((u, v)); } }
    }
    edges.extend([(0, 5), (1, 6)]);
    let mut rng = Rng(7);
    let cuts: Vec<usize> = (0..200).map(|_| karger_once(10, &edges, &mut rng)).collect();
    let best = *cuts.iter().min().unwrap();
    println!("edges: {} best cut: {}", edges.len(), best);
    println!("runs that found it: {} of 200", cuts.iter().filter(|&&c| c == best).count());
}
M64 = (1 << 64) - 1
class Rng:                               # the same splitmix64 as before
    def __init__(self, seed): self.s = seed
    def next(self):
        self.s = (self.s + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M64
        z = self.s
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M64
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M64
        return z ^ (z >> 31)

def find(parent, x):                     # union-find: which super-node is x in?
    while parent[x] != x:
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def karger_once(n, edges, rng):
    order = edges[:]
    for i in range(len(order) - 1, 0, -1):          # random shuffle of the edges
        j = rng.next() % (i + 1)
        order[i], order[j] = order[j], order[i]
    parent, groups = list(range(n)), n
    for u, v in order:                   # contract edges in random order
        ru, rv = find(parent, u), find(parent, v)
        if ru != rv and groups > 2:
            parent[ru] = rv
            groups -= 1
    return sum(1 for u, v in edges if find(parent, u) != find(parent, v))

# Two groups of 5 nodes, each fully linked, plus 2 bridge edges.
edges = [(u, v) for g in (0, 5) for u in range(g, g + 5) for v in range(u + 1, g + 5)]
edges += [(0, 5), (1, 6)]
rng = Rng(7)
cuts = [karger_once(10, edges, rng) for _ in range(200)]
print("edges:", len(edges), "best cut:", min(cuts))
print("runs that found it:", cuts.count(min(cuts)), "of 200")
edges: 22 best cut: 2
runs that found it: 49 of 200

Karger's algorithm (1993) is very short. Pick a random edge. Contract it: merge its two ends into one super-node. Keep parallel edges, but drop the edges inside a super-node. Repeat until two super-nodes are left. The edges between them form a cut.

The code does the same thing in another way. It shuffles the edges once, then merges along them with union-find. Taking edges in a random order and skipping inner edges gives the same random choices. One run found the cut of size 2 in about one run out of four.

Let C be a minimum cut of a connected graph with n nodes. One run of random contraction returns exactly C with probability at least \frac{2}{n(n-1)} = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}.

Proof

Let C have c edges. Every node has degree at least c. If not, the edges around that one node would be a smaller cut. So a graph with i nodes has at least ic/2 edges. A random edge is in C with chance at most c / (ic/2) = 2/i. The run returns C if it never contracts an edge of C. The chance of that is at least \prod_{i=3}^{n}\left(1 - \frac{2}{i}\right) = \prod_{i=3}^{n} \frac{i-2}{i} = \frac{2}{n(n-1)}. The product telescopes: almost every factor cancels.

For n = 10 the bound is 2/90, about 2.2%. Our graph did much better, about 25%, because its groups are dense. The bound is a floor that holds for every graph. Now amplify. Run it T = \binom{n}{2} \ln n times and keep the best cut. The chance that every run fails is at most (1 - 1/\binom{n}{2})^T \le e^{-\ln n} = 1/n.

A nice side result follows. Each minimum cut is found with chance at least 1/\binom{n}{2}. One run returns only one cut, so these events cannot overlap. So a graph has at most \binom{n}{2} minimum cuts. Karger and Stein (1996) made the method much faster. They share the early contractions between many runs, because the risky steps come at the end.

You can also find a global minimum cut with flows. Fix one node s and run a max flow to every other node t. The smallest s-t cut is the global minimum. See Network flow and linear programming. Karger's method is simpler and needs no flows.

Do not delete parallel edges after a contraction. If two super-nodes are joined by three edges, a random pick must hit that pair three times as often. Deleting copies changes the chances, and the proof breaks. Self-loops, edges inside one super-node, are the only ones to drop.

Approximation algorithms

Many useful problems are NP-hard. No fast exact algorithm is known for them. See Complexity theory. But often a fast answer that is provably close to the best is good enough.

An algorithm is an \alpha-approximation if, for every input, its answer costs at most \alpha times the best cost. For a minimum problem, \alpha \ge 1, and smaller is better. The hard part is the proof. We usually do not know the best cost, so we compare with a lower bound on it.

Vertex cover: a factor of 2

Take a star: one centre joined to five leaves. The best vertex cover is just the centre, size 1. Now use this rule. While some edge has no chosen end, choose both its ends. On the star, the first edge chooses the centre and one leaf. All edges are now covered. The answer has size 2, twice the best.

The rule "while an edge is uncovered, take both its ends" returns a vertex cover of size at most twice the minimum.

Proof

The edges the rule picks share no node, so they form a matching M. Any vertex cover needs a different node for each edge of M, so the best size is at least |M|. The rule takes 2|M| nodes. So the answer is at most twice the best.

The star shows the factor 2 can really happen. Nobody knows a polynomial algorithm with factor 2 - \varepsilon. Under a famous unproved assumption, the Unique Games Conjecture, none exists.

Set cover: the greedy rule

In set cover we have a universe of items and a list of sets. We want the fewest sets that cover every item. Think of choosing test cases that cover all features, or documents that cover all topics. The greedy rule takes the set that covers the most items still uncovered.

use std::collections::BTreeSet;

fn greedy_cover(universe: &BTreeSet<u32>, sets: &[(&str, BTreeSet<u32>)]) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut left = universe.clone();
    let mut chosen = vec![];
    while !left.is_empty() {
        // Pick the set that covers the most elements still left.
        let (name, set) = sets.iter()
            .max_by_key(|(name, s)| (s.intersection(&left).count(), std::cmp::Reverse(*name)))
            .unwrap();
        let new: BTreeSet<u32> = set.intersection(&left).copied().collect();
        println!("pick {name}: covers {} new, {} left", new.len(), left.len() - new.len());
        chosen.push(name.to_string());
        left = &left - &new;
    }
    chosen
}

fn main() {
    let sets = vec![
        ("A", (1..8).collect()),           // 1..7
        ("B", (8..15).collect()),          // 8..14
        ("C1", BTreeSet::from([1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11])),
        ("C2", BTreeSet::from([5, 6, 12, 13])),
        ("C3", BTreeSet::from([7, 14])),
    ];
    println!("greedy: {}", greedy_cover(&(1..15).collect(), &sets).join(", "));
    println!("best:   A, B");
}
SETS = {
    "A": set(range(1, 8)),               # 1..7
    "B": set(range(8, 15)),              # 8..14
    "C1": {1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11},
    "C2": {5, 6, 12, 13},
    "C3": {7, 14},
}

def greedy_cover(universe, sets):
    left, chosen = set(universe), []
    while left:
        # Pick the set that covers the most elements still left.
        name = max(sorted(sets), key=lambda s: len(sets[s] & left))
        new = sets[name] & left
        print(f"pick {name}: covers {len(new)} new, {len(left) - len(new)} left")
        chosen.append(name)
        left -= new
    return chosen

print("greedy:", ", ".join(greedy_cover(range(1, 15), SETS)))
print("best:   A, B")
pick C1: covers 8 new, 6 left
pick C2: covers 4 new, 2 left
pick C3: covers 2 new, 0 left
greedy: C1, C2, C3
best:   A, B

Greedy took 3 sets. The best uses 2. The big set C1 looked good, but it split both halves. Bigger copies of this trap make greedy worse and worse, but only slowly.

If the best cover uses k sets and the universe has n items, greedy uses at most H(n) \cdot k sets, where H(n) = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \dots + \tfrac{1}{n} \le \ln n + 1.

Proof idea

Say r items are still uncovered. The best k sets cover them, so one of those sets covers at least r/k of them. Greedy takes a set at least that good. So each step leaves at most r(1 - 1/k) items. After t steps at most n(1 - 1/k)^t \lt n e^{-t/k} items are left. With t = k \ln n this is less than 1, so nothing is left. This count gives about k \ln n + 1 sets. Spreading the cost of each set over its new items gives the exact H(n) bound.

This is close to the best possible. Dinur and Steurer (2014) proved that a factor of (1 - \varepsilon)\ln n is NP-hard for every \varepsilon \gt 0. So unless P = NP, greedy is as good as any fast algorithm, up to small terms.

Travelling salesman with the triangle inequality

The travelling salesman problem, or TSP, asks for the shortest round trip through all cities. In general it cannot be approximated at all, unless P = NP. But real distances obey the triangle inequality: d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z). With this rule, a simple trick gives factor 2.

Four cities

A(0,0), B(4,0), C(4,3), D(0,3). The sides are 4 and 3. The diagonals are 5. The best tour goes round the rectangle: 14.

Build a minimum spanning tree

Take D-A (3), B-C (3) and A-B (4). The tree costs 10. See Graph algorithms for Kruskal and Prim.

A tour is never cheaper than the tree

Remove one edge from the best tour. What is left is a spanning tree. So the best tour costs at least 10.

Walk round the tree

Walk every tree edge twice: D-A-B-C-B-A-D. The walk costs 2 × 10 = 20. It visits some cities twice.

Take shortcuts

Skip cities you have seen: D-A-B-C-D. By the triangle inequality a shortcut is never longer. The tour costs 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14.

The promise

In general: tour ≤ walk = 2 × tree ≤ 2 × best tour. Here we were lucky and got the best tour itself.

If the distances obey the triangle inequality, the double-tree tour costs at most twice the shortest tour.

Christofides (1976), and on his own Serdyukov, improved this to 1.5. They add a cheap matching on the odd-degree nodes of the tree instead of doubling every edge. For over forty years nobody beat 1.5. Then Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan (published at STOC 2021) found a randomised algorithm with factor 1.5 - \varepsilon, for an \varepsilon above 10^{-36}. The gain is tiny, but it broke an old wall.

An approximation ratio is a worst-case promise, not a typical result. On real inputs these methods are often within a few percent of the best. Also, do not confuse them with heuristics, such as simulated annealing. Heuristics can be very good, but they carry no proof.

Online algorithms and paging

You go skiing, but you do not know for how many days. Renting skis costs 10 euros a day. Buying costs 100 euros. If you knew the number of days, the choice would be easy. You do not. A safe rule is: rent for 9 days, then buy on day 10. If you ski 5 days, you pay 50, the best possible. If you ski 30 days, you pay 90 + 100 = 190, while the best was 100. You never pay more than 1.9 times the best.

An online algorithm must act on each request before it sees the next one. We compare it with the best offline algorithm, OPT, which knows the future. An online algorithm is c-competitive if, for every request sequence \sigma, \text{ALG}(\sigma) \le c \cdot \text{OPT}(\sigma) + b for some fixed b. The smallest such c is the competitive ratio. Our ski rule is 1.9-competitive.

Now paging. A fast cache holds k pages. A request for a page in the cache is a hit. Otherwise it is a fault, and we must evict a page to make room. Three rules:

  • FIFO evicts the page that came in first.
  • LRU evicts the least recently used page.
  • OPT evicts the page whose next request is farthest in the future. This is Belady's rule. It is optimal, but it needs to see the future.
fn faults(reqs: &[u32], k: usize, policy: &str) -> usize {
    let (mut cache, mut count): (Vec<u32>, usize) = (vec![], 0); // cache[0] is evicted next
    for (i, &p) in reqs.iter().enumerate() {
        if let Some(pos) = cache.iter().position(|&q| q == p) {
            if policy == "LRU" {         // a hit makes p the most recent
                cache.remove(pos);
                cache.push(p);
            }
            continue;
        }
        count += 1;
        if cache.len() == k {
            if policy == "OPT" {         // evict the page used farthest away
                let rest = &reqs[i + 1..];
                let next_use = |q: u32| rest.iter().position(|&r| r == q).unwrap_or(rest.len());
                let far = (0..k).max_by_key(|&j| next_use(cache[j])).unwrap();
                cache.remove(far);
            } else {                     // FIFO and LRU evict the front
                cache.remove(0);
            }
        }
        cache.push(p);
    }
    count
}

fn main() {
    let seq = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    for k in [3, 4] {
        let r: Vec<String> = ["FIFO", "LRU", "OPT"].iter()
            .map(|p| format!("{p} {}", faults(&seq, k, p))).collect();
        println!("k={k}: {}", r.join(", "));
    }
    let cycle: Vec<u32> = [1, 2, 3, 4].repeat(6); // k+1 pages in a loop: the worst case for LRU
    println!("cycle, k=3: LRU {}, OPT {}", faults(&cycle, 3, "LRU"), faults(&cycle, 3, "OPT"));
}
def faults(reqs, k, policy):
    cache, count = [], 0                 # cache[0] is the next to evict
    for i, p in enumerate(reqs):
        if p in cache:
            if policy == "LRU":          # a hit makes p the most recent
                cache.remove(p)
                cache.append(p)
            continue
        count += 1
        if len(cache) == k:
            if policy == "OPT":          # evict the page used farthest away
                rest = reqs[i + 1:]
                far = max(cache, key=lambda q: rest.index(q) if q in rest else len(rest))
                cache.remove(far)
            else:                        # FIFO and LRU evict the front
                cache.pop(0)
        cache.append(p)
    return count

seq = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
for k in (3, 4):
    print(f"k={k}:", ", ".join(f"{p} {faults(seq, k, p)}" for p in ("FIFO", "LRU", "OPT")))
cycle = [1, 2, 3, 4] * 6                 # k+1 pages in a loop: the worst case for LRU
print("cycle, k=3:", ", ".join(f"{p} {faults(cycle, 3, p)}" for p in ("LRU", "OPT")))
k=3: FIFO 9, LRU 10, OPT 7
k=4: FIFO 10, LRU 8, OPT 6
cycle, k=3: LRU 24, OPT 10

Look at the last line. Four pages in a loop with a cache of 3 is the worst case for LRU. It always evicts the page that comes next, so every request faults. OPT faults about once every 3 requests. The ratio moves towards 3, which is k.

With a cache of k pages, for every request sequence \sigma: \text{LRU}(\sigma) \le k \cdot \text{OPT}(\sigma) + k. FIFO has the same bound. No deterministic online algorithm has a competitive ratio below k.

Proof

Upper bound. Cut the sequence into phases. Each phase is as long as possible while it asks for at most k different pages. Inside one phase, LRU faults at most once per different page, so at most k times. A page loaded in the phase stays, because only k different pages are asked. Now let p be the first page of a phase. From the next request up to the first request of the following phase, we see at least k different pages that are not p. OPT has p in its cache at the start, so it holds at most k - 1 of them. It must fault at least once. So OPT faults at least once per phase, except maybe the last.

Lower bound. Use k + 1 pages. An enemy always asks for the page that the online algorithm does not hold. The algorithm faults every time. OPT, which evicts the page needed farthest away, faults at most once every k requests.

Sleator and Tarjan proved this in 1985. Their paper also compared LRU with a smaller optimal cache. Randomness helps here. The marking algorithm evicts a random unmarked page. It is O(\log k)-competitive, and no randomised rule beats about \ln k.

The competitive ratio is very pessimistic. With k = 1000, "1000 times worse than OPT" sounds terrible. Real programs have locality, and LRU does well on them. Use the ratio to compare rules in the worst case, not to predict real hit rates. Many real systems use cheaper cousins of LRU, such as the CLOCK algorithm.

Streaming sketches

A router sees millions of packets per second. It cannot store them. It still wants to know: which addresses are most common? How many different users came today? In the streaming model we see each item once, in order. Memory must be far smaller than the stream. A sketch is such a small summary.

Reservoir sampling

Problem one: keep a fair random sample of k items from a stream of unknown length. Fill the first k slots. Then keep item number i (counting from 1) with chance k/i. If you keep it, it replaces a random slot.

struct Rng(u64);                           // the same splitmix64 as before
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
        let mut z = self.0;
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
        z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

fn reservoir(stream: impl Iterator<Item = u64>, k: usize, rng: &mut Rng) -> Vec<u64> {
    let mut sample = Vec::with_capacity(k);
    for (i, x) in stream.enumerate() {     // i counts from 0
        if i < k {
            sample.push(x);                // fill the reservoir first
        } else {
            let j = (rng.next() % (i as u64 + 1)) as usize; // keep x with chance k/(i+1)
            if j < k { sample[j] = x; }    // it replaces a random old item
        }
    }
    sample
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng = Rng(3);
    println!("one sample of 5 from 1..1000: {:?}", reservoir(1..=1000, 5, &mut rng));
    let mut hits = [0; 10];
