    for _ in 0..10_000 {                   // sample 2 of 10, many times
        for x in reservoir(0..10, 2, &mut rng) { hits[x as usize] += 1; }
    }
    println!("times each item was chosen: {:?}", hits);
}
M64 = (1 << 64) - 1
class Rng:                                 # the same splitmix64 as before
    def __init__(self, seed): self.s = seed
    def next(self):
        self.s = (self.s + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M64
        z = self.s
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M64
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M64
        return z ^ (z >> 31)

def reservoir(stream, k, rng):
    sample = []
    for i, x in enumerate(stream):         # i counts from 0
        if i < k:
            sample.append(x)               # fill the reservoir first
        else:
            j = rng.next() % (i + 1)       # keep x with chance k/(i+1)
            if j < k:
                sample[j] = x              # it replaces a random old item
    return sample

rng = Rng(3)
print("one sample of 5 from 1..1000:", reservoir(range(1, 1001), 5, rng))
hits = [0] * 10
for _ in range(10_000):                    # sample 2 of 10, many times
    for x in reservoir(range(10), 2, rng):
        hits[x] += 1
print("times each item was chosen:", hits)
one sample of 5 from 1..1000: [212, 8, 709, 586, 536]
times each item was chosen: [1968, 1957, 2055, 1975, 1975, 1976, 1988, 2052, 2020, 2034]

Each of the 10 items was chosen about 2000 times, as expected: 10{,}000 \times 2/10. Why is it fair? Item i enters with chance k/i. At a later step j, it is thrown out with chance (k/j)(1/k) = 1/j. So it stays to the end with chance \frac{k}{i} \cdot \frac{i}{i+1} \cdot \frac{i+1}{i+2} \cdots \frac{n-1}{n} = \frac{k}{n}. This method is called Algorithm R. Knuth credits it to Alan Waterman. Vitter (1985) made it faster by skipping items.

Count-min sketch: how often?

Problem two: estimate how many times each item appeared. The count-min sketch by Cormode and Muthukrishnan (2005) keeps d rows of w counters. Each row has its own universal hash function. To add an item, add 1 to one counter in every row. To ask for an item, take the smallest of its d counters.

const P: u64 = (1 << 61) - 1;

struct Rng(u64);                           // the same splitmix64 as before
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
        let mut z = self.0;
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
        z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let (eps, delta) = (0.01_f64, 0.01_f64);
    let w = (std::f64::consts::E / eps).ceil() as usize;  // 272
    let d = (1.0 / delta).ln().ceil() as usize;           // 5
    let mut rng = Rng(1);
    let rows: Vec<(u64, u64)> = (0..d).map(|_| { let a = 1 + rng.next() % (P - 1); (a, rng.next() % P) }).collect();
    let mut table = vec![vec![0u64; w]; d];
    // one cell in each row
    let cell = |r: usize, x: u64| (((rows[r].0 as u128 * x as u128 + rows[r].1 as u128) % P as u128) % w as u128) as usize;
    let truth: Vec<u64> = (0..1000).map(|i| 1000 / (i + 1)).collect(); // item i appears 1000/(i+1) times
    for (x, &c) in truth.iter().enumerate() {
        for r in 0..d { table[r][cell(r, x as u64)] += c; }
    }
    let n: u64 = truth.iter().sum();
    println!("w={w} d={d} N={n} error limit eps*N={:.0}", eps * n as f64);
    for x in [0u64, 1, 9, 99, 999] {
        let est = (0..d).map(|r| table[r][cell(r, x)]).min().unwrap();
        println!("item {x}: true {}, estimate {est}", truth[x as usize]);
    }
}
import math
P, M64 = (1 << 61) - 1, (1 << 64) - 1

class Rng:                                 # the same splitmix64 as before
    def __init__(self, seed): self.s = seed
    def next(self):
        self.s = (self.s + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M64
        z = self.s
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M64
        z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M64
        return z ^ (z >> 31)

eps, delta = 0.01, 0.01
w, d = math.ceil(math.e / eps), math.ceil(math.log(1 / delta))   # 272 x 5
rng = Rng(1)
rows = [(1 + rng.next() % (P - 1), rng.next() % P) for _ in range(d)]
table = [[0] * w for _ in range(d)]

def cells(x):                              # one cell in each row
    return [(r, ((a * x + b) % P) % w) for r, (a, b) in enumerate(rows)]

true = {i: 1000 // (i + 1) for i in range(1000)}   # item i appears 1000/(i+1) times
for x, c in true.items():
    for r, j in cells(x):
        table[r][j] += c
N = sum(true.values())
print(f"w={w} d={d} N={N} error limit eps*N={eps * N:.0f}")
for x in (0, 1, 9, 99, 999):
    est = min(table[r][j] for r, j in cells(x))
    print(f"item {x}: true {true[x]}, estimate {est}")
w=272 d=5 N=7069 error limit eps*N=71
item 0: true 1000, estimate 1006
item 1: true 500, estimate 506
item 9: true 100, estimate 103
item 99: true 10, estimate 15
item 999: true 1, estimate 1

With w = \lceil e/\varepsilon \rceil and d = \lceil \ln(1/\delta) \rceil, each estimate \hat a of a true count a obeys a \le \hat a \le a + \varepsilon N with probability at least 1 - \delta. Here N is the length of the stream.

The estimate never goes below the truth, because other items only add to a counter. In one row, the expected extra is at most N/w = \varepsilon N / e. By Markov's inequality, the extra passes \varepsilon N with chance at most 1/e. All d rows must fail together, which has chance at most e^{-d} \le \delta. Here 1360 counters summarised 7069 events, and every error stayed under 71.

HyperLogLog: how many different?

Problem three: count the different items. Hash each item to a random-looking bit string. About half of the hashes start with a 0 bit. About a quarter start with 00. If the longest run of leading zeros you ever saw is 20, you probably saw around 2^{20} different items. Duplicates give the same hash, so they change nothing.

fn mix(x: u64) -> u64 {                    // a 64-bit hash of an integer
    let mut z = x.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
    z ^ (z >> 31)
}

fn hll_count(items: impl Iterator<Item = u64>, b: u32) -> f64 {
    let m = 1usize << b;                   // 1024 registers
    let mut reg = vec![0u32; m];
    for x in items {
        let h = mix(x);
        let j = (h >> (64 - b)) as usize;  // the first b bits choose a register
        let rest = h << b;                 // the other bits
        let rank = rest.leading_zeros().min(64 - b) + 1; // leading zeros + 1
        reg[j] = reg[j].max(rank);
    }
    let mf = m as f64;
    let alpha = 0.7213 / (1.0 + 1.079 / mf);
    let mut est = alpha * mf * mf / reg.iter().map(|&r| 2f64.powi(-(r as i32))).sum::<f64>();
    let zeros = reg.iter().filter(|&&r| r == 0).count();
    if est <= 2.5 * mf && zeros > 0 {      // small counts: use linear counting
        est = mf * (mf / zeros as f64).ln();
    }
    est
}

fn main() {
    for n in [1000u64, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000] {
        let stream = (0..2 * n).map(|i| i % n); // every value appears twice
        let est = hll_count(stream, 10);
        println!("distinct {n}: estimate {est:.0}, error {:+.1}%", 100.0 * (est - n as f64) / n as f64);
    }
}
import math
M64 = (1 << 64) - 1

def mix(x):                                # a 64-bit hash of an integer
    z = (x + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M64
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M64
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M64
    return z ^ (z >> 31)

def hll_count(items, b=10):
    m = 1 << b                             # 1024 registers
    reg = [0] * m
    for x in items:
        h = mix(x)
        j = h >> (64 - b)                  # the first b bits choose a register
        rest = (h << b) & M64              # the other bits
        rank = min(64 - rest.bit_length(), 64 - b) + 1   # leading zeros + 1
        reg[j] = max(reg[j], rank)
    alpha = 0.7213 / (1 + 1.079 / m)
    est = alpha * m * m / sum(2.0 ** -r for r in reg)
    zeros = reg.count(0)
    if est <= 2.5 * m and zeros:           # small counts: use linear counting
        est = m * math.log(m / zeros)
    return est

for n in (1000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
    stream = (i % n for i in range(2 * n))  # every value appears twice
    est = hll_count(stream)
    print(f"distinct {n}: estimate {est:.0f}, error {100 * (est - n) / n:+.1f}%")
distinct 1000: estimate 986, error -1.4%
distinct 10000: estimate 9782, error -2.2%
distinct 100000: estimate 103224, error +3.2%
distinct 1000000: estimate 1045085, error +4.5%

One run of zeros is too noisy. HyperLogLog (Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet and Meunier, 2007) uses m small registers. The first bits of the hash choose a register. Each register keeps its longest run. A harmonic mean combines them. The standard error is about 1.04/\sqrt{m}. With m = 1024 that is about 3.3%, and our errors fit. The 1024 registers fit in under 1 KB if each one uses 6 bits. That stays the same, whether you count a thousand items or a million.

Redis has HyperLogLog built in, with the commands PFADD, PFCOUNT and PFMERGE. Its documentation says one HyperLogLog uses at most 12 KB, with a standard error of 0.81%. Two sketches merge by taking the larger value in each register. So each server can count its own users, and you can merge the sketches later.

Three sketches side by side
SketchQuestionMemoryErrorMergeable?
Reservoira fair sample of k itemsk itemsnone: exact samplingwith care (weights)
Count-minhow often is x?\frac{e}{\varepsilon} \ln\frac{1}{\delta} countersover by at most \varepsilon Nyes: add the tables
HyperLogLoghow many different items?m small registersabout 1.04/\sqrt{m}yes: take the maximum

Count-min is good for frequent items and bad for rare ones. Item 99 above has a true count of 10, but the estimate is 15: a 50% error. The promise is about \varepsilon N, not about each count. Also, HyperLogLog counts different items. It cannot tell you how many times one item appeared.

String matching

Find the pattern "ababaca" in the text "abababacababacab". The simple way tries every start position and compares letter by letter. On a text of n letters and a pattern of m, that can take O(nm) steps. Think of the text "aaaa…a" and the pattern "aaab". Every try matches three letters, then fails, then starts again.

Knuth-Morris-Pratt

After a failure we already know some of the text. The KMP algorithm (1977) never reads a text letter twice in a forward way. It uses a table, the failure function. For each prefix of the pattern, it stores the length of the longest border. A border is a part that is both a proper start and an end. For "ababa" the longest border is "aba", length 3.

// fail[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pat[..=i]
// that is also a suffix of it.
fn failure(pat: &[u8]) -> Vec<usize> {
    let (mut fail, mut k) = (vec![0; pat.len()], 0);
    for i in 1..pat.len() {
        while k > 0 && pat[i] != pat[k] {
            k = fail[k - 1];               // fall back to a shorter border
        }
        if pat[i] == pat[k] { k += 1; }
        fail[i] = k;
    }
    fail
}

fn kmp_search(text: &[u8], pat: &[u8]) -> (Vec<usize>, usize) {
    let (fail, mut k, mut found, mut steps) = (failure(pat), 0, vec![], 0);
    for (i, &ch) in text.iter().enumerate() { // i only moves forward
        while k > 0 && ch != pat[k] {
            k = fail[k - 1];
            steps += 1;
        }
        steps += 1;
        if ch == pat[k] { k += 1; }
        if k == pat.len() {                // a full match ends at i
            found.push(i + 1 - k);
            k = fail[k - 1];
        }
    }
    (found, steps)
}

fn main() {
    println!("failure of ababaca: {:?}", failure(b"ababaca"));
    let text = b"abababacababacab";
    let (found, steps) = kmp_search(text, b"ababaca");
    println!("matches at {found:?}, {steps} comparisons, text length {}", text.len());
}
def failure(pat):
    # fail[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pat[:i+1]
    # that is also a suffix of it.
    fail, k = [0] * len(pat), 0
    for i in range(1, len(pat)):
        while k > 0 and pat[i] != pat[k]:
            k = fail[k - 1]                # fall back to a shorter border
        if pat[i] == pat[k]:
            k += 1
        fail[i] = k
    return fail

def kmp_search(text, pat):
    fail, k, found, steps = failure(pat), 0, [], 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(text):          # i only moves forward
        while k > 0 and ch != pat[k]:
            k = fail[k - 1]
            steps += 1
        steps += 1
        if ch == pat[k]:
            k += 1
        if k == len(pat):                  # a full match ends at i
            found.append(i - k + 1)
            k = fail[k - 1]
    return found, steps

print("failure of ababaca:", failure("ababaca"))
text = "abababacababacab"
found, steps = kmp_search(text, "ababaca")
print(f"matches at {found}, {steps} comparisons, text length {len(text)}")
failure of ababaca: [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1]
matches at [2, 8], 17 comparisons, text length 16

The pattern appears at positions 2 and 8. KMP used only 17 comparisons on 16 letters. Why is it always linear? The match length k goes up by at most 1 per text letter. Every fallback makes k smaller. So the total number of fallbacks is at most n. The search costs O(n), and the table costs O(m), so KMP runs in O(n + m).

Rabin-Karp

Rabin-Karp (1987) compares numbers instead of letters. Read each window of the text as a number, and keep it modulo a prime. Moving the window by one letter updates the number in O(1). This is a rolling hash.

  1. The pattern 263 gives 263 \bmod 7 = 4.
  2. First window 415: 415 \bmod 7 = 2. No match.
  3. Roll: drop the 4, add the 2. (415 - 4 \cdot 100) \cdot 10 + 2 = 152, and 152 \bmod 7 = 5. No match.
  4. Window 526 gives 1. Window 263 gives 4: a hash hit. Compare the letters. They are equal: a real match at position 3.
  5. Window 633 gives 3. Window 333 gives 4: another hit. Compare the letters. 333 is not 263. This is a false hit, so we go on.

With a random large prime, false hits are rare. The expected time is O(n + m), but the worst case is O(nm). Rabin-Karp shines when you search for many patterns of the same length at once. Put all pattern hashes in a set, then roll once over the text.

Suffix arrays

What if the text stays the same and the patterns change? Then prepare the text once. A suffix array lists the start positions of all suffixes of the text, sorted. A suffix is an end part of the text.

fn main() {
    let s = "banana";
    let mut sa: Vec<usize> = (0..s.len()).collect();
    sa.sort_by_key(|&i| &s[i..]);          // sort the suffixes
    println!("suffix array: {sa:?}");
    for &i in &sa { println!("{i} {}", &s[i..]); }

    let pat = "an";                        // suffixes that start with pat sit together
    let key = |i: usize| &s[i..(i + pat.len()).min(s.len())]; // the first len(pat) letters
    let lo = sa.partition_point(|&i| key(i) < pat);
    let hi = sa.partition_point(|&i| key(i) <= pat);
    println!("'{pat}' occurs at positions {:?}", &sa[lo..hi]);
}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

s = "banana"
sa = sorted(range(len(s)), key=lambda i: s[i:])   # sort the suffixes
print("suffix array:", sa)
for i in sa:
    print(i, s[i:])

pat = "an"                                # suffixes that start with pat sit together
key = lambda i: s[i:i + len(pat)]         # look only at the first len(pat) letters
lo, hi = bisect_left(sa, pat, key=key), bisect_right(sa, pat, key=key)
print(f"{pat!r} occurs at positions {sa[lo:hi]}")
suffix array: [5, 3, 1, 0, 4, 2]
5 a
3 ana
1 anana
0 banana
4 na
2 nana
'an' occurs at positions [3, 1]

Every pattern that occurs is the start of some suffix. In sorted order, all suffixes that start with "an" sit next to each other. Two binary searches find them in O(m \log n) time. Manber and Myers introduced suffix arrays around 1990. Our simple sort can be slow on long texts, because one comparison can read many letters. Prefix doubling builds the array in O(n \log n). The SA-IS algorithm (Nong, Zhang and Chan, 2009) builds it in O(n). Suffix arrays, and the related Burrows-Wheeler transform, power DNA search tools and the bzip2 compressor.

Your language already has a good search. Since Python 3.10, str.find and in sometimes use the Two-Way algorithm of Crochemore and Perrin. It avoids quadratic time on long strings. Rust's str::find also uses a Two-Way searcher for string patterns. I checked this in the Rust 1.99 standard library source.

In Rabin-Karp, do not report a hash hit as a match without checking the letters. Two different windows can share a hash, like 263 and 333 above. Also, in Rust, slicing a &str at a byte position in the middle of a multi-byte letter panics. Work on bytes, as our KMP code does.

Parallel algorithm basics

Add up the numbers from 1 to 10 million with 4 threads. Each thread adds one quarter. Then we add the four results.

use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let data: Vec<u64> = (1..=10_000_000).collect();
    let p = 4;                                       // number of threads
    let chunk = data.len().div_ceil(p);
    let total: u64 = thread::scope(|s| {
        let handles: Vec<_> = data.chunks(chunk)     // one chunk per thread
            .map(|c| s.spawn(move || c.iter().sum::<u64>()))
            .collect();
        handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum()
    });
    println!("sum = {total}");
    let n = data.len() as u64;
    let work = n - 1;                                // additions in a tree sum
    let span = 64 - (n - 1).leading_zeros() as u64;  // tree depth: ceil(log2 n)
    println!("work = {work}, span = {span}, Brent limit for p={p}: {}", work / p as u64 + span);
}
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import math

data = list(range(1, 10_000_001))
p = 4                                       # number of threads
chunk = math.ceil(len(data) / p)
parts = [data[i:i + chunk] for i in range(0, len(data), chunk)]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=p) as pool:
    total = sum(pool.map(sum, parts))        # one chunk per thread
print(f"sum = {total}")
n = len(data)
work = n - 1                                # additions in a tree sum
span = math.ceil(math.log2(n))              # tree depth
print(f"work = {work}, span = {span}, Brent limit for p={p}: {work // p + span}")
sum = 50000005000000
work = 9999999, span = 24, Brent limit for p=4: 2500023

To reason about speed, we use two numbers. The work W is the total number of steps. The span S is the longest chain of steps that must wait for each other. Adding n numbers in a tree has work n - 1 and span \lceil \log_2 n \rceil. For 10 million numbers that is 24 levels. The ratio W/S is the parallelism. More processors than that cannot help.

A computation with work W and span S runs on p processors, with a greedy scheduler, in time T_p \le \frac{W}{p} + S. No schedule can beat \max(W/p,\ S), so greedy is always within a factor of 2 of the best.

Proof idea

In each time step, either all p processors are busy, or some are idle. Busy steps do p units of work, so there are at most W/p of them. In a step with an idle processor, every ready task runs. So the longest remaining chain gets one step shorter. There are at most S such steps.

Work and span of basic parallel patterns
PatternWorkSpanExample
map: the same job on every itemO(n)O(1)resize every image
reduce: combine all itemsO(n)O(\log n)sum, max, count
scan: all running totalsO(n)O(\log n)prefix sums, stream compaction
merge sort with parallel mergeO(n \log n)O(\log^3 n) with a simple parallel mergesort a big array

In Rust, the Rayon library turns iter() into par_iter() and does this splitting for you. In Python, the normal build has a GIL. Our thread pool gives the right answer, but no real speed-up for pure Python work. Python 3.14 officially supports a free-threaded build without the GIL (PEP 779). For CPU work on the normal build, use processes, or libraries like NumPy that work outside the GIL.

More threads do not always mean more speed. Starting threads costs time, and memory bandwidth is shared. A fixed serial part limits the speed-up, as Amdahl's law says. And an algorithm with a long span, like a loop where each step needs the last one, cannot be fast in parallel at all.

Patterns for randomised, approximate, streaming and string algorithms
