Practice

An algorithm always returns a correct answer, but its running time depends on coin flips. What kind is it?

  • Las Vegas
  • Monte Carlo
  • Approximation

Las Vegas algorithms are always correct. Only their time is random, like randomised quicksort.

A hash family is universal. Two different keys x and y, and m = 100 buckets. What is the most the collision chance can be?

  • 1/2
  • 1/100
  • 0

Universal means \Pr[h(x) = h(y)] \le 1/m for every pair of different keys.

Why does the count-min sketch take the minimum of its counters?

  • Because counters can go below the true count
  • Because every counter is at least the true count, and other items only add extra
  • Because the minimum is the average of the rows

Each counter holds the true count plus noise from other items. The smallest counter has the least noise.

A cache holds k = 4 pages. What is the best competitive ratio a deterministic online paging rule can have?

  • 1
  • 2
  • 4

LRU reaches k, and an enemy with k + 1 pages forces every deterministic rule to k.

Karger's algorithm returns a fixed minimum cut of a graph with 5 nodes with chance at least 1 in ?.

The failure function of the pattern "aabaa" is [0, 1, 0, 1, ?].

A computation has work 1000 and span 10. On 10 processors, Brent's bound says it takes at most ? steps.

  1. Run the vertex cover rule on the path a-b-c-d. Take the edges in the order a-b, b-c, c-d. What do you get, and what is the best?
    Answer

    Edge a-b is uncovered, so take a and b. Edge b-c is covered by b. Edge c-d is uncovered, so take c and d. The answer is {a, b, c, d}, size 4. The best is {b, c}, size 2. The ratio is exactly 2, as the theorem allows.

  2. Reservoir sampling with k = 1 on a stream of 4 items. What is the chance that item 2 is the final sample? Show the product.
    Answer

    Item 2 enters with chance 1/2. Item 3 does not replace it with chance 2/3. Item 4 does not replace it with chance 3/4. So \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{4}. Every item has the same chance, 1/4.

  3. Ski rental: renting costs 1 a day and buying costs 50. Give a rule and its competitive ratio.
    Answer

    Rent for 49 days, then buy on day 50. If you ski at most 49 days you pay the best price. Otherwise you pay 49 + 50 = 99, while the best was 50. The ratio is 99/50 = 1.98 = 2 - 1/50.

  4. Why does the double-tree proof need the triangle inequality? What goes wrong without it?
    Answer

    The shortcut step jumps over cities we have seen. The triangle inequality says the jump is never longer than the path it replaces. Without it, a jump can cost much more, so the tour can be far longer than twice the tree. In fact, general TSP has no constant-factor approximation unless P = NP.

  5. Expert. Show that a graph with n nodes has at most \binom{n}{2} different global minimum cuts.
    Answer

    Fix one run of Karger's algorithm. For each minimum cut C, the event "the run returns exactly C" has chance at least 1/\binom{n}{2}. One run returns only one cut, so these events cannot happen together. Their chances add up to at most 1. So there are at most \binom{n}{2} of them.

  6. Expert. You must count different visitors over 100 web servers, with little memory and traffic between them. Which sketch do you choose, and how do you combine the servers?
    Answer

    Use HyperLogLog with the same hash function and register count on every server. Each server keeps its own sketch. To combine, take the maximum of each register across all 100 sketches. Then estimate from the merged registers. Visitors seen on many servers are counted once, because they set the same register to the same value.

Key takeaways

  • Las Vegas algorithms are always right with a random time. Monte Carlo algorithms have a fixed time and a small, shrinkable error.
  • A hash function chosen at random from a universal family gives expected chain length 1 + n/m on every input.
  • Karger's random contractions find a minimum cut with chance at least 2/(n(n-1)). Repeat to make failure rare.
  • Approximation proofs compare with a lower bound: a matching for vertex cover, a spanning tree for metric TSP.
  • Greedy set cover is within \ln n + 1 of the best, and doing much better is NP-hard.
  • The competitive ratio compares an online algorithm with an all-knowing OPT. LRU is k-competitive, and no deterministic rule does better.
  • Sketches answer questions about huge streams in small memory: reservoir samples, count-min counts, HyperLogLog distinct counts.
  • KMP and Rabin-Karp search in linear time (Rabin-Karp in expectation). Suffix arrays prepare a text for fast repeated searches.
  • Parallel speed depends on work and span: T_p \le W/p + S.

Sources

  • Princeton COS 521, Fall 2025: Karger's Min Cut Algorithm. The contraction algorithm, its success chance and the Karger-Stein idea.
  • MIT 6.854 notes: Online algorithms. Competitive ratio, ski rental, the LRU proof by phases, lower bounds and the marking algorithm.
  • Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan: A (Slightly) Improved Approximation Algorithm for Metric TSP. The first improvement on the 1.5 factor.
  • Count-min sketch. The width and depth formulas and the error guarantee.
  • Redis docs: HyperLogLog. PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE, the 12 KB limit and the 0.81% standard error.
  • Rust std: HashMap. The default SipHash 1-3 hasher, random seeding and HashDoS resistance.

Automata and formal languages

A machine reads a text one symbol at a time. At the end it says yes or no. This simple picture explains regular expressions, lexers, parsers and even the grammars that keep an LLM's JSON output valid. This chapter builds the machines from the weakest to the strongest and shows what each one cannot do.

  • Describe a language as a set of strings and build a DFA or an NFA for it.
  • Turn an NFA into a DFA and a regular expression into an automaton.
  • Prove that a language is not regular with the pumping lemma or Myhill-Nerode.
  • Write a context-free grammar, explain a pushdown automaton, and run the CYK parser.
  • Place a real problem in the Chomsky hierarchy and pick the right tool for it.

Alphabets, strings and languages

Look at three questions. Is 2026-11-15 a date in the right format? Is this text valid JSON? Does this program ever stop? Each question takes a piece of text and wants yes or no. They look alike. But the first is easy, the second needs more memory, and the third has no answer at all. This part of the book explains why.

We start with exact words for "text" and "question".

  • An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. We write it \Sigma. Examples: \{0, 1\}, the 26 letters, or all Unicode code points.
  • A string is a finite row of symbols. The string 0110 has length 4. We write |w| = 4.
  • The empty string has length 0. We write it \varepsilon.
  • \Sigma^* is the set of all strings over \Sigma, including \varepsilon.
  • A language is any set of strings. It can be finite or infinite.

Every yes-or-no question about text is a language: the set of strings with the answer yes. "Valid JSON" is the set of all valid JSON texts. So "solve the problem" and "decide if a string is in the language" mean the same thing. We build languages from smaller ones with three operations.

Three operations on languages, with A = \{\texttt{a}, \texttt{b}\} and B = \{\texttt{c}\}
OperationMeaningExample
Union A \cup Ba string from either language\{\texttt{a}, \texttt{b}, \texttt{c}\}
Concatenation ABa string from A, then one from B\{\texttt{ac}, \texttt{bc}\}
Star A^*zero or more strings from A, joined\{\varepsilon, \texttt{a}, \texttt{b}, \texttt{aa}, \texttt{ab}, \dots\}

The empty language \emptyset and the language \{\varepsilon\} are different. The first has no strings at all. The second has one string, the empty one. Also note: \emptyset^* = \{\varepsilon\}, because the star always allows "zero pieces".

Deterministic finite automata

Here is a small machine. It reads a binary number from left to right. It tells you if the number is a multiple of 3. It remembers only one thing: the remainder so far. Reading a bit b changes the value from v to 2v + b. So the new remainder is (2r + b) \bmod 3.

This machine is a deterministic finite automaton (DFA). "Deterministic" means there is exactly one move for each state and symbol. "Finite" means the number of states is fixed before we read anything.

A DFA has five parts: a finite set of states Q, an alphabet \Sigma, a transition function \delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q, a start state q_0, and a set of accepting states F \subseteq Q. It accepts w when the run on w ends in F.

// A DFA for binary numbers that are multiples of 3.
// The state is the remainder of the number read so far.
const DELTA: [[usize; 2]; 3] = [[0, 1], [2, 0], [1, 2]]; // DELTA[state][bit]

fn accepts(word: &str) -> bool {
    let mut state = 0; // start state: remainder 0
    for ch in word.chars() {
        let bit = match ch {
            '0' => 0,
            '1' => 1,
            _ => return false, // not in the alphabet
        };
        state = DELTA[state][bit]; // exactly one move per symbol
    }
    state == 0 // accept when the remainder is 0
}

fn main() {
    for w in ["11", "110", "111", "1001", "10010", "12"] {
        let value = u32::from_str_radix(w, 2).ok();
        println!("{w:>5}  value={value:?}  accepted={}", accepts(w));
    }
}
# A DFA for binary numbers that are multiples of 3.
# The state is the remainder of the number read so far.
DELTA = {(0, "0"): 0, (0, "1"): 1,
         (1, "0"): 2, (1, "1"): 0,
         (2, "0"): 1, (2, "1"): 2}

def accepts(word: str) -> bool:
    state = 0                          # start state: remainder 0
    for ch in word:
        if ch not in "01":
            return False               # not in the alphabet
        state = DELTA[(state, ch)]     # exactly one move per symbol
    return state == 0                  # accept when the remainder is 0

for w in ["11", "110", "111", "1001", "10010", "12"]:
    value = int(w, 2) if set(w) <= {"0", "1"} else None
    print(f"{w:>5}  value={value}  accepted={accepts(w)}")
   11  value=Some(3)  accepted=true
  110  value=Some(6)  accepted=true
  111  value=Some(7)  accepted=false
 1001  value=Some(9)  accepted=true
10010  value=Some(18)  accepted=true
   12  value=None  accepted=false

That is the Rust output. Python prints 3 instead of Some(3) and True with a capital letter. A DFA reads each symbol once, so it runs in time O(n) and uses O(1) memory. A language is regular when some DFA accepts it.

Regular languages are closed under many operations. "Closed" means the result is regular again.

  • Complement. Swap accepting and non-accepting states. Now the DFA accepts "not a multiple of 3".
  • Intersection. Run two DFAs side by side. A state is a pair (p, q). This is the product construction. A 3-state and a 2-state DFA give 6 pairs.
  • Union, concatenation and star. These are easy with NFAs, in the next section.

A DFA needs a move for every symbol in every state. Drawings often leave some arrows out. Those missing arrows go to a hidden dead state. Before you complement a DFA, add the dead state. Otherwise the swap gives the wrong answer for strings that fall into it.

Nondeterminism and the subset construction

Take the language "the third symbol from the end is 1". A DFA reads from the left. It does not know where the end is. So it must remember the last three symbols: 8 possible states. A different kind of machine can simply guess. When it sees a 1, it guesses: "this is the third from the end". Then it checks that exactly two symbols follow.

That machine is a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA). From one state, a symbol can lead to several states or to none. It may also have epsilon moves, which read nothing. An NFA accepts when at least one path ends in an accepting state. Wrong guesses just die.

Can every NFA be turned into a DFA? Yes. The trick is to follow all guesses at once. A DFA state is the set of NFA states we could be in now.

Three NFA states

State 0 loops on 0 and 1. On 1 it may also guess and go to state 1. State 1 goes to state 2 on any symbol. State 2 accepts and has no moves.

Start with {0}

On 0, state 0 can only go to 0. So {0} goes to {0}. On 1, it can go to 0 or 1. So {0} goes to {0, 1}.

Process {0, 1}

On 0: state 0 gives 0, state 1 gives 2. Result {0, 2}. On 1: state 0 gives 0 and 1, state 1 gives 2. Result {0, 1, 2}.

Process {0, 2}

State 2 has no moves, so it adds nothing. On 0 we get {0}. On 1 we get {0, 1}. Both sets are known already.

Process {0, 1, 2}

On 0 we get {0, 2}. On 1 we get {0, 1, 2}. No new set appears, so we stop.

A DFA with 4 states

The states are {0}, {0, 1}, {0, 2} and {0, 1, 2}. The accepting ones contain NFA state 2: {0, 2} and {0, 1, 2}.

For every NFA with n states there is a DFA with at most 2^n states that accepts exactly the same language.

Proof

Let the NFA have states Q. First define the epsilon closure E(S) of a set S. It is S plus every state reachable from S by epsilon moves. Build a DFA whose states are subsets of Q. Its start state is E(\{q_0\}). From a set S on symbol a, go to E of all states reachable from S by one a-move. A set is accepting when it contains an accepting NFA state.

Now use induction on the length of the input. After reading w, the DFA is in exactly the set of NFA states that some path on w can reach. For w = \varepsilon this is the start set. One more symbol follows the definition of the move. So the DFA accepts w exactly when some NFA path on w ends in an accepting state. There are 2^n subsets of Q, which gives the bound.

In simple words: an NFA is not more powerful than a DFA. It is only shorter to write. Here is the cost. We build the NFA for "the k-th symbol from the end is 1" and count the DFA states we reach.

use std::collections::{BTreeSet, HashMap, VecDeque};

type Set = BTreeSet<usize>;

// NFA for "the k-th symbol from the end is 1". States 0..=k. State k accepts.
fn nfa_step(k: usize, q: usize, c: char) -> Vec<usize> {
    match (q, c) {
        (0, '1') => vec![0, 1],         // guess "this 1 is k-th from the end", or wait
        (0, _) => vec![0],              // keep waiting
        (q, _) if q < k => vec![q + 1], // count the symbols after the guess
        _ => vec![],                    // state k has no moves: a wrong guess dies
    }
}

// Subset construction: each DFA state is a set of NFA states.
fn build_dfa(k: usize) -> HashMap<Set, [Set; 2]> {
    let mut dfa = HashMap::new();
    let mut todo = VecDeque::from([Set::from([0])]);
    while let Some(s) = todo.pop_front() {
        if dfa.contains_key(&s) { continue; }
        let next = ['0', '1'].map(|c| s.iter().flat_map(|&q| nfa_step(k, q, c)).collect::<Set>());
        todo.extend(next.iter().cloned()); // visit the new sets later
        dfa.insert(s, next);
    }
    dfa
}

fn dfa_accepts(dfa: &HashMap<Set, [Set; 2]>, k: usize, word: &str) -> bool {
    let mut s = Set::from([0]);
    for c in word.chars() {
        s = dfa[&s][(c == '1') as usize].clone(); // one move per symbol
    }
    s.contains(&k) // accept if any NFA path accepts
}

fn main() {
    for k in 1..=6 {
        println!("k={k}: NFA has {} states, DFA has {} states", k + 1, build_dfa(k).len());
    }
    let dfa = build_dfa(3);
    for w in ["0100", "0010", "1111000"] {
        println!("k=3 {w}: {}", dfa_accepts(&dfa, 3, w));
    }
}
from collections import deque

def nfa_step(k: int, q: int, c: str) -> set[int]:
    """NFA for 'the k-th symbol from the end is 1'. States 0..k. State k accepts."""
    if q == 0:
        return {0, 1} if c == "1" else {0}   # guess, or keep waiting
    if q < k:
        return {q + 1}                       # count the symbols after the guess
    return set()                             # state k has no moves: a wrong guess dies

def build_dfa(k: int) -> dict:
    """Subset construction: each DFA state is a set of NFA states."""
    dfa, todo = {}, deque([frozenset({0})])
    while todo:
        s = todo.popleft()
        if s in dfa:
            continue
        nxt = tuple(frozenset(r for q in s for r in nfa_step(k, q, c)) for c in "01")
        todo.extend(nxt)                     # visit the new sets later
        dfa[s] = nxt
    return dfa

def dfa_accepts(dfa: dict, k: int, word: str) -> bool:
    s = frozenset({0})
    for c in word:
        s = dfa[s][c == "1"]                 # one move per symbol
    return k in s                            # accept if any NFA path accepts

for k in range(1, 7):
    print(f"k={k}: NFA has {k + 1} states, DFA has {len(build_dfa(k))} states")
dfa = build_dfa(3)
for w in ["0100", "0010", "1111000"]:
    print(f"k=3 {w}: {dfa_accepts(dfa, 3, w)}")
k=1: NFA has 2 states, DFA has 2 states
k=2: NFA has 3 states, DFA has 4 states
k=3: NFA has 4 states, DFA has 8 states
k=4: NFA has 5 states, DFA has 16 states
k=5: NFA has 6 states, DFA has 32 states
k=6: NFA has 7 states, DFA has 64 states
k=3 0100: true
k=3 0010: false
k=3 1111000: false

Python prints the same lines, with True and False in capitals. The NFA grows by one state for each step of k. The DFA doubles. The Myhill-Nerode theorem, later in this chapter, shows that no smaller DFA exists for this language. So the exponential cost is real, not a weakness of our method. This is why some regex engines build the DFA lazily, one state at a time, and keep only a cache of states.

"Nondeterministic" does not mean "random". The machine does not flip a coin. It accepts if some sequence of choices works. Think of it as a perfect guesser, or as running all choices in parallel.

Regular expressions and Kleene's theorem

The NFA above has a short description: (0|1)*1(0|1)(0|1). Read it as "anything, then a 1, then two more symbols". This is a regular expression. It is built from six rules.

  1. \emptyset means the empty language. \varepsilon means \{\varepsilon\}. A symbol \texttt{a} means \{\texttt{a}\}.
  2. If R and S are regular expressions, so are R \mid S (union), RS (concatenation) and R^* (star).

Star binds strongest, then concatenation, then union. So ab*|c means (\texttt{a}(\texttt{b}^*)) \mid \texttt{c}. Tools add short forms. R+ means RR^*. R? means R \mid \varepsilon. [0-9] means one digit.

A language is regular exactly when some regular expression describes it. So regular expressions, NFAs and DFAs all describe the same class of languages.

Proof idea

Expression to NFA (Thompson's construction). Build a small NFA for each base case. Then glue NFAs with epsilon moves. For R \mid S, add a new start with epsilon moves into both. For RS, link each accepting state of R to the start of S. For R^*, add a new accepting start and loop back from the end. Each rule adds at most two states, so the NFA has O(m) states for an expression of size m. By the subset construction, a DFA exists too.

DFA to expression (state elimination). Let arrows carry whole expressions, not single symbols. Remove states one by one. When you remove state q with a loop L, replace each path p \to q \to r by one arrow p \to r labelled A L^* B. In the end one arrow from start to accept remains. Its label is the expression.

Real regex engines come in two families. The difference matters for speed and for security.

Automata engines. RE2, Go's regexp and Rust's regex crate simulate an NFA or a lazy DFA. The Rust crate documents a worst case of O(m \cdot n) for regex size m and text length n. The price: no backreferences and no look-around.

Backtracking engines. PCRE, Python's re, Java and JavaScript try one choice and go back when it fails. They support backreferences like (.+)\1. But some patterns take exponential time.

We test the classic trap ^(a+)+$ on the text "aaa…ab". The pattern cannot match. A backtracking engine tries every way to split the a's between the inner and outer loop. That is about 2^n ways.

use regex::Regex;
use std::time::Instant;

fn main() {
    let pattern = Regex::new(r"^(a+)+$").unwrap(); // the same trap pattern
    for n in [16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 100_000] {
        let text = "a".repeat(n) + "b"; // almost matches, then fails at the end
        let t0 = Instant::now();
        let found = pattern.is_match(&text);
        let ms = t0.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1000.0;
        println!("n={n}  match={found}  time={ms:8.3} ms");
    }
}
import re
import time

pattern = re.compile(r"^(a+)+$")        # nested repetition: a classic trap
for n in [16, 18, 20, 22, 24]:
    text = "a" * n + "b"                 # almost matches, then fails at the end
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    found = pattern.match(text) is not None
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    print(f"n={n}  match={found}  time={ms:8.1f} ms")
Rust (release build):            Python 3.14:
n=16  match=false  time=   0.031 ms    n=16  match=False  time=     2.3 ms
n=18  match=false  time=   0.000 ms    n=18  match=False  time=     9.3 ms
n=20  match=false  time=   0.000 ms    n=20  match=False  time=    34.8 ms
n=22  match=false  time=   0.000 ms    n=22  match=False  time=   135.5 ms
n=24  match=false  time=   0.000 ms    n=24  match=False  time=   544.7 ms
n=100000  match=false  time=   0.069 ms

Each extra character doubles Python's time. At n = 40 it would take about ten hours. The Rust engine handles a text of 100,000 characters in under a millisecond. Your times will differ, but the shape will not. This attack is called ReDoS.

On 2 July 2019, Cloudflare deployed a new firewall rule. Its regular expression contained the part .*(?:.*=.*). The backtracking PCRE engine used all the CPU on its HTTP servers worldwide. The service went down for 27 minutes. One fix on their list was to move to RE2 or the Rust regex engine, which both guarantee run time.

Python 3.11 added atomic groups (?>...) and possessive quantifiers like a*+. They forbid backtracking into a part of the pattern, which can stop the blow-up. They help, but you must use them by hand.

A "regex" in a programming language is not always a regular expression in the theory sense. With a backreference, ^(.+)\1$ matches strings of the form ww, like abcabc. That language is not regular. It is not even context-free. Theory results, like linear time, hold only for true regular expressions.

What finite memory cannot do

Try to build a DFA for \{\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n : n \ge 0\}: some a's, then the same number of b's. The machine must count the a's. Say it has 5 states. After reading 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 a's, it has seen six different counts. By the pigeonhole principle, two counts end in the same state. From then on, the machine cannot tell them apart. This idea gives two tools.

If L is regular, there is a number p \ge 1 with this property. Every w \in L with |w| \ge p can be split as w = xyz with |xy| \le p and |y| \ge 1, and then xy^iz \in L for every i \ge 0.

Proof

Take a DFA for L with p states. Run it on w, where |w| \ge p. The first p symbols visit p + 1 states, counting the start. By the pigeonhole principle, some state q appears twice among them. Let x be the part before the first visit to q. Let y be the part between the two visits, and z the rest. The part y is a loop from q back to q. So we can go around it zero times, or many times, and still end in the same accepting state. Since both visits happen in the first p symbols, |xy| \le p.

In simple words: every long string of a regular language has a short loop near the start. You can repeat the loop or cut it out, and you stay in the language. We use the lemma backwards. If no split works, the language is not regular.

  1. Suppose L = \{\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n\} is regular, with pumping number p.
  2. Choose w = \texttt{a}^p\texttt{b}^p. It is in L and |w| = 2p \ge p.
  3. Take any split w = xyz with |xy| \le p and |y| \ge 1. The first p symbols are all a's. So y = \texttt{a}^k with k \ge 1.
  4. Pump with i = 2. We get \texttt{a}^{p+k}\texttt{b}^p. It has more a's than b's, so it is not in L.
  5. Every split fails. This contradicts the lemma. So L is not regular.

The pumping lemma only works in one direction. A stronger tool gives an exact answer. Two strings x and y are equivalent for L, written x \equiv_L y, when every ending z treats them the same: xz \in L exactly when yz \in L. An ending that treats them differently is a distinguishing extension.

A language L is regular exactly when \equiv_L has finitely many classes. The number of classes equals the number of states of the smallest DFA for L.

Proof idea

If a DFA ends in the same state on x and on y, then x \equiv_L y. So a DFA with k states gives at most k classes. In the other direction, build a DFA whose states are the classes themselves. The class of x moves on symbol a to the class of xa. This is well defined because equivalent strings stay equivalent after adding a. It accepts the classes of strings in L. This DFA has one state per class, and no DFA can have fewer.

Three uses, with numbers.

  • Multiples of 3. The strings \varepsilon, 1 and 10 have remainders 0, 1 and 2. The ending 1 distinguishes \varepsilon from 1, because 1 is not a multiple of 3 but 11 is. So there are exactly 3 classes. Our 3-state DFA is the smallest.
  • \texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n. For i \ne j, the ending \texttt{b}^i distinguishes \texttt{a}^i from \texttt{a}^j. That gives infinitely many classes. So the language is not regular.
  • k-th symbol from the end. Any two different strings of length k differ at some place. Add enough 0s to move that place to position k from the end. So all 2^k strings are in different classes. The DFA needs 2^k states.

The theorem also gives DFA minimisation. Start with two groups: accepting and not accepting. Split a group when one symbol sends its states into different groups. Repeat until nothing splits. Each final group becomes one state. Hopcroft's version of this runs in O(n \log n) for a fixed alphabet.

In a pumping proof, you choose w, but you do not choose the split. You must show that every allowed split fails. Also, passing the pumping test does not prove that a language is regular. Some non-regular languages pass it. Myhill-Nerode has no such gap.

Context-free grammars and pushdown automata

Brackets in code must match. (()()) is fine. ())( is not. We just saw that finite memory cannot count. So we need a new kind of description. Here is a grammar for balanced brackets.

S -> ( S ) S
S -> ε

Start with S. Replace S by one of its right sides. Repeat until no S is left. For example: S \Rightarrow (S)S \Rightarrow ((S)S)S \Rightarrow (()S)S \Rightarrow (())S \Rightarrow (()). Each step is part of a derivation.

A context-free grammar (CFG) has variables, terminals, rules of the form "variable \to string", and a start variable. "Context-free" means a variable is rewritten the same way wherever it stands. A language is context-free when some CFG generates it. Here is a grammar for sums and products.

E -> E + T | T        an expression is a sum of terms
T -> T * F | F        a term is a product of factors
F -> ( E ) | num      a factor is a number or a bracketed expression

A parse tree shows the structure of a string. A grammar is ambiguous when a string has two parse trees. The grammar E -> E - E | num is ambiguous. For 5 − 2 − 1 it gives (5 − 2) − 1 = 2 and 5 − (2 − 1) = 4. The layered grammar above removes this problem. Each level of precedence gets its own variable. The left recursion E -> E + T makes operators group from the left.

Which machine matches grammars? Add a stack to an NFA. The result is a pushdown automaton (PDA). For \texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n: push a mark for each a. Pop a mark for each b. Accept when the input and the stack are both empty at the end.

A language is generated by some context-free grammar exactly when some (nondeterministic) pushdown automaton accepts it.

Proof idea

Grammar to PDA. Push the start variable. If a variable is on top, replace it by the right side of some rule: a guess. If a terminal is on top, it must match the next input symbol, so pop it. Accept when the stack is empty at the end of the input. PDA to grammar. First change the PDA so each move pushes or pops one symbol. For each pair of states p, q, make a variable A_{pq}. It generates the strings that take the PDA from p to q with the stack the same at both ends.

Nondeterminism matters here, unlike for finite automata. Even-length palindromes, like abba, need a PDA that guesses the middle. No deterministic PDA can accept them. Compilers use grammars that a deterministic PDA can parse, so they run in linear time. The Compilers chapter covers these LL and LR parsers.

If L is context-free, there is p \ge 1 such that every w \in L with |w| \ge p splits as w = uvxyz with |vxy| \le p and |vy| \ge 1, and uv^ixy^iz \in L for all i \ge 0.

Proof idea

A long string has a tall parse tree. A tall path has more nodes than the grammar has variables. By the pigeonhole principle, some variable A repeats on the path. The subtree under the upper A can replace the subtree under the lower A, again and again. That repeats v and y together. Use it on \texttt{a}^p\texttt{b}^p\texttt{c}^p. The window vxy is at most p long, so it touches at most two of the three letters. Pumping breaks the balance. So \{\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n\texttt{c}^n\} is not context-free.

Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and star. They are not closed under intersection. The languages \{\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n\texttt{c}^m\} and \{\texttt{a}^m\texttt{b}^n\texttt{c}^n\} are both context-free. Their intersection is \{\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n\texttt{c}^n\}, which is not. But the intersection of a context-free language with a regular language is always context-free.

Do not parse HTML, JSON or code with one regular expression. Nesting needs a stack, and a regular expression has none. Use a real parser. A regex is fine for the small pieces, such as numbers and names.

Parsing with CYK

Given a grammar and a string, is the string in the language? For any CFG, one clean method is the CYK algorithm. It needs the grammar in a special shape first.

A grammar is in Chomsky normal form (CNF) when every rule is A \to BC (two variables) or A \to a (one terminal). The start variable may also have S \to \varepsilon. Every CFG can be changed into CNF with the same language.

Here is a CNF grammar for non-empty balanced brackets. L stands for "(" and R for ")". A stands for "a balanced string, then a closing bracket".

S -> S S | L R | L A
A -> S R
L -> (
R -> )

CYK is dynamic programming, the method of the dynamic programming chapter. For each piece of the string, it finds the set of variables that can generate that piece. It handles short pieces first. A piece of length \ell is split in every way into a left part and a right part. If B makes the left part, C makes the right part, and A \to BC is a rule, then A makes the piece.

  1. Length 1. The four symbols give L, L, R, R.
  2. Length 2. "((" and "))" give nothing. The middle "()" is L then R, so it gives S.
  3. Length 3. "(()" gives nothing. "())" splits as "()" + ")", which is S then R. The rule A → S R gives A.
  4. Length 4. "(())" splits as "(" + "())", which is L then A. The rule S → L A gives S.
  5. S makes the whole string, so "(())" is balanced.
// CYK for balanced brackets. The grammar is in Chomsky normal form:
// S -> S S | L R | L A    A -> S R    L -> (    R -> )
const S: u8 = 1; const A: u8 = 2; const L: u8 = 4; const R: u8 = 8; // one bit each
const RULES: [(u8, u8, u8); 4] = [(S, S, S), (S, L, R), (S, L, A), (A, S, R)];

fn cyk(word: &str) -> bool {
    let w: Vec<char> = word.chars().collect();
    let n = w.len();
    if n == 0 { return false; }
    // t[len][i] = set of variables that make the piece of length len starting at i
    let mut t = vec![vec![0u8; n]; n + 1];
    for (i, &c) in w.iter().enumerate() {
        t[1][i] = match c { '(' => L, ')' => R, _ => 0 };
    }
    for len in 2..=n {
        for i in 0..=n - len {
            for split in 1..len { // left part has length split
                let (left, right) = (t[split][i], t[len - split][i + split]);
                for &(head, b, c) in &RULES {
                    if left & b != 0 && right & c != 0 { t[len][i] |= head; }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    t[n][0] & S != 0 // does S make the whole word?
}

fn main() {
    for w in ["()", "(()())", "())(", "((()", "(()(()))"] {
        println!("{w:<10} {}", cyk(w));
    }
}
# CYK for balanced brackets. The grammar is in Chomsky normal form:
# S -> S S | L R | L A    A -> S R    L -> (    R -> )
RULES = [("S", "S", "S"), ("S", "L", "R"), ("S", "L", "A"), ("A", "S", "R")]
TERMINALS = {"(": {"L"}, ")": {"R"}}

def cyk(word: str) -> bool:
    n = len(word)
    if n == 0:
        return False
    # t[length][i] = set of variables that make the piece of that length at i
    t = [[set() for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i, c in enumerate(word):
        t[1][i] = set(TERMINALS.get(c, set()))
    for length in range(2, n + 1):
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            for split in range(1, length):      # left part has length split
                left, right = t[split][i], t[length - split][i + split]
                for head, b, c in RULES:
                    if b in left and c in right:
                        t[length][i].add(head)
    return "S" in t[n][0]                       # does S make the whole word?

for w in ["()", "(()())", "())(", "((()", "(()(()))"]:
    print(f"{w:<10} {cyk(w)}")
()         true
(()())     true
())(       false
((()       false
(()(()))   true

Python prints the same, with True and False. There are three nested loops over the string: length, start and split. So CYK costs O(n^3 \cdot |G|), where |G| is the size of the grammar. For 1,000 tokens that is already about 10^9 / 6 steps. That is fine for short inputs and research, but too slow for a compiler. Other general methods exist. Earley's parser is also cubic in the worst case, but linear on many practical grammars. GLR parsers follow several LR choices at once. In 1975 Valiant showed that CFG recognition can run as fast as matrix multiplication.

Exams often give a small CNF grammar and a string of length 4 or 5. They ask you to fill the CYK triangle. Write the table with length on one axis and start position on the other. Check each split, and list every variable you find, not only S.

The Chomsky hierarchy and real software

In the late 1950s, Noam Chomsky described grammars of growing power. Each level allows more general rules. Each level also matches a stronger kind of machine.

The Chomsky hierarchy
TypeGrammar rulesMachineExample languageIn real software
3: regularA \to aB or A \to aDFA or NFAmultiples of 3lexers, input checks, protocol states
2: context-freeA \to any stringpushdown automaton\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n, bracketsparsers, JSON, LLM grammar decoding
1: context-sensitive\alpha A \beta \to \alpha \gamma \beta, \gamma not emptylinear bounded automaton\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n\texttt{c}^nrarely used directly
0: unrestricted\alpha \to \betaTuring machineprograms that haltany general program

Type 0 is the world of Turing machines. The next chapter, Computability, shows that some type-0 questions have no algorithm at all. Here is where the lower levels appear in real systems.

Lexers and search tools (type 3)

A compiler first cuts the source into tokens: names, numbers, operators. Each token kind is a regular expression. Lexer generators such as lex and flex join them into one DFA. Ken Thompson's 1968 paper turned regular expressions into NFAs for searching text. Tools like grep grew from that work.

Protocols and user interfaces (type 3)

A TCP connection moves through named states such as LISTEN, SYN-SENT and ESTABLISHED. The TCP standard (RFC 9293) defines this state machine. Checkout flows, traffic lights and game menus are finite automata too. Writing them as an explicit state table makes illegal moves impossible.

Parsers (type 2)

Since Python 3.9, CPython uses a PEG parser (PEP 617) in place of its old LL(1) parser. Many editors use tree-sitter, a parser generator that updates the syntax tree after each edit. Compilers often use hand-written recursive descent: one function per grammar variable.

Structured output for LLMs (types 3 and 2)

An LLM picks one token at a time. A grammar engine can mask the tokens that would break the format. Outlines (Willard and Louf, 2023) compiles a regular expression into a finite automaton for this. XGrammar (2024) runs a pushdown automaton for context-free grammars such as JSON. It precomputes most of the token mask ahead of time. The llguidance library combines an Earley parser with a regex-based lexer. Its README says it has powered OpenAI's JSON Schema structured outputs since May 2025.

Beyond context-free

"Every variable is declared before use" is not context-free. Neither is "the types match". So compilers parse with a CFG first. Then they check these rules in a separate step, with a symbol table. This split keeps each step simple and fast.

A bigger language is not a harder language. \Sigma^* contains every string, and a one-state DFA accepts it. Difficulty is about the structure of memory the machine needs. Finite states, one stack, or an unlimited tape.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for automata and formal languages
PatternPurposeModelNote
State = what you must rememberDesign a DFAMultiples of 3: the state is the remainderAdd the dead state before complementing.
Product of two DFAsIntersection of two regular languages3 states × 2 states = 6 pairsUnion works the same way with a different accept rule.
Guess and checkWrite a small NFAGuess the 1 that is third from the endNondeterministic is not random.
Set of statesTurn an NFA into a DFA{0}, {0,1}, {0,2}, {0,1,2}Can need 2^n states, so build lazily.
Glue with epsilon movesRegex to NFA (Thompson)R|S: new start into bothThe NFA stays O(m) in size.
Automata regex engineMatch untrusted text safelyRust regex: O(m \cdot n)No backreferences or look-around.
Pump the loopProve a language is not regular\texttt{a}^{p+k}\texttt{b}^p leaves the languageYou pick w, not the split.
Distinguishing extensionsCount the states of the smallest DFA\texttt{b}^i separates \texttt{a}^i from \texttt{a}^jInfinitely many classes means not regular.
One variable per precedence levelWrite an unambiguous expression grammarE -> E + T | TLeft recursion groups from the left.
Push on open, pop on closeMatch nesting with a PDABrackets, \texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^nPalindromes need a guess: nondeterminism.
Table by piece lengthParse any CFG (CYK)S → L A makes "(())"Convert to CNF first. It costs O(n^3).
Grammar mask on tokensKeep LLM output validAutomaton for a regex, PDA for JSONThe mask limits format, not truth.

Practice

An NFA has 5 states. What is the largest number of states the subset construction can give?

  • 5
  • 25
  • 32

Each DFA state is a subset of the 5 NFA states, and there are 2^5 = 32 subsets.

Which language is regular?

  • Strings with the same number of a's and b's
  • Strings with an even number of a's
  • Balanced brackets

Two states are enough: "even so far" and "odd so far". The other two need to count without a limit.

Which machine matches context-free grammars exactly?

  • Deterministic finite automaton
  • Nondeterministic pushdown automaton
  • Deterministic pushdown automaton

Deterministic PDAs are weaker. Even-length palindromes need a guess for the middle.

The regular expression (0|1)*1(0|1) describes strings whose ? symbol from the end is 1.

The smallest DFA for binary multiples of 5 has ? states.

CYK on a string of length n costs O(n^{\text{?}}) with ? = ?.

  1. Draw a DFA over {a, b} for "contains the substring ab". How many states does it need?
    Answer

    Three states. State 0: no progress. State 1: the last symbol was a. State 2: we have seen ab, and it loops on both symbols. From 0, a goes to 1 and b stays at 0. From 1, a stays at 1 and b goes to 2. Only state 2 accepts.

  2. Write a regular expression for binary strings that do not contain 11.
    Answer

    One answer: (0|10)*(1|ε). Every 1 inside the string must be followed by a 0. A single 1 may stand at the very end.

  3. Use Myhill-Nerode to show that the palindromes over {a, b} are not regular.
    Answer

    Take the strings \texttt{a}^i\texttt{b} for i = 0, 1, 2, \dots. For i \ne j, add the ending \texttt{a}^i. Then \texttt{a}^i\texttt{b}\texttt{a}^i is a palindrome, but \texttt{a}^j\texttt{b}\texttt{a}^i is not. So the strings are in infinitely many different classes.

  4. Give a context-free grammar for \{\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n : n \ge 0\} and derive aabb.
    Answer

    S -> a S b | ε. Derivation: S \Rightarrow \texttt{a}S\texttt{b} \Rightarrow \texttt{aa}S\texttt{bb} \Rightarrow \texttt{aabb}.

  5. Expert: an API gateway checks request paths with user-supplied patterns. Which kind of regex engine should it use, and what limit should it still set?
    Answer

    Use an automata engine such as RE2 or Rust's regex, so matching is O(m \cdot n) and cannot blow up on the text. A huge pattern can still make a huge automaton. So also limit the pattern size, for example with the crate's size limit setting. Reject patterns that need backreferences.

Key takeaways

  • A language is a set of strings. Every yes-or-no question about text is a language.
  • DFAs, NFAs and regular expressions describe the same class: the regular languages.
  • The subset construction turns an NFA into a DFA, but it can need 2^n states.
  • The pumping lemma proves non-regularity. Myhill-Nerode gives the exact size of the smallest DFA.
  • Automata regex engines run in O(m \cdot n). Backtracking engines can take exponential time: ReDoS.
  • Context-free grammars match pushdown automata. A stack is what nesting needs.
  • CYK parses any grammar in CNF in O(n^3). Compilers use faster deterministic subsets.
  • The Chomsky hierarchy has four levels. Real tools use the lowest level that does the job.

Sources

  • Jeff Erickson, Models of Computation notes. Free notes on strings, regular languages, automata, nondeterminism and context-free languages.
  • Rust regex crate documentation. The O(m \cdot n) guarantee, ReDoS and the missing features.
  • Python re module. Backtracking, backreferences, atomic groups and possessive quantifiers (added in 3.11).
  • Cloudflare: Details of the outage on July 2, 2019. The regex, the 27 minutes and the action items.
  • XGrammar: Flexible and Efficient Structured Generation Engine for Large Language Models. Pushdown automata for grammar-guided decoding.
  • llguidance on GitHub. Earley parser with a regex-derivative lexer, and its integrations.

Computability

Some problems have no algorithm. The reason is not slow hardware or a missing idea. We can prove that no program can ever solve them. This chapter gives that proof step by step. Then it shows what the limit means for compilers, static analysis and AI agents that check code.

  • Describe a Turing machine and run one by hand and in code.
  • Explain the Church-Turing thesis and the universal machine.
  • Tell decidable, recognisable and co-recognisable problems apart.
  • Prove that the halting problem is undecidable with the diagonal argument.
  • Use reductions and Rice's theorem to judge what a code checker or an AI agent can promise.

Turing machines

The previous chapter showed that \{\texttt{a}^n\texttt{b}^n\texttt{c}^n\} is not context-free. One stack is not enough memory for it. But a person with a pencil can check it easily. Cross off one a, one b and one c. Go back to the start. Repeat. At the end, everything must be crossed off.

In 1936 Alan Turing turned this "person with a pencil" into a mathematical machine. A Turing machine has three parts.

  • A tape of cells, unlimited to the right. At the start it holds the input. All other cells are blank.
  • A head that sits on one cell. It reads the cell, writes a symbol and moves one step left or right.
  • A finite set of states with a rule table: "in state q, reading a: write b, move, go to state r".

The machine stops when it enters an accept state, or when no rule fits, which means reject. But it may also run forever. So a Turing machine has three possible outcomes on an input: accept, reject or loop. Here is our crossing-off machine, written as data. Each rule is five words: state, read, write, move, next state.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// The machine is data: "state read write move next", five words per rule.
// It decides { a^n b^n c^n }. X, Y, Z mark crossed-off a, b, c. '_' is blank.
const MACHINE: &str = "
q0 a X R q1  q0 Y Y R q4  q0 _ _ R accept
q1 a a R q1  q1 Y Y R q1  q1 b Y R q2
q2 b b R q2  q2 Z Z R q2  q2 c Z L q3
q3 a a L q3  q3 b b L q3  q3 Y Y L q3  q3 Z Z L q3  q3 X X R q0
q4 Y Y R q4  q4 Z Z R q4  q4 _ _ R accept";

#[derive(Debug)]
#[allow(dead_code)] // the step counts are only printed with {:?}
enum Outcome { Accept(usize), Reject(usize), OutOfFuel }

fn run(machine: &str, input: &str, fuel: usize) -> Outcome {
    let w: Vec<&str> = machine.split_whitespace().collect();
    let rules: HashMap<(&str, &str), (&str, &str, &str)> =
        w.chunks(5).map(|r| ((r[0], r[1]), (r[2], r[3], r[4]))).collect();
    let mut tape: Vec<String> = input.chars().map(String::from).collect();
    let (mut state, mut head) = ("q0", 0usize);
    for step in 0..fuel {
        if state == "accept" { return Outcome::Accept(step); }
        if head == tape.len() { tape.push("_".into()); } // the tape grows on demand
        let Some(&(write, mv, next)) = rules.get(&(state, tape[head].as_str())) else {
            return Outcome::Reject(step); // no rule for this case: reject
        };
        tape[head] = write.into();
        head = if mv == "R" { head + 1 } else { head.saturating_sub(1) };
        state = next;
    }
    Outcome::OutOfFuel // we gave up; we do NOT know if it would halt
}

fn main() {
    for input in ["abc", "aabbcc", "aabbc", "abcabc", ""] {
        println!("{input:>7}: {:?}", run(MACHINE, input, 10_000));
    }
    println!("aaabbbccc with fuel 20: {:?}", run(MACHINE, "aaabbbccc", 20));
    for n in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32] {
        let input = "a".repeat(n) + &"b".repeat(n) + &"c".repeat(n);
        println!("n={n:>2}: {:?}", run(MACHINE, &input, 1_000_000));
    }
}
# The machine is data: "state read write move next", five words per rule.
# It decides { a^n b^n c^n }. X, Y, Z mark crossed-off a, b, c. '_' is blank.
MACHINE = """
q0 a X R q1  q0 Y Y R q4  q0 _ _ R accept
q1 a a R q1  q1 Y Y R q1  q1 b Y R q2
q2 b b R q2  q2 Z Z R q2  q2 c Z L q3
q3 a a L q3  q3 b b L q3  q3 Y Y L q3  q3 Z Z L q3  q3 X X R q0
q4 Y Y R q4  q4 Z Z R q4  q4 _ _ R accept"""

def run(machine: str, text: str, fuel: int) -> str:
    w = machine.split()
    rules = {(w[i], w[i + 1]): (w[i + 2], w[i + 3], w[i + 4]) for i in range(0, len(w), 5)}
    tape, state, head = list(text), "q0", 0
    for step in range(fuel):
        if state == "accept":
            return f"Accept({step})"
        if head == len(tape):
            tape.append("_")                   # the tape grows on demand
        if (state, tape[head]) not in rules:
            return f"Reject({step})"           # no rule for this case: reject
        tape[head], move, state = rules[(state, tape[head])]
        head = head + 1 if move == "R" else max(head - 1, 0)
    return "OutOfFuel"                         # we gave up; we do NOT know if it would halt

for text in ["abc", "aabbcc", "aabbc", "abcabc", ""]:
    print(f"{text:>7}: {run(MACHINE, text, 10_000)}")
print("aaabbbccc with fuel 20:", run(MACHINE, "aaabbbccc", 20))
for n in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]:
    print(f"n={n:>2}: {run(MACHINE, 'a' * n + 'b' * n + 'c' * n, 1_000_000)}")
    abc: Accept(8)
 aabbcc: Accept(23)
  aabbc: Reject(13)
 abcabc: Reject(7)
       : Accept(1)
aaabbbccc with fuel 20: OutOfFuel
n= 1: Accept(8)
n= 2: Accept(23)
n= 4: Accept(77)
n= 8: Accept(281)
n=16: Accept(1073)
n=32: Accept(4193)

Both versions print the same lines. Doubling n multiplies the steps by about 4, so this machine takes O(n^2) steps. Look at the line with fuel 20. The simulator gave up. That does not mean the machine loops. It only means we stopped watching. Keep this in mind for the rest of the chapter.

A Turing machine has a finite set of states Q, an input alphabet \Sigma, a tape alphabet \Gamma \supseteq \Sigma \cup \{\_\}, a transition function \delta : Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L, R\}, a start state, an accept state and a reject state. A configuration is the current state, the tape contents and the head position.

Many variants exist: several tapes, a tape unlimited in both directions, or nondeterministic choices. All of them recognise the same languages. A machine with k tapes can be simulated on one tape with at most a square slowdown: t steps become O(t^2).

Do not think "if it does not accept, it rejects". A Turing machine can loop forever. Many proofs go wrong at exactly this point. Always ask: does this machine halt on every input?

The Church-Turing thesis

In the 1930s, several people tried to define "algorithm" exactly. Their definitions looked very different. But they all turned out to compute the same functions.

  1. 1928 The decision problem. Hilbert and Ackermann ask for a method that decides if any statement of first-order logic is valid.
  2. 1931 Gödel. His incompleteness theorem shows limits of formal proof. The Logic and formal methods chapter covers it.
  3. 1936 Church and Turing. Church uses the lambda calculus. Turing uses his machines. Both show that the decision problem has no solution.
  4. 1938 Kleene. He proves the recursion theorem: programs can refer to their own code.
  5. 1946 Post. He finds an undecidable puzzle about matching strings, the Post correspondence problem.
  6. 1953 Rice. Every non-trivial question about what programs compute is undecidable.
  7. 1970 Matiyasevich. He finishes the proof that Hilbert's tenth problem, solving whole-number equations, is undecidable.
  8. 2024 Busy Beaver 5. An online team proves the value of BB(5) with a computer-checked proof.

Every function that can be computed by an effective method, step by step and without insight, can be computed by a Turing machine.

This is a thesis, not a theorem. "Effective method" is an everyday idea, not a mathematical object. So no proof is possible. The evidence is strong, though. Turing machines, the lambda calculus, general recursive functions, register machines and every normal programming language compute exactly the same functions. A system that can simulate a Turing machine, given enough memory, is Turing complete. Python and Rust are Turing complete. So are C++ templates and Conway's Game of Life.

If you can describe a method in clear steps, a Turing machine can run it. So when we prove "no Turing machine can do X", we really prove "no program in any language can do X".

"Turing complete" says nothing about speed. It is about what can be computed at all, with unlimited time and memory. Also, a real computer has finite memory. In theory it is a finite automaton with a huge number of states. We still model it as a Turing machine, because that number is far too big to use.

The universal machine

Look at the simulator again. The machine is a string. The simulator reads that string and the input, and it runs the machine. One fixed program runs every Turing machine. Turing described such a machine in his 1936 paper.

To do this, we write a machine M as a string. We call it the encoding of M and write it \langle M \rangle. Our five-word rule format is one encoding. Any clear format works.

There is a Turing machine U such that, for every machine M and input w, U on \langle M, w \rangle accepts if M accepts w, rejects if M rejects w, and loops if M loops on w.

Proof idea

U keeps three things on its tapes: the rule table \langle M \rangle, the tape of M, and the current state of M. In each round it finds the rule for the current state and symbol. It updates the simulated tape, head and state. It stops exactly when M stops. Our Rust and Python programs do the same thing. By the Church-Turing thesis, a Turing machine can do it too.

This idea is everywhere. A CPU runs any program stored in memory, the stored-program idea from the How computers compute chapter. The Python interpreter runs any Python file. A WebAssembly runtime runs any module. An agent framework runs any tool call it is given. Code is data, and data can be run.

A universal machine can run any program. It cannot predict any program. To know what M does, U must simulate it. If M loops, U loops too. The next sections show that no shortcut exists.

Decidable and recognisable

Ask two questions about a program P. First: "does P print hi within 1,000 steps?" Run it for 1,000 steps and look. You always get an answer. Second: "does P ever print hi?" Run it and wait. If it prints hi, you can say yes. If it does not, you wait forever and never know.

  • A language is decidable when some Turing machine halts on every input and answers correctly. That machine is a decider.
  • A language is recognisable (also called recursively enumerable) when some machine accepts exactly its strings. On other strings, that machine may reject or loop.
  • A language is co-recognisable when its complement is recognisable. You can confirm every "no" answer.

Decidable problems include: does a DFA accept w? Is the language of a DFA empty? Do two DFAs accept the same language? Does a context-free grammar generate w? The CYK algorithm answers the last one. Recognisers can search through infinitely many cases with dovetailing. To test "does P halt on some input?", run 1 step on input 1. Then 2 steps on inputs 1 and 2. Then 3 steps on inputs 1, 2 and 3, and so on. If any run halts, you find it.

A language is decidable exactly when it is both recognisable and co-recognisable.

Proof

If L is decidable, its decider recognises L. Swap accept and reject, and you recognise the complement. In the other direction, let R_1 recognise L and R_2 recognise its complement. On input w, run both in turns, one step each. Every w is in L or in its complement. So one of them accepts after finitely many steps. If R_1 accepts, say yes. If R_2 accepts, say no. This always halts.

"Recognisable" is not "half decidable" in a weak sense. A recogniser gives a correct yes for every yes-instance. What it cannot promise is an answer for no-instances. If you add a timeout, you get a third answer: "unknown". That is honest. Calling it "no" is a bug.

The diagonal argument

Before the halting problem, here is a simpler fact. There are more problems than programs. So most problems have no program at all. The proof idea comes from Georg Cantor, who used it in 1891 to show that there are more real numbers than whole numbers.

Every program is a finite string. So we can list all programs: P_1, P_2, P_3, \dots, first by length, then in alphabetical order. A set we can list like this is countable. Now make a table. Row i is program P_i. Column j is the input string w_j. The cell says whether P_i accepts w_j.

The set of all programs is countable, but the set of all languages over \{0, 1\} is not. So some languages are not recognised by any Turing machine.

Proof

Suppose we could list all languages L_1, L_2, \dots. List all strings w_1, w_2, \dots too. Define D = \{ w_i : w_i \notin L_i \}. For every i, D and L_i disagree on w_i. So D is not in the list. This contradicts the claim that the list holds every language. Programs can be listed, so they cover only countably many languages. Most languages are left without a program.

This proof says "most problems are unsolvable", but it does not name one we care about. The halting problem does. Its proof uses the same diagonal trick on a table of programs and inputs.

The new row must differ from every row in at least one place. Flipping only the diagonal does this, because row i is checked in column i. Students sometimes flip a random cell. Then row D might still equal some other row.

The halting problem, step by step

Define \mathrm{HALT} = \{ \langle P, x \rangle : \text{program } P \text{ halts on input } x \}. A perfect halting checker would be wonderful. It would find every infinite loop before you ship. It would also settle open problems in mathematics. For example, write a program that searches for a counterexample to a conjecture and stops when it finds one. Ask the checker if it halts.

Assume a checker

Suppose a program H(P, x) exists. It always halts. It says yes when P halts on x, and no when P loops on x.

Build a troublemaker

Write D(P). It runs H(P, P): "does P halt when given its own code?" If the answer is yes, D loops forever. If no, D halts.

D is a real program

D only calls H and adds an if and a loop. If H is a program, so is D. So we may feed D its own code: D(D).

Case 1: D(D) halts

Then H(D, D) says yes. But on yes, D loops forever. So D(D) does not halt. Contradiction.

Case 2: D(D) loops

Then H(D, D) says no. But on no, D halts at once. So D(D) halts. Contradiction again.

So H cannot exist

Both cases are impossible. The only assumption was that H exists. So it does not. D is the flipped diagonal: it differs from every program P on the input P.

No Turing machine decides \mathrm{HALT}. But \mathrm{HALT} is recognisable. So its complement, "P loops on x", is not recognisable.

Proof

Undecidable: this is the argument in the slides above. Recognisable: on \langle P, x \rangle, run the universal machine on P and x. If the simulation halts, accept. Complement: if it were recognisable too, then \mathrm{HALT} would be recognisable and co-recognisable. By the theorem of the last section it would be decidable. That is false.

We can watch the proof work. The code below takes any claimed checker and builds the troublemaker for it. Then it compares the checker's answer with what really happens. A program "halts" here if it stops within its step budget. The troublemaker that loops uses up any budget you give it.

use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

// A program we can run with a step budget. It returns true if it halts in time.
struct Program { run: Box<dyn Fn(u64) -> bool> }

// Someone claims: "this function tells you if a program halts".
type Checker = fn(&Program) -> bool;

// Build the program that asks the checker about itself, then does the opposite.
fn trouble(check: Checker) -> Rc<Program> {
    Rc::new_cyclic(|me: &Weak<Program>| {
        let me = me.clone(); // the program gets a handle to its own code
        Program {
            run: Box::new(move |fuel| {
                if check(&me.upgrade().unwrap()) {
                    for _ in 0..fuel {} // "halts", says the checker: so loop forever
                    false               // (here: until the budget is gone)
                } else {
                    true // "loops", says the checker: so halt at once
                }
            }),
        }
    })
}

fn always_yes(_: &Program) -> bool { true }
fn always_no(_: &Program) -> bool { false }

fn main() {
    for (name, check) in [("always_yes", always_yes as Checker), ("always_no", always_no)] {
        let t = trouble(check);
        let says = check(&t);
        let really = (t.run)(1_000_000);
        println!("{name}: says halts={says}, halts in 10^6 steps={really}, wrong={}", says != really);
    }
}
import inspect

def make_trouble(check):
    """Build the program that asks the checker about itself, then does the opposite."""
    def trouble(fuel: int) -> bool:        # True means "it halted within the budget"
        if check(trouble):                 # the program can name itself
            for _ in range(fuel):          # "halts", says the checker: so loop forever
                pass                       # (here: until the budget is gone)
            return False
        return True                        # "loops", says the checker: so halt at once
    return trouble

def always_yes(prog) -> bool:
    return True

def always_no(prog) -> bool:
    return False

def reads_source(prog) -> bool:
    """A 'smarter' checker: it says 'loops' when the code contains a loop."""
    code = inspect.getsource(prog)
    return "for " not in code and "while " not in code

for check in [always_yes, always_no, reads_source]:
    t = make_trouble(check)
    says, really = check(t), t(1_000_000)
    print(f"{check.__name__}: says halts={says}, halts in 10^6 steps={really}, wrong={says != really}")
Rust:
always_yes: says halts=true, halts in 10^6 steps=false, wrong=true
always_no: says halts=false, halts in 10^6 steps=true, wrong=true
Python:
always_yes: says halts=True, halts in 10^6 steps=False, wrong=True
always_no: says halts=False, halts in 10^6 steps=True, wrong=True
reads_source: says halts=False, halts in 10^6 steps=True, wrong=True

Every checker is wrong on its own troublemaker. The Python version adds a checker that reads the source code. It fails too. You could try a checker that simulates the program. On the troublemaker, that checker calls itself again and again, and it never answers. Note the Rust trick: Rc::new_cyclic gives the program a handle to itself. A later section shows that every real language allows this.

Among all 5-state Turing machines on a blank tape that halt, which runs longest? In 2024 the Busy Beaver Challenge team proved the answer: 47,176,870 steps. Their proof checks all the machines, and it is verified in the Coq proof assistant, now called Rocq. For 6 states, nobody knows. In June 2025 a 6-state machine was found whose step count needs towers of powers of 10, stacked inside each other, just to write down. One 6-state machine behaves like an open problem similar to the Collatz problem. The busy beaver function grows faster than every computable function.

The theorem does not say "we cannot tell if this program halts". For most real programs we can. It says no single program answers correctly for all programs. Also, the name "halting problem" is not Turing's own. It is usually credited to Martin Davis in the 1950s.

Reductions and Rice's theorem

Is it decidable whether a program ever prints hello? Suppose a checker C for that existed. Given any \langle P, x \rangle, build a new program Q. Q runs P on x with all printing switched off. If that run ends, Q prints hello. So Q prints hello exactly when P halts on x. Then C(Q) would decide HALT. That is impossible, so C cannot exist.

This method is a reduction. We write A \le_m B when a computable function f maps each instance of A to an instance of B, and x \in A exactly when f(x) \in B.

  • If A \le_m B and B is decidable, then A is decidable.
  • So if A \le_m B and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable.
reduce(P, x):                 # an instance of HALT
    return program Q(y):      # an instance of "prints hello"
        run P on x, printing nothing
        print "hello"         # reached only if P halts on x

Look at the right end of the map. Some undecidable problems have nothing to do with programs. Is a context-free grammar ambiguous? Does a grammar generate every string? Does a whole-number equation have a solution? All undecidable. Rice's theorem gives a whole family at once.

A semantic property is a property of a program's language, or behaviour, not of its text. "Accepts the string 42" is semantic. "Has fewer than 100 lines" is not. A property is non-trivial when some programs have it and some do not.

Let S be a non-trivial property of recognisable languages. Then \{ \langle M \rangle : L(M) \text{ has property } S \} is undecidable.

Proof

We may assume the empty language does not have S. Otherwise use the complement of S, which is also non-trivial. Since S is non-trivial, some machine M_1 has a language with S. Now reduce HALT. Given \langle P, x \rangle, build Q. On input y, Q first runs P on x. If that halts, Q runs M_1 on y.

If P halts on x, then L(Q) = L(M_1), which has S. If P loops, Q accepts nothing, so L(Q) = \emptyset, which does not have S. A decider for S would therefore decide HALT. That is impossible.

In simple words: you cannot write a perfect tool that answers any interesting question about what code does. Examples of undecidable questions: Does this function ever divide by zero? Does it return 0 on all inputs? Is it equal to this other function? Is this program malware?

Rice's theorem is about behaviour only. Questions about the text are often decidable: "does the code call eval?" Questions with a fixed budget are decidable: "does it halt within 1,000 steps on input 7?" Do not use Rice to give up on these. Also, a reduction goes from the known hard problem to the new one. Reversing it proves nothing.

Kleene's recursion theorem

Can a program print its own source code, without reading its file? Yes. Such a program is called a quine. Here are two. Each one prints exactly itself.

fn main() {
    let s = "fn main() {\n    let s = {:?};\n    print!(\"{}\", s.replacen(\"{:?}\", &format!(\"{:?}\", s), 1));\n}\n";
    print!("{}", s.replacen("{:?}", &format!("{:?}", s), 1));
}
s = 's = %r\nprint(s %% s)'
print(s % s)
$ rustc --edition 2024 quine.rs -o quine && ./quine > out.rs && diff quine.rs out.rs && echo same
same
$ python3.14 quine.py > out.py && diff quine.py out.py && echo same
same

The trick has two parts. The string s is a template of the whole program, with a hole where the string itself goes. Then the program fills the hole with a quoted copy of s. Rust's {:?} and Python's %r both make the quoted form. A quine cannot contain comments, because the comments would have to print themselves too.

Let T be any computable function that takes a program and an input. Then there is a program R such that, for every input w, R on w behaves exactly like T(\langle R \rangle, w).

Proof idea

Build R from two parts, A and B, like the quine. B is fixed: it reads a description \langle X \rangle, builds the program "print \langle X \rangle", joins it in front of X, and passes the result with w to T. Let A be the program that prints \langle B \rangle. Run R = AB. A prints \langle B \rangle. B then builds "print \langle B \rangle" followed by B, which is exactly \langle AB \rangle = \langle R \rangle. So T receives the code of R itself.

In simple words: any program may assume it has a copy of its own code. A quine is the case where T prints its first argument. The theorem gives a two-line proof of undecidability. Suppose H decides HALT. Build R: "get my own code, ask H about me on this input, then do the opposite". This is exactly the Rust new_cyclic trick, now justified for all languages. A fixed-point form says more. For every computable transformation f of programs, some program e behaves exactly like f(e).

In his Turing Award lecture, published in 1984 as "Reflections on Trusting Trust", Ken Thompson described a compiler that inserts a backdoor into the login program. It also inserts the backdoor code into new compilers that it compiles, using quine-like self-copying. So reading the compiler's source code does not reveal it. Computer viruses use the same self-copying idea.

A program that opens and prints its own file is not a quine. It reads data from outside. The theorem says the self-reference can be built into the program, with no outside help.

What this means for program analysis and AI agents

A compiler warns: "this variable might be used before it is set". Sometimes the warning is wrong. The code may set the variable on every real path. Why does the compiler not just know? Rice's theorem says it cannot know in every case. So every analysis tool must give something up.

  • A sound checker never misses a real bug of its kind. The price is false positives.
  • A complete checker never raises a false alarm. The price is false negatives.
  • No checker of a non-trivial semantic property is both sound and complete, and always halts. Pick two of the three, at most.
How real tools live with undecidability
StrategyReal exampleWhat it gives up
Be sound, reject some good programsRust's borrow checker and type checkerSome safe programs do not compile
Restrict the languageThe Linux eBPF verifier: loops were banned, then bounded loops came in Linux 5.3Programs must provably end
Demand a proof of terminationLean and Rocq accept recursion that clearly shrinks, or a proofThe programmer does more work
Set a budgetWasmtime fuel: the call traps with OutOfFuel"Unknown" becomes "stopped"
Test, do not proveUnit tests, fuzzingTests show bugs, not their absence
Use heuristicsLinters, bug finders, LLM code reviewMisses some bugs and raises some false alarms

Since Linux 5.17, eBPF also has a bpf_loop helper for up to 2^{23}, about 8 million, iterations. The design idea is clear. If the halting question is undecidable for a full language, make the language smaller until the question becomes easy.

Now apply this to an AI agent that reviews or tests code. The agent is a program, so all the limits above apply to it. No agent, however large its model, can always answer correctly "does this patch ever crash?" or "does this function always terminate?". A good agent design accepts this and works with it.

  1. Run code only in a sandbox, with a time limit, a memory limit and a step or fuel budget.
  2. Report three answers: "found a problem", "checked and fine for these cases", and "unknown". Never turn a timeout into "safe".
  3. Prefer checks that are decidable: types, tests with fixed inputs, linters, size limits.
  4. For key properties, ask for proofs in a restricted setting, such as a type system, a proof assistant or a bounded model checker.
  5. Treat an LLM verdict as a heuristic. Back it with tests that a machine checks.

A common exam task: "Is it decidable whether a Turing machine M ...?" First ask: is this about the language of M, or about its code or a fixed number of steps? If it is about the language and non-trivial, cite Rice's theorem. Otherwise, try to build a decider, or reduce HALT to it.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for computability
PatternPurposeModelNote
Machine as dataBuild a universal machine or an interpreterFive words per rule: q0 a X R q1Running a program is not predicting it.
Three outcomesReason about any machineAccept, reject, loopNot accepting does not mean rejecting.
Fuel or timeoutRun unknown code safelyWasmtime OutOfFuelOut of fuel means "unknown", not "loops".
DovetailingSearch infinitely many runsStep 1 on input 1, then 2 steps on inputs 1 and 2Gives a recogniser, not a decider.
Run both recognisersShow a problem is decidableRecogniser for L and for its complementAlternate steps, never run one to the end first.
Flip the diagonalShow something is missing from a listRow D differs from row i in column iFlip every diagonal cell.
Assume, then contradictProve the halting problem undecidableD(D) halts exactly when it loopsThe only assumption is that H exists.
Reduce from HALTShow a new problem is undecidableQ prints hello only if P halts on xThe arrow goes from the known hard problem.
Rice's theoremSpot an impossible semantic checker"Never divides by zero" is undecidableNot for questions about the text or a fixed budget.
Template plus quoted copyMake a program use its own codeQuine: print(s % s)Comments break a quine.
Sound or completeDesign a code checkerBorrow checker: sound, rejects some safe codeYou cannot have both and always halt.
Shrink the languageMake termination checkableeBPF bounded loopsLess power, more guarantees.

Practice

A simulator runs a Turing machine for one million steps and the machine has not stopped. What can you conclude?

  • The machine loops forever.
  • The machine will reject.
  • Nothing yet. It may halt later.

A budget only shows that the machine did not halt so far. Busy beavers halt after very long runs.

Which problem is decidable?

  • Does program P ever print hello?
  • Does program P print hello within 500 steps on input 3?
  • Do programs P and Q compute the same function?

With a fixed input and a fixed step budget, just run it. The other two are semantic and non-trivial, so Rice's theorem applies.

HALT is recognisable. What does that tell you about its complement?

  • It is decidable.
  • It is recognisable too.
  • It is not recognisable.

If both were recognisable, HALT would be decidable. It is not.

The Church-Turing thesis cannot be proved, because "effective method" is not a ? definition.

A checker that never misses a real bug but sometimes gives false alarms is called ?.

The value BB(5), proved in 2024, is ? steps.

  1. Trace the crossing-off machine on abc. Which rules does it use, in order?
    Answer

    q0 reads a: writes X, moves right, q1. q1 reads b: writes Y, right, q2. q2 reads c: writes Z, left, q3. q3 reads Y: left. q3 reads X: right, q0. q0 reads Y: right, q4. q4 reads Z: right. q4 reads blank: right, accept. That is 8 moves, matching Accept(8).

  2. Explain why "does P halt on some input?" is recognisable.
    Answer

    Use dovetailing. In round k, run P for k steps on each of the first k inputs. If P halts on some input x after t steps, round \max(t, \text{index of } x) finds it, and we accept. If P never halts, we run forever, which a recogniser may do.

  3. Show with a reduction that "does program P return 0 on input 5?" is undecidable.
    Answer

    Given \langle M, x \rangle, build Q: on any input, run M on x, then return 0. If M halts on x, Q returns 0 on input 5. If not, Q never returns. A decider for our problem would decide HALT. Rice's theorem gives the same answer directly.

  4. Is it decidable whether a given Turing machine has more than 10 states? Why does Rice's theorem not apply?
    Answer

    Yes, it is decidable: read the encoding and count. Rice's theorem is about the language of the machine. Two machines with the same language can have 5 or 50 states. So this is a property of the code, not of the behaviour.

  5. Expert: a team wants an AI agent that blocks every pull request that "can cause an infinite loop", with no false alarms. Explain why this is impossible, and propose a design that is still useful.
    Answer

    Blocking exactly the patches that can loop forever would decide a non-trivial semantic property. Rice's theorem says no program can do that, and the agent is a program. A useful design gives up one goal. Make the check sound but cautious: flag loops without a clear bound, and let a human approve them. Add tests with timeouts in a sandbox. Report "unknown" honestly. For critical code, require a termination argument, such as a loop variant or a proof assistant.

Key takeaways

  • A Turing machine has finite states and an unlimited tape. On each input it accepts, rejects or loops.
  • The Church-Turing thesis says Turing machines capture every effective method. It is evidence-based, not proved.
  • A universal machine runs any machine given as data. Interpreters and CPUs are universal machines.
  • Decidable means recognisable and co-recognisable. A timeout gives "unknown", never "no".
  • The diagonal argument shows there are more problems than programs.
  • The halting problem is undecidable but recognisable. Its complement is not recognisable.
  • Reductions spread undecidability. Rice's theorem makes every non-trivial semantic property undecidable.
  • Programs can use their own code (the recursion theorem). Real tools and AI agents must choose: sound, complete or always halting.
