  • Wasmtime: Interrupting Wasm execution. Fuel, epochs and the OutOfFuel trap.

Complexity theory

Some problems are easy to solve. Some are easy to check but seem very hard to solve. Complexity theory sorts problems by the time and memory they need. It tells you when to stop looking for a fast exact algorithm and what to do instead.

  • Explain time and space classes, and the classes P, NP, coNP and PSPACE.
  • Show that a problem is in NP with a verifier, and that it is NP-hard with a reduction.
  • State the Cook-Levin, hierarchy, Savitch, IP = PSPACE and PCP theorems in simple words.
  • Use randomness to check a result fast, and know what the classes BPP, RP and ZPP mean.
  • Choose a practical plan for a hard problem: special cases, solvers, approximation or heuristics.

Measuring hardness: time and space classes

Take two jobs. Job one: sort 60 numbers. Job two: try every subset of 60 numbers to find one with a given sum. Sorting needs a few hundred steps. The subsets number 2^{60}, about 10^{18}. At a billion checks per second, that is more than 30 years.

Complexity theory studies decision problems. "Does this formula have a solution?" is one. We measure cost as a function of the input size n, in bits. We use the worst input of each size.

  • \text{TIME}(f(n)) is the set of problems a Turing machine solves in O(f(n)) steps.
  • \text{SPACE}(f(n)) is the set of problems it solves with O(f(n)) cells of memory.
  • A complexity class is such a set of problems.

The most important classes collect all polynomial or exponential bounds:

\text{P} = \bigcup_{k} \text{TIME}(n^k), \qquad \text{PSPACE} = \bigcup_{k} \text{SPACE}(n^k), \qquad \text{EXP} = \bigcup_{k} \text{TIME}(2^{n^k}).

Why polynomials? Real machines, Turing machines and RAM models can simulate each other with a polynomial slowdown. So the class P is the same on every reasonable model. Polynomials are also closed: a polynomial number of calls to a polynomial routine is still polynomial. The computability chapter defines the Turing machine itself.

"P means fast" is not exact. An n^{100} algorithm is in P but useless. And some exponential problems, like SAT, are solved every day on huge inputs. P is a clean line for theory. It is a good first guess for practice, not a promise.

P, NP and verifiers

A friend gives you a solved Sudoku. You check every row, column and box in a minute. Solving the empty grid took her an hour. Checking is easy. Finding is hard. This gap is the heart of NP.

A problem is in NP when every "yes" input has a short certificate, and a polynomial-time verifier checks it. Short means polynomial in n. For a "no" input, no certificate makes the verifier say yes.

The name NP means "nondeterministic polynomial time". A nondeterministic machine may guess the certificate and then run the verifier. The two definitions give the same class. Every problem in P is also in NP: the verifier can ignore the certificate and just solve.

Here is SAT. The input is a formula in conjunctive normal form (CNF). The certificate is a true or false value for each variable. The verifier needs one pass. The brute-force solver may need 2^n tries.

// A literal is a variable number. A minus sign means NOT.
type Clause = [i32; 3];

// The verifier: one pass over the formula. Time grows with its size.
fn verify(cnf: &[Clause], value: &[bool]) -> bool {
    cnf.iter().all(|c| c.iter().any(|&lit| value[lit.unsigned_abs() as usize] == (lit > 0)))
}

// The solver: try all 2^n assignments, one after another.
fn brute_force(cnf: &[Clause], n: usize) -> (Option<String>, u64) {
    let mut tried = 0;
    for mask in 0..(1u64 << n) {
        tried += 1;
        // value[0] is not used, so value[i] belongs to variable i
        let value: Vec<bool> = (0..=n).map(|i| i > 0 && (mask >> (i - 1)) & 1 == 1).collect();
        if verify(cnf, &value) {
            let text = value[1..].iter().map(|&b| if b { 'T' } else { 'F' }).collect();
            return (Some(text), tried);
        }
    }
    (None, tried)
}

fn main() {
    let cnf = [[1, 2, -4], [1, -2, 4], [2, 3, 4], [2, 3, -4],
               [2, -3, 4], [-2, 3, -4], [-1, -2, 4]];
    let certificate = [false, true, false, true, true]; // x1=T x2=F x3=T x4=T
    println!("certificate ok: {}", verify(&cnf, &certificate));
    let (found, tried) = brute_force(&cnf, 4);
    println!("brute force tried {tried} of 16, found {}", found.unwrap_or("none".into()));
    for n in [20, 40, 60] {
        println!("n = {n}: up to {} assignments", 1u64 << n);
    }
}
# A literal is a variable number. A minus sign means NOT.

def verify(cnf, value):
    """The verifier: one pass over the formula. Time grows with its size."""
    return all(any(value[abs(lit)] == (lit > 0) for lit in c) for c in cnf)

def brute_force(cnf, n):
    """The solver: try all 2^n assignments, one after another."""
    tried = 0
    for mask in range(2 ** n):
        tried += 1
        # value[0] is not used, so value[i] belongs to variable i
        value = [False] + [(mask >> (i - 1)) & 1 == 1 for i in range(1, n + 1)]
        if verify(cnf, value):
            return "".join("T" if b else "F" for b in value[1:]), tried
    return None, tried

cnf = [[1, 2, -4], [1, -2, 4], [2, 3, 4], [2, 3, -4],
       [2, -3, 4], [-2, 3, -4], [-1, -2, 4]]
certificate = [False, True, False, True, True]   # x1=T x2=F x3=T x4=T
print("certificate ok:", str(verify(cnf, certificate)).lower())
found, tried = brute_force(cnf, 4)
print(f"brute force tried {tried} of 16, found {found or 'none'}")
for n in [20, 40, 60]:
    print(f"n = {n}: up to {2 ** n} assignments")
certificate ok: true
brute force tried 14 of 16, found TFTT
n = 20: up to 1048576 assignments
n = 40: up to 1099511627776 assignments
n = 60: up to 1152921504606846976 assignments

The big open question is whether \text{P} = \text{NP}. If every easy-to-check problem were also easy to solve, much of cryptography would break. Most researchers believe \text{P} \neq \text{NP}. Nobody has a proof. The Clay Mathematics Institute lists it as an unsolved Millennium Prize Problem.

NP does not mean "not polynomial". It means "polynomial with a good guess". P is inside NP. So "this problem is in NP" alone does not say it is hard. Sorting is in NP too.

Polynomial reductions

You know how to boil water. A friend asks you to make tea. You turn tea into boiling water plus one easy step. That is a reduction. In complexity, we turn one problem into another with cheap work.

A polynomial reduction from A to B is a function f, computable in polynomial time, with x \in A \iff f(x) \in B for every input x. We write A \le_p B. It means "A is no harder than B".

If A \le_p B and B is in P, then A is in P. Just translate and solve. Read it the other way too: if A is hard, then B is hard.

Here is a classic. We reduce 3-SAT to INDEPENDENT SET. An independent set is a set of vertices with no edge inside it. The question is: does the graph have an independent set of size k?

  1. For each clause, make three vertices, one per literal. Join them in a triangle.
  2. Join every vertex x to every vertex \neg x in other clauses.
  3. Set k to the number of clauses m.
  4. An independent set of size m takes exactly one vertex from each triangle. It never takes x and \neg x together. So making the chosen literals true satisfies every clause.
  5. The other way: a satisfying assignment makes one literal true in each clause. Pick that vertex in each triangle. No two picks clash.
// Reduce 3-SAT to INDEPENDENT SET. One vertex per literal in each clause.
fn reduce(cnf: &[[i32; 3]]) -> (Vec<i32>, Vec<(usize, usize)>) {
    let lits: Vec<i32> = cnf.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
    let mut edges = Vec::new();
    for a in 0..lits.len() {
        for b in a + 1..lits.len() {
            let same_clause = a / 3 == b / 3;     // triangle inside a clause
            let opposite = lits[a] == -lits[b];   // x and NOT x cannot both be chosen
            if same_clause || opposite {
                edges.push((a, b));
            }
        }
    }
    (lits, edges)
}

fn main() {
    let cnf = [[1, 2, 3], [-1, -2, 3], [-1, 2, -3]];
    let (lits, edges) = reduce(&cnf);
    let m = cnf.len(); // we need an independent set of size m
    println!("{} vertices, {} edges, k = {m}", lits.len(), edges.len());
    // A set of size m must take one vertex from each triangle: 3^m choices.
    for code in 0..3usize.pow(m as u32) {
        let group: Vec<usize> = (0..m).map(|i| 3 * i + code / 3usize.pow((m - 1 - i) as u32) % 3).collect();
        if edges.iter().all(|(a, b)| !(group.contains(a) && group.contains(b))) {
            let chosen: Vec<i32> = group.iter().map(|&v| lits[v]).collect();
            println!("independent set (as literals): {chosen:?}");
            // make every chosen literal true; other variables can be anything
            let x = |v: i32| if chosen.contains(&-v) { 'F' } else { 'T' };
            println!("assignment: x1={} x2={} x3={}", x(1), x(2), x(3));
            break;
        }
    }
}
from itertools import combinations, product

def reduce(cnf):
    """Reduce 3-SAT to INDEPENDENT SET. One vertex per literal in each clause."""
    lits = [lit for clause in cnf for lit in clause]
    edges = []
    for a, b in combinations(range(len(lits)), 2):
        same_clause = a // 3 == b // 3       # triangle inside a clause
        opposite = lits[a] == -lits[b]       # x and NOT x cannot both be chosen
        if same_clause or opposite:
            edges.append((a, b))
    return lits, edges

cnf = [[1, 2, 3], [-1, -2, 3], [-1, 2, -3]]
lits, edges = reduce(cnf)
m = len(cnf)  # we need an independent set of size m
print(f"{len(lits)} vertices, {len(edges)} edges, k = {m}")
# A set of size m must take one vertex from each triangle: 3^m choices.
for pick in product(range(3), repeat=m):
    group = [3 * i + p for i, p in enumerate(pick)]
    if all(not (a in group and b in group) for a, b in edges):
        chosen = [lits[v] for v in group]
        print("independent set (as literals):", chosen)
        # make every chosen literal true; other variables can be anything
        x = lambda v: "F" if -v in chosen else "T"
        print(f"assignment: x1={x(1)} x2={x(2)} x3={x(3)}")
        break
9 vertices, 15 edges, k = 3
independent set (as literals): [1, -2, -3]
assignment: x1=T x2=F x3=F

The reduction itself is fast: O(m^2) edges at most. Only our final search is slow. Two more reductions are almost free. A set S is independent exactly when the other vertices form a vertex cover. And S is independent in G exactly when it is a clique in the complement graph.

The direction matters. To show your problem B is hard, reduce a known hard problem A to B: A \le_p B. Reducing B to SAT shows only that B is in NP, not that it is hard.

NP-completeness and the Cook-Levin theorem

Some problems in NP are the hardest ones. A fast algorithm for any one of them would give a fast algorithm for all of NP.

A problem B is NP-hard when A \le_p B for every A in NP. It is NP-complete when it is NP-hard and also in NP.

SAT is NP-complete. The same holds for 3-SAT, where each clause has at most three literals.

Proof idea

SAT is in NP: the verifier above checks an assignment. For hardness, take any problem A in NP with a verifier that runs in time n^k. We build a formula that is satisfiable exactly when some certificate makes the verifier accept. The carousel below shows the steps. The formula has about n^{2k} variables, so the translation is polynomial. To reach 3-SAT, split a long clause (a \lor b \lor c \lor d) into (a \lor b \lor y) \land (\neg y \lor c \lor d) with a new variable y.

Write the run as a table

The verifier runs for T = n^k steps. Write each moment as one row: the tape, the head and the state. The table has T rows and T columns.

One variable per fact

Make a variable for "cell (i, j) holds symbol s". There are about T^2 cells and a fixed number of symbols.

Each cell holds one symbol

Add clauses that say: at least one symbol per cell, and no two symbols in the same cell.

The first row is the start

Fix the input bits in row 1. Leave the certificate bits free. The formula will "guess" them.

Each row follows from the row above

A cell depends only on three cells above it. So a small fixed set of clauses for each 2 by 3 window checks every legal step.

The run accepts

Add one clause: some cell shows the accept state. Now the formula is satisfiable exactly when some certificate is accepted.

In simple words: SAT can describe any computation that checks evidence. So SAT is a universal NP problem. Stephen Cook proved this in 1971. Leonid Levin found it on his own, published in 1973. In 1972 Richard Karp reduced SAT to 21 famous problems. Clique, vertex cover, set cover, Hamiltonian cycle, knapsack and partition were among them. Thousands of problems are now known to be NP-complete.

After Cook-Levin, a new hardness proof needs only one reduction from any known NP-complete problem. The graph shows a map of classic reductions. Each arrow means "reduces to".

Real software meets these problems often. Picking package versions that fit all constraints is NP-complete. Russ Cox showed the 3-SAT reduction for language package managers. The uv documentation also calls resolution NP-complete in the worst case. Register allocation in a compiler is graph colouring, as the compilers chapter shows.

A problem is NP-complete, not an input. "My 20-node input is NP-complete" makes no sense. Small inputs are fine: 2^{20} is about a million. Also, a special case may be easy. 2-SAT is in P, and so is Hamiltonian path in a DAG.

coNP, PSPACE and the cost of memory

Proving that a formula has a solution is easy: show it. How do you prove that it has none? No short proof is known in general. This is the class coNP.

  • coNP holds the problems whose "no" answers have short certificates. UNSAT ("this formula has no solution") and TAUTOLOGY ("this formula is always true") are coNP-complete.
  • If \text{NP} \neq \text{coNP}, then \text{P} \neq \text{NP}. Most people believe both.
  • Some problems are in \text{NP} \cap \text{coNP}. "Does N have a factor below k?" is one. The factors themselves are proof both ways. No fast classical algorithm is known.
  • Primality was a famous example. In 2002 Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena showed that PRIMES is in P.

A SAT solver that says UNSAT can now give a proof that a checker reads. These proofs can be huge. That fits the belief that coNP has no short certificates. The logic and formal methods chapter explains these solvers.

PSPACE allows polynomial memory and any amount of time. Its typical problem is TQBF: is a formula with quantifiers true, like \exists x\, \forall y\, \exists z\, \varphi? Read it as a game. Player "exists" picks x. Player "for all" picks y. Does the first player always win? Many games on an n \times n board are PSPACE-hard. Plan existence in classical AI planning (STRIPS) is PSPACE-complete, as Bylander showed in 1994. That matters for AI agents that plan long chains of actions.

Below P sit two small-memory classes. L uses O(\log n) memory, enough for a few counters. NL is the same with guessing. Reachability in a directed graph is NL-complete. Now the surprise: guessing does not help much with memory.

For every space-constructible s(n) \ge \log n: \text{NSPACE}(s(n)) \subseteq \text{SPACE}(s(n)^2). As a result, \text{NPSPACE} = \text{PSPACE}.

Proof idea

A nondeterministic machine with space s has at most 2^{O(s)} configurations. It accepts when the accept configuration is reachable from the start. Ask "is there a path from u to v with at most 2^k steps?" Try every middle point w and ask the same question for u \to w and w \to v with 2^{k-1} steps. The two halves run one after the other, so they reuse memory. The recursion has depth O(s), and each level stores O(s) bits. Total: O(s^2).

// Is there a path from u to v with at most 2^k steps? Guess the middle vertex.
fn reach(adj: &[Vec<bool>], u: usize, v: usize, k: u32, depth: u32, st: &mut (u64, u32)) -> bool {
    st.0 += 1;                      // count calls (time)
    st.1 = st.1.max(depth);         // deepest recursion (space)
    if k == 0 {
        return u == v || adj[u][v]; // a path of 0 or 1 step
    }
    // Try every middle vertex w. The two halves reuse the same memory.
    (0..adj.len()).any(|w| reach(adj, u, w, k - 1, depth + 1, st) && reach(adj, w, v, k - 1, depth + 1, st))
}

fn main() {
    let n = 8;
    let mut adj = vec![vec![false; n]; n];
    for i in 0..n - 1 {
        adj[i][i + 1] = true; // a line: 0 -> 1 -> ... -> 7
    }
    let mut st = (0, 0);
    let ok = reach(&adj, 0, 7, 3, 1, &mut st); // 2^3 = 8 steps are enough
    println!("path 0 to 7: {ok}, calls: {}, deepest: {}", st.0, st.1);
    let mut st = (0, 0);
    let ok = reach(&adj, 7, 0, 3, 1, &mut st);
    println!("path 7 to 0: {ok}, calls: {}, deepest: {}", st.0, st.1);
}
def reach(adj, u, v, k, depth, st):
    """Is there a path from u to v with at most 2^k steps? Guess the middle vertex."""
    st["calls"] += 1                          # count calls (time)
    st["deepest"] = max(st["deepest"], depth) # deepest recursion (space)
    if k == 0:
        return u == v or adj[u][v]            # a path of 0 or 1 step
    # Try every middle vertex w. The two halves reuse the same memory.
    return any(reach(adj, u, w, k - 1, depth + 1, st) and reach(adj, w, v, k - 1, depth + 1, st)
               for w in range(len(adj)))

n = 8
adj = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
for i in range(n - 1):
    adj[i][i + 1] = True                      # a line: 0 -> 1 -> ... -> 7
for u, v in [(0, 7), (7, 0)]:
    st = {"calls": 0, "deepest": 0}
    ok = reach(adj, u, v, 3, 1, st)           # 2^3 = 8 steps are enough
    print(f"path {u} to {v}: {str(ok).lower()}, calls: {st['calls']}, deepest: {st['deepest']}")
path 0 to 7: true, calls: 443, deepest: 4
path 7 to 0: false, calls: 820, deepest: 4

The recursion is only 4 frames deep for 8 vertices: \log_2 8 + 1. Each frame keeps a few vertex numbers. But it makes hundreds of calls, where BFS needs about 15 steps. Savitch trades a lot of time for little memory. In 2025 Ryan Williams showed a new trade the other way round. Any multitape machine that runs in time t can be simulated in about \sqrt{t \log t} space.

Savitch does not say \text{NP} = \text{P}. It is about memory, and memory can be reused. Time cannot be reused. The simulation in the proof takes time 2^{O(s^2)}.

Hierarchy theorems: more time really helps

Is \text{TIME}(n^3) bigger than \text{TIME}(n^2)? It feels obvious. Proving it is not. The tool is the same diagonal argument that proves the halting problem undecidable in the computability chapter.

Let f and g be time-constructible with f(n) \log f(n) = o(g(n)). Then \text{TIME}(f(n)) \subsetneq \text{TIME}(g(n)). Some problem is solvable in time g but not in time f.

Proof idea

Build a machine D. On input x, it reads x as the code of a machine M_x. It simulates M_x on x for about g(|x|) steps with a universal machine. If M_x answers in time, D gives the opposite answer. Otherwise D says no. Now suppose some machine M solved D's problem in time f. The simulation costs only a \log f factor more, so for a long enough code x of M, D finishes the simulation. Then D(x) \neq M(x). This contradicts the claim that M solves the same problem.

Example with numbers: f(n) = n^2 and g(n) = n^3. Then n^2 \log n^2 = 2n^2 \log n, which is o(n^3). So some problem needs more than n^2 time but fits in n^3. The space version is even sharper. If f = o(g) for space-constructible functions, then \text{SPACE}(f) \subsetneq \text{SPACE}(g). The log factor goes away because a universal machine wastes only constant extra space.

  • \text{P} \subsetneq \text{EXP}. So some problems in EXP are truly not in P.
  • \text{L} \subsetneq \text{PSPACE}.
  • We know \text{P} \subseteq \text{NP} \subseteq \text{PSPACE} \subseteq \text{EXP}. At least one of these steps is strict. We do not know which.

Why can diagonalization not settle P against NP? Baker, Gill and Solovay (1975) built oracles where P equals NP and others where it does not. Diagonal proofs keep working when you add any oracle. So they cannot decide the question. Later barriers, "natural proofs" and "algebrization", block other common methods too.

Randomness and interaction

A GPU sends back C = A \times B for two big matrices. Recomputing costs O(n^3). Freivalds' check costs O(n^2). Pick a random 0/1 vector r. Compare A(Br) with Cr. If C is wrong, one round catches it with probability at least one half.

// A tiny random number generator (xorshift), so both languages agree.
fn next(s: &mut u64) -> u64 {
    *s ^= *s << 13;
    *s ^= *s >> 7;
    *s ^= *s << 17;
    *s
}

fn mul_vec(m: &[[i64; 3]; 3], v: &[i64; 3]) -> [i64; 3] {
    let mut out = [0; 3];
    for i in 0..3 {
        out[i] = (0..3).map(|j| m[i][j] * v[j]).sum();
    }
    out
}

// One round costs O(n^2): three matrix-vector products, no matrix product.
fn freivalds_round(a: &[[i64; 3]; 3], b: &[[i64; 3]; 3], c: &[[i64; 3]; 3], s: &mut u64) -> bool {
    let r = [next(s) as i64 & 1, next(s) as i64 & 1, next(s) as i64 & 1]; // random 0/1 vector
    mul_vec(a, &mul_vec(b, &r)) == mul_vec(c, &r)
}

fn main() {
    let a = [[2, 1, 0], [1, 3, 1], [0, 1, 4]];
    let b = [[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 1], [3, 1, 0]];
    let good = [[2, 1, 5], [4, 4, 5], [12, 5, 1]]; // the true product A x B
    let mut bad = good;
    bad[1][2] = 6; // one wrong number
    let mut s = 2026u64;
    for (name, c) in [("good", good), ("bad", bad)] {
        let passed = (0..20).filter(|_| freivalds_round(&a, &b, &c, &mut s)).count();
        println!("{name}: passed {passed} of 20 rounds");
    }
    println!("a wrong C survives 20 rounds with chance at most 1/{}", 1u32 << 20);
}
MASK = (1 << 64) - 1

def next_rand(state):
    """A tiny random number generator (xorshift), so both languages agree."""
    s = state[0]
    s ^= (s << 13) & MASK
    s ^= s >> 7
    s ^= (s << 17) & MASK
    state[0] = s
    return s

def mul_vec(m, v):
    return [sum(m[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)]

def freivalds_round(a, b, c, state):
    """One round costs O(n^2): three matrix-vector products, no matrix product."""
    r = [next_rand(state) & 1 for _ in range(3)]      # random 0/1 vector
    return mul_vec(a, mul_vec(b, r)) == mul_vec(c, r)

a = [[2, 1, 0], [1, 3, 1], [0, 1, 4]]
b = [[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 1], [3, 1, 0]]
good = [[2, 1, 5], [4, 4, 5], [12, 5, 1]]   # the true product A x B
bad = [row[:] for row in good]
bad[1][2] = 6                                # one wrong number
state = [2026]
for name, c in [("good", good), ("bad", bad)]:
    passed = sum(freivalds_round(a, b, c, state) for _ in range(20))
    print(f"{name}: passed {passed} of 20 rounds")
print(f"a wrong C survives 20 rounds with chance at most 1/{2 ** 20}")
good: passed 20 of 20 rounds
bad: passed 12 of 20 rounds
a wrong C survives 20 rounds with chance at most 1/1048576

The bad matrix failed 8 rounds. One failed round is already proof that C is wrong. The correct matrix never fails. This is one-sided error. Repeating the test makes the error tiny: 2^{-20} after 20 rounds.

Randomised classes (all with polynomial expected or worst-case time)
ClassErrors allowedExample
ZPPNever wrong. Running time is random, polynomial on average.Las Vegas algorithms
RPMay say "no" on a yes input, with chance at most 1/2. Never wrong on "no" inputs.Testing that a polynomial is not zero
BPPWrong with chance at most 1/3 on any input.Monte Carlo algorithms

We know \text{P} \subseteq \text{ZPP} \subseteq \text{RP} \subseteq \text{BPP} \subseteq \text{PSPACE}, and \text{RP} \subseteq \text{NP}. Many researchers believe \text{BPP} = \text{P}. Strong circuit lower bounds would imply it. The story of primality fits this belief. Fast random tests came first. A deterministic polynomial test came in 2002.

Now add a conversation. In an interactive proof, an all-powerful prover talks with a polynomial-time random verifier. Here is a classic protocol for "these two graphs are not the same up to renaming".

  1. The verifier secretly flips a coin and picks graph G_0 or G_1.
  2. It renames the vertices at random and sends the result H.
  3. The prover says which graph H came from.
  4. If the graphs are truly different, the prover can always tell. It answers right every time.
  5. If they are the same, H looks the same either way. The prover guesses right only half the time. After 20 rounds, a cheating prover survives with chance 2^{-20}.

The problems with interactive proofs (polynomially many rounds) are exactly the problems in PSPACE: \text{IP} = \text{PSPACE}.

Proof idea

\text{IP} \subseteq \text{PSPACE}: the verifier is polynomial. So a PSPACE machine can try all its random choices. It finds the best prover answers and reuses memory. \text{PSPACE} \subseteq \text{IP}: use TQBF. Turn the formula into a polynomial over a finite field ("arithmetization"). AND becomes multiplication. The prover sends small polynomials, one variable at a time. The verifier checks each one at a random point. A lie survives a random check only with tiny probability, because two different low-degree polynomials agree on few points.

The result came in 1990. Lund, Fortnow, Karloff and Nisan put #SAT in IP. Soon after, Shamir proved \text{IP} = \text{PSPACE}. In simple words: a weak but random checker can be convinced of any PSPACE fact. Note that NP proofs are a special case with one message and no randomness.

Approximation hardness and the PCP theorem

For an NP-hard optimisation problem, we can still hope for a near-best answer. The approximation ratio says how near. Some problems allow any ratio. Others resist even rough answers. The PCP theorem explains why.

Imagine a 300-page proof. You want to know if it is correct. You are allowed to read only three random letters. That sounds impossible. The PCP theorem says it is possible, if the proof is written in a special, very redundant format.

\text{NP} = \text{PCP}(\log n, 1). Every NP problem has a special proof format and a verifier. The verifier uses O(\log n) random bits. It reads only a constant number of bits of the proof. A correct proof is always accepted. If the input is a "no" instance, every proof is rejected with probability at least 1/2.

Proof idea

The first proof came around 1992 and was published in 1998. Its authors were Arora and Safra, and Arora, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy. It used error-correcting codes and low-degree polynomials. Irit Dinur gave a more combinatorial proof in 2007. Her method takes a constraint graph with a tiny fraction of broken constraints. Each round doubles the broken fraction, while the graph grows only by a constant factor. After about \log n rounds, a "no" instance has a constant fraction of broken constraints. Then a few random checks find one.

The PCP theorem has an equal form about gaps. There is a constant \epsilon \gt 0 with this property. Look at two kinds of 3-SAT formulas. Some are satisfiable. In the others, every assignment breaks at least an \epsilon fraction of the clauses. Telling the two kinds apart is NP-hard. A good approximation algorithm could tell these two cases apart. So it cannot exist unless \text{P} = \text{NP}.

Best known algorithms and matching hardness (unless P = NP)
ProblemSimple algorithmHardness
MAX-3SATA random assignment meets 7/8 of the clauses (for exactly 3 literals each)Better than 7/8 + \epsilon is NP-hard (Håstad, 2001)
Set coverGreedy gets within about \ln n(1 - \epsilon) \ln n is NP-hard (Dinur and Steurer, 2014)
Vertex coverFactor 2 with a maximal matchingFactor 2 - \epsilon is hard if the Unique Games Conjecture holds
KnapsackAny factor 1 + \epsilon, in time polynomial in n and 1/\epsilonNo gap: it is "easy to approximate"
General TSPNoneNo constant factor at all

So the greedy set cover algorithm in the advanced algorithms chapter is the best possible, up to small terms. That is a strong statement about a five-line algorithm.

"NP-hard" does not mean "every approximation is hard". Knapsack is NP-hard but has very good approximations. Always check the approximation status of your exact problem.

  1. 1965 Hartmanis and Stearns. Time hierarchy: more time solves more problems.
  2. 1970 Savitch. Guessing saves at most a square in memory.
  3. 1971 Cook. SAT is NP-complete. Levin's paper follows in 1973.
  4. 1972 Karp. 21 classic problems are NP-complete.
  5. 1990 LFKN and Shamir. IP = PSPACE.
  6. 1992 The PCP theorem. Journal papers in 1998, Gödel Prize in 2001.
  7. 2002 Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena. PRIMES is in P.
  8. 2007 Dinur. A combinatorial proof of the PCP theorem.
  9. 2025 Williams. Time t fits in about \sqrt{t \log t} space.

What to do with a hard problem in practice

Your boss wants the best schedule for 500 jobs. You recognise an NP-hard problem. Do not give up, and do not search for a magic polynomial algorithm. Work through a plan.

  • Check the size. 2^{25} is about 33 million. A laptop does that in seconds.
  • Look for structure. Many NP-hard graph problems are easy on trees. Knapsack has a pseudo-polynomial DP in O(nW) time. It is fast when the capacity W is small. See dynamic programming.
  • Use a solver. Modern SAT, SMT and integer programming solvers handle millions of variables on many industrial inputs. Encode the problem and let the solver search. See linear programming.
  • Use a parameter. If the answer k is small, a fixed-parameter algorithm may work. For vertex cover, pick an edge. One end must be in the cover. Try both: 2^k branches, each with linear work.
  • Approximate. Accept a proven ratio, like 2 for vertex cover.
  • Use heuristics. Local search, simulated annealing or a greedy rule. They give no guarantee but often work well.
  • Change the problem. Add a time limit. Accept "good enough". Ask whether the business needs the true optimum at all.

An AI example: an agent must choose documents for its context window. Each document has a token cost and a usefulness score. The window holds 8,000 tokens. That is knapsack. With token counts as integers, the DP needs about n \times 8{,}000 steps, which is cheap. A greedy rule by score per token is even faster and usually close.

Fine-grained complexity asks for exact exponents. The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) of Impagliazzo and Paturi says 3-SAT needs 2^{cn} time for some c \gt 0. It is a belief, not a theorem. Many tight lower bounds for real algorithms rest on it.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for complexity theory
PatternPurposeModelNote
Certificate + verifierShow a problem is in NPAn assignment for SAT, checked in one passThe certificate must be short and the check polynomial.
Known hard \le_p newShow a problem is NP-hard3-SAT \le_p independent set with trianglesReduce from the known hard problem, not to it.
Prove both directionsMake a reduction correctSatisfiable \iff independent set of size mCheck yes maps to yes and no maps to no.
Swap yes and noPlace a problem in coNPUNSAT, tautologyA short proof of "no" is usually not known.
Guess the middleSave memorySavitch: reach(u, w) and reach(w, v)Time grows a lot. Space only squares.
DiagonalizeSeparate classes\text{P} \subsetneq \text{EXP}It cannot decide P against NP.
Random check, repeatVerify a result cheaplyFreivalds on A \times BEach round halves the error. Use 20 or more.
Spot-check a robust proofHardness of approximationPCP: read a constant number of bitsNeeds a special proof format.
Gap reductionShow a ratio is hardMAX-3SAT above 7/8The gap, not the exact value, gives the bound.
DP on small numbersSolve knapsack-like problemsO(nW) for an 8,000-token windowPseudo-polynomial: slow when W is huge.
Branch on a small parameterExact answer for small kVertex cover in O(2^k m)Only helps when k is really small.
Encode for a solverSolve industrial NP-hard inputsPackage versions as SAT variablesSet a time limit. Worst cases still exist.

Practice

A problem is in NP. What can you say for sure?

  • It cannot be solved in polynomial time.
  • A "yes" answer has a certificate that can be checked in polynomial time.
  • It is NP-complete.

NP is defined by fast checking. It contains P, so membership alone says nothing about hardness.

You want to prove that your new problem X is NP-hard. Which reduction do you build?

  • From X to SAT
  • From 3-SAT (or another NP-complete problem) to X
  • From X to a problem in P

A fast solver for X would then solve 3-SAT. Hardness flows from the known hard problem to X.

What does Savitch's theorem prove?

  • P = NP
  • NP = coNP
  • PSPACE = NPSPACE

Nondeterministic space s fits in deterministic space s^2. A polynomial squared is still a polynomial.

A 3-SAT formula has 5 clauses. The reduction to independent set builds a graph with ? vertices and asks for a set of size ?.

Freivalds' test has error at most 1/2 per round. After 10 rounds, a wrong product survives with chance at most 1 in ?.

A brute-force search over 30 Boolean variables tries up to 2^{30}, which is about ? assignments.

  1. Show that CLIQUE is in NP. Say what the certificate is and what the verifier does.
    Answer

    The certificate is a list of k vertices. The verifier checks that they are distinct and that each of the k(k-1)/2 pairs is an edge. That is O(k^2) edge tests, which is polynomial.

  2. Use the reduction in this chapter to show that VERTEX COVER is NP-hard.
    Answer

    S is independent exactly when V \setminus S covers every edge. An edge inside S is an edge the rest misses, and the other way round. So G has an independent set of size k exactly when it has a vertex cover of size n - k. The map (G, k) \mapsto (G, n - k) is fast. Independent set is NP-hard, so vertex cover is NP-hard.

  3. The time hierarchy theorem: does it separate \text{TIME}(n) from \text{TIME}(n \log n)? Explain with the condition.
    Answer

    No, not in this form. We need f \log f = o(g). With f = n, f \log f = n \log n, which is not o(n \log n). The theorem does separate \text{TIME}(n) from \text{TIME}(n \log^2 n).

  4. Why does "if NP is not equal to coNP, then P is not equal to NP" hold?
    Answer

    P is closed under complement: swap the yes and no outputs of a fast algorithm. If \text{P} = \text{NP}, then \text{coNP} = \text{coP} = \text{P} = \text{NP}. So \text{NP} \neq \text{coNP} forces \text{P} \neq \text{NP}.

  5. An agent picks tools for a task. Each tool has a cost in dollars and a value. The budget is 200 dollars. There are 40 tools with integer costs. Which method do you pick and how many steps does it take?
    Answer

    This is 0-1 knapsack. Use the DP over budget: about 40 \times 200 = 8{,}000 table cells. Brute force would try 2^{40}, about 10^{12}, subsets. The DP is pseudo-polynomial, but here the numbers are small, so it is fast.

  6. Expert: a startup claims a polynomial algorithm that approximates MAX-3SAT within 0.95 on every satisfiable formula with exactly 3 literals per clause. What do you conclude?
    Answer

    0.95 is bigger than 7/8 = 0.875. By Håstad's result, beating 7/8 + \epsilon on satisfiable instances is NP-hard. So the claim would imply \text{P} = \text{NP}. Most likely the algorithm is wrong, or it works only on a special family of inputs, or it is not polynomial.

Key takeaways

  • P is "solvable in polynomial time". NP is "checkable in polynomial time with a certificate". Whether they are equal is open.
  • A reduction A \le_p B moves hardness from A to B. Cook-Levin makes SAT the first NP-complete problem.
  • coNP holds problems with short "no" proofs. PSPACE holds games, quantified formulas and planning.
  • Savitch: guessing costs at most a square in memory, so PSPACE = NPSPACE.
  • Hierarchy theorems prove that more time or space gives more power, for example P is not EXP.
  • Randomness checks results cheaply (Freivalds). Interaction with randomness reaches all of PSPACE.
  • The PCP theorem turns NP-hardness into hardness of approximation, with tight ratios like 7/8 for MAX-3SAT.
  • For a hard problem in practice: check size and structure, use solvers, parameters, approximation or heuristics.

Sources

  • Sanjeev Arora and Boaz Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach (draft). Statements of the hierarchy, Savitch, Cook-Levin, IP = PSPACE and PCP theorems, and Håstad's 7/8 result.
  • Clay Mathematics Institute: P vs NP. The problem is still listed as unsolved.
  • Ryan Williams, Simulating Time With Square-Root Space. The 2025 time-space result (STOC 2025).
  • Irit Dinur and David Steurer, Analytical Approach to Parallel Repetition. Set cover is NP-hard to approximate within (1 - \epsilon) \ln n.
  • Russ Cox, Version SAT. Package version selection is NP-complete, with the 3-SAT reduction.
  • uv documentation: resolver internals. uv uses PubGrub and notes that resolution is NP-complete in the worst case.

Logic and formal methods

Tests check some inputs. Formal methods check all of them. This chapter shows the logic under them and the solvers that do the work. It also shows how big companies use these tools to prove that code and designs are right.

  • Write software rules in propositional and first-order logic, and check them with a SAT or SMT solver.
  • Explain how DPLL and CDCL solvers search, propagate and learn.
  • Prove a loop correct with a Hoare triple and a loop invariant.
  • Check a concurrent design with a model checker and temporal logic, and read a small TLA+ spec.
  • Explain "types as proofs", what Lean and Rocq do, and where industry uses formal methods today.

Propositional logic for software

Here is an access rule from a real-looking code base. A user may edit a file in two cases. They are an admin, or they own the file and it is not locked.

allow = admin || (owner && !locked)

allow = (admin || owner) && !locked

A colleague says the two rules are the same. Are they? Each name is a proposition. The symbols AND (\land), OR (\lor) and NOT (\neg) are connectives. With three propositions there are only 2^3 = 8 cases. We can check them all.

Truth table for the two rules. The rows marked "differ" are bugs.
adminownerlockedoldnew
FFFFF
FFTFF
FTFTT
FTTFF
TFFTT
TFTTFdiffer
TTFTT
TTTTFdiffer

The new rule locks out admins from locked files. A test suite may never try that case. A truth table finds it at once.

  • A formula is satisfiable if some choice of values makes it true.
  • A formula is valid (a tautology) if every choice makes it true.
  • F is valid exactly when \neg F is not satisfiable. So one tool, a satisfiability checker, answers both questions.
  • Two rules are equal exactly when "old differs from new" is not satisfiable.

Solvers want formulas in conjunctive normal form (CNF). A literal is a variable or its negation. Any formula can be turned into CNF of about the same size by adding helper variables. This trick is the Tseitin encoding. The discrete maths chapter covers the basic laws, and the how computers compute chapter builds gates from them.

"A \Rightarrow B" is true when A is false. "If the build is red, the deploy stops" says nothing about green builds. In code, a implies b is !a || b, not a && b.

First-order logic: talking about all things

"Every order has a customer." Propositional logic cannot say this for a million orders. First-order logic adds variables for things, predicates and two quantifiers.

\forall o\, \big(\text{Order}(o) \Rightarrow \exists c\, (\text{Customer}(c) \land \text{PlacedBy}(o, c))\big)

Read \forall as "for all" and \exists as "there exists". This is the language of database constraints, API contracts and specifications. A foreign key in SQL says the same thing as the formula above.

\forall x\, \exists y\, \text{Likes}(x, y). Everyone likes someone. Each person may like a different person.

\exists y\, \forall x\, \text{Likes}(x, y). There is one person whom everyone likes. This is a much stronger claim.

First-order logic is powerful, and the power has a price.

  • Gödel's completeness theorem (1929) says every valid formula has a proof. So a program can list all proofs and find one, if it exists.
  • Church and Turing (1936) showed that no program decides validity in general. A search for a proof may run forever when there is none. See the computability chapter.
  • Some useful parts are decidable. Linear arithmetic over integers (Presburger arithmetic) is one. Many SMT theories are others.

The order of quantifiers changes the meaning. "For every request there is a server that handles it" allows load balancing. "There is a server that handles every request" means one server does all the work. Write the quantifiers first, in the right order, before you write code.

SAT solvers: DPLL and CDCL

SAT is NP-complete, as the complexity theory chapter shows. Yet modern solvers decide industrial formulas with millions of clauses. They do not try all assignments. They search, deduce and learn.

The base algorithm is DPLL (Davis, Putnam, Logemann and Loveland, 1960 and 1962). It has two moves.

  • Unit propagation. If every literal in a clause is false except one unset literal, that literal must be true. It is a unit clause. No choice is needed.
  • Decide and backtrack. When nothing is forced, pick a variable and guess a value. If this leads to a conflict, undo the guess and try the other value.
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
type Assign = BTreeMap<i32, bool>;

// Some(true), Some(false), or None (variable not set yet).
fn value(lit: i32, a: &Assign) -> Option<bool> { a.get(&lit.abs()).map(|&v| v == (lit > 0)) }

fn dpll(cnf: &[Vec<i32>], mut a: Assign, depth: usize) -> Option<Assign> {
    let pad = "  ".repeat(depth);
    loop { // unit propagation
        let mut unit = None;
        for c in cnf.iter().filter(|c| !c.iter().any(|&l| value(l, &a) == Some(true))) {
            let free: Vec<i32> = c.iter().copied().filter(|&l| value(l, &a).is_none()).collect();
            if free.is_empty() {
                println!("{pad}conflict in {c:?}"); // every literal is false
                return None;
            }
            if free.len() == 1 { unit = Some(free[0]); break; }
        }
        let Some(u) = unit else { break };
        a.insert(u.abs(), u > 0); // forced: no choice
        println!("{pad}unit {u}");
    }
    if cnf.iter().all(|c| c.iter().any(|&l| value(l, &a) == Some(true))) { return Some(a); }
    let x = cnf.iter().flatten().map(|l| l.abs()).filter(|v| !a.contains_key(v)).min()?;
    for choice in [true, false] { // decide, and undo on failure
        println!("{pad}decide x{x}={}", if choice { 'T' } else { 'F' });
        let mut next = a.clone();
        next.insert(x, choice);
        if let Some(model) = dpll(cnf, next, depth + 1) { return Some(model); }
    }
    None
}

fn main() {
    let cnf = vec![vec![-1, 2], vec![-1, 3], vec![-2, -3], vec![1, 4], vec![-4, 5], vec![-5, -2, 3]];
    let model = dpll(&cnf, Assign::new(), 0).unwrap();
    let text: Vec<String> = model.iter().map(|(k, &v)| format!("x{k}={}", if v { 'T' } else { 'F' })).collect();
    println!("model: {}", text.join(" "));
}
def value(lit, assign):
    """True, False, or None (variable not set yet)."""
    v = assign.get(abs(lit))
    return None if v is None else v == (lit > 0)

def dpll(cnf, assign, depth=0):
    pad = "  " * depth
    while True:                                  # unit propagation
        unit = None
        for c in cnf:
            vals = [value(l, assign) for l in c]
            if True in vals:
                continue                         # clause already true
            free = [l for l, v in zip(c, vals) if v is None]
            if not free:
                print(f"{pad}conflict in {c}")
                return None                      # every literal is false
            if len(free) == 1:
                unit = free[0]
                break
        if unit is None:
            break
        assign = assign | {abs(unit): unit > 0}  # forced: no choice
        print(f"{pad}unit {unit}")
    if all(True in [value(l, assign) for l in c] for c in cnf):
        return assign
    x = min(abs(l) for c in cnf for l in c if abs(l) not in assign)
    for choice in (True, False):                 # decide, and undo on failure
        print(f"{pad}decide x{x}={'T' if choice else 'F'}")
        result = dpll(cnf, assign | {x: choice}, depth + 1)
        if result is not None:
            return result
    return None

cnf = [[-1, 2], [-1, 3], [-2, -3], [1, 4], [-4, 5], [-5, -2, 3]]
model = dpll(cnf, {})
print("model:", " ".join(f"x{k}={'T' if v else 'F'}" for k, v in sorted(model.items())))
decide x1=T
  unit 2
  unit 3
  conflict in [-2, -3]
decide x1=F
  unit 4
  unit 5
  decide x2=T
    unit -3
    conflict in [-5, -2, 3]
  decide x2=F
model: x1=F x2=F x4=T x5=T

The model leaves x_3 unset. Every clause is already true, so x_3 can be anything. Notice the waste, though. DPLL hit two conflicts and forgot why each one happened. On a big formula it would make the same mistake again in another branch.

CDCL fixes this. GRASP (Marques-Silva and Sakallah, mid-1990s) added learning and long jumps back. Chaff (2001) made it fast with clever data structures. Here is one CDCL step on the same formula.

Decide

Set x_1 = T. This is decision level 1.

Propagate and keep the reasons

(\neg x_1 \lor x_2) forces x_2. (\neg x_1 \lor x_3) forces x_3. The solver records each reason clause. The reasons form an implication graph.

Conflict

(\neg x_2 \lor \neg x_3) is now false. Something earlier was wrong.

Analyse by resolution

Combine the conflict clause with the reasons. (\neg x_2 \lor \neg x_3) and (\neg x_1 \lor x_2) give (\neg x_1 \lor \neg x_3). With (\neg x_1 \lor x_3) this gives (\neg x_1).

Learn

Add the learned clause (\neg x_1) to the formula. It says: x_1 = T can never work. It follows from the formula, so no solution is lost.

Jump back

Go back to the lowest level where the learned clause becomes a unit clause. This is a backjump. Here it is level 0: x_1 = F is now a fact for the rest of the search.

Next conflict, next lesson

Later, x_2 = T forces \neg x_3 and breaks (\neg x_5 \lor \neg x_2 \lor x_3). Resolution gives (\neg x_2 \lor \neg x_5). Since x_5 is already true, this forces x_2 = F.

Real solvers add four more ideas.

  • Two watched literals. Each clause watches only two of its literals. Propagation looks at a clause only when a watched literal becomes false. This makes the inner loop cheap.
  • Activity-based choice (VSIDS). Variables that appear in recent conflicts get a higher score and are picked first.
  • Restarts. Every so often the solver drops all decisions but keeps its learned clauses. It escapes a bad early guess.
  • Clause deletion. Learned clauses that are rarely useful are thrown away to save memory.

When a solver says "satisfiable", you check the model in linear time. When it says "unsatisfiable", you would have to trust it. Many solvers can therefore write a proof of unsatisfiability. A small separate checker then verifies it. DRAT is a common format for such proofs.

SMT solvers: logic plus theories

Binary search has a famous bug. With 32-bit integers, (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow when both numbers are large. Many libraries shipped this bug for years. An SMT solver finds it in milliseconds.

SMT means "satisfiability modulo theories". A theory gives the solver knowledge of one data type. Common theories are integers, real numbers, arrays, strings and bit-vectors. Z3 (from Microsoft Research) and cvc5 are two widely used open-source SMT solvers.

use z3::ast::BV;
use z3::{SatResult, Solver};

fn main() {
    let lo = BV::new_const("lo", 32); // 32-bit machine integers (like i32)
    let hi = BV::new_const("hi", 32);
    let zero = BV::from_i64(0, 32);
    let two = BV::from_i64(2, 32);
    let bad = lo.bvadd(&hi).bvsdiv(&two);            // the classic midpoint
    let good = lo.bvadd(&hi.bvsub(&lo).bvsdiv(&two)); // the safe midpoint
    for (name, mid) in [("(lo + hi) / 2", bad), ("lo + (hi - lo) / 2", good)] {
        let s = Solver::new();
        s.assert(lo.bvsge(&zero)); // what binary search knows
        s.assert(hi.bvsge(&lo));
        s.assert(!(lo.bvsle(&mid) & mid.bvsle(&hi))); // ask for a counterexample
        match s.check() {
            SatResult::Sat => {
                let m = s.get_model().unwrap();
                let v = |x: &BV| m.eval(x, true).unwrap().as_i64().unwrap() as i32;
                println!("{name}: BUG, lo={} hi={} mid={}", v(&lo), v(&hi), v(&mid));
            }
            _ => println!("{name}: proved for all 2^64 inputs"),
        }
    }
}
from z3 import BitVecs, Solver, And, Not, sat

lo, hi = BitVecs("lo hi", 32)          # 32-bit machine integers (like i32)
pre = And(lo >= 0, hi >= lo)           # what binary search knows
bad = (lo + hi) / 2                    # the classic midpoint
good = lo + (hi - lo) / 2              # the safe midpoint

for name, mid in [("(lo + hi) / 2", bad), ("lo + (hi - lo) / 2", good)]:
    s = Solver()
    s.add(pre, Not(And(lo <= mid, mid <= hi)))   # ask for a counterexample
    if s.check() == sat:
        m = s.model()
        print(f"{name}: BUG, lo={m[lo].as_signed_long()} hi={m[hi].as_signed_long()} "
              f"mid={m.eval(mid).as_signed_long()}")
    else:
        print(f"{name}: proved for all 2^64 inputs")
(lo + hi) / 2: BUG, lo=268435456 hi=1879048192 mid=-1073741824
lo + (hi - lo) / 2: proved for all 2^64 inputs

Check the bug by hand. 268435456 + 1879048192 = 2^{31}. That is one more than the largest i32, so it wraps to -2^{31}. Half of it is -2^{30} = -1073741824, far outside the range. The second answer is a proof, not a test. "Unsatisfiable" means no pair of the 2^{64} inputs breaks the rule. We ran the Python version with z3-solver 5.4.1 from PyPI. The Rust version uses the z3 crate, linked to the same Z3 library.

All SMT solvers read one shared text format, SMT-LIB. The same question looks like this:

; Is there a 32-bit lo, hi with 0 <= lo <= hi where (lo + hi) / 2 leaves [lo, hi]?
(set-logic QF_BV)
(declare-const lo (_ BitVec 32))
(declare-const hi (_ BitVec 32))
(define-fun mid () (_ BitVec 32) (bvsdiv (bvadd lo hi) #x00000002))
(assert (bvsge lo #x00000000))
(assert (bvsge hi lo))
(assert (not (and (bvsle lo mid) (bvsle mid hi))))
(check-sat)
sat

How does it work inside? Most solvers use the DPLL(T) idea.

  1. Replace each theory fact, like x + y \gt 3, with a plain Boolean variable.
  2. Let the CDCL engine find an assignment for these Boolean variables.
  3. Ask a theory solver: can these facts be true together? For linear arithmetic it runs a form of the simplex method.
  4. If not, the theory solver returns a short reason. It becomes a learned clause, and the SAT search goes on.

Do not model machine integers with the mathematical integer theory. In Int, x + 1 \gt x is always true. In 32-bit bit-vectors, it is false for the largest number. Pick the theory that matches the real machine.

Hoare logic and loop invariants

Here is a loop that divides by repeated subtraction. We want to prove that it is right for every input, not only for the ones we test.

// {x >= 0 and y > 0}
//   q = 0; r = x; while r >= y { r = r - y; q = q + 1 }
// {x == q*y + r and 0 <= r < y}
fn divide(x: u32, y: u32) -> (u32, u32) {
    assert!(y > 0); // precondition (x >= 0 is given by the type u32)
    let (mut q, mut r) = (0, x);
    assert_eq!(x, q * y + r); // invariant holds before the loop
    while r >= y {
        r -= y; // the variant r gets smaller each time
        q += 1;
        assert_eq!(x, q * y + r); // invariant still holds after the body
        println!("q = {q}, r = {r}, q*y + r = {}", q * y + r);
    }
    assert!(x == q * y + r && r < y); // invariant + exit condition = postcondition
    (q, r)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", divide(17, 5));
}
# {x >= 0 and y > 0}
#   q = 0; r = x; while r >= y { r = r - y; q = q + 1 }
# {x == q*y + r and 0 <= r < y}
def divide(x: int, y: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
    assert x >= 0 and y > 0                  # precondition
    q, r = 0, x
    assert x == q * y + r and r >= 0         # invariant holds before the loop
    while r >= y:
        r -= y                               # the variant r gets smaller each time
        q += 1
        assert x == q * y + r and r >= 0     # invariant still holds after the body
        print(f"q = {q}, r = {r}, q*y + r = {q * y + r}")
    assert x == q * y + r and 0 <= r < y     # invariant + exit condition = postcondition
    return q, r

print(divide(17, 5))
q = 1, r = 12, q*y + r = 17
q = 2, r = 7, q*y + r = 17
q = 3, r = 2, q*y + r = 17
(3, 2)

The value of q \cdot y + r stays 17 in every round. That fact is the loop invariant. Runtime asserts check it for one input. Hoare logic proves it for all inputs.

A Hoare triple \{P\}\ C\ \{Q\} means: if C starts in a state where P holds, and C finishes, then Q holds at the end. P is the precondition. Q is the postcondition. Tony Hoare published the rules in 1969.

The core rules of Hoare logic
RuleShapeIn words
Assignment\{Q[e/x]\}\ x := e\ \{Q\}To get Q after the assignment, Q with e in place of x must hold before.
Sequence\{P\}\,C_1\,\{R\} and \{R\}\,C_2\,\{Q\} give \{P\}\,C_1; C_2\,\{Q\}Chain two steps through a middle condition.
If\{P \land b\}\,C_1\,\{Q\} and \{P \land \neg b\}\,C_2\,\{Q\}Both branches must reach Q.
While\{I \land b\}\,C\,\{I\} gives \{I\}\ \text{while } b\ \text{do } C\ \{I \land \neg b\}If the body keeps I, then I holds at the end, and the condition is false.
ConsequenceP \Rightarrow P', \{P'\}\,C\,\{Q'\}, Q' \Rightarrow QYou may strengthen the precondition and weaken the postcondition.

Apply them to divide with I = (x = q \cdot y + r \land r \ge 0).

  1. Start. After q = 0; r = x we get x = 0 \cdot y + x, and x \ge 0 from the precondition. So I holds.
  2. Body keeps I. Assume I and r \ge y. After the body, the new values are q + 1 and r - y. Then (q + 1)y + (r - y) = qy + r = x. Also r - y \ge 0 because r \ge y.
  3. End. The while rule gives I \land \neg(r \ge y). That is x = qy + r and 0 \le r \lt y, the postcondition.
  4. Termination. r is a natural number and drops by y \ge 1 each round. It cannot drop forever. This decreasing number is the variant.

Hoare triples prove partial correctness. Add a variant, and you get total correctness. Tools work backwards with the weakest precondition. For example \text{wp}(x := x + 1,\ x \gt 5) = (x + 1 \gt 5) = (x \gt 4). Tools like Dafny and Verus (for Rust) compute such conditions and send them to an SMT solver.

Suppose a triple \{P\}\ C\ \{Q\} can be derived with the rules. Suppose also that every implication used in the consequence rule is true. Then the triple is valid. For every start state that satisfies P, if C terminates, the final state satisfies Q.

Proof idea

Use induction on the derivation. Each rule takes valid triples to a valid triple. Assignment: the final state gives x the old value of e, so Q holds exactly when Q[e/x] held before. Sequence: run C_1 to reach R, then C_2 to reach Q. While: use a second induction on the number of rounds. The invariant holds after 0 rounds, and each round keeps it. When the loop stops, b is false. Stephen Cook showed the other direction, called relative completeness. Every valid triple can be derived, if we may use all true facts about the data.

In simple words: if the rules say a program is right, it is right. Example: the derivation above for divide is valid, so divide(17, 5) must return a pair with 17 = 5q + r and r \lt 5. It does: (3, 2).

A weak invariant like r \ge 0 is true but useless. It does not give the postcondition. A good invariant mentions every variable the loop changes and links them to the goal. Ask: "what stays the same while everything changes?"

Model checking and temporal logic

Two threads share a printer. Each one checks a flag, then sets its own flag, then prints. Is it safe? Testing may pass a million times and fail once in production. A model checker explores every order of steps.

Model checking turns a design into a graph of states. It then checks a property on every reachable state. Our checker uses breadth-first search, so the first bug it finds has the shortest trace.

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};
type State = ([u8; 2], [bool; 2], usize); // program counters, flags, turn

// Breadth-first search over every reachable state. Invariant: not both in crit.
fn check(step: fn(State, usize) -> Option<State>, crit: u8) -> String {
    let start: State = ([0, 0], [false, false], 0);
    let mut parent: HashMap<State, Option<State>> = HashMap::from([(start, None)]);
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([start]);
    while let Some(s) = queue.pop_front() {
        if s.0 == [crit, crit] { // mutual exclusion is broken
            let (mut trace, mut cur) = (vec![], Some(s));
            while let Some(c) = cur {
                trace.push(format!("{},{}", c.0[0], c.0[1]));
                cur = parent[&c];
            }
            trace.reverse();
            return format!("BUG after {} steps: {}", trace.len() - 1, trace.join(" -> "));
        }
        for i in 0..2 {
            if let Some(t) = step(s, i).filter(|t| !parent.contains_key(t)) {
                parent.insert(t, Some(s));
                queue.push_back(t);
            }
        }
    }
    format!("safe: checked all {} reachable states", parent.len())
}

// Look at the other flag, then raise my own. 2 = critical section.
fn naive((mut pc, mut flag, turn): State, i: usize) -> Option<State> {
    match pc[i] {
        0 if flag[1 - i] => return None,   // wait
        0 => pc[i] = 1,                    // the other flag is down
        1 => (flag[i], pc[i]) = (true, 2), // raise my flag, enter
        2 => pc[i] = 3,                    // leave the critical section
        _ => (flag[i], pc[i]) = (false, 0),
    }
    Some((pc, flag, turn))
}
from collections import deque

def check(step, crit):
    """Breadth-first search over every reachable state. Invariant: not both in crit."""
    start = ((0, 0), (False, False), 0)        # program counters, flags, turn
    parent = {start: None}
    queue = deque([start])
    while queue:
        s = queue.popleft()
        if s[0] == (crit, crit):               # mutual exclusion is broken
            trace = []
            while s is not None:
                trace.append("%d,%d" % s[0])
                s = parent[s]
            return f"BUG after {len(trace) - 1} steps: " + " -> ".join(reversed(trace))
        for i in (0, 1):
            t = step(s, i)
            if t is not None and t not in parent:
                parent[t] = s
                queue.append(t)
    return f"safe: checked all {len(parent)} reachable states"

def naive(s, i):
    """Look at the other flag, then raise my own. 2 = critical section."""
    pc, flag, turn = list(s[0]), list(s[1]), s[2]
    if pc[i] == 0:
        if flag[1 - i]:
            return None                        # wait
        pc[i] = 1                              # the other flag is down
    elif pc[i] == 1:
        flag[i], pc[i] = True, 2               # raise my flag, enter
    elif pc[i] == 2:
        pc[i] = 3                              # leave the critical section
    else:
        flag[i], pc[i] = False, 0
    return tuple(pc), tuple(flag), turn

Now add Peterson's algorithm to the same file. Each thread raises its flag, then politely gives the turn to the other thread, then waits.

// Raise my flag, give the turn away, wait. 3 = critical section.
fn peterson((mut pc, mut flag, mut turn): State, i: usize) -> Option<State> {
    let j = 1 - i;
    match pc[i] {
        0 => (flag[i], pc[i]) = (true, 1),            // I want to enter
        1 => (turn, pc[i]) = (j, 2),                  // but you may go first
        2 if flag[j] && turn == j => return None,     // wait
        2 => pc[i] = 3,                               // enter
        3 => pc[i] = 4,                               // leave the critical section
        _ => (flag[i], pc[i]) = (false, 0),
    }
    Some((pc, flag, turn))
}

fn main() {
    println!("naive: {}", check(naive, 2));
    println!("peterson: {}", check(peterson, 3));
}
def peterson(s, i):
    """Raise my flag, give the turn away, wait. 3 = critical section."""
    pc, flag, turn = list(s[0]), list(s[1]), s[2]
    j = 1 - i
    if pc[i] == 0:
        flag[i], pc[i] = True, 1               # I want to enter
    elif pc[i] == 1:
        turn, pc[i] = j, 2                     # but you may go first
    elif pc[i] == 2:
        if flag[j] and turn == j:
            return None                        # wait
        pc[i] = 3                              # enter
    elif pc[i] == 3:
        pc[i] = 4                              # leave the critical section
    else:
        flag[i], pc[i] = False, 0
    return tuple(pc), tuple(flag), turn

print("naive:", check(naive, 2))
print("peterson:", check(peterson, 3))
naive: BUG after 4 steps: 0,0 -> 1,0 -> 1,1 -> 2,1 -> 2,2
peterson: safe: checked all 26 reachable states

Read the bug trace. Both threads see the other flag down (states 1,0 and 1,1). Then both raise their flags and enter. Peterson's version passes in all 26 reachable states. That is a proof for this model, not a lucky test.

Properties over time need temporal logic. Amir Pnueli brought it to computer science in 1977. Linear temporal logic (LTL) has four main operators.

LTL operators, with examples from the printer
OperatorMeaningExample
\mathbf{G}\,palways p\mathbf{G}\,\neg(\text{cs}_0 \land \text{cs}_1): never both printing
\mathbf{F}\,peventually p\mathbf{F}\,\text{cs}_0: thread 0 prints some day
\mathbf{X}\,pin the next state\mathbf{X}\,\text{flag}_0
p\ \mathbf{U}\ qp holds until q happens\text{waiting}_0\ \mathbf{U}\ \text{cs}_0
  • A safety property says "nothing bad happens", like \mathbf{G}\,\neg(\text{cs}_0 \land \text{cs}_1). A finite trace shows a violation, as above.
  • A liveness property says "something good happens", like \mathbf{G}(\text{want}_0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{F}\,\text{cs}_0). A violation is an endless cycle where the good thing never comes.

The big enemy is state explosion. Ten threads with ten program points each give 10^{10} combinations. Tools fight back in several ways. Symbolic model checking stores sets of states as compact formulas. Bounded model checking unrolls k steps into one big SAT formula. Partial order reduction skips orders of steps that do not matter. Clarke, Emerson and Sifakis received the 2007 Turing Award for model checking.

"The model checker says safe" means the model is safe. Our checker assumed that each step is atomic and that memory is sequentially consistent. Real CPUs reorder memory writes. Peterson's algorithm on real hardware needs memory fences or atomics. See the concurrency chapter.

TLA+: specifying whole systems

TLA+ is a language for designs, not for code. Leslie Lamport created it. You describe a system as a set of states and the allowed steps between them. The TLC model checker then explores the states, just like our small checker.

Here is the naive lock as a TLA+ spec. Init gives the start states. Next gives the allowed steps. A primed variable like pc' means "the value in the next state".

---- MODULE NaiveLock ----
EXTENDS Naturals
VARIABLES pc, flag
Procs == {0, 1}

Init == pc = [i \in Procs |-> "check"] /\ flag = [i \in Procs |-> FALSE]

Check(i) == /\ pc[i] = "check" /\ ~flag[1 - i]
            /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "set"] /\ UNCHANGED flag
Set(i)   == /\ pc[i] = "set" /\ flag' = [flag EXCEPT ![i] = TRUE]
            /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "cs"]
Leave(i) == /\ pc[i] = "cs" /\ flag' = [flag EXCEPT ![i] = FALSE]
            /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "check"]

Next == \E i \in Procs : Check(i) \/ Set(i) \/ Leave(i)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<pc, flag>>

MutualExclusion == ~(pc[0] = "cs" /\ pc[1] = "cs")
====

You ask TLC to check MutualExclusion as an invariant. It reports a violation with a trace, like our checker did. The Spec line is a temporal formula. It says: start in Init, and every step is a Next step or changes nothing. We did not run this spec with TLC here. Our Rust and Python checkers explore the same model with the leave step split in two.

Why do engineers like it? A design bug is cheapest to fix before any code exists. Engineers at Amazon Web Services wrote about their use of TLA+ in 2015. They used it on S3, DynamoDB and other core services. A DynamoDB spec found subtle bugs. One of them needed a 35-step trace to show, which no normal test would ever reach. Today the TLA+ Foundation, part of the Linux Foundation, supports the tools. Its listed members include AWS, Oracle and NVIDIA.

Start small. Model only the protocol, with two or three nodes and small numbers. Most design bugs show up in tiny models. This idea is called the small scope hypothesis.

Types as proofs and proof assistants

Look at this Rust function: fn and_swap<A, B>(p: (A, B)) -> (B, A). Read the type as logic: "from A and B, conclude B and A". The body that compiles is a proof of that claim.

// Each function type is a claim. A function body that compiles is its proof.

// A and B implies B and A: swap the pair.
fn and_swap<A, B>(p: (A, B)) -> (B, A) { (p.1, p.0) }

// "A or B" is an enum with two cases.
enum Or<A, B> { Left(A), Right(B) }
fn or_swap<A, B>(p: Or<A, B>) -> Or<B, A> {
    match p { Or::Left(a) => Or::Right(a), Or::Right(b) => Or::Left(b) }
}

// (A implies B) and (B implies C) give (A implies C).
fn chain<A, B, C>(f: impl Fn(A) -> B, g: impl Fn(B) -> C) -> impl Fn(A) -> C {
    move |a| g(f(a))
}

// False is a type with no values. From False, anything follows.
enum False {}
fn absurd<A>(f: False) -> A { match f {} }

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", and_swap((1, 2.5)));
    if let Or::Right(x) = or_swap::<i32, &str>(Or::Left(7)) { println!("Right({x})"); }
    println!("{}", chain(|n: i32| n + 1, |n: i32| n * 10)(4));
    let _never_called: fn(False) -> i32 = absurd;
}
# Each function type is a claim. A body that passes the type checker is its proof.
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Never

def and_swap[A, B](p: tuple[A, B]) -> tuple[B, A]:      # A and B implies B and A
    return (p[1], p[0])

@dataclass
class Left[A]:
    value: A

@dataclass
class Right[B]:
    value: B

def or_swap[A, B](p: Left[A] | Right[B]) -> Left[B] | Right[A]:   # A or B implies B or A
    match p:
        case Left(a):
            return Right(a)
        case Right(b):
            return Left(b)

def chain[A, B, C](f: Callable[[A], B], g: Callable[[B], C]) -> Callable[[A], C]:
    return lambda a: g(f(a))                               # A->B and B->C give A->C

def absurd[A](f: Never, goal: type[A]) -> A:               # from False, anything follows
    return f

def inc(n: int) -> int: return n + 1
def times10(n: int) -> int: return n * 10

print(and_swap((1, 2.5)))
r: Left[str] | Right[int] = or_swap(Left(7))
if isinstance(r, Right):
    print(f"Right({r.value})")
print(chain(inc, times10)(4))
(2.5, 1)
Right(7)
50

Now try to prove a false claim: "from any A, get any B". The checker refuses.

// A false claim: "every A implies every B". No body can prove it.
fn bad<A, B>(a: A) -> B { a }
fn main() {}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> bad.rs:2:27
  |
2 | fn bad<A, B>(a: A) -> B { a }
  |        -  -           -   ^ expected type parameter `B`, found type parameter `A`
def bad[A, B](a: A, goal: type[B]) -> B:   # a false claim: "every A implies every B"
    return a
bad.py:2: error: Incompatible return value type (got "A", expected "B")  [return-value]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

Proofs in intuitionistic natural deduction correspond one to one with programs in the typed lambda calculus. Propositions are types. A proof of a proposition is a program of that type. Simplifying a proof is running the program.

Proof idea

Go rule by rule. The rule "from A and B, conclude A \land B" builds a pair. The rule "from A \land B, conclude A" takes the first part. The rule "assume A, prove B, conclude A \Rightarrow B" builds a function. Modus ponens is function call. Each rule has exactly one matching typing rule. A detour in a proof builds something and takes it apart at once. That is a beta reduction: calling a function you just wrote. Curry saw the link for implication in 1934. Howard wrote it out in full in 1969, published in 1980.

The dictionary between logic and types
LogicTypesRust
A \land Bpair (product)(A, B)
A \lor Btagged union (sum)enum Or<A, B>
A \Rightarrow Bfunctionimpl Fn(A) -> B
Trueunit type()
Falseempty typeenum False {} or !
\forall x\, P(x)dependent functionnot in Rust (Lean, Rocq)

The last row needs dependent types. A proof assistant has them. Lean 4 and the Rocq Prover (called Coq until its renaming) are the best known. Isabelle/HOL is another. You write the claim as a type and build the proof with tactics. A small trusted kernel checks the result.

-- A proof is a program: swap the two parts of the pair.
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p := ⟨h.2, h.1⟩

-- Lean checks this one by computation.
example : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl

-- The safe midpoint stays in range, for all natural numbers.
-- The omega tactic decides linear arithmetic over Nat and Int.
theorem mid_ok (lo hi : Nat) (h : lo ≤ hi) :
    lo ≤ lo + (hi - lo) / 2 ∧ lo + (hi - lo) / 2 ≤ hi := by
  omega

Note that Lean's Nat has no overflow. This proof is about mathematical numbers, not about i32. For machine code you need bit-vector types, or a tool like Verus or Kani.

There is a hard limit on all such systems, found long before computers.

Let T be a consistent theory whose axioms a program can list, and which can express basic arithmetic. Then some sentence G in the language of T is neither provable nor refutable in T.

Proof idea

Here is a simpler version that uses the halting problem and assumes T proves only true statements. Suppose T could prove or refute "machine M halts on input x" for every M and x. Then this program decides halting. List all proofs of T one by one. Stop when you find a proof of "halts" or of "does not halt". One of them must come, and it is true. That contradicts the undecidability of halting. So for some M and x, T proves neither. Gödel's own 1931 proof builds a sentence that says "I am not provable". Rosser (1936) showed that plain consistency is enough.

In simple words: no fixed set of rules proves every true fact about whole numbers. For daily work in Lean or Rocq this rarely matters. Normal theorems about programs are far from this edge. It does mean that no proof assistant, and no AI that writes proofs, can ever be complete.

A proof is only as good as its specification. Say the spec demands "the output is sorted" but forgets "it is a permutation of the input". Then a function that returns an empty list passes the proof. Review the spec as carefully as the code.

Where industry uses formal methods

Formal methods are no longer only for research. Here are real cases. Each one is described in public papers or on the project's own site.

Formal methods in use (checked against public sources, November 2026)
Who and whatMethodResult
AWS: S3, DynamoDB, EBSTLA+ and model checkingDesign bugs found before release, one with a 35-step trace
AWS IAM policies (Zelkova)SMT solversAnswers questions like "can anyone outside read this bucket?" Runs many millions of times a day
AWS Cedar policy languageLeanFormal proofs about the authorization engine
seL4 microkernelIsabelle/HOLThe C code is proved to match its specification (first published 2009)
CompCert C compilerRocqThe compiled code behaves as the source says. Qualified in 2026 for ATR 42/72 avionics software
Kani for RustModel checkingChecks panics, overflow and undefined behaviour in Rust code
Google DeepMind AlphaProofLeanAn AI system whose proofs are checked by Lean

For AI engineers this is good news. An AI coding agent can write code and a specification, and a solver can check them. The checker does not get tired and does not trust the agent. A failed proof gives a precise counterexample, which is perfect feedback for the next attempt. Lean is used in this way for AI-written mathematics.

  1. 1931 Gödel. Incompleteness of arithmetic.
  2. 1936 Church and Turing. First-order validity is undecidable.
  3. 1962 DPLL. Search with unit propagation and backtracking.
  4. 1969 Hoare. Axioms for proving programs. Howard writes the Curry-Howard notes.
  5. 1977 Pnueli. Temporal logic for programs.
  6. 1981 Model checking. Clarke and Emerson, then Queille and Sifakis.
  7. 2001 Chaff. Fast CDCL with watched literals and VSIDS.
  8. 2009 seL4. A full OS kernel proved correct.
  9. 2015 AWS paper. TLA+ in daily industry use.
  10. 2026 CompCert in avionics. A verified compiler qualified for aircraft software.

Exams often ask you to name the method for a task. Hardware or protocol with finite states: model checking. Arithmetic or bit-level bugs in one function: SMT. A deep theorem about a compiler or kernel: a proof assistant. A loop: an invariant and a variant.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for logic and formal methods
PatternPurposeModelNote
Equal \iff "differ" is UNSATCheck a refactorOld rule XOR new ruleA model of "differ" is a ready-made test case.
Valid \iff negation is UNSATProve a property with a solverAssert NOT(property), check"sat" means you found a counterexample.
Unit propagationDeduce forced values(\neg x_1 \lor x_2) with x_1 = T forces x_2Most solver time is spent here.
Learn from a conflictNever repeat a mistakeLearned clause (\neg x_1)The clause follows from the formula, so no solution is lost.

\{P\}\ C\ \{Q\}State what code promises\{y \gt 0\} divide \{x = qy + r\}Partial correctness: says nothing if C never stops.

VariantProve the loop stopsr drops by y each roundMust be a natural number that strictly drops.
