Practice

You want to prove that formula F is valid with a SAT solver. What do you ask the solver?

  • Is F satisfiable?
  • Is \neg F satisfiable? If not, F is valid.
  • Is F \land \neg F satisfiable?

F is true in every case exactly when no case makes \neg F true.

What does CDCL add to DPLL?

  • It tries all assignments in a smarter order.
  • It learns a new clause from each conflict and can jump back several levels.
  • It removes unit propagation to save time.

Learned clauses stop the same conflict from happening again in other branches.

"The server never sends two replies to one request." Which kind of property is this?

  • A safety property
  • A liveness property
  • Neither

It says something bad never happens. A finite trace with two replies would show a violation.

\text{wp}(x := 2x,\ x \gt 10) is x \gt ?.

With 4 propositions, a truth table has ? rows.

In the Curry-Howard dictionary, the logical "and" corresponds to the ? type.

  1. Write "every admin is also a user" in first-order logic.
    Answer

    \forall x\, (\text{Admin}(x) \Rightarrow \text{User}(x)). Note the arrow. \forall x\, (\text{Admin}(x) \land \text{User}(x)) would say that everything is an admin and a user.

  2. Find a loop invariant for this loop and prove the postcondition s = n(n+1)/2: s = 0; i = 0; while i < n { i = i + 1; s = s + i }.
    Answer

    Use I = (s = i(i+1)/2 \land i \le n). Start: s = 0 = 0 \cdot 1 / 2 and 0 \le n. Body: from I and i \lt n, after the body s' = i(i+1)/2 + (i + 1) = (i+1)(i+2)/2 and i + 1 \le n. Exit: I and i \ge n give i = n, so s = n(n+1)/2. The variant is n - i.

  3. Run DPLL by hand on (x_1 \lor x_2) \land (\neg x_1 \lor x_2) \land (\neg x_2 \lor x_3) \land (\neg x_3 \lor \neg x_1). Try x_1 = T first.
    Answer

    Decide x_1 = T. Clause 2 forces x_2. Clause 3 forces x_3. Clause 4 becomes (\neg x_3), which is false: conflict. Undo, decide x_1 = F. Clause 1 forces x_2. Clause 3 forces x_3. Clause 4 is true because \neg x_1 is true. Model: x_1 = F, x_2 = T, x_3 = T.

  4. Our naive lock failed. A friend suggests: "raise my flag first, then wait until the other flag is down". Is it safe? What can go wrong?
    Answer

    It is safe: mutual exclusion holds, because a thread enters only when its flag is up and the other flag is down. But both threads can raise their flags at the same time and then wait for each other forever. That is a deadlock, a liveness failure. Peterson's "turn" variable breaks the tie.

  5. Why can no proof assistant prove every true statement about the natural numbers?
    Answer

    A proof assistant's rules can be listed by a program, and they are consistent (we hope). They also express arithmetic. By Gödel's first incompleteness theorem, some arithmetic sentence is neither provable nor refutable. One of that sentence and its negation is true, so some true statement has no proof.

  6. Expert: an SMT query to check x + 1 > x returns "unsat" for the negation with Int, but "sat" with 32-bit bit-vectors. Explain both answers and say which one matters for Rust code.
    Answer

    With mathematical integers, x + 1 \gt x is always true, so its negation has no model. With 32-bit signed bit-vectors, x = 2^{31} - 1 wraps to -2^{31}, so the negation has a model. Rust's i32 is a 32-bit bit-vector. In debug builds the addition panics, and in release builds it wraps by default. So the bit-vector answer is the one that describes the real program.

Key takeaways

  • Propositional logic checks rules over all cases. Validity and equivalence reduce to "is this formula unsatisfiable?".
  • First-order logic adds "for all" and "there exists". It is undecidable in general, but many useful parts are decidable.
  • DPLL searches with unit propagation and backtracking. CDCL learns a clause from every conflict and jumps back.
  • SMT solvers add theories like bit-vectors and arrays. They find real bugs such as integer overflow, or prove that none exist.
  • Hoare logic proves code with pre- and postconditions. A loop needs an invariant, and a variant for termination. The rules are sound.
  • Model checking explores all states. Temporal logic states safety and liveness. TLA+ applies this to whole system designs.
  • Curry-Howard: types are propositions and programs are proofs. Lean and Rocq build on this idea.
  • Gödel's theorem is a hard limit, but industry uses formal methods every day: AWS, seL4, CompCert, Kani and more.

Sources

  • Marques-Silva, Lynce and Malik: Conflict-Driven Clause Learning SAT Solvers. Handbook of Satisfiability chapter on DPLL, GRASP, Chaff, watched literals and restarts.
  • Backes et al.: Semantic-based Automated Reasoning for AWS Access Policies using SMT. Zelkova, FMCAD 2018.
  • Abridged version of "How Amazon Web Services Uses Formal Methods". TLA+ at AWS, on Leslie Lamport's TLA+ site.
  • Philip Wadler: Propositions as Types. The history of Curry-Howard, with Curry 1934 and Howard 1969.
  • Lean. The Lean language and proof assistant, with Mathlib, AWS Cedar and AlphaProof as users.
  • CompCert. The verified C compiler, its Rocq proofs and its 2026 avionics qualification.

Computer architecture

Two loops can do the same work and differ in speed by ten times. The reason is the machine under the code. This chapter opens the processor: instructions, pipelines, caches, virtual memory, many cores and vector units. Every idea comes with a real measurement from this book's laptop.

  • Read a short program in RISC-V, Arm and x86 assembly, and say how the three instruction sets differ.
  • Trace an instruction through a five-stage pipeline and find data and control hazards.
  • Split an address into tag, index and offset, and name the kind of every cache miss.
  • Explain the TLB, cache coherence and false sharing, and measure their effects.
  • Use Amdahl's and Gustafson's laws to predict the speed-up from more cores.

All timings in this chapter come from one laptop. It is an Apple M2 Pro with 6 performance cores and 4 efficiency cores. It runs macOS 26.6, Rust 1.99 and Python 3.14. The timings were measured in November 2026. The machine was busy with other work, so some numbers vary between runs. Your numbers will differ. The shape of the results is what matters.

Instruction sets: the contract with the hardware

Here is one small C function. It adds up a list of numbers. We compiled it on the test machine for two kinds of processor.

long sum(const long *a, long n) {
    long s = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) s += a[i];
    return s;
}
_sum:                     ; x0 = pointer a, x1 = n
    cmp   x1, #1
    b.lt  LBB0_4          ; n < 1: return 0
    mov   x8, #0          ; s = 0
LBB0_2:
    ldr   x9, [x0], #8    ; load a[i], then move the pointer 8 bytes
    add   x8, x9, x8      ; s += a[i]
    subs  x1, x1, #1      ; n -= 1 and set the flags
    b.ne  LBB0_2          ; repeat while n != 0
    mov   x0, x8          ; the result goes in x0
    ret
LBB0_4:
    mov   x8, #0
    mov   x0, x8
    ret
_sum:                           ## rdi = pointer a, rsi = n
    pushq  %rbp
    movq   %rsp, %rbp
    testq  %rsi, %rsi
    jle    LBB0_1               ## n <= 0: return 0
    xorl   %ecx, %ecx           ## i = 0
    xorl   %eax, %eax           ## s = 0
LBB0_4:
    addq   (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax  ## s += a[i]: load and add in one instruction
    incq   %rcx
    cmpq   %rcx, %rsi
    jne    LBB0_4
    popq   %rbp
    retq
LBB0_1:
    xorl   %eax, %eax
    popq   %rbp
    retq
sum:                    # a0 = pointer a, a1 = n
    li    a2, 0         # s = 0
    blez  a1, done      # n <= 0: skip the loop
loop:
    ld    a3, 0(a0)     # load a[i]
    add   a2, a2, a3    # s += a[i]
    addi  a0, a0, 8     # move the pointer 8 bytes
    addi  a1, a1, -1    # n -= 1
    bnez  a1, loop      # repeat while n != 0
done:
    mv    a0, a2        # the result goes in a0
    ret

The Arm and x86 listings are real compiler output from Apple clang. Apple clang on this machine has no RISC-V target. So we wrote the RISC-V version by hand, in the same shape. Look at the loop in each one. Arm and RISC-V load first and add second. x86 does the load and the add in one instruction.

An instruction set architecture (ISA) is a contract. Software promises to use only these instructions. Hardware promises to run them with the stated meaning. A register holds one value inside the processor. Instructions work on registers and on memory addresses.

There are two old styles. RISC uses simple instructions of one fixed size. Only loads and stores touch memory. CISC has many instructions of different sizes, and many can use memory directly.

Three instruction sets in brief
RISC-VArm (AArch64)x86-64
StyleRISCRISCCISC
Instruction size32 bits (16 with the C extension)32 bits1 to 15 bytes
Integer registers32 (x0 is always zero)31 general, plus a zero register16 (Intel APX adds 16 more)
Who owns itOpen standard (RISC-V International)Arm, licensed to chip makersIntel and AMD
Where you meet itMicrocontrollers, research, new AI chipsPhones, Apple Macs, many cloud serversMost PCs and servers

Today the old fight between RISC and CISC matters less. A modern x86 core splits each instruction into small micro-ops. Inside, it works much like a RISC core. The ISA still matters for decoding, code size and software.

"x86 is slow because it is CISC." This is not true for modern chips. Speed comes mostly from the microarchitecture: pipelines, caches and predictors. The same ISA can run on a slow chip and on a fast chip.

The datapath and the pipeline

Take one instruction: ld x5, 8(x10). It means "read 8 bytes at address x10 + 8, and put them in x5". The processor does this in five steps.

Instruction fetch

The program counter holds an address. The processor reads the instruction at that address. It adds 4 to the program counter.

Instruction decode

The control unit reads the bits. "This is a load." It reads register x10 from the register file.

Execute

The ALU adds x10 and 8. The result is the memory address.

Memory

The processor reads 8 bytes from data memory at that address.

Write back

The value goes into register x5. The instruction is done.

The parts that do this work form the datapath. The program counter (PC) says where the next instruction is. The register file holds the registers. The ALU does the arithmetic. The control unit sets the switches for each instruction.

Now the key trick. A laundry has a washer and a dryer. You do not wait for load 1 to dry before you wash load 2. A pipeline does the same with instructions. In every clock cycle, each stage works on a different instruction.

A pipeline does not make one instruction faster. Its latency stays at 5 cycles. It improves throughput. With k stages and n instructions, the pipeline needs k + n - 1 cycles instead of k \cdot n. For large n, the speed-up gets close to k.

The time a program takes on one core is

\text{CPU time} = \text{instructions} \times \text{CPI} \times \text{clock period}

Here CPI is the average number of cycles per instruction.

Why it is true

Time is cycles times the length of one cycle. The number of cycles is the number of instructions times the average cycles for each one. Put the two together.

Example: a program runs 2 billion instructions. CPI is 0.5, because the core starts two instructions per cycle. The clock runs at 3 GHz, so one cycle is \frac{1}{3} ns. The time is 2 \cdot 10^9 \times 0.5 \times \frac{1}{3} ns, about 0.33 seconds. The law shows the three levers: fewer instructions (compiler, ISA), lower CPI (microarchitecture) and a faster clock (circuits).

Hazards

A pipeline breaks when instructions depend on each other. A hazard forces the pipeline to wait. Look at this code.

ld   x5, 0(x10)     # x5 arrives at the end of MEM
add  x6, x5, x7     # needs x5 in EX: one cycle too early
sub  x8, x6, x9     # needs x6: forwarding gives it in time
beq  x8, x0, done   # which instruction comes next? not known yet
  • A data hazard: an instruction needs a result that is not ready. The fix is forwarding. The sub gets x6 straight from the ALU output.
  • A load-use hazard: even with forwarding, the add needs x5 one cycle before memory gives it. The pipeline inserts a bubble. This wait is called a stall.
  • A control hazard: after beq, the next address is not known until the compare is done. The next section shows the fix.
  • A structural hazard: two instructions need the same part in the same cycle. Separate instruction and data caches remove the most common case.

"A deeper pipeline is always faster." More stages allow a faster clock. But every stall and every wrong branch guess now costs more cycles. Intel's Pentium 4 used a very deep pipeline. Later Intel designs went back to shorter ones.

Expert: beyond the simple pipeline

A superscalar core starts several instructions in each cycle. An out-of-order core keeps a window of hundreds of instructions. It runs each one when its inputs are ready. Register renaming removes false dependencies, where two instructions only reuse a register name. A reorder buffer makes the results appear in program order. This is how real cores reach a CPI well below 1.

Branch prediction

This Rust program counts the bytes that are 128 or more. It runs twice on the same 10 million bytes. The first time, they are in random order. The second time, they are sorted.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

fn count_big(data: &[u8]) -> u64 {
    let mut count = 0u64;
    for &x in data {
        if x >= 128 {
            count = black_box(count + 1); // black_box stops branch-free tricks
        }
    }
    count
}

fn main() {
    let mut seed = 7u64;
    let mut data: Vec<u8> = (0..10_000_000)
        .map(|_| {
            seed = seed.wrapping_mul(6364136223846793005).wrapping_add(1);
            (seed >> 56) as u8 // a pseudo-random byte
        })
        .collect();

    let t = Instant::now();
    let a = count_big(&data);
    println!("random order: {:>3} ms, count {}", t.elapsed().as_millis(), a);

    data.sort_unstable(); // now all small values come first
    let t = Instant::now();
    let b = count_big(&data);
    println!("sorted order: {:>3} ms, count {}", t.elapsed().as_millis(), b);
}
import random
import time

random.seed(7)
data = [random.randrange(256) for _ in range(10_000_000)]

def count_big(xs):
    count = 0
    for x in xs:
        if x >= 128:
            count += 1
    return count

t = time.perf_counter()
a = count_big(data)
print(f"random order: {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:4.0f} ms, count {a}")
data.sort()                                # all small values come first
t = time.perf_counter()
b = count_big(data)
print(f"sorted order: {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:4.0f} ms, count {b}")
random order:  32 ms, count 5000856
sorted order:   4 ms, count 5000856

Rust 1.99, rustc -O

random order:  215 ms, count 4996637
sorted order:  175 ms, count 4996637

Python 3.14

Same data, same work, but Rust is 8 times faster on sorted data. Why? The processor guesses the result of each branch before it knows it. On sorted data the answer is "no, no, no ... yes, yes, yes". The guess is almost always right. On random data it is wrong half the time.

A branch predictor keeps a history of each branch. The core then runs the guessed path at once. This is speculative execution. A right guess costs nothing. A wrong guess throws away all work after the branch. Our numbers give the cost. About 5 million wrong guesses added about 28 ms. That is about 5.5 ns per wrong guess. Apple does not list the clock speed. At an assumed 3 to 3.5 GHz, this is roughly 16 to 19 cycles.

The simplest good predictor is a saturating counter with two bits. One wrong guess does not flip a strong state.

Real cores use much bigger predictors. They look at the history of many recent branches. A BTB remembers where each taken branch jumps. A return stack predicts where functions return.

In Python, the gap is only about 20%. Each loop step runs many instructions inside the interpreter. One wrong guess is a small part of that work.

Our first Rust test showed no difference at all. The compiler had removed the branch. It used a conditional select instead. Always check that your test measures what you think. Here black_box keeps the branch.

Expert: Spectre

Wrong-path work is thrown away, but it leaves traces in the cache. In 2018 the Spectre attacks used this. They trained the predictor to go the wrong way. The wrong path read a secret and touched a cache line that depended on it. A timing test then revealed the secret. Defences include fences after bounds checks and separate predictor state for each process.

Caches

Memory is far away from the core. A cache keeps copies of data the program used recently. Here is a tiny cache simulator. Addresses 0 and 128 take turns, ten times.

// A tiny cache simulator with LRU replacement inside each set.
fn misses(addrs: &[u64], sets: u64, ways: usize, line: u64) -> usize {
    let mut cache: Vec<Vec<u64>> = vec![Vec::new(); sets as usize];
    let mut miss = 0;
    for &a in addrs {
        let block = a / line;              // which memory block
        let set = &mut cache[(block % sets) as usize];
        if let Some(i) = set.iter().position(|&b| b == block) {
            set.remove(i);                 // hit: move it to the back (newest)
        } else {
            miss += 1;
            if set.len() == ways { set.remove(0); } // full: evict the oldest
        }
        set.push(block);
    }
    miss
}

fn main() {
    // 8 lines of 16 bytes = 128 bytes of cache. Addresses 0 and 128 take turns.
    let addrs: Vec<u64> = (0..10).map(|i| if i % 2 == 0 { 0 } else { 128 }).collect();
    println!("direct-mapped (8 sets x 1 way): {} misses of 10", misses(&addrs, 8, 1, 16));
    println!("2-way         (4 sets x 2 way): {} misses of 10", misses(&addrs, 4, 2, 16));
    println!("fully assoc.  (1 set  x 8 way): {} misses of 10", misses(&addrs, 1, 8, 16));
}
# A tiny cache simulator with LRU replacement inside each set.
def misses(addrs, sets, ways, line):
    cache = [[] for _ in range(sets)]
    miss = 0
    for a in addrs:
        block = a // line                  # which memory block
        s = cache[block % sets]
        if block in s:
            s.remove(block)                # hit: move it to the back (newest)
        else:
            miss += 1
            if len(s) == ways:
                s.pop(0)                   # full: evict the oldest
        s.append(block)
    return miss

# 8 lines of 16 bytes = 128 bytes of cache. Addresses 0 and 128 take turns.
addrs = [0 if i % 2 == 0 else 128 for i in range(10)]
print(f"direct-mapped (8 sets x 1 way): {misses(addrs, 8, 1, 16)} misses of 10")
print(f"2-way         (4 sets x 2 way): {misses(addrs, 4, 2, 16)} misses of 10")
print(f"fully assoc.  (1 set  x 8 way): {misses(addrs, 1, 8, 16)} misses of 10")
direct-mapped (8 sets x 1 way): 10 misses of 10
2-way         (4 sets x 2 way): 2 misses of 10
fully assoc.  (1 set  x 8 way): 2 misses of 10

The cache has room for 8 blocks, and we use only 2. Still, the first cache misses every time. Both addresses want the same place.

A cache moves data in fixed blocks called cache lines. A hit is fast. A miss is slow. The cache is split into sets. Each set has some ways. A block can only go into one set, but into any way of that set.

  • Direct-mapped: one way per set. Simple and fast, but two blocks can fight over one place.
  • Set-associative: a few ways per set, often 4 to 16. This is the normal choice.
  • Fully associative: one set with all the ways. No fights, but every way must be checked. Small structures like the TLB use it.

The hardware cuts each address into three parts. The offset picks the byte in the line. The index picks the set. The tag is stored next to the data and compared on each lookup.

  1. Lines: 32768 / 64 = 512. Sets: 512 / 8 = 64.
  2. Offset bits: \log_2 64 = 6. Index bits: \log_2 64 = 6. With 48-bit addresses, the tag has 48 - 12 = 36 bits.
  3. Take address 0x12345, which is 74565. Offset: 74565 \bmod 64 = 5.
  4. Block number: \lfloor 74565 / 64 \rfloor = 1165. Index: 1165 \bmod 64 = 13.
  5. Tag: \lfloor 74565 / 4096 \rfloor = 18. So the byte lives in set 13, if a way there holds tag 18.

Every miss has a reason. Computer architects use the "three Cs".

Compulsory miss

The first use of a block. It was never in the cache. Prefetching helps. A bigger cache does not.

Capacity miss

The data you use is bigger than the cache. Even a fully associative cache would miss. A bigger cache or a smaller working set helps.

Conflict miss

The cache has room, but too many blocks map to one set. Our direct-mapped test had only conflict misses after the first two. More ways help.

Coherence miss (the fourth C)

Another core wrote to the line, so this copy was thrown out. It appears in multicore programs. A later section shows it.

When the cache writes, it has two choices. Write-through sends every write to the next level. Write-back marks the line dirty and writes it later. Most CPU caches use write-back.

Programs reuse data they used recently (temporal locality). They also use data near data they used recently (spatial locality).

This is an observation about real programs, not a proof. Loops reuse their variables. Arrays are read in order. Caches work because of locality. A program without locality gets almost nothing from a cache.

\text{AMAT} = \text{hit time} + \text{miss rate} \times \text{miss penalty}

With two levels, the miss penalty of level 1 is the AMAT of level 2.

Why it is true

Every access pays the hit time, because the cache is always checked first. A fraction of the accesses, the miss rate, also pays the extra time to fetch from the next level. Take the average over all accesses.

Example: L1 hit time 1 ns, miss rate 5%, and memory takes 100 ns. AMAT is 1 + 0.05 \times 100 = 6 ns. Now add an L2 with a 5 ns hit time. It misses on 20% of the accesses it gets. AMAT is 1 + 0.05 \times (5 + 0.2 \times 100) = 2.25 ns. A small second level cuts the average time by more than half.

Exams love three calculations. The first is tag, index and offset bits. The second is AMAT with two levels. The third is the pipeline speed-up \frac{nk}{k + n - 1}. Write the units at every step. Say clearly if a miss rate is local (of the accesses that reach this level) or global (of all accesses).

The memory hierarchy, measured

How slow is a miss, really? The program below builds a random cycle through an array. Then it follows the cycle 20 million times. Each load needs the result of the one before. So the processor cannot overlap the loads. This is called pointer chasing.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

// Follow a random cycle through `bytes` of memory. Return ns per load.
fn ns_per_load(bytes: usize) -> f64 {
    let n = bytes / 8;
    let mut order: Vec<usize> = (0..n).collect();
    let mut seed = 42u64;
    for i in (1..n).rev() {
        seed ^= seed << 13; seed ^= seed >> 7; seed ^= seed << 17; // xorshift
        order.swap(i, (seed % (i as u64 + 1)) as usize);          // shuffle
    }
    let mut next = vec![0usize; n];
    for k in 0..n {
        next[order[k]] = order[(k + 1) % n]; // each slot points to the next one
    }
    let steps = 20_000_000;
    let mut p = 0;
    let t = Instant::now();
    for _ in 0..steps {
        p = next[p]; // this load needs the result of the last load
    }
    black_box(p);
    t.elapsed().as_nanos() as f64 / steps as f64
}

fn main() {
    for kib in [16, 64, 128, 256, 1024, 4096, 16384, 32768, 65536, 262144] {
        println!("{:>7} KiB: {:6.1} ns per load", kib, ns_per_load(kib * 1024));
    }
}
import random
import time
from array import array

def ns_per_load(nbytes):
    n = nbytes // 8
    order = list(range(n))
    random.seed(42)
    random.shuffle(order)
    nxt = array("q", bytes(8 * n))           # 8-byte slots, side by side
    for k in range(n):
        nxt[order[k]] = order[(k + 1) % n]   # each slot points to the next
    steps = 2_000_000
    p = 0
    t = time.perf_counter_ns()
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = nxt[p]                           # each load needs the one before
    return (time.perf_counter_ns() - t) / steps

for kib in [16, 256, 4096, 65536, 262144]:
    print(f"{kib:>7} KiB: {ns_per_load(kib * 1024):6.1f} ns per load")
     16 KiB:    1.3 ns per load
     64 KiB:    1.3 ns per load
    128 KiB:    1.3 ns per load
    256 KiB:    3.7 ns per load
   1024 KiB:    5.8 ns per load
   4096 KiB:    7.9 ns per load
  16384 KiB:   24.8 ns per load
  32768 KiB:   49.7 ns per load
  65536 KiB:  104.9 ns per load
 262144 KiB:  126.7 ns per load

Rust, M2 Pro

    256 KiB:   22.0 ns per load

The steps match the caches. The macOS tool sysctl reports these sizes for this chip:

Cache sizes on the test machine, as sysctl reports them
LevelSizeOur measured time
L1 data, per performance core128 KiBabout 1.3 ns
L2, performance cores (shared by 3 cores)16 MiBabout 4 to 8 ns

Up to 128 KiB, every load hits L1. From 256 KiB to 4 MiB, the loads hit L2. Past 16 MiB the data no longer fits, and the time climbs to main memory speed. In other runs, the 16 MiB point varied from 25 to 51 ns, and the 256 MiB point from 124 to 181 ns. Large arrays also cause TLB misses, which the next section explains.

Caches are made of SRAM. Main memory is DRAM. SRAM is fast but large and costly. DRAM is dense but slow. So every computer uses a memory hierarchy. Python adds about 22 ns of interpreter work to every load. That hides L1 and L2. But main memory still shows: 108 ns against 22 ns.

Other levels are much slower. These well-known estimates come from Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig. They are from about 2012, not from our machine.

Rough latency numbers (Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig, about 2012)
ActionTimeIf an L1 hit took 1 second
L1 cache hit0.5 ns1 second
Main memory access100 ns3 minutes
Read 4 KB at random from an SSD150 µs3.5 days
Round trip inside one data centre500 µs12 days
Disk seek10 ms8 months
Packet from California to the Netherlands and back150 ms9.5 years

Modern SSDs are faster than the 2012 figure. Measure your own hardware when it matters.

Testing memory speed with a simple loop over an array. The hardware prefetcher sees the pattern and loads the lines early. You then measure bandwidth, not latency. Random pointer chasing defeats the prefetcher.

Virtual memory and the TLB

Every process sees its own addresses, starting near zero. Two processes can both use address 0x1000. They still do not see each other's data. How?

A program uses virtual addresses. The hardware turns each one into a physical address. Memory is split into pages. A page table maps each virtual page to a physical page. The MMU does the translation on every load and store.

Page size depends on the system. Most x86 and Linux systems use 4 KiB pages. On the test machine, sysctl hw.pagesize prints 16384. Apple Silicon Macs use 16 KiB pages.

The page table lives in memory. On x86-64 it has four levels, or five on newer systems. A full translation could cost four extra memory reads. That would make every load five times slower. So the MMU keeps a small cache of recent translations: the TLB.

  1. Take a TLB with 64 entries. This is an example size, not a measured one.
  2. With 4 KiB pages, the TLB covers 64 \times 4 KiB = 256 KiB. This is its reach.
  3. With 16 KiB pages, the reach is 1 MiB.
  4. With 2 MiB huge pages, the reach is 128 MiB.
  5. A program that jumps around 64 MiB of memory misses the TLB often with small pages, and rarely with huge pages.

Real cores have several TLB levels with more entries. The idea is the same. The operating system builds the page tables. The hardware walks them on a TLB miss. On a context switch the TLB may need a flush, or it tags entries with an address space id. The chapter Operating systems: memory and storage covers page faults and replacement.

"Virtual memory means swapping to disk." Swapping is only one use. The main jobs are isolation and a simple, private address space for each process. A system with no swap file still uses virtual memory on every instruction.

Multicore and cache coherence

Two threads each add 1 to their own counter, 50 million times. They never touch the same counter. Only the distance between the two counters changes.

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

#[repr(C, align(256))] // the block starts on a 256-byte boundary
struct Block([AtomicU64; 32]); // 32 counters of 8 bytes = 256 bytes

// Two threads each add 1 to their own counter, 50 million times.
fn run(gap_bytes: usize) -> u128 {
    let block = Block(std::array::from_fn(|_| AtomicU64::new(0)));
    let (a, b) = (&block.0[0], &block.0[gap_bytes / 8]);
    let t = Instant::now();
    thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..50_000_000 { a.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); });
        s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..50_000_000 { b.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); });
    });
    t.elapsed().as_millis()
}

fn main() {
    for gap in [8, 64, 128] {
        println!("counters {gap:>3} bytes apart: {:>4} ms", run(gap));
    }
}
counters   8 bytes apart:  552 ms
counters  64 bytes apart:  201 ms
counters 128 bytes apart:  108 ms

Counters 8 bytes apart are 5 times slower than counters 128 bytes apart. In six runs, 128 bytes was the fastest in five. There is no Python tab here. In the standard CPython build, threads take turns running Python code, so they cannot show this effect.

A multicore chip gives each core its own L1 cache. Now two caches can hold copies of one line. If one core writes, the other copy is wrong. Cache coherence keeps the copies in agreement. The common protocol is MESI.

The four MESI states of a cache line
StateMeaningWrite without asking?
ModifiedOnly this cache has it, and it changed itYes
ExclusiveOnly this cache has it, and it equals memoryYes (it becomes Modified)
SharedSeveral caches may hold it, read onlyNo: first make the others Invalid
InvalidThis copy must not be usedNo: first fetch the line

Here is what happened when the counters were 8 bytes apart.

  1. Core A writes counter a. Its line becomes Modified. Core B's copy becomes Invalid.
  2. Core B writes counter b. Counter b is in the same line. B must take the line from A. Now B has it Modified, and A's copy is Invalid.
  3. Core A writes again. The line moves back to A.
  4. The line bounces between the cores again and again. Each move is a slow trip from one cache to another.

This is false sharing. The threads share no data, but they share a line. The fix is padding: put each hot counter on its own line. Our result also answers a real question. Apple Silicon reports a 128-byte cache line in sysctl. Some engineers say the L1 lines are 64 bytes. On our machine, 64 bytes of distance helped, but 128 bytes helped more. So pad to 128 bytes on this chip.

Small chips find copies by snooping. Big chips with many cores use a directory, because sending every request to every core does not scale.

Expert: coherence is not the memory model

Coherence speaks about one address. A memory model speaks about the order of writes to different addresses. x86 uses a strong model called TSO. Arm and RISC-V use weaker models. They let the hardware reorder more. Programs then need fences or atomic operations with acquire and release order. The chapter Concurrency and parallelism builds on this.

How much faster can more cores make a program?

A program has a serial part, a fraction s of its time on one core. The rest, 1 - s, can be split over n cores. The job size is fixed. Then the speed-up is

S(n) = \frac{1}{s + \frac{1 - s}{n}} \lt \frac{1}{s}
Proof

Let the time on one core be T. The serial part still takes sT. The parallel part takes (1 - s)T / n. The speed-up is the old time over the new time: \frac{T}{sT + (1 - s)T/n}. Cancel T. As n grows, the second term goes to 0, so the speed-up stays below \frac{1}{s}.

In simple words: the serial part sets a ceiling. With s = 0.05, even a million cores give less than 20 times the speed.

Now let the job grow with the machine. On n cores, a fraction s of the run time is serial. The same work on one core would take s + (1 - s)n times as long. This is the scaled speed-up:

S(n) = s + (1 - s)\,n = n - (n - 1)\,s
Proof

Measure one run on n cores and call its time 1. The serial part takes s. The parallel part takes 1 - s, with all n cores busy. One core alone would need s for the serial part and n(1 - s) for the parallel part. The ratio of the two times is s + n(1 - s).

// Speed-up with n cores when a share s of the work is serial.
fn amdahl(s: f64, n: f64) -> f64 { 1.0 / (s + (1.0 - s) / n) }   // fixed job size
fn gustafson(s: f64, n: f64) -> f64 { s + (1.0 - s) * n }        // job grows with n

fn main() {
    let s = 0.05; // 5% of the time is serial
    println!("cores  amdahl  gustafson");
    for n in [1.0, 4.0, 16.0, 64.0, 1024.0] {
        println!("{:>5}  {:>6.2}  {:>9.2}", n, amdahl(s, n), gustafson(s, n));
    }
}
# Speed-up with n cores when a share s of the work is serial.
def amdahl(s, n):
    return 1 / (s + (1 - s) / n)       # fixed job size

def gustafson(s, n):
    return s + (1 - s) * n             # job grows with n

s = 0.05                               # 5% of the time is serial
print("cores  amdahl  gustafson")
for n in [1, 4, 16, 64, 1024]:
    print(f"{n:>5}  {amdahl(s, n):>6.2f}  {gustafson(s, n):>9.2f}")
cores  amdahl  gustafson
    1    1.00       1.00
    4    3.48       3.85
   16    9.14      15.25
   64   15.42      60.85
 1024   19.64     972.85

The two laws do not disagree. They answer different questions. Amdahl asks: "How much faster is this job?" Gustafson asks: "How much bigger a job can I do in the same time?" Training a large AI model is a Gustafson case. More GPUs let you train a bigger model on more data in the same weeks.

Using the same s in both laws. In Amdahl, s is the serial share of the one-core time. In Gustafson, it is the serial share of the n-core time. A program that is 5% serial on 1024 cores was far less serial on one core. Mixing the two makes the laws look like they disagree.

SIMD and GPUs

Here are two ways to sum a million 32-bit floats. The first keeps one running total. The second keeps eight.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

// One running total: every add waits for the add before it.
fn sum_one(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    let mut s = 0.0;
    for &x in xs { s += x; }
    s
}

// Eight totals: the compiler can keep them in SIMD registers.
fn sum_eight(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    let mut acc = [0.0f32; 8];
    for chunk in xs.chunks_exact(8) {
        for i in 0..8 { acc[i] += chunk[i]; } // 8 adds, no chain between them
    }
    acc.iter().sum()
}

fn main() {
    let xs = vec![0.5f32; 1 << 20]; // 4 MiB of f32
    for (name, f) in [("one total", sum_one as fn(&[f32]) -> f32), ("eight totals", sum_eight)] {
        let t = Instant::now();
        let mut s = 0.0;
        for _ in 0..100 { s = f(black_box(&xs)); }
        println!("{name:>12}: {:>4} us per pass, sum {s}", t.elapsed().as_micros() / 100);
    }
}
import time
import numpy as np

xs = np.full(1 << 20, 0.5, dtype=np.float32)   # 4 MiB of f32
lst = xs.tolist()

t = time.perf_counter()
s = 0.0
for x in lst:                     # one value at a time, in the interpreter
    s += x
print(f"Python loop: {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e6:6.0f} us, sum {s}")

xs.sum()                          # warm up once
t = time.perf_counter()
s = float(xs.sum())               # NumPy: one compiled loop in C
print(f"NumPy sum:   {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e6:6.0f} us, sum {s}")
   one total:  960 us per pass, sum 524288
eight totals:  117 us per pass, sum 524288

Rust 1.99

Python loop:  41732 us, sum 524288.0
NumPy sum:      188 us, sum 524288.0

Python 3.14 with NumPy 2.5.4 (uv run --with numpy)

Eight totals run 8 times faster. Why? Float addition is not associative. (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) in the last bits. So the compiler must keep the order of the first loop. Each add waits for the one before it. In the second loop we chose a new order ourselves. Now the compiler can use SIMD.

SIMD means one instruction works on a short vector of values. Each value sits in a lane. Arm's NEON registers are 128 bits wide, so they hold four f32 values. x86 has SSE (128 bits), AVX2 (256 bits) and AVX-512 (512 bits). Arm's SVE lets the vector length vary from chip to chip. RISC-V's V extension has the same idea.

A GPU takes this idea very far. It runs thousands of threads. NVIDIA GPUs group 32 threads into a warp. The threads of a warp run the same instruction on different data. NVIDIA calls this SIMT.

CPU core

  • A few fast, clever cores
  • Big caches and branch predictors
  • Built for low latency on one task

GPU

  • Thousands of simple lanes
  • Hides memory latency by switching between warps
  • Built for high throughput on many tasks

Putting an if that splits the threads of one warp. If 16 threads take one path and 16 take the other, the warp runs both paths, one after the other. Half the lanes rest each time. This is divergence. Arrange the data so that neighbour threads take the same path.

Expert: compute-bound or memory-bound?

The arithmetic intensity of a task is its operations per byte of memory traffic. Adding two f32 vectors does 1 operation per 12 bytes: two loads and one store. No machine can feed that fast enough, so it is memory-bound. Multiplying two n \times n matrices does about 2n^3 operations on 3n^2 values. The intensity grows with n, so large matrix products are compute-bound. That is why GPUs add special matrix units. The same idea explains why a language model making one token at a time is often limited by memory bandwidth. It must read every weight for each token.

Why layout in memory changes speed

A 4096 by 4096 grid of floats is stored row by row. We sum it two ways: along the rows and along the columns.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

const N: usize = 4096; // a 4096 x 4096 grid of f32: 64 MiB

fn main() {
    let grid = vec![1.0f32; N * N]; // row-major: row r starts at r * N
    let t = Instant::now();
    let mut s = 0.0f32;
    for r in 0..N {
        for c in 0..N {
            s += grid[r * N + c]; // next item is the next address
        }
    }
    println!("by rows:    {:>4} ms (sum {})", t.elapsed().as_millis(), black_box(s));

    let t = Instant::now();
    let mut s = 0.0f32;
    for c in 0..N {
        for r in 0..N {
            s += grid[r * N + c]; // next item is 16 KiB away
        }
    }
    println!("by columns: {:>4} ms (sum {})", t.elapsed().as_millis(), black_box(s));
}
import time
import numpy as np

N = 4096
grid = np.ones((N, N), dtype=np.float32)  # row-major (C order): 64 MiB

t = time.perf_counter()
s = sum(float(grid[r, :].sum()) for r in range(N))   # one row: 4096 neighbours
print(f"by rows:    {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:4.0f} ms (sum {s:.0f})")

t = time.perf_counter()
s = sum(float(grid[:, c].sum()) for c in range(N))   # one column: stride 16 KiB
print(f"by columns: {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:4.0f} ms (sum {s:.0f})")
by rows:      32 ms (sum 16777216)
by columns:  310 ms (sum 16777216)

Rust 1.99

by rows:      13 ms (sum 16777216)
by columns:   81 ms (sum 16777216)

Python 3.14 with NumPy

Same numbers, same sum, about 10 times slower in Rust. The row loop uses every byte of each cache line. The prefetcher sees the pattern too. The column loop jumps 4096 \times 4 = 16384 bytes each step. That is exactly one page on this machine. So every step needs a new cache line and a new TLB entry. Also, the jump is a power of two, so many of the lines fall into the same cache sets. A pure Python loop showed only 8.1 s against 9.2 s. The interpreter's own work hid most of the gap.

The same idea decides how to store records. An array of structs (AoS) keeps each record together. A struct of arrays (SoA) keeps each field together.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

#[allow(dead_code)] // we only read x in this test
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Particle { x: f64, y: f64, z: f64, vx: f64, vy: f64, vz: f64, mass: f64, id: u64 } // 64 bytes

fn main() {
    let n = 4_000_000;
    let aos = vec![Particle { x: 1.0, y: 0.0, z: 0.0, vx: 0.0, vy: 0.0, vz: 0.0, mass: 1.0, id: 0 }; n];
    let xs = vec![1.0f64; n]; // the same x values, stored alone

    let t = Instant::now();
    let s: f64 = black_box(&aos).iter().map(|p| p.x).sum(); // uses 8 of every 64 bytes
    println!("array of structs: {:>3} ms, sum {s}", t.elapsed().as_millis());

    let t = Instant::now();
    let s: f64 = black_box(&xs).iter().sum(); // uses every byte it loads
    println!("struct of arrays: {:>3} ms, sum {s}", t.elapsed().as_millis());
}
import time
import numpy as np

n = 4_000_000
fields = ["x", "y", "z", "vx", "vy", "vz", "mass", "id"]
aos = np.zeros(n, dtype=[(f, np.float64) for f in fields])  # 64 bytes per record
aos["x"] = 1.0
xs = np.ones(n)                                              # x values alone

t = time.perf_counter()
s = aos["x"].sum()                     # a strided view: 8 of every 64 bytes
print(f"array of structs: {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:3.0f} ms, sum {s:.0f}")

t = time.perf_counter()
s = xs.sum()                           # one tight block
print(f"struct of arrays: {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:3.0f} ms, sum {s:.0f}")
array of structs:  25 ms, sum 4000000
struct of arrays:   4 ms, sum 4000000

Rust 1.99

array of structs:  30 ms, sum 4000000
struct of arrays:   4 ms, sum 4000000

Python 3.14 with NumPy

To sum only x, the AoS version loads 64 bytes to use 8. The SoA version uses every byte it loads. Game engines, databases with column storage and data-frame libraries use SoA for this reason.

Here are the main layout rules.

  • Walk memory in the order it is stored. In row-major arrays, the last index changes fastest.
  • Keep the fields you use together. Move cold fields to another place.
  • Prefer arrays to linked structures. Each list node is a possible cache miss.
  • Give hot data shared by threads its own cache line. Do not pack writers' counters together.
  • Process big data in blocks that fit in the cache. This is called tiling. Fast matrix multiplication does this.

Thinking that O(n) tells you the speed. Both grid loops are O(n^2) in the side length. One is still 10 times slower. Big-O counts operations. It does not count cache misses. Measure with real data on real hardware.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for computer architecture
PatternPurposeModelNote
Time = instructions × CPI × periodFind which lever to pull2 \cdot 10^9 \times 0.5 \times \frac{1}{3} ns ≈ 0.33 sA faster clock with a higher CPI can be slower.

Name the CChoose the right fix for missescompulsory, capacity, conflict, coherenceMore ways fix conflict misses only.
Chase pointers to measure latencyDefeat the prefetcherL1 1.3 ns, DRAM about 105 ns (M2 Pro)A plain loop measures bandwidth instead.
Entries × page sizeTLB reach64 × 16 KiB = 1 MiBHuge pages raise the reach a lot.
Pad hot data to a lineStop false sharing8 bytes apart: 552 ms, 128 apart: 108 msUse 128 bytes on Apple Silicon.

s + (1-s)nScaled speed-up (Gustafson)1024 cores: 973Here s is measured on the n-core run.
