Practice

Which statement about pipelining is true?

  • It makes each instruction finish in fewer cycles.
  • It lets one instruction finish in most cycles, while each still takes several cycles.
  • It removes the need for a clock.

A pipeline improves throughput, not latency. Each instruction still passes through every stage.

A loop reads a 64 KiB array again and again. The cache is 32 KiB and fully associative. What kind of misses does it get after the first pass?

  • Compulsory
  • Capacity
  • Conflict

The data is bigger than the whole cache. Even a fully associative cache misses, so these are capacity misses.

Two threads write to two different variables. The program is slow, and a profiler shows many coherence misses. What is the likely cause?

  • A data race
  • False sharing: the variables sit in one cache line
  • A TLB miss on every write

The threads share no data but share a line. Each write takes the line away from the other core. Padding fixes it.

A program is 10% serial on one core. By Amdahl's law, what is the best speed-up with any number of cores?

  • 9 times
  • 10 times
  • No limit

The ceiling is 1 / s = 1 / 0.1 = 10. Real programs get less, because of communication costs.

Why does a GPU run an if slowly when half the threads of a warp take each path?

  • The GPU has no branch instructions.
  • The warp runs both paths one after the other, with half the lanes idle each time.
  • Each thread needs its own cache.

The threads of a warp share one instruction stream. Divergent paths are run in turn, with the inactive lanes masked off.

A 5-stage pipeline with no stalls runs 100 instructions in ? cycles.

A cache has 64-byte lines. The offset part of an address has ? bits.

A TLB has 32 entries and pages are 16 KiB. Its reach is ?.

With s = 0.1 and 10 cores, Gustafson's scaled speed-up is ?.

  1. Compute the AMAT. L1: hit time 1 ns, miss rate 10%. L2: hit time 6 ns, local miss rate 25%. Memory: 120 ns.
    Answer

    The L1 miss penalty is the L2 AMAT: 6 + 0.25 \times 120 = 36 ns. Then AMAT = 1 + 0.1 \times 36 = 4.6 ns.

  2. A 16 KiB, 4-way cache has 32-byte lines and 32-bit addresses. How many bits are in the tag, the index and the offset?
    Answer

    Lines: 16384 / 32 = 512. Sets: 512 / 4 = 128. Offset: \log_2 32 = 5 bits. Index: \log_2 128 = 7 bits. Tag: 32 - 7 - 5 = 20 bits.

  3. Reorder this code to remove the load-use stall: ld x1, 0(x9), add x2, x1, x3, sub x4, x5, x6.
    Answer

    Move the independent sub between the load and the add: ld x1, 0(x9), sub x4, x5, x6, add x2, x1, x3. Now x1 is ready in time, through forwarding from the MEM stage. Compilers do this reordering. It is called instruction scheduling.

  4. The column loop over the 4096 by 4096 grid was slow. Change the grid width to 4100 floats per row, but still use 4096 columns. Explain why the column loop may get faster, although it does the same work.
    Answer

    With 4096 floats per row, the stride is 16384 bytes, a power of two. Many column items then map to the same cache sets, which causes conflict misses. With 4100 floats per row, the stride is 16400 bytes. The items spread over different sets. The extra 4 floats per row are padding. The TLB cost stays, because each step still lands on a new page.

  5. Your team says: "Our service is 2% serial. We will buy 200 cores and get 200 times the speed." Answer with both laws.
    Answer

    By Amdahl, for a fixed job: 1 / (0.02 + 0.98/200) \approx 40. The ceiling is 50. So 200 times is impossible for the same job. Gustafson's law fits when each batch grows with the machine. If the serial share of the 200-core run stays at 2%, the scaled speed-up is 0.02 + 0.98 \times 200 \approx 196. So the answer depends on whether the work grows. Also check for false sharing and memory bandwidth limits.

  6. Expert. Explain why our pointer-chasing test reports latency, but a simple loop that sums the same array would report something much smaller per item.
    Answer

    In pointer chasing, each address comes from the previous load. The core cannot start the next load early, so the times add up. A simple sum has known addresses. The prefetcher loads lines early, and an out-of-order core keeps many misses in flight at once. One 128-byte line also holds 16 items of 8 bytes. So the cost per item reflects bandwidth, not latency.

Key takeaways

  • An ISA is the contract between software and hardware. RISC-V and Arm are RISC. x86 is CISC outside but runs micro-ops inside.
  • CPU time is instructions times CPI times the clock period. Pipelines lower CPI by overlapping instructions.
  • Hazards break the overlap. Forwarding fixes most data hazards. Branch prediction fixes most control hazards. A wrong guess costs many cycles.
  • Caches work because of locality. A cache cuts each address into tag, index and offset. Misses are compulsory, capacity, conflict or coherence.
  • On the M2 Pro test machine, an L1 hit took about 1.3 ns and main memory about 100 to 130 ns. That is a gap of almost 100 times.
  • Virtual memory gives each process its own addresses. The TLB caches translations. Huge pages raise its reach.
  • Coherence keeps core caches in agreement. False sharing makes independent threads fight over one line. Pad hot data.
  • Amdahl's law limits a fixed job by its serial part. Gustafson's law shows that growing jobs can use many cores well.
  • SIMD and GPUs run one instruction on many values. Layout in memory often matters more than the number of operations.

Sources

  • The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I (version 20260120): RV32I. The 32 registers, x0 fixed at zero, and the fixed 32-bit instruction formats.
  • John L. Gustafson: Reevaluating Amdahl's Law (Communications of the ACM, 1988). The original short paper on scaled speed-up.
  • Yuan Shi: Reevaluating Amdahl's Law and Gustafson's Law. Why the serial fraction means different things in the two laws.
  • Latency numbers every programmer should know. The Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig estimates from about 2012.
  • NVIDIA: PTX ISA documentation. The SIMT model, warps of 32 threads, and how divergent branches run.
  • Arpaci-Dusseau: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces. Free chapters on address translation, TLBs and paging.

Operating systems: processes and scheduling

Your laptop runs hundreds of programs on a few cores. Each program thinks it owns the machine. The operating system makes this true enough, and it keeps the programs safe from each other. This chapter shows how: kernel mode, processes and threads, scheduling, locks, deadlock, pipes and signals.

  • Explain kernel mode, user mode and system calls, and measure what a system call costs.
  • Compare processes and threads, and say what a context switch saves and costs.
  • Compute waiting and response times for FIFO, SJF and round robin, and prove that SJF is best for average waiting time.
  • Use mutexes, semaphores and condition variables correctly in Rust and Python.
  • Name the four Coffman conditions, and prevent, avoid or detect deadlock.

All timings come from one laptop, measured in November 2026. It is an Apple M2 Pro with macOS 26.6, Rust 1.99 and Python 3.14. macOS is a Unix system, so the ideas match Linux. Other chapter authors were running work at the same time, so timings vary between runs. Linux facts in this chapter come from the Linux documentation and man pages, not from this machine.

Kernel mode, user mode and system calls

This Rust program prints a line without the C library. It asks the macOS kernel directly.

use std::arch::asm;

// macOS on Apple Silicon only. Apple does not promise this interface: use libc in real code.
fn raw_write(fd: u64, msg: &[u8]) -> u64 {
    let ret: u64;
    unsafe {
        asm!(
            "svc #0x80",                 // trap into the kernel
            in("x16") 4u64,              // system call number 4 = write
            inlateout("x0") fd => ret,   // argument 1 in, result out
            inlateout("x1") msg.as_ptr() => _, // argument 2: address of the bytes
            in("x2") msg.len(),          // argument 3: how many bytes
            options(nostack),
        );
    }
    ret
}

fn main() {
    let n = raw_write(1, b"hello from the kernel\n"); // fd 1 is standard output
    println!("the kernel wrote {n} bytes");
}
import os

# os.write is a thin wrapper: it calls the C library, which runs the write system call.
n = os.write(1, b"hello from the kernel\n")   # fd 1 is standard output
print(f"the kernel wrote {n} bytes")
hello from the kernel
the kernel wrote 22 bytes

The program cannot touch the screen or a file itself. It puts a number and three arguments in registers. Then the svc instruction jumps into the kernel. The kernel does the work and returns the result in x0.

The kernel runs in kernel mode. Normal programs run in user mode. In user mode, the processor refuses instructions that change page tables, talk to devices or turn off interrupts. A program that needs such work makes a system call.

The privilege levels of three instruction sets
User programsKernelSystem call instruction
x86-64ring 3ring 0syscall
Arm (AArch64)EL0EL1svc
RISC-VU modeS modeecall

Three kinds of event enter the kernel. A system call is a planned entry. An exception is an accident, like a bad memory access. An interrupt comes from outside, like a timer tick or a network packet. All three are called traps. In every case, the hardware jumps to an address that the kernel set at boot. A program cannot choose where it enters the kernel.

Prepare

The C library puts the call number and arguments in registers.

Trap

svc switches to kernel mode. The hardware saves the user program counter and jumps to the kernel's entry point.

Check

The kernel saves the user registers. It looks up call number 4 in its table. It checks that the file is open and the buffer belongs to the process.

Work

The kernel copies the bytes and gives them to the file or device driver.

Return

The kernel puts the result in x0, restores the registers and returns to user mode.

How much does this trip cost? We wrote one byte to /dev/null a million times. We compared it with a plain function call.

use std::fs::File;
use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::Write;
use std::time::Instant;

#[inline(never)]
fn add_one(x: u64) -> u64 { x + 1 } // a plain function call, no kernel

fn main() {
    let n = 1_000_000;
    let t = Instant::now();
    let mut x = 0;
    for _ in 0..n { x = add_one(black_box(x)); }
    println!("function call:  {:>6.1} ns", t.elapsed().as_nanos() as f64 / n as f64);

    let mut f = File::create("/dev/null").unwrap();
    let t = Instant::now();
    for _ in 0..n { f.write_all(b"x").unwrap(); } // each write is one system call
    println!("write() syscall: {:>5.1} ns", t.elapsed().as_nanos() as f64 / n as f64);
    black_box(x);
}
import os
import time

def add_one(x):
    return x + 1                       # a plain function call, no kernel

n = 1_000_000
t = time.perf_counter_ns()
x = 0
for _ in range(n):
    x = add_one(x)
print(f"function call:   {(time.perf_counter_ns() - t) / n:5.1f} ns")

fd = os.open("/dev/null", os.O_WRONLY)
t = time.perf_counter_ns()
for _ in range(n):
    os.write(fd, b"x")                 # each write is one system call
print(f"write() syscall: {(time.perf_counter_ns() - t) / n:5.1f} ns")
function call:     2.1 ns
write() syscall: 452.8 ns

Rust 1.99

function call:    49.0 ns
write() syscall: 554.0 ns

Python 3.14

On this machine, a system call costs about 200 times more than a function call. That is why buffered I/O exists. Rust's BufWriter and Python's normal file objects collect many small writes in memory. Then they make one big system call.

Writing a log line with one unbuffered write per line in a hot loop. A million lines then cost a million kernel trips. Wrap the file in a buffer, and flush it at the end or at safe points.

Expert: calls that skip the kernel

Linux maps a small library called the vDSO into every process. It answers calls like clock_gettime in user mode, from data that the kernel keeps updated. Fast locks work in a similar way. They try an atomic instruction first and enter the kernel only when they must sleep. Linux calls this a futex.

Processes and threads

We started 200 processes, then 10,000 threads. Each one did nothing and ended. We timed the start and the wait.

use std::process::Command;
use std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

fn main() {
    // 1. Start a new process and wait for it.
    let n = 200;
    let t = Instant::now();
    for _ in 0..n { Command::new("/usr/bin/true").status().unwrap(); }
    println!("new process: {:>7.1} us", t.elapsed().as_micros() as f64 / n as f64);

    // 2. Start a new thread and wait for it.
    let n = 10_000;
    let t = Instant::now();
    for _ in 0..n { thread::spawn(|| ()).join().unwrap(); }
    println!("new thread:  {:>7.1} us", t.elapsed().as_micros() as f64 / n as f64);

    // 3. Two threads pass a token back and forth: each pass wakes the other thread.
    let (to_b, from_a) = sync_channel::<u32>(0);
    let (to_a, from_b) = sync_channel::<u32>(0);
    let n = 100_000;
    let b = thread::spawn(move || for v in from_a { to_a.send(v + 1).unwrap(); });
    let t = Instant::now();
    for i in 0..n { to_b.send(i).unwrap(); from_b.recv().unwrap(); }
    println!("round trip:  {:>7.1} us", t.elapsed().as_micros() as f64 / n as f64);
    drop(to_b);
    b.join().unwrap();
}
import os
import subprocess
import threading
import time

n = 200
t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(n):
    subprocess.run(["/usr/bin/true"])          # start a process and wait
print(f"new process: {(time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1e6:7.1f} us")

n = 10_000
t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(n):
    th = threading.Thread(target=lambda: None)
    th.start()
    th.join()                                   # start a thread and wait
print(f"new thread:  {(time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1e6:7.1f} us")

# Two processes pass one byte back and forth through two pipes.
a_r, a_w = os.pipe()
b_r, b_w = os.pipe()
n = 100_000
if os.fork() == 0:                              # the child process
    for _ in range(n):
        os.write(b_w, os.read(a_r, 1))
    os._exit(0)
t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(n):
    os.write(a_w, b"x")
    os.read(b_r, 1)                             # wait for the child's answer
print(f"round trip:  {(time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1e6:7.1f} us")
os.wait()
new process:  1198.3 us
new thread:     22.3 us
round trip:      3.1 us

Rust 1.99 (round trip between two threads)

new process:  2010.9 us
new thread:     30.2 us
round trip:      7.2 us

Python 3.14 (round trip between two processes)

A new process cost about 1.2 ms. A new thread cost about 20 µs, about 50 times less. Why is a process so much more expensive?

A process is a program in action. It has its own address space, open files and permissions. A thread is one line of execution inside a process. All threads of a process share its memory and files. Each thread has only its own stack, registers and program counter. So a new process needs a new address space and a new program loaded from disk. A new thread needs only a stack.

What threads share and what they keep for themselves
Shared by all threads of a processPrivate to each thread
Code, global data, heapStack
Open files and socketsRegisters and program counter
Process id, user id, working directoryThread id, scheduling state

The kernel keeps a record for each process, the PCB. It holds the saved registers, the state, the page table and the open files. Linux calls it task_struct. In Linux, a thread is also a task. Threads of one process are tasks that share an address space.

On Unix, a process is born in two steps. fork() makes a copy of the calling process. exec() replaces the copy's program with a new one. The parent then calls wait() to collect the exit status. The copy is cheap because of copy-on-write. Many libraries, Rust's Command among them, use posix_spawn when they can. It does both steps in one call.

Forgetting to call wait(). A child that has ended but was never collected stays a zombie. It keeps a slot in the process table. A server that starts many children and never waits slowly fills the table.

The context switch

In the round-trip test above, each pass of the token wakes the other thread. One round trip took about 3 µs in Rust. That is about 7 times a system call. It includes two wake-ups and two switches.

A context switch moves a core from one thread to another. It happens in two cases. In a voluntary switch, the thread blocks: it waits for I/O, a lock or a sleep. In an involuntary switch, the kernel takes the core away, for example when the time slice ends.

  1. A timer interrupt or a system call enters the kernel.
  2. The kernel saves the old thread's registers, stack pointer and program counter in its record.
  3. The scheduler picks the next thread.
  4. If the new thread is in another process, the kernel switches the page table. The TLB may need a flush.
  5. The kernel loads the new thread's registers and returns to user mode in the new thread.

The direct cost is the saving and loading. The hidden cost is often bigger. The new thread finds the caches and the TLB full of the old thread's data. It runs slowly until they warm up again. The chapter Computer architecture measured how slow a cache miss is.

Starting one thread per request in a busy server. Each thread costs a stack and a start, and thousands of threads cause many switches. Use a thread pool, or async tasks that share a few threads. The chapter Concurrency and parallelism covers async.

Scheduling: FIFO, SJF and round robin

Three jobs arrive at time 0. Job A needs 100 ms of CPU time. Jobs B and C need 10 ms each. In which order should one core run them? This program tries four policies.

// All jobs arrive at time 0. A job is (name, CPU time in ms).
fn run_to_end(order: &[(char, u32)]) -> (f64, f64) {
    let (mut t, mut wait) = (0, 0);
    for &(_, burst) in order {
        wait += t; // this job waited until now
        t += burst;
    }
    let avg = wait as f64 / order.len() as f64;
    (avg, avg) // no preemption: response time = waiting time
}

fn round_robin(jobs: &[(char, u32)], q: u32) -> (f64, f64) {
    let n = jobs.len();
    let mut left: Vec<u32> = jobs.iter().map(|j| j.1).collect();
    let (mut first, mut done, mut t) = (vec![None; n], vec![0; n], 0);
    while left.iter().any(|&r| r > 0) {
        for i in 0..n {
            if left[i] == 0 { continue; }
            first[i].get_or_insert(t); // the first time this job runs
            let slice = q.min(left[i]);
            t += slice;
            left[i] -= slice;
            if left[i] == 0 { done[i] = t; }
        }
    }
    let wait: u32 = (0..n).map(|i| done[i] - jobs[i].1).sum();
    let resp: u32 = first.iter().map(|f| f.unwrap()).sum();
    (wait as f64 / n as f64, resp as f64 / n as f64)
}

fn main() {
    let jobs = [('A', 100), ('B', 10), ('C', 10)];
    let mut sjf = jobs.to_vec();
    sjf.sort_by_key(|j| j.1); // shortest job first
    let rows = [("FIFO", run_to_end(&jobs)), ("SJF", run_to_end(&sjf)),
                ("RR q=10", round_robin(&jobs, 10)), ("RR q=1", round_robin(&jobs, 1))];
    for (name, (w, r)) in rows {
        println!("{name:<8} average wait {w:5.1} ms, average response {r:5.1} ms");
    }
}
# All jobs arrive at time 0. A job is (name, CPU time in ms).
def run_to_end(order):
    t = wait = 0
    for _, burst in order:
        wait += t                      # this job waited until now
        t += burst
    avg = wait / len(order)
    return avg, avg                    # no preemption: response time = waiting time

def round_robin(jobs, q):
    left = [burst for _, burst in jobs]
    first, done, t = [None] * len(jobs), [0] * len(jobs), 0
    while any(left):
        for i in range(len(jobs)):
            if left[i] == 0:
                continue
            if first[i] is None:
                first[i] = t           # the first time this job runs
            piece = min(q, left[i])
            t += piece
            left[i] -= piece
            if left[i] == 0:
                done[i] = t
    n = len(jobs)
    wait = sum(done[i] - jobs[i][1] for i in range(n))
    return wait / n, sum(first) / n

jobs = [("A", 100), ("B", 10), ("C", 10)]
sjf = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1])  # shortest job first
rows = [("FIFO", run_to_end(jobs)), ("SJF", run_to_end(sjf)),
        ("RR q=10", round_robin(jobs, 10)), ("RR q=1", round_robin(jobs, 1))]
for name, (w, r) in rows:
    print(f"{name:<8} average wait {w:5.1f} ms, average response {r:5.1f} ms")
FIFO     average wait  70.0 ms, average response  70.0 ms
SJF      average wait  10.0 ms, average response  10.0 ms
RR q=10  average wait  16.7 ms, average response  10.0 ms
RR q=1   average wait  19.7 ms, average response   1.0 ms

The scheduler decides which ready thread runs next. We judge a policy with a few numbers.

  • Turnaround time: from arrival to the end.
  • Waiting time: turnaround time minus the CPU time.
  • Response time: from arrival to the first run. Users feel this one.
  • Fairness and throughput also matter.

FIFO (first in, first out) runs jobs in arrival order, each to the end. It is simple, but short jobs can wait behind a long one. This is the convoy effect. SJF (shortest job first) runs the shortest job first. In our example it cut the average wait from 70 ms to 10 ms.

All jobs arrive at time 0 and run to the end without interruption. Then running them from shortest to longest gives the smallest possible average waiting time.

Proof (exchange argument)

Take any order where a longer job L runs just before a shorter job S, with L \gt S. Let both start after time t. Before the swap, L waits t and S waits t + L. The sum is 2t + L.

Swap them. Now S waits t and L waits t + S. The sum is 2t + S, which is smaller. Jobs before the pair do not change. Jobs after the pair still start at t + L + S. So every swap of such a pair lowers the total wait.

Keep swapping until no longer job comes before a shorter one. The order is then sorted, and the total wait only went down. So the sorted order is the best.

Another view: with jobs p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n in this order, job p_i makes the n - i jobs after it wait. The total waiting time is

W = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (n - i)\, p_i

The first job has the largest weight, n - 1. So it should be the smallest job. Check with our jobs in SJF order 10, 10, 100: W = 2 \cdot 10 + 1 \cdot 10 + 0 \cdot 100 = 30. The average is 10 ms, as the program printed.

If jobs arrive at different times, the preemptive version wins. SRTF always runs the job with the least work left, and stops the running job if a shorter one arrives. But there is a catch. The kernel does not know how long a job will run. It can only guess from the past.

Round robin (RR) gives each job a short time slice, also called a quantum, in turn. With a 1 ms slice, the average response time fell to 1 ms. But the average wait rose to 19.7 ms. Round robin is good for response and bad for turnaround.

Choosing a very small time slice "for fairness". Each switch costs microseconds and cold caches. With a 10 µs slice and a 3 µs switch, almost a quarter of the time is lost. Real systems use slices of about a millisecond or more.

Scheduling: priority, MLFQ and fair share

A video call and a large file compression run at once. The call needs the CPU often, for a short time. The compression wants all the CPU it can get. How can the scheduler favour the call, without knowing what either program is?

Priority scheduling always runs the ready thread with the highest priority. The danger is starvation. A low-priority job may never run. The fix is aging.

The multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) learns from behaviour. Its rules, as the OSTEP textbook gives them, are:

  1. If A has a higher priority than B, A runs.
  2. If A and B have the same priority, they share the CPU in round robin.
  3. A new job starts at the highest priority.
  4. When a job uses up its time allowance at a level, it moves down one level. It does not matter how many times it gave up the CPU.
  5. After a fixed period, move every job back to the top level.

Short interactive jobs stay at the top. Long CPU-bound jobs sink. Rule 5 stops starvation, and it lets a job that changes behaviour rise again. Rule 4 stops a trick. Without it, a job could give up the CPU just before its slice ends. It would then stay at the top forever.

Fair share scheduling gives each job a share of the CPU instead. Lottery scheduling gives each job tickets and draws a random winner for each slice. A job with 75 of 100 tickets gets about 75% of the CPU. Linux uses a fair-share design too. Its CFS gave each task a virtual run time and ran the task with the smallest one. Since Linux 6.6, the kernel has moved to EEVDF. EEVDF gives each task a lag and a virtual deadline. A task with positive lag is owed CPU time. Among tasks with lag zero or more, it runs the one with the earliest virtual deadline.

The nice value sets the weight of a Linux task, from -20 (most CPU) to 19 (least). Each step changes the CPU share by about 10%.

  1. 1962 CTSS. Fernando Corbató's time-sharing system uses several priority queues, an early form of MLFQ.
  2. 1994 Lottery scheduling. Waldspurger and Weihl publish proportional share with tickets.
  3. 1995 EEVDF paper. Stoica and Abdel-Wahab describe Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First.
  4. 2007 CFS. Linux 2.6.23 ships the Completely Fair Scheduler.
  5. 2023 EEVDF in Linux. Linux 6.6 starts the move from CFS to EEVDF.

Priority inversion. A low-priority thread holds a lock. A high-priority thread waits for the lock. A medium-priority thread now runs instead of both. In 1997, NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander kept resetting because of this bug. The fix is priority inheritance.

Exams often give a table of jobs with arrival times and CPU times. They ask for a Gantt chart and the average waiting time for FIFO, SJF, SRTF and RR. Draw the chart first. Then compute each job's finish time. Waiting time is finish time minus arrival time minus CPU time.

Synchronisation: locks, semaphores and condition variables

Four threads each add 1 to a counter, 10,000 times. The answer should be 40,000. In the wrong version, each thread reads the value, lets the scheduler switch, and then writes.

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering::SeqCst};
use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    // Wrong: read, then write. Another thread can run in between.
    let hits = AtomicU64::new(0);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..4 {
            s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..10_000 {
                let v = hits.load(SeqCst); // 1. read
                thread::yield_now();       //    (let the scheduler switch here)
                hits.store(v + 1, SeqCst); // 2. write: may erase another update
            });
        }
    });
    println!("read then write: {}", hits.load(SeqCst));

    // Right: the lock makes read-and-write one step for other threads.
    let hits = Mutex::new(0u64);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..4 {
            s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..10_000 {
                let mut g = hits.lock().unwrap(); // only one thread at a time
                thread::yield_now();
                *g += 1;
            }); // the guard is dropped here: unlock
        }
    });
    println!("with a mutex:    {}", hits.lock().unwrap());
}
import threading
import time

hits = 0

def wrong():
    global hits
    for _ in range(10_000):
        v = hits                       # 1. read
        time.sleep(0)                  #    (let the scheduler switch here)
        hits = v + 1                   # 2. write: may erase another update

lock = threading.Lock()

def right():
    global hits
    for _ in range(10_000):
        with lock:                     # only one thread at a time
            v = hits
            time.sleep(0)
            hits = v + 1

for name, fn in [("read then write", wrong), ("with a lock", right)]:
    hits = 0
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=fn) for _ in range(4)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"{name + ':':<16} {hits}")
read then write: 10207
with a mutex:    40000

Rust 1.99

read then write: 10012
with a lock:     40000

Python 3.14

About three quarters of the updates were lost. The exact number changes from run to run. A thread read 500, another thread wrote 501, and then the first thread also wrote 501. This is a race condition. Note that the Rust code compiles. Rust stops data races, where two threads touch memory at once without atomics. It cannot stop every wrong order of correct steps.

The code between the read and the write is a critical section. A mutex guards it. lock() waits until the mutex is free and takes it. Unlock gives it back. In Rust the guard unlocks when it goes out of scope, and the data lives inside the mutex. So you cannot touch the data without the lock.

  • A spinlock waits by looping. It is good only for very short waits, often inside the kernel.
  • A sleeping mutex asks the kernel to block the thread. A futex tries a fast atomic step first and sleeps only if the lock is taken.

A semaphore is a counter s \ge 0 with two atomic operations. wait (P): if s \gt 0, take one, s \leftarrow s - 1. Otherwise sleep until that is possible. signal (V): s \leftarrow s + 1, and wake one sleeper.

A semaphore that starts at 1 works like a mutex. A semaphore that starts at 5 lets at most 5 threads in at once, for example 5 open database connections. Edsger Dijkstra described semaphores in the 1960s.

Sometimes a thread must wait for a condition, not only for a lock. "Wait until the buffer has an item." A condition variable lets a thread sleep and release the mutex in one step. Another thread changes the state and calls notify. A monitor puts the data, the mutex and the condition variables together. Java objects and Python's threading.Condition follow this idea.

Here is the classic bounded buffer. A producer makes 10 items. A consumer takes them. The buffer holds at most 3.

use std::collections::VecDeque;
use std::sync::{Condvar, Mutex};
use std::thread;

const CAP: usize = 3; // the buffer holds at most 3 items

fn main() {
    let buf = Mutex::new(VecDeque::new());
    let (not_full, not_empty) = (Condvar::new(), Condvar::new());
    thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| for item in 1..=10 { // producer
            let mut q = buf.lock().unwrap();
            while q.len() == CAP {
                q = not_full.wait(q).unwrap(); // sleep and unlock; relock on wake
            }
            q.push_back(item);
            not_empty.notify_one();
        });
        s.spawn(|| { // consumer
            let (mut sum, mut most) = (0, 0);
            for _ in 0..10 {
                let mut q = buf.lock().unwrap();
                while q.is_empty() {
                    q = not_empty.wait(q).unwrap(); // check again after waking
                }
                most = most.max(q.len());
                sum += q.pop_front().unwrap();
                not_full.notify_one();
            }
            println!("sum {sum}, most items seen in the buffer: {most}");
        });
    });
}
import threading
from collections import deque

CAP = 3                                # the buffer holds at most 3 items
buf = deque()
cond = threading.Condition()           # one lock with a waiting room

def producer():
    for item in range(1, 11):
        with cond:
            while len(buf) == CAP:
                cond.wait()            # sleep and unlock; relock on wake
            buf.append(item)
            cond.notify_all()

def consumer():
    total = most = 0
    for _ in range(10):
        with cond:
            while not buf:
                cond.wait()            # check again after waking
            most = max(most, len(buf))
            total += buf.popleft()
            cond.notify_all()
    print(f"sum {total}, most items seen in the buffer: {most}")

threads = [threading.Thread(target=producer), threading.Thread(target=consumer)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
sum 55, most items seen in the buffer: 3

Both versions printed this line. The sum is always 55. The second number depends on timing, but it can never be more than 3.

Using if instead of while around wait(). A thread can wake up although the condition is false. Another thread may have taken the item first, or the wake-up may be spurious. The Rust documentation warns about spurious wake-ups. Always check the condition again in a loop.

Deadlock

Two threads need the same two locks. Thread T1 takes lock a, then b. Thread T2 takes lock b, then a. Each thread waits 1 second for its second lock before it gives up.

use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::thread::{scope, sleep};
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

fn worker(name: &str, first: &Mutex<()>, second: &Mutex<()>) {
    let _g1 = first.lock().unwrap();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)); // both threads now hold one lock
    let start = Instant::now();
    while start.elapsed() < Duration::from_secs(1) { // a real program would wait forever
        if let Ok(_g2) = second.try_lock() {
            println!("{name} finished");
            return;
        }
        sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
    }
    println!("{name} gave up after 1 s: deadlock");
}

fn main() {
    let (a, b) = (Mutex::new(()), Mutex::new(()));
    // Wrong: opposite order. Right: the same global order (a before b).
    for (label, x, y) in [("opposite order", &b, &a), ("same order", &a, &b)] {
        println!("-- {label}");
        scope(|s| {
            s.spawn(|| worker("T1", &a, &b));
            s.spawn(|| worker("T2", x, y));
        });
    }
}
import threading
import time

a, b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()

def worker(name, first, second):
    with first:
        time.sleep(0.1)                         # both threads now hold one lock
        if second.acquire(timeout=1):           # a real program would wait forever
            second.release()
            print(name, "finished")
        else:
            print(name, "gave up after 1 s: deadlock")

# Wrong: opposite order. Right: the same global order (a before b).
for label, order2 in [("opposite order", (b, a)), ("same order", (a, b))]:
    print("--", label)
    t1 = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("T1", a, b))
    t2 = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("T2", *order2))
    t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join()
-- opposite order
T1 gave up after 1 s: deadlock
T2 gave up after 1 s: deadlock
-- same order
T1 finished
T2 finished

This is the Python output. The Rust output has the same lines, but the two "gave up" lines may come in the other order. With the opposite order, each thread holds what the other needs. Neither can move. This is a deadlock. With one global order, the problem is gone.

A deadlock can happen only if all four conditions hold at the same time:

  1. Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one thread at a time.
  2. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while it waits for another.
  3. No preemption: nobody can take a resource away from its holder.
  4. Circular wait: there is a cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource that the next one holds.
Proof idea

Take a deadlocked group. Each thread waits forever for a resource held by another thread in the group. If resources could be shared, nobody would wait, so mutual exclusion holds. The waiting threads hold resources that others need, so hold and wait holds. If the system could take a resource away, the waiting would end, so no preemption holds. Now follow the "waits for" arrows from any thread. Each step reaches another thread of the group. The group is finite, so the path must come back to a thread it has seen. That is a circular wait.

Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani listed these conditions in 1971. They are necessary, so breaking any one of them makes deadlock impossible. When each resource has only one unit, a cycle in the graph means deadlock. With several units of a resource, a cycle can exist without a deadlock.

Prevention: break one condition by design

Lock ordering breaks circular wait. It is the most common fix in real code. Taking all locks at once breaks hold and wait. try_lock with back-off breaks no preemption: a thread gives up its locks and tries again. Lock-free data structures avoid mutual exclusion.

Avoidance: refuse requests that could lead to deadlock

Each process declares its maximum need in advance. The system grants a request only if the result is still safe. Dijkstra's Banker's algorithm does this. It is rare in general operating systems, because programs seldom know their maximum needs.

Detection and recovery: let it happen, then fix it

Build the wait-for graph and look for a cycle. Then end one thread or roll back one transaction. Databases do this. PostgreSQL checks for a deadlock after a lock wait passes a timeout, then cancels one transaction.

Ignore it

Many operating systems do not handle deadlock between user programs at all. A deadlock there is a bug in the program. This is sometimes called the ostrich method.

A state is safe if some order lets every process finish. Find a process whose remaining need fits in the free resources. Pretend it runs to the end and gives back everything it holds. Repeat. If every process finishes, the state is safe. Grant a request only if the state after it is safe.

Here is a small cluster with 4 GPUs and 6 database connections, shared by three processes.

// Banker's safety test: is there an order in which every process can finish?
fn safe_order(mut avail: Vec<u32>, alloc: &[Vec<u32>], need: &[Vec<u32>]) -> Option<Vec<usize>> {
    let mut done = vec![false; alloc.len()];
    let mut order = Vec::new();
    while order.len() < alloc.len() {
        let next = (0..alloc.len()).find(|&p| {
            !done[p] && need[p].iter().zip(&avail).all(|(n, a)| n <= a)
        })?; // nobody can finish: unsafe
        for r in 0..avail.len() { avail[r] += alloc[next][r]; } // it finishes and returns all
        done[next] = true;
        order.push(next);
    }
    Some(order)
}

// Pretend to grant the request. Keep it only if the new state is safe.
fn try_request(p: usize, req: &[u32], avail: &[u32], alloc: &[Vec<u32>], need: &[Vec<u32>]) {
    let (mut av, mut al, mut ne) = (avail.to_vec(), alloc.to_vec(), need.to_vec());
    for r in 0..req.len() { av[r] -= req[r]; al[p][r] += req[r]; ne[p][r] -= req[r]; }
    match safe_order(av, &al, &ne) {
        Some(o) => println!("P{p} asks {req:?}: grant, safe order {o:?}"),
        None => println!("P{p} asks {req:?}: wait, the state would be unsafe"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Two resource types: [GPUs, database connections]. 4 GPUs and 6 connections in total.
    let alloc = vec![vec![1, 2], vec![1, 1], vec![1, 2]];
    let max = vec![vec![2, 4], vec![2, 2], vec![3, 3]];
    let need: Vec<Vec<u32>> = (0..3).map(|p| (0..2).map(|r| max[p][r] - alloc[p][r]).collect()).collect();
    let avail = vec![4 - 3, 6 - 5];
    println!("now: safe order {:?}", safe_order(avail.clone(), &alloc, &need).unwrap());
    try_request(2, &[1, 0], &avail, &alloc, &need);
    try_request(1, &[1, 0], &avail, &alloc, &need);
}
# Banker's safety test: is there an order in which every process can finish?
def safe_order(avail, alloc, need):
    avail, done, order = list(avail), [False] * len(alloc), []
    while len(order) < len(alloc):
        for p in range(len(alloc)):
            if not done[p] and all(n <= a for n, a in zip(need[p], avail)):
                break
        else:
            return None                # nobody can finish: unsafe
        avail = [a + x for a, x in zip(avail, alloc[p])]  # it finishes and returns all
        done[p] = True
        order.append(p)
    return order

# Pretend to grant the request. Keep it only if the new state is safe.
def try_request(p, req, avail, alloc, need):
    av = [a - r for a, r in zip(avail, req)]
    al = [row[:] for row in alloc]
    ne = [row[:] for row in need]
    al[p] = [a + r for a, r in zip(al[p], req)]
    ne[p] = [n - r for n, r in zip(ne[p], req)]
    order = safe_order(av, al, ne)
    if order is None:
        print(f"P{p} asks {req}: wait, the state would be unsafe")
    else:
        print(f"P{p} asks {req}: grant, safe order {order}")

# Two resource types: [GPUs, database connections]. 4 GPUs and 6 connections in total.
alloc = [[1, 2], [1, 1], [1, 2]]
mx = [[2, 4], [2, 2], [3, 3]]
need = [[m - a for m, a in zip(mx[p], alloc[p])] for p in range(3)]
avail = [4 - 3, 6 - 5]
print(f"now: safe order {safe_order(avail, alloc, need)}")
try_request(2, [1, 0], avail, alloc, need)
try_request(1, [1, 0], avail, alloc, need)
now: safe order [1, 0, 2]
P2 asks [1, 0]: wait, the state would be unsafe
P1 asks [1, 0]: grant, safe order [1, 0, 2]

Both requests ask for the last free GPU. P2 still needs more after it, so the system could get stuck. P1 needs nothing more except one connection, which is free. So P1 can finish and return everything. An unsafe state is not yet a deadlock. It is a state from which the system can no longer promise to avoid one.

Calling unknown code while you hold a lock. A callback or a log hook may take another lock, in an order you cannot see. Keep critical sections short. Copy the data out, unlock, and then call other code.

Expert: livelock and starvation

The "try, give up, try again" fix can cause a livelock. Two threads keep stepping back at the same moment, like two people in a narrow corridor. Random back-off times break the pattern. Ethernet used random back-off for the same reason.

Inter-process communication and signals

Our program sends text to a child process through a pipe. Then it stops another child with a signal.

use std::io::Write;
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt; // Unix only: read the signal number
use std::process::{Command, Stdio};

fn main() {
    // 1. A pipe: our process writes, the child `tr` reads and answers.
    let mut child = Command::new("tr").arg("a-z").arg("A-Z")
        .stdin(Stdio::piped()).stdout(Stdio::piped()).spawn().unwrap();
    child.stdin.take().unwrap().write_all(b"hello from the parent\n").unwrap();
    let out = child.wait_with_output().unwrap(); // stdin is closed: tr sees the end
    print!("child said: {}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout));

    // 2. A signal: start a long sleep, then end it with SIGKILL.
    let mut sleeper = Command::new("sleep").arg("30").spawn().unwrap();
    sleeper.kill().unwrap(); // sends SIGKILL on Unix
    let status = sleeper.wait().unwrap();
    println!("sleep ended: code {:?}, signal {:?}", status.code(), status.signal());
}
import os
import signal
import subprocess

# 1. A pipe: our process writes, the child `tr` reads and answers.
out = subprocess.run(["tr", "a-z", "A-Z"], input=b"hello from the parent\n",
                     capture_output=True)
print("child said:", out.stdout.decode(), end="")

# 2. A signal: start a long sleep, then end it with SIGKILL.
sleeper = subprocess.Popen(["sleep", "30"])
sleeper.kill()                         # sends SIGKILL on Unix
print("sleep ended: return code", sleeper.wait())   # minus the signal number

# 3. Catch a signal in our own process.
def on_usr1(signum, frame):
    print("handler got signal", signal.Signals(signum).name)

signal.signal(signal.SIGUSR1, on_usr1)
os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGUSR1)   # send it to ourselves
child said: HELLO FROM THE PARENT
sleep ended: code None, signal Some(9)

Rust 1.99

child said: HELLO FROM THE PARENT
sleep ended: return code -9
handler got signal SIGUSR1

Python 3.14

Processes do not share memory by default. That is the point of isolation. So they need inter-process communication (IPC). Every way goes through the kernel, at least to set it up.

Common IPC methods on Unix
MethodWhat it isTypical use
PipeA one-way byte stream with a buffer in the kernells | grep txt, parent and child
Named pipe (FIFO)A pipe with a name in the file systemUnrelated processes on one machine
Unix domain socketA two-way socket inside one machineDocker, databases, desktop services
Shared memoryThe same physical pages mapped into two processesLarge data, very fast, needs its own locks
Message queueThe kernel keeps whole messages in orderSmall typed messages
SignalA small numbered event, with no dataStop, reload, child ended

A pipe connects a writer to a reader. If the reader is slow, the pipe buffer fills, and the writer blocks. This is free flow control. When the writer closes its end, the reader gets end-of-file. In our test, tr printed its result only after we closed its input.

A signal is like a tap on the shoulder. The kernel stops the process at a safe point and runs a signal handler, or a default action. Rust's kill() sent SIGKILL, number 9. Python reports a death by signal as a negative return code, so -9.

Signals you will meet (numbers as on Linux x86 and Arm)
SignalNumberUsual causeDefault action
SIGINT2Ctrl + C in a terminalEnd the process
SIGKILL9kill -9End it. Cannot be caught.
SIGSEGV11Bad memory accessEnd it and dump core
SIGTERM15A polite request to stopEnd the process
SIGCHLD17A child process endedIgnore
SIGSTOP19Pause a processStop it. Cannot be caught.

Signal numbers differ between systems. For example, SIGCHLD is 20 on macOS. Use the names in code, never the numbers. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. So a process cannot refuse to die or to pause.

Doing real work inside a C or Rust signal handler. The handler can run in the middle of any instruction, even inside malloc or while a lock is held. Only async-signal-safe functions are allowed there. The safe pattern is to set a flag or write one byte to a pipe. The main loop then does the real work. Python already works this way. Its C handler only sets a flag, and the Python handler runs later in the main thread.

Containers and services use signals every day. docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits, and then sends SIGKILL. A good server catches SIGTERM, stops taking new requests, finishes the current ones and exits.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for processes and scheduling
PatternPurposeModelNote
Trap into the kernelAsk for privileged worksvc, syscall, ecallThe kernel, not the program, picks the entry point.
Buffer, then write onceFewer system callsBufWriter::new(file)Flush at the end, or the last data is lost.
Thread for sharing, process for isolationChoose the unit of workthread 20 µs, process 1.2 ms (M2 Pro)A memory fault in one thread ends the whole process.
fork, exec, waitStart a program on UnixCommand::new("tr").spawn()Always wait, or zombies pile up.
Shortest firstLowest average waiting time10, 10, 100: average wait 10 msNeeds run times you rarely know.
Round robin with a sliceFast responseq = 1: response 1 ms, wait 19.7 msToo small a slice wastes time on switches.
Demote the CPU hogsFavour interactive jobs (MLFQ)charge the whole allowance at each levelBoost everyone now and then to stop starvation.
Weights, not ordersFair share75 of 100 tickets: about 75% of the CPULinux uses EEVDF since 6.6.
Lock, change, unlockProtect a critical sectionlet mut g = m.lock().unwrap();Rust stops data races, not race conditions.
while around waitWait for a conditionwhile q.is_empty() { q = cv.wait(q).unwrap(); }Never use if: wake-ups can be spurious.
Counter semaphoreLimit how many enterstart at 5 for 5 connectionsEvery wait needs a matching signal.
One global lock orderPrevent deadlockalways a before bWrite the order down in the code.
Grant only if safeAvoid deadlock (Banker's)P2 waits, P1 is grantedNeeds each process's maximum in advance.
Pipe for streamsConnect two processesls | grep txtClose the write end, or the reader waits forever.

Practice

Which of these needs a system call?

  • Adding two numbers in a register
  • Reading 100 bytes from a file
  • Calling a function in your own program

Files are owned by the kernel. User mode cannot reach the disk or the file system directly, so the program must ask the kernel.

Two threads of the same process share which of these?

  • Their stacks
  • Their program counters
  • Their heap and open files

Threads share the address space and files. Each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter.

Which policy gives the best average response time for many short interactive jobs?

  • FIFO
  • Round robin with a small time slice
  • SJF without preemption

Round robin gives every job a turn soon. Our test showed a 1 ms average response with a 1 ms slice.

A program takes locks in the order a, then b, everywhere. Which Coffman condition can never hold?

  • Mutual exclusion
  • Hold and wait
  • Circular wait

A cycle would need a thread that holds b and waits for a. With one global order, no thread does that.

Which signal can a process catch to shut down cleanly?

  • SIGKILL
  • SIGTERM
  • SIGSTOP

SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. SIGTERM is the polite request that a program can handle.

Jobs of 6, 2 and 4 ms arrive at time 0. With SJF the average waiting time is ? ms.

A semaphore starts at 2. Three threads call wait. The number of threads that sleep is ?.

A Python child process was ended by SIGTERM. Its return code is ?.

  1. Jobs A (8 ms), B (4 ms) and C (2 ms) arrive at time 0, in this order. Compute the average waiting time for FIFO and for round robin with a 2 ms slice.
    Answer

    FIFO: A waits 0, B waits 8, C waits 12. The average is 20/3 \approx 6.67 ms. Round robin with a 2 ms slice: A 0-2, B 2-4, C 4-6 (C done), A 6-8, B 8-10 (B done), A 10-14 (A done). Waits: A 14 - 8 = 6, B 10 - 4 = 6, C 6 - 2 = 4. The average is 16/3 \approx 5.33 ms.

  2. Use the formula W = \sum (n - i)\, p_i to show that FIFO in the order 8, 4, 2 is the worst order for these jobs.
    Answer

    W = 2 \cdot 8 + 1 \cdot 4 + 0 \cdot 2 = 20. The largest weight sits on the largest job, and the smallest weight on the smallest job. This is the reverse of SJF, so it gives the largest total: SJF gives 2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 4 + 0 = 8.

  3. Why does MLFQ charge a job for its whole time allowance at a level, even if it gave up the CPU many times?
    Answer

    Without this rule, a job could run for 99% of its slice and then do a tiny I/O. It would look interactive and stay at the top level. It could take almost all the CPU. Counting the total time used at the level stops this trick.

  4. The bounded buffer used notify_one in Rust but notify_all in Python. Why is notify_one safe in Rust here?
    Answer

    The Rust version has two condition variables: one for "not full" and one for "not empty". A notify on not_empty can only wake a consumer, which can use the new item. The Python version has one condition for both kinds of waiter. A single notify might wake the wrong kind of thread, which goes back to sleep, and the right thread is never woken. notify_all avoids that.

  5. A web server takes lock users, then lock sessions in one handler. Another handler takes them in the other order. It hangs about once a week. Explain the bug with the Coffman conditions, and give two fixes.
    Answer

    All four conditions can hold. The locks are exclusive. Each handler holds one lock while it waits for the other. Locks cannot be taken away. When both handlers run at the same moment, they form a cycle. Fix 1: one global order, for example always users before sessions. Fix 2: merge the two locks into one, or use try_lock with a timeout and back-off. It happens once a week because the two handlers must interleave at exactly the wrong moment.

  6. Expert. A real-time thread at high priority waits for a lock held by a low-priority logging thread. A medium-priority video encoder runs for seconds. What is this, and how does priority inheritance fix it?
    Answer

    This is priority inversion. The high-priority thread is blocked by the low one, and the medium thread keeps the low one from running. With priority inheritance, the logging thread runs at the high priority while it holds the lock. The encoder can no longer preempt it. The logger releases the lock soon, drops back to low priority, and the real-time thread runs.

Key takeaways

  • The kernel runs in kernel mode. Programs run in user mode and ask the kernel for help with system calls. On the test machine, a system call cost about 450 ns, against 2 ns for a function call.
  • A process owns an address space and resources. Threads share them and keep only a stack and registers. A new process cost 1.2 ms, a new thread about 20 µs.
  • A context switch saves one thread's registers and loads another's. Cold caches and TLB entries are a large hidden cost.
  • FIFO suffers from the convoy effect. SJF minimises average waiting time, and an exchange argument proves it. Round robin gives fast response.
  • MLFQ learns which jobs are interactive. Fair-share schedulers like CFS and EEVDF share the CPU by weight. Linux moved to EEVDF from version 6.6.
  • Mutexes guard critical sections. Semaphores count. Condition variables wait for a state and need a while loop.
  • Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions. Lock ordering is the usual fix. The Banker's algorithm avoids unsafe states.
  • Pipes, sockets and shared memory move data between processes. Signals are small events. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught.

Sources

  • Arpaci-Dusseau: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces. Free chapters on processes, limited direct execution, scheduling, MLFQ, lottery scheduling, locks, condition variables, semaphores and concurrency bugs.
  • Linux kernel documentation: EEVDF Scheduler. Lag, virtual deadlines and the move from CFS starting in Linux 6.6.
  • Linux manual page: signal(7). Default actions, signal numbers, and the two signals that cannot be caught.
  • Python documentation: signal. Python handlers run in the main thread, after the C handler sets a flag.
  • Rust standard library: Condvar. Waiting with a mutex guard, and the warning about spurious wake-ups.
  • University of Virginia CS 3130: Deadlock. The four conditions from Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani (1971), and why they are necessary but not sufficient.

Operating systems: memory and storage

Every program thinks it owns a huge private memory. It also thinks a file is a simple named list of bytes. Both ideas are illusions. The operating system builds them on top of small RAM chips and slow disks. This chapter shows how the kernel does it, and what each trick costs.

  • Translate a virtual address through a multi-level page table by hand.
  • Simulate FIFO, LRU, Clock and OPT page replacement, and prove that OPT is the best.
  • Explain how allocators, inodes, journals and copy-on-write file systems work.
  • Compare blocking I/O, epoll and io_uring, and pick one for a server.
  • Say what a virtual machine and a container share, and what they keep apart.

Address spaces

A program makes a value on the heap. Then it splits into two processes with fork. The child changes the value. Both processes print the value and its address.

// Two processes, one virtual address, two different values.
unsafe extern "C" {
    fn fork() -> i32;                                   // from the C library
    fn waitpid(pid: i32, status: *mut i32, options: i32) -> i32;
}

fn main() {
    let mut value = Box::new(100u64);                   // lives on the heap
    let addr = &*value as *const u64;
    let pid = unsafe { fork() };                        // now there are two processes
    if pid == 0 {
        *value = 999;                                   // the child writes its copy
        println!("child : value {} at {:p}", value, addr);
        return;
    }
    unsafe { waitpid(pid, std::ptr::null_mut(), 0) };   // wait for the child
    println!("parent: value {} at {:p}", value, addr);
}
# Two processes, one virtual address, two different values.
import os

value = [100]                        # a list object on the heap
addr = hex(id(value))                # in CPython, id() is the address
pid = os.fork()                      # now there are two processes
if pid == 0:
    value[0] = 999                   # the child writes its copy
    print(f"child : value {value[0]} at {addr}", flush=True)
    os._exit(0)
os.waitpid(pid, 0)                   # wait for the child
print(f"parent: value {value[0]} at {addr}")
$ ./fork
child : value 999 at 0x104f9dba0
parent: value 100 at 0x104f9dba0
$ ./fork
child : value 999 at 0x1034fdba0
parent: value 100 at 0x1034fdba0

Python prints the same pattern with other addresses. Look at the first run. Both processes use the same address. But they see different values. So the address is not a place in the RAM chips. It is a virtual address. The real place in RAM is the physical address. A unit in the CPU, the MMU, translates every address on every memory access.

The set of virtual addresses a process can use is its address space. A typical address space has these parts, from low to high addresses:

  • Code: the machine instructions. It is read-only.
  • Data: global and static variables.
  • Heap: memory from malloc, Box or Python objects. It grows up.
  • Mapped regions: shared libraries and files mapped with mmap.
  • Stack: function calls and local variables. It grows down.
  • Kernel: the top part. User code cannot touch it.

Now look at the second run. The address changed. This is ASLR. The kernel puts the heap, stack and libraries at random places on each run. An attacker then cannot guess where useful code lives. See Systems and software security.

Address spaces give four things. Programs cannot read each other's memory. Every program can use the same simple layout. The total memory in use can be bigger than RAM. And many processes can share one copy of a library. On x86-64 with 4-level page tables, a virtual address has 48 bits. The user part is about 128 TiB. With 5-level tables, it has 57 bits, and the user part is about 64 PiB.

Sending a raw pointer to another process, for example through a file or a pipe. The number means nothing in the other address space. Even in shared memory, the region can sit at a different address in each process. Store offsets or indexes, not pointers.

Paging and page tables

The MMU does not translate byte by byte. It cuts memory into fixed blocks. Here is how x86-64 cuts a 48-bit address.

// Split a 48-bit x86-64 virtual address into four table indexes and an offset.
fn split(va: u64) -> ([u64; 4], u64) {
    let offset = va & 0xfff;                       // low 12 bits: 4 KiB page
    let mut idx = [0u64; 4];
    for level in 0..4 {
        let shift = 39 - 9 * level as u64;         // 39, 30, 21, 12
        idx[level] = (va >> shift) & 0x1ff;        // 9 bits: 512 entries
    }
    (idx, offset)
}

fn main() {
    for va in [0x0000_7ffd_1234_5678u64, 0x0000_0000_0040_1a2c] {
        let (i, off) = split(va);
        println!("{va:#016x} -> L4 {:3} L3 {:3} L2 {:3} L1 {:3} offset {off:#05x}",
                 i[0], i[1], i[2], i[3]);
    }
}
# Split a 48-bit x86-64 virtual address into four table indexes and an offset.
def split(va):
    offset = va & 0xFFF                       # low 12 bits: 4 KiB page
    idx = [(va >> (39 - 9 * level)) & 0x1FF   # 9 bits: 512 entries
           for level in range(4)]             # shifts 39, 30, 21, 12
    return idx, offset

for va in [0x0000_7FFD_1234_5678, 0x0000_0000_0040_1A2C]:
    i, off = split(va)
    print(f"{va:#016x} -> L4 {i[0]:3} L3 {i[1]:3} L2 {i[2]:3} L1 {i[3]:3} offset {off:#05x}")
0x007ffd12345678 -> L4 255 L3 500 L2 145 L1 325 offset 0x678
0x00000000401a2c -> L4   0 L3   0 L2   2 L1   1 offset 0xa2c

A page is a block of virtual memory. A frame is a block of RAM of the same size. The low 12 bits are the offset inside a 4 KiB page. The offset does not change in translation. The high bits form the page number. A page table maps page numbers to frame numbers.

Why four levels and not one big table? Count the cost. A flat table for 48 bits and 4 KiB pages needs 2^{36} entries. At 8 bytes each, that is 512 GiB for every process. A multi-level table stores only the parts in use. Each table has 512 entries of 8 bytes, so it fills exactly one 4 KiB page. A small program may need only about ten tables, which is 40 KiB.

  1. Pages are 4 KiB, so the offset is the low 12 bits. Address 0x3A7F has page 3 and offset 0xA7F.
  2. Read entry 3 of the page table. It says: present, writable, frame 9.
  3. Join frame and offset. The physical address is 0x9A7F.
  4. If the entry said "not present", the CPU would stop and call the kernel. That is a page fault.

A page table entry holds the frame number and some flag bits:

  • present: the page is in RAM now.
  • writable and user: who may write, and whether user mode may touch it.
  • accessed and dirty: the CPU sets them when the page is read or written.
  • no-execute: the CPU refuses to run code from this page.

A full walk costs four extra memory reads. That would make every access five times slower. So the CPU keeps recent translations in a small cache, the TLB. The hardware side of the TLB is in Computer architecture. Huge pages stop the walk early. A 2 MiB page skips table 1, and one TLB entry then covers 512 times more memory. Page sizes differ between machines. On the Apple M2 Pro used for this book, pagesize prints 16384, so pages are 16 KiB.

Expert: other page table designs

An inverted page table has one entry per frame, not per page. Its size grows with RAM, not with the address space. A lookup hashes the page number. Some older PowerPC and IA-64 systems used this idea. Most systems today use radix trees like the one above, because the hardware can walk them fast.

Mixing up pages and frames. A page is virtual and belongs to one address space. A frame is physical and can hold different pages over time. Two processes can map the same frame, as shared libraries do.

Page faults

A program calls malloc for 1 GiB. The call returns at once, and RAM use hardly changes. The memory appears only when the program touches it, one page at a time. Each first touch is a page fault.

The CPU traps

The program reads an address. The TLB has no translation. The page walk finds an entry with present = 0. The CPU stops the instruction and jumps into the kernel.

Is the address legal?

The kernel looks up the region of the address space that holds the address. No region? Then the program gets a segmentation fault and usually dies.

Find a frame

The kernel takes a free frame. If none is free, it evicts a page. A dirty page must be written to disk first.

Fill the frame

A new heap page is filled with zeros. A file page or a swapped page is read from disk. During a disk read, the process sleeps and others run.

Retry

The kernel writes the frame number into the entry and sets present = 1. It returns to the program. The CPU runs the same instruction again, and now it works.

This is demand paging. A minor fault needs no disk read, for example a fresh zero page. A major fault must wait for the disk. The space on disk for evicted heap pages is swap.

Now the fork example makes sense. fork does not copy memory. It is copy-on-write. Parent and child share every frame, marked read-only. The child's write causes a fault. The kernel copies just that one page, and the child gets its own frame.

Let m be the time of a normal memory access, F the time to serve a fault, and p the chance that an access faults. The expected time per access is

\text{EAT} = (1 - p)\,m + p\,F .

It is the average memory access time formula from Computer architecture, with a page fault as the miss. Put in numbers. Let m = 100 ns, and let a major fault from a hard disk take F = 8 ms = 8{,}000{,}000 ns. With one fault in 1,000 accesses, \text{EAT} \approx 99.9 + 8000 \approx 8100 ns. The program runs about 80 times slower. To lose less than 10%, we need p \lt 10 / 8{,}000{,}000. That is about one fault per 800,000 accesses. Faults must be very rare.

Trusting a successful malloc. Linux usually allows overcommit. The big allocation succeeds, but no frames exist yet. If RAM runs out when the pages are touched, the out-of-memory killer ends a process. Your error check after malloc never runs.

Page replacement and the working set

RAM is full and a fault needs a frame. Which page should go? Four rules compete on the request list 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5.

// Count page faults for FIFO, LRU, Clock and OPT.
fn faults(refs: &[u32], frames: usize, policy: &str) -> usize {
    let (mut mem, mut used): (Vec<u32>, Vec<bool>) = (vec![], vec![]);
    let (mut count, mut hand) = (0, 0);
    for (t, &p) in refs.iter().enumerate() {
        if let Some(i) = mem.iter().position(|&q| q == p) {
            used[i] = true;                                  // Clock: mark as used
            if policy == "LRU" { let q = mem.remove(i); mem.push(q); }
            continue;
        }
        count += 1;                                          // a page fault
        if mem.len() < frames { mem.push(p); used.push(true); continue; }
        let victim = match policy {
            "OPT" => {                                       // farthest next use
                let next = |q: u32| refs[t + 1..].iter().position(|&r| r == q).unwrap_or(usize::MAX);
                (0..frames).max_by_key(|&i| next(mem[i])).unwrap()
            }
            "Clock" => {
                while used[hand] { used[hand] = false; hand = (hand + 1) % frames; }
                let v = hand; hand = (hand + 1) % frames; v
            }
            _ => { mem.remove(0); mem.push(p); continue; }   // FIFO and LRU: drop the front
        };
        mem[victim] = p;
        used[victim] = true;
    }
    count
}

fn main() {
    let refs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    for frames in [3, 4] {
        let row: Vec<String> = ["FIFO", "LRU", "Clock", "OPT"].iter()
            .map(|p| format!("{p} {}", faults(&refs, frames, p))).collect();
        println!("{frames} frames: {}", row.join(", "));
    }
}
# Count page faults for FIFO, LRU, Clock and OPT.
def faults(refs, frames, policy):
    mem, count, hand, ref_bit = [], 0, 0, {}
    for t, p in enumerate(refs):
        if p in mem:
            if policy == "LRU":
                mem.remove(p); mem.append(p)          # move to "most recent"
            ref_bit[p] = 1                            # Clock: mark as used
            continue
        count += 1                                    # a page fault
        if len(mem) < frames:
            mem.append(p); ref_bit[p] = 1
            continue
        if policy in ("FIFO", "LRU"):
            mem.pop(0)                                # oldest or least recent
        elif policy == "OPT":                         # farthest next use
            future = refs[t + 1:]
            nxt = lambda q: future.index(q) if q in future else len(refs)
            mem.remove(max(mem, key=nxt))
        elif policy == "Clock":
            while ref_bit[mem[hand]]:                 # give a second chance
                ref_bit[mem[hand]] = 0
                hand = (hand + 1) % frames
            mem.pop(hand)                             # evict, keep the hand here
        if policy == "Clock":
            mem.insert(hand, p); hand = (hand + 1) % frames
        else:
            mem.append(p)
        ref_bit[p] = 1
    return count

refs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
for frames in (3, 4):
    row = [f"{p} {faults(refs, frames, p)}" for p in ("FIFO", "LRU", "Clock", "OPT")]
    print(f"{frames} frames: {', '.join(row)}")
3 frames: FIFO 9, LRU 10, Clock 9, OPT 7
4 frames: FIFO 10, LRU 8, Clock 10, OPT 6
  • FIFO evicts the page that came in first. It ignores use.
  • LRU evicts the least recently used page. It bets that the recent past predicts the near future.
  • Clock keeps pages in a circle with a hand. A page with its accessed bit set gets a second chance: the bit is cleared and the hand moves on. Clock is a cheap copy of LRU, because the CPU sets the bits for free.
  • OPT evicts the page whose next use is farthest away. It needs to know the future.

(Belady, 1966.) Memory has k frames, and the whole future request list is known. On a fault with full memory, evict the page whose next request is farthest in the future. A page never used again counts as farthest. No other policy makes fewer faults on that list. This policy is called OPT or MIN.

Proof idea: an exchange argument

Take any policy A. Suppose A agrees with OPT until some fault. There OPT evicts page p, but A evicts page q. By the rule, q is needed before p. Build a new policy A'. It evicts p instead of q, and then copies A. Now A and A' differ in one page only: A' holds q where A holds p.

If A ever evicts p, A' evicts q at that moment, and the two become equal with the same faults. Otherwise, q is requested first. There A faults and A' does not, so A' gains one fault. Later, when p is requested, A' may fault where A does not. It loses at most the one it gained. So A' never faults more than A, and it agrees with OPT for one more step. Repeat this until the policy is OPT. OPT is never worse than A.

In simple words: keep the pages you need soon. Nobody knows the future, so OPT is not a real policy. It is the yardstick. On our list, LRU made 10 faults with 3 frames and OPT made 7. The online view of this gap is in Randomised, approximate, streaming and string algorithms. There, LRU is shown to be at most k times worse than OPT.

More memory gave FIFO more faults. This surprise is Belady's anomaly. LRU and OPT can never show it.

For LRU and OPT, the pages in memory with k frames are always a subset of the pages in memory with k + 1 frames, at every step. So every hit with k frames is also a hit with k + 1 frames. Faults can only go down as memory grows.

Why does the subset rule hold for LRU? With k frames, LRU holds the k most recently used pages. With k + 1 frames, it holds the k + 1 most recent pages. The first set is inside the second. FIFO has no such order, because arrival time and use do not match.

Real kernels use cheap LRU copies. Older Linux kept an active list and an inactive list of pages. Linux 6.1, released in December 2022, added the multi-gen LRU. It groups pages into generations of similar age. Many large distributions now turn it on.

The working set

Programs have locality. A loop touches the same few pages again and again. The principle of locality is in Computer architecture. Denning built a model on this in 1968. The working set W(t, \tau) is the set of pages a process used in the window of its last \tau references, up to time t.

A process runs well only when its working set W(t, \tau) is in RAM. So run a group of processes only if the sum of their working set sizes fits in RAM. If it does not fit, suspend one process and give its frames to the others. Never let the sum stay above RAM.

Why the principle holds

By locality, the pages used in the next short window are mostly the pages used in the last window. If they are all in RAM, the fault rate p stays tiny. If one of them is missing, it will be needed soon, so it faults soon. Then the process evicts a page of its own working set, which also faults soon. The fault rate jumps, and by the formula above every access becomes thousands of times slower.

Example. RAM is 2 GiB. Three processes have working sets of 600, 900 and 700 MiB. The sum is 2.2 GiB, which is too big. All three fault all the time and the disk is always busy. This is thrashing. Suspend the 700 MiB process. The other two now fit in 1.5 GiB and run at full speed.

Fixing thrashing by adding more processes or faster disks. The CPU looks idle during thrashing, so a naive scheduler starts more work, and it gets worse. The fix is less load or more RAM. Measure the fault rate, not only the CPU use.

Memory allocators

Paging gives a process whole pages. But programs ask for 24 bytes here and 3,000 bytes there. A heap allocator cuts pages into small blocks. This Rust program counts every call to the allocator. The Python version uses tracemalloc.

// Wrap the system allocator and count every call to it.
use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, Layout, System};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering::Relaxed};

struct Counting;
static CALLS: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
static BYTES: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);

unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for Counting {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
        CALLS.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
        BYTES.fetch_add(layout.size(), Relaxed);
        unsafe { System.alloc(layout) }                 // the real work
    }
    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {
        unsafe { System.dealloc(ptr, layout) }
    }
}

#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: Counting = Counting;                     // every Box, Vec, String uses it

fn measure(name: &str, f: impl Fn()) {
    let (c0, b0) = (CALLS.load(Relaxed), BYTES.load(Relaxed));
    f();
    println!("{name:<28} {:>4} allocations, {:>6} bytes",
             CALLS.load(Relaxed) - c0, BYTES.load(Relaxed) - b0);
}

fn main() {
    measure("push 1000 items", || { let mut v = Vec::new(); for i in 0..1000u32 { v.push(i); } });
    measure("with_capacity(1000)", || { let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(1000); for i in 0..1000u32 { v.push(i); } });
    measure("1000 small Boxes", || { let _b: Vec<Box<u32>> = (0..1000).map(Box::new).collect(); });
}
push 1000 items                 9 allocations,   8176 bytes
with_capacity(1000)             1 allocations,   4000 bytes
1000 small Boxes             1001 allocations,  12000 bytes
# Watch the allocator with tracemalloc from the standard library.
import tracemalloc

def measure(name, f):
    tracemalloc.start()
    keep = f()                                        # keep the result alive
    current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
    tracemalloc.stop()
    print(f"{name:<28} now {current:>7} bytes, peak {peak:>7} bytes")

measure("list of 1000 ints", lambda: [i for i in range(1000)])
measure("1000 small dicts", lambda: [{"id": i} for i in range(1000)])
measure("bytearray of 100000", lambda: bytearray(100_000))
list of 1000 ints            now   31872 bytes, peak   31872 bytes
1000 small dicts             now  209520 bytes, peak  209520 bytes
bytearray of 100000          now  100057 bytes, peak  100057 bytes

Growing a vector one push at a time made 9 allocations: capacity 4, 8, 16 and so on up to 1024. Reserving the space first made one. A thousand small boxes made a thousand allocations. Each allocation costs time, and it also wastes space. I asked the macOS C allocator for real block sizes with malloc_size:

Request (bytes)Block given (bytes)Waste
41675%
173247%
10011211%
5,0005,1202%
100,000114,68813%

Waste inside a block is internal fragmentation. Free space cut into pieces that are too small to use is external fragmentation. An allocator fights both, and it must be fast. These are the main designs:

  • Free list. Keep the free blocks in a linked list. First fit is fast. Best fit leaves less waste but searches more. On free, join neighbour blocks, which is called coalescing.
  • Buddy allocator. All blocks are powers of two. A big block splits into two halves, the buddies. A block of size s at address a has its buddy at a \oplus s, so joining is one XOR. The Linux page allocator works this way.
  • Slab allocator. Keep a cache for each object kind, for example one for inodes. A slab is a few pages cut into equal slots. There is no external fragmentation inside a slab. Bonwick designed it for Solaris in 1994. Linux uses a version called SLUB.
  • Size classes and thread caches. Round each request up to a class, such as 16, 32, 48 or 64 bytes. Each thread keeps its own free lists, so it needs no lock. jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc work this way.
  • Arena or bump allocator. Move a pointer forward for each request, and free everything at once. It is the fastest design when many objects die together, such as all the nodes of one request.
  1. Round 100 KiB up to a power of two: 128 KiB.
  2. Split 1 MiB into two 512 KiB buddies. Split one into two 256 KiB buddies. Split one of those into two 128 KiB buddies.
  3. Hand out one 128 KiB block. 28 KiB of it is internal fragmentation.
  4. On free, check the buddy at address XOR 128 KiB. If it is free, join them into 256 KiB, and go on up.

Python has its own layer. For objects of 512 bytes or less, CPython uses pymalloc. It takes memory in arenas of 1 MiB on 64-bit systems, and it uses the C allocator for bigger requests. The free-threaded build of Python 3.14 uses mimalloc instead, with one heap per thread.

Allocating in the hot loop. A thousand tiny boxes cost a thousand allocator calls and up to 75% waste each. Reserve capacity, reuse buffers, or store values in one vector and refer to them by index. Measure first. The count above took twenty lines of code.

File systems

A file has two names. One name is deleted. Does the file still exist? This program makes a hard link and a symbolic link, then removes the first name.

// A name points to an inode. A hard link is a second name for it.
use std::fs;
use std::os::unix::fs::{symlink, MetadataExt};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    std::env::set_current_dir("fsdemo")?;
    fs::write("a.txt", "hello\n")?;
    fs::hard_link("a.txt", "b.txt")?;                   // hard link: same inode
    symlink("a.txt", "c.txt")?;                         // symbolic link: a path to a name

    for name in ["a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt"] {
        let m = fs::symlink_metadata(name)?;            // do not follow symlinks
        println!("{name}: inode {}, links {}", m.ino(), m.nlink());
    }

    fs::remove_file("a.txt")?;                          // delete one name only
    println!("b.txt still reads: {}", fs::read_to_string("b.txt")?.trim());
    println!("c.txt exists? {}", fs::exists("c.txt")?); // follows the dead path
    Ok(())
}
a.txt: inode 304048616, links 2
b.txt: inode 304048616, links 2
c.txt: inode 304048619, links 1
b.txt still reads: hello
c.txt exists? false
# A name points to an inode. A hard link is a second name for it.
import os

os.chdir("fsdemo")
with open("a.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("hello\n")
os.link("a.txt", "b.txt")             # hard link: same inode
os.symlink("a.txt", "c.txt")          # symbolic link: a path to a name

for name in ("a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt"):
    s = os.lstat(name)                # lstat: do not follow symlinks
    print(f"{name}: inode {s.st_ino}, links {s.st_nlink}")

os.remove("a.txt")                    # delete one name only
print("b.txt still reads:", open("b.txt").read().strip())
print("c.txt exists?", os.path.exists("c.txt"))   # follows the dead path
a.txt: inode 304048587, links 2
b.txt: inode 304048587, links 2
c.txt: inode 304048590, links 1
b.txt still reads: hello
c.txt exists? False

The file lives on. A file is really an inode. The inode stores the size, owner, permissions, times and the list of data blocks. It does not store a name. A directory is a file of entries, and each entry maps a name to an inode number. A hard link is a second entry for the same inode, so the link count became 2. A symbolic link stores only a path. When that path dies, the link dangles. The kernel frees an inode when its link count is 0 and no process has it open.

With 4 KiB blocks and 4-byte pointers, one block holds 1024 pointers. So the pointers alone allow 12 + 1024 + 1024^2 + 1024^3 blocks, about 4 TiB. Other fields set lower real limits. A big file with many pointers wastes space. So ext4 and most modern systems use extents. One extent says "blocks 5000 to 5999", where the old way needed 1000 pointers.
