To open /home/ana/notes.txt, the kernel reads the root directory, finds home, reads that directory, and so on. Each step can be a disk read. So the kernel caches directory entries and inodes in RAM. It also keeps file data in the page cache, the same frames that paging uses.

Crash consistency

Appending one block to a file needs three writes. The data block, the inode with its new size and pointer, and the bitmap that marks the block as used. The power can fail between any two of them. Then the inode may point to garbage, or a block may be lost forever. There are four ways out:

  • Check after the crash. The old tool fsck scans the whole disk. On a big disk this takes hours.
  • Journaling. First write what you plan to do into a log, then do it.
  • Copy-on-write. Never overwrite a live block. Write new blocks, then switch one root pointer. ZFS and btrfs work this way, and APFS does it for its metadata. Snapshots become almost free.
  • Log-structured. Write everything, data and inodes, at the end of one big log. Rosenblum and Ousterhout proposed this in 1991. A cleaner later copies live blocks out of old segments. F2FS on Linux uses this design for flash.
  1. Write the new data block to its home on disk. This is "ordered" mode.
  2. Write a transaction to the journal: begin, new inode, new bitmap.
  3. Write a commit record. After the commit is on disk, the update is safe.
  4. Checkpoint: copy the inode and bitmap to their home places.
  5. Free the journal space. After a crash, replay every committed transaction and ignore the rest.

ext4 has three modes. data=journal puts data in the journal too, and it is the slowest. data=ordered journals only metadata but writes data first, and it is the default. data=writeback journals only metadata, in any order, so a file can hold old garbage after a crash. The kernel documentation now marks data=journal as deprecated.

Thinking that write means "on disk". It means "in the page cache". To save a file safely, write a temporary file, call fsync on it, rename it over the old name, then fsync the directory. The rename is atomic, but without the second fsync it may not survive a crash. Databases do the same with a write-ahead log, see Relational databases.

Disks, SSDs and RAID

A hard disk spins at 7200 turns per minute. One turn takes 60 / 7200 s = 8.33 ms. On average the head waits half a turn, 4.17 ms, for the right sector. Moving the arm, the seek, adds a few more milliseconds. So one random 4 KiB read takes about 10 ms. That is about 100 random reads per second, or 0.4 MB/s. The same disk reads more than 100 MB/s in order. Order matters 250 times.

An SSD has no moving parts. A random read takes tens of microseconds. But flash has strange rules:

  • You read and write one flash page at a time, often a few KiB.
  • You cannot overwrite a page. You must first erase it, and you can only erase a whole erase block of many pages.
  • Each block survives only a limited number of erases.

So the SSD has a small computer inside, the FTL. It maps each logical block number to a flash page, much like a page table. A write goes to a fresh page, and the old page is marked dead. Garbage collection later copies the live pages out of a block and erases it. This extra copying is write amplification. The TRIM command tells the SSD which blocks the file system no longer uses, so it copies less. Log-structured and copy-on-write file systems fit flash well, because they never overwrite in place.

Disks fail. RAID, described by Patterson, Gibson and Katz in 1988, spreads data over many disks. A stripe is one row of blocks across the disks. With N disks of capacity C:

LevelIdeaUsable spaceDisk failures survivedSmall write
RAID 0stripe blocks over disksN C01 write
RAID 1mirror every blockN C / 21 per mirror pair2 writes
RAID 5stripe plus one parity block(N - 1) C12 reads, 2 writes
RAID 6stripe plus two parity blocks(N - 2) C23 reads, 3 writes
RAID 10stripe over mirror pairsN C / 21 per pair2 writes

RAID 5 parity is the XOR of the data blocks in a stripe. XOR has a magic property: a \oplus b \oplus b = a. So any one lost block equals the XOR of all the others.

// RAID 5 idea: parity = XOR of the data blocks. Lose one disk, rebuild it.
fn xor(blocks: &[&[u8]]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut out = vec![0u8; blocks[0].len()];
    for b in blocks {
        for (o, x) in out.iter_mut().zip(b.iter()) { *o ^= x; }
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    let mut disks: Vec<Vec<u8>> = vec![b"AAAA".to_vec(), b"BBBB".to_vec(), b"CCCC".to_vec()];
    let mut parity = xor(&[&disks[0], &disks[1], &disks[2]]);   // on a fourth disk
    let hex: String = parity.iter().map(|b| format!("{b:02x}")).collect();
    println!("parity : {hex}");

    let rebuilt = xor(&[&disks[0], &disks[2], &parity]);        // disk 1 died
    println!("rebuilt: {}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&rebuilt));

    let new = b"bBBB".to_vec();                                 // small write to disk 1
    parity = xor(&[&parity, &disks[1], &new]);                  // old ^ old data ^ new data
    disks[1] = new;
    println!("check  : {}", parity == xor(&[&disks[0], &disks[1], &disks[2]]));
}
# RAID 5 idea: parity = XOR of the data blocks. Lose one disk, rebuild it.
from functools import reduce

def xor(blocks):
    return bytes(reduce(lambda a, b: a ^ b, col) for col in zip(*blocks))

disks = [b"AAAA", b"BBBB", b"CCCC"]          # three data blocks in one stripe
parity = xor(disks)                          # stored on a fourth disk
print("parity :", parity.hex())

lost = 1                                     # disk 1 dies
alive = [d for i, d in enumerate(disks) if i != lost] + [parity]
print("rebuilt:", xor(alive))                # XOR of everything left

new = b"bBBB"                                # small write to disk 1
parity = xor([parity, disks[1], new])        # new parity = old ^ old data ^ new data
disks[1] = new
print("check  :", parity == xor(disks))
parity : 40404040
rebuilt: BBBB
check  : true

The Python version prints b'BBBB' and True. The last part shows the small-write cost. To change one block, RAID 5 reads the old data and old parity, then writes the new data and new parity. That is four disk operations for one write.

Using RAID as a backup. RAID survives a dead disk. It does not survive a deleted file, ransomware or a bad rm, because it copies the mistake to every disk at once. Also, a rebuild of a big disk can take many hours. A second failure during the rebuild loses a RAID 5 array.

I/O models

A server has 10,000 open connections, and most are idle. How does one program wait on all of them? First see the basic tool: a read that does not wait.

// Non-blocking reads: the kernel says "not now" instead of making you wait.
use std::io::{ErrorKind, Read, Write};
use std::os::unix::net::UnixStream;

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let (mut a, mut b) = UnixStream::pair()?;           // two connected sockets
    b.set_nonblocking(true)?;
    let mut buf = [0u8; 100];

    match b.read(&mut buf) {                            // nothing to read yet
        Err(e) if e.kind() == ErrorKind::WouldBlock => println!("read: would block"),
        other => println!("read: {other:?}"),
    }

    a.write_all(b"ping")?;
    let n = b.read(&mut buf)?;                          // data is there now
    println!("read: {:?}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&buf[..n]));
    Ok(())
}
# Non-blocking reads and a readiness selector (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS).
import selectors, socket

a, b = socket.socketpair()            # two connected sockets
b.setblocking(False)
try:
    b.recv(100)                       # nothing to read yet
except BlockingIOError:
    print("recv: would block")

sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()
print("selector:", type(sel).__name__)
sel.register(b, selectors.EVENT_READ)
print("ready before write:", sel.select(timeout=0))   # empty list

a.send(b"ping")
for key, _ in sel.select(timeout=1):  # the kernel says: b is readable
    print("ready after write :", key.fileobj.recv(100))
read: would block
read: "ping"
recv: would block
selector: KqueueSelector
ready before write: []
ready after write : b'ping'

The first output is from Rust, the second from Python on macOS. There are three big models:

  • Blocking I/O. read puts the thread to sleep until data comes. Use one thread per connection. It is simple, but 10,000 threads cost memory for stacks and time for context switches. Context switches are in Operating systems: processes and scheduling.
  • Readiness. Make every socket non-blocking. Ask the kernel which ones are ready, then read only those. select and poll pass the whole list on every call, so the cost grows with the number of sockets. epoll keeps an interest list inside the kernel and returns only the ready ones. It came in Linux 2.5.44. macOS and the BSDs have kqueue.
  • Completion. Hand the kernel the whole job: "read into this buffer". Later it says "done, 512 bytes". io_uring came in Linux 5.1 in 2019. Windows has had this model for a long time, as I/O completion ports.

How does io_uring work? The program and the kernel share two rings in memory. The program puts a request, an SQE, on the submission queue. The kernel puts a result, a CQE, on the completion queue. Each result carries the user_data tag of its request, because results can come back in any order. One io_uring_enter system call can submit hundreds of requests. In polling mode, a kernel thread watches the ring, and the program often makes no system call at all.

Readiness says "you can read now without waiting". Completion says "your read is done". The difference matters for disk files. select and poll always report a regular file as ready, even when the read will wait for the disk. epoll refuses regular files. Neither one helps. So readiness servers send file reads to a thread pool, and io_uring can do them directly. Async runtimes such as Tokio build on epoll and kqueue. The theory of async tasks is in Concurrency and parallelism.

Using epoll in edge-triggered mode and reading only once. Edge mode reports a socket only when new data arrives. If you leave bytes in the buffer, no new event comes, and the connection hangs. Read until you get "would block". Also check where io_uring is allowed. In June 2023 Google wrote that about 60% of the kernel exploits sent to its bug bounty used io_uring. It turned io_uring off on ChromeOS and on its production servers. This can change, so check your platform.

Virtual machines and containers

Two teams share one big server. Team A runs a whole Windows system. Team B runs fifty small Linux services. A gets a virtual machine. B gets containers. What is the difference?

A hypervisor runs whole operating systems as guests. Each guest believes it owns the hardware. A type 1 hypervisor runs on the bare machine, like Xen, Hyper-V or ESXi. KVM turns the Linux kernel itself into one. A type 2 hypervisor runs as a program on a normal system, like VirtualBox.

The classic method is trap and emulate. Guest code runs directly on the CPU. When it tries a privileged instruction, the CPU traps to the hypervisor, which fakes the result. Popek and Goldberg showed in 1974 when this works. Every instruction that can change or reveal machine state must trap. Early x86 broke this rule. So VMware rewrote guest code on the fly, and Xen changed the guest kernel. Later, Intel VT-x and AMD-V added hardware support.

Memory needs two translations: guest virtual to guest physical, then guest physical to host physical. With nested paging (Intel EPT, AMD NPT), the CPU walks both tables. Each of the guest's 4 levels needs a host walk too. A TLB miss can then cost up to 24 memory reads, so huge pages help a lot in VMs. Devices are usually faked with virtio drivers.

A container is just a group of processes on the host kernel. Two kernel features make it feel like its own machine:

  • Namespaces change what a process can see. Linux has eight kinds: mount, PID, network, UTS (host name), IPC, user, cgroup and time.
  • cgroups limit what it can use. In cgroup v2, controllers include cpu, memory, io and pids. The file memory.max sets a hard memory limit.

An image adds a layered file system such as overlayfs. A container starts in milliseconds, because it is only a process. But all containers share one kernel. One kernel bug can let a process escape from every container on the host. In between sit microVMs. Firecracker uses KVM. Its site says a microVM boots in under 125 ms, with under 5 MiB of memory overhead. AWS Lambda runs on it. gVisor takes another path: a kernel written in user space catches the container's system calls.

Treating a container as a strong security wall. Do you run code you do not trust, such as code from an AI agent? Then use a VM or a microVM, or at least gVisor. Containers are fine for packaging your own code. See Systems and software security.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for memory and storage
PatternPurposeModelNote
Translate through a treeBig sparse address space, small tables9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 12 bits on x86-64Each level is one more memory read. The TLB hides it.
Load on first touchUse RAM only for pages in usemalloc(1 GiB) returns at onceOvercommit can kill you later, not at malloc.
Copy on writeCheap copies of big datafork, ZFS snapshotsThe first write pays for the copy.
Evict the farthest next useThe best possible paging, as a yardstickOPT: 7 faults where LRU had 10Needs the future. Use LRU or Clock in practice.
Second chance with a bitCheap LRU copyClock clears accessed bits as the hand movesLike FIFO, it can show Belady's anomaly.
Keep the working set in RAMAvoid thrashingSuspend one of three processesIdle CPU plus a busy disk means thrashing.
Size classes plus thread cachesFast small allocations without locks4 bytes become a 16-byte blockReserve capacity in hot loops.
Names point to inodesMany names, one filehard link: link count 2A symbolic link breaks when its target name goes.
Log first, then writeSurvive a crash in the middleext4 data=orderedwrite is not durable. Call fsync.
Never overwrite in placeCrash safety and flash friendlinesscopy-on-write, log-structured file systemsNeeds a cleaner or garbage collector.
Parity by XORRebuild one lost diskRAID 5: p = a \oplus b \oplus cRAID is not a backup.
Ask what is readyMany idle connections, one threadepoll, kqueue, selectorsEdge mode: read until "would block".
Submit and collectBatch I/O with few system callsio_uring SQE and CQE ringsMatch results by user_data. Some platforms disable it.
Share the kernel or notChoose isolation strengthcontainer for your code, microVM for untrusted codeA container escape is one kernel bug away.

Practice

Two processes print the same pointer value but different data. Why?

  • One of them reads stale cache.
  • Each process has its own page table, so the same virtual address maps to different frames.
  • The kernel moved the data between the two prints.

Addresses in a process are virtual. After the child's write, copy-on-write gave it a new frame. The two page tables now map that page to different frames.

Which policy can make more faults when you add a frame?

  • LRU
  • OPT
  • FIFO

FIFO is not a stack algorithm, so it can show Belady's anomaly. On 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 it makes 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4.

You delete a.txt. A hard link b.txt to it exists. What happens to the data?

  • It is deleted. b.txt now gives an error.
  • It stays. The inode's link count drops from 2 to 1.
  • It stays, but b.txt becomes a symbolic link.

Deleting removes one directory entry. The inode is freed only when its link count is 0 and no process has it open.

A server reads many files from a slow disk. Which model avoids blocking without a thread pool?

  • epoll in level-triggered mode
  • io_uring
  • select

select and poll report regular files as always ready, so the read still waits for the disk. epoll does not accept regular files at all. io_uring is completion-based and can run file reads in the background.

With 4 KiB pages, the offset is the low ? bits of an address.

RAID 6 with 8 disks of 4 TB gives ? TB of usable space.

The parity of the bytes 0x41, 0x42 and 0x43 is 0x?.

  1. Run OPT by hand with 3 frames on 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4. How many faults?
    Answer

    7, 0 and 1 fault and fill the frames: 3 faults. Request 2 faults. The next uses are 0 at once, 1 never, 7 never. Evict 7 (or 1, both are never used). Frames 2 0 1. Request 0 hits. Request 3 faults. Next uses: 0 soon, 1 and 2 never. Evict 1. Frames 2 0 3. Request 0 hits. Request 4 faults. Evict 2 or 3. Total: 6 faults.

  2. A 32-bit machine uses 4 KiB pages and a flat page table with 4-byte entries. How big is the table of one process? Why is a two-level table better?
    Answer

    There are 2^{32} / 2^{12} = 2^{20} pages, so 2^{20} \cdot 4 = 4 MiB per process, even for a tiny program. A two-level table splits the 20 bits into 10 + 10. The top table has 1024 entries, 4 KiB. Second-level tables exist only for regions in use. A small program needs about three tables: 12 KiB.

  3. Memory access is 100 ns. A major fault from an SSD costs 100 microseconds. What fault rate keeps the slowdown under 10%?
    Answer

    We need p \cdot F \lt 0.1 \cdot m roughly, so p \lt 10 / 100{,}000 = 10^{-4}. At most one fault in 10,000 accesses. With a hard disk at 8 ms, the limit was one in 800,000. The SSD gives 80 times more room.

  4. Explain why write, then rename, then nothing else can lose a config file after a power cut. Give the safe order.
    Answer

    Both changes may still sit in the page cache. The rename can reach the disk before the data. After the crash the new name points to an empty or half-written file. Safe order: write the temp file, fsync it, rename it over the old name, then fsync the directory so the new entry is durable.

  5. Expert. A buddy allocator owns 1 MiB. It serves 200 KiB, then 60 KiB, then 300 KiB. Which block sizes does it hand out, and how much is internal fragmentation?
    Answer

    200 KiB becomes 256 KiB: split 1 MiB into 512 + 512, then one 512 into 256 + 256. 60 KiB becomes 64 KiB: split the free 256 into 128 + 128, then one 128 into 64 + 64. 300 KiB becomes 512 KiB: the other half of the first split is still free. The program asked for 560 KiB but got 256 + 64 + 512 = 832 KiB. Waste: 56 + 4 + 212 = 272 KiB, about a third. Buddy allocators are fast but can waste a lot.

  6. Expert. Your agent platform runs code written by users. Compare running each job in a container, in gVisor and in a Firecracker microVM.
    Answer

    A container starts fastest and uses the least memory. But it shares the host kernel, so one kernel bug can let the code escape. gVisor catches the system calls in a user-space kernel. The attack surface on the host kernel is much smaller, and some calls get slower. A microVM gives each job its own kernel behind KVM and the hardware's virtualisation support. It costs a short boot and a few MiB per job. For untrusted code, microVMs or gVisor are the usual choice.

Key takeaways

  • Every address a program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it through a multi-level page table, and the TLB caches the result.
  • Pages load on first touch. Copy-on-write makes fork and snapshots cheap. Faults must be very rare, because a major fault costs millions of nanoseconds.
  • OPT, which evicts the page used farthest in the future, is provably the best. LRU and Clock copy it from the past. FIFO can get worse with more memory.
  • Run only as many processes as their working sets allow. Otherwise the system thrashes.
  • Allocators trade speed against fragmentation with free lists, buddies, slabs, size classes and arenas.
  • A file is an inode. Directories map names to inodes. Journals, copy-on-write and logs keep the disk consistent after a crash. Durability needs fsync.
  • Hard disks hate random access. SSDs hate overwrites. RAID survives disk failures but is not a backup.
  • Blocking, readiness (epoll, kqueue) and completion (io_uring) are the three I/O models. Containers share one kernel. Virtual machines do not.

Sources

  • Arpaci-Dusseau: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces. A free textbook. Chapters on paging, page replacement policies, free space, file systems, journaling, LFS, SSDs, RAID and virtual machines.
  • Linux kernel documentation: x86-64 memory map. User space sizes with 4-level and 5-level page tables.
  • Linux kernel documentation: ext4. The journal, ordered and writeback modes, and the default.
  • io_uring(7) manual page. Submission and completion rings, SQEs, CQEs and user_data. The epoll(7) page in the same set gives the epoll history.
  • Python 3.14 documentation: Memory management. pymalloc, its 512-byte limit and 1 MiB arenas, and mimalloc in the free-threaded build.
  • Firecracker. The microVM monitor built on KVM, with its boot time and memory overhead.

Concurrency and parallelism

Modern computers have many cores, and servers wait on many slow things at once. Programs must do several things at the same time. This is easy to start and hard to get right. This chapter gives the theory under threads, locks and atomics: memory models, linearisability and lock-free design.

  • Tell concurrency from parallelism, and threads from async tasks.
  • Explain data races, memory models and the DRF-SC guarantee, and show how Rust's Send and Sync stop data races.
  • Prevent deadlock with a lock order, and write a correct compare-and-swap loop.
  • Explain the ABA problem, linearisability and why compare-and-swap can build any wait-free object.
  • Use actors and data parallelism, and measure speed-up honestly.

Threads, tasks and async

A web service calls four other services. Each call waits 100 ms. One after another, the user waits 400 ms. All at the same time, the user waits about 100 ms.

// Four jobs that each wait 100 ms: one after another, then on four threads.
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

fn job(id: u32) -> u32 {
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100));   // stands for a network call
    id * 10
}

fn main() {
    let t = Instant::now();
    let seq: Vec<u32> = (1..=4).map(job).collect();
    println!("sequential: {seq:?} in {} ms", t.elapsed().as_millis());

    let t = Instant::now();
    let handles: Vec<_> = (1..=4).map(|id| thread::spawn(move || job(id))).collect();
    let par: Vec<u32> = handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).collect();
    println!("4 threads : {par:?} in {} ms", t.elapsed().as_millis());
}
# Four jobs that each wait 100 ms: one after another, on threads, and as async tasks.
import asyncio, time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def job(i):
    time.sleep(0.1)                      # stands for a network call
    return i * 10

async def ajob(i, blocking):
    if blocking:
        time.sleep(0.1)                  # wrong: blocks the whole event loop
    else:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)         # right: gives control back to the loop
    return i * 10

async def run_all(blocking):
    return await asyncio.gather(*(ajob(i, blocking) for i in range(1, 5)))

def timed(name, f):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = f()
    print(f"{name:<14}: {out} in {round((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)} ms")

timed("sequential", lambda: [job(i) for i in range(1, 5)])
with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as pool:
    timed("4 threads", lambda: list(pool.map(job, range(1, 5))))
timed("async", lambda: asyncio.run(run_all(False)))
timed("async, blocked", lambda: asyncio.run(run_all(True)))
sequential: [10, 20, 30, 40] in 416 ms
4 threads : [10, 20, 30, 40] in 105 ms
sequential    : [10, 20, 30, 40] in 412 ms
4 threads     : [10, 20, 30, 40] in 105 ms
async         : [10, 20, 30, 40] in 102 ms
async, blocked: [10, 20, 30, 40] in 421 ms

The first output is from Rust, the second from Python. The jobs mostly wait, so one core is enough. That is concurrency: many jobs are in progress at once. Parallelism is different. It means work really runs at the same instant on several cores. Concurrency is about the structure of a program. Parallelism is about how it runs.

  • A thread is scheduled by the kernel. The kernel can stop it at any moment. This is preemptive scheduling. Each thread has its own stack. In Rust it is 2 MiB of virtual memory by default, and only touched pages use RAM.
  • A task is scheduled by a runtime inside the program, such as Tokio or asyncio. Thousands of tasks share a few threads.
  • An async function returns a future. In Rust, the compiler turns it into a state machine. The runtime polls it. At each await that is not ready, the task stops and another one runs. This is cooperative scheduling.

A runtime learns that I/O is ready from epoll, kqueue or io_uring. These are in Operating systems: memory and storage. Threads and context switches are in Operating systems: processes and scheduling. The Coding book has the hands-on Rust chapters on threads and on async.

A blocking call inside an async task. Look at the last Python line. time.sleep does not give control back, so the whole event loop stops, and four tasks took 421 ms. Use the async version of the call, or move blocking work to a thread, with asyncio.to_thread in Python or spawn_blocking in Tokio.

Data races and memory models

Recall the lost update from Operating systems: processes and scheduling. Two threads read a counter, both add 1, and both write. One update vanishes. A lock fixes it. This section asks a deeper question. When threads share memory, what may a read return?

A race condition is any bug that depends on timing. A data race is a narrower thing. Two threads access the same location. At least one access is a write. At least one is a plain, non-atomic access. And nothing orders the two. In Rust and C++, a data race is undefined behaviour. The compiler may then produce any result.

In Python, the GIL lets only one thread run Python code at a time. It hides many such bugs, but it promises nothing. A thread switch can still fall between a read and a write. Python 3.14 also has an officially supported free-threaded build without the GIL. There, threads really run in parallel, so these bugs show up more easily. Safe Rust refuses to compile a plain counter that two threads write, as the next section shows.

What can a read see?

Here is a famous test. Thread A writes x = 1 and then reads y. Thread B writes y = 1 and then reads x. Both start at 0. Can both reads give 0? Think of any order of the four steps. Some write always comes first, so at least one read must see a 1. Now run it a million times on the Apple M2 Pro used for this book.

// Store buffering test: can both threads read 0?
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, AtomicUsize, Ordering, Ordering::*};
use std::thread;

static X: AtomicU32 = AtomicU32::new(0);
static Y: AtomicU32 = AtomicU32::new(0);
static R: [AtomicU32; 2] = [AtomicU32::new(0), AtomicU32::new(0)];
static ARRIVED: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
static ROUND: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);

fn barrier() {                                   // both threads meet here, spinning
    let r = ROUND.load(Acquire);
    if ARRIVED.fetch_add(1, AcqRel) == 1 { ARRIVED.store(0, Relaxed); ROUND.fetch_add(1, Release); }
    else { while ROUND.load(Acquire) == r { std::hint::spin_loop(); } }
}

fn round(me: usize, ord: Ordering) {
    let (mine, other) = if me == 0 { (&X, &Y) } else { (&Y, &X) };
    barrier();
    mine.store(1, ord);                          // write my flag
    R[me].store(other.load(ord), Relaxed);       // read the other flag
    barrier();
}

fn run(ord: Ordering, rounds: usize) -> usize {
    let mut both_zero = 0;
    thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..rounds { round(1, ord); barrier(); });
        for _ in 0..rounds {
            round(0, ord);
            if R[0].load(Relaxed) == 0 && R[1].load(Relaxed) == 0 { both_zero += 1; }
            X.store(0, Relaxed); Y.store(0, Relaxed);
            barrier();                           // reset done, start the next round
        }
    });
    both_zero
}

fn main() {
    for ord in [Relaxed, SeqCst] {
        println!("{ord:?}: both read 0 in {} of 1000000 rounds", run(ord, 1_000_000));
    }
}
Relaxed: both read 0 in 1065 of 1000000 rounds
SeqCst: both read 0 in 0 of 1000000 rounds

With Relaxed, both threads read 0 in about a thousand rounds. The count changes a lot from run to run. In five runs we saw between 272 and 10,047. The program uses only atomics, so it has no data race. The result is still impossible in any simple order of steps.

Hardware is faster than simple interleaving. A core puts a write in its store buffer and goes on. x86 allows exactly this store-then-load reordering. ARM allows more. Compilers also move loads and stores when one thread cannot tell the difference. So every language needs a memory model.

The simple ideal is sequential consistency, defined by Lamport in 1979. The result must look like all steps ran in one single order, and each thread's steps keep their program order. Rust uses the C++20 memory model. Its key idea is happens-before. Each atomic operation takes an ordering:

  • Relaxed: the operation itself is atomic, but it orders nothing else.
  • Release on a store and Acquire on a load: if the load reads the stored value, everything before the store happens before everything after the load.
  • SeqCst: as above, plus all SeqCst operations fall into one total order. That is why the second test line shows 0.

Release and acquire are the normal way to publish data. Here a flag publishes one value:

// Message passing with release and acquire: if you see the flag, you see the data.
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicU64, Ordering::*};
use std::thread;

static DATA: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);
static READY: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);

fn main() {
    thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| {
            DATA.store(42, Relaxed);             // 1. write the data
            READY.store(true, Release);          // 2. publish: everything before stays before
        });
        s.spawn(|| {
            while !READY.load(Acquire) {         // 3. wait for the flag
                std::hint::spin_loop();
            }
            println!("data = {}", DATA.load(Relaxed));  // 4. always 42
        });
    });
}
data = 42

(Adve and Hill, 1990.) Suppose no sequentially consistent run of a program has a data race. Then every run of the program is sequentially consistent. In C++ and Rust this holds when the program synchronises only with locks and SeqCst atomics.

Proof idea

Compilers and CPUs only reorder steps that no other thread can see without a race. Between two synchronisation points, a thread's plain accesses touch data that no other thread touches at the same time. So their inner order is invisible. The synchronisation points themselves keep one global order. The outcome therefore equals some interleaving of whole steps.

In simple words: avoid data races and use the strong tools, and you may think in simple interleavings. The weak orderings are for experts who need the last bit of speed. The Java and C++ memory models were both built on this promise.

"It passed all tests on my laptop." A wrong ordering can look correct on x86, which keeps stores in order. Then it fails on ARM phones and servers. It can also fail only once in a million runs, as above. Think about orderings on paper. Then test with tools such as ThreadSanitizer or the Rust model checker loom.

How Send and Sync prevent data races

Here are three small Rust programs that do not compile, and a fixed version. The error messages are shortened.

// The same counter in Rust. This program does not compile.
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let mut count = 0;
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..2 {
            s.spawn(|| {
                for _ in 0..200_000 { count += 1; }   // two threads write
            });
        }
    });
    println!("{count}");
}
error[E0499]: cannot borrow `count` as mutable more than once at a time
 --> race.rs:8:21
  |
8 |             s.spawn(|| {
  |                     ^^ `count` was mutably borrowed here in the previous iteration of the loop
9 |                 for _ in 0..200_000 { count += 1; }   // two threads write
  |                                       ----- borrows occur due to use of `count` in closure
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let hits = Rc::new(0u64);                    // Rc: a counter without atomics
    let h = Rc::clone(&hits);
    thread::spawn(move || println!("{h}")).join().unwrap();
}
error[E0277]: `Rc<u64>` cannot be sent between threads safely
  = help: within `{closure@send.rs:7:19: 7:26}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<u64>`
use std::cell::Cell;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let flag = Cell::new(false);                 // Cell: change through a shared reference
    thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| flag.set(true));
    });
}
error[E0277]: `Cell<bool>` cannot be shared between threads safely
  = help: the trait `Sync` is not implemented for `Cell<bool>`
  = note: required for `&Cell<bool>` to implement `Send`
// The fix: Arc counts owners with atomics, AtomicBool changes safely.
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicU64, Ordering::SeqCst};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let hits = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0));      // Arc<T>: Send + Sync when T is
    let flag = AtomicBool::new(false);           // atomic: Sync
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..4 {
            let h = Arc::clone(&hits);
            s.spawn(move || { h.fetch_add(1, SeqCst); });
        }
        s.spawn(|| flag.store(true, SeqCst));    // shares &flag: needs Sync
    });
    println!("hits = {}, flag = {}", hits.load(SeqCst), flag.load(SeqCst));
}
hits = 4, flag = true

Two marker traits carry the rules:

  • A type is Send if a value of it may move to another thread.
  • A type is Sync if many threads may use it through shared references. Formally, T is Sync exactly when &T is Send. The last note of the Cell error says just this.

Both are auto traits. A struct is Send when all its fields are. They are also unsafe traits: a wrong manual impl can cause undefined behaviour.

TypeSendSyncWhy
Rc<T>nonoIts owner count changes without atomics.
Arc<T>if T is Send + Syncif T is Send + SyncThe count is atomic.
Cell<T>, RefCell<T>if T is SendnoThey change data through & with no synchronisation.
Mutex<T>if T is Sendif T is SendThe lock orders every access.
MutexGuard<T>noif T is SyncIt must unlock on the thread that locked.
AtomicU64yesyesEvery access is atomic.
raw pointersnonoA safety default for unknown ownership.

Why does this stop every data race in safe Rust? Follow the definition. A data race needs two threads that reach the same location, with one unsynchronised write.

  1. A value reaches a second thread only by a move or a reference. A move needs Send. A shared reference needs &T: Send, that is T: Sync.
  2. A &mut T is unique, by the borrow rules. So two threads can never both hold one.
  3. So a write through a shared reference needs interior mutability. Among such types, only the synchronised ones are Sync: atomics, Mutex, RwLock.
  4. So every shared write is atomic or under a lock. No data race is possible.

Add DRF-SC from the last section. If a safe Rust program also uses only locks and SeqCst, every run is sequentially consistent. The store buffering test was safe Rust, but it used Relaxed, so it showed a weak result without a data race. Rust does not stop race conditions or deadlocks. Those are logic bugs, and the next sections deal with them.

Writing unsafe impl Send for MyType {} to silence the compiler. You now promise that the type is safe across threads. If it holds an Rc or a raw pointer to shared data, the promise is false, and the data races come back.

Mutexes and lock ordering

Eight threads count events into one total. Three designs: every thread takes one shared lock, every thread adds to one shared atomic, or every thread counts privately and the totals are added at the end.

// 8 threads count 8 million events: one lock, one atomic, or a counter each.
use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering::Relaxed};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

const THREADS: u64 = 8;
const EACH: u64 = 1_000_000;

fn timed(name: &str, f: impl Fn() -> u64) {
    let t = Instant::now();
    let total = f();
    println!("{name:<16} total {total}  in {:>4} ms", t.elapsed().as_millis());
}

fn main() {
    timed("one Mutex", || {
        let m = Mutex::new(0u64);
        thread::scope(|s| for _ in 0..THREADS {
            s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..EACH { *m.lock().unwrap() += 1; });   // every add takes the lock
        });
        m.into_inner().unwrap()
    });
    timed("one AtomicU64", || {
        let a = AtomicU64::new(0);
        thread::scope(|s| for _ in 0..THREADS {
            s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..EACH { a.fetch_add(1, Relaxed); });    // one shared cache line
        });
        a.into_inner()
    });
    timed("counter each", || {
        thread::scope(|s| {
            let hs: Vec<_> = (0..THREADS).map(|_| s.spawn(|| {
                let mut local = 0u64;                                     // private: no sharing
                for _ in 0..EACH { local = std::hint::black_box(local + 1); }
                local
            })).collect();
            hs.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum()               // combine once at the end
        })
    });
}
one Mutex        total 8000000  in  151 ms
one AtomicU64    total 8000000  in   72 ms
counter each     total 8000000  in    2 ms
# 4 threads count 800,000 events: one shared lock, or a counter each.
import threading, time

THREADS, EACH = 4, 200_000

def timed(name, f):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    total = f()
    print(f"{name:<14} total {total}  in {round((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000):>4} ms")

def run(target):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=target, args=(i,)) for i in range(THREADS)]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()

def one_lock():
    lock, box = threading.Lock(), [0]
    def work(_):
        for _ in range(EACH):
            with lock:                       # every add takes the lock
                box[0] += 1
    run(work)
    return box[0]

def counter_each():
    results = [0] * THREADS
    def work(i):
        local = 0                            # private: no sharing
        for _ in range(EACH):
            local += 1
        results[i] = local
    run(work)
    return sum(results)                      # combine once at the end

timed("one Lock", one_lock)
timed("counter each", counter_each)
one Lock       total 800000  in   74 ms
counter each   total 800000  in   13 ms

A mutex lets one thread at a time into a critical section. All three designs give the right total. But in this Rust run, the shared designs were 36 to 75 times slower than private counters. In Python, the lock made the job about 6 times slower. The times are noisy. In five Rust runs the mutex took 138 to 186 ms, and the atomic took 72 to 265 ms. So an atomic is not always faster than a lock. The big win is less sharing, not a cleverer lock.

  • Contention. One big lock is simple, but threads wait in line for it. Many small locks run in parallel, but they bring ordering bugs. Start coarse, measure, then split.
  • Sharding. Split one hot value into many parts, one per thread or per key range, and combine them when you read. The "counter each" design is the extreme case.
  • Readers and writers. An RwLock lets many readers in at once, or one writer. It helps only when reads are long and writes are rare.

A free mutex costs very little. On Linux, Rust's Mutex is built on the futex. Taking a free lock is one atomic instruction, with no system call. Only a thread that must wait asks the kernel to sleep.

Lock ordering

With more than one lock comes deadlock. Thread 1 locks account A and then wants B. Thread 2 locks B and then wants A. A demo of exactly this, and the four Coffman conditions, are in Operating systems: processes and scheduling. Here is the theory of the most common fix.

Give every lock a rank. If every thread takes locks only in increasing rank, no set of threads can deadlock on these locks.

Proof

Suppose threads T_1, \dots, T_n deadlock. Then there is a cycle: T_i holds lock L_i and waits for L_{i+1}, and T_n waits for L_1. A thread asks only for locks above all locks it holds, so \text{rank}(L_i) \lt \text{rank}(L_{i+1}). Around the cycle, \text{rank}(L_1) \lt \text{rank}(L_2) \lt \dots \lt \text{rank}(L_n) \lt \text{rank}(L_1). A number cannot be less than itself. So no cycle exists, and the circular wait condition never holds.

In practice, rank locks by account id, by memory address, or by layers of the program. Linux checks its own lock order at run time with a tool called lockdep.

Priority inversion is another lock problem. In 1997 the Mars Pathfinder lander kept resetting. A low-priority task held a lock that a high-priority task needed, and medium tasks kept the low one from running. Engineers fixed it from Earth by turning on priority inheritance for that lock.

Holding a lock during slow work, such as a disk read, a network call or an await. Every other thread then waits for the slow work too, and the lock becomes the bottleneck. In async Rust, a std::sync::MutexGuard held across an await can even stall the runtime. Copy the data out, release the lock, then do the slow part.

Atomics and compare-and-swap

Eight threads sell tickets. At most one million may be sold. The first version checks the count, then adds one. The second uses compare-and-swap.

// Sell at most a million tickets to 8 threads. Check-then-act against a CAS loop.
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering::*};
use std::thread;

const LIMIT: u32 = 1_000_000;

fn naive(sold: &AtomicU32) -> bool {
    if sold.load(SeqCst) < LIMIT {               // check ...
        sold.fetch_add(1, SeqCst);               // ... then act: another thread can come between
        return true;
    }
    false
}

fn with_cas(sold: &AtomicU32, retries: &AtomicU32) -> bool {
    let mut cur = sold.load(Relaxed);
    loop {
        if cur >= LIMIT { return false; }        // sold out
        match sold.compare_exchange_weak(cur, cur + 1, AcqRel, Relaxed) {
            Ok(_) => return true,                // nobody changed it: we won
            Err(now) => { cur = now; retries.fetch_add(1, Relaxed); }  // retry with the new value
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    for use_cas in [false, true] {
        let (sold, retries) = (AtomicU32::new(0), AtomicU32::new(0));
        thread::scope(|s| {
            for _ in 0..8 {
                s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..200_000 {
                    if use_cas { with_cas(&sold, &retries); } else { naive(&sold); }
                });
            }
        });
        let name = if use_cas { "CAS loop" } else { "check-then-act" };
        println!("{name:<15} sold {} (limit {LIMIT}), retries {}", sold.load(SeqCst), retries.load(SeqCst));
    }
}
check-then-act  sold 1000005 (limit 1000000), retries 0
CAS loop        sold 1000000 (limit 1000000), retries 2755894
# Sell at most 1000 tickets to 8 threads. Check-then-act against a CAS loop.
import threading, time

LIMIT = 1000

class AtomicInt:                         # Python has no CAS: a lock stands in
    def __init__(self):                  # for the single CPU instruction
        self.value, self._lock = 0, threading.Lock()
    def compare_exchange(self, expected, new):
        with self._lock:
            if self.value == expected:
                self.value = new
                return True, expected
            return False, self.value     # failed: report the real value

def naive(sold):
    if sold.value < LIMIT:               # check ...
        time.sleep(0)                    # (let another thread in, as real CPUs do)
        sold.value += 1                  # ... then act

def with_cas(sold):
    cur = sold.value
    while cur < LIMIT:
        ok, cur = sold.compare_exchange(cur, cur + 1)   # on failure, cur is the new value
        if ok:
            return True                  # nobody changed it: we won
    return False                         # sold out

for use_cas in (False, True):
    sold = AtomicInt()
    work = (lambda: [with_cas(sold) for _ in range(300)]) if use_cas \
        else (lambda: [naive(sold) for _ in range(300)])
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(8)]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
    print(f"{'CAS loop' if use_cas else 'check-then-act':<15} sold {sold.value} (limit {LIMIT})")
check-then-act  sold 1007 (limit 1000)
CAS loop        sold 1000 (limit 1000)

Check-then-act oversold. Each step was atomic, but another thread came between the check and the add. An atomic operation is one indivisible step. A read-modify-write operation, such as fetch_add, reads and writes as one step. The most powerful one is compare-and-swap (CAS):

CAS(location, expected, new):        // all one atomic step
    if *location == expected:
        *location = new
        return success
    return failure, *location        // tell the caller the real value

The pattern is the CAS loop. Read the value. Compute the new value from it. Try a CAS. If it fails, someone changed the value, so start again with the value you got back. The loop never holds a lock. In the Rust run, threads retried about 2.8 million times, but the limit held. Other runs gave between 0.9 and 2.8 million retries.

  • x86 has one instruction, lock cmpxchg.
  • ARM first had a pair: LL/SC (ldxr and stxr). The store fails if anyone wrote the location since the load. ARMv8.1 added a real cas instruction. The program above, built for the M2 Pro, uses cas and ldadd, as otool shows.
  • compare_exchange_weak may fail even when the value matches. This is a spurious failure, allowed for LL/SC machines. Inside a loop it costs nothing, so use the weak form there.

Atomics are not free. To write a location, a core must own its cache line. Under contention, the line jumps between cores, and every retry costs more. Two atomics that share one cache line slow each other down, even when they are different variables. This is false sharing. Cache lines and coherence are in Computer architecture.

Building one decision from two atomic steps: if x.load() < LIMIT { x.fetch_add(1) }. Each step is atomic. The pair is not. Use one CAS loop, or one lock around both steps. This bug is a race condition without any data race, so Rust cannot catch it.

Lock-free structures and the ABA problem

What if a thread holding a lock is paused, for example by a page fault? All other threads wait. Non-blocking structures avoid this. They promise progress at different strengths:

  • Obstruction-free: a thread finishes if it runs alone for a while.
  • Lock-free: the system as a whole always makes progress. One thread may starve, but some thread finishes.
  • Wait-free: every thread finishes in a bounded number of its own steps.

The classic lock-free structure is the Treiber stack, from 1986. It is a linked list with one atomic pointer, top.

push(n):  loop { old = top;  n.next = old;  if CAS(top, old, n): return }
pop():    loop { old = top;  next = old.next;  if CAS(top, old, next): return old }

The CAS loop is lock-free. A CAS fails only if another thread's CAS succeeded, so some thread always makes progress. But this pop has a famous bug.

Start

The stack is A, then B, then C. Thread 1 starts pop. It reads old = A and next = B. Then the scheduler pauses it.

Thread 2 pops twice

Thread 2 pops A, then pops B. It now owns B. The stack is just C.

Thread 2 pushes A again

Thread 2 pushes node A back, maybe a reused memory block. The stack is A, then C. top is A again.

Thread 1 wakes up

It runs CAS(top, A, B). top is A, so the CAS succeeds. The stack is now B, then C.

Damage

B is on the stack, but thread 2 owns it and may free it. The value went A, B, A, and the CAS could not see the change. This is the ABA problem.

This program replays the five steps, first with a plain CAS, then with a version tag.

// Replay the ABA problem on a lock-free stack, step by step.
const NIL: usize = usize::MAX;
const NAME: [&str; 3] = ["A", "B", "C"];

fn replay(use_tag: bool) {
    let mut next = [1, 2, NIL];                       // the stack: A -> B -> C
    let mut top = (0usize, 0u32);                     // (node, version tag)
    let cas = |top: &mut (usize, u32), old: (usize, u32), new: (usize, u32)| {
        let same = top.0 == old.0 && (!use_tag || top.1 == old.1);
        if same { *top = new; }
        same
    };

    let mut old = top;                                // thread 1 starts pop(): reads A ...
    let mut new = (next[old.0], old.1 + 1);           // ... and plans top = B. Paused.

    for _ in 0..2 { top = (next[top.0], top.1 + 1); } // thread 2: pop A, pop B
    next[0] = top.0;                                  // thread 2: push A again
    top = (0, top.1 + 1);

    while !cas(&mut top, old, new) {                  // thread 1 wakes up
        old = top;                                    // CAS failed: read again, retry
        new = (next[old.0], old.1 + 1);
    }

    let (mut stack, mut node) = (vec![], top.0);
    while node != NIL { stack.push(NAME[node]); node = next[node]; }
    println!("tag={use_tag:<5} stack after both pops: {stack:?}  (correct: [\"C\"])");
}

fn main() {
    replay(false);
    replay(true);
}
# Replay the ABA problem on a lock-free stack, step by step.
def replay(use_tag):
    nxt = {"A": "B", "B": "C", "C": None}         # the stack: A -> B -> C
    top = ["A", 0]                                # [node, version tag]

    def cas(expected, new):
        same = top[0] == expected[0] and (not use_tag or top[1] == expected[1])
        if same:
            top[:] = new
        return same

    old = list(top)                               # thread 1 starts pop(): reads A ...
    new = [nxt[old[0]], old[1] + 1]               # ... and plans to set top = B. Paused.

    for _ in range(2):                            # thread 2: pop A, pop B
        top[:] = [nxt[top[0]], top[1] + 1]
    nxt["A"] = top[0]                             # thread 2: push A again
    top[:] = ["A", top[1] + 1]

    while not cas(old, new):                      # thread 1 wakes up
        old = list(top)                           # CAS failed: read again, retry
        new = [nxt[old[0]], old[1] + 1]

    stack, node = [], top[0]
    while node:
        stack.append(node)
        node = nxt[node]
    print(f"tag={use_tag!s:<5} stack after both pops: {stack}  (correct: ['C'])")

replay(False)
replay(True)
tag=false stack after both pops: ["B", "C"]  (correct: ["C"])
tag=true  stack after both pops: ["C"]  (correct: ["C"])

The Python output has the same stacks. The ABA problem hits CAS on pointers whenever memory is reused. The fixes:

  • Version tag. Store a counter next to the pointer and add 1 on every change. The CAS compares both. This needs a double-width CAS, or spare bits in the pointer.
  • LL/SC. The store fails after any write, even one that restores the old value.
  • Safe memory reclamation. Never reuse a node while a thread may still read it. Hazard pointers (Michael, 2004) and epoch-based reclamation do this. Rust's crossbeam-epoch crate uses epochs.
  • Garbage collection. In Java, a node is not reused while anyone holds it. So the Michael-Scott lock-free queue from 1996 is simpler there. Java's ConcurrentLinkedQueue is based on it.

Writing your own lock-free structure for production. They are very hard to prove, and they are not always faster than a good mutex. Under heavy contention, CAS retries waste work. Use tested libraries such as crossbeam or java.util.concurrent, and measure.

Linearisability and the power of compare-and-swap

How do we say a concurrent stack is correct? Its operations overlap in time. Look at a history of one register that starts at 0. Each bar is one operation, from its call to its return.

The program below tries every order of the operations. It checks two rules. Linearisable: keep real-time order, so an operation that ended before another began comes first. Sequentially consistent: keep only each thread's own order.

// Brute-force check of a register history: linearisable? sequentially consistent?
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Op { thread: u8, write: bool, value: i32, start: u32, end: u32 }

const fn op(thread: u8, write: bool, value: i32, start: u32, end: u32) -> Op {
    Op { thread, write, value, start, end }
}

// Try to place the ops one by one. An op may go next only if every op that
// must come before it is already placed, and a read must see the current value.
fn search(h: &[Op], placed: &mut Vec<bool>, value: i32, rt: bool) -> bool {
    if placed.iter().all(|&p| p) { return true; }
    for i in 0..h.len() {
        if placed[i] { continue; }
        let blocked = (0..h.len()).any(|j| !placed[j] && j != i && h[j].end < h[i].start
                                            && (rt || h[j].thread == h[i].thread));
        if blocked || (!h[i].write && h[i].value != value) { continue; }
        placed[i] = true;
        let next = if h[i].write { h[i].value } else { value };
        if search(h, placed, next, rt) { return true; }
        placed[i] = false;                       // undo and try another op
    }
    false
}

fn check(h: &[Op], rt: bool) -> bool { search(h, &mut vec![false; h.len()], 0, rt) }

fn main() {
    let h1 = [op(1, true, 1, 0, 4), op(2, false, 0, 1, 2), op(2, false, 1, 3, 5)];
    let h2 = [op(1, true, 1, 0, 2), op(2, false, 1, 3, 4), op(3, false, 0, 5, 6)];
    for (name, h) in [("H1", &h1), ("H2", &h2)] {
        println!("{name}: linearisable {}, sequentially consistent {}", check(h, true), check(h, false));
    }
}
# Brute-force check of a register history: linearisable? sequentially consistent?
from itertools import permutations

# (thread, kind, value, start time, end time); the register starts at 0
H1 = [("T1", "w", 1, 0, 4), ("T2", "r", 0, 1, 2), ("T2", "r", 1, 3, 5)]
H2 = [("T1", "w", 1, 0, 2), ("T2", "r", 1, 3, 4), ("T3", "r", 0, 5, 6)]

def legal(order):                        # does this order obey a register?
    value = 0
    for _, kind, v, _, _ in order:
        if kind == "w":
            value = v
        elif v != value:
            return False
    return True

def respects(order, before):             # keeps every "a must come before b"?
    pos = {op: i for i, op in enumerate(order)}
    return all(pos[a] < pos[b] for a in order for b in order if before(a, b))

real_time = lambda a, b: a[4] < b[3]                     # a ended before b started
same_thread = lambda a, b: a[0] == b[0] and a[4] < b[3]  # program order only

def check(history, before):
    return any(legal(p) and respects(p, before) for p in permutations(history))

for name, h in (("H1", H1), ("H2", H2)):
    print(f"{name}: linearisable {check(h, real_time)}, "
          f"sequentially consistent {check(h, same_thread)}")
H1: linearisable true, sequentially consistent true
H2: linearisable false, sequentially consistent true

In H1, the read of 0 overlaps the write, so it may take effect before it. H2 is sequentially consistent, because the order "read 0, write 1, read 1" keeps each thread's order. But it breaks real time, so it is not linearisable.

A history lists the calls and returns of operations. Herlihy and Wing gave the definition in 1990. A history is linearisable if each operation seems to take effect at one instant between its call and its return. Also, the results must match a correct sequential object. That instant is the linearisation point. In the Treiber stack, it is the successful CAS.

ConditionAboutKeeps real time?Typical place
Sequential consistencysingle operationsno, only program orderhardware memory models
Linearisabilitysingle operations on objectsyesconcurrent objects, registers in distributed stores
Serialisabilitytransactions of many operationsnodatabases
Strict serialisabilitytransactionsyesSpanner-style databases

A history H is linearisable if and only if, for every object x, the sub-history H|x of the operations on x is linearisable.

Proof idea

"Only if" is easy. Take a linearisation of H and keep only the operations on x. For "if", take one linearisation for each object. Join all of them with the real-time order of H. Each object's order already respects real time. So a cycle in the joined order would need operations that each end before the next one starts, all the way round. Time cannot run in a circle. So the joined order has no cycle, and any total order that extends it is a linearisation of H.

In simple words: if every object is linearisable on its own, the whole program is. You can build and test each object alone, then combine them freely. This is why libraries can promise "this map is linearisable", and it stays true inside your program.

Expert: sequential consistency is not local

Take two FIFO queues, p and q. Thread A runs p.enq(x), q.enq(x), p.deq() → y. Thread B runs q.enq(y), p.enq(y), q.deq() → x. Each queue alone is sequentially consistent. But together, A's dequeue needs p.enq(y) before p.enq(x), and B's needs q.enq(x) before q.enq(y). With the program orders this makes a cycle: p.enq(y), p.enq(x), q.enq(x), q.enq(y), p.enq(y). So the whole history is not sequentially consistent. Correct parts do not give a correct whole.

Checking linearisability is NP-complete in general, as Gibbons and Korach showed in 1997. Our brute-force checker is exponential. Real tools, such as Jepsen's Knossos and the Porcupine checker, prune the search well. They test databases this way. Consistency models for distributed systems continue in Distributed systems.

How strong is compare-and-swap?

In the consensus problem, each of n threads proposes a value. All must decide the same value, and it must be one of the proposals. Here is consensus for any number of threads with one CAS:

// Wait-free consensus for any number of threads with one CAS.
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering::SeqCst};
use std::sync::Barrier;
use std::thread;

const EMPTY: usize = usize::MAX;

fn decide(cell: &AtomicUsize, proposal: usize) -> usize {
    match cell.compare_exchange(EMPTY, proposal, SeqCst, SeqCst) {
        Ok(_) => proposal,                       // I was first: my value wins
        Err(winner) => winner,                   // someone was first: take theirs
    }
}

fn main() {
    for run in 1..=3 {
        let (cell, start) = (AtomicUsize::new(EMPTY), Barrier::new(8));
        let votes: Vec<usize> = thread::scope(|s| {
            let hs: Vec<_> = (0..8).map(|id| {
                let (c, b) = (&cell, &start);
                s.spawn(move || { b.wait(); decide(c, id * 100) })   // all start together
            }).collect();
            hs.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).collect()
        });
        println!("run {run}: decisions {votes:?}");
    }
}
run 1: decisions [700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700]
run 2: decisions [200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200]
run 3: decisions [300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300]
# Wait-free consensus for any number of threads with one CAS.
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

class CasCell:                           # a lock stands in for the CAS instruction
    def __init__(self):
        self.value, self._lock = None, threading.Lock()
    def compare_exchange(self, expected, new):
        with self._lock:
            old = self.value
            if old == expected:
                self.value = new
            return old

def decide(cell, start, proposal):
    start.wait()                         # all threads start together
    old = cell.compare_exchange(None, proposal)
    return proposal if old is None else old   # first writer wins, others adopt it

for run in range(1, 4):
    cell, start = CasCell(), threading.Barrier(8)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as pool:
        votes = list(pool.map(lambda i: decide(cell, start, i * 100), range(8)))
    print(f"run {run}: decisions {votes}")
run 1: decisions [700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700]
run 2: decisions [700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700]
run 3: decisions [700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700, 700]

The winner changes from run to run, but all threads always agree. Each thread takes two steps, so it is wait-free.

The consensus number of an object type is the largest n such that objects of this type, plus read-write registers, solve wait-free consensus for n threads. It can be infinite.

ObjectConsensus number
read-write registers (plain loads and stores)1
test-and-set, swap, fetch-and-add, queue, stack2
compare-and-swap, LL/SCinfinite

(Herlihy, 1991.) CAS solves wait-free consensus for any number of threads. With consensus objects and registers, every object with a sequential specification has a wait-free, linearisable implementation. So CAS is universal.

Proof idea: the universal construction

The program above gives consensus. Now build any object, say a queue. Keep a shared log of operations as a list of cells. Each cell has its own consensus object that decides which operation goes in that cell. To run an operation, a thread first announces it in its slot of an array. Then it helps fill the cells: for cell k, every thread proposes the pending operation of thread k \bmod n if there is one, else its own.

Because of this helping, every announced operation lands in the log within n cells. So each thread finishes in a bounded number of steps, which is wait-free. To get its result, a thread replays the log on a private copy of the sequential queue. The cell where an operation lands is its linearisation point.

In simple words: plain loads and stores cannot even let two threads agree without waiting. fetch_add works for two threads but not for three. CAS works for any number, and so it can build anything. That is why every modern CPU offers CAS or LL/SC. The universal construction is slow, so real structures are designed by hand. The same impossibility appears for message passing as the FLP result in Distributed systems.

Thinking that linearisable operations make your sequence of operations atomic. With a linearisable map, if !map.contains(k) { map.insert(k, v) } is still a race. Each call is atomic, the pair is not. Use one operation that does both, like entry in Rust or putIfAbsent in Java.

Actors and message passing

Another way to avoid shared-memory bugs is to share nothing. Here one thread owns a bank balance. Other threads may only send it messages.

// An actor owns the balance. Others can only send it messages.
use std::sync::mpsc::{sync_channel, Sender, channel};
use std::thread;

enum Msg {
    Deposit(u64),
    Withdraw(u64, Sender<bool>),                 // the reply goes back on its own channel
    Balance(Sender<u64>),
}

fn main() {
    let (tx, rx) = sync_channel::<Msg>(16);      // bounded mailbox: senders wait when full
    let actor = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut balance = 0u64;                  // private state: no lock needed
        for msg in rx {                          // one message at a time
            match msg {
                Msg::Deposit(n) => balance += n,
                Msg::Withdraw(n, reply) => {
                    let ok = n <= balance;
                    if ok { balance -= n; }
                    reply.send(ok).unwrap();
                }
                Msg::Balance(reply) => reply.send(balance).unwrap(),
            }
        }
    });
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..4 {
            let tx = tx.clone();
            s.spawn(move || for _ in 0..1000 { tx.send(Msg::Deposit(1)).unwrap(); });
        }
    });
    let (rtx, rrx) = channel();
    tx.send(Msg::Withdraw(5000, rtx.clone())).unwrap();
    tx.send(Msg::Withdraw(1500, rtx)).unwrap();
    println!("withdraw 5000: {}, withdraw 1500: {}", rrx.recv().unwrap(), rrx.recv().unwrap());
    let (btx, brx) = channel();
    tx.send(Msg::Balance(btx)).unwrap();
    println!("balance: {}", brx.recv().unwrap());
    drop(tx);                                    // close the mailbox: the actor's loop ends
    actor.join().unwrap();
}
# An actor owns the balance. Others can only send it messages.
import queue, threading

def account_actor(mailbox):
    balance = 0                               # private state: no lock needed
    while (msg := mailbox.get()) is not None: # one message at a time; None = stop
        kind, amount, reply = msg
        if kind == "deposit":
            balance += amount
        elif kind == "withdraw":
            ok = amount <= balance
            if ok:
                balance -= amount
            reply.put(ok)
        elif kind == "balance":
            reply.put(balance)

mailbox = queue.Queue(maxsize=16)             # bounded: senders wait when it is full
actor = threading.Thread(target=account_actor, args=(mailbox,))
actor.start()

def client():
    for _ in range(1000):
        mailbox.put(("deposit", 1, None))

clients = [threading.Thread(target=client) for _ in range(4)]
for c in clients: c.start()
for c in clients: c.join()

reply = queue.Queue()
mailbox.put(("withdraw", 5000, reply))
mailbox.put(("withdraw", 1500, reply))
print(f"withdraw 5000: {reply.get()}, withdraw 1500: {reply.get()}")
mailbox.put(("balance", 0, reply))
print("balance:", reply.get())
mailbox.put(None)                             # close the mailbox: the actor stops
actor.join()
withdraw 5000: false, withdraw 1500: true
balance: 2500

Four clients deposited 4000 in total, with no lock. Python prints the same, with False and True. This is the actor model of Hewitt, Bishop and Steiger from 1973. An actor has private state and a mailbox. It handles one message at a time. For each message it may send messages, create new actors, and choose how to handle the next message. No two actors share memory, so there are no data races.

  • Erlang and Elixir run millions of tiny actor processes. A supervisor restarts an actor that crashes. This style is called "let it crash".
  • Akka (on the JVM) and Orleans (on .NET) bring actors to other platforms.
  • CSP, from Hoare in 1978, is a close cousin. Processes talk through named channels, not addresses. Go's goroutines and channels and Rust's channels follow it.

Actors also map well onto AI agents that talk by messages. See Orchestrators and coordinators for agents. Actors are not magic. They have their own problems:

  • Two actors can deadlock. A waits for a reply from B while B waits for a reply from A.
  • A mailbox with no limit can grow until memory runs out. A bounded mailbox, like sync_channel(16) above, makes fast senders wait. This is back-pressure.
  • Order is kept only between one sender and one receiver. Messages from two senders can arrive in any order.
  • One busy actor is a single-threaded bottleneck. Split its state across many actors to scale.

Making a request-reply cycle between actors. If actor A handles a message by asking B and waiting, and B does the same back to A, both stop. Send replies without waiting, or make the call graph a tree with no cycle.

Data parallelism and measuring speed-up

Counting primes below six million is the same small job on many numbers. Split the numbers into blocks and give the blocks to p workers. How much faster is it?

// Count primes below 6 million with 1 to 10 threads. Measure the speed-up.
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

fn is_prime(n: u64) -> bool {
    if n < 2 { return false; }
    let mut d = 2;
    while d * d <= n { if n % d == 0 { return false; } d += 1; }
    true
}

fn count(limit: u64, threads: u64) -> usize {
    thread::scope(|s| {
        let hs: Vec<_> = (0..threads).map(|t| s.spawn(move || {
            // blocks of 1000 numbers, dealt out like cards: thread t takes t, t+T, ...
            (0..limit / 1000).filter(|b| b % threads == t)
                .map(|b| (b * 1000..(b + 1) * 1000).filter(|&n| is_prime(n)).count()).sum::<usize>()
        })).collect();
        hs.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum()
    })
}

fn main() {
    let limit = 6_000_000;
    let mut t1 = 0.0;
    for p in [1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10] {
        let mut times: Vec<f64> = (0..5).map(|_| {
            let t = Instant::now();
            let n = count(limit, p);
            assert_eq!(n, 412_849);              // the right answer
            t.elapsed().as_secs_f64()
        }).collect();
        times.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap());
        let med = times[2];                      // median of 5 runs
        if p == 1 { t1 = med; }
        let s = t1 / med;
        println!("p={p:>2}: {:.3} s  speed-up {s:.2}  efficiency {:.0}%", med, 100.0 * s / p as f64);
    }
}
p= 1: 0.737 s  speed-up 1.00  efficiency 100%
p= 2: 0.387 s  speed-up 1.91  efficiency 95%
p= 4: 0.192 s  speed-up 3.84  efficiency 96%
p= 6: 0.146 s  speed-up 5.04  efficiency 84%
p= 8: 0.145 s  speed-up 5.07  efficiency 63%
p=10: 0.132 s  speed-up 5.59  efficiency 56%
# Count primes below 600,000 with 1 to 10 processes. Measure the speed-up.
import statistics, time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 1
    return True

def count_block(b):                       # one block of 1000 numbers
    return sum(is_prime(n) for n in range(b * 1000, (b + 1) * 1000))

def count(limit, workers):
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(workers) as pool:   # processes: each has its own GIL
        return sum(pool.map(count_block, range(limit // 1000), chunksize=8))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t1 = None
    for p in (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10):
        times = []
        for _ in range(3):
            t = time.perf_counter()
            assert count(600_000, p) == 49_098       # the right answer
            times.append(time.perf_counter() - t)
        med = statistics.median(times)
        t1 = t1 or med
        print(f"p={p:>2}: {med:.3f} s  speed-up {t1 / med:.2f}  efficiency {100 * t1 / med / p:.0f}%")
p= 1: 1.155 s  speed-up 1.00  efficiency 100%
p= 2: 0.615 s  speed-up 1.88  efficiency 94%
p= 4: 0.371 s  speed-up 3.11  efficiency 78%
p= 6: 0.323 s  speed-up 3.58  efficiency 60%
p= 8: 0.366 s  speed-up 3.15  efficiency 39%
p=10: 0.286 s  speed-up 4.03  efficiency 40%

Data parallelism applies one operation to many items. It is the easiest parallelism, because the items do not talk to each other. The common shapes are map and reduce, and fork-join. Libraries such as Rayon in Rust use work stealing, an idea from the Cilk language. Each worker keeps a queue of tasks, and an idle worker steals from the far end of another worker's queue. SIMD and GPUs apply data parallelism inside the chip, see Computer architecture.

Now measure. The speed-up on p workers is S(p) = T_1 / T_p. The efficiency is E(p) = S(p) / p. Amdahl's law says that a serial fraction 1 - f caps the speed-up at 1 / (1 - f), no matter how many workers you add. Gustafson's law says that bigger problems often have a bigger parallel part. Both are in Computer architecture. To find the serial fraction from a measurement, use this formula:

(Karp and Flatt, 1990.) Measure the speed-up S on p \gt 1 workers. The experimentally determined serial fraction is

e = \frac{1/S - 1/p}{1 - 1/p} .

If the program follows Amdahl's law exactly, e equals the serial fraction 1 - f for every p.

Put in the Rust numbers. At p = 4, S = 3.84: e = (0.260 - 0.250) / 0.75 \approx 0.014. At p = 6, e \approx 0.038. At p = 10, S = 5.59: e = (0.179 - 0.100) / 0.9 \approx 0.088. The value grows with p. So the problem is not a fixed serial part. Something grows with p. Here there are two causes. The four extra cores are slower efficiency cores, and other programs were busy on the machine.

The Python curve has another cause. Starting a process pool is serial work that comes before any counting, so it acts like a serial part. Threads are no help in Python with the GIL. With 4 threads the same job took 1.12 s, against 1.11 s on one thread. The theory of work and span gives the limits: T_p \ge \max(T_1 / p, T_\infty). Brent's bound says that a greedy scheduler gets close to it. See Randomised, approximate, streaming and string algorithms.

  1. Check the answer in every run. The programs above assert 412,849 and 49,098 primes.
  2. Compare with the best sequential program, not the parallel program on one worker.
  3. Warm up, repeat, and report the median. Note the spread.
  4. Use a quiet machine, and say which one: core count, core types, and load.
  5. Say whether you keep the problem size fixed (strong scaling) or grow it with p (weak scaling).
  6. Use inputs big enough that start-up costs do not dominate.

Reporting "speed-up 8" against a slow baseline. If the parallel version on one worker is twice as slow as a plain loop, its speed-up looks twice as good as it is. Another trap is a tiny input. Then thread start-up dominates, and more workers make the program slower.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for concurrency and parallelism
PatternPurposeModelNote
Overlap the waitingMany slow I/O calls at oncefour 100 ms calls in 102 ms with asyncio.gatherA blocking call stops the whole event loop.
