Practice

One core runs a web server that serves 1,000 connections by switching between them. What is this?

  • Parallelism, but not concurrency
  • Concurrency, but not parallelism
  • Neither

Many jobs are in progress at once, which is concurrency. Only one runs at any instant, so there is no parallelism.

Which of these is a data race in Rust's memory model?

  • Two threads call fetch_add on the same AtomicU64.
  • One thread writes a plain variable through a raw pointer while another reads it, with no lock or atomic between them.
  • Two threads read the same plain variable at the same time.

A data race needs a write, a plain non-atomic access and no ordering. Atomic operations never race. Two reads never race.

Why is Rc<T> not Send?

  • Because it lives on the heap.
  • Because two threads could change its owner count at once without atomics.
  • Because T might be large.

Clone and drop change the count with plain reads and writes. Arc uses atomic operations for the count, so it can be Send.

A CAS on a pointer succeeds, but the structure is now broken. The pointer had changed and then changed back. What is this called?

  • Priority inversion
  • False sharing
  • The ABA problem

CAS compares values only. A, then B, then A again looks unchanged. A version tag or safe memory reclamation fixes it.

The consensus number of fetch-and-add is ?.

A program has speed-up 6 on 8 workers. Its efficiency is ?.

In Rust, T is Sync exactly when &T is ?.

  1. Explain why the store buffering test can show "both read 0" with Relaxed, but never with SeqCst.
    Answer

    With Relaxed, each core may keep its write in its store buffer and read the other variable first. Both reads then see the old 0. With SeqCst, all four operations fall into one total order that keeps program order. In that order one of the writes is first, and the other thread's later read must see it. On ARM the compiler adds the needed instructions to make this true.

  2. Three threads take locks: T1 takes A then B, T2 takes B then C, T3 takes C then A. Can they deadlock? Give a fix.
    Answer

    Yes. T1 holds A and waits for B, T2 holds B and waits for C, T3 holds C and waits for A. That is a cycle. Fix: rank the locks A < B < C and always lock in rank order. T3 must then take A before C. A cycle is now impossible by the lock-order theorem.

  3. Is this history of a register (start value 0) linearisable? T1: write(1) from time 0 to 10. T2: read gives 1, from 2 to 3. T3: read gives 0, from 4 to 5.
    Answer

    No. T2's read ended at 3 before T3's read started at 4, so T2's read comes first. T2 saw 1, so the write must be before T2's read. Then T3's read comes after the write and must see 1, not 0. It is sequentially consistent, though. Use the order: T3 reads 0, write 1, T2 reads 1.

  4. Write the pop of a Treiber stack in pseudocode and mark its linearisation point. Why is it lock-free but not wait-free?
    Answer

    loop { old = top; if old == null: return empty; next = old.next; if CAS(top, old, next): return old }. The linearisation point is the successful CAS. An empty pop linearises at the read of top. A CAS fails only when another thread's CAS succeeded, so the system always makes progress: lock-free. But one unlucky thread can lose every race forever, so it has no bound on its own steps: not wait-free.

  5. Expert. A program shows speed-up 3.0 on 4 workers and 4.0 on 8 workers. Compute the Karp-Flatt metric for both. What do you conclude?
    Answer

    For p = 4: e = (1/3 - 1/4) / (3/4) = 0.0833 / 0.75 \approx 0.111. For p = 8: e = (0.25 - 0.125) / 0.875 \approx 0.143. The value grows with p. So there is more than a fixed serial part: overhead grows with the number of workers. Look for lock contention, false sharing, load imbalance or communication. A fixed serial part would give a constant e.

  6. Expert. Explain why plain loads and stores cannot solve wait-free consensus for two threads, but CAS can.
    Answer

    Idea of the proof: look at a state where the decision is still open, and both next steps would fix it. Each thread is about to read or write a register. Try every case. A read changes nothing the other thread can see. Writes to different registers can be done in either order with the same result. A write to the same register overwrites the other one. In every case, the thread that moves second cannot tell which order happened. So it cannot know the decision without waiting. With CAS, the first CAS on an empty cell wins, and the second thread reads the winner from its own failed CAS. So CAS decides in one step.

Key takeaways

  • Concurrency is many jobs in progress. Parallelism is many jobs running at the same instant. Threads are preemptive and scheduled by the kernel. Async tasks are cooperative and scheduled by a runtime.
  • A data race is undefined behaviour. Hardware and compilers reorder memory steps, so languages define a memory model. Data-race-free programs that use locks and SeqCst behave as simple interleavings.
  • Rust's Send and Sync, with the borrow rules, make data races in safe code a compile error. Race conditions and deadlocks remain your job.
  • Taking locks in one global order makes deadlock impossible, because it breaks the circular wait.
  • Compare-and-swap enables lock-free loops. Watch for check-then-act bugs, contention, false sharing and the ABA problem.
  • Linearisability means each operation seems to happen at one instant inside its call. It is local, so correct objects compose.
  • CAS has an infinite consensus number and can build any wait-free object. Registers alone cannot even give two threads agreement.
  • Actors share nothing and talk by messages. Data parallelism splits the data. Measure speed-up with care, and use the Karp-Flatt metric to find what grows with p.

Sources

  • Herlihy and Wing: Linearizability, a correctness condition for concurrent objects (1990). The definition and the locality theorem.
  • Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization (1991). Consensus numbers, the hierarchy and the universal construction.
  • Rust standard library: std::sync::atomic. Rust follows the C++20 memory model, and data races are undefined behaviour.
  • The Rustonomicon: Send and Sync. The definitions, the rule that T is Sync when &T is Send, and which types are neither.
  • Mara Bos: Rust Atomics and Locks. A free book on memory ordering, x86 and ARM hardware, and building locks.
  • What's new in Python 3.14. The officially supported free-threaded build and its single-thread cost.

Compilers

A compiler turns a program that people can read into code that a machine can run. It works like a factory line. Each station does one small job and passes its result on. This chapter builds a tiny compiler in Rust and Python, station by station, and shows how LLVM, V8 and CPython do the same jobs at full size.

  • Name the phases of a compiler and say what each phase takes in and gives out.
  • Write a lexer and a parser for expressions, and compare LL, LR and Pratt parsing.
  • Check names and types, then lower a tree to three-address code in SSA form.
  • Run classic optimisations and allocate registers by colouring an interference graph.
  • Compare kinds of garbage collection and explain where JIT compilers and LLVM fit.

The compiler pipeline

Take one line of a small program: let b = x * (a + 1);. Follow it through a compiler. Each step below is a separate pass.

  1. Lexer. Characters become words: let, b, =, x, *, (, a, +, 1, ), ;.
  2. Parser. The words become a tree. The sum a + 1 sits under the product.
  3. Checker. Are a and x defined? Do the types fit?
  4. IR builder. The tree becomes simple steps: t2 = t1 + 1, then t3 = x * t2.
  5. Optimiser. t1 is the constant 6. So t2 is 7, and the line becomes t3 = x * 7.
  6. Code generator. It picks machine instructions and registers: r2 = r0 * 7.

A compiler is this chain of passes. The passes share data in an intermediate representation (IR). Compiler writers group the passes into three parts.

  • The front end reads the source text and checks it.
  • The middle end improves the IR.
  • The back end writes code for one kind of processor.

Why split the work like this? Say you have 5 languages and 4 chips. Without a shared IR you need 5 \times 4 = 20 compilers. With one shared IR you need 5 + 4 = 9 parts. This is the idea of LLVM. Clang (C and C++), rustc and Swift all produce LLVM IR. LLVM then does the optimising and the code for each chip.

"Compiled language" and "interpreted language" are not exact terms. They describe one implementation, not the language. CPython compiles your source to bytecode and then interprets it. PyPy and CPython's new JIT compile hot code to machine code while it runs.

The Rust and Python code blocks in this chapter form one tiny compiler. Paste the blocks of one language into one file, in order, and it runs. The full output is in the code generation section. The tiny language has numbers, the operators + - * /, brackets, let lines and one input variable x.

Lexing with regular expressions

Look at this text: let letter = 12;. A lexer cuts it into five tokens: LET, NAME(letter), OP(=), NUM(12), OP(;). Why is letter one name and not LET followed by ter? Two simple rules decide this.

  • Longest match. Read as far as the pattern still fits. So letter is one name, x12 is one name, and >= is one token, not > and =. People call this maximal munch.
  • Priority. If two patterns match the same longest text, the earlier rule wins. The text let fits both LET and NAME. LET comes first, so it is a keyword.

Each token kind is a regular expression. Numbers are [0-9]+. Names are [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. By Kleene's theorem, each one is a finite automaton. A lexer generator such as flex joins all of them into one DFA. So the lexer reads each character once, in linear time.

use std::collections::{BTreeSet, HashMap, HashSet}; // used by later blocks

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Tok { Num(i64), Name(String), Let, Op(char), Eof }

// A hand-written lexer. Each branch is one small DFA from the automata chapter.
fn lex(src: &str) -> Result<Vec<Tok>, String> {
    let cs: Vec<char> = src.chars().collect();
    let (mut i, mut out) = (0, Vec::new());
    while i < cs.len() {
        let (c, start) = (cs[i], i);
        if c.is_whitespace() {
            i += 1; // spaces and new lines make no token
        } else if c.is_ascii_digit() {
            while i < cs.len() && cs[i].is_ascii_digit() { i += 1; } // longest match
            let text: String = cs[start..i].iter().collect();
            out.push(Tok::Num(text.parse().map_err(|_| "number too big")?));
        } else if c.is_alphabetic() || c == '_' {
            while i < cs.len() && (cs[i].is_alphanumeric() || cs[i] == '_') { i += 1; }
            let word: String = cs[start..i].iter().collect();
            out.push(if word == "let" { Tok::Let } else { Tok::Name(word) }); // keyword?
        } else if "+-*/()=;".contains(c) {
            out.push(Tok::Op(c));
            i += 1;
        } else {
            return Err(format!("unexpected character {c:?} at {i}"));
        }
    }
    out.push(Tok::Eof);
    Ok(out)
}
import re

# One regular expression per token kind. Python tries them in this order.
SPEC = [("NUM", r"\d+"), ("LET", r"let\b"), ("NAME", r"[A-Za-z_]\w*"),
        ("OP", r"[-+*/()=;]"), ("SKIP", r"\s+"), ("BAD", r".")]
MASTER = re.compile("|".join(f"(?P<{kind}>{rx})" for kind, rx in SPEC))

def lex(src):
    tokens = []
    for m in MASTER.finditer(src):
        kind, text = m.lastgroup, m.group()
        if kind == "SKIP":
            continue                       # spaces and new lines make no token
        if kind == "BAD":
            raise SyntaxError(f"unexpected character {text!r} at {m.start()}")
        tokens.append((kind, int(text) if kind == "NUM" else text))
    tokens.append(("EOF", None))
    return tokens

The Rust lexer is written by hand. Each while loop is a tiny automaton that runs as long as it can. The Python lexer builds one regular expression from a list of rules. Both drop spaces. A real lexer also drops comments and keeps the line and column of each token for error messages.

Python's re tries the alternatives from left to right and takes the first one that matches. It does not look for the longest. Without \b, the rule let would match the start of letter and leave ter. flex works differently: it always takes the longest match first.

Some real lexers need more than a DFA. Python's indentation is one case. The tokenizer keeps a stack of indent widths and makes INDENT and DEDENT tokens. A stack is more than a finite automaton can do. Another case is Vec<Vec<i32>>. Longest match makes >> one token, the shift operator. Rust and C++ parsers split it back into two closing brackets when the grammar needs that.

Parsing: top-down and bottom-up

The parser gets tokens and builds a tree. Here is a grammar for sums and products. The Automata chapter shows its parse tree for 2 + 3 * 4.

E -> E + T | T        a sum of terms
T -> T * F | F        a product of factors
F -> num | ( E )      a number or a bracketed sum

Any grammar can be parsed in cubic time with CYK. A compiler wants linear time. So it uses grammars that a deterministic machine can parse. There are two families.

Top-down (LL). Start at E. Look at the next token and choose a rule. Grow the tree from the root to the leaves. LL(1) means one token of lookahead is enough to choose.

Bottom-up (LR). Read tokens onto a stack. When the top of the stack is a full right side of a rule, replace it by the rule's left side. Grow the tree from the leaves to the root.

Recursive descent

The easiest top-down parser is recursive descent. Each grammar variable becomes one function. The function for F checks the next token. A number means F -> num. A ( means F -> ( E ). The two rules start with different tokens, so the choice is easy. The set of tokens that can start a rule is its FIRST set. LL(1) needs the FIRST sets of the rules for one variable to be disjoint.

But the rule E -> E + T is a trap. The function parse_E would call parse_E first, before it reads any token. It loops forever. This is left recursion. The fix is a loop:

parse_E():
    left = parse_T()
    while next token is '+':
        take the '+'
        left = Add(left, parse_T())   # the loop builds the tree to the left
    return left

Do not fix left recursion by turning E -> E - T into E -> T - E. The language stays the same, but the tree changes. Then 8 - 3 - 2 means 8 - (3 - 2) = 7, not (8 - 3) - 2 = 3. Use the loop. It keeps the grouping from the left.

Shift and reduce

An LR parser has two moves. Shift moves the next token onto the stack. Reduce replaces a right side on top of the stack by its variable. Here is the parse of 2 + 3 * 4 with the grammar above.

Shift 2

Stack: 2. Input left: + 3 * 4. A number is a factor, so reduce: F, then T, then E.

Shift + and 3

Stack: E + 3. Reduce the 3 to F, then to T. Stack: E + T.

The key choice

The stack E + T matches the rule E -> E + T. But the lookahead is *. A product binds tighter. So the parser shifts and does not reduce.

Shift * and 4

Stack: E + T * 4. Reduce 4 to F. Now T * F is on top. Reduce it to T. Stack: E + T.

End of input

The lookahead is the end marker. Now reduce E + T to E. The stack holds only E, so the parser accepts.

The tree

The reduces, in order, build the tree from the bottom. The product was reduced first, so it is lower in the tree: 2 + 12 = 14.

When to shift and when to reduce comes from a table. A parser generator builds that table from the grammar. yacc and GNU Bison are classic examples. Bison makes LALR(1) tables by default and can also make canonical LR(1) and GLR parsers. An LR parser is a deterministic pushdown automaton: a DFA that reads the stack, plus the stack itself.

Sometimes the table has two moves in one cell. This is a conflict. The classic one is the dangling else: if a then if b then s else t. Does the else belong to the first if or the second? Tools prefer shift, so the else goes with the nearest if.

LL and LR side by side
QuestionLL (top-down)LR (bottom-up)
Tree growsfrom the rootfrom the leaves
Left recursionnot allowed, use loopsfine, even better
Grammars it acceptsfewermore: every LL(k) grammar is LR(k)
Written by hand?yes, oftenrarely, use a generator
ToolsANTLR 4 (ALL(*)), hand-written codeyacc, Bison

Large compilers often write their parser by hand anyway. Clang, GCC and rustc use hand-written recursive descent. The reason is error messages. A hand-written parser can say "you forgot a semicolon here" and then go on parsing. CPython is different. Since Python 3.9 it uses a generated PEG parser.

Pratt parsing and the abstract syntax tree

Expressions have many operators and levels. One function per level gets long. Vaughan Pratt showed a shorter way in 1973. Give each operator a number, its binding power. Here are the numbers for our tiny language.

Binding powers in the tiny compiler
OperatorLeft powerRight powerMeaning
+ -1011weak, group from the left
* /2021stronger than +
prefix -none30strongest: -2 * 3 is (-2) \cdot 3

The parser function expr(min_bp) reads one value first. Then it looks at the next operator. If the operator's left power is lower than min_bp, it stops and returns. Otherwise it takes the operator and reads the right side with expr(right_power). Watch it on 8 - 3 - 2.

  1. Read the value 8. The next operator is - with left power 10. Since 10 \ge 0, take it.
  2. Call expr(11) for the right side. It reads 3. The next - has left power 10. Since 10 \lt 11, it stops and returns 3.
  3. Now the tree is (8 - 3). The next - has power 10 \ge 0. Take it and call expr(11), which returns 2.
  4. The tree is ((8 - 3) - 2), which is 3. The grouping is from the left, as it should be.
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Expr { Num(i64), Var(String), Neg(Box<Expr>), Bin(char, Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>) }

// Binding power (left, right). Higher binds tighter. right = left + 1: group from the left.
fn infix_bp(op: char) -> Option<(u8, u8)> {
    match op { '+' | '-' => Some((10, 11)), '*' | '/' => Some((20, 21)), _ => None }
}
const PREFIX: u8 = 30; // unary minus binds tightest

struct Parser { toks: Vec<Tok>, i: usize }

impl Parser {
    fn next(&mut self) -> Tok { self.i += 1; self.toks[self.i - 1].clone() }
    fn expect(&mut self, want: Tok) -> Result<(), String> {
        let got = self.next();
        if got == want { Ok(()) } else { Err(format!("expected {want:?}, got {got:?}")) }
    }
    fn expr(&mut self, min_bp: u8) -> Result<Expr, String> {
        let mut left = match self.next() {
            Tok::Num(n) => Expr::Num(n),
            Tok::Name(s) => Expr::Var(s),
            Tok::Op('-') => Expr::Neg(Box::new(self.expr(PREFIX)?)),
            Tok::Op('(') => { let e = self.expr(0)?; self.expect(Tok::Op(')'))?; e }
            t => return Err(format!("unexpected {t:?}")),
        };
        loop {
            let Tok::Op(op) = self.toks[self.i] else { return Ok(left) }; // look ahead
            let Some((l_bp, r_bp)) = infix_bp(op) else { return Ok(left) };
            if l_bp < min_bp { return Ok(left); } // weaker operator: let the caller take it
            self.next();
            left = Expr::Bin(op, Box::new(left), Box::new(self.expr(r_bp)?));
        }
    }
}
# Binding power (left, right). Higher binds tighter. right = left + 1: group from the left.
INFIX = {"+": (10, 11), "-": (10, 11), "*": (20, 21), "/": (20, 21)}
PREFIX = 30                                # unary minus binds tightest

class Parser:
    def __init__(self, tokens):
        self.toks, self.i = tokens, 0

    def next(self):
        self.i += 1
        return self.toks[self.i - 1]

    def expect(self, want):
        kind, value = self.next()
        if want not in (kind, value):
            raise SyntaxError(f"expected {want}, got {value!r}")
        return value

    def expr(self, min_bp=0):
        kind, value = self.next()
        if kind == "NUM":    left = ("num", value)
        elif kind == "NAME": left = ("var", value)
        elif value == "-":   left = ("neg", self.expr(PREFIX))
        elif value == "(":   left = self.expr(0); self.expect(")")
        else: raise SyntaxError(f"unexpected {value!r}")
        while True:
            op = self.toks[self.i][1]          # look ahead at the next token
            if op not in INFIX or INFIX[op][0] < min_bp:
                return left                    # weaker operator: let the caller take it
            self.next()
            left = ("bin", op, left, self.expr(INFIX[op][1]))

The parser returns an abstract syntax tree (AST). A parse tree has a node for every grammar step, like E, T and F. An AST keeps only what matters. Brackets disappear: their job was to shape the tree, and the tree now has that shape.

The two powers of an operator must differ on purpose. If - had powers (10, 10), the check 10 \lt 10 fails in step 2, so the inner call keeps going. Then 8 - 3 - 2 becomes 8 - (3 - 2) = 7. That is right only for operators that group from the right, like power: give ^ the powers (31, 30). Then 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 2^9 = 512.

Names, scopes and types

This program has the right shape. The parser accepts it.

let a = b + 1;
a

But b means nothing. Our tiny compiler stops with this message:

Rust:   error: name "b" is not defined
Python: NameError: name 'b' is not defined

The parser checks syntax. The next pass checks semantics that can be known before the program runs. Two jobs are common to almost every language: names and types.

Names and scopes

The compiler keeps a symbol table. A scope is a region where a name is visible. Blocks inside blocks give a stack of tables. Entering a block pushes a new table. Leaving it pops the table. A lookup searches from the top of the stack down.

fn main() {
    let x = 1;
    {
        let x = x + 10; // a new x; it hides (shadows) the outer x
        println!("inner x = {x}");
    }
    println!("outer x = {x}"); // the outer table is back
}
inner x = 11
outer x = 1

The inner let adds a new entry to the inner table. This is shadowing. The right side x + 10 still sees the outer x, because the new name is visible only after its line.

In our tiny compiler, the symbol table is the map scope in block 3 below. It maps each source name to the IR operand that holds its value.

Types as rules

Type rules are written as fractions. Above the line are the facts you need. Below the line is the fact you get. The letter \Gamma (gamma) is the type environment: the symbol table with a type for each name.

\frac{\Gamma \vdash e_1 : \text{int} \quad \Gamma \vdash e_2 : \text{int}}{\Gamma \vdash e_1 + e_2 : \text{int}} \qquad \frac{x : \tau \in \Gamma}{\Gamma \vdash x : \tau}

Read the first rule like this: "if e_1 is an int and e_2 is an int, then e_1 + e_2 is an int". The second rule says: a name has the type the table gives it. Take \Gamma = \{x : \text{int},\ ok : \text{bool}\}. Then x + 1 is an int. But x + ok matches no rule, so it is a type error. The checker walks the AST from the leaves up and uses one rule at each node.

The checker may also change the tree. In C, 1 + 2.5 adds an int and a double. The checker puts a hidden "convert to double" node around the 1. Rust does not do this. It asks you to write the conversion yourself.

Languages differ in when they check. rustc checks names, types and borrows before it makes any code. CPython checks names and types only when the line runs. A wrong name is a NameError at run time. Tools like mypy add a static checker on top. The chapter on programming language theory shows how types can be inferred and why a sound type system removes whole classes of bugs.

Do not try to put "declared before use" or "types match" into the grammar. These rules are not context-free. Keep the grammar simple. Check meaning in a separate pass with a symbol table.

Intermediate code and SSA

A tree is good for checking. It is not good for optimising. So the compiler lowers the AST to a flat list of small steps. Here is the IR our tiny compiler makes for the program below.

let a = 2 * 3;
let b = x * (a + 1);
let unused = b * 100;
let c = b - x / a;
c * c + a * x
t1 = 2 * 3
t2 = t1 + 1
t3 = x * t2
t4 = t3 * 100
t5 = x / t1
t6 = t3 - t5
t7 = t6 * t6
t8 = t1 * x
t9 = t7 + t8

This is three-address code. Each step has one operator and at most three names: the result and two inputs. The names t1, t2 and so on are temporaries. There are as many as we like. The back end later maps them to the few real registers.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
enum Val { Const(i64), Temp(String) } // an operand: a number or a temp
type Ins = (String, char, Val, Val);  // dst = a op b
fn program(p: &mut Parser) -> Result<(Vec<(String, Expr)>, Expr), String> {
    let mut lets = Vec::new();
    while p.toks[p.i] == Tok::Let { // let name = expr ;
        p.next();
        let Tok::Name(name) = p.next() else { return Err("expected a name".into()) };
        p.expect(Tok::Op('='))?;
        lets.push((name, p.expr(0)?));
        p.expect(Tok::Op(';'))?;
    }
    let body = p.expr(0)?;
    p.expect(Tok::Eof)?;
    Ok((lets, body))
}

fn lower_expr(e: &Expr, scope: &HashMap<String, Val>, code: &mut Vec<Ins>) -> Result<Val, String> {
    let (op, a, b) = match e {
        Expr::Num(n) => return Ok(Val::Const(*n)),
        Expr::Var(s) => return scope.get(s).cloned().ok_or(format!("name {s:?} is not defined")),
        Expr::Neg(x) => ('-', Val::Const(0), lower_expr(x, scope, code)?), // -a becomes 0 - a
        Expr::Bin(op, l, r) => (*op, lower_expr(l, scope, code)?, lower_expr(r, scope, code)?),
    };
    let dst = format!("t{}", code.len() + 1); // each temp is assigned once: SSA
    code.push((dst.clone(), op, a, b));
    Ok(Val::Temp(dst))
}

fn lower(lets: &[(String, Expr)], body: &Expr) -> Result<(Vec<Ins>, Val), String> {
    let mut scope = HashMap::from([("x".to_string(), Val::Temp("x".into()))]); // symbol table
    let mut code = Vec::new();
    for (name, e) in lets {
        let v = lower_expr(e, &scope, &mut code)?;
        scope.insert(name.clone(), v); // the name is visible only after its line
    }
    let result = lower_expr(body, &scope, &mut code)?;
    Ok((code, result))
}
def program(p):
    lets = []
    while p.toks[p.i][0] == "LET":         # let name = expr ;
        p.next()
        name = p.expect("NAME"); p.expect("=")
        lets.append((name, p.expr())); p.expect(";")
    body = p.expr(); p.expect("EOF")
    return lets, body

def lower(lets, body, params=("x",)):
    code = []
    scope = {p: p for p in params}         # symbol table: source name -> IR name

    def lower_expr(e):                     # returns the operand that holds the value
        if e[0] == "num":
            return e[1]
        if e[0] == "var":
            if e[1] not in scope:
                raise NameError(f"name {e[1]!r} is not defined")
            return scope[e[1]]
        if e[0] == "neg":
            op, args = "-", (0, lower_expr(e[1]))   # -a becomes 0 - a
        else:
            op, args = e[1], (lower_expr(e[2]), lower_expr(e[3]))
        dst = f"t{len(code) + 1}"          # each temp is assigned once: SSA
        code.append((dst, op, *args))
        return dst

    for name, e in lets:
        scope[name] = lower_expr(e)        # the name is visible only after its line
    return code, lower_expr(body)

Static single assignment

Look at the IR again. Every temporary gets a value exactly once. This form has a name: static single assignment (SSA). Straight-line code is easy to put in SSA: give each new value a new name. Branches are harder.

if x > 0 { y = 1 } else { y = 2 }
z = y + x                 which y is this?

Split the code into basic blocks and draw arrows for the jumps. This is the control-flow graph (CFG). In SSA the two assignments get different names, y1 and y2. Where the paths meet, a φ-function joins them: y3 = φ(y1, y2). It picks y1 if control came from the then-block and y2 if it came from the else-block.

Where exactly do φ-functions go? We need two ideas about graphs.

Block D dominates block N when every path from the entry to N passes through D. Every block dominates itself. D strictly dominates N when it dominates N and D \ne N. The dominance frontier \operatorname{DF}(X) is the set of blocks Y such that X dominates a predecessor of Y but does not strictly dominate Y.

In simple words: \operatorname{DF}(X) is where the area ruled by X ends. In the graph above, B1 dominates every block. B2 dominates only itself. B4 has a predecessor dominated by B2, but B2 does not dominate B4. So \operatorname{DF}(B2) = \{B4\}, and also \operatorname{DF}(B3) = \{B4\}. That is exactly where the φ for y went.

Let S be the set of blocks that assign a variable v, plus the entry block. Let \operatorname{DF}^{+}(S) be the iterated dominance frontier: start with \operatorname{DF}(S), add the frontier of every new block, and repeat until nothing changes. Then v needs a φ-function exactly at the blocks of \operatorname{DF}^{+}(S). Placing them there gives a correct SSA form with no extra φ-functions of this kind (Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman and Zadeck, 1991).

Proof idea

A block Z needs a φ for v when two different definitions of v reach Z on two paths that first meet at Z. Take a definition in block X and a path from X onward. While the path stays in blocks that X strictly dominates, no other definition can sneak in from outside. The first block on the path that X does not strictly dominate is in \operatorname{DF}(X). There, another path from the entry (which counts as a definition) can arrive. So the meeting points are frontier blocks.

A φ-function is itself a new definition of v. So its block can create new meeting points further on. That is why we iterate to \operatorname{DF}^{+}. In the other direction, every block in the frontier really is a meeting point of two definitions. So no placed φ is extra.

Here is a loop with numbers. It sums 0 + 1 + \dots + (n-1).

B1: i = 0; s = 0                    entry
B2: if i < n goto B3 else B4        loop test
B3: s = s + i; i = i + 1; goto B2   loop body
B4: return s

Now \operatorname{DF}(B3) = \{B2\}, because B3 jumps back to B2 and does not dominate it. Also \operatorname{DF}(B2) = \{B2\}. Both i and s are assigned in B1 and B3. So \operatorname{DF}^{+}(\{B1, B3\}) = \{B2\}. The loop test gets i1 = φ(i0, i2) and s1 = φ(s0, s2). The first input comes from B1, the second from B3.

Why do compilers love SSA? Each use of a name has exactly one definition. So "where did this value come from?" has a one-word answer. Constant propagation and dead code elimination become simple walks. LLVM IR is in SSA form, and GCC's middle end works on SSA too. Most compilers cheat at the start. A front end writes each variable to a stack slot. Then LLVM's mem2reg pass turns the slots into SSA values and places φ-functions with the dominance frontier.

Real IR from rustc and CPython

Here is a small function in both languages. It has a constant to fold and a dead line.

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn f(x: i64) -> i64 {
    let a = 2 * 3;
    let _unused = x * 100; // dead code
    let b = x * (a + 1);
    b + a
}
import dis

def f(x):
    a = 2 * 3
    unused = x * 100   # dead code
    b = x * (a + 1)
    return b + a

dis.dis(f)
define i64 @f(i64 %x) unnamed_addr #0 !guid !4 {
start:
  %_unused = mul i64 %x, 100
  %b = mul i64 %x, 7
  %_0 = add i64 %b, 6
  ret i64 %_0
}
define noundef i64 @f(i64 noundef %x) unnamed_addr #0 !guid !4 {
start:
  %b = mul i64 %x, 7
  %_0 = add i64 %b, 6
  ret i64 %_0
}
  3           RESUME                   0

  4           LOAD_SMALL_INT           6
              STORE_FAST               1 (a)

  5           LOAD_FAST_BORROW         0 (x)
              LOAD_SMALL_INT         100
              BINARY_OP                5 (*)
              STORE_FAST               2 (unused)

  6           LOAD_FAST_BORROW_LOAD_FAST_BORROW 1 (x, a)
              LOAD_SMALL_INT           1
              BINARY_OP                0 (+)
              BINARY_OP                5 (*)
              STORE_FAST               3 (b)

  7           LOAD_FAST_BORROW_LOAD_FAST_BORROW 49 (b, a)
              BINARY_OP                0 (+)
              RETURN_VALUE

The Rust output comes from rustc --emit=llvm-ir with rustc 1.99.0. The opt-level 0 run also used -C overflow-checks=off to keep it short. Some constant folding happens even at level 0, while the IR is built. The dead multiply by 100 is still there. At level 2 the LLVM passes delete it.

CPython folds 2 * 3 into 6 when it compiles. But it keeps x * 100. Why? x can be any object. Its * can print, fail or change a file. Without types, the compiler cannot prove the line is dead. Optimisation needs facts, and types are facts.

Classic optimisations

Our tiny optimiser runs two passes over the SSA list. First it computes every step whose inputs are all known numbers. Then it walks backwards and keeps only the steps that the result needs.

fn apply(op: char, a: i64, b: i64) -> i64 {
    match op { '+' => a + b, '-' => a - b, '*' => a * b, _ => a / b }
}

fn optimise(code: Vec<Ins>, result: Val) -> (Vec<Ins>, Val) {
    let mut known: HashMap<String, i64> = HashMap::new(); // temp -> constant value
    let get = |v: &Val, known: &HashMap<String, i64>| match v {
        Val::Temp(t) if known.contains_key(t) => Val::Const(known[t]),
        other => other.clone(),
    };
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for (dst, op, a, b) in code { // 1. constant propagation and folding
        let (a, b) = (get(&a, &known), get(&b, &known));
        match (&a, &b) {
            (Val::Const(x), Val::Const(y)) if !(op == '/' && *y == 0) => {
                known.insert(dst, apply(op, *x, *y)); // computed now, at compile time
            }
            _ => out.push((dst, op, a, b)),
        }
    }
    let result = get(&result, &known);
    let (mut live, mut kept) = (HashSet::from([result.clone()]), Vec::new());
    for ins in out.into_iter().rev() { // 2. dead code elimination, backwards
        if live.contains(&Val::Temp(ins.0.clone())) {
            live.extend([ins.2.clone(), ins.3.clone()]);
            kept.push(ins);
        }
    }
    kept.reverse();
    (kept, result)
}
OPS = {"+": lambda a, b: a + b, "-": lambda a, b: a - b,
       "*": lambda a, b: a * b, "/": lambda a, b: a // b}

def optimise(code, result):
    known, out = {}, []                    # known: temp -> constant value
    for dst, op, a, b in code:             # 1. constant propagation and folding
        a, b = known.get(a, a), known.get(b, b)
        if isinstance(a, int) and isinstance(b, int) and not (op == "/" and b == 0):
            known[dst] = OPS[op](a, b)     # computed now, at compile time
        else:
            out.append((dst, op, a, b))
    result = known.get(result, result)
    live, kept = {result}, []              # 2. dead code elimination, backwards
    for dst, op, a, b in reversed(out):
        if dst in live:
            kept.append((dst, op, a, b))
            live |= {a, b}
    return kept[::-1], result
t1 = 2 * 3
t2 = t1 + 1
t3 = x * t2
t4 = t3 * 100
t5 = x / t1
t6 = t3 - t5
t7 = t6 * t6
t8 = t1 * x
t9 = t7 + t8
t3 = x * 7
t5 = x / 6
t6 = t3 - t5
t7 = t6 * t6
t8 = 6 * x
t9 = t7 + t8

t1 and t2 became the numbers 6 and 7. This is constant folding plus constant propagation. t4 was never used, so dead code elimination removed it. Nine steps became six. SSA made both passes one short loop each.

More classic optimisations
NameBeforeAfter
Common subexpression eliminationa = x*y; b = x*ya = x*y; b = a
Copy propagationb = a; c = b + 1c = a + 1
Strength reductiony = x * 8y = x << 3
Loop-invariant code motionloop { k2 = k * 2; ... }k2 = k * 2; loop { ... }
Inliningy = sq(x)y = x * x
Tail-call eliminationreturn f(n - 1)jump back to the start of f

Inlining is the most important one in practice. Alone it saves only a call. But after inlining, the caller's constants flow into the body. Then folding and dead code elimination can do much more. LLVM names its passes after these jobs, for example instcombine, gvn, licm, sccp and inline.

Data-flow analysis

With branches and loops, a pass must collect facts over the whole CFG. The classic example is liveness. A variable is live at a point when its value may still be read later.

For each block n, let \mathrm{use}[n] be the variables read before any write in n, and \mathrm{def}[n] the variables written in n. Then \mathrm{in}[n] = \mathrm{use}[n] \cup (\mathrm{out}[n] \setminus \mathrm{def}[n]), \qquad \mathrm{out}[n] = \bigcup_{s \in \mathrm{succ}(n)} \mathrm{in}[s]. Start with empty sets and repeat until nothing changes.

The sets only grow, and there are finitely many variables. So the loop always stops. This is a fixed point, like in the Knaster-Tarski theorem. Many analyses have the same shape: reaching definitions, available expressions, constant propagation. Only the sets and the join operation change.

Optimisations must not change behaviour

An optimisation is correct only if the program does the same visible things. Three traps catch new compiler writers.

fn main() {
    let (a, b, c) = (0.1_f64, 0.2, 0.3);
    println!("(a + b) + c = {}", (a + b) + c);
    println!("a + (b + c) = {}", a + (b + c)); // same maths, different float result
    println!("-7 / 2 = {}", -7 / 2);           // Rust rounds toward zero
}
a, b, c = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3
print("(a + b) + c =", (a + b) + c)
print("a + (b + c) =", a + (b + c))   # same maths, different float result
print("-7 // 2 =", -7 // 2)            # Python rounds down
(a + b) + c = 0.6000000000000001
a + (b + c) = 0.6
-7 / 2 = -3
(a + b) + c = 0.6000000000000001
a + (b + c) = 0.6
-7 // 2 = -4
  1. Floating point is not associative. (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) give different floats. So compilers do not reorder float sums unless you allow it, for example with GCC's -ffast-math.
  2. Use the target language's rules. -7 divided by 2 is -3 in Rust and -4 in Python. A folding pass must compute what the program would compute at run time.
  3. Never crash the compiler. Folding 1 / 0 must not stop the build. Our optimiser skips division by zero and leaves it for run time.

The order of passes matters. Inlining before folding finds more constants. But each pass can open or close chances for the others. No single order is best for every program. This is the phase-ordering problem. Real compilers use fixed pass lists that work well on typical code.

Code generation and register allocation

The back end has three main jobs.

  1. Instruction choice. Cover the IR with real machine instructions. For example, x86-64 has lea, which can compute a + b * 4 in one instruction.
  2. Register allocation. Put each temporary in one of the few real registers. x86-64 has 16 general registers. Our IR can have thousands of temporaries.
  3. Scheduling. Reorder instructions so the processor does not wait.

Register allocation is the hard one. Two temporaries can share a register only if they are never live at the same time. So first we compute liveness, walking backwards. Then we build a graph.

The interference graph has one node per temporary. It has an edge between two temporaries when one is defined while the other is live.

type Edges = BTreeSet<(String, String)>;

fn temps(vs: &[&Val]) -> Vec<String> {
    vs.iter().filter_map(|v| if let Val::Temp(t) = v { Some(t.clone()) } else { None }).collect()
}

fn interference(code: &[Ins], result: &Val) -> Edges {
    let mut live: HashSet<String> = temps(&[result]).into_iter().collect();
    let mut edges = Edges::new();
    for (dst, _, a, b) in code.iter().rev() { // walk backwards, track live temps
        live.remove(dst); // dst is born here
        for o in &live { // both alive at the same time
            let (p, q) = if dst < o { (dst, o) } else { (o, dst) };
            edges.insert((p.clone(), q.clone()));
        }
        live.extend(temps(&[a, b]));
    }
    edges
}
def interference(code, result):
    live, edges = {result}, set()          # walk backwards, track live temps
    for dst, op, a, b in reversed(code):
        live.discard(dst)                  # dst is born here
        for other in live:
            edges.add(frozenset((dst, other)))   # both alive at the same time
        live |= {v for v in (a, b) if isinstance(v, str)}
    return edges

For our optimised code, the walk finds six edges. Look at the line t5 = x / 6. Just after it, x, t3 and t5 are all live. That makes a triangle.

Give each temporary one register for its whole life. Then the temporaries fit in k registers exactly when the interference graph has a proper k-colouring: a colour for each node, with different colours at the ends of every edge. Also, every graph is the interference graph of some program. So deciding whether k registers are enough is NP-complete for k \ge 3 (Chaitin and others, 1981 and 1982).

Proof idea

Colouring gives registers. Name the colours r_0, \dots, r_{k-1}. Two temporaries with the same colour have no edge. So they are never live at the same time, and one register can hold both. Registers give a colouring. If an allocation works, two temporaries in the same register are never live together. So no edge joins them, and the register numbers are a colouring.

Every graph appears. Given any graph, write a program that defines one temporary per node. Add uses so that each pair joined by an edge is live at the same point, and other pairs are not. Then k-colouring, which is NP-complete for k \ge 3, reduces to register allocation.

In simple words: registers are colours, and "live at the same time" means "must have different colours". Our triangle needs 3 colours, so it needs 3 registers. With 2 registers, something must go to memory. Moving a temporary to memory is called a spill.

Colouring is NP-complete, so Chaitin used a fast rule of thumb. If a node has fewer than k neighbours, it can always get a colour later. Whatever its neighbours take, one colour is left.

Simplify: while the graph has nodes, remove a node with fewer than k neighbours and push it on a stack. If every node has k or more, choose one to spill and remove it. Select: pop the nodes one by one. Give each the lowest colour that its already-coloured neighbours do not use.

fn colour(nodes: &[String], edges: &Edges, k: usize) -> (HashMap<String, usize>, Vec<String>) {
    let mut adj: HashMap<&String, Vec<&String>> = nodes.iter().map(|n| (n, vec![])).collect();
    for (p, q) in edges { adj.get_mut(p).unwrap().push(q); adj.get_mut(q).unwrap().push(p); }
    let mut left: BTreeSet<&String> = nodes.iter().collect();
    let (mut stack, mut spilled) = (Vec::new(), Vec::new());
    while !left.is_empty() { // Chaitin: remove a node with fewer than k neighbours
        let degree = |n: &&String| adj[*n].iter().filter(|m| left.contains(*m)).count();
        let n = match left.iter().find(|n| degree(n) < k) {
            Some(&n) => { stack.push(n); n }
            None => { // stuck: spill the busiest node
                let &n = left.iter().rev().max_by_key(|n| degree(n)).unwrap();
                spilled.push(n.clone()); n }
        };
        left.remove(n);
    }
    let mut reg = HashMap::new();
    for n in stack.into_iter().rev() { // put nodes back, pick a free colour
        let used: Vec<usize> = adj[n].iter().filter_map(|m| reg.get(*m).copied()).collect();
        reg.insert(n.clone(), (0..k).find(|c| !used.contains(c)).unwrap());
    }
    (reg, spilled)
}
def colour(nodes, edges, k):
    adj = {n: set() for n in nodes}
    for p, q in edges:
        adj[p].add(q); adj[q].add(p)
    stack, left, spilled = [], set(nodes), []
    while left:                            # Chaitin: remove a node with fewer than k neighbours
        degree = lambda n: len(adj[n] & left)
        easy = [n for n in sorted(left) if degree(n) < k]
        if easy:
            n = easy[0]; stack.append(n)
        else:                              # stuck: spill the busiest node
            n = max(sorted(left), key=degree); spilled.append(n)
        left.discard(n)
    reg = {}
    for n in reversed(stack):              # put nodes back, pick a free colour
        reg[n] = min(set(range(k)) - {reg[m] for m in adj[n] if m in reg})
    return reg, spilled

The last two blocks write the assembly, run it on a tiny register machine, and print every stage.

fn emit(code: &[Ins], result: &Val, reg: &HashMap<String, usize>) -> Vec<String> {
    let r = |v: &Val| match v { Val::Temp(t) => format!("r{}", reg[t]), Val::Const(c) => c.to_string() };
    let mut asm: Vec<String> = code.iter()
        .map(|(d, op, a, b)| format!("r{} = {} {op} {}", reg[d], r(a), r(b))).collect();
    asm.push(format!("ret {}", r(result)));
    asm
}

fn run(asm: &[String], regs: &mut [i64; 3]) -> i64 { // a tiny machine to test the output
    let val = |s: &str, regs: &[i64; 3]| match s.strip_prefix('r') {
        Some(n) => regs[n.parse::<usize>().unwrap()],
        None => s.parse().unwrap(),
    };
    for line in asm {
        let w: Vec<&str> = line.split(' ').collect();
        if w[0] == "ret" { return val(w[1], regs); }
        let op = w[3].chars().next().unwrap();
        regs[w[0][1..].parse::<usize>().unwrap()] = apply(op, val(w[2], regs), val(w[4], regs));
    }
    unreachable!("no ret")
}
def emit(code, result, reg):
    r = lambda v: f"r{reg[v]}" if isinstance(v, str) else str(v)
    return [f"r{reg[d]} = {r(a)} {op} {r(b)}" for d, op, a, b in code] + [f"ret {r(result)}"]

def run(asm, regs):                        # a tiny machine to test the output
    val = lambda s: regs[int(s[1:])] if s[0] == "r" else int(s)
    for line in asm:
        w = line.split()
        if w[0] == "ret":
            return val(w[1])
        regs[int(w[0][1:])] = OPS[w[3]](val(w[2]), val(w[4]))
fn show(title: &str, code: &[Ins]) {
    let f = |v: &Val| match v { Val::Temp(t) => t.clone(), Val::Const(c) => c.to_string() };
    println!("{title}");
    for (d, op, a, b) in code { println!("  {d} = {} {op} {}", f(a), f(b)); }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let src = "let a = 2 * 3;
let b = x * (a + 1);
let unused = b * 100;
let c = b - x / a;
c * c + a * x";
    let (lets, body) = program(&mut Parser { toks: lex(src)?, i: 0 })?;
    let (code, res) = lower(&lets, &body)?;
    show("IR:", &code);
    let (code, res) = optimise(code, res);
    show("optimised:", &code);
    let edges = interference(&code, &res);
    let pairs: Vec<String> = edges.iter().map(|(p, q)| format!("{p}-{q}")).collect();
    println!("interference: {}", pairs.join(" "));
    let mut nodes = vec!["x".to_string()]; // every variable gets a node
    nodes.extend(code.iter().map(|ins| ins.0.clone()));
    let mut reg = HashMap::new();
    for k in [2, 3] {
        let (r, spilled) = colour(&nodes, &edges, k);
        let note = if spilled.is_empty() { "no spill".into() } else { format!("spill {}", spilled.join(" ")) };
        println!("k={k}: {note}");
        reg = r;
    }
    let asm = emit(&code, &res, &reg);
    println!("assembly:");
    for line in &asm { println!("  {line}"); }
    let mut regs = [0i64; 3];
    regs[reg["x"]] = 10; // the input arrives in x's register
    println!("run with x=10: {}", run(&asm, &mut regs));
    Ok(())
}
def show(title, code):
    print(title)
    for d, op, a, b in code:
        print(f"  {d} = {a} {op} {b}")

SRC = """let a = 2 * 3;
let b = x * (a + 1);
let unused = b * 100;
let c = b - x / a;
c * c + a * x"""
lets, body = program(Parser(lex(SRC)))
code, res = lower(lets, body)
show("IR:", code)
code, res = optimise(code, res)
show("optimised:", code)
edges = interference(code, res)
print("interference:", " ".join(sorted("-".join(sorted(e)) for e in edges)))
nodes = ["x"] + [ins[0] for ins in code]   # every variable gets a node
for k in (2, 3):
    reg, spilled = colour(nodes, edges, k)
    print(f"k={k}:", f"spill {' '.join(spilled)}" if spilled else "no spill")
asm = emit(code, res, reg)
print("assembly:", *asm, sep="\n  ")
regs = [0, 0, 0]
regs[reg["x"]] = 10                        # the input arrives in x's register
print("run with x=10:", run(asm, regs))
IR:
  t1 = 2 * 3
  t2 = t1 + 1
  t3 = x * t2
  t4 = t3 * 100
  t5 = x / t1
  t6 = t3 - t5
  t7 = t6 * t6
  t8 = t1 * x
  t9 = t7 + t8
optimised:
  t3 = x * 7
  t5 = x / 6
  t6 = t3 - t5
  t7 = t6 * t6
  t8 = 6 * x

interference: t3-t5 t3-x t5-x t6-x t7-t8 t7-x
