run with x=10: 4821

Both languages print exactly these lines. Check the answer by hand: a = 6, b = 70, c = 70 - 1 = 69, and 69 \cdot 69 + 60 = 4821. Now read the assembly. x lives in r0. After t8 = 6 * x, x is dead, so t8 reuses r0. Three registers are enough for nine temporaries.

In strict SSA form, where each definition dominates all its uses, the interference graph is chordal. A chordal graph can be coloured with the fewest colours in linear time. That number equals the largest number of values live at one point.

Proof idea

If two SSA values interfere, one of them is live where the other is defined. Order the values by the dominance of their definitions. When a value is defined, the values it interferes with that came earlier are all live at that point, so they form a group where every pair interferes. That gives a perfect elimination order, which is the definition of chordal. Greedy colouring in that order uses exactly as many colours as the biggest group. Several groups proved this around 2005 and 2006. The CMU notes in the sources build an allocator on it.

Our example agrees. At most 3 values are live at once, and 3 registers were enough. The hard part moves elsewhere. Leaving SSA turns φ-functions into copies, and those copies must also be placed well. LLVM's default allocator is called greedy. It splits long live ranges and tries to keep the spill cost low. At opt-level 0 LLVM uses a much simpler fast allocator. Many JIT compilers use linear scan (Poletto and Sarkar, 1999), which is quicker and a little worse.

A spill is not free. Every use of a spilled value needs a load from memory, and every definition needs a store. In a hot loop this can cost more than all the other work. Good allocators spill values that are used rarely, not simply the node with the most edges.

Runtimes: garbage collection and JIT compilers

A compiler does not stop at code. The program also needs a runtime. Two big parts of many runtimes are the garbage collector and the JIT compiler.

Garbage collection

Here are two objects that point to each other. Then we drop our names for them.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

struct Node { name: &'static str, next: RefCell<Option<Rc<Node>>> }

impl Drop for Node {
    fn drop(&mut self) { println!("free {}", self.name); } // runs when the count hits 0
}

fn main() {
    let a = Rc::new(Node { name: "a", next: RefCell::new(None) });
    let b = Rc::new(Node { name: "b", next: RefCell::new(None) });
    *a.next.borrow_mut() = Some(Rc::clone(&b)); // a -> b
    {
        let c = Rc::new(Node { name: "c", next: RefCell::new(None) });
        println!("c count = {}", Rc::strong_count(&c));
    } // c is freed here: its count drops to 0
    *b.next.borrow_mut() = Some(Rc::clone(&a)); // b -> a: a cycle
    println!("a count = {}, b count = {}", Rc::strong_count(&a), Rc::strong_count(&b));
    drop(a);
    drop(b);
    println!("end of main: a and b were never freed");
}
import gc, sys

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.next = name, None
    def __del__(self):
        print("free", self.name)           # runs when the object is freed

gc.collect(); gc.disable()                 # clean start, then no automatic cycle collection
a, b = Node("a"), Node("b")
a.next = b                                 # a -> b
c = Node("c")
print("c count =", sys.getrefcount(c) - 1) # -1: the call itself holds one reference
del c                                      # count drops to 0: freed at once
b.next = a                                 # b -> a: a cycle
del a, b                                   # counts are still 1, nothing is freed
print("cycle collector found:", gc.collect())   # tracing finds the unreachable cycle
c count = 1
free c
a count = 2, b count = 2
end of main: a and b were never freed
c count = 1
free c
free a
free b
cycle collector found: 2

c is freed at once in both: its count fell to 0. But a and b keep each other's count at 1. Rust's Rc uses only counting, so they leak. Python also counts, but it has a second collector. That collector traced the objects, found that no one could reach them, and freed both.

An object is garbage when no chain of pointers from a root reaches it. Roots are local variables, global variables and registers. Collectors find garbage in two basic ways.

Reference counting

Each object counts the pointers to it. When the count reaches 0, free it. Memory comes back at once, and pauses are short. But every pointer copy changes a count, which costs time and is slow across threads. Cycles never reach 0, as we just saw. CPython, Swift and Rust's Rc and Arc use counting. In Rust you break cycles with Weak pointers.

Mark and sweep

Start at the roots and mark everything you can reach. Then sweep the heap and free everything not marked. Cycles are no problem. Objects never move. The heap can get full of small holes, called fragmentation.

Copying

Split the heap in two halves. Copy every reachable object from the full half to the empty half, then swap. Cheney's 1970 algorithm does this with no extra stack. The cost depends only on the live objects, and free memory is one big block. The price: half the memory waits empty, and pointers must be updated.

Mark and compact

Mark as before, then slide the live objects together. No half of the heap is wasted, and fragmentation is gone. It costs more passes over the heap.

Generational

Most objects die young. So keep new objects in a small young area and collect it often, usually by copying. Objects that survive a few times move to the old area, which is collected rarely. The JVM, .NET and V8 work this way.

Incremental and concurrent

A collector that stops the program for a whole collection can pause it for a long time. An incremental collector does a little work at a time. A concurrent one runs on another thread while the program runs. Both need the tri-colour rule below and a write barrier.

In most programs, most objects become garbage soon after they are made. So a collector that looks at young objects often and old objects rarely does less work for the same result.

Paint objects white (not seen yet), grey (seen, but its pointers not scanned yet) and black (seen and scanned). Marking ends when no grey object is left. A concurrent collector is correct if no black object ever points to a white object (Dijkstra and others, 1978). The write barrier keeps this rule when the program changes a pointer during marking.

Garbage collection in real systems (checked November 2026)
SystemKindRecent news
CPythonreference counting plus a tracing cycle collector3.14.0 to 3.14.4 had an incremental cycle collector. Version 3.14.5 went back to the generational one from 3.13 after reports of memory pressure.
Gotracing, concurrent, mark-sweep, non-movingThe new Green Tea collector is the default since Go 1.26. The release notes expect 10 to 40% less GC overhead in GC-heavy programs.
Java (HotSpot)generational; G1 is the defaultZGC is a low-pause option for very large heaps.
Rustno collectorOwnership decides at compile time where each value is freed. Rc and Arc are opt-in counting.

JIT compilers

A JIT compiler (just in time) compiles while the program runs. It has one big advantage over a normal compiler: it can watch the program first. If a + b has added two small integers 10,000 times, the JIT can make machine code for that case only. This is speculation.

  1. Start in an interpreter. It is slow but starts at once. It counts calls and records the types it sees.
  2. When a function gets hot, compile it with a quick, simple compiler.
  3. When it gets very hot, compile it again with a slow, strong optimiser that uses the recorded types.
  4. Put a guard before each guess, for example "is a still a small integer?".
  5. If a guard fails, jump back to the interpreter. This is deoptimisation. Later the JIT may compile again with better guesses.

V8, the JavaScript engine in Chrome and Node.js, has four tiers. Ignition is the interpreter. Sparkplug (2021) is a fast baseline compiler. Maglev (Chrome M117, 2023) is a middle optimiser. TurboFan is the strongest optimiser. Java's HotSpot has an interpreter and two compilers, C1 and C2. CPython 3.11 added a specialising interpreter (PEP 659). CPython 3.13 added an experimental JIT that uses copy-and-patch (PEP 744). It is off by default. Check the official pages before you rely on these details. They change often.

Do not measure JIT code with one short run. The first runs use the interpreter and include compile time. Warm up first, then measure many runs. Tools like JMH for Java do this for you.

A short history

  1. 1957 FORTRAN I. John Backus's team at IBM ships the first big optimising compiler.
  2. 1965 LR parsing. Donald Knuth defines LR(k) grammars and their parsers.
  3. 1973 Pratt parsing. Vaughan Pratt presents top-down operator precedence.
  4. 1978 Tri-colour marking. Dijkstra and others describe on-the-fly garbage collection.
  5. 1981 Graph colouring. Chaitin and others allocate registers by colouring.
  6. 1991 SSA. Cytron and others build SSA with dominance frontiers.
  7. 2003 LLVM 1.0. A shared, reusable optimiser and back end. Version 23.1.5 is listed on llvm.org in November 2026.
  8. 2024 CPython 3.13. Python gets an experimental copy-and-patch JIT.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for compilers
PatternPurposeModelNote
Front, middle, backShare work between languages and chips5 languages + 4 chips = 9 parts, not 20The IR is the contract between them.
Longest match, then priorityCut text into tokensletter is a name, let a keywordPython's re takes the first alternative, not the longest.
One function per variableWrite a recursive-descent parserparse_E, parse_T, parse_FTurn left recursion into a loop.
Shift or reduceParse bottom-up with a stackShift on * when E + T is on topTwo moves in one cell is a conflict.
Binding power (left, right)Parse operators with Pratt- is (10, 11), ^ is (31, 30)Equal powers group from the right.
Stack of tablesResolve names in nested scopesInner x = 11, outer x = 1A new name is visible after its line.
Rule per nodeCheck typesint + int gives intNo matching rule means a type error.
New name per assignmentBuild SSAy3 = φ(y1, y2)φ goes in the iterated dominance frontier.
Fold, then sweepConstant propagation and dead code removal9 steps become 6Never fold 1 / 0. Use the target's rules.
Grow sets to a fixed pointData-flow analysisLiveness: in = use ∪ (out − def)It stops because the sets only grow.
Registers are coloursAllocate registersTriangle x, t3, t5 needs 3General colouring is NP-complete. Use simplify and select.
Count or traceFree memoryRc cycle leaks, Python's collector frees itCounting alone cannot free cycles.
Interpret, watch, compileMake a JIT fastIgnition, Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFanEvery guess needs a guard and a way back.

Practice

Which pass reports the error in let = 5; (no name after let)?

  • The lexer
  • The parser
  • The register allocator

Every token is fine: LET, OP(=), NUM(5), OP(;). The order of the tokens is wrong. Order is syntax, so the parser finds it.

A recursive-descent parser hangs forever on every input. What is the most likely cause?

  • A FIRST set is empty
  • A left-recursive rule such as E -> E + T
  • Too many temporaries

The function for E calls itself before it reads any token. Nothing changes between the calls, so it never ends.

Two Python objects point only to each other. Which part of CPython frees them?

  • Reference counting
  • The cycle collector
  • The JIT compiler

Each count stays at 1 because of the other object. Only tracing from the roots shows that nothing can reach them.

Registers correspond to ? in the interference graph.

In SSA, the pseudo step that joins two values where paths meet is the ?.

With binding powers (10, 11) for -, the expression 10 - 4 - 3 has the value ?.

  1. Turn t1 = 4; t2 = t1 * 2; t3 = y + t2; t4 = y * 0; return t3 into optimised code. Name each step you used.
    Answer

    Constant propagation makes t2 = 4 * 2, and folding makes it 8. Then t3 = y + 8. t4 is never used, so dead code elimination removes it. The result is t3 = y + 8; return t3. Note: for integers y * 0 is 0, but for floats it can be -0.0 or NaN, so be careful with algebra rules.

  2. Rewrite the grammar L -> L , id | id (a comma list) so that recursive descent can parse it.
    Answer

    L -> id { , id }. As code: read an id, then loop while the next token is a comma: take the comma and read another id. The loop keeps the order from the left.

  3. Put this code in SSA form: x = 1; if c { x = x + 1 }; print(x).
    Answer

    x1 = 1. In the then-block: x2 = x1 + 1. After the if: x3 = φ(x1, x2) and print(x3). The join block is in the dominance frontier of the then-block, so the φ goes there. The first input comes from the path that skips the then-block.

  4. The live sets after each line of some code are {a, b}, {a, b, c}, {b, c}, {c, d}. What is the smallest number of registers? Which pairs interfere?
    Answer

    Three registers, because three values (a, b, c) are live at one point. Edges: a-b, a-c, b-c, c-d. A colouring: a = r0, b = r1, c = r2, d = r0. In straight-line SSA code the maximum live count is always enough.

  5. Give binding powers for a new operator ? that binds weaker than + and groups from the right.
    Answer

    Any pair below 10 with the right power lower than the left, for example (6, 5). Then a ? b ? c means a ? (b ? c), and a + b ? c means (a + b) ? c.

  6. Expert: a JIT compiled f(a, b) = a + b for small integers. Then a call passes two strings. What happens, step by step?
    Answer

    The guard "a and b are small integers" fails. The runtime deoptimises: it rebuilds the interpreter's frame from the optimised frame and goes on in the interpreter, which handles strings. The JIT notes the new types. If f stays hot, it may compile again, with code for both cases or with a general path. Too many failures can stop the JIT from optimising f at all.

Key takeaways

  • A compiler is a chain of passes: lexer, parser, checker, IR builder, optimiser, code generator.
  • A shared IR lets M languages and N chips need M + N parts, not M × N. LLVM is the main example.
  • Lexers are regular expressions turned into one automaton. They use longest match and rule priority.
  • LL parsers grow the tree from the root, LR parsers from the leaves. Pratt parsing handles operators with binding powers.
  • Name and type checks need symbol tables and type rules, not a bigger grammar.
  • SSA gives each value one definition. φ-functions go in the iterated dominance frontier.
  • Constant folding, propagation and dead code elimination are short loops on SSA. They must keep the program's behaviour.
  • Register allocation is graph colouring. It is NP-complete in general, but SSA graphs are chordal and easy.
  • Reference counting frees memory at once but leaks cycles. Tracing collectors find cycles. JITs speculate, guard and deoptimise.

Sources

  • LLVM: The LLVM Target-Independent Code Generator. Register allocators (fast, basic, greedy, PBQP), spilling and φ elimination.
  • CMU 15-411 lecture notes: Register Allocation. Liveness, interference graphs and chordal colouring for SSA.
  • Crafting Interpreters: Compiling Expressions. A full Pratt parser with a rule table.
  • V8 blog: Maglev, V8's fastest optimizing JIT. The four tiers Ignition, Sparkplug, Maglev and TurboFan.
  • PEP 744: JIT Compilation. CPython's experimental copy-and-patch JIT and its status.
  • A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector. Tracing, mark-sweep, non-moving and concurrent collection.

Programming language theory

Programming language theory asks exact questions about programs. What does this program mean? Which programs can go wrong, and how can a compiler know before they run? It answers with very small mathematical languages. This chapter starts with the smallest one, the lambda calculus, and ends with the ideas under Rust's ownership, Python's type checkers and modern effect handlers.

  • Reduce lambda terms by hand and in code, and encode booleans, numbers and recursion as functions.
  • Read and write small-step and big-step rules, and find stuck programs.
  • Type a program with simple types, and explain progress, preservation and type soundness.
  • Infer types with Hindley-Milner, and decide when one type is a subtype of another.
  • Explain ownership as a linear or affine type, and effects and continuations in simple words.

The lambda calculus

Look at the Python function lambda x: x + 1. It has no name. It takes x and gives back x + 1. Now give it 2: the result is 3. That is the whole idea of the lambda calculus. Alonzo Church wrote it down in the 1930s. It has only three kinds of terms.

The three kinds of lambda terms
KindWrittenPythonMeaning
Variablexxa name
Abstraction\lambda x.\, Mlambda x: Ma function with input x and body M
ApplicationM\, NM(N)call M with N

Two writing rules save brackets. Application groups to the left: f\,a\,b means (f\,a)\,b. A body goes as far right as it can: \lambda x.\, x\,y means \lambda x.\, (x\,y). Functions take one input. For two inputs, return a function: \lambda x.\, \lambda y.\, x takes x, then y, and gives back x. This trick is called currying.

Free and bound names

In \lambda x.\, x\,y, the name x is bound by the lambda. The name y is free. The names of bound variables do not matter. \lambda x.\, x and \lambda z.\, z are the same function. Renaming a bound variable is called alpha conversion.

Beta reduction

Running a program means one rule, again and again:

(\lambda x.\, M)\, N \to_\beta M[x := N]

Read M[x := N] as "M with each free x replaced by N". A term of the form (\lambda x.\, M)\, N is a redex. Reducing it is a beta step. Example: (\lambda x.\, x\,x)\,(\lambda y.\, y) \to (\lambda y.\, y)\,(\lambda y.\, y) \to \lambda y.\, y. Two steps, and no redex is left. A term with no redex is in normal form.

Substitution must not capture free names. Take (\lambda x.\, \lambda y.\, x)\, y. The answer should be "a function that ignores its input and returns the outer y". Plain text replacement gives \lambda y.\, y, the identity. That is wrong. First rename the inner y to a new name: \lambda v_1.\, y. Now it is right.

Here is substitution in code. The renaming step is the important line.

use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};

#[derive(Debug)]
enum Term { Var(String), Lam(String, Rc<Term>), App(Rc<Term>, Rc<Term>) }
use Term::*;

fn free_vars(t: &Term) -> HashSet<String> {
    match t {
        Var(x) => HashSet::from([x.clone()]),
        Lam(x, b) => { let mut s = free_vars(b); s.remove(x); s }
        App(f, a) => &free_vars(f) | &free_vars(a),
    }
}

static FRESH: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(1); // counter for new names v1, v2, ...

fn subst(t: &Rc<Term>, x: &str, s: &Rc<Term>) -> Rc<Term> { // t[x := s] without capture
    match &**t {
        Var(y) => if y == x { s.clone() } else { t.clone() },
        App(f, a) => Rc::new(App(subst(f, x, s), subst(a, x, s))),
        Lam(y, _) if y == x => t.clone(), // x is bound again here: stop
        Lam(y, body) if free_vars(s).contains(y) => { // rename y first, or s would be captured
            let z = format!("v{}", FRESH.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed));
            let body = subst(body, y, &Rc::new(Var(z.clone())));
            Rc::new(Lam(z, subst(&body, x, s)))
        }
        Lam(y, body) => Rc::new(Lam(y.clone(), subst(body, x, s))),
    }
}
import itertools, re

def free_vars(t):
    if t[0] == "var": return {t[1]}
    if t[0] == "lam": return free_vars(t[2]) - {t[1]}
    return free_vars(t[1]) | free_vars(t[2])

fresh = (f"v{i}" for i in itertools.count(1))

def subst(t, x, s):                        # t[x := s] without capture
    if t[0] == "var":
        return s if t[1] == x else t
    if t[0] == "app":
        return ("app", subst(t[1], x, s), subst(t[2], x, s))
    y, body = t[1], t[2]
    if y == x:
        return t                           # x is bound again here: stop
    if y in free_vars(s):                  # rename y first, or s would be captured
        z = next(fresh)
        y, body = z, subst(body, y, ("var", z))
    return ("lam", y, subst(body, x, s))

Reduction order and the Church-Rosser theorem

A term can have many redexes. Which one do we reduce first? Look at this term. Its argument is \Omega, a term that never stops.

\Omega = (\lambda x.\, x\,x)\,(\lambda x.\, x\,x) \to (\lambda x.\, x\,x)\,(\lambda x.\, x\,x) \to \dots

Now reduce (\lambda x.\, y)\, \Omega. The function throws its input away.

  • Normal order: reduce the leftmost, outermost redex first. One step gives y. Done.
  • Applicative order: reduce the argument first. We reduce \Omega forever and never finish.

Programming languages use these orders too. Rust, Python and C use call by value, like applicative order. Haskell uses call by need, a lazy version of normal order. A reduction strategy is this choice. Our interpreter uses normal order.

fn step(t: &Rc<Term>) -> Option<Rc<Term>> { // one normal-order step, None if done
    match &**t {
        App(f, a) => match &**f {
            Lam(x, body) => Some(subst(body, x, a)), // beta: (\x. b) a  ->  b[x := a]
            _ => step(f).map(|f2| Rc::new(App(f2, a.clone())))
                .or_else(|| step(a).map(|a2| Rc::new(App(f.clone(), a2)))),
        },
        Lam(x, b) => step(b).map(|b2| Rc::new(Lam(x.clone(), b2))),
        Var(_) => None,
    }
}

fn normalise(mut t: Rc<Term>, limit: usize) -> (Option<Rc<Term>>, usize) {
    for n in 0..limit {
        match step(&t) { Some(next) => t = next, None => return (Some(t), n) }
    }
    (None, limit)
}
def step(t):                               # one normal-order step, None if done
    if t[0] == "app":
        f, a = t[1], t[2]
        if f[0] == "lam":
            return subst(f[2], f[1], a)    # beta: (\x. b) a  ->  b[x := a]
        if (f2 := step(f)) is not None:
            return ("app", f2, a)
        if (a2 := step(a)) is not None:
            return ("app", f, a2)
    if t[0] == "lam" and (b := step(t[2])) is not None:
        return ("lam", t[1], b)
    return None

def normalise(t, limit=10_000):
    for n in range(limit):
        if (nxt := step(t)) is None:
            return t, n                    # normal form after n steps
        t = nxt
    return None, limit

Different orders can differ in whether they finish. Can they differ in the answer? No. This is the most important fact about the lambda calculus.

Beta reduction is confluent. If M \to^{*} N_1 and M \to^{*} N_2, then there is a term P with N_1 \to^{*} P and N_2 \to^{*} P. Here \to^{*} means zero or more beta steps (Church and Rosser, 1936).

Proof idea

One beta step does not close a diamond by itself. A step can copy a redex, so the other side may need two steps to catch up. The trick is a new relation, parallel reduction, written \Rightarrow. It reduces any chosen set of existing redexes in one move. You show three facts. Every beta step is a parallel step. Every parallel step is a few beta steps. And \Rightarrow has the diamond property: two parallel steps from M can each be finished by one parallel step to a common term. That last fact is proved by induction on the term (Tait and Martin-Löf). Then you tile the diamonds, like bricks in a wall, to join any two long paths.

In simple words: the order of work may change if you finish, but never what you get. So a term has at most one normal form, up to renaming. If P and P' were two different normal forms of M, the theorem would give a common term below both. But a normal form cannot step. So P = P'.

If a term has a normal form, normal-order reduction reaches it. It follows from the standardisation theorem of Curry and Feys. So the strategy in our interpreter is the safest one.

Programming with only functions

The lambda calculus has no numbers, no if and no loops. Yet it can compute everything a computer can. The trick is to encode data as functions.

  1. Booleans choose. \mathtt{TRUE} = \lambda a.\, \lambda b.\, a and \mathtt{FALSE} = \lambda a.\, \lambda b.\, b. Then "if c then x else y" is just c\,x\,y.
  2. Numbers repeat. The Church numeral \overline{n} applies a function n times: \overline{n} = \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, f^{n}(x). So \overline{2} = \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, f\,(f\,x).
  3. Arithmetic composes. \mathtt{PLUS} = \lambda m.\, \lambda n.\, \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, m\,f\,(n\,f\,x): do f n times, then m more times.
  4. Recursion uses a fixed point. Y = \lambda f.\, (\lambda x.\, f\,(x\,x))\,(\lambda x.\, f\,(x\,x)). Then Y\,g reduces to g\,(Y\,g). So g gets itself as an input and can call itself.

A fixed point of g is a value x with g\,x = x. Y finds one for every g, and that is enough for loops. The next two blocks finish the interpreter. They add a small parser for terms like \x. x and run the encodings.

fn parse(src: &str) -> Rc<Term> { // \x. body   f a b   (term)
    let spaced = src.replace('\\', " \\ ").replace('.', " . ").replace('(', " ( ").replace(')', " ) ");
    let toks: Vec<&str> = spaced.split_whitespace().collect();
    term(&toks, &mut 0)
}

fn term(toks: &[&str], pos: &mut usize) -> Rc<Term> {
    if toks[*pos] == "\\" {
        *pos += 3; // skip  \ name .
        return Rc::new(Lam(toks[*pos - 2].to_string(), term(toks, pos)));
    }
    let mut t = atom(toks, pos);
    while *pos < toks.len() && toks[*pos] != ")" {
        t = Rc::new(App(t, atom(toks, pos))); // application groups to the left
    }
    t
}

fn atom(toks: &[&str], pos: &mut usize) -> Rc<Term> {
    if toks[*pos] == "\\" { return term(toks, pos); }
    *pos += 1;
    if toks[*pos - 1] != "(" { return Rc::new(Var(toks[*pos - 1].to_string())); }
    let t = term(toks, pos);
    *pos += 1; // skip the closing bracket
    t
}

fn show(t: &Term) -> String {
    match t {
        Var(x) => x.clone(),
        Lam(x, b) => format!("λ{x}.{}", show(b)),
        App(f, a) => {
            let fs = if matches!(**f, Lam(..)) { format!("({})", show(f)) } else { show(f) };
            let xs = if matches!(**a, Var(_)) { show(a) } else { format!("({})", show(a)) };
            format!("{fs} {xs}")
        }
    }
}
def parse(src):                            # \x. body   f a b   (term)
    toks, pos = re.findall(r"[\\.()]|\w+", src), 0
    def term():
        nonlocal pos
        if toks[pos] == "\\":
            pos += 3                           # skip  \ name .
            return ("lam", toks[pos - 2], term())
        t = atom()
        while pos < len(toks) and toks[pos] != ")":
            t = ("app", t, atom())             # application groups to the left
        return t
    def atom():
        nonlocal pos
        if toks[pos] == "\\":
            return term()
        pos += 1
        if toks[pos - 1] != "(":
            return ("var", toks[pos - 1])
        t = term(); pos += 1                   # skip the closing bracket
        return t
    return term()

def show(t):
    if t[0] == "var": return t[1]
    if t[0] == "lam": return f"λ{t[1]}.{show(t[2])}"
    f = show(t[1]) if t[1][0] != "lam" else f"({show(t[1])})"
    a = show(t[2]) if t[2][0] == "var" else f"({show(t[2])})"
    return f"{f} {a}"
fn main() {
    let defs = [ // each name may use the names above it
        ("TRUE", r"\a.\b. a"), ("FALSE", r"\a.\b. b"), ("AND", r"\p.\q. p q p"),
        ("ZERO", r"\f.\x. x"), ("TWO", r"\f.\x. f (f x)"), ("THREE", r"\f.\x. f (f (f x))"),
        ("SUCC", r"\n.\f.\x. f (n f x)"), ("PLUS", r"\m.\n.\f.\x. m f (n f x)"),
        ("MULT", r"\m.\n.\f. m (n f)"), ("ISZERO", r"\n. n (\x. FALSE) TRUE"),
        ("PRED", r"\n.\f.\x. n (\g.\h. h (g f)) (\u. x) (\u. u)"),
        ("Y", r"\f. (\x. f (x x)) (\x. f (x x))"),
        ("FACT", r"Y (\r.\n. ISZERO n (SUCC ZERO) (MULT n (r (PRED n))))"),
        ("OMEGA", r"(\x. x x) (\x. x x)"),
    ];
    let mut terms: Vec<(&str, Rc<Term>)> = Vec::new();
    let expand = |src: &str, terms: &[(&str, Rc<Term>)]| // parse, then replace the known names
        terms.iter().fold(parse(src), |t, (name, def)| subst(&t, name, def));
    for (name, src) in defs {
        let t = expand(src, &terms);
        terms.push((name, t));
    }
    for src in ["AND TRUE FALSE", "PLUS TWO THREE", "MULT TWO THREE", "PRED THREE",
                "FACT THREE", r"(\x. y) OMEGA", "OMEGA"] {
        let (nf, steps) = normalise(expand(src, &terms), 10_000);
        let text = nf.map(|t| show(&t)).unwrap_or("no normal form".into());
        println!("{src:15} -> {text} ({steps} step{})", if steps == 1 { "" } else { "s" });
    }
}
DEFS = {                                   # each name may use the names above it
    "TRUE": r"\a.\b. a", "FALSE": r"\a.\b. b", "AND": r"\p.\q. p q p",
    "ZERO": r"\f.\x. x", "TWO": r"\f.\x. f (f x)", "THREE": r"\f.\x. f (f (f x))",
    "SUCC": r"\n.\f.\x. f (n f x)", "PLUS": r"\m.\n.\f.\x. m f (n f x)",
    "MULT": r"\m.\n.\f. m (n f)", "ISZERO": r"\n. n (\x. FALSE) TRUE",
    "PRED": r"\n.\f.\x. n (\g.\h. h (g f)) (\u. x) (\u. u)",
    "Y": r"\f. (\x. f (x x)) (\x. f (x x))",
    "FACT": r"Y (\r.\n. ISZERO n (SUCC ZERO) (MULT n (r (PRED n))))",
    "OMEGA": r"(\x. x x) (\x. x x)",
}
TERMS = {}

def expand(src):                           # parse, then replace the known names
    t = parse(src)
    for name, term in TERMS.items():
        t = subst(t, name, term)
    return t

for name, src in DEFS.items():
    TERMS[name] = expand(src)

for src in ["AND TRUE FALSE", "PLUS TWO THREE", "MULT TWO THREE", "PRED THREE",
            "FACT THREE", r"(\x. y) OMEGA", "OMEGA"]:
    nf, steps = normalise(expand(src))
    text = show(nf) if nf else "no normal form"
    print(f"{src:15} -> {text} ({steps} step{'' if steps == 1 else 's'})")
AND TRUE FALSE  -> λa.λb.b (4 steps)
PLUS TWO THREE  -> λf.λx.f (f (f (f (f x)))) (6 steps)
MULT TWO THREE  -> λf.λx.f (f (f (f (f (f x))))) (7 steps)
PRED THREE      -> λf.λx.f (f x) (11 steps)
FACT THREE      -> λf.λx.f (f (f (f (f (f x))))) (664 steps)
(\x. y) OMEGA   -> y (1 step)
OMEGA           -> no normal form (10000 steps)

Both languages print these lines. 2 + 3 gives five fs, and 2 \times 3 gives six. The factorial of 3 is 6 and takes 664 steps, with no number type and no loop in the language. Normal order throws \Omega away in one step. \Omega alone never reaches a normal form, so we stop after 10,000 steps.

The lambda calculus can express every computable function. That is one form of the Church-Turing thesis. It also means the halting problem appears here: no algorithm can decide whether any term has a normal form.

Y loops forever under call by value. The argument x\,x is reduced before the call, again and again. Strict languages use the Z combinator instead. It wraps the self-application in one more lambda: \lambda v.\, x\,x\,v. A lambda body is not reduced until the lambda is called.

Operational semantics

What does if 1 + 2 < 4 then 10 + 5 else 0 mean? A semantics answers this with exact rules. We use a tiny language with numbers, booleans, +, < and if. Operational semantics describes meaning as running. There are two styles.

Small-step rules

A small-step rule t \to t' says what one step does. Rules are fractions: if the top holds, the bottom holds. A value v is a number or a boolean.

\frac{t_1 \to t_1'}{t_1 + t_2 \to t_1' + t_2} \qquad \frac{t_2 \to t_2'}{v_1 + t_2 \to v_1 + t_2'} \qquad \frac{n = n_1 + n_2}{n_1 + n_2 \to n} \mathtt{if}\ \mathtt{true}\ \mathtt{then}\ t_2\ \mathtt{else}\ t_3 \to t_2 \qquad \mathtt{if}\ \mathtt{false}\ \mathtt{then}\ t_2\ \mathtt{else}\ t_3 \to t_3

The first two rules fix the order: left side first, then right side. The third does the addition. The rules for < look the same. One more rule reduces the test of an if first. Here is our example, one rule per step.

  1. The test is not a value. Inside it, 1 + 2 steps to 3.
  2. Now 3 < 4 steps to true.
  3. The if rule for true picks the then-branch: 10 + 5.
  4. 10 + 5 steps to 15, a value. Done.
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
enum T { Int(i64), Bool(bool), Add(Box<T>, Box<T>), Lt(Box<T>, Box<T>), If(Box<T>, Box<T>, Box<T>) }
use T::*;

fn is_value(t: &T) -> bool { matches!(t, Int(_) | Bool(_)) }

fn step(t: &T) -> Option<T> { // one small step, or None if no rule applies
    let b = |x: T| Box::new(x);
    let rebuild = |x, y| if matches!(t, Add(..)) { Add(x, y) } else { Lt(x, y) };
    match t {
        Add(x, y) | Lt(x, y) if !is_value(x) => Some(rebuild(b(step(x)?), y.clone())), // parts first
        Add(x, y) | Lt(x, y) if !is_value(y) => Some(rebuild(x.clone(), b(step(y)?))),
        Add(x, y) => match (&**x, &**y) { (Int(m), Int(n)) => Some(Int(m + n)), _ => None },
        Lt(x, y) => match (&**x, &**y) { (Int(m), Int(n)) => Some(Bool(m < n)), _ => None },
        If(c, yes, no) if !is_value(c) => Some(If(b(step(c)?), yes.clone(), no.clone())),
        If(c, yes, no) => match **c { // if true then yes else no  ->  yes
            Bool(v) => Some(if v { (**yes).clone() } else { (**no).clone() }),
            _ => None,
        },
        _ => None, // a value, or something like true + 1
    }
}
# Terms: ("int", n) ("bool", b) ("add", a, b) ("lt", a, b) ("if", test, yes, no)
def is_value(t):
    return t[0] in ("int", "bool")

def step(t):                               # one small step, or None if no rule applies
    k = t[0]
    if is_value(t):
        return None
    parts = [1] if k == "if" else [1, 2]   # reduce the parts first, left to right
    for i in parts:
        if not is_value(t[i]):
            s = step(t[i])
            return None if s is None else t[:i] + (s,) + t[i + 1:]
    a, b = t[1], t[2]
    if k == "if":                          # if true then yes else no  ->  yes
        return (t[2] if a[1] else t[3]) if a[0] == "bool" else None
    if a[0] == b[0] == "int":
        return ("int", a[1] + b[1]) if k == "add" else ("bool", a[1] < b[1])
    return None                            # for example: true + 1

Now try true + 3. It is not a value. But no rule fits: addition needs two numbers. The term is stuck. A stuck term is the formal picture of a crash, like TypeError in Python. Keep this word in mind. Type soundness is about it.

Big-step rules

A big-step rule t \Downarrow v says "t runs to the value v". It jumps to the end in one go.

\frac{t_1 \Downarrow n_1 \quad t_2 \Downarrow n_2}{t_1 + t_2 \Downarrow n} \;(n = n_1 + n_2) \qquad \frac{t_1 \Downarrow \mathtt{true} \quad t_2 \Downarrow v}{\mathtt{if}\ t_1\ \mathtt{then}\ t_2\ \mathtt{else}\ t_3 \Downarrow v}

A big-step proof is a tree, and the tree is exactly a recursive interpreter. Small steps are better for proofs about stuck states, loops and threads. With big steps, a program that loops and a program that is stuck both just have "no rule". Small steps tell them apart.

Denotational semantics maps each program to a mathematical object, for example a function from inputs to outputs. Axiomatic semantics gives meaning through proof rules, like Hoare logic in the logic and formal methods chapter. All three styles should agree on the same language.

Simple types and normalisation

Stuck terms come from mixing kinds of values. A type system sorts terms before they run. The simply typed lambda calculus (STLC) has base types like \mathtt{Int} and \mathtt{Bool}, and function types T_1 \to T_2. The arrow groups to the right: \mathtt{Int} \to \mathtt{Int} \to \mathtt{Int} is \mathtt{Int} \to (\mathtt{Int} \to \mathtt{Int}).

A typing judgement \Gamma \vdash t : T reads "with the names in \Gamma, the term t has type T". Three rules type the lambda part.

\frac{x : T \in \Gamma}{\Gamma \vdash x : T} \qquad \frac{\Gamma, x : T_1 \vdash t : T_2}{\Gamma \vdash \lambda x{:}T_1.\, t : T_1 \to T_2} \qquad \frac{\Gamma \vdash t_1 : T_1 \to T_2 \quad \Gamma \vdash t_2 : T_1}{\Gamma \vdash t_1\, t_2 : T_2}
  1. Inside the body, \Gamma = \{x : \mathtt{Int}\}. By the variable rule, x : \mathtt{Int}. By the rule for +, x + 1 : \mathtt{Int}.
  2. By the lambda rule, \lambda x{:}\mathtt{Int}.\, x + 1 : \mathtt{Int} \to \mathtt{Int}.
  3. The argument 2 has type \mathtt{Int}, which matches the input type.
  4. By the application rule, the whole term has type \mathtt{Int}.

For our small language with if, the rules are: + needs two ints and gives an int, < needs two ints and gives a bool, and if needs a bool test and two branches of the same type. Here they are as code.

fn type_of(t: &T) -> Result<&'static str, String> {
    match t {
        Int(_) => Ok("int"),
        Bool(_) => Ok("bool"),
        Add(a, b) | Lt(a, b) => { // both sides must be int
            let name = if matches!(t, Add(..)) { "add" } else { "lt" };
            if type_of(a)? != "int" || type_of(b)? != "int" {
                return Err(format!("{name} needs two ints"));
            }
            Ok(if name == "add" { "int" } else { "bool" })
        }
        If(c, yes, no) => {
            if type_of(c)? != "bool" { return Err("the test is not a bool".into()); }
            let (y, n) = (type_of(yes)?, type_of(no)?);
            if y != n { return Err("the branches have different types".into()); }
            Ok(y)
        }
    }
}
def type_of(t):
    k = t[0]
    if k in ("int", "bool"):
        return k
    if k in ("add", "lt"):                 # both sides must be int
        if type_of(t[1]) != "int" or type_of(t[2]) != "int":
            raise TypeError(f"{k} needs two ints")
        return "int" if k == "add" else "bool"
    if type_of(t[1]) != "bool":            # the test of an if must be a bool
        raise TypeError("the test is not a bool")
    yes, no = type_of(t[2]), type_of(t[3])
    if yes != no:
        raise TypeError("the branches have different types")
    return yes

Types do more than stop crashes. Try to type \Omega. In x\,x, the variable x must be a function T \to S and also its own input T. So T = T \to S. No finite type solves this. \Omega and Y have no simple type, and that is no accident.

In the simply typed lambda calculus, every well-typed term is strongly normalising. Every sequence of beta steps from it is finite, whatever order you choose (Tait, 1967).

Proof idea

Induction on the term does not work directly. An application t_1\,t_2 can create new redexes that are bigger than both parts. Tait's idea: define a stronger property by induction on the type. A term of base type is "reducible" when it is strongly normalising. A term of type T_1 \to T_2 is reducible when it maps every reducible input of type T_1 to a reducible output of type T_2. Then show two things. Every reducible term is strongly normalising. And every well-typed term is reducible, by induction on the typing proof. This method is now called logical relations.

In simple words: if the types fit, the program stops. That is great for logic and bad for programming. A language where every program stops cannot express every computable function. So real languages add a recursion operator such as fix, or named recursive functions. They give up normalisation and keep soundness. Total languages such as Agda and Lean keep normalisation on purpose. There a well-typed term is a proof, which is the Curry-Howard correspondence.

Type soundness: progress and preservation

Robin Milner put the goal in a short slogan in 1978: well-typed programs cannot go wrong. "Go wrong" has an exact meaning now: become stuck. Wright and Felleisen showed in 1994 how to prove it with two simple lemmas.

If \vdash t : T (a closed, well-typed term), then t is a value or there is a t' with t \to t'.

If \Gamma \vdash t : T and t \to t', then \Gamma \vdash t' : T. One step keeps the type.

If \vdash t : T and t \to^{*} t', then t' is not stuck. It is a value, or it can take another step. Every value it reaches has type T.

Proof

Induction on the number of steps. With zero steps, t' = t, and progress says t is not stuck. Now say t \to^{*} t'' \to t'. By the induction hypothesis and preservation, t'' has type T. By preservation again, t' has type T. By progress, t' is a value or can step. So it is not stuck.

Progress is proved by induction on the typing proof. For t_1 + t_2, each part is a value or steps. If both are values of type int, they are numbers, so the addition rule fits. Preservation is also by induction. The hard case is a beta step. It needs the substitution lemma: if \Gamma, x : S \vdash t : T and \Gamma \vdash s : S, then \Gamma \vdash t[x := s] : T.

Our small evaluator can show both lemmas at work. It prints every step with its type.

fn show(t: &T) -> String {
    let side = |u: &T| if is_value(u) { show(u) } else { format!("({})", show(u)) };
    match t {
        Int(n) => n.to_string(),
        Bool(v) => v.to_string(),
        If(c, y, n) => format!("if {} then {} else {}", show(c), show(y), show(n)),
        Add(a, b) => format!("{} + {}", side(a), side(b)),
        Lt(a, b) => format!("{} < {}", side(a), side(b)),
    }
}

fn trace(mut t: T) {
    loop {
        let ty = match type_of(&t) { Ok(ty) => ty.to_string(), Err(e) => format!("type error: {e}") };
        println!("  {:34} : {ty}", show(&t));
        match step(&t) {
            Some(next) => t = next,
            None => {
                println!("  {}", if is_value(&t) { "done: a value" } else { "STUCK: no rule applies" });
                return;
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let n = |v| Box::new(Int(v));
    trace(If(Box::new(Lt(Box::new(Add(n(1), n(2))), n(4))), Box::new(Add(n(10), n(5))), n(0)));
    trace(Add(Box::new(Lt(n(1), n(2))), n(3)));
}
def show(t):
    k = t[0]
    if k == "int": return str(t[1])
    if k == "bool": return "true" if t[1] else "false"
    if k == "if": return f"if {show(t[1])} then {show(t[2])} else {show(t[3])}"
    side = lambda u: show(u) if is_value(u) else f"({show(u)})"
    return f"{side(t[1])} {'+' if k == 'add' else '<'} {side(t[2])}"

def trace(t):
    while True:
        try:
            ty = type_of(t)
        except TypeError as err:
            ty = f"type error: {err}"
        print(f"  {show(t):34} : {ty}")
        if (nxt := step(t)) is None:
            print("  done: a value" if is_value(t) else "  STUCK: no rule applies")
            return
        t = nxt

N = lambda n: ("int", n)
trace(("if", ("lt", ("add", N(1), N(2)), N(4)), ("add", N(10), N(5)), N(0)))
trace(("add", ("lt", N(1), N(2)), N(3)))
  if (1 + 2) < 4 then 10 + 5 else 0  : int
  if 3 < 4 then 10 + 5 else 0        : int
  if true then 10 + 5 else 0         : int
  10 + 5                             : int
  15                                 : int
  done: a value
  (1 < 2) + 3                        : type error: add needs two ints
  true + 3                           : type error: add needs two ints
  STUCK: no rule applies

The first program has type int at every step. That is preservation. It never stops before it reaches a value. That is progress. The second program is rejected by the checker. If we run it anyway, it gets stuck at true + 3. Soundness says the checker is right to reject it.

What soundness buys, and what it does not

A sound type system removes whole classes of bugs, not single bugs. Which classes depend on what the types track.

Bug classes and the type feature that removes them
Bug classType featureExample
Wrong kind of valuebasic typesAdding a bool to an int will not compile.
Null dereferenceoption typesRust's Option<T> must be checked before use.
Use after free, double freeownershipA moved value cannot be used again.
Data racesownership plus marker traitsRust's Send and Sync control what crosses threads.
Missing casesum types with exhaustive matchA match that forgets a variant will not compile.

Soundness does not mean "no crashes at all". Division by zero and an index out of range are still possible. A sound language turns them into defined run-time errors, like a Rust panic, instead of undefined behaviour. They are values or steps in the semantics, not stuck states.

Not every type system is sound, and some are unsound on purpose. The TypeScript handbook says its type system allows some operations that are not known to be safe. It chose this for easier JavaScript patterns. Java arrays are covariant, so a String[] can pass as an Object[]. Java stays safe only by a run-time check that throws ArrayStoreException. C's casts and unions break soundness completely.

Polymorphism and type inference

The identity function \lambda x.\, x works on ints, on bools and on functions. In STLC you must write a new copy for each type. Polymorphism fixes this. There are three kinds.

Parametric polymorphism uses type variables. The identity has the type \forall \alpha.\, \alpha \to \alpha: for every type \alpha, a function from \alpha to \alpha. In Rust this is fn id<T>(x: T) -> T. The \forall part is a type scheme.

Hindley-Milner in simple words

ML, OCaml, F# and Haskell find these types with no annotations at all. The method is Hindley-Milner (HM). Roger Hindley found it in 1969 and Robin Milner in 1978. It has three ideas.

  1. Unknowns. Give every unknown type a variable: 'a, 'b, and so on.
  2. Equations. Each use creates an equation. If f x appears, then the type of f equals "type of x \to some result".
  3. Solving. Solve all equations by unification. Variables still free at a let become \forall variables.

Unknowns

Say f : 'a and x : 'b. We know nothing yet.

The inner call f x

f is applied to a 'b. So 'a = 'b -> 'c for a new result 'c. The value of f x has type 'c.

The outer call f (f x)

Now f is applied to a 'c. So 'b -> 'c = 'c -> 'd. Unification gives 'b = 'c and 'c = 'd.

Put it together

The whole term has type 'a -> 'b -> 'd. Replace what we learned: ('b -> 'b) -> 'b -> 'b.

Clean up

Rename the variable to 'a. The answer is ('a -> 'a) -> 'a -> 'a: "give me a function from a type to itself, and a value of that type".

If two types can be made equal by some substitution, then there is a most general one: every other solution is that one followed by more replacements. Robinson's algorithm (1965) finds it or reports that none exists.

If a term has a type in the Hindley-Milner system, it has a principal type scheme, and Algorithm W finds it. Every other type of the term is an instance of the principal one (Damas and Milner, 1982).

In simple words: HM never has to guess. The answer it finds is the most general one, so it never rejects a use that some other typing would allow. For fun x -> x it finds 'a -> 'a. The type int -> int is an instance of it.

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Ty { Var(usize), Int, Bool, Fun(Box<Ty>, Box<Ty>) } // Var(n): the n-th unknown

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Scheme { generic: Vec<usize>, ty: Ty } // forall generic. ty

enum E { Int, Bool, Var(&'static str), Fun(&'static str, Box<E>), App(Box<E>, Box<E>),
         If(Box<E>, Box<E>, Box<E>), Let(&'static str, Box<E>, Box<E>) }

fn fun(a: Ty, b: Ty) -> Ty { Ty::Fun(Box::new(a), Box::new(b)) }

fn free(t: &Ty, out: &mut Vec<usize>) { // the unknowns inside a (resolved) type
    match t {
        Ty::Var(v) => if !out.contains(v) { out.push(*v) },
        Ty::Fun(a, b) => { free(a, out); free(b, out) }
        _ => {}
    }
}

fn show(t: &Ty, names: &mut Vec<usize>) -> String { // print unknowns as 'a, 'b, ...
    match t {
        Ty::Var(v) => {
            if !names.contains(v) { names.push(*v) }
            let i = names.iter().position(|n| n == v).unwrap();
            format!("'{}", (b'a' + i as u8) as char)
        }
        Ty::Int => "int".into(),
        Ty::Bool => "bool".into(),
        Ty::Fun(a, b) => {
            let left = show(a, names);
            let left = if matches!(**a, Ty::Fun(..)) { format!("({left})") } else { left };
            format!("{left} -> {}", show(b, names))
        }
    }
}
import itertools

class TVar:                                # an unknown type; ref is set by unify
    ids = itertools.count()
    def __init__(self):
        self.id, self.ref = next(TVar.ids), None

INT, BOOL = ("int",), ("bool",)
def Fun(a, b): return ("->", a, b)

def prune(t):                              # follow the links to the current type
    while isinstance(t, TVar) and t.ref is not None:
        t = t.ref
    return t

def free(t):                               # the unknowns inside a type
    t = prune(t)
    if isinstance(t, TVar):
        return {t}
    return set().union(*(free(s) for s in t[1:]))

def unify(a, b):                           # make a and b equal, or fail
    a, b = prune(a), prune(b)
    if isinstance(a, TVar):
        if a is not b:
            if a in free(b):
                raise TypeError("infinite type (occurs check)")
            a.ref = b
    elif isinstance(b, TVar):
        unify(b, a)
    elif a[0] != b[0]:
        raise TypeError(f"cannot unify {show(a)} with {show(b)}")
    else:
        for x, y in zip(a[1:], b[1:]):
            unify(x, y)
struct Infer { links: Vec<Option<Ty>> } // links[n]: what unknown n was unified with

impl Infer {
    fn fresh(&mut self) -> Ty { self.links.push(None); Ty::Var(self.links.len() - 1) }
    fn resolve(&self, t: &Ty) -> Ty { // follow the links to the current type
        match t {
            Ty::Var(v) => match &self.links[*v] { Some(u) => self.resolve(u), None => t.clone() },
            Ty::Fun(a, b) => fun(self.resolve(a), self.resolve(b)),
            _ => t.clone(),
        }
    }
    fn unify(&mut self, a: &Ty, b: &Ty) -> Result<(), String> { // make a and b equal, or fail
        match (self.resolve(a), self.resolve(b)) {
            (Ty::Var(v), t) | (t, Ty::Var(v)) => {
                if t == Ty::Var(v) { return Ok(()); }
                let mut inside = vec![];
                free(&t, &mut inside);
                if inside.contains(&v) { return Err("infinite type (occurs check)".into()); }
                self.links[v] = Some(t);
                Ok(())
            }
            (Ty::Fun(a1, b1), Ty::Fun(a2, b2)) => { self.unify(&a1, &a2)?; self.unify(&b1, &b2) }
            (x, y) if x == y => Ok(()),
            (x, y) => Err(format!("cannot unify {} with {}", show(&x, &mut vec![]), show(&y, &mut vec![]))),
        }
    }

    fn instantiate(&mut self, s: &Scheme) -> Ty { // forall a. t  ->  t with a new unknown for a
        let new: HashMap<usize, Ty> = s.generic.iter().map(|&v| (v, self.fresh())).collect();
        fn copy(t: &Ty, new: &HashMap<usize, Ty>) -> Ty {
            match t {
                Ty::Var(v) => new.get(v).cloned().unwrap_or(t.clone()),
                Ty::Fun(a, b) => fun(copy(a, new), copy(b, new)),
                _ => t.clone(),
            }
        }
        copy(&self.resolve(&s.ty), &new)
    }
}
def instantiate(scheme):                   # forall a. t  ->  t with a new unknown for a
    names, t = scheme
    new = {v: TVar() for v in names}
    def copy(t):
        t = prune(t)
        if isinstance(t, TVar):
            return new.get(t, t)
        return (t[0], *map(copy, t[1:]))
    return copy(t)

def infer(env, e):                         # env: name -> (generic unknowns, type)
    k = e[0]
    if k in ("int", "bool"):
        return INT if k == "int" else BOOL
    if k == "var":
        return instantiate(env[e[1]])
    if k == "fun":                         # fun x -> body
        a = TVar()
        return Fun(a, infer({**env, e[1]: ([], a)}, e[2]))
    if k == "app":                         # f x: f must be a function from x's type
        f, x, r = infer(env, e[1]), infer(env, e[2]), TVar()
        unify(f, Fun(x, r))
        return r
    if k == "if":
        unify(infer(env, e[1]), BOOL)
        t = infer(env, e[2])
        unify(t, infer(env, e[3]))
        return t
    t1 = infer(env, e[2])                  # let x = e1 in e2: generalise here
    busy = set().union(*(free(t) - set(names) for names, t in env.values()))
    return infer({**env, e[1]: (free(t1) - busy, t1)}, e[3])
impl Infer {
    fn infer(&mut self, env: &HashMap<&'static str, Scheme>, e: &E) -> Result<Ty, String> {
        Ok(match e {
            E::Int => Ty::Int,
            E::Bool => Ty::Bool,
            E::Var(x) => self.instantiate(&env[x]),
            E::Fun(x, body) => { // fun x -> body
                let a = self.fresh();
                let mut inner = env.clone();
                inner.insert(x, Scheme { generic: vec![], ty: a.clone() });
                fun(a, self.infer(&inner, body)?)
            }
            E::App(f, x) => { // f x: f must be a function from x's type
                let (tf, tx, r) = (self.infer(env, f)?, self.infer(env, x)?, self.fresh());
                self.unify(&tf, &fun(tx, r.clone()))?;
                r
            }
            E::If(c, yes, no) => {
                let tc = self.infer(env, c)?;
                self.unify(&tc, &Ty::Bool)?;
                let (ty, tn) = (self.infer(env, yes)?, self.infer(env, no)?);
                self.unify(&ty, &tn)?;
                ty
            }
            E::Let(x, e1, e2) => { // let x = e1 in e2: generalise here
                let t1 = self.infer(env, e1)?;
                let t1 = self.resolve(&t1);
                let mut busy = vec![];
                for s in env.values() { free(&self.resolve(&s.ty), &mut busy) }
                let mut generic = vec![];
                free(&t1, &mut generic);
                generic.retain(|v| !busy.contains(v));
                let mut inner = env.clone();
                inner.insert(x, Scheme { generic, ty: t1 });
                self.infer(&inner, e2)?
            }
        })
    }
}
def show(t, names=None):                   # print unknowns as 'a, 'b, ...
    names = {} if names is None else names
    t = prune(t)
    if isinstance(t, TVar):
        return names.setdefault(t, "'" + "abcdefgh"[len(names)])
    if t[0] != "->":
        return t[0]
    left = show(t[1], names)
    if isinstance(prune(t[1]), tuple) and prune(t[1])[0] == "->":
        left = f"({left})"                 # arrows group to the right
    return f"{left} -> {show(t[2], names)}"
fn main() {
    let b = |e: E| Box::new(e);
    let (v, id_fn) = (E::Var, || E::Fun("x", Box::new(E::Var("x"))));
    let app = |f: E, x: E| E::App(Box::new(f), Box::new(x));
    let body = || E::If(b(app(v("id"), E::Bool)), b(app(v("id"), E::Int)), b(E::Int));
    let tests = [
        ("fun x -> x", id_fn()),
        ("fun f -> fun x -> f (f x)", E::Fun("f", b(E::Fun("x", b(app(v("f"), app(v("f"), v("x")))))))),
        ("let id = fun x -> x in ...", E::Let("id", b(id_fn()), b(body()))),
        ("fun id -> ...", E::Fun("id", b(body()))),
        ("fun x -> x x", E::Fun("x", b(app(v("x"), v("x"))))),
    ];
    for (text, e) in tests {
        let mut inf = Infer { links: vec![] };
        match inf.infer(&HashMap::new(), &e) {
            Ok(t) => println!("{text:28} : {}", show(&inf.resolve(&t), &mut vec![])),
            Err(err) => println!("{text:28} : type error, {err}"),
        }
    }
}
def V(x): return ("var", x)
def app(f, x): return ("app", f, x)
I = ("fun", "x", V("x"))
body = ("if", app(V("id"), ("bool", True)), app(V("id"), ("int", 1)), ("int", 0))
tests = {
    "fun x -> x": I,
    "fun f -> fun x -> f (f x)": ("fun", "f", ("fun", "x", app(V("f"), app(V("f"), V("x"))))),
    "let id = fun x -> x in ...": ("let", "id", I, body),
    "fun id -> ...": ("fun", "id", body),
    "fun x -> x x": ("fun", "x", app(V("x"), V("x"))),
}
for text, e in tests.items():
    try:
        print(f"{text:28} : {show(infer({}, e))}")
    except TypeError as err:
        print(f"{text:28} : type error, {err}")
fun x -> x                   : 'a -> 'a
fun f -> fun x -> f (f x)    : ('a -> 'a) -> 'a -> 'a
let id = fun x -> x in ...   : int
fun id -> ...                : type error, cannot unify bool with int
fun x -> x x                 : type error, infinite type (occurs check)

The ... stands for if id true then id 1 else 0. With let, the name id gets the scheme \forall \alpha.\, \alpha \to \alpha. Each use gets fresh unknowns, so id true and id 1 both work. As a lambda input, id has one unknown type. The first use fixes it to bool, and the second needs int. This is let-polymorphism. The last test fails the occurs check: 'a = 'a -> 'b has no finite solution, just like \Omega before.

"HM is fast" is true in practice, not in theory. Deciding ML typability is complete for exponential time (Mairson; Kfoury, Tiuryn and Urzyczyn, 1990). Nested lets can make types double in size again and again. Real programs never do this. Also, Rust and TypeScript do not use full HM. They ask for types on function signatures and infer only inside bodies.

Subtyping and variance

A function that wants an Animal should accept a Dog. A type S is a subtype of T, written S \lt: T, when an S can be used wherever a T is expected. One rule, called subsumption, makes this part of the type system.

\frac{\Gamma \vdash t : S \quad S \lt: T}{\Gamma \vdash t : T} \qquad \frac{T_1 \lt: S_1 \quad S_2 \lt: T_2}{S_1 \to S_2 \lt: T_1 \to T_2}

The second rule is for functions. Look at it closely. The output goes the same way: a function that returns a Dog can stand in for one that returns an Animal. The input goes the other way. A function that accepts any Animal can stand in for one that accepts only Dogs, but not the reverse.

  • Covariant: S \lt: T gives F[S] \lt: F[T]. Function outputs and read-only containers.
  • Contravariant: S \lt: T gives F[T] \lt: F[S]. Function inputs.
  • Invariant: no relation either way. Containers you can read and write.

Why must a mutable list be invariant? If list[Dog] were a subtype of list[Animal], you could add a Cat to a list of dogs. Here is that bug in Python. Python itself runs it. The type checker mypy (version 2.4.1 here) rejects it.

// &mut T is invariant in T: the compiler may not shrink the lifetime inside.
fn set<'a>(slot: &mut &'a str, value: &'a str) {
    *slot = value;
}

fn main() {
    let mut kept: &'static str = "forever";
    {
        let local = String::from("short life");
        set(&mut kept, &local); // would put a short-lived &str into kept
    } // local is freed here
    println!("{kept}"); // kept would point to freed memory
}
class Animal: ...
class Cat(Animal): ...
class Dog(Animal):
    def bark(self) -> str:
        return "woof"

def add_cat(pets: list[Animal]) -> None:
    pets.append(Cat())                # fine for a list of animals

dogs: list[Dog] = [Dog()]
add_cat(dogs)                         # mypy: list is invariant, so this is an error
print(dogs[-1].bark())                # at run time the last "dog" is a Cat
error[E0597]: `local` does not live long enough
  --> variance.rs:10:24
   |
 7 |     let mut kept: &'static str = "forever";
   |                   ------------ type annotation requires that `local` is borrowed for `'static`
 8 |     {
 9 |         let local = String::from("short life");
   |             ----- binding `local` declared here
10 |         set(&mut kept, &local); // would put a short-lived &str into kept
   |                        ^^^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
11 |     } // local is freed here
   |     - `local` dropped here while still borrowed
variance.py:11: error: Argument 1 to "add_cat" has incompatible type "list[Dog]"; expected "list[Animal]"  [arg-type]
variance.py:11: note: "list" is invariant -- see https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/common_issues.html#variance
variance.py:11: note: Consider using "Sequence" instead, which is covariant
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "variance.py", line 12, in <module>
    print(dogs[-1].bark())                # at run time the last "dog" is a Cat
          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'Cat' object has no attribute 'bark'

Rust has very little subtyping. The Rust Reference says it exists only for lifetimes (and higher-ranked types). &'static str is a subtype of &'a str, because a longer-lived reference can stand in for a shorter one. &'a T is covariant in T. But &'a mut T is invariant in T, for the same reason as the Python list. In the Rust example, kept has type &'static str. Invariance forces 'a to be 'static, so &local is rejected. Without that rule, kept would point to freed memory.

Memory trick: if you can only read it, it is covariant. If you can only write into it, like a function input, it is contravariant. If you can do both, it is invariant.

Ownership and linear types

Normal logic lets you use a fact many times, or not at all. Two structural rules allow this. Weakening lets you drop an assumption. Contraction lets you copy one. Jean-Yves Girard's linear logic (1987) removes them. Then each assumption is a resource. It is used exactly once.

Substructural type systems
SystemRule removedEach value is usedSeen in
Normalnoneany number of timesPython, Java
Affinecontractionat most onceRust moves
Linearcontraction and weakeningexactly oncelinear types in Haskell (an extension)

Philip Wadler's 1990 paper made the idea practical. If a value has only one owner, the compiler knows when it dies. It can free it or change it in place safely. Rust is built on this. A non-Copy value is affine: you may move it once, or drop it. A dropped value is freed exactly once, when its owner goes out of scope.

fn total(v: Vec<i32>) -> i32 { v.iter().sum() } // takes ownership of v

fn main() {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let s = total(v);          // v moves into total: used once
    println!("{s} {}", v.len()); // error: v was moved

    let mut w = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let first = &w[0];         // a shared borrow into w
    w.push(4);                 // error: push may move w's memory
    println!("{first}");
}
def total(v):
    s = sum(v)
    v.clear()                  # the callee can change our list
    return s

v = [1, 2, 3]
s = total(v)
print(s, len(v))               # 6 0: v changed behind our back

w = {"a": 1}
for key in w:
    w["b"] = 2                 # change the dict while we walk it
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `v`
 --> own.rs:6:24
  |
4 |     let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
  |         - move occurs because `v` has type `Vec<i32>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
5 |     let s = total(v);          // v moves into total: used once
  |                   - value moved here
6 |     println!("{s} {}", v.len()); // error: v was moved
  |                        ^ value borrowed here after move

error[E0502]: cannot borrow `w` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
  --> own.rs:10:5
   |
 9 |     let first = &w[0];         // a shared borrow into w
   |                  - immutable borrow occurs here
10 |     w.push(4);                 // error: push may move w's memory
   |     ^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
11 |     println!("{first}");

6 0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "own.py", line 11, in <module>
    for key in w:
               ^
RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

Rust finds both problems before the program runs. Python finds the second one only while running, and only for dicts. The first one it never reports: the list just changes behind our back. A move uses up the value. A borrow lends it for a while. The borrow rules say: many shared borrows or one mutable borrow, never both. A lifetime names the region where a borrow is valid. This is region typing, an older idea from research languages.

Is Rust's type system really sound? The RustBelt project (Jung and others, POPL 2018) built a formal model of a core of Rust in the Coq proof assistant, now called Rocq. It proved the core sound. It also proved that some standard library types that use unsafe inside, such as Rc and Cell, are safe to use from safe code.

Ownership does not mean "no memory leaks". Leaking is safe in Rust. std::mem::forget and Rc cycles both leak, as the Compilers chapter shows. Rust is affine, not linear: a value may be used at most once, and skipping its destructor is allowed.

Effects and continuations

A function in maths only maps inputs to outputs. Real functions also print, read files, throw errors, change memory or wait for the network. These are effects. An effect system puts them into the types.

  • Java's checked exceptions: throws IOException is part of the method type.
  • Rust's async fn marks code that can pause. unsafe fn marks code with extra rules. const fn marks code that can run at compile time.
  • Haskell's IO type marks code with side effects.

Continuations

At any point in a program, "what happens next" is a thing too. It is called the continuation. In print(1 + f(x)), the continuation of the call f(x) is "add 1, then print". In continuation-passing style (CPS), every function takes its continuation as an extra input and calls it with the result.

// Factorial in continuation-passing style: never return, always call k.
fn fact(n: u64, k: Box<dyn FnOnce(u64) -> u64>) -> u64 {
    if n == 0 {
        k(1)
    } else {
        fact(n - 1, Box::new(move |r| k(n * r))) // the rest: multiply by n, then go on
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", fact(5, Box::new(|r| r)));        // the last continuation: identity
    println!("{}", fact(5, Box::new(|r| r + 1000))); // the caller decides what comes next
}
# Factorial in continuation-passing style: never return a result, always call k.
def fact(n, k):
    if n == 0:
        return k(1)
    return fact(n - 1, lambda r: k(n * r))   # the rest: multiply by n, then go on

print(fact(5, lambda r: r))                  # the last continuation: identity
print(fact(5, lambda r: r + 1000))           # the caller decides what comes next
120
1120

CPS makes the order of work explicit. Every call becomes a tail call. Compilers for functional languages use CPS as an IR, and so do some JavaScript tools. Scheme's call/cc gives a program its current continuation as a value. Generators and async/await are limited forms. A paused generator is a continuation that can be resumed once.

Effect handlers

An effect handler is like an exception handler with one extra power. It receives the continuation. So it can answer the request and resume the code where it stopped. Below, the program asks for two numbers. It does not know who answers. Two different handlers give two different results.

// A program that asks for values. Each Ask holds "the rest of the program":
// a continuation that takes the answer and goes on.
enum Prog {
    Done(String),
    Ask(&'static str, Box<dyn FnOnce(i64) -> Prog>),
}

fn program() -> Prog {
    Prog::Ask("width", Box::new(|w| {
        Prog::Ask("height", Box::new(move |h| Prog::Done(format!("area = {}", w * h))))
    }))
}

// A handler answers each request and resumes the continuation.
fn run(mut p: Prog, answer: impl Fn(&str) -> i64) -> String {
    loop {
        match p {
            Prog::Done(result) => return result,
            Prog::Ask(question, rest) => p = rest(answer(question)),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", run(program(), |q| if q == "width" { 3 } else { 4 })); // a test handler
    println!("{}", run(program(), |_| 10));                                // another handler
}
# A program that asks for values. At each yield it stops; the paused
# generator is "the rest of the program": a continuation.
def program():
    w = yield "width"
    h = yield "height"
    return f"area = {w * h}"

# A handler answers each request and resumes the continuation.
def run(gen, answer):
    try:
        question = next(gen)
        while True:
            question = gen.send(answer(question))
    except StopIteration as done:
        return done.value

print(run(program(), lambda q: 3 if q == "width" else 4))   # a test handler
print(run(program(), lambda q: 10))                         # another handler
area = 12
area = 100

This pattern is called algebraic effects (Plotkin and Pretnar, 2009). The program says what it needs. The handler says how. A test can use a fake handler with no real files or network. OCaml 5.0 added effect handlers to the language. Its manual calls them a generalisation of exception handlers. OCaml 5.3 added special syntax for them. OCaml's continuations are one-shot: each must be resumed at most once. The language Koka puts effects in every function type.

Async functions in Rust and Python compile to state machines. Each await is a point where the continuation is saved. An executor such as tokio or asyncio is a handler for the "wait" effect. It resumes the continuation when the data is ready.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for programming language theory
PatternPurposeModelNote
Replace the input by the argumentRun a lambda term (beta step)(\lambda x.\, x\,x)\,a \to a\,aRename bound names first to avoid capture.
Leftmost, outermost firstReach a normal form if one exists(\lambda x.\, y)\,\Omega \to yCall by value would loop here.
Paths meet againTrust that the answer is uniqueChurch-RosserThe order can change termination, not the result.
Data as behaviourEncode values with functions\overline{2} = \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, f\,(f\,x)Use Z, not Y, under call by value.
Premises over a lineWrite semantics and type rulesif int and int, then intRead from top to bottom.
Not a value, no ruleSpot a stuck termtrue + 3Stuck is the formal word for a crash.
Progress + preservationProve type soundnessint at every step, ends in 15Run-time errors like division by zero stay possible.
Define by induction on typesProve normalisationTait's reducible termsPlain induction on terms fails.

Practice

What is the normal form of (\lambda x.\, \lambda y.\, x)\, a\, b?

  • a
  • b
  • \lambda y.\, a

First step: \lambda y.\, a. Second step: apply it to b, which is thrown away. The result is a. This function is \mathtt{TRUE}.

A term is well typed in the simply typed lambda calculus. What does strong normalisation promise?

  • It runs in linear time
  • Every reduction sequence from it is finite
  • It has no free variables

Whatever order you reduce in, you reach a normal form. Nothing is said about how many steps it takes.

Which Rust type is invariant in T?

  • &'a T
  • Box<T>
  • &'a mut T

Through a mutable reference you can both read and write. Like a mutable list, it must be invariant.

A closed, well-typed term is a value or can take a step. This lemma is called ?.

In Hindley-Milner, only names bound by ? get a type with \forall.

A type system where each value is used at most once is called ?.

  1. Compute \mathtt{SUCC}\ \overline{1} by hand, with \mathtt{SUCC} = \lambda n.\, \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, f\,(n\,f\,x) and \overline{1} = \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, f\,x.
    Answer

    Step 1: replace n by \overline{1}. You get \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, f\,(\overline{1}\,f\,x). Step 2: \overline{1}\,f becomes \lambda x.\, f\,x. No renaming is needed, because the argument f has no x in it. Step 3: applied to x, it gives f\,x. Result: \lambda f.\, \lambda x.\, f\,(f\,x), which is \overline{2}.

  2. Write the small-step steps for (2 + 3) < (1 + 1).
    Answer

    (2 + 3) < (1 + 1) → 5 < (1 + 1) (left side first) → 5 < 2 → false. Three steps, and the type stays bool all the way.

  3. Infer the type of fun f -> fun g -> fun x -> f (g x) by hand.
    Answer

    Let x : 'a. Then g : 'a -> 'b and f : 'b -> 'c. The result is 'c. So the type is ('b -> 'c) -> ('a -> 'b) -> 'a -> 'c. This is function composition.

  4. Is Callable[[Animal], Dog] a subtype of Callable[[Dog], Animal]? Explain with the function rule.
    Answer

    Yes. Inputs are contravariant: we need Dog <: Animal, which holds. Outputs are covariant: we need Dog <: Animal, which holds. A function that accepts any animal and returns a dog can stand in for one that accepts dogs and returns animals.

  5. Why can Rust not let you keep let first = &w[0]; across w.push(4)? Answer with what happens in memory.
    Answer

    push may need more room. Then the vector allocates a new buffer, copies the items and frees the old buffer. first would still point into the old, freed buffer: a use after free. The borrow rule "shared or mutable, not both" stops this at compile time.

  6. Expert: the language of the simply typed lambda calculus with ints cannot write an interpreter for itself. Why not? Use strong normalisation.
    Answer

    Every well-typed program halts, so every function you can write is total. Suppose a self-interpreter eval existed, also total. Then diagonalise: build bad(n) = eval(n, n) + 1. It is a program with some code m, and bad(m) = eval(m, m) + 1 = bad(m) + 1, which is impossible. This is the same diagonal argument as for the halting problem, and it is why total languages cannot be universal.

Key takeaways

  • The lambda calculus has variables, functions and calls. Beta reduction is its only rule.
  • Church-Rosser: different reduction orders may differ in stopping, never in the final answer.
  • Booleans, numbers and recursion can all be encoded as functions. The Y combinator gives recursion.
  • Small-step semantics shows each step and makes "stuck" exact. Big-step semantics is a recursive interpreter.
  • Simple types make every program stop (strong normalisation). Real languages add recursion and keep soundness.
  • Soundness = progress + preservation. A well-typed program never gets stuck.
  • Hindley-Milner infers the most general type with unknowns, equations and unification. Only let generalises.
  • Variance: read-only is covariant, function inputs are contravariant, read-write is invariant.
  • Rust ownership is an affine type system. Borrows and lifetimes control aliasing. RustBelt proved a core of it sound.
  • Effects are what code does besides returning. Continuations are "the rest of the program". Handlers combine both.

Sources

  • Software Foundations, vol. 2: Properties of STLC. Progress, preservation and soundness, checked in Rocq.
  • Software Foundations, vol. 2: Normalization of STLC. The logical-relations proof that well-typed terms halt.
  • Cornell CS 3110: Type Inference. Hindley-Milner with constraints, unification and let-polymorphism.
  • The Rust Reference: Subtyping and Variance. Lifetime subtyping and the variance table.
  • TypeScript Handbook: Type Compatibility. Its note on soundness and on function parameter bivariance.
  • OCaml manual: Effect handlers. Effects since OCaml 5.0, deep-handler syntax since 5.3, one-shot continuations.

Computer networks

A network moves bytes from one program to another program far away. It does this with layers. Each layer solves one problem and trusts the layer below. This chapter follows one web request through every layer, from signals on a wire to HTTP/3, and adds the maths of speed and delay.

  • Name the layers and say what each header adds to a packet.
  • Compute subnets, read routing tables and explain link state, distance vector and BGP.
  • Trace a TCP connection, its flow control and its congestion control, and compare it with QUIC.
  • Explain DNS, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and the TLS 1.3 handshake in round trips.
  • Estimate delay and throughput with simple formulas, and use ping, traceroute, dig and tcpdump.

Layers, packets and the end-to-end argument

You type https://example.com in a browser. About ten things happen before the page appears. Here they are, in order.

  1. DNS turns the name example.com into an IP address.
  2. The browser opens a connection to that address: TCP, or QUIC for HTTP/3.
  3. TLS agrees on keys, so nobody on the path can read or change the data.
  4. The browser sends an HTTP request: "GET /".
  5. IP carries each piece across many routers, one hop at a time.
  6. On each hop, Ethernet or Wi-Fi moves the bits to the next box.
  7. The server answers. The same layers carry the answer back.

Each step belongs to a layer. The common teaching model has five layers. The older OSI model has seven. It splits the top layer into application, presentation and session.

LayerJobUnitExamples
5 ApplicationWhat the program meansmessageHTTP, DNS, SMTP
4 TransportProgram to program, by portsegment or datagramTCP, UDP, QUIC
3 NetworkHost to host, across many hopspacketIPv4, IPv6, ICMP
2 LinkBox to box on one wire or radioframeEthernet, Wi-Fi
1 PhysicalBits as signalsbitcopper, fibre, radio

A layer works by encapsulation. TCP puts its header in front of the HTTP bytes. IP puts its header in front of that. Ethernet adds a header and a check value at the end. The receiver removes the headers in the opposite order.

Where should a job like "check that the data is correct" live? In every layer? Only at the ends? A famous paper by Saltzer, Reed and Clark answered this in 1984.

Some jobs can be done fully and correctly only by the programs at the two end points. Examples are checking that a file arrived unchanged, encryption, and removing duplicates. For such a job, the network in the middle cannot give a full answer. A lower layer may still do a partial version, but only to make the system faster.

Why it holds: the careful file transfer

A file goes from disk A to disk B. Errors can happen in many places. The disk can return a wrong block. A bug in the copy program can change bytes. Memory on host B can flip a bit after the network checked it. The network sees only the middle part of this path.

Say the path has n parts and each part works with probability p. The whole path works with probability p^n, as in the chain rule for agents. Making the network perfect still leaves the disks and the programs. So the receiver must compute a checksum of the final file and compare it with the sender's. If they differ, it asks again. That end check catches every error, wherever it happened. A per-link check now only saves time: it fixes errors early, so fewer full retries happen.

In simple words: the ends must check the result anyway. The middle can help, but it cannot replace that check. This is why the Internet core is simple. IP only tries its best. Reliability, order and security live in the end hosts, in TCP, QUIC and TLS.

A number shows the idea. A path has 5 hops. Each hop loses 0.1% of packets. The path delivers 0.999^5 \approx 0.995, so 99.5% of packets. Only an end-to-end retry brings this close to 100%.

"TCP has a checksum, so my file is safe." The TCP checksum is only 16 bits. It misses about one in 65,536 random corruptions, and it does not see bugs in your own program. Real systems add their own end check. Package managers compare a SHA-256 hash. Databases check each page. This is the end-to-end argument at work.

Links: signals, Ethernet and switches

A Wi-Fi channel is 20 MHz wide. The signal is 1,000 times stronger than the noise. How fast can it ever go? A formula from 1948 gives a hard limit.

A channel has bandwidth B hertz. Its signal-to-noise ratio is S/N, as a power ratio. The noise is random Gaussian noise. Then the highest rate with as few errors as you want is

C = B \log_2\!\left(1 + \frac{S}{N}\right) \ \text{bits per second.}

Above C, no code can make the error rate small.

Proof idea

Look at n samples of the signal as one point in n dimensions. Noise moves the point a little, into a small ball of radius about \sqrt{nN}. All received points lie in a big ball of radius about \sqrt{n(S+N)}. The receiver can tell messages apart if their small balls do not overlap. The number of small balls that fit is about \left(\sqrt{(S+N)/N}\right)^n. That is \frac{1}{2}\log_2(1 + S/N) bits per sample. A channel of width B carries 2B samples per second (Nyquist). Multiply, and you get C. Shannon's noisy channel coding theorem shows that good codes really reach this limit.

Engineers write S/N in decibels. 30 dB means 10^{30/10} = 1000. So the Wi-Fi channel gives C = 20 \times 10^6 \cdot \log_2(1001) \approx 199 Mbit/s. Two lessons follow. Capacity grows in a straight line with bandwidth. It grows only with the logarithm of the signal power. Doubling the power adds just 1 bit per second per hertz. That is why new Wi-Fi and 5G versions use wider channels and many antennas.
