check("S3", "r1(X) r1(Y) r2(X) r2(Y) w1(X) w2(Y)")
S1: edges T1->T2  serialisable as [1, 2]
S2: edges T1->T2 T2->T1  CYCLE, not serialisable
S3: edges T1->T2 T2->T1  CYCLE, not serialisable

S2 is the lost update. S3 is the write skew from the story: X and Y are Ana's and Ben's rows.

How can a database make sure that every schedule is serialisable? The classic answer is locking. A shared lock allows reading. An exclusive lock allows writing. A shared lock blocks exclusive locks, and an exclusive lock blocks everything else.

Say every transaction follows two-phase locking (2PL). In the growing phase it only takes locks. In the shrinking phase it only releases locks. Then every schedule that the locks allow is conflict-serialisable.

Proof

The lock point of a transaction is the moment it takes its last lock. Take an arrow T_i \to T_j in the precedence graph. Then T_i and T_j had conflicting operations on some item, and T_i went first. The locks conflict, so T_i released its lock on that item before T_j got its lock. T_i released something, so its lock point had already passed. T_j took a lock, so its lock point is at that moment or later. So \text{LP}(T_i) \lt \text{LP}(T_j).

Now suppose there is a cycle T_1 \to T_2 \to \dots \to T_k \to T_1. Then \text{LP}(T_1) \lt \text{LP}(T_2) \lt \dots \lt \text{LP}(T_1), which is impossible. So the graph has no cycle. A graph without a cycle has a topological order. Sorting the transactions by lock point gives an equal serial order.

In simple words: once you release a lock, you may not take a new one. Then the transactions line up in the order of their lock points. Example: T1 locks A, locks B, unlocks A, unlocks B. T2 waits for A, then locks A and B. T2's lock point comes after T1's, so the result equals "T1, then T2".

Real systems use strict 2PL: they hold locks until commit. Then no transaction reads data that may still roll back. 2PL can deadlock: T1 holds A and waits for B, while T2 holds B and waits for A. PostgreSQL looks for wait cycles after deadlock_timeout (one second by default) and aborts one transaction.

PostgreSQL mostly avoids read locks with MVCC. An update does not overwrite a row. It writes a new row version. Each version records the transaction that created it (xmin) and the one that deleted it (xmax). Watch the real system columns before and after an update:

SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM acct;
UPDATE acct SET balance = 80 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM acct;
SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct', 0));
ctid  | xmin | xmax | id | owner | balance
------+------+------+----+-------+--------
(0,1) | 801  | 0    | 1  | Ana   | 100
(0,2) | 801  | 0    | 2  | Ben   | 50
(2 rows)

ctid  | xmin | xmax | id | owner | balance
------+------+------+----+-------+--------
(0,2) | 801  | 0    | 2  | Ben   | 50
(0,3) | 802  | 0    | 1  | Ana   | 80
(2 rows)

lp | t_xmin | t_xmax | t_ctid
---+--------+--------+-------
1  | 801    | 802    | (0,3)
2  | 801    | 0      | (0,2)
3  | 802    | 0      | (0,3)
(3 rows)

Ana's row moved from slot (0,1) to slot (0,3). The new version has xmin = 802, the updating transaction. The page still holds the old version in slot 1, with xmax = 802 and a pointer to slot 3. A transaction whose snapshot started before 802 committed still sees balance 100. So readers never wait for writers, and writers never wait for readers.

Old versions must be cleaned up later. VACUUM does this. After VACUUM acct, slot 1 had lp_flags = 2: it was only a redirect to slot 3. The old data was gone. Writers still lock rows against other writers, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks rows on request. Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) adds tracking of read-write dependencies on top of snapshots. PostgreSQL has used SSI for its serializable level since version 9.1.

Read-modify-write in the application at read committed. The program reads the balance 100, computes 90 in Python, and writes SET balance = 90. Two such programs lose an update. Write SET balance = balance - 10 instead, so the database computes it on the newest version. Or use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or the serializable level with retries.

Write-ahead logging and recovery

A commit must survive a crash. But writing every changed 8 KB page to disk at every commit would be slow. The answer is a log. This is the real log that PostgreSQL wrote for two small updates right after a checkpoint, decoded with pg_waldump. The lines are shortened to fit.

pg_waldump -p data/pg_wal -s 0/3878AB8 -e 0/3878C70
rmgr: XLOG        len (rec/tot):  49/ 209, tx:   0, lsn: 0/03878AB8, desc: FPI_FOR_HINT , blkref #0: rel 1663/5/14141 blk 0 FPW
rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):  71/  71, tx: 804, lsn: 0/03878B90, desc: HOT_UPDATE old_off: 4, new_off: 5, blkref #0: rel 1663/5/14141 blk 0
rmgr: Transaction len (rec/tot):  34/  34, tx: 804, lsn: 0/03878BD8, desc: COMMIT
rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):  71/  71, tx: 805, lsn: 0/03878C00, desc: HOT_UPDATE old_off: 5, new_off: 6, blkref #0: rel 1663/5/14141 blk 0
rmgr: Transaction len (rec/tot):  34/  34, tx: 805, lsn: 0/03878C48, desc: COMMIT

Each update is one small record of 71 bytes plus a 34-byte commit record. Each record has a LSN. The first change after the checkpoint also logged a copy of the whole page (FPW). This page was almost empty, so the copy was only 209 bytes.

The rule is write-ahead logging (WAL):

  1. A change is made to the page in memory and described in a log record.
  2. The log record must reach disk before the changed page reaches disk.
  3. At COMMIT, the database flushes the log up to the commit record with fsync. Then it answers "committed".
  4. Changed data pages are written later, in the background, in big batches.
  5. A checkpoint writes all changed pages and records where recovery must start.

Why is this fast? The log is written in order, at the end of one file. One fsync can commit many transactions together: this is group commit. Random page writes happen later, and a page changed ten times is written once.

After a crash, PostgreSQL starts at the last checkpoint and redoes every log record after it. Pages become exactly as they were at the crash. What about transactions that never committed? Their row versions are on the pages, but the commit log says they did not commit. MVCC makes them invisible, and VACUUM removes them later. So PostgreSQL needs only redo.

Many other systems follow ARIES (IBM, 1992), which updates rows in place. It has three phases. Analysis reads the log from the last checkpoint to find unfinished transactions and dirty pages. Redo repeats history: it replays every change, even from losers. Undo rolls back the losers and logs each undo step, so a crash during recovery is safe too.

Expert: torn pages and full page writes

A database page is 8 KB, but a disk may write only 4 KB at a time. A crash in the middle leaves a torn page. A small redo record cannot fix a page that is half old and half new. So after each checkpoint, the first change to a page logs a full copy of the page. Recovery starts from that copy. This is full_page_writes = on, the default, as the settings query showed. The empty middle of the page is left out, which is why the copy above was small.

The WAL has more uses. Streaming the WAL to another server keeps a live copy for failover. Saving old WAL files allows point-in-time recovery: restore a backup, then replay the log up to 10:41 yesterday. Logical decoding turns the WAL into a stream of row changes for other systems. See Distributed systems and Modern data systems.

Turning off fsync to make tests fast, and then keeping it off in production. With fsync = off, a power failure can corrupt the whole database. The safe speed switch is synchronous_commit = off. A crash may lose the last few commits, but the data stays consistent.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for relational databases
PatternPurposeModelNote
Select, join, then projectWrite a question as algebra\pi_{\text{name}}(\sigma(\ldots) \bowtie \sigma(\ldots))Push selections down, before joins.
NOT EXISTS over NOT INFind rows with no matchWHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...)One NULL makes NOT IN return nothing.
Closure test for an FDCheck if X → Y follows{cid}+ contains officeFDs come from meaning, not from sample data.
Split on the bad FDReach 3NF or BCNFcourse(cid, title, teacher)Shared columns must be a key of one side.
One B-tree per hot queryFast lookups and rangesCREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id)Every index slows every write.
Leftmost columns firstUse a composite index(customer_id, created)Does not help a filter on created alone.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE, compare rowsFind why a query is slowrows=20 against actual rows=16Big gaps mean bad statistics.
Small outer side plus indexNested loop joinWHERE c.id = 7, cost 86Terrible for two big inputs.
Build on the small sideHash join for big equal joinshash 10,000 customers, probe 200,000 ordersOnly for = conditions.
Compute in SQL, not in the appAvoid lost updatesSET balance = balance - 10Read then write in the app loses updates.
Serializable plus retryStop write skewretry on SQLSTATE 40001Without a retry loop, users see errors.
Grow, then shrinkTwo-phase lockinglock A, lock B, unlock A, unlock BCan deadlock. The database then aborts one.
Log first, pages laterFast durable commits71-byte WAL record per updateNever run production with fsync off.

Practice

Which relational algebra operation removes columns?

  • Selection \sigma
  • Projection \pi
  • Natural join \bowtie

Projection keeps some columns and drops the rest. Selection keeps some rows.

What does SELECT 1 WHERE 3 NOT IN (1, NULL) return?

  • One row, because 3 is not 1
  • No rows
  • An error

3 <> NULL is unknown, so the whole NOT IN is unknown. WHERE drops rows that are not true.

Table R(A, B, C) has the FDs A → B and B → C. What is its candidate key?

  • {A}
  • {A, B}
  • {B}

{A}+ = {A, B, C}, so A alone is a key. {A, B} is a superkey but not minimal. {B}+ = {B, C} misses A.

In PostgreSQL, which isolation level prevents write skew?

  • Read committed
  • Repeatable read
  • Serializable

Repeatable read is snapshot isolation, which allows write skew. Serializable uses SSI and aborts one of the transactions.

A query reads 90% of a big table. The column has a B-tree index. What will a good optimiser usually choose?

  • An index scan, because indexes are always faster
  • A sequential scan
  • A hash index

Reading most pages in order is cheaper than jumping from the index to scattered pages. The real plan for customer_id < 9000 did exactly this.

A B+ tree has fan-out 400. With 3 levels it can hold about ? keys.

The anomaly where two transactions read 100, both add 10, and the result is 110 is called a ?.

A table has 500 pages and 40,000 rows. With PostgreSQL's default costs and no filter, a sequential scan costs ?.

  1. Write relational algebra for "names of students who take no course".
    Answer

    \pi_{\text{name}}\big(\text{students} \bowtie (\pi_{\text{sid}}(\text{students}) - \pi_{\text{sid}}(\text{enrolled}))\big). The difference finds the ids with no enrolment. The join brings back the names. Join on the id, not on the name, because two students may share a name.

  2. R(A, B, C, D) has FDs A → B, B → C, C → D. Is it in 3NF? If not, decompose it into BCNF.
    Answer

    The key is {A}. B → C and C → D have left sides that are not superkeys, and C and D are not part of a key. So R is not even in 3NF. Split on the violation C → D: R1(C, D) and R2(A, B, C). The shared column C is the key of R1, so the split is lossless. In R2, B → C still breaks BCNF. Split again: R21(B, C) and R22(A, B). The result is (A, B), (B, C), (C, D). Each table is in BCNF, and every FD lives inside one table.

  3. Prove that augmentation and transitivity give the union rule: if X → Y and X → Z, then X → YZ.
    Answer

    Augment X → Y with X: X → XY. Augment X → Z with Y: XY → YZ. By transitivity of X → XY and XY → YZ: X → YZ.

  4. Is the schedule r1(A) w2(A) w1(A) r2(B) w1(B) conflict-serialisable? Draw the precedence graph.
    Answer

    r1(A) before w2(A): T1 → T2. w2(A) before w1(A): T2 → T1. r2(B) before w1(B): T2 → T1. The arrows T1 → T2 and T2 → T1 make a cycle, so it is not conflict-serialisable.

  5. A query SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created is slow on a table of 50 million rows. What index would you create, and why?
    Answer

    Create CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created). The first column finds the customer's rows. Inside one customer, the rows are already sorted by created, so no sort step is needed. Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. If the query reads only a few columns, adding them with INCLUDE can allow an index-only scan.

  6. Expert. Explain why PostgreSQL needs only redo after a crash, while an ARIES system needs undo too. What extra work does PostgreSQL pay for this?
    Answer

    An ARIES system writes changes in place, so a page on disk may hold changes of an uncommitted transaction. Recovery must undo them. PostgreSQL never overwrites a row in place. It writes new versions, and visibility depends on whether the creating transaction committed, which is stored in the commit log. Versions from aborted transactions are simply invisible. The price is cleanup: dead versions take space until VACUUM removes them, tables can bloat, and transaction ids must be "frozen" before the 32-bit counter wraps around.

Key takeaways

  • A relation is a set of tuples. Relational algebra (σ, π, ×, ∪, −, ρ, ⋈) answers questions, and Codd's theorem says safe calculus is equally strong.
  • SQL is declarative algebra on bags with NULLs and three-valued logic. Beware NOT IN with NULLs.
  • Functional dependencies define keys. Armstrong's axioms are sound and complete, so the closure algorithm is a full test.
  • Normal forms remove repeated facts. 3NF always keeps every FD. BCNF removes all FD redundancy but may lose FDs.
  • B+ trees give lookups and ranges in three or four page reads. Indexes cost writes.
  • The optimiser picks plans by estimated cost from statistics. Compare estimated and actual rows when a plan is slow.
  • Nested loop, hash and merge joins each win in different cases: small with index, big with equality, already sorted.
  • Isolation levels allow different anomalies. Two-phase locking and SSI give serialisable results. MVCC lets readers and writers not block each other.
  • Write-ahead logging makes commits durable with one sequential flush. Recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint.

Sources

  • PostgreSQL 18 documentation: Transaction Isolation. The isolation table, snapshot behaviour, SSI and the 40001 error.
  • PostgreSQL 18 documentation: Using EXPLAIN. Plan nodes, startup and total cost, and the sequential scan cost formula.
  • PostgreSQL 18 documentation: Write-Ahead Logging. Why the log is flushed before data pages, and redo recovery.
  • E. F. Codd: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (1970). The paper that started the relational model.
  • Berenson and others: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels (1995). Snapshot isolation and the anomalies the SQL standard misses.
  • CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems (Fall 2025). A university course on storage, indexes, joins, optimisation, concurrency control and recovery.

Modern data systems

One relational database is the right start for most programs. But some jobs need other shapes: huge write rates, data spread over many machines, scans over billions of rows, or a stream of events. This chapter shows the main families of data systems, the structures inside them, and how to choose.

  • Describe key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores, and model one example in each.
  • Compare LSM trees with B-trees using read, write and space amplification, and state the RUM conjecture.
  • Explain why column stores and vectorised execution make analytic queries fast.
  • Explain distributed SQL, streaming logs and lakehouse tables in terms of logs, snapshots and consensus.
  • Choose a store for a workload with a decision tree, and defend the choice.

Four families beyond the table

A shop stores one customer with two orders. Here is the same data in four kinds of store.

GET customer:42        -> {"name":"Ana","city":"Oslo"}
GET orders:42          -> [1001, 1002]
GET session:9f3c       -> "customer 42, expires 18:00"
{ "_id": 42, "name": "Ana", "city": "Oslo",
  "orders": [ { "id": 1001, "total": 30.5, "items": ["pen", "ink"] },
              { "id": 1002, "total": 12.0, "items": ["paper"] } ] }
partition key: customer_id = 42      (decides the machine)
  clustering key: order_day DESC      (decides the order on disk)
  2026-11-14 | order 1002 | 12.00
  2026-11-02 | order 1001 | 30.50
(:Customer {id: 42, name: "Ana"})-[:PLACED]->(:Order {id: 1001})
(:Order {id: 1001})-[:CONTAINS]->(:Product {name: "pen"})
(:Customer {id: 42})-[:FOLLOWS]->(:Customer {id: 7})

Each shape makes some questions cheap and others hard.

  • A key-value store answers "give me the value for this key" very fast. It knows nothing about the inside of the value. Examples: Redis and Valkey in memory, Amazon DynamoDB as a service.
  • A document store keeps one nested record per id. "Load customer 42 with all orders" is one read. Joins across documents are weak. Example: MongoDB.
  • A wide-column store spreads partitions over many machines and keeps rows sorted inside each partition. It is built for huge write rates and queries that you know in advance. Examples: Apache Cassandra, Google Bigtable, Apache HBase.
  • A graph store keeps nodes and edges and follows links quickly. Examples: Neo4j and other property graph databases.

Two words help. OLTP means many small transactions, like "place this order". OLAP means large scans, like "revenue per city per month". Row stores suit OLTP. Column stores suit OLAP.

The line between families is not sharp. PostgreSQL stores documents in jsonb columns and indexes them with GIN. This ran on 50,000 product documents in PostgreSQL 18.3:

CREATE INDEX products_doc_idx ON products USING gin (doc jsonb_path_ops);
SELECT id, doc FROM products WHERE doc @> '{"tags": ["rust"]}' ORDER BY id LIMIT 2;
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM products WHERE doc @> '{"tags": ["rust"]}';
id  | doc
----+---------------------------------------------------------
100 | {"name": "item 100", "tags": ["rust", "db"], "price": 0}
200 | {"name": "item 200", "tags": ["rust", "db"], "price": 0}
(2 rows)

Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (cost=18.14..729.14 rows=1010 width=4)
  Recheck Cond: (doc @> '{"tags": ["rust"]}'::jsonb)
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on products_doc_idx  (cost=0.00..17.88 rows=1010 width=0)
        Index Cond: (doc @> '{"tags": ["rust"]}'::jsonb)

Choosing a NoSQL store "because it scales" before you know your queries. In a wide-column or key-value store, you design tables around the exact queries. A new kind of question later often means a new copy of the data. In a relational database, a new question usually needs only a new index. Start from the access patterns, not from the brand.

B-trees against LSM trees

A B-tree updates pages in place. That means random writes. A log-structured merge tree (LSM tree) never updates in place. Here is a toy version.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

// A toy LSM tree. None is a tombstone (a "deleted" marker).
struct Lsm { mem: BTreeMap<u32, Option<u32>>, runs: Vec<Vec<(u32, Option<u32>)>>, written: usize }

impl Lsm {
    fn put(&mut self, k: u32, v: Option<u32>) {
        self.mem.insert(k, v);                         // fast: memory only (plus a WAL in real life)
        if self.mem.len() == 4 {                       // memtable full: flush a sorted run
            let run: Vec<_> = std::mem::take(&mut self.mem).into_iter().collect();
            self.written += run.len();
            self.runs.insert(0, run);                  // newest run first
        }
    }
    fn get(&self, k: u32) -> (Option<u32>, usize) {
        if let Some(v) = self.mem.get(&k) { return (*v, 0); }
        for (i, run) in self.runs.iter().enumerate() { // newest to oldest
            if let Ok(p) = run.binary_search_by_key(&k, |e| e.0) { return (run[p].1, i + 1); }
        }
        (None, self.runs.len())
    }
    fn compact(&mut self) {                            // merge all runs; newest value wins
        let mut merged = BTreeMap::new();
        for run in self.runs.iter().rev() { for (k, v) in run { merged.insert(*k, *v); } }
        let run: Vec<_> = merged.into_iter().filter(|e| e.1.is_some()).collect(); // drop tombstones
        self.written += run.len();
        self.runs = vec![run];
    }
}

fn show((v, runs): (Option<u32>, usize)) -> String {
    format!("{} (runs read: {runs})", v.map_or("none".to_string(), |x| x.to_string()))
}

fn main() {
    let mut t = Lsm { mem: BTreeMap::new(), runs: vec![], written: 0 };
    for i in 0..20u32 { t.put(i * 3 % 8, Some(i)); } // 20 writes to 8 keys
    t.put(5, None);                                  // delete key 5
    t.put(6, Some(99)); t.put(2, Some(98)); t.put(7, Some(97));
    println!("runs: {}, get(1) = {}, get(5) = {}", t.runs.len(), show(t.get(1)), show(t.get(5)));
    t.compact();
    println!("after compaction: runs: {}, get(1) = {}, get(5) = {}", t.runs.len(), show(t.get(1)), show(t.get(5)));
    println!("user writes: 24, entries written to runs: {}", t.written);
}
import bisect

# A toy LSM tree. None is a tombstone (a "deleted" marker).
class Lsm:
    def __init__(self):
        self.mem, self.runs, self.written = {}, [], 0

    def put(self, k, v):
        self.mem[k] = v                           # fast: memory only (plus a WAL in real life)
        if len(self.mem) == 4:                    # memtable full: flush a sorted run
            run = sorted(self.mem.items())
            self.written += len(run)
            self.runs.insert(0, run)              # newest run first
            self.mem = {}

    def get(self, k):
        if k in self.mem:
            return self.mem[k], 0
        for i, run in enumerate(self.runs):       # newest to oldest
            p = bisect.bisect_left(run, (k,))
            if p < len(run) and run[p][0] == k:
                return run[p][1], i + 1
        return None, len(self.runs)

    def compact(self):                            # merge all runs; newest value wins
        merged = {}
        for run in reversed(self.runs):
            merged.update(run)
        run = sorted((k, v) for k, v in merged.items() if v is not None)  # drop tombstones
        self.written += len(run)
        self.runs = [run]

def show(r):
    v, runs = r
    return f"{'none' if v is None else v} (runs read: {runs})"

t = Lsm()
for i in range(20):
    t.put(i * 3 % 8, i)                           # 20 writes to 8 keys
t.put(5, None)                                    # delete key 5
t.put(6, 99); t.put(2, 98); t.put(7, 97)
print(f"runs: {len(t.runs)}, get(1) = {show(t.get(1))}, get(5) = {show(t.get(5))}")
t.compact()
print(f"after compaction: runs: {len(t.runs)}, get(1) = {show(t.get(1))}, get(5) = {show(t.get(5))}")
print(f"user writes: 24, entries written to runs: {t.written}")
runs: 6, get(1) = 19 (runs read: 2), get(5) = none (runs read: 1)
after compaction: runs: 1, get(1) = 19 (runs read: 1), get(5) = none (runs read: 1)
user writes: 24, entries written to runs: 31

Before compaction, the newest value of key 1 was in the second run, so a read checked two runs. Key 5 was found as a tombstone in the newest run, so the answer is "none". After compaction, one run is left and every read checks one run. The 24 user writes caused 31 entry writes: that is the write amplification, here about 1.3.

Log it

The write is appended to a write-ahead log on disk. If the machine crashes, the log rebuilds the memory part.

Memtable

The write goes into a sorted structure in memory, the memtable. The user gets "OK" now. No random disk write happened.

Flush

When the memtable is full, it is written out as one sorted, immutable file: an SSTable. This is one big sequential write.

Bloom filter

Each SSTable gets a Bloom filter. A read can skip a file when its filter says "certainly not here".

Compaction

In the background, files are merged into bigger sorted files in lower levels. Old versions and tombstones are dropped. Each level is about 10 times bigger than the one above.

Read

A read checks the memtable, then the files from newest to oldest. The first match wins. Filters keep most checks in memory.

The same three costs decide every storage design. Read amplification is how much extra you read. Write amplification is how much extra you write. Space amplification is how much extra you store.

B-tree (PostgreSQL, InnoDB)LSM tree (RocksDB, Cassandra)
Write pathchange a page in place, plus WALappend to WAL and memtable
Disk patternrandom page writeslarge sequential writes
Point readone root-to-leaf path, 3 to 4 pagesmemtable plus several files, helped by Bloom filters
Range readwalk linked leavesmerge a cursor from every level
Write amplificationa whole page per small changeeach item rewritten once per level. RocksDB says often above 10.
Spacepages partly emptyold versions until compaction
Best forread-heavy, mixed OLTPwrite-heavy, time series, logs

Two compaction styles exist. Leveled compaction keeps one sorted run per level. Reads are cheaper, writes more expensive. Tiered compaction lets several runs collect before a merge. Writes are cheaper, reads and space more expensive. RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra and many time-series databases use LSM trees.

"An LSM tree is always faster for writes." The first writes are fast. But compaction must keep up. If the write rate stays above what compaction can merge, files pile up, reads slow down and the system finally stalls writes. Measure throughput over hours, not over the first minute.

The RUM conjecture

Every structure above pays somewhere. A plain log file is cheap to write but slow to search. A sorted array is fast to search but slow to change. A 2016 paper by Athanassoulis, Idreos and others gave this pattern a name.

Measure an access method by three overheads, each a ratio that is at least 1. Read overhead R is data read divided by data wanted. Update overhead U is data written divided by data changed. Memory overhead M is space used divided by the size of the base data. The conjecture: an access method that sets an upper bound on two of R, U and M must accept a lower bound on the third. You can make two small, but not all three.

Why people believe it

It is a conjecture, so there is no proof. The evidence comes from the corners. To make reads cheap, you add help: indexes, sorted order, copies. Help costs space and must be updated on every write. To make writes cheap, you delay work and keep changes on the side, as an LSM tree does. Then reads must merge those changes, and old versions use space. To make space small, you drop help and compress. Then reads must scan, and writes must re-compress. No known structure escapes all three.

In simple words: read, update, memory. Pick two. Here are known structures with small numbers for N = 10^9 keys and pages of 512 keys.

StructureReadUpdateMemoryGood at
Append-only logscan N: badone append: bestabout 1: bestU, M
Sorted array\log_2 N \approx 30 stepsshift half: badabout 1R, M
Hash indexabout 1 pageabout 1 pageextra slots, often 1.5 or moreR, U
B+ tree\log_{512} N \approx 3.3 pagesabout 3 pagespages often two thirds fullbalanced
LSM treeseveral files, fewer with filterssmall, but rewritten per levelold versions until compactionU

The RUM view turns "which database is best?" into a better question: "which overhead can I afford?" Flash drives wear out with writes, so they favour low U. Small caches favour low M. Interactive apps favour low R.

The conjecture links to Data structures. A Bloom filter spends a little memory to cut reads. A B-tree's wide nodes cut reads by using the page size. Each tuning knob, like Bloom filter bits per key or the level size ratio, moves a design inside the RUM triangle.

Column stores and vectorised execution

An analyst asks: "What is the sum of one column over two million rows?" The program stores the same eight columns in two layouts and times the sum. The Rust version was built with rustc -O.

use std::time::Instant;

const N: usize = 2_000_000;

fn main() {
    // Row layout: each row keeps its 8 values side by side (64 bytes).
    let rows: Vec<[i64; 8]> = (0..N).map(|i| [i as i64; 8]).collect();
    // Column layout: each column is its own array.
    let cols: Vec<Vec<i64>> = (0..8).map(|_| (0..N).map(|i| i as i64).collect()).collect();

    let best = |f: &dyn Fn() -> i64| {             // best time of 5 runs, in ms
        (0..5).map(|_| { let t = Instant::now(); std::hint::black_box(f()); t.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e3 })
              .fold(f64::MAX, f64::min)
    };
    let r = best(&|| rows.iter().map(|row| row[3]).sum());   // touches 64 bytes per value
    let c = best(&|| cols[3].iter().sum());                   // touches 8 bytes per value
    println!("sum of one column, row layout:    {r:.2} ms ({} MB touched)", N * 64 / 1_000_000);
    println!("sum of one column, column layout: {c:.2} ms ({} MB touched)", N * 8 / 1_000_000);

    // Run-length encoding: a sorted column with few values shrinks a lot.
    let city: Vec<u8> = (0..N).map(|i| (i * 5 / N) as u8).collect(); // 5 cities, sorted
    let runs = 1 + city.windows(2).filter(|w| w[0] != w[1]).count();
    println!("city column: {N} values -> {runs} (value, count) pairs");
}
import time
from array import array

N = 2_000_000
rows = [(i,) * 8 for i in range(N)]                        # row layout: tuples of 8 values
cols = [array("q", range(N)) for _ in range(8)]           # column layout: 8 typed arrays

def best(f):                                               # best time of 5 runs, in ms
    times = []
    for _ in range(5):
        t = time.perf_counter(); f(); times.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3)
    return min(times)

r = best(lambda: sum(row[3] for row in rows))              # visits every row object
c = best(lambda: sum(cols[3]))                             # one tight array of integers
print(f"sum of one column, row layout:    {r:.2f} ms")
print(f"sum of one column, column layout: {c:.2f} ms")

# Run-length encoding: a sorted column with few values shrinks a lot.
city = [i * 5 // N for i in range(N)]                      # 5 cities, sorted
runs = 1 + sum(1 for a, b in zip(city, city[1:]) if a != b)
print(f"city column: {N} values -> {runs} (value, count) pairs")
sum of one column, row layout:    2.42 ms (128 MB touched)
sum of one column, column layout: 0.28 ms (16 MB touched)
city column: 2000000 values -> 5 (value, count) pairs
sum of one column, row layout:    35.48 ms
sum of one column, column layout: 15.28 ms
city column: 2000000 values -> 5 (value, count) pairs

Why? The CPU loads memory in cache lines. In the row layout, each wanted value drags its whole 64-byte row along. In the column layout, every byte loaded is a wanted value, and the CPU can add several values per instruction with SIMD. See Computer architecture.

A column store builds on this. It reads only the columns a query names. It also compresses well, because one column holds similar values.

  • Run-length encoding: a sorted city column became 5 pairs like (Oslo, 400,000) instead of two million values.
  • Dictionary encoding: store each distinct string once and keep small integer codes.
  • Bit packing: values from 0 to 9 need 4 bits, not 64.
  • Zone maps: keep the minimum and maximum of each block, so a filter can skip whole blocks.

The engine matters too. The classic Volcano model passes one row at a time between operators. Each row costs a function call and a branch. Vectorised execution passes a batch of values instead. DuckDB uses batches of 2,048 values by default. The loop over one batch is tight, fits in cache, and uses SIMD. The MonetDB/X100 project (2005) showed this idea. Other engines compile the whole query to machine code instead.

Here is a real run with DuckDB 2.0.0, installed from PyPI on the test machine. It writes two million orders to a Parquet file, then queries it.

import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()                                   # an in-memory database
con.sql("""
    CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS id, i % 10000 AS customer_id,
           ['Oslo', 'Lima', 'Pune', 'Kyiv', 'Accra'][i % 5 + 1] AS city,
           (i * 37 % 20000) / 100.0 AS total,
           DATE '2026-01-01' + (i // 10000)::INT AS day
    FROM range(2000000) t(i)
""")
con.sql("COPY orders TO 'orders.parquet' (FORMAT parquet, ROW_GROUP_SIZE 500000)")
# Parquet keeps min and max per row group and column: readers can skip groups.
print(con.sql("""
    SELECT row_group_id, path_in_schema AS col, stats_min, stats_max, compression
    FROM parquet_metadata('orders.parquet') WHERE path_in_schema IN ('day', 'city')
    ORDER BY row_group_id, col
"""))
plan = con.sql("""
    EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT city, sum(total) FROM 'orders.parquet'
    WHERE day >= DATE '2026-07-01' GROUP BY city
""").fetchall()
print(plan[0][1])

Look at "Row Groups Scanned: 1 / 4". The filter wants days from July. The statistics show that only row group 3 reaches July, so DuckDB skipped three of the four groups. It also read only the columns city, total and day. In total it read about 1 MB.

Using a column store for OLTP. Changing one order means touching every column file, often a compressed block in each. Column stores like DuckDB, ClickHouse and Snowflake shine for scans. A row store like PostgreSQL shines for many small writes. Many companies run both and copy data from one to the other.

Distributed SQL

One PostgreSQL server holds the shop. Then the shop goes global. One machine cannot hold or serve all the data. Distributed SQL systems keep the SQL and transactions, but spread the data. Examples are Google Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB.

  1. Split. The key space is cut into ranges (also called shards, regions or tablets). A range that grows too big splits in two.
  2. Copy. Each range has usually three copies on different machines or zones.
  3. Agree. The copies of one range form a consensus group, usually Raft. A write commits when a majority, 2 of 3, has it in its log. One machine can die without data loss.
  4. Coordinate. A transaction that touches several ranges uses a commit protocol across their leaders, like two-phase commit on top of Raft groups.
  5. Order. The system gives each transaction a timestamp. Spanner uses TrueTime: clocks with a known error bound from GPS and atomic clocks. It waits out the uncertainty, a few milliseconds, before it reports a commit. CockroachDB uses hybrid logical clocks instead.

Hash or range? Hash partitioning spreads keys evenly but breaks range scans. Range partitioning keeps neighbours together, so scans are cheap. But new keys that always grow, like timestamps, all land in the last range and make a hot spot.

The price is latency. A commit must reach a majority. With three copies in one region, that is a round trip of about 1 ms. With copies in three regions 70 ms apart, every write waits at least 70 ms. Consensus, quorums and two-phase commit are explained step by step in Distributed systems.

Using an always-increasing primary key, like a sequence or a timestamp, in a range-partitioned database. Every insert goes to the same range and the same leader. One node does all the work. Use a random or hashed key part, such as a UUID version 4, or put a hash bucket in front of the time.

Streaming logs

A shop has many services: orders, payments, email, analytics. Each one wants to hear about every order. Instead of calling each other, they share a log. The toy below shows the idea behind Apache Kafka.

// A toy partitioned log, the idea behind Kafka topics.
fn partition(key: &str, n: usize) -> usize {
    key.bytes().map(|b| b as usize).sum::<usize>() % n  // same key -> same partition
}

fn main() {
    let n = 3;
    let mut parts: Vec<Vec<String>> = vec![Vec::new(); n];   // append-only lists
    let events = [("ana", "login"), ("ben", "login"), ("ana", "add cart"),
                  ("max", "login"), ("ben", "pay"), ("ana", "pay"), ("max", "logout")];
    for (key, what) in events {
        let p = partition(key, n);
        parts[p].push(format!("{key}:{what}"));              // the offset is the index
    }
    for (p, log) in parts.iter().enumerate() { println!("partition {p}: {}", log.join(", ")); }

    // A consumer group: consumer A owns partitions 0 and 2, consumer B owns 1.
    let mut committed = vec![0usize; n];                     // next offset to read
    for p in [0, 2] {
        for off in committed[p]..parts[p].len() { println!("A reads p{p}@{off} {}", parts[p][off]); }
        committed[p] = parts[p].len();                       // commit after processing
    }
    // A new event arrives; A reads only what is new. Replay = move the offset back.
    parts[2].push("max:login".into());
    for off in committed[2]..parts[2].len() { println!("A reads p2@{off} {}", parts[2][off]); }
    println!("replay p0 from offset 0: {}", parts[0][0..].join(", "));
}
# A toy partitioned log, the idea behind Kafka topics.
def partition(key, n):
    return sum(key.encode()) % n                         # same key -> same partition

n = 3
parts = [[] for _ in range(n)]                           # append-only lists
events = [("ana", "login"), ("ben", "login"), ("ana", "add cart"),
          ("max", "login"), ("ben", "pay"), ("ana", "pay"), ("max", "logout")]
for key, what in events:
    parts[partition(key, n)].append(f"{key}:{what}")     # the offset is the index
for p, log in enumerate(parts):
    print(f"partition {p}: {', '.join(log)}")

# A consumer group: consumer A owns partitions 0 and 2, consumer B owns 1.
committed = [0] * n                                      # next offset to read
for p in [0, 2]:
    for off in range(committed[p], len(parts[p])):
        print(f"A reads p{p}@{off} {parts[p][off]}")
    committed[p] = len(parts[p])                         # commit after processing
# A new event arrives; A reads only what is new. Replay = move the offset back.
parts[2].append("max:login")
for off in range(committed[2], len(parts[2])):
    print(f"A reads p2@{off} {parts[2][off]}")
print(f"replay p0 from offset 0: {', '.join(parts[0][0:])}")
partition 0: ben:login, ben:pay
partition 1: ana:login, ana:add cart, ana:pay
partition 2: max:login, max:logout
A reads p0@0 ben:login
A reads p0@1 ben:pay
A reads p2@0 max:login
A reads p2@1 max:logout
A reads p2@2 max:login

The last output line is replay p0 from offset 0: ben:login, ben:pay. Every event of one user stayed in one partition, in order. Consumer A remembered where it stopped and read only the new event.

The Kafka words map onto the toy:

  • A topic is a named stream, such as orders.
  • A partition is an ordered, append-only log. Order is kept inside a partition, not across partitions. The key decides the partition.
  • An offset is an event's position. Consumers store their own offsets.
  • A consumer group shares the work. Each partition goes to one consumer in the group. More partitions allow more parallel consumers.
  • Events stay for a set time or size, not until they are read. A new service can start from offset 0 and replay history. With log compaction, Kafka keeps only the newest event per key, like a table.

Each partition is copied to several brokers, with one leader. Since Kafka 4.0 (March 2025), Kafka manages this metadata with its own Raft-based mode, KRaft, and no longer uses ZooKeeper. The newest release on the official download page in November 2026 was 4.4.0. Check that page, because this changes often.

Why does this matter so much? A log of changes is the most basic form of data. A table is the result of replaying a log. The database WAL from Relational databases is such a log. Change data capture reads it and publishes every row change to a topic. Search indexes, caches and warehouses then follow the database without changing the application.

Expecting "exactly once" for free. A consumer that processes an event and then crashes before it saves its offset will see the event again. So the normal promise is "at least once". Make handlers idempotent, for example with an event id that you store with the result. Kafka's idempotent producers and transactions give exactly-once processing only inside Kafka to Kafka pipelines.

Lakehouse tables

A company keeps years of events as Parquet files in object storage, such as Amazon S3. Files are cheap and any engine can read them. But a folder of files is not a table. Two writers can clash. A reader can see half of a job's files. Nobody knows which files form "the table" right now. A table format fixes this. The toy below shows the central trick.

// A toy table format: immutable snapshots plus one pointer that changes atomically.
struct Catalog { snapshots: Vec<Vec<String>>, current: usize }   // snapshot id = index

impl Catalog {
    // Optimistic commit: succeed only if nobody committed since we read `base`.
    fn commit(&mut self, base: usize, add: &[&str], remove: &[&str]) -> Result<usize, String> {
        if self.current != base {
            return Err(format!("conflict: you read v{base}, table is at v{}", self.current));
        }
        let mut files: Vec<String> = self.snapshots[base].iter()
            .filter(|f| !remove.contains(&f.as_str())).cloned().collect();
        files.extend(add.iter().map(|f| f.to_string()));       // data files are never edited
        self.snapshots.push(files);
        self.current = self.snapshots.len() - 1;               // the atomic pointer swap
        Ok(self.current)
    }
}

fn show(r: Result<usize, String>) -> String {
    match r { Ok(v) => format!("ok, now v{v}"), Err(e) => format!("rejected, {e}") }
}

fn main() {
    let mut cat = Catalog { snapshots: vec![vec![]], current: 0 };
    cat.commit(0, &["a.parquet", "b.parquet"], &[]).unwrap();   // v1
    cat.commit(1, &["c.parquet"], &[]).unwrap();                // v2
    let (x_base, y_base) = (cat.current, cat.current);          // two writers read v2
    let v = cat.commit(y_base, &["ab.parquet"], &["a.parquet", "b.parquet"]); // compaction
    println!("writer Y: {}", show(v));
    let v = cat.commit(x_base, &["d.parquet"], &[]);
    println!("writer X: {}", show(v));
    let v = cat.commit(cat.current, &["d.parquet"], &[]);       // retry on the new snapshot
    println!("writer X retry: {}", show(v));
    println!("current v{}: {}", cat.current, cat.snapshots[cat.current].join(", "));
    println!("time travel v1: {}", cat.snapshots[1].join(", "));
}
# A toy table format: immutable snapshots plus one pointer that changes atomically.
class Catalog:
    def __init__(self):
        self.snapshots, self.current = [[]], 0                  # snapshot id = index

    def commit(self, base, add, remove=()):
        """Optimistic commit: succeed only if nobody committed since we read base."""
        if self.current != base:
            return f"rejected, conflict: you read v{base}, table is at v{self.current}"
        files = [f for f in self.snapshots[base] if f not in remove]
        files += add                                            # data files are never edited
        self.snapshots.append(files)
        self.current = len(self.snapshots) - 1                  # the atomic pointer swap
        return f"ok, now v{self.current}"

cat = Catalog()
cat.commit(0, ["a.parquet", "b.parquet"])                       # v1
cat.commit(1, ["c.parquet"])                                    # v2
x_base = y_base = cat.current                                   # two writers read v2
print("writer Y:", cat.commit(y_base, ["ab.parquet"], ["a.parquet", "b.parquet"]))  # compaction
print("writer X:", cat.commit(x_base, ["d.parquet"]))
print("writer X retry:", cat.commit(cat.current, ["d.parquet"]))  # retry on the new snapshot
print(f"current v{cat.current}:", ", ".join(cat.snapshots[cat.current]))
print("time travel v1:", ", ".join(cat.snapshots[1]))
writer Y: ok, now v3
writer X: rejected, conflict: you read v2, table is at v3
writer X retry: ok, now v4
current v4: c.parquet, ab.parquet, d.parquet
time travel v1: a.parquet, b.parquet

Two writers started from version 2. Writer Y compacted two small files into one and won. Writer X's commit was rejected, because the table had moved on. X tried again on version 3 and won. A reader can still ask for version 1. This is time travel.

Real table formats work the same way, with more layers. In Apache Iceberg:

  1. Data lives in immutable Parquet, ORC or Avro files.
  2. Manifests list data files with statistics, such as min and max per column.
  3. A manifest list names the manifests of one snapshot. A snapshot is the table at one moment.
  4. A table metadata file holds the schema, the partitioning and the list of snapshots.
  5. The catalog holds one pointer to the current metadata file. A commit writes new files, then swaps this pointer atomically. If the pointer moved, the writer retries.

The Iceberg specification has format versions 1, 2 and 3. Version 2 added row-level deletes. Version 3 added types such as variant and geospatial types, default values, row lineage and binary deletion vectors. Version 4 is still being designed. Delta Lake and Apache Hudi solve the same problem with different metadata layouts.

A lakehouse is this setup: open files in cheap storage, a table format for transactions, and many engines on top. Spark, Trino, DuckDB and warehouses can all read the same table.

Streaming many tiny commits into a lakehouse table. Each commit adds files and metadata. Thousands of 10 KB files make every query slow, because opening a file costs more than reading it. Batch the writes, and run regular compaction and snapshot expiry, as writer Y did above.

Vector and graph databases: a short bridge

Two more families feed the AI systems part of this book. They get only a short visit here.

A vector database finds the nearest neighbours of an embedding. Exact search compares the query with every vector. Approximate indexes such as HNSW and IVF answer much faster with a small loss of recall. Vector search fits the RUM view too: HNSW spends memory on graph links to make reads fast. PostgreSQL with pgvector, and dedicated systems, are compared in Vector search and vector databases.

A graph question: "Whom can Ana reach in at most three hops?" In SQL, a recursive query does it. This ran on PostgreSQL 18.3.

WITH RECURSIVE reach(person, hops) AS (
  SELECT dst, 1 FROM follows WHERE src = 'ana'
  UNION
  SELECT f.dst, r.hops + 1 FROM reach r JOIN follows f ON f.src = r.person WHERE r.hops < 3
)
SELECT person, min(hops) AS hops FROM reach GROUP BY person ORDER BY hops, person;
person | hops
-------+-----
ben    | 1
eva    | 1
cai    | 2
dan    | 2
fay    | 3
(5 rows)

A graph database writes the same question as a path pattern. The Cypher below is for comparison only. It was not run for this chapter.

MATCH p = (a:Person {name: 'ana'})-[:FOLLOWS*1..3]->(b:Person)
RETURN b.name AS person, min(length(p)) AS hops
ORDER BY hops, person;

Graph stores keep each node's edges next to the node. Following an edge is a pointer jump, not an index lookup. This is called index-free adjacency. It pays off for deep, many-hop queries. ISO published GQL, a standard graph query language based on Cypher ideas, as ISO/IEC 39075 in April 2024. SQL:2023 added property graph queries to SQL itself (SQL/PGQ). Context graphs and GraphRAG are in Context graphs and GraphRAG.

A rule of thumb for graphs: up to two or three fixed hops, SQL joins are fine. Variable-length paths, shortest paths and graph algorithms on big graphs favour a graph engine or a graph extension.

Choosing a store

A team must pick storage for a new service. Walk down this tree.

  1. Trips and payments. Money needs transactions. Start with PostgreSQL. At 2,000 trips per minute, that is about 33 writes per second, which is easy for one server.
  2. Driver positions. 100,000 drivers send a position every 4 seconds. That is 25,000 writes per second, and only the newest position matters. Use an in-memory key-value store with a short expiry.
  3. Events. Trip started, trip ended, payment done: put them on a partitioned log keyed by trip id, so each trip's events stay in order.
  4. Reports. Copy the events into a lakehouse table or a column store. Analysts scan months of trips there without touching the live database.
  5. Check the RUM costs. Positions need cheap updates and small memory, and reads can be slightly stale. Payments need correct reads. Different parts, different stores.

Ask these questions before you choose:

  • What are the top five queries, and how often does each run?
  • What is the write rate at peak, and the data size in three years?
  • Which data needs transactions? Which can be a few seconds stale?
  • Who runs it at 3 a.m.? A managed service may cost more but save people.
  • How will data move between stores? Prefer a log and change data capture over writing to two stores from the app.

System design interviews reward reasons, not names. Say the access pattern, the numbers and the trade-off: "Writes are 50,000 per second and reads are by key, so an LSM-based wide-column store. We give up ad hoc joins and accept compaction cost." Then name a product as an example.

The "dual write": the application writes an order to the database and then sends an event to the log. If it crashes between the two, they disagree forever. Write once, to the database, and let change data capture publish the event. Or write the event into an outbox table in the same transaction, and publish it from there.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for modern data systems
PatternPurposeModelNote
Design tables per queryModel a wide-column or key-value storepartition by customer_id, cluster by dayNew questions may need new copies.
Buffer, flush, mergeFast writes with an LSM treememtable, then SSTables, then compactionCompaction must keep up with writes.
Tombstone, then compactDelete in an append-only storeput(5, None)Space comes back only after compaction.
Pick two of R, U, MReason about storage trade-offshash index: fast R and U, more MNo structure wins all three.
Read only needed columnsFast analytic scans16 MB instead of 128 MBBad for many small updates.
Min and max per blockSkip data without reading itRow Groups Scanned: 1 / 4Works best when data is sorted by the filter column.
Batches, not rowsVectorised execution2,048 values per call in DuckDBToo big a batch falls out of cache.
Range, copy three times, agreeDistributed SQLRaft group per rangeEvery commit waits for a majority.
Key decides the partitionOrder per entity in a logall events of trip 77 in one partitionNo order across partitions.
At least once plus idempotenceSafe event handlingstore the event id with the resultExactly once is not free.
Immutable files, atomic pointerTransactions on object storagecommit v4 only if the table is still at v3Retry on conflict.
Log first, derive the restKeep many stores in syncchange data capture from the WALAvoid dual writes from the application.

Practice

A service writes 200,000 sensor readings per second and reads them by sensor and time range. Which storage structure fits best?

  • A B-tree updated in place
  • An LSM tree with time-ordered keys per sensor
  • A hash index

An LSM tree turns the writes into sequential flushes. Keys like (sensor, time) keep each sensor's range sorted. A hash index cannot answer time ranges.

Why does a column store read less data for SELECT sum(total) FROM orders?

  • It caches the answer.
  • It reads only the total column, and that column compresses well.
  • It uses a B-tree on total.

The other columns are never read. Similar values in one column also compress with dictionary, run-length or bit-packing encodings.

In Kafka, where is the order of events guaranteed?

  • Across the whole topic
  • Inside one partition
  • Inside one consumer group

A partition is one append-only log. Events with the same key go to the same partition, so they keep their order.

Two jobs commit to the same Iceberg table from the same base snapshot. What happens to the second one?

  • Its files overwrite the first job's files.
  • The pointer swap fails, and it must retry on the new snapshot.
  • Both commits are lost.

The catalog swaps the metadata pointer only if it still points to the base the writer read. This is optimistic concurrency.

According to the RUM conjecture, what does a hash index usually give up?

  • Fast reads
  • Fast updates
  • Low memory overhead

Hash indexes give about one page per read and update, but they need extra empty slots and cannot answer ranges.

A distributed SQL range has 5 copies. A write commits after ? copies have it.

A table has 4 Parquet row groups, and the zone maps show only 1 can match. The engine scans ? row group(s).

An LSM tree got 1 GB of user writes and wrote 12 GB to disk. Its write amplification is ?.

  1. Model "the last 20 messages in a chat room" for a wide-column store. Give the partition key and the clustering key.
    Answer

    Partition key: room_id, so one room's messages live together. Clustering key: sent_at DESC (or a time-based id), so the newest come first. "Last 20 messages" is then one partition read that stops after 20 rows. A very busy room can make one partition too big, so add a time bucket, such as the day, to the partition key.

  2. Explain with the RUM conjecture why an LSM tree is good on flash drives but needs Bloom filters.
    Answer

    Flash drives wear out with writes and prefer sequential writes. An LSM tree lowers random update cost: writes go to memory and are flushed in large sequential files. The price moves to reads, which may check several files, and to space, which holds old versions. Bloom filters spend a little memory to cut the read overhead back down. That is the trade inside the RUM triangle: some M to fix R.

  3. A shop's order service writes to PostgreSQL and then publishes to Kafka. Sometimes events are missing. Why, and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    This is a dual write. A crash or a network error between the database commit and the Kafka send loses the event. Fix it with the outbox pattern: write the order and an outbox row in one transaction, then publish outbox rows to Kafka. Or use change data capture on PostgreSQL's WAL. Consumers must still be idempotent, because a publish can be repeated.

  4. A table is range-partitioned by created_at. Writes are slow, and one node is at 100% CPU. Explain and fix.
    Answer

    All new rows have the newest timestamps, so they all fall in the last range. That range's leader takes every insert: a hot spot. Fix it with a key that spreads load, such as (hash(user_id) mod 16, created_at), or a random UUID primary key with a secondary index on time. Time-range queries then fan out to 16 buckets, which is the trade-off.

  5. Estimate the data DuckDB must read for SELECT avg(total) FROM events on 1 billion rows with 20 columns of 8 bytes each. Compare a row store and a column store with 4 times compression.
    Answer

    Row store: 1 billion × 20 × 8 bytes = 160 GB. Column store: one column is 1 billion × 8 bytes = 8 GB, and 4 times compression gives 2 GB. That is 80 times less data. At 2 GB/s, that is about 1 second instead of 80 seconds.

  6. Expert. A global payment system needs serialisable transactions in three regions, 80 ms apart. Estimate the minimum commit latency for a distributed SQL database with one copy per region, and suggest ways to reduce it.
    Answer

    A commit needs a majority, 2 of 3 copies. The leader must reach at least one other region: one round trip of about 80 ms. With a transaction across two ranges whose leaders are in different regions, the commit protocol adds more round trips, so 160 ms or more is realistic. Ways to reduce it: put the leaders of each customer's data in that customer's home region, use five copies with two in the home region so a majority is nearer, keep transactions to one range, or split the work so only the payment step is global.

Key takeaways

  • Key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores each make some queries cheap. Design them around known access patterns.
  • B-trees update in place and favour reads. LSM trees buffer and merge and favour writes. Compaction and Bloom filters decide their read cost.
  • The RUM conjecture: read, update and memory overheads cannot all be minimal. Every design picks two.
  • Column stores read only needed columns, compress them, and skip blocks with min and max statistics. Vectorised engines process batches of values.
  • Distributed SQL splits keys into ranges, copies each range, and agrees with Raft. Every commit pays at least one majority round trip.
  • A partitioned log keeps order per key, lets consumers replay, and connects services. Plan for at-least-once delivery.
  • Lakehouse table formats add snapshots and atomic commits to files in object storage, with optimistic concurrency and time travel.
  • Vector and graph databases serve AI systems. PostgreSQL can often start as a document, vector or graph store before you need a dedicated one.

Sources

  • Athanassoulis and others: Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture (EDBT 2016). The definitions of read, update and memory overhead and the conjecture.
  • RocksDB wiki: Leveled Compaction. Levels, L0 files, compaction scores and write amplification above 10.
  • DuckDB documentation: Vectors. Vectorised execution and the default vector size of 2,048 values.
  • Apache Iceberg table specification. Format versions, snapshots, manifests and the atomic commit with retries.
  • Apache Kafka downloads. Release history, including 4.0.0 in March 2025 and the current release.
  • PostgreSQL 18 documentation: JSON types. The jsonb type, containment and GIN indexing used in the document example.

Distributed systems

A distributed system is many computers that work as one. They talk only by messages, and messages can be late or lost. This chapter shows what can go wrong and which problems have no solution. Then it shows how real systems like Raft, Cassandra and MapReduce still work well.

  • Name the failure models and timing models, and explain the two generals problem.
  • Order events with Lamport clocks and vector clocks.
  • Compare leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication, and size a quorum.
  • Place a system on the ladder of consistency models, and state FLP, CAP and the Byzantine bound.
  • Walk through Raft step by step, and choose between two-phase commit, sagas and CRDTs.

What can go wrong: failure models

Start with a small example. Three servers keep copies of a shopping cart. Server C stops answering. Is it dead? Is it slow? Is the network cable broken? Server A cannot know. It only sees silence.

A node is one computer in the system. Nodes talk by messages. A network partition happens when some nodes cannot reach others. To reason about a system, we first say which faults we expect. That choice is the failure model.

Node faults, from easy to hard
ModelWhat a faulty node doesExample
Crash-stopStops foreverA disk dies and the server is removed
Crash-recoveryStops, then comes back with what it saved on diskA server reboots after a power cut
OmissionLoses some messagesA full network buffer drops packets
ByzantineAnything at all, even liesA bug, a bit flip, or an attacker

We also choose a timing model. In a synchronous system, every message arrives within a known time. In an asynchronous system, there is no time limit at all. Real networks are in between. They are partially synchronous: usually fast, but sometimes slow for a while.

Now the oldest problem. Two generals must attack a city at the same time. They send messengers through a valley. The enemy can catch any messenger.

Two parties talk over a channel that can lose any message. No protocol with a finite number of messages makes both parties sure that they agree. So a sender can never be sure that its last message arrived.

Proof idea

Take the shortest protocol that works. Its last message can be lost. The sender of that last message acts the same either way, because it cannot see the loss. So the protocol must also work without that message. Then a shorter protocol works, which is a contradiction. Jim Gray gave the problem its name in 1978.

In practice this means: a timeout does not tell you what happened. The request may be lost, or only the reply. The chapter Making AI systems fast and reliable shows the practical answer: retry until you get a reply, and make the receiver idempotent with keys.

"No reply in 2 seconds, so the node is dead." A timeout only means "no reply yet". A slow node may wake up and act on old orders. Good designs stay correct even when the timeout guess is wrong.

Time and order of events

Server A writes name = "Ann" at 10:00:00.010 by its clock. Server B writes name = "Bo" at 10:00:00.005 by its clock. B's clock is 30 ms slow. The rule "the latest timestamp wins" keeps Ann, but Bo really came last. Physical clocks drift, so we cannot trust them to order events.

Leslie Lamport gave a better idea in 1978. Use the happens-before relation, written a \to b. It holds in three cases. Both events are in one process and a comes first. Or a sends a message and b receives it. Or a chain of such steps links them. If neither a \to b nor b \to a, the two events are concurrent, written a \parallel b.

A Lamport clock is one counter per process. Before each event, add 1. Put the counter on every message. On receive, set the counter to the larger of yours and the message's, then add 1. A vector clock keeps one counter for every process. On receive, take the larger value in each position, then add 1 to your own position.

Lamport clocks: if a \to b then L(a) \lt L(b). The opposite is not true. Vector clocks: a \to b exactly when V(a) \le V(b) in every position and V(a) \ne V(b).

The code runs the picture above and checks three pairs of events.

// Lamport clocks and vector clocks for three processes A, B, C.
const N: usize = 3; // processes 0=A, 1=B, 2=C

struct Sim {
    lamport: [u32; N],
    vector: [[u32; N]; N],
    stamps: Vec<(&'static str, u32, [u32; N])>, // event, Lamport, vector
}

impl Sim {
    fn tick(&mut self, p: usize, name: &'static str) { // local event or send
        self.lamport[p] += 1;
        self.vector[p][p] += 1;
        self.stamps.push((name, self.lamport[p], self.vector[p]));
    }
    fn receive(&mut self, p: usize, name: &'static str, msg: &str) {
        let (l_msg, v_msg) = self.get(msg); // the stamp travels with the message
        self.lamport[p] = self.lamport[p].max(l_msg) + 1;
        for i in 0..N {
            self.vector[p][i] = self.vector[p][i].max(v_msg[i]);
        }
        self.vector[p][p] += 1;
        self.stamps.push((name, self.lamport[p], self.vector[p]));
    }
    fn get(&self, name: &str) -> (u32, [u32; N]) {
        let s = self.stamps.iter().find(|s| s.0 == name).unwrap();
        (s.1, s.2)
    }
    fn order(&self, x: &str, y: &str) -> &'static str {
        let (vx, vy) = (self.get(x).1, self.get(y).1);
        let le = |a: [u32; N], b: [u32; N]| (0..N).all(|i| a[i] <= b[i]) && a != b;
        if le(vx, vy) { "->" } else if le(vy, vx) { "<-" } else { "||" } // || = concurrent
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut s = Sim { lamport: [0; N], vector: [[0; N]; N], stamps: vec![] };
    s.tick(0, "a1"); s.tick(0, "a2_send"); // A works, then sends m1 to B
    s.tick(2, "c1"); // C works on its own
    s.receive(1, "b1_recv", "a2_send"); s.tick(1, "b2_send"); // B gets m1, sends m2 to C
    s.receive(2, "c2_recv", "b2_send"); s.tick(0, "a3");
    for (name, l, v) in &s.stamps {
        println!("{name:8} L={l}  V={v:?}");
    }
    for (x, y) in [("a1", "c2_recv"), ("c1", "b1_recv"), ("a3", "b2_send")] {
        println!("{x} {} {y}   (L: {} vs {})", s.order(x, y), s.get(x).0, s.get(y).0);
    }
}
# Lamport clocks and vector clocks for three processes A, B, C.
N = 3                                   # processes 0=A, 1=B, 2=C
lamport = [0] * N
vector = [[0] * N for _ in range(N)]
stamps = {}                             # event name -> (Lamport, vector)


def tick(p: int, name: str) -> None:    # local event or send
    lamport[p] += 1
    vector[p][p] += 1
    stamps[name] = (lamport[p], vector[p][:])


def receive(p: int, name: str, msg: str) -> None:
    l_msg, v_msg = stamps[msg]          # the stamp travels with the message
    lamport[p] = max(lamport[p], l_msg) + 1
    vector[p] = [max(a, b) for a, b in zip(vector[p], v_msg)]
    vector[p][p] += 1
    stamps[name] = (lamport[p], vector[p][:])


def order(x: str, y: str) -> str:
    vx, vy = stamps[x][1], stamps[y][1]
    if all(a <= b for a, b in zip(vx, vy)) and vx != vy:
        return "->"                     # x happened before y
    if all(b <= a for a, b in zip(vx, vy)) and vx != vy:
        return "<-"
    return "||"                         # concurrent


tick(0, "a1"); tick(0, "a2_send")       # A works, then sends m1 to B
tick(2, "c1")                           # C works on its own
receive(1, "b1_recv", "a2_send"); tick(1, "b2_send")   # B gets m1, sends m2 to C
receive(2, "c2_recv", "b2_send"); tick(0, "a3")
for name, (l, v) in stamps.items():
    print(f"{name:8} L={l}  V={v}")
for x, y in [("a1", "c2_recv"), ("c1", "b1_recv"), ("a3", "b2_send")]:
    print(f"{x} {order(x, y)} {y}   (L: {stamps[x][0]} vs {stamps[y][0]})")
a1       L=1  V=[1, 0, 0]
a2_send  L=2  V=[2, 0, 0]
c1       L=1  V=[0, 0, 1]
b1_recv  L=3  V=[2, 1, 0]
b2_send  L=4  V=[2, 2, 0]
c2_recv  L=5  V=[2, 2, 2]
a3       L=3  V=[3, 0, 0]
a1 -> c2_recv   (L: 1 vs 5)
c1 || b1_recv   (L: 1 vs 3)
a3 || b2_send   (L: 3 vs 4)

Look at c1 and b1_recv. The Lamport values are 1 and 3, so they look ordered. The vector clocks show the truth: they are concurrent. Vector clocks cost more space, one number per process. Dynamo used them to find conflicting writes. Fidge and Mattern described vector clocks in 1988.

Some databases mix both worlds. Google Spanner uses TrueTime. It gives each timestamp as an interval of uncertainty, and a commit waits until the interval has passed. CockroachDB uses hybrid logical clocks.

Using "last write wins" with wall-clock time and thinking no data is lost. When clocks drift, a newer write can lose to an older one, and nobody sees an error. If lost writes matter, detect concurrent writes with version vectors, or use a CRDT.

Replication and quorums

Replication keeps copies of data on several nodes. Each copy is a replica. Replicas give more read capacity and survive crashes. The hard part is keeping the copies the same while data changes.

Three ways to replicate
StyleHow writes flowGood atHard partExample
Single leaderAll writes go to one leader. Followers copy its log.Simple order of writesFailover when the leader diesPostgreSQL streaming replication
Multi-leaderSeveral leaders, often one per data centreWrites near the user, offline workWrite conflictsCalendar apps, multi-region setups
LeaderlessThe client writes to many replicas and reads from manyNo failover stepStale reads, conflict repairDynamo, Cassandra

A leader can send changes synchronously or asynchronously. With asynchronous copies, followers lag behind. A user writes to the leader, then reads from a follower, and sees old data. This delay is called replication lag.

Leaderless systems use voting. Take N = 3 replicas. A write waits for W = 2 replicas to say OK. A read asks R = 2 replicas and keeps the newest version. Any two replicas out of three share at least one replica. So the read always reaches someone who has the new write.

A value has N replicas. Every write waits for W replicas and every read asks R replicas. If R + W \gt N, then every read set and every write set share at least one replica.

Proof

Put the W write replicas and the R read replicas into N boxes. If no box got both, they would need R + W different boxes. But R + W \gt N, so that is impossible. This is the pigeonhole principle. In fact the overlap is at least R + W - N. A set of replicas that is large enough to vote is called a quorum. Gifford used weighted voting like this in 1979.

When R + W \le N, a read can miss the write. The chance is easy to compute: all R read replicas come from the N - W old ones. So P(\text{stale}) = \binom{N-W}{R} / \binom{N}{R}. The simulation checks the formula with the same seeded generator in both languages.

// Leaderless replication: write to W random replicas, read from R random replicas.
struct Lcg(u64); // same LCG as the Python version
impl Lcg {
    fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_mul(6364136223846793005).wrapping_add(1442695040888963407);
        self.0 >> 33
    }
    fn pick(&mut self, n: usize, k: usize) -> Vec<bool> { // k distinct replicas out of n
        let mut ids: Vec<usize> = (0..n).collect();
        for i in 0..k { // partial Fisher-Yates shuffle
            let j = i + (self.next_u32() % (n - i) as u64) as usize;
            ids.swap(i, j);
        }
        let mut chosen = vec![false; n];
        for &id in &ids[..k] { chosen[id] = true; }
        chosen
    }
}

fn comb(n: usize, k: usize) -> f64 {
    if k > n { return 0.0; }
    (0..k).fold(1.0, |acc, i| acc * (n - i) as f64 / (i + 1) as f64)
}

fn main() {
    const TRIALS: u32 = 100_000;
    let mut rng = Lcg(42);
    println!(" N  R  W  R+W>N  stale reads  formula");
    for (n, r, w) in [(3, 1, 1), (3, 1, 2), (3, 2, 2), (5, 1, 3), (5, 2, 3), (5, 3, 3)] {
        let mut stale = 0;
        for _ in 0..TRIALS {
            let written = rng.pick(n, w); // replicas that got the new value
            let read = rng.pick(n, r); // replicas the reader asks
            if !(0..n).any(|i| written[i] && read[i]) { stale += 1; } // no overlap
        }
        let exact = comb(n - w, r) / comb(n, r); // choose all R from the N-W old replicas
        let ok = if r + w > n { "yes" } else { "no" };
        let sim = stale as f64 / TRIALS as f64 * 100.0;
        println!("{n:2} {r:2} {w:2}  {ok:>5}  {sim:9.2}%  {:6.2}%", exact * 100.0);
    }
}
# Leaderless replication: write to W random replicas, read from R random replicas.
from math import comb

MASK = (1 << 64) - 1
seed = 42


def rand_u32() -> int:                  # same LCG as the Rust version
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 6364136223846793005 + 1442695040888963407) & MASK
    return seed >> 33


def pick(n: int, k: int) -> set[int]:   # k distinct replicas out of n
    ids = list(range(n))
    for i in range(k):                  # partial Fisher-Yates shuffle
        j = i + rand_u32() % (n - i)
        ids[i], ids[j] = ids[j], ids[i]
    return set(ids[:k])


TRIALS = 100_000
print(" N  R  W  R+W>N  stale reads  formula")
for n, r, w in [(3, 1, 1), (3, 1, 2), (3, 2, 2), (5, 1, 3), (5, 2, 3), (5, 3, 3)]:
    stale = 0
    for _ in range(TRIALS):
        written = pick(n, w)            # replicas that got the new value
        read = pick(n, r)               # replicas the reader asks
        if not written & read:          # no overlap: the reader sees only old data
            stale += 1
    exact = comb(n - w, r) / comb(n, r)  # choose all R from the N-W old replicas
    ok = "yes" if r + w > n else "no"
    print(f"{n:2} {r:2} {w:2}  {ok:>5}  {stale / TRIALS:10.2%}  {exact:7.2%}")
 N  R  W  R+W>N  stale reads  formula
 3  1  1     no      66.67%   66.67%
 3  1  2     no      33.23%   33.33%
 3  2  2    yes       0.00%    0.00%
 5  1  3     no      39.82%   40.00%
 5  2  3     no      10.03%   10.00%
 5  3  3    yes       0.00%    0.00%

Cassandra lets you choose per query. Its docs say a write always goes to all replicas. The consistency level only says how many replies to wait for. QUORUM means a majority, so with 3 replicas, quorum reads and quorum writes always overlap. Dynamo-style stores also use hinted handoff and read repair to bring old copies up to date.

"R + W > N, so my store is linearizable." Not by itself. Two writes can race. A read can overlap a write that is half done. A sloppy quorum writes to stand-in nodes, so the overlap is gone. Cassandra also resolves conflicts by timestamp, so clock drift matters again.

Consistency models and the CAP theorem

A user changes her profile name to "Mia" and presses reload. The page shows the old name. Then it shows "Mia". Then the old name again. Is that a bug? It depends on the promise the store makes. That promise is its consistency model.

  • Linearizable. The system acts like one copy. Every operation seems to happen at one instant between its start and its end. Once a write is done, every later read sees it. See Concurrency and parallelism.
  • Sequential. All nodes see one order of all operations. Each process keeps its own order, but the order may lag real time.
  • Causal. Events with a cause come in order. A reply never appears before its question. Concurrent events may appear in any order.
  • Session guarantees. Read your writes, monotonic reads (never go back in time), monotonic writes.
  • Eventual. If writes stop, replicas agree in the end. Before that, anything goes.

Jepsen's map also says what survives a partition. Linearizable, sequential and serializable stores cannot stay available on both sides. Causal and read-your-writes can stay available if a client keeps talking to the same server. Jepsen calls that "sticky available". The weakest models can stay totally available.

Suppose the network can lose all messages between two groups of nodes. Then a replicated store cannot give both of these: linearizable reads and writes (C), and a reply from every working node to every request (A). During a partition (P) it must give up one of them.

Proof idea

Take two nodes, G1 and G2, with value v_0. Cut every message between them. A client writes v_1 to G1. By availability, G1 must say OK. Then another client reads from G2. By availability, G2 must answer. But no message from G1 can reach G2, so G2 can only return v_0. The read after a finished write returns the old value, so the store is not linearizable. Eric Brewer stated the idea in 2000. Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved it in 2002.

So the real choice is between C and A during a partition. A bank ledger picks C: some nodes refuse requests. A shopping cart picks A: it accepts writes and repairs conflicts later. The PACELC idea adds the normal case: even without a partition, stronger consistency costs latency, because nodes must wait for each other.

"Pick two of three: C, A, P." Partitions are not a choice. Networks fail. Also, the C in CAP means linearizable, which is not the C in ACID. And the A means every working node answers, which is stronger than "99.9% uptime".

Consensus: FLP, Paxos and Raft

Five servers run a lock service. A client asks for lock 7. Two servers think client X has it. Two think client Y has it. That is a disaster. The servers must agree on one history. This is consensus.

Each node proposes a value. A consensus protocol must give three things.

  • Agreement. No two nodes decide different values.
  • Validity. The decided value was proposed by some node.
  • Termination. Every working node decides in the end.

In an asynchronous system, no deterministic protocol solves consensus if even one node may crash. Every such protocol has a run that never decides.

Here deterministic means: the same inputs and messages always give the same steps.

Proof idea

Call a state bivalent if both answers, 0 and 1, can still happen. Step 1: some start state is bivalent. Step 2: from any bivalent state, an adversary can delay one message. It does this so that the next state is bivalent again. A slow node and a dead node look the same, so the protocol cannot just wait. Repeat step 2 forever. Every message still arrives in the end, yet the run never decides. Fischer, Lynch and Paterson published this in 1985.

FLP does not say consensus is useless. It says you cannot have all three properties with no timing help at all. Real systems keep agreement always and give up termination only in bad periods. They use timeouts, which assume partial synchrony, or randomness. When the network calms down, they decide.

A crash-tolerant protocol needs a majority. With n = 2f + 1 nodes it survives f crashes: 3 nodes survive 1, and 5 nodes survive 2. Two majorities always share a node, by the quorum theorem. That shared node carries decisions from one leader to the next.

Paxos in one paragraph

Lamport's Paxos has proposers and acceptors. Phase 1: a proposer picks a ballot number b and asks a majority to promise to ignore lower ballots. Each acceptor answers with the value it accepted before, if any. Phase 2: the proposer must reuse the value with the highest ballot from those answers. Only if there is none may it use its own value. Once a majority accepts the value for ballot b, it is chosen. Paxos is correct but famously hard to learn, and the full system around it has many details.

Raft step by step

Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout designed Raft in 2014 to be easier to understand. It keeps a replicated log. Every server applies the same commands in the same order. So all copies of the state machine stay the same.

Terms

Time is cut into terms: 1, 2, 3 and so on. Each term starts with an election. A term has at most one leader. A server that sees a higher term moves to it at once.

Heartbeats

The leader sends empty AppendEntries messages as heartbeats. Each follower has an election timer. The paper suggests a random value such as 150 to 300 ms. Each heartbeat resets the timer.

Election

The leader crashes. The follower whose timer fires first becomes a candidate. It adds 1 to the term, votes for itself and sends RequestVote to everyone.

Voting rules

A server votes at most once per term. It refuses a candidate whose log is less up to date than its own. Compare the last entry's term first, then the log length. With votes from a majority, the candidate becomes leader.

Log replication

A client sends a command to the leader. The leader adds it to its log and sends AppendEntries. Each message carries the index and term of the entry just before the new ones.

Consistency check

A follower rejects AppendEntries if its log has no entry with that index and term. The leader then steps back one entry and tries again. In the end the follower's log matches the leader's.

Commit

An entry from the current term is committed once a majority stores it. Older entries become committed with it. Then servers apply it and the leader answers the client.

Split vote

Two candidates start at almost the same time. Each gets two votes out of five. Nobody wins. Both time out again, with new random timeouts, and the next term usually has one clear winner.

Why is the timeout random? The simulation below tests that. Five servers, message delays of 5 to 10 ms, 1,000 crashes per setting. It is a simplified model, not the real protocol: logs are equal and all candidates of one round share a term.

// Raft leader election after a crash: 5 servers, random election timeouts.
struct Lcg(u64); // same LCG as the Python version
impl Lcg {
    fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_mul(6364136223846793005).wrapping_add(1442695040888963407);
        self.0 >> 33
    }
    fn between(&mut self, lo: u64, hi: u64) -> u64 {
        lo + self.next_u32() % (hi - lo + 1)
    }
}

const N: usize = 5;
const MAJORITY: usize = 3;
const D: (u64, u64) = (5_000, 10_000); // message delay 5 to 10 ms (in µs)

fn election(rng: &mut Lcg, lo: u64, hi: u64) -> (Option<u64>, u32) {
    let mut deadline: Vec<u64> = (0..N).map(|_| rng.between(lo, hi)).collect(); // last heartbeat at 0
    for rnd in 0..50 { // one round = one term
