        let (mut cands, mut first, mut arrive) = (vec![], [u64::MAX; N], [[0u64; N]; N]);
        let mut order: Vec<usize> = (0..N).collect();
        order.sort_by_key(|&i| deadline[i]);
        for j in order {
            if deadline[j] < first[j] { // timer fires before any vote request
                cands.push(j);
                for k in (0..N).filter(|&k| k != j) {
                    arrive[j][k] = deadline[j] + rng.between(D.0, D.1);
                    first[k] = first[k].min(arrive[j][k]);
                }
            }
        }
        let mut votes: Vec<Vec<u64>> = (0..N).map(|c| vec![deadline[c]]).collect(); // self vote
        let mut voted_at = [0u64; N];
        for k in (0..N).filter(|k| !cands.contains(k)) { // vote for the first request
            let c = *cands.iter().min_by_key(|&&c| arrive[c][k]).unwrap();
            voted_at[k] = arrive[c][k];
            votes[c].push(arrive[c][k] + rng.between(D.0, D.1));
        }
        for &c in &cands {
            if votes[c].len() >= MAJORITY { // a majority: c is the new leader
                votes[c].sort();
                return (Some(votes[c][MAJORITY - 1]), rnd);
            }
        }
        for i in 0..N { // split vote: wait again, new term
            let base = if cands.contains(&i) { deadline[i] } else { voted_at[i] };
            deadline[i] = base + rng.between(lo, hi);
        }
    }
    (None, 50)
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng = Lcg(42);
    println!("timeout ms  median ms  worst ms  split rounds  no leader");
    for (lo, hi) in [(150, 150), (150, 155), (150, 175), (150, 200), (150, 300)] {
        let runs: Vec<_> = (0..1000).map(|_| election(&mut rng, lo * 1000, hi * 1000)).collect();
        let mut times: Vec<u64> = runs.iter().filter_map(|r| r.0).collect();
        times.sort();
        let splits: u32 = runs.iter().map(|r| r.1).sum();
        let ms = |t: u64| format!("{:.0}", t as f64 / 1000.0);
        let (med, worst) = match times.last() {
            Some(&w) => (ms(times[times.len() / 2]), ms(w)),
            None => ("-".to_string(), "-".to_string()),
        };
        println!("{lo}-{hi:<6} {med:>9}  {worst:>8}  {splits:12}  {:9}", 1000 - times.len());
    }
}
# Raft leader election after a crash: 5 servers, random election timeouts.
MASK = (1 << 64) - 1
seed = 42


def rand_u32() -> int:                       # same LCG as the Rust version
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 6364136223846793005 + 1442695040888963407) & MASK
    return seed >> 33


def between(lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    return lo + rand_u32() % (hi - lo + 1)


N, MAJORITY, D_LO, D_HI = 5, 3, 5_000, 10_000  # message delay 5 to 10 ms (in µs)


def election(lo: int, hi: int):
    deadline = [between(lo, hi) for _ in range(N)]  # last heartbeat at time 0
    for rnd in range(50):                    # one round = one term
        cands, first, arrive = [], [10**12] * N, {}
        for j in sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: deadline[i]):
            if deadline[j] < first[j]:       # timer fires before any vote request
                cands.append(j)
                for k in range(N):
                    if k != j:
                        arrive[j, k] = deadline[j] + between(D_LO, D_HI)
                        first[k] = min(first[k], arrive[j, k])
        votes = {c: [deadline[c]] for c in cands}   # each candidate votes for itself
        voted_at = {}
        for k in range(N):
            if k not in cands:               # vote for the first request that arrives
                c = min(cands, key=lambda c: arrive[c, k])
                voted_at[k] = arrive[c, k]
                votes[c].append(arrive[c, k] + between(D_LO, D_HI))
        for c in cands:
            if len(votes[c]) >= MAJORITY:    # a majority: c is the new leader
                return sorted(votes[c])[MAJORITY - 1], rnd
        for i in range(N):                   # split vote: wait again, new term
            deadline[i] = (deadline[i] if i in cands else voted_at[i]) + between(lo, hi)
    return None, 50


print("timeout ms  median ms  worst ms  split rounds  no leader")
for lo, hi in [(150, 150), (150, 155), (150, 175), (150, 200), (150, 300)]:
    runs = [election(lo * 1000, hi * 1000) for _ in range(1000)]
    times = sorted(t for t, _ in runs if t is not None)
    splits = sum(s for _, s in runs)
    med, worst = (f"{times[len(times) // 2] / 1000:.0f}", f"{times[-1] / 1000:.0f}") if times else ("-", "-")
    print(f"{lo}-{hi:<6} {med:>9}  {worst:>8}  {splits:12}  {1000 - len(times):9}")
timeout ms  median ms  worst ms  split rounds  no leader
150-150            -         -         50000       1000
150-155         1378      7470          9696          1
150-175          170       958           304          0
150-200          172       666            64          0
150-300          185       469            10          0

With equal timeouts, every server becomes a candidate at once, every time. No leader is ever elected. With only 5 ms of randomness, split votes are common. A wider range almost removes them. The Raft paper saw the same shape on a real five-server cluster. With no randomness, elections took more than 10 seconds. With 50 ms of randomness, the worst of 1,000 trials was 513 ms. Our numbers differ because our model is simpler.

The paper also gives a timing rule. The broadcast time must be much smaller than the election timeout. The timeout must be much smaller than the time between failures. Broadcast time is often 0.5 to 20 ms, because servers write to disk before they reply.

The five safety properties of Raft (paper, Figure 3)
PropertyMeaning
Election safetyAt most one leader in each term
Leader append-onlyA leader never deletes or overwrites its own log entries
Log matchingSame index and same term means the logs match up to there
Leader completenessA committed entry is in the log of every later leader
State machine safetyNo two servers apply different commands at the same index

Raft runs in many real systems. etcd uses it, and Kubernetes keeps its cluster state in etcd. Apache Kafka 4.0, released in March 2025, removed ZooKeeper. Kafka now keeps its metadata with KRaft, a protocol based on Raft.

Running 4 or 6 consensus nodes. A majority of 4 is 3, so 4 nodes survive only 1 crash, like 3 nodes. Use odd sizes: 3 or 5. And do not stretch one consensus group across slow links without measuring, because every commit waits for a majority.

Know why a Raft leader does not count replicas for entries from older terms. An old entry stored on a majority can still be overwritten by a later leader. The Raft paper shows this case in its Figure 8. Committing a current-term entry on top makes the old entries safe.

Distributed transactions: two-phase commit and sagas

An online shop has two services. The order service saves the order. The payment service takes the money. The order fails, but the money is gone. A transaction across several nodes must commit everywhere or nowhere. This is atomic commit.

  1. A coordinator sends PREPARE to every participant.
  2. Each participant writes the changes to disk and locks the rows. Then it votes YES or NO. A YES is a promise: "I can commit, whatever happens."
  3. If all votes are YES, the coordinator writes COMMIT to its own log. That moment is the decision.
  4. The coordinator sends COMMIT to all. If any vote was NO, it sends ABORT.
  5. Participants apply the decision, release locks and answer DONE.

2PC is correct but it can block. Say a participant voted YES and then the coordinator crashes. The participant may not commit alone, and it may not abort alone. It must hold its locks and wait. Real systems run the coordinator on top of consensus to avoid this. Spanner does that. For the database side of transactions, see Relational databases.

Long business processes cannot hold locks for minutes. A saga splits the work into local transactions. Each step has a compensating action. Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem described sagas in 1987.

A travel booking saga
StepActionCompensation if a later step fails
1Reserve flightCancel flight
2Reserve hotelCancel hotel
3Charge cardRefund card
4Send ticketNone needed, this is the last step

If step 3 fails, the saga runs "cancel hotel", then "cancel flight". Each step and each compensation must be idempotent, because the saga runner retries after crashes. Durable execution engines run sagas this way.

Thinking a compensation is a rollback. It is not. Between the step and its undo, other people saw the effect. The hotel room looked taken. An email may have gone out. Sagas give no isolation, so design each step so that others can see it safely.

CRDTs: agreeing without consensus

Two phones share a "likes" counter. Both are offline. Phone A adds 3 likes. Phone B adds 2 likes. Later they sync. The answer must be 5, on both phones, in any sync order. Consensus cannot help when phones are offline. A different tool can.

A CRDT is a data type whose copies can always merge. Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero and Zawirski defined them in 2011. The simplest is a grow-only counter, the G-Counter. Each replica keeps one number per replica. A replica only adds to its own number. Merge takes the larger value in each position. The counter's value is the sum.

  1. Start: A has \{A{:}\,0, B{:}\,0\}. B has the same.
  2. Offline: A adds 3, so A has \{A{:}\,3, B{:}\,0\}. B adds 2, so B has \{A{:}\,0, B{:}\,2\}.
  3. Sync: merge takes the larger value per position. Both get \{A{:}\,3, B{:}\,2\}.
  4. Value: 3 + 2 = 5 on both phones. Merging again changes nothing.

Suppose merge is commutative (a \sqcup b = b \sqcup a), associative and idempotent (a \sqcup a = a). Suppose every update only grows the state. Then replicas that got the same updates have the same state. Order, delay and duplicates do not matter. This is called strong eventual consistency.

Other CRDTs build on the same idea. A PN-Counter is two G-Counters, one for adds and one for subtracts. An observed-remove set tags each add with a unique id, so a remove only removes what it has seen. Text CRDTs give every character a unique position id. Automerge and Yjs are open-source CRDT libraries for shared documents.

Using a CRDT for a rule that needs agreement, like "the balance must never go below zero". Two offline phones can each spend the last 10 dollars. Merging gives a valid CRDT state but breaks the rule. Rules like this need coordination or consensus.

Byzantine faults

Three generals must agree: attack or retreat. One may be a traitor. The commander tells lieutenant 1 "attack" and lieutenant 2 "retreat". Lieutenant 2 tells lieutenant 1 "the commander said retreat". Who is lying? Lieutenant 1 cannot tell. A lying lieutenant 2 would look exactly the same.

With unsigned messages, n nodes can reach agreement despite f Byzantine nodes only if n \gt 3f, that is n \ge 3f + 1.

Proof idea

Lower bound: the three-generals story shows that 3 nodes cannot handle 1 traitor. For general f, split 3f nodes into three groups of f. Each group acts like one general, so a solution for 3f nodes would solve the three-general case. Upper bound idea: with n = 3f + 1, use quorums of 2f + 1. Two such quorums share at least 2(2f + 1) - (3f + 1) = f + 1 nodes. At least one of them is honest, so honest decisions cannot conflict. Lamport, Shostak and Pease published the bound in 1982.

So 4 nodes tolerate 1 Byzantine node, and 7 nodes tolerate 2. Compare with crashes: 3 nodes tolerate 1 crash. Lying costs more nodes than dying. Digital signatures help. With signed messages and fixed time limits, the 1982 paper solves the problem for any number of traitors. But with unknown network delays, n \ge 3f + 1 is needed even with signatures. Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer showed this in 1988.

Who uses Byzantine fault tolerance? Blockchains and some systems run by many companies that do not trust each other. PBFT by Castro and Liskov (1999) was the first fast practical protocol. A normal company database usually trusts its own servers. It uses crash-fault protocols like Raft, and defends against bugs with checksums.

Thinking Raft or Paxos survive one bad node that lies. They do not. A Raft node that claims a false term or a fake log can break safety. Raft and Paxos assume crash faults only.

Partitioning and dataflow

Consistent hashing

One machine cannot hold all the data. We split the data into parts, called partitions or shards. A simple rule is server = hash(key) mod N. It works until N changes. Go from 4 servers to 5, and most keys move.

Consistent hashing fixes this. Karger and others described it in 1997. Put servers on a circle by hashing their names. Hash each key onto the same circle. A key belongs to the first server clockwise. When a server joins, it takes keys only from its neighbours. Each server gets many points on the circle, called virtual nodes, so the load is even.

// How many keys move when a 5th server joins 4 servers?
fn hash64(text: &str) -> u64 { // FNV-1a, then a mixing step
    let mut h: u64 = 0xCBF29CE484222325;
    for byte in text.bytes() {
        h = (h ^ byte as u64).wrapping_mul(0x100000001B3);
    }
    h = (h ^ (h >> 33)).wrapping_mul(0xFF51AFD7ED558CCD); // spread the bits
    h ^ (h >> 33)
}

fn ring(servers: usize, points: usize) -> Vec<(u64, usize)> {
    let mut r: Vec<(u64, usize)> = (0..servers)
        .flat_map(|s| (0..points).map(move |v| (hash64(&format!("server-{s}#{v}")), s)))
        .collect();
    r.sort();
    r
}

fn owner(r: &[(u64, usize)], h: u64) -> usize {
    let i = r.partition_point(|p| p.0 < h); // first point at or after the key
    r[i % r.len()].1 // past the end: wrap to the start
}

fn main() {
    let keys: Vec<u64> = (0..100_000).map(|i| hash64(&format!("user:{i}"))).collect();
    println!("method              keys moved  biggest server (ideal 20%)");
    for (name, points) in [("hash mod N", 0), ("ring, 1 point", 1), ("ring, 100 points", 100)] {
        let (old, new): (Vec<usize>, Vec<usize>) = if points == 0 {
            keys.iter().map(|&h| ((h % 4) as usize, (h % 5) as usize)).unzip()
        } else {
            let (r4, r5) = (ring(4, points), ring(5, points));
            keys.iter().map(|&h| (owner(&r4, h), owner(&r5, h))).unzip()
        };
        let n = keys.len() as f64;
        let moved = old.iter().zip(&new).filter(|(a, b)| a != b).count() as f64 / n;
        let biggest = (0..5).map(|s| new.iter().filter(|&&x| x == s).count()).max().unwrap() as f64 / n;
        println!("{name:18}  {:9.1}%  {:8.1}%", moved * 100.0, biggest * 100.0);
    }
}
# How many keys move when a 5th server joins 4 servers?
from bisect import bisect_left

MASK = (1 << 64) - 1


def hash64(text: str) -> int:             # FNV-1a, then a mixing step
    h = 0xCBF29CE484222325
    for byte in text.encode():
        h = ((h ^ byte) * 0x100000001B3) & MASK
    h = ((h ^ (h >> 33)) * 0xFF51AFD7ED558CCD) & MASK   # spread the bits
    return h ^ (h >> 33)


def ring(servers: int, points: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    return sorted((hash64(f"server-{s}#{v}"), s) for s in range(servers) for v in range(points))


def owner(r: list[tuple[int, int]], h: int) -> int:
    i = bisect_left(r, (h, -1))           # first point at or after the key
    return r[i % len(r)][1]               # past the end: wrap to the start


keys = [hash64(f"user:{i}") for i in range(100_000)]
print("method              keys moved  biggest server (ideal 20%)")
for name, points in [("hash mod N", 0), ("ring, 1 point", 1), ("ring, 100 points", 100)]:
    if points == 0:
        old, new = [h % 4 for h in keys], [h % 5 for h in keys]
    else:
        r4, r5 = ring(4, points), ring(5, points)
        old, new = [owner(r4, h) for h in keys], [owner(r5, h) for h in keys]
    moved = sum(a != b for a, b in zip(old, new)) / len(keys)
    biggest = max(new.count(s) for s in range(5)) / len(keys)
    print(f"{name:18}  {moved:10.1%}  {biggest:9.1%}")
method              keys moved  biggest server (ideal 20%)
hash mod N               80.0%      20.2%
ring, 1 point            22.1%      42.2%
ring, 100 points         21.1%      21.5%

The mod rule moves 80% of the keys. The ring moves about 20%, close to the ideal 1/5. With one point per server, one server gets 42% of the keys. With 100 points, the biggest gets 21.5%. Cassandra and Dynamo use rings with virtual nodes. The nginx option hash $key consistent uses the ketama ring.

MapReduce and dataflow

You must count words in 1 TB of logs. Say one disk reads 200 MB per second. Then one machine needs about 80 minutes just to read the data. Split the logs into 1,000 parts of 1 GB and use 1,000 machines. Each part takes about 5 seconds to read. Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat published MapReduce at Google in 2004.

  1. Map. Each worker reads one part and emits pairs like ("error", 1).
  2. Shuffle. Pairs go to reducer number hash(word) mod R. All pairs with the same word meet at one reducer.
  3. Reduce. Each reducer adds up the counts for its words and writes the result.
  4. Failures. If a worker dies, the master runs its task again on another machine. Near the end, it starts backup copies of slow tasks and keeps the first result.

Re-running a task is safe only because map and reduce are deterministic. Later systems, such as Apache Spark, Apache Flink and Apache Beam, generalise MapReduce into a dataflow graph. Data flows through many steps, often in memory, and also as a never-ending stream. The chapter Data science and information retrieval uses these models for big data.

A map function that calls the current time, a random number or an outside API. A re-run gives a different result, and the final output mixes both. Keep tasks deterministic, or save the input they used.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for distributed systems
PatternPurposeModelNote
Timeout means "unknown"Handle lost replies safelyretry with the same idempotency keyNever read a timeout as "it failed".
Lamport clockOrder events by causeL = max(mine, message) + 1Cannot detect concurrent events.
Vector clockDetect concurrent writes[2, 1, 0] vs [0, 0, 1] means concurrentSize grows with the number of writers.
Single leaderOne clear order of writesPostgreSQL primary with replicasReads from followers can be stale.
Quorum R + W > NReads overlap the latest writeN = 3, W = 2, R = 2Not linearizable by itself.
Majority of 2f + 1Survive f crashes5 nodes survive 2 crashesEven sizes add cost, not safety.
Random election timeoutAvoid split votes150 to 300 ms in the Raft paperTimeout must be much larger than broadcast time.
Commit on a majorityNever lose a decided entryRaft entry on 3 of 5 logsCount only current-term entries.
Two-phase commitAtomic commit across nodesPREPARE, votes, COMMITBlocks if the coordinator dies.
Saga with compensationsLong processes without locksbook, then cancel on failureNo isolation between steps.
CRDT mergeOffline edits that always mergeG-Counter: max per positionCannot keep rules like "balance at least 0".
3f + 1 nodesSurvive f lying nodes4 nodes, 1 traitorRaft does not handle lies.
Consistent hashingMove few keys when servers changering with 100 points per serverUse virtual nodes for even load.
Deterministic tasksSafe re-run after a crashmap and reduce in MapReduceNo clocks or random numbers inside.

Practice

A store has N = 5 replicas and writes wait for W = 3. What is the smallest R that makes every read overlap every write?

  • 1
  • 3
  • 5

We need R + W \gt N, so R + 3 \gt 5, so R \ge 3.

Event x has vector clock [2, 0, 1]. Event y has [1, 3, 1]. How are they related?

  • x happened before y
  • y happened before x
  • They are concurrent

x is bigger in the first position, and y is bigger in the second. Neither vector is less than or equal in every position.

During a network partition, a store keeps answering on both sides. Which property must it give up, by CAP?

  • Partition tolerance
  • Linearizable consistency
  • Durability

If both sides answer, a read on one side cannot see a write on the other side. That breaks linearizability.

A Raft cluster has 7 servers. It can survive ? crashed servers.

To tolerate 2 Byzantine nodes, you need at least ? nodes.

A Lamport clock shows 4. A message arrives with the value 9. After the receive event, the clock shows ?.

  1. A follower's timer fires, but the leader is only slow, not dead. What happens in Raft, and why is it still safe?
    Answer

    The follower starts a new term and may win. The old leader's next message carries an old term. Servers reject it, and the old leader steps down when it sees the higher term. Each term has at most one leader, and commits need a majority, so the old leader cannot commit anything new. The only cost is a short pause.

  2. N = 5, R = 1, W = 3. Use the formula to find the chance of a stale read. Then check the simulation output.
    Answer

    P = \binom{2}{1} / \binom{5}{1} = 2/5 = 40\%. The read must hit one of the 2 replicas without the write. The simulation gave 39.82%, which is close.

  3. In 2PC, a participant voted YES. Then it loses contact with the coordinator. Why may it not abort on its own?
    Answer

    The coordinator may already have decided COMMIT and told other participants. If this participant aborts, some nodes commit and others abort, which breaks atomicity. A YES vote is a promise to follow the coordinator's decision, so it must wait or ask other participants.

  4. Design a shopping cart that stays available during partitions. Which tool fits: consensus, 2PC or a CRDT? What can go wrong?
    Answer

    A CRDT, such as an observed-remove set of items. Both sides accept adds and removes, and merge later. A remove only deletes adds it has seen, so a concurrent add survives. Something to watch: stock checks need coordination, because two carts can buy the last item. Check stock again at checkout.

  5. Explain in your own words why FLP does not stop etcd from working every day.
    Answer

    FLP is about fully asynchronous systems, where a slow node and a dead node look the same forever. etcd uses Raft with timeouts. Raft never breaks agreement, even when timing is bad. It only fails to make progress while the network is very slow. When messages flow on time again, a leader is elected and work goes on.

  6. You add a sixth cache server to five, using hash(key) mod N. About what share of keys move? What share would move with a good consistent hashing ring?
    Answer

    With mod N, a key stays only if h mod 5 equals h mod 6. That is true for about 1 key in 6, so about 83% move. With a ring, the new server takes its fair share, about 1/6 \approx 17\%, and only those keys move.

What does the two generals problem prove?

Over a lossy channel, no finite protocol makes both sides sure they agree.

What does FLP prove?

No deterministic protocol solves consensus in an asynchronous system if one node may crash.

What is the quorum rule?

If R + W > N, every read set meets every write set.

How many nodes for f Byzantine faults?

At least 3f + 1.

Why are Raft timeouts random?

So that one server usually times out first and wins before others start. This avoids split votes.

Key takeaways

  • Choose a failure model and a timing model first. A timeout means "unknown", never "failed".
  • Lamport clocks respect cause and effect. Vector clocks also detect concurrent events.
  • Replication can use one leader, many leaders or none. Quorums with R + W > N make reads meet writes.
  • Consistency models form a ladder. By CAP, during a partition you choose linearizability or availability.
  • FLP rules out consensus with no timing help. Raft uses random timeouts, terms and majorities to work in practice.
  • 2PC gives atomic commit but can block. Sagas avoid locks but give no isolation. CRDTs merge without coordination.
  • Lying nodes need 3f + 1 nodes. Consistent hashing moves few keys. MapReduce re-runs deterministic tasks.

Sources

  • In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm. The Raft paper by Ongaro and Ousterhout (USENIX ATC 2014): rules, safety properties and election timing results.
  • Distributed Systems lecture notes. Martin Kleppmann's Cambridge course: system models, two generals, Byzantine bound, clocks, quorums.
  • Jepsen consistency models. The map of models, which implies which, and what stays available in a partition.
  • Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process. The FLP paper (Journal of the ACM, 1985).
  • Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services. Gilbert and Lynch's proof of CAP (2002).
  • Cassandra: Dynamo architecture. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes, tunable consistency, hinted handoff and read repair.

Cloud and system design

System design is the art of turning "it works on my laptop" into "it works for ten million people". You add servers, caches and queues, and you learn to protect them from overload. This chapter gives the tools, two laws with numbers, a design method, and three full designs.

  • Scale a service up and out, keep it stateless, and choose a load-balancing method.
  • Use caches, queues, rate limits, idempotency keys and retries without making things worse.
  • Size a system with Little's law and explain why fan-out makes the tail slow.
  • Define SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, and alert on burn rate.
  • Follow a design method and estimate capacity for a URL shortener, a chat app and an AI retrieval service.

Scaling up and scaling out

A small web shop runs on one server. At lunch time, CPU use hits 95% and pages take 3 seconds. You have two choices.

Scale up. Buy a bigger machine: 16 cores become 64. No code changes. But big machines cost more per core. There is a largest size. And one machine is still one point of failure.

Scale out. Run 4 copies of the app behind a load balancer (see the next section). Add more copies when traffic grows. One copy can die and the others carry on. But the copies must not keep private state.

Scaling up is often right for a database. Scaling out is right for the app servers in front of it. To scale out, the app servers must be stateless. Every request carries what the server needs, or the server reads it from a shared store.

The login session lives in the memory of server 2. The load balancer sends the next request to server 3. The user is logged out.

The session lives in Redis or in a signed cookie. Any server can handle any request. A server can restart at any time.

State does not disappear. It moves to places built for it: a database, a cache, a queue, an object store. Then those places become the hard part. The chapter Distributed systems shows how they replicate and split data.

Scaling out the app servers while the database is the real bottleneck. Ten app servers now open ten times more database connections, and the database gets slower. Measure first. Find the resource that is full.

Load balancing

Four app servers stand behind one address. Who decides where each request goes? A load balancer. A layer 4 balancer sees only IP addresses and ports. A layer 7 balancer reads HTTP, so it can route /api and /images to different groups.

Common balancing methods (nginx names in brackets)
MethodHow it picksGood for
Round robin (default)Each server in turn, with optional weightsEqual servers, short equal requests
Least connections (least_conn)The server with the fewest open connectionsRequests of very different lengths
Consistent hash (hash $key consistent)Same key, same server, few moves when servers changeCaches, sticky data
Two random choices (random two least_conn)Pick two servers at random, use the less busy oneMany balancers with old load data

The last method is the power of two choices. It sounds too simple, but it works very well. Put n jobs on n servers at random, and the busiest server gets about \log n / \log \log n jobs. Pick the better of two random servers, and it drops to about \log \log n. One extra look gives most of the benefit.

upstream app {
    random two least_conn;           # power of two choices
    server 10.0.0.11 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 10.0.0.12 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 10.0.0.13 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
}

A balancer must also stop sending traffic to sick servers. In open-source nginx, this is passive. After max_fails failed tries within fail_timeout, the server rests for fail_timeout. The defaults are 1 and 10 seconds. Many balancers also send active health checks.

A health check that only says "the process is running". The server answers 200 OK while its database connection is broken, and it fails every real request fast. Fast failures look like low latency, so this sick server even gets more traffic. Check the real dependencies, and watch the error rate per server.

Caching layers and invalidation

A product page needs 40 ms of database work. It gets 2,000 views per second, but the product changes once a day. Doing the same work 2,000 times per second is waste. A cache keeps the result close and returns it in 1 ms.

Caches sit at many layers. A CDN keeps copies of pages and images close to users. The app keeps a small cache in its own memory and a big shared one in Redis.

The effect of a cache is easy to compute. With hit ratio h, the mean time is T = h \cdot T_{hit} + (1 - h) \cdot T_{miss}. With T_{hit} = 1 ms and T_{miss} = 40 ms, a hit ratio of 0.9 gives 4.9 ms. A hit ratio of 0.99 gives 1.39 ms. The database load also drops from 2,000 to 200, then to 20 queries per second.

Ways to write with a cache
PatternHow it worksRisk
Cache-asideRead cache. On a miss, read the database and fill the cache. On a write, update the database and delete the cache key.A short window of stale data
Write-throughEvery write goes to the cache and the database togetherSlower writes
Write-backWrite to the cache now, to the database laterData loss if the cache dies

The hard part is invalidation: knowing when a copy is old. Use three tools together. A TTL puts an upper limit on staleness. Deleting the key on write keeps hot data fresh. A version in the key, like product:42:v7, makes old copies unreachable at once.

Watch out for a cache stampede. A hot key expires. A thousand requests miss at the same moment, and all of them query the database. Let only one request refill the key while the others wait for it. Also add jitter to TTLs, so that keys do not all expire together.

Caching a page that depends on who is asking, under a key that ignores it. User A's private data is then shown to user B. Put everything that changes the answer in the key: user or tenant, language, permissions. Or do not cache it at that layer.

Queues, back-pressure and Little's law

A video site gets uploads. Converting one video takes 2 minutes. If the upload request waited for that, users would see timeouts. Instead, the server puts a job in a queue and answers at once: "processing". Workers take jobs from the queue at their own speed.

Queues smooth bursts and decouple services. But a queue cannot fix a system that is too slow on average. If 12 jobs arrive per minute and the workers finish 10, the queue grows forever. How many workers do you need? Little's law answers.

In a stable system, the average number of items inside, L, equals the average arrival rate, \lambda, times the average time each item stays, W:

L = \lambda W
Proof idea

Draw the number of items inside over a long time T. The area under that curve is the total time all items spent inside. Count it another way: about \lambda T items arrived, and each stayed W on average, so the area is \lambda T W. The average height is the area divided by T, which is \lambda W. John Little proved it in full in 1961. It needs no assumption about how arrivals are spread.

  1. Workers. 12 videos arrive per minute, \lambda = 0.2 per second. Each takes W = 120 s. Busy workers: L = 0.2 \cdot 120 = 24. With 30 workers, they are 80% busy.
  2. Database pool. 2,000 queries per second, 5 ms each. Busy connections: L = 2000 \cdot 0.005 = 10. A pool of 20 leaves room for bursts.
  3. Waiting time. A queue holds 600 jobs, and 10 jobs leave per second. A new job waits about W = L / \lambda = 600 / 10 = 60 s.

When work arrives faster than it leaves, something must give. Back-pressure pushes the problem back to the sender. Give every queue a size limit. When it is full, reject new work with HTTP 429 or 503 and a Retry-After header. Or drop the least important work first. That is called load shedding.

Why not let the queue grow? Waiting time explodes as servers get close to 100% busy. The M/M/1 model in Making AI systems fast and reliable shows it. At 95% busy, a request spends 10 times longer inside than at 50% busy. A queue with no limit turns overload into long delays, then into memory errors.

An unbounded queue "so we never lose a job". During an outage it fills with hours of work. Users gave up long ago, but the workers still process every old job, and new jobs wait behind them. Set a limit and a deadline per job. Drop jobs that nobody waits for any more.

Rate limits, idempotency keys and retries

Rate limiting with a token bucket

One customer's script sends 500 requests per second and slows down everyone. A rate limit protects the shared service. The most common method is the token bucket. Tokens drip into a bucket at rate r. The bucket holds at most b tokens. Each request takes one token. With no token, the answer is 429 Too Many Requests.

So a client can send a short burst of b requests, but over a long time no more than r per second. Amazon API Gateway documents its throttling this way: the rate is how fast tokens are added and the burst is the bucket size.

// Token bucket: 5 requests per second on average, bursts of up to 10.
struct TokenBucket {
    rate: u64,   // milli-tokens added per ms
    cap: u64,    // whole numbers only: 1 token = 1000
    tokens: u64,
    last: u64,
}

impl TokenBucket {
    fn new(rate_per_s: u64, capacity: u64) -> Self {
        TokenBucket { rate: rate_per_s, cap: capacity * 1000, tokens: capacity * 1000, last: 0 } // start full
    }
    fn allow(&mut self, now_ms: u64) -> bool {
        self.tokens = self.cap.min(self.tokens + (now_ms - self.last) * self.rate);
        self.last = now_ms; // refill lazily, only when asked
        if self.tokens >= 1000 {
            self.tokens -= 1000; // one request costs one token
            return true;
        }
        false // caller answers 429 Too Many Requests
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut bucket = TokenBucket::new(5, 10);
    let phases: [(&str, Vec<u64>); 3] = [
        ("burst at 0 s", vec![0; 15]),
        ("10 per second for 2 s", (100..=2000).step_by(100).collect()),
        ("burst after 2 s of rest", vec![4000; 15]),
    ];
    println!("{:24} sent  allowed  denied", "phase");
    for (name, times) in &phases {
        let ok = times.iter().filter(|&&t| bucket.allow(t)).count();
        println!("{name:24} {:4}  {ok:7}  {:6}", times.len(), times.len() - ok);
    }
}
# Token bucket: 5 requests per second on average, bursts of up to 10.
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate_per_s: int, capacity: int):
        self.rate = rate_per_s              # milli-tokens added per ms
        self.cap = capacity * 1000          # whole numbers only: 1 token = 1000
        self.tokens, self.last = self.cap, 0  # start full

    def allow(self, now_ms: int) -> bool:
        self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now_ms - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now_ms                  # refill lazily, only when asked
        if self.tokens >= 1000:
            self.tokens -= 1000             # one request costs one token
            return True
        return False                        # caller answers 429 Too Many Requests


bucket = TokenBucket(rate_per_s=5, capacity=10)
phases = [("burst at 0 s", [0] * 15),
          ("10 per second for 2 s", list(range(100, 2001, 100))),
          ("burst after 2 s of rest", [4000] * 15)]
print(f"{'phase':24} sent  allowed  denied")
for name, times in phases:
    ok = sum(bucket.allow(t) for t in times)
    print(f"{name:24} {len(times):4}  {ok:7}  {len(times) - ok:6}")
phase                    sent  allowed  denied
burst at 0 s               15       10       5
10 per second for 2 s      20       10      10
burst after 2 s of rest    15       10       5

The full bucket lets 10 requests through at once. At 10 requests per second, only 5 per second pass, the refill rate. After a rest, the bucket is full again. With many servers, keep the bucket in a shared store such as Redis, or give each server a share of the limit.

Idempotency keys

A phone app sends "pay 20 dollars". The network drops the reply. The app retries. Without protection, the customer pays twice. The client adds an idempotency key, a random id per operation. The server saves the key with the result. A repeat with the same key gets the saved result and changes nothing.

Stripe's API shows the details. Keys can be up to 255 characters. Stripe may remove a key once it is at least 24 hours old. If a retry uses the same key with different parameters, Stripe returns an error. For its v1 API, Stripe saves the first result even when it is a 500 error. The IETF is writing a standard Idempotency-Key HTTP header. On 2026-11-15 it is still a draft (revision 08), not an RFC.

Retries with backoff and jitter

The chapter Making AI systems fast and reliable gives the code for retries with full jitter. Here is the system view. A retry is selfish: it spends more of the server's capacity to raise your own chance. That is fine for rare errors and harmful during overload. So follow the AWS Builders' Library rules:

  • Set a timeout on every remote call. Choose it from measured latency, for example the 99.9th percentile, plus some margin.
  • Retry at one layer only. Five layers that each try 3 times can send 3^5 = 243 calls to the database for one user click.
  • Limit retries with a token bucket. Retry freely while tokens last, then slowly. AWS added this to its SDKs in 2016.
  • Use capped exponential backoff with jitter, so clients do not retry in step.
  • Retry only safe operations: reads, and writes with idempotency keys. Do not retry 400 or 409.

A client retries a timed-out payment with a new idempotency key on each try. Now every retry looks like a new payment. The key must be made once per operation and saved before the first try.

The tail at scale

A search page asks 100 servers in parallel and waits for all of them. Each server answers in about 10 ms. But 1 request in 100 takes a full second, because of a garbage collection pause or a busy disk. How often is the page slow?

A request waits for n independent parts. Each part is slow with probability p. Then the request is slow with probability

P_{slow} = 1 - (1 - p)^n \ge 1 - e^{-np},

which is close to np when np is small, and goes to 1 as n grows.

Proof

The request is fast only if all n parts are fast. Each part is fast with probability 1 - p, and the parts are independent, so all are fast with probability (1 - p)^n. Take this from 1. For the bound, use 1 - p \le e^{-p}, so (1 - p)^n \le e^{-np}. The union bound gives the other side: P_{slow} \le np.

With p = 0.01 and n = 100: 1 - 0.99^{100} \approx 0.634. So 63% of pages are slow, though each server is slow only 1% of the time. Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso gave this exact example in "The Tail at Scale" (2013).

Their paper also shows a real Google service. The 99th percentile for one random leaf was 10 ms. Waiting for all leaves, the 99th percentile was 140 ms. Waiting for 95% of the leaves, it was 70 ms. The slowest 5% of leaves caused half of the tail.

One fix is a hedged request. If a part has not answered by about its 95th percentile, send the same request to another replica and use the first answer. The paper reports a BigTable test: 1,000 keys over 100 servers, a hedge after 10 ms. The 99.9th percentile fell from 1,800 ms to 74 ms, with just 2% more requests. The simulation below tries the idea with the same seeded generator in both languages.

// The tail at scale: a request waits for its slowest leaf.
struct Lcg(u64); // same LCG as the Python version
impl Lcg {
    fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_mul(6364136223846793005).wrapping_add(1442695040888963407);
        self.0 >> 33
    }
    fn between(&mut self, lo: u64, hi: u64) -> u64 {
        lo + self.next_u32() % (hi - lo + 1)
    }
    fn leaf(&mut self) -> u64 { // one leaf reply time in ms
        let r = self.next_u32() % 100;
        if r == 0 {
            return self.between(500, 1500); // 1 in 100: a slow pause
        }
        if r < 5 { self.between(16, 60) } else { self.between(5, 15) }
    }
}

fn request(rng: &mut Lcg, fan_out: u32, hedge: Option<u64>) -> (u64, u32) {
    let (mut worst, mut extra) = (0, 0);
    for _ in 0..fan_out {
        let mut t = rng.leaf();
        if let Some(h) = hedge.filter(|&h| t > h) { // no reply yet: ask another replica
            extra += 1;
            t = t.min(h + rng.leaf());
        }
        worst = worst.max(t);
    }
    (worst, extra)
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng = Lcg(42);
    println!("fan-out  hedge  p50 ms  p99 ms  over 400 ms  theory  extra");
    for (fan_out, hedge) in [(1, None), (10, None), (100, None), (100, Some(15))] {
        let (mut times, mut extra) = (Vec::new(), 0);
        for _ in 0..10_000 {
            let (t, e) = request(&mut rng, fan_out, hedge);
            times.push(t);
            extra += e;
        }
        times.sort();
        let slow = times.iter().filter(|&&t| t > 400).count() as f64 / 10_000.0 * 100.0;
        let p: f64 = if hedge.is_none() { 0.01 } else { 0.01 * 0.01 }; // a hedged leaf is slow only if both are
        let theory = (1.0 - (1.0 - p).powf(fan_out as f64)) * 100.0;
        let h = hedge.map_or("none".to_string(), |h| format!("{h} ms"));
        let ex = extra as f64 / (10_000.0 * fan_out as f64) * 100.0;
        println!("{fan_out:7}  {h:>5}  {:6}  {:6}  {slow:10.1}%  {theory:5.1}%  {ex:4.1}%",
                 times[5000], times[9900]);
    }
}
# The tail at scale: a request waits for its slowest leaf.
MASK = (1 << 64) - 1
seed = 42


def rand_u32() -> int:                    # same LCG as the Rust version
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 6364136223846793005 + 1442695040888963407) & MASK
    return seed >> 33


def between(lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    return lo + rand_u32() % (hi - lo + 1)


def leaf() -> int:                        # one leaf reply time in ms
    r = rand_u32() % 100
    if r == 0:
        return between(500, 1500)         # 1 in 100: a slow pause
    return between(16, 60) if r < 5 else between(5, 15)


def request(fan_out: int, hedge: int | None) -> tuple[int, int]:
    worst, extra = 0, 0
    for _ in range(fan_out):
        t = leaf()
        if hedge is not None and t > hedge:   # no reply yet: ask another replica
            extra += 1
            t = min(t, hedge + leaf())
        worst = max(worst, t)
    return worst, extra


print("fan-out  hedge  p50 ms  p99 ms  over 400 ms  theory  extra")
for fan_out, hedge in [(1, None), (10, None), (100, None), (100, 15)]:
    times, extra = [], 0
    for _ in range(10_000):
        t, e = request(fan_out, hedge)
        times.append(t)
        extra += e
    times.sort()
    slow = sum(t > 400 for t in times) / len(times)
    p = 0.01 if hedge is None else 0.01 * 0.01   # a hedged leaf is slow only if both are
    theory = 1 - (1 - p) ** fan_out
    h = f"{hedge} ms" if hedge else "none"
    print(f"{fan_out:7}  {h:>5}  {times[5000]:6}  {times[9900]:6}  {slow:11.1%}"
          f"  {theory:6.1%}  {extra / (10_000 * fan_out):5.1%}")
fan-out  hedge  p50 ms  p99 ms  over 400 ms  theory  extra
      1   none      10     601         1.1%    1.0%   0.0%
     10   none      15    1414         9.4%    9.6%   0.0%
    100   none     808    1493        63.6%   63.4%   0.0%
    100  15 ms      29      75         0.9%    1.0%   5.0%

Read the rows. With one leaf, the median is 10 ms. With 100 leaves, even the median request is slow: 808 ms. Hedging after 15 ms, about the 95th percentile of one leaf, cuts the 99th percentile from 1,493 ms to 75 ms. It costs 5% more requests, the same share the paper predicts for a hedge at the 95th percentile.

Other fixes from the same paper: tied requests, many small partitions that can move away from a busy machine, and good-enough answers from most leaves. In the end, you design for the tail, not for the average.

Reporting the average latency. An average of 30 ms can hide a 99th percentile of 1.5 seconds. Users who make many requests meet the tail often. Always report percentiles, and know how many backends each request touches.

Observability, SLOs and error budgets

At 3 a.m. users say "the app is slow". Which of 40 services is the cause? You can only answer if the system tells you about itself. That is observability. It rests on three kinds of data.

  • Metrics are cheap numbers over time. Good for dashboards and alerts.
  • Logs record single events with details. Good for "what exactly happened".
  • Traces follow one request across services as a tree of timed steps. Good for "where did the time go".

OpenTelemetry is the open standard for all three. Its docs list traces, metrics, logs and baggage as supported signals, and profiles as still in development. Google's SRE book names four golden signals to watch on every service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. It also warns: measure the latency of failed requests separately, because fast errors make latency look good.

Now make it a promise. An SLI is a measurement, for example "share of requests that succeed in under 300 ms". An SLO is the target: "99.9% over 30 days". An SLA is a contract with money attached, and it is usually looser than the SLO.

  1. SLO: 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. The error budget is 0.1%.
  2. In time: 30 days is 43,200 minutes. 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes of full outage.
  3. In requests: at 2 million requests per day, that is 60 million per month and 60,000 allowed failures.
  4. A bad deploy fails 2% of requests for 1 hour: about 83{,}333 \cdot 0.02 \approx 1{,}667 failures, or 2.8% of the budget.
  5. Policy: while budget remains, ship. When it is gone, freeze risky releases and work on reliability.

The SRE book says the same: the budget is a shared tool for product and SRE teams, and a spent budget slows releases. To alert, use burn rate. A burn rate of 1 spends the budget in exactly 30 days. The SRE workbook suggests a page when the burn rate is 14.4 over 1 hour. That speed spends 2% of the budget in one hour. The alert also checks a 5-minute window, so it stops soon after the problem ends.

Allowed downtime for common targets
SLOPer 30 daysPer year
99%7.2 hours3.65 days
99.9%43.2 minutes8.76 hours
99.99%4.32 minutes52.56 minutes
99.999%26 seconds5.26 minutes

Setting the SLO to 100%. Then every small error is a crisis, nobody can ship, and you still miss it. Users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% when their own phone network fails more often. Pick the lowest target that keeps users happy.

A design method

A design interview or a real design review gives you a vague goal: "design a chat app". Do not draw boxes at once. Follow steps, and write numbers next to each box.

Requirements

List what the system must do: the main use cases. List the qualities: latency, availability, consistency, cost. Ask what is out of scope.

Estimates

Users, requests per second at the busy hour, read to write ratio, data size per year. Round numbers are fine. One day is about 10^5 seconds.

API

Write the main calls with inputs and outputs. Mark which calls change data. Those need idempotency keys.

Data model

Main tables or documents, keys and access patterns. Choose the store from the access pattern, not from fashion.

High-level design

Draw clients, balancers, stateless services, stores, caches and queues. Follow one request through the picture.

Deep dives

Pick the two hardest parts. Scale them with numbers: partitions, replicas, cache hit ratio, Little's law.

Failures

Kill each box in your head. What happens? Add timeouts, retries, idempotency, back-pressure and fallbacks.

Operations

SLOs, dashboards, alerts, safe rollouts, cost per month. Say what you would build first and what later.

Interviewers grade the reasoning, not the final picture. Say each trade-off out loud: "I choose a cache here. The cost is up to 60 seconds of stale data, which is fine for this page." State numbers with units, and check them. For example, 1 million requests per day is only about 12 per second.

Three worked designs

All numbers below are assumptions for practice, not measurements of real products. Change them to your own measured numbers.

1. A URL shortener

Users turn a long link into a short one, like sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x. A click on the short link redirects to the long one.

  1. Writes. 100 million new links per month. 10^8 / (30 \cdot 86{,}400) \approx 39 per second on average. With a busy-hour factor of 3, about 120 per second.
  2. Reads. 100 clicks per link: about 3,900 per second on average, 11,600 at the busy hour.
  3. Storage. In 5 years, 6 \cdot 10^9 links. At 500 bytes each, that is 3 TB.
  4. Key length. Keys use 62 characters: a to z, A to Z, 0 to 9. Seven characters give 62^7 \approx 3.5 \cdot 10^{12} keys. We use only 0.17% of them.
  5. Cache. Assume the hottest 20 million links get most clicks. At 500 bytes, that is 10 GB: it fits in one Redis node, with replicas. With a 90% hit ratio, the database sees about 1,160 reads per second at peak.
  6. Servers. Little's law: 11,600 requests per second at 5 ms each means 58 requests in flight. A few stateless servers are enough. Run at least 3 for failures.

Design choices. Keys come from a counter in base 62, where each server takes a block of 10,000 numbers at a time. Or keys are random, and an insert that finds the key taken simply tries again. A 301 redirect is permanent, so browsers cache it and later clicks never reach you. A 302 is temporary, so every click reaches you and you can count it. Link creation gets a token-bucket limit per API key, to stop spam.

2. A chat service

Users send messages to one person or to small groups. Messages must arrive in order, once, even after a phone loses signal.

  1. Load. 10 million daily users send 40 messages each: 400 million per day, about 4,600 per second, and 14,000 at the busy hour.
  2. Deliveries. The average conversation has 5 members, so 4 receivers per message: 56,000 deliveries per second at peak.
  3. Storage. 300 bytes per message with metadata: 120 GB per day, about 44 TB per year before replication.
  4. Connections. At peak, 30% of users are online: 3 million open WebSocket connections. If one gateway holds 50,000 (measure your own), you need 60 gateways, so plan 80.

The key ideas come from earlier chapters. Each conversation lives in one partition, so one leader gives every message a sequence number. The phone sends a client message id, which is an idempotency key. A retry after lost signal is saved only once. Delivery is at least once, and phones drop duplicates by id. When a phone reconnects, it asks: "send me everything after sequence 1,041".

3. A retrieval service for an AI app

An assistant answers questions from company documents. For each question, the retrieval service must return the 8 best text chunks, with permission checks, fast.

  1. Data. 2 million documents, 10 chunks each: 20 million chunks.
  2. Vector size. 1,024 dimensions as 4-byte floats is 4 KB per chunk, so 80 GB in total. As half-precision floats it is 40 GB. As one bit per dimension, it is 128 bytes per chunk, or 2.6 GB. The index graph comes on top.
  3. Shards. Split the vectors into 4 shards of 5 million, each with a replica. Each shard fits in the memory of one machine.
  4. Latency budget. Embed the question 30 ms. Vector and keyword search in parallel, 40 ms. Rerank 100 candidates, 120 ms. Fetch text 20 ms. Total about 210 ms, against an SLO of 400 ms at the 99th percentile.
  5. Load. At peak, 50 questions per second. Little's law: L = 50 \cdot 0.21 \approx 11 requests in flight. The reranker is busy 50 \cdot 0.12 = 6 calls at a time, so it needs batching or 8 workers.
  6. Tail. Each request waits for 4 shards. If each is slow 1% of the time, 1 - 0.99^4 \approx 3.9\% of requests are slow. Hedge a shard query after its 95th percentile.

Cache two things. Cache the question embedding by exact text. Cache results with a short TTL, under a key that includes the index version and the user's permission groups. When documents are re-indexed, bump the index version, and old results disappear at once. New documents go through a bounded ingest queue. Back-pressure there slows the uploads, not the search. A freshness SLO says: 99% of new documents are searchable within 5 minutes. The chapter Vector search and vector databases explains the index itself.

Filtering permissions after the search. Maybe the top 8 results all come from files this user may not open. Then the answer is empty. Or worse, private text leaks through the cache. Filter during the search, and put permissions in every cache key.

Practice

A service gets 400 requests per second, and each request takes 50 ms. On average, how many requests are in flight?

  • 8
  • 20
  • 200

Little's law: L = \lambda W = 400 \times 0.05 = 20.

A token bucket has rate 2 per second and size 6. A client has been quiet for a minute, then sends 10 requests at once. How many pass?

  • 2
  • 6
  • 10

The bucket is full after a long rest, so it holds 6 tokens. Six requests pass, and four get 429.

A request waits for 50 backends. Each is slow 2% of the time. About how often is the request slow?

  • 2%
  • 10%
  • 64%

1 - 0.98^{50} \approx 0.64. Fan-out turns a small tail into a common problem.

An SLO of 99.9% over 30 days allows ? minutes of full outage.

With a hit ratio of 0.95, a hit time of 1 ms and a miss time of 21 ms, the mean time is ? ms.

Four layers each try a call 3 times. One user click can cause ? calls at the bottom layer.

  1. Your app servers keep shopping carts in memory and use sticky sessions. Name two problems and a fix.
    Answer

    When a server dies or restarts, its users lose their carts. Load is uneven, because sticky users cannot move to a free server. Fix: keep carts in a shared store such as Redis or a database. Then any server can serve any user, and you can drop sticky sessions.

  2. A queue grows by 2,000 jobs every hour, all day. You add a second queue in front of it. Does that help? What should you do?
    Answer

    No. Arrivals are higher than the service rate, so any queue grows forever. Add workers until the service rate is above the arrival rate, or make each job cheaper. Also put a size limit on the queue and reject or drop work you cannot finish in time.

  3. The error budget of a 99.9% SLO is half spent after 10 days. The team wants to ship a large risky change. What does the burn rate tell you, and what do you suggest?
    Answer

    Half the budget in a third of the window is a burn rate of about 1.5. At that speed the budget runs out around day 20. Ship the risky change only with a canary (a release to a small share of users first) and a fast rollback, or wait. Spend some time on the causes of the errors first.

  4. Redo the URL shortener numbers for 1 billion new links per month, with the same read ratio and record size. Find peak reads per second and 5-year storage. Is 7 characters still enough?
    Answer

    Writes: 10^9 / 2{,}592{,}000 \approx 386 per second, peak about 1,160. Reads at 100 times: about 38,600 per second, peak about 116,000. In 5 years: 6 \cdot 10^{10} links times 500 bytes is 30 TB. Seven characters give 3.5 \cdot 10^{12} keys, so we use about 1.7%. That is still enough, but random keys will hit a taken key a little more often.

  5. In the retrieval design, the reranker becomes slow: 300 ms instead of 120 ms. What happens to the latency budget and to the work in flight? Suggest two fixes.
    Answer

    Total time grows to about 390 ms, very close to the 400 ms SLO, so the 99th percentile will break it. Work in flight at the reranker grows to 50 \cdot 0.3 = 15 calls. Fixes: rerank fewer candidates, for example 50 instead of 100. Batch calls on a GPU. Cache rerank results for repeated questions. Or skip the reranker when the first-stage scores are clearly separated.

Key takeaways

  • Scale up for simplicity, scale out for size and safety. Stateless services make scaling out easy.
  • Balance load with least connections, consistent hashing or two random choices, and check real health.
  • Caches need TTLs, deletion on write, versioned keys and protection from stampedes.
  • Little's law, L = \lambda W, sizes pools and workers. Bounded queues and load shedding stop overload.
  • Token buckets limit rate. Idempotency keys make retries safe. Retry at one layer with backoff and jitter.
  • Fan-out makes the tail common: 1 - (1 - p)^n. Hedged requests cut it for a small extra cost.
  • Measure with metrics, logs and traces. Set SLOs, spend the error budget on purpose, and alert on burn rate.

Sources

  • The Tail at Scale. Dean and Barroso (Communications of the ACM, February 2013): fan-out maths, Google measurements and hedged requests.
  • Embracing Risk. Google SRE book chapter on SLOs and error budgets.
  • Alerting on SLOs. Google SRE workbook: burn rate and multi-window alerts.
  • Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter. AWS Builders' Library: timeouts, retry layers, retry token buckets.
  • Idempotent requests. Stripe API reference: key length, key lifetime and saved results.
  • nginx upstream module. Load-balancing methods, consistent hashing and passive health checks.

Cryptography

Every web page, every git push and every passkey sign-in uses cryptography. It keeps data secret. It finds changes. It proves who sent a message. This chapter builds the main tools one by one, from the one-time pad to the post-quantum standards. Every tool comes with tested Rust and Python code.

  • Name the three goals of cryptography and choose the right tool for each one.
  • Use authenticated encryption, hashes, MACs and signatures correctly in Rust and Python.
  • Compute toy RSA and Diffie-Hellman by hand, and prove why RSA decrypts correctly.
  • Explain the TLS 1.3 handshake, certificates and safe password storage.
  • Describe ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA, and say what "secure" means in a formal game.

The toy examples here use tiny numbers so you can follow them by hand. Never use toy code to protect real data. In real work, use a well-known library, such as RustCrypto, ring or pyca/cryptography. All attacks in this chapter run only against our own toy code.

Goals, attackers and Kerckhoffs's principle

Ana sends a message to her bank: "pay Bo 100". Three bad things can happen on the way.

  • Eve reads the message. Now she knows Ana's business.
  • Mallory changes "100" to "1000". The bank pays the wrong amount.
  • Mallory writes a new message and puts Ana's name on it.

The readable message is the plaintext. The scrambled form is the ciphertext. A cipher does the scrambling. A key controls it. The attacker is everyone we do not trust: Eve listens, and Mallory also changes things.

The goals of cryptography and their tools
GoalQuestionToolIn this chapter
Confidentiality (secrecy)Can others read it?EncryptionAES-GCM, ML-KEM
IntegrityDid anyone change it?MAC, authenticated encryptionHMAC-SHA256
AuthenticityWho sent it?MAC (shared key) or signatureEd25519
Non-repudiationCan the sender deny it later?Signature onlyEd25519, ML-DSA

Now a key question. Should the cipher itself be secret? In 1883 Auguste Kerckhoffs gave the answer that cryptographers still use.

A cryptosystem must stay secure when the attacker knows everything about it except the key.

In simple words: assume the attacker has your source code. Only the key is secret. Claude Shannon later said it even more shortly: "the enemy knows the system".

Here is why it works. AES has been public since 2001. Thousands of experts have attacked it for over 20 years. A secret home-made cipher had no such tests. And if a key leaks, you change one key. If a secret design leaks, you must replace every device that uses it.

"Nobody knows our algorithm, so it is safe." This is called security through obscurity. Base64 is not encryption. XOR with a fixed string is not encryption. Reverse engineers find hidden designs quickly. Use public, reviewed algorithms and keep only the keys secret.

Perfect secrecy and the one-time pad

Start with the simplest cipher. Take a random key as long as the message. Combine each message byte with one key byte using XOR. XOR the ciphertext with the same key, and the message comes back.

// One-time pad: XOR each byte of the message with one byte of the key.
fn xor(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    a.iter().zip(b).map(|(x, y)| x ^ y).collect()
}

fn hex(b: &[u8]) -> String {
    b.iter().map(|x| format!("{:02x}", x)).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let key = [0x3a, 0x91, 0x5c, 0x07, 0xe2, 0x48, 0xbd, 0x16]; // truly random, used once
    let m1 = b"PAY BO 9";
    let c1 = xor(m1, &key);
    println!("cipher 1: {}", hex(&c1));
    println!("decrypt : {}", String::from_utf8(xor(&c1, &key)).unwrap());

    // The mistake: use the same key for a second message.
    let m2 = b"PAY EVE7";
    let c2 = xor(m2, &key);
    let leak = xor(&c1, &c2); // the key cancels out: c1 ^ c2 = m1 ^ m2
    println!("c1 ^ c2 : {}", hex(&leak));
    println!("m1 ^ m2 : {}", hex(&xor(m1, m2)));
}
# One-time pad: XOR each byte of the message with one byte of the key.
def xor(a: bytes, b: bytes) -> bytes:
    return bytes(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b))

key = bytes([0x3a, 0x91, 0x5c, 0x07, 0xe2, 0x48, 0xbd, 0x16])  # truly random, used once
m1 = b"PAY BO 9"
c1 = xor(m1, key)
print("cipher 1:", c1.hex())
print("decrypt :", xor(c1, key).decode())

# The mistake: use the same key for a second message.
m2 = b"PAY EVE7"
c2 = xor(m2, key)
leak = xor(c1, c2)  # the key cancels out: c1 ^ c2 = m1 ^ m2
print("c1 ^ c2 :", leak.hex())
print("m1 ^ m2 :", xor(m1, m2).hex())
cipher 1: 6ad00527a0079d2f
decrypt : PAY BO 9
c1 ^ c2 : 000000000719650e
m1 ^ m2 : 000000000719650e

This is the one-time pad. With a fresh random key, the ciphertext 6ad00527a0079d2f could come from any 8-byte message. Shannon made this idea exact in 1949.

A cipher has perfect secrecy when, for every message m and every ciphertext c, P(M = m \mid C = c) = P(M = m). Then:

  1. The one-time pad with a uniform random key, used once, has perfect secrecy.
  2. Every cipher with perfect secrecy has at least as many keys as messages: |\mathcal{K}| \ge |\mathcal{M}|.
Proof

Part 1. Messages, keys and ciphertexts are n-bit strings. For a fixed m and c, exactly one key works: k = m \oplus c. Each key has probability 2^{-n}. So P(C = c \mid M = m) = 2^{-n} for every m. The ciphertext does not depend on the message. By Bayes' rule, P(M = m \mid C = c) = P(M = m).

Part 2. Take a ciphertext c that can appear. Decrypt it with every key. You get at most |\mathcal{K}| different messages. If |\mathcal{K}| \lt |\mathcal{M}|, some possible message m' is never a result. Then P(M = m' \mid C = c) = 0, but P(M = m') \gt 0. This breaks perfect secrecy.

In simple words: perfect secrecy costs one key byte for every message byte, forever. A 1 GB file needs 1 GB of fresh random key. You must share that key safely in advance. That is why real systems aim for a weaker goal. We only need security against attackers with limited computing time.

Using a pad twice. Look at the output: c1 ^ c2 equals m1 ^ m2. The key is gone. The six zero bytes show that both messages start with the same six characters. In the 1940s Soviet spies reused some pad pages. The American Venona project then read many of their messages.

Symmetric encryption: AES, modes and AEAD

In symmetric encryption, Ana and Bo share one key. The most used cipher is AES. It is a block cipher: it turns 16 bytes into 16 bytes. Keys have 128, 192 or 256 bits. The other big choice is ChaCha20, a stream cipher. It is fast on phones without AES hardware.

But a message is rarely 16 bytes. A mode of operation says how to handle long messages.

Modes of operation
ModeHow it worksProblem or strengthUse it?
ECBEncrypt each block aloneEqual blocks give equal ciphertext. Patterns show.Never
CBCXOR each block with the previous ciphertext blockNeeds a random start value and padding. Padding errors leaked data in old TLS.Old systems only
CTREncrypt a counter, XOR the result with the dataFast and parallel. No integrity at all.As a part of GCM
GCMCTR plus a 16-byte tagSecrecy and integrity in one stepYes (TLS 1.3)
ChaCha20-Poly1305Stream cipher plus a 16-byte tagSecrecy and integrity, fast in softwareYes (TLS 1.3, WireGuard)

GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are AEAD modes. They need a nonce for each message. Here is AES-256-GCM in both languages.

// AES-256-GCM: authenticated encryption with the RustCrypto aes-gcm crate.
use aes_gcm::aead::{Aead, AeadCore, KeyInit, OsRng};
use aes_gcm::Aes256Gcm;

fn main() {
    let key = Aes256Gcm::generate_key(OsRng);      // 32 random bytes
    let cipher = Aes256Gcm::new(&key);
    let msg = b"pay Bo 100";

    let n1 = Aes256Gcm::generate_nonce(&mut OsRng); // 12 bytes, new for EVERY message
    let n2 = Aes256Gcm::generate_nonce(&mut OsRng);
    let c1 = cipher.encrypt(&n1, msg.as_ref()).unwrap();
    let c2 = cipher.encrypt(&n2, msg.as_ref()).unwrap();
    println!("message {} bytes, ciphertext {} bytes", msg.len(), c1.len());
    println!("same message, same ciphertext? {}", c1 == c2);

    let back = cipher.decrypt(&n1, c1.as_ref()).unwrap();
    println!("decrypt: {}", String::from_utf8(back).unwrap());

    let mut bad = c1.clone();
    bad[0] ^= 1; // the attacker flips one bit
    println!("after one flipped bit: {:?}", cipher.decrypt(&n1, bad.as_ref()).map(|_| ()));
}
# AES-256-GCM: authenticated encryption with the pyca/cryptography package.
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)   # 32 random bytes
cipher = AESGCM(key)
msg = b"pay Bo 100"

n1, n2 = os.urandom(12), os.urandom(12)     # 12 bytes, new for EVERY message
c1 = cipher.encrypt(n1, msg, None)
c2 = cipher.encrypt(n2, msg, None)
print(f"message {len(msg)} bytes, ciphertext {len(c1)} bytes")
print("same message, same ciphertext?", c1 == c2)
print("decrypt:", cipher.decrypt(n1, c1, None).decode())

bad = bytearray(c1)
bad[0] ^= 1                                 # the attacker flips one bit
try:
    cipher.decrypt(n1, bytes(bad), None)
except InvalidTag:
    print("after one flipped bit: InvalidTag")
message 10 bytes, ciphertext 26 bytes
same message, same ciphertext? false
decrypt: pay Bo 100
after one flipped bit: Err(Error)

Read the output line by line. The ciphertext has 26 bytes: 10 bytes of data and a 16-byte tag. The same message gives two different ciphertexts, because the nonces differ. One flipped bit makes decryption fail. Python prints True, False and InvalidTag in the same places.

Reusing a nonce with the same GCM key. The key stream repeats, so you get the two-time pad again. Worse, the attacker can learn the tag key and forge messages. With random 12-byte nonces, NIST SP 800-38D allows at most 2^{32} messages per key. Use a counter as the nonce, or change keys often.

Hashes, MACs and the birthday bound

A hash function turns any input into a short fingerprint. SHA-256 always gives 32 bytes. Change one letter, and about half the output bits change. This is the avalanche effect. The program below shows it. Then it keeps only the first 4 bytes of each hash and waits for two inputs to match.

// SHA-256, the avalanche effect, and a birthday collision on 32 bits.
use sha2::{Digest, Sha256};
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn hex(b: &[u8]) -> String { b.iter().map(|x| format!("{:02x}", x)).collect() }

fn main() {
    println!("hello -> {}", hex(&Sha256::digest(b"hello")));
    println!("hellp -> {}", hex(&Sha256::digest(b"hellp")));

    // Keep only the first 4 bytes (32 bits) and wait for two inputs to match.
    let mut seen: HashMap<[u8; 4], u64> = HashMap::new();
    for i in 0u64.. {
        let h = Sha256::digest(format!("msg-{i}").as_bytes());
        let short = [h[0], h[1], h[2], h[3]];
        if let Some(j) = seen.insert(short, i) {
            println!("msg-{j} and msg-{i} share the prefix {}", hex(&short));
            println!("tries: {}, square root of 2^32: {}", i + 1, 1u64 << 16);
            break;
        }
    }
}
# SHA-256, the avalanche effect, and a birthday collision on 32 bits.
import hashlib
from itertools import count

print("hello ->", hashlib.sha256(b"hello").hexdigest())
print("hellp ->", hashlib.sha256(b"hellp").hexdigest())

# Keep only the first 4 bytes (32 bits) and wait for two inputs to match.
seen = {}
for i in count():
    short = hashlib.sha256(f"msg-{i}".encode()).digest()[:4]
    if short in seen:
        print(f"msg-{seen[short]} and msg-{i} share the prefix {short.hex()}")
        print(f"tries: {i + 1}, square root of 2^32: {2**16}")
        break
    seen[short] = i
hello -> 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824
hellp -> fdd7585e08c4e2afd71dcabdb4636c89d557a3f42db9e2040c8bbd1708aa4ce7
msg-108856 and msg-114806 share the prefix 38b4f97a
tries: 114807, square root of 2^32: 65536

There are over 4 billion 32-bit values. Yet we found a match after about 115,000 tries. A good hash must resist three attacks:

  • Preimage resistance: from the hash alone, you cannot find an input.
  • Second-preimage resistance: you cannot find a second input with the same hash as a given one.
  • Collision resistance: you cannot find any two inputs with the same hash.

Collisions must exist, because there are more inputs than outputs. This is the pigeonhole principle. The question is how fast you can find one.

Pick q values independently and uniformly from N possible values. The probability of at least one collision satisfies

1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)} \le P(\text{collision}) \le \frac{q(q-1)}{2N}.

So about q \approx 1.18\sqrt{N} values give a 50% chance.

Proof

Upper bound. There are \binom{q}{2} = q(q-1)/2 pairs. Each pair collides with probability 1/N. The union bound adds these: q(q-1)/(2N).

Lower bound. The i-th value misses all earlier ones with probability 1 - (i-1)/N. So P(\text{no collision}) = \prod_{i=1}^{q-1} (1 - i/N). Use 1 - x \le e^{-x} on each factor. The product is at most e^{-\sum i/N} = e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)}. Set this equal to 1/2 and solve: q \approx \sqrt{2 \ln 2 \cdot N} \approx 1.18\sqrt{N}.

In simple words: collisions come at the square root of the output size, not at the full size. With 23 people, 1 - e^{-23 \cdot 22/730} = 1 - e^{-0.693} \approx 0.50. For our 32-bit test, \sqrt{2^{32}} = 65{,}536. The expected number of tries is about \sqrt{\pi N / 2} \approx 82{,}000. Our run needed 114,807, which is normal luck. The rule for design: an n-bit hash gives only about n/2 bits of collision resistance. SHA-256 gives 128 bits.

Today, use SHA-256 or SHA-512 (the SHA-2 family, FIPS 180-4), SHA-3 (FIPS 202) or BLAKE2. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken. The first public SHA-1 collision came in 2017. NIST plans to stop all use of SHA-1 by the end of 2030.

MACs: a hash with a key

A hash alone does not stop Mallory. She changes the message and computes a new hash. A MAC mixes in a secret key. Without the key, Mallory cannot make a valid tag. The standard choice is HMAC.

// HMAC-SHA256: a tag that only holders of the key can make.
use hmac::{Hmac, Mac};
use sha2::Sha256;

type HmacSha256 = Hmac<Sha256>;

fn tag(key: &[u8], msg: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut mac = HmacSha256::new_from_slice(key).unwrap();
    mac.update(msg);
    mac.finalize().into_bytes().to_vec()
}

fn check(key: &[u8], msg: &[u8], t: &[u8]) -> bool {
    let mut mac = HmacSha256::new_from_slice(key).unwrap();
    mac.update(msg);
    mac.verify_slice(t).is_ok() // compares in constant time
}

fn main() {
    let key = b"a 32-byte secret shared by A & B"; // demo only: real keys are random
    let t = tag(key, b"pay Bo 100");
    let hex: String = t.iter().map(|x| format!("{:02x}", x)).collect();
    println!("tag: {}", hex);
    println!("pay Bo 100  -> {}", check(key, b"pay Bo 100", &t));
    println!("pay Bo 1000 -> {}", check(key, b"pay Bo 1000", &t));
}
# HMAC-SHA256: a tag that only holders of the key can make.
import hashlib
import hmac

def tag(key: bytes, msg: bytes) -> bytes:
    return hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).digest()

def check(key: bytes, msg: bytes, t: bytes) -> bool:
    return hmac.compare_digest(tag(key, msg), t)  # constant time, never ==

key = b"a 32-byte secret shared by A & B"  # demo only: real keys are random
t = tag(key, b"pay Bo 100")
print("tag:", t.hex())
print("pay Bo 100  ->", check(key, b"pay Bo 100", t))
print("pay Bo 1000 ->", check(key, b"pay Bo 1000", t))
tag: eba13286d12ed3b7f5c4f9e66a448ba59c9fb31011252b7c14bb536a15c58fce
pay Bo 100  -> true
pay Bo 1000 -> false

Two classic bugs. First, tag = SHA-256(key || message) looks fine but is not. With SHA-2, an attacker can add data to the end and compute a valid new tag. This is a length extension attack. HMAC is safe from it. Second, comparing tags with == can stop at the first wrong byte. The time difference tells the attacker how many bytes are right. Always use a constant-time comparison.

Public keys: Diffie-Hellman, RSA and elliptic curves

Symmetric crypto has one big problem. How do Ana and Bo get a shared key in the first place? In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman showed a way. Two people can agree on a secret over a public line.

  1. Everyone knows the prime p = 23 and the base g = 5.
  2. Ana picks a secret a = 6. She sends A = 5^6 \bmod 23 = 8.
  3. Bo picks a secret b = 15. He sends B = 5^{15} \bmod 23 = 19.
  4. Ana computes B^a = 19^6 \bmod 23 = 2.
  5. Bo computes A^b = 8^{15} \bmod 23 = 2. Both have the secret 2, because both equal g^{ab} \bmod p.
  6. Eve saw 23, 5, 8 and 19. To get 2, she must find a from 5^a \bmod 23 = 8.

Finding a is the discrete logarithm problem. With a 23 it is easy. With a 3072-bit prime, no known normal computer can do it in a useful time. Today we use the same idea on elliptic curves, as X25519.

Plain Diffie-Hellman does not say who is on the other side. Mallory can sit in the middle and run one exchange with Ana and another with Bo. This is a man-in-the-middle attack. The fix is to sign the exchange. TLS does exactly this, as you will see below.

RSA

RSA came in 1977, from Rivest, Shamir and Adleman. It uses a key pair. Here is how to make one:

  1. Pick two secret primes p and q. Compute n = pq and \varphi(n) = (p-1)(q-1).
  2. Pick e with no common factor with \varphi(n). Often e = 65537.
  3. Compute d with ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(n)}. The public key is (n, e). The private key is d.
  4. Encrypt: c = m^e \bmod n. Decrypt: m = c^d \bmod n.
// Toy RSA with tiny primes. For learning only: real keys use 3072-bit n and padding.
fn modpow(mut b: u128, mut e: u128, m: u128) -> u128 {
    let mut r = 1;
    b %= m;
    while e > 0 {
        if e & 1 == 1 { r = r * b % m; } // multiply when the bit is 1
        b = b * b % m;                    // square for the next bit
        e >>= 1;
    }
    r
}

// Inverse of a mod m with the extended Euclidean algorithm.
fn inverse(a: i128, m: i128) -> i128 {
    let (mut r0, mut r1, mut s0, mut s1) = (m, a, 0, 1);
    while r1 != 0 {
        let q = r0 / r1;
        (r0, r1) = (r1, r0 - q * r1);
        (s0, s1) = (s1, s0 - q * s1);
    }
    s0.rem_euclid(m)
}

fn main() {
    let (p, q) = (47u128, 59u128);
    let n = p * q;
    let phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1);
    let e = 17;
    let d = inverse(e as i128, phi as i128) as u128;
    println!("n = {n}, phi = {phi}, e = {e}, d = {d}");
    let m = 1234;
    let c = modpow(m, e, n);
    println!("encrypt {m} -> {c}, decrypt -> {}", modpow(c, d, n));
    let s = modpow(m, d, n); // sign with the private key
    println!("sign {m} -> {s}, verify -> {}", modpow(s, e, n));
}
# Toy RSA with tiny primes. For learning only: real keys use 3072-bit n and padding.
p, q = 47, 59
n = p * q
phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)
e = 17
d = pow(e, -1, phi)          # modular inverse (Python 3.8+)
print(f"n = {n}, phi = {phi}, e = {e}, d = {d}")
m = 1234
c = pow(m, e, n)             # fast modular power
print(f"encrypt {m} -> {c}, decrypt -> {pow(c, d, n)}")
s = pow(m, d, n)             # sign with the private key
print(f"sign {m} -> {s}, verify -> {pow(s, e, n)}")
n = 2773, phi = 2668, e = 17, d = 157
encrypt 1234 -> 1793, decrypt -> 1234
sign 1234 -> 726, verify -> 1234

Check d by hand: 17 \times 157 = 2669 = 2668 + 1. So ed \equiv 1 \pmod{2668}. But why does decryption give back exactly 1234?

Let p \ne q be primes, n = pq, and ed \equiv 1 \pmod{(p-1)(q-1)}. Then for every whole number m with 0 \le m \lt n:

(m^e)^d \equiv m \pmod{n}.
Proof

Write ed = 1 + k(p-1)(q-1) for some whole number k \ge 0. First work modulo p.

Case 1: p does not divide m. Fermat's little theorem says m^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p. So m^{ed} = m \cdot (m^{p-1})^{k(q-1)} \equiv m \cdot 1 = m \pmod p.

Case 2: p divides m. Then both m^{ed} and m are 0 modulo p.

In both cases m^{ed} \equiv m \pmod p. The same steps give m^{ed} \equiv m \pmod q. So p and q both divide m^{ed} - m. They are different primes, so pq = n divides it too. This is the Chinese remainder theorem in its simplest form.

In simple words: raising to e and then to d is a full trip around a circle of size \varphi(n). You land where you started. Breaking RSA seems to need the factors p and q. Factoring 2773 is easy. Factoring a 3072-bit n is far beyond any normal computer.

"Textbook RSA" as in our toy code is not secure. It is deterministic, so equal messages give equal ciphertexts. It is also malleable: c_1 c_2 is a valid encryption of m_1 m_2. Real RSA adds random padding: OAEP for encryption and PSS for signatures. Use at least 2048-bit keys, and 3072 bits for 128-bit security.

Elliptic curves

An elliptic curve is a set of points that solve an equation like y^2 = x^3 + 7. This one is used in Bitcoin. Over the real numbers it looks like the picture below. In cryptography we use the same equation modulo a large prime.

You can "add" two points. Draw a line through them. It meets the curve at a third point. Reflect that point in the x-axis, and you have the sum. Adding a point P to itself k times gives kP. Computing kP is fast with "double and add", the same trick as modpow above. Finding k from P and kP is the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. It is much harder than factoring for keys of the same size.

Sizes for about 128 bits of security (NIST SP 800-57)
FamilyExampleKey sizeMain use
SymmetricAES-128128 bitsBulk encryption
FactoringRSA-30723072 bitsOld signatures and key transport
Elliptic curveX25519, Ed25519, P-256256 bitsKey exchange and signatures

Shor's algorithm (1994) solves factoring, discrete logs and elliptic curve discrete logs fast on a large quantum computer. No such computer exists today. But RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves all fall to the same attack. The post-quantum section below covers the replacements.

Signatures, certificates and TLS 1.3

A digital signature is a MAC with two keys. Only the private key can sign. Anyone with the public key can check. Here is Ed25519, a fast elliptic-curve signature.

// Ed25519 signatures with the ed25519-dalek crate.
use ed25519_dalek::{Signer, SigningKey, Verifier};
use rand::rngs::OsRng;

fn main() {
    let sk = SigningKey::generate(&mut OsRng); // private key: keep it secret
    let vk = sk.verifying_key();               // public key: give it to everyone
