Classical AI and reinforcement learning

Before language models, AI meant search, logic and probability. These ideas still run route planners, game engines, schedulers and robots. Reinforcement learning adds learning from reward, and it is part of how language models are trained today.

  • Describe a problem as search and choose BFS, DFS, uniform cost search or A*.
  • Prove that A* with an admissible heuristic finds a cheapest path.
  • Play games with minimax, alpha-beta pruning and Monte Carlo tree search.
  • Solve constraint and planning problems, and reason with Bayesian networks and hidden Markov models.
  • Solve a Markov decision process with value iteration, learn it with Q-learning and explain the policy gradient theorem.

Search problems and uninformed search

Look at the 8-puzzle. Eight numbered tiles sit in a 3 × 3 box with one empty square. You slide a tile into the gap. The goal is the order 1 to 8 with the gap last. What is the shortest list of moves?

A computer sees this as a search problem. It has five parts:

  • States. Every possible layout of the tiles. Half of the 9! layouts can reach the goal: 181,440 states.
  • Initial state. The layout we start from.
  • Actions. Move the gap up, down, left or right.
  • Transition model. Which state each action leads to.
  • Goal test and cost. Is this the goal? Each move costs 1.

A search algorithm keeps a frontier. It takes one state out, makes its neighbours and adds them to the frontier. This is called expanding the state. A set of visited states stops it from expanding the same state twice. The only difference between the algorithms is the order in which they take states out.

Uninformed search. b = branching factor, d = depth of the best goal, m = largest depth, C* = best cost, ε = smallest step cost.
AlgorithmTakes out nextFinds a goal?Cheapest?TimeMemory
Breadth-first (BFS)the oldest state (queue)yesif all steps cost the sameO(b^d)O(b^d)
Depth-first (DFS)the newest state (stack)not on infinite pathsnoO(b^m)O(bm)
Iterative deepeningDFS with limit 1, 2, 3, ...yesif all steps cost the sameO(b^d)O(bd)
Uniform cost (UCS)the cheapest path so faryes, if \varepsilon \gt 0yesO(b^{1 + C^*/\varepsilon})same as time

Uniform cost search is Dijkstra's algorithm that stops at the goal. The chapter Graph algorithms proves that BFS and Dijkstra find shortest paths. Here we care about one number: memory.

  1. Take b = 10 and a goal at depth d = 8. BFS may hold about 10^8 states.
  2. At 100 bytes per state, that is 10 GB of memory.
  3. Iterative deepening holds only about b \cdot d = 80 states. It repeats the top levels, but the last level dominates, so the time is about the same.

Running DFS on a graph without a visited set. In the 8-puzzle, moving the gap left and then right gives the start state again. DFS can loop forever. Keep a visited set, or at least never undo the last move.

A* and heuristics

Uniform cost search spreads out in all directions. It does not know where the goal is. A heuristic h(n) gives it a sense of direction. A* takes out the state with the smallest

f(n) = g(n) + h(n),

where g(n) is the cost so far. Hart, Nilsson and Raphael published A* in 1968. Let us try three heuristics on one hard puzzle.

  • zero: h = 0. This is uniform cost search.
  • misplaced: the number of tiles in the wrong square.
  • manhattan: for each tile, the rows plus columns to its home square.
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap};

type State = [u8; 9]; // 0 is the empty square
const GOAL: State = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 0];

fn zero(_: &State) -> u32 { 0 } // no guess: uniform cost search
fn misplaced(s: &State) -> u32 { (0..9).filter(|&i| s[i] != 0 && s[i] != GOAL[i]).count() as u32 }
fn manhattan(s: &State) -> u32 { // sum of each tile's grid distance
    let d = |i: usize, t: usize| (i / 3).abs_diff(t / 3) + (i % 3).abs_diff(t % 3);
    (0..9).filter(|&i| s[i] != 0).map(|i| d(i, s[i] as usize - 1) as u32).sum()
}

fn neighbours(s: &State) -> Vec<State> {
    let z = s.iter().position(|&t| t == 0).unwrap(); // move the gap up, down, left, right
    let moves = [(z >= 3, z.wrapping_sub(3)), (z < 6, z + 3),
                 (z % 3 > 0, z.wrapping_sub(1)), (z % 3 < 2, z + 1)];
    moves.iter().filter(|m| m.0).map(|&(_, n)| { let mut t = *s; t.swap(z, n); t }).collect()
}

fn astar(start: State, h: fn(&State) -> u32) -> (u32, u32) {
    let mut frontier = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((h(&start), 0u32, start))]); // by f = g + h
    let (mut best, mut expanded) = (HashMap::from([(start, 0u32)]), 0);
    while let Some(Reverse((_, g, s))) = frontier.pop() {
        if g > best[&s] { continue; } // an old, worse copy: skip it
        if s == GOAL { return (g, expanded); }
        expanded += 1;
        for n in neighbours(&s) {
            if g + 1 < *best.get(&n).unwrap_or(&u32::MAX) { // every move costs 1
                best.insert(n, g + 1);
                frontier.push(Reverse((g + 1 + h(&n), g + 1, n)));
            }
        }
    }
    unreachable!()
}

fn main() {
    let start: State = [7, 8, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 1, 0];
    let hs: [(&str, fn(&State) -> u32); 3] =
        [("zero", zero), ("misplaced", misplaced), ("manhattan", manhattan)];
    for (name, h) in hs {
        let (cost, expanded) = astar(start, h);
        println!("{name:<10} path cost {cost}  expanded {expanded}");
    }
}
import heapq

GOAL = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 0)               # 0 is the empty square

def zero(s): return 0                             # no guess: uniform cost search
def misplaced(s): return sum(1 for i in range(9) if s[i] and s[i] != GOAL[i])
def manhattan(s):                                 # sum of each tile's grid distance
    return sum(abs(i // 3 - (s[i] - 1) // 3) + abs(i % 3 - (s[i] - 1) % 3)
               for i in range(9) if s[i])

def neighbours(s):
    z = s.index(0)                                # move the gap up, down, left, right
    for ok, n in [(z >= 3, z - 3), (z < 6, z + 3), (z % 3 > 0, z - 1), (z % 3 < 2, z + 1)]:
        if ok:
            t = list(s)
            t[z], t[n] = t[n], t[z]
            yield tuple(t)

def astar(start, h):
    frontier = [(h(start), 0, start)]             # a heap ordered by f = g + h
    best, expanded = {start: 0}, 0
    while frontier:
        f, g, s = heapq.heappop(frontier)
        if g > best[s]:
            continue                              # an old, worse copy: skip it
        if s == GOAL:
            return g, expanded
        expanded += 1
        for n in neighbours(s):
            if g + 1 < best.get(n, 10**9):        # every move costs 1
                best[n] = g + 1
                heapq.heappush(frontier, (g + 1 + h(n), g + 1, n))

start = (7, 8, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 1, 0)
for h in (zero, misplaced, manhattan):
    cost, expanded = astar(start, h)
    print(f"{h.__name__:<10} path cost {cost}  expanded {expanded}")
zero       path cost 24  expanded 121054
misplaced  path cost 24  expanded 16790
manhattan  path cost 24  expanded 798

All three paths cost 24, the true minimum. Why can we trust that? Because both heuristics never guess too high.

Let h^*(n) be the true cheapest cost from n to a goal. A heuristic is admissible if h(n) \le h^*(n) for every state. It is consistent if h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n') for every step from n to n', and h(\text{goal}) = 0.

Let all step costs be at least some \varepsilon \gt 0. If h is admissible, A* returns a cheapest path to a goal (when it may re-open a state after finding a cheaper path to it, as our code does). If h is also consistent, A* never needs to re-open a state.

Proof

Let C^* be the cheapest cost. Suppose A* takes out a goal G_2 with cost g(G_2) \gt C^*. Since h(G_2) = 0, we have f(G_2) = g(G_2) \gt C^*.

Look at a cheapest path to a goal. Before G_2 comes out, some state n on this path is on the frontier with its true best cost, g(n) = g^*(n). (The start is such a state. When such a state is expanded, its successor on the path gets its best cost.)

Admissibility gives f(n) = g^*(n) + h(n) \le g^*(n) + h^*(n) = C^*. So f(n) \le C^* \lt f(G_2). A* always takes out the smallest f. So it takes out n before G_2. The same holds for the next state on the path, and so on, until the cheap goal comes out first. This contradicts the start of the proof.

With consistency, f never decreases along a path. So the first time A* takes out a state, its g is already the best. No re-opening is needed.

In simple words: an honest optimist never misses the best path. Uniform cost search is the case h = 0, so the theorem includes Dijkstra.

Where do good heuristics come from? From a relaxed problem. "Misplaced" is the exact cost if a tile could jump anywhere. "Manhattan" is the exact cost if tiles could slide over each other. A relaxed problem is easier, so its cost is never higher. Manhattan is never below misplaced, so it dominates it and expands fewer states.

One number summarises the gain. The effective branching factor b^* solves N + 1 = 1 + b^* + (b^*)^2 + \dots + (b^*)^d. For our runs with d = 24: zero gives b^* \approx 1.56, misplaced 1.43, Manhattan 1.23.

"A bigger heuristic is always better." Only while it stays admissible. Twice the Manhattan distance is faster but can return a longer path. Sometimes that trade is fine. Weighted A* uses f = g + w \cdot h. With an admissible h, its path costs at most w times the best. Choose it on purpose, not by accident.

Games: minimax, alpha-beta and Monte Carlo tree search

In a game, an opponent answers every move. Two players, MAX and MIN, take turns. MAX wants a high score and MIN wants a low score. Look at this small game tree. MAX moves first, then MIN, then the game ends with the scores at the leaves.

The minimax value of a position is its score if it is final. At a MAX position, it is the largest value of the children. At a MIN position, it is the smallest value of the children.

MIN a gives 4. At MIN b the first leaf is 2. MIN will pick 2 or less there. But MAX already has 4 from a, so MAX will never choose b. The other two leaves of b do not matter. This is alpha-beta pruning. The search keeps two numbers. \alpha is the best score MAX is sure of. \beta is the best score MIN is sure of. When \alpha \ge \beta, the rest of the branch is skipped.

const LINES: [[usize; 3]; 8] =
    [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8], [0, 3, 6], [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], [0, 4, 8], [2, 4, 6]];

fn winner(b: &[u8; 9]) -> i32 {
    for [x, y, z] in LINES {
        if b[x] != b'.' && b[x] == b[y] && b[y] == b[z] {
            return if b[x] == b'X' { 1 } else { -1 }; // +1: X (MAX) wins, -1: O (MIN) wins
        }
    }
    0
}

fn value(b: &mut [u8; 9], max: bool, mut alpha: i32, mut beta: i32,
         prune: bool, visits: &mut u64) -> i32 {
    *visits += 1; // count every position we look at
    let w = winner(b);
    if w != 0 || !b.contains(&b'.') {
        return w; // the game is over
    }
    let mut best = if max { -2 } else { 2 };
    for i in 0..9 {
        if b[i] == b'.' {
            b[i] = if max { b'X' } else { b'O' };
            let v = value(b, !max, alpha, beta, prune, visits);
            b[i] = b'.'; // undo the move
            if max { best = best.max(v); alpha = alpha.max(v); }
            else { best = best.min(v); beta = beta.min(v); }
            if prune && alpha >= beta {
                break; // the other player will never allow this
            }
        }
    }
    best
}

fn main() {
    for prune in [false, true] {
        let mut visits = 0;
        let v = value(&mut [b'.'; 9], true, -2, 2, prune, &mut visits);
        let on = if prune { "on" } else { "off" };
        println!("pruning {on:<3}  value {v}  positions visited {visits}");
    }
}
LINES = [(0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6, 7, 8), (0, 3, 6),     # the 8 ways to win
         (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 8), (0, 4, 8), (2, 4, 6)]
visits = 0

def winner(b):
    for x, y, z in LINES:
        if b[x] != "." and b[x] == b[y] == b[z]:
            return 1 if b[x] == "X" else -1      # +1: X (MAX) wins, -1: O (MIN) wins
    return 0

def value(b, player, alpha, beta, prune):
    global visits
    visits += 1                                  # count every position we look at
    w = winner(b)
    if w != 0 or "." not in b:
        return w                                 # the game is over
    best = -2 if player == "X" else 2
    for i in range(9):
        if b[i] == ".":
            v = value(b[:i] + player + b[i + 1:], "O" if player == "X" else "X",
                      alpha, beta, prune)
            if player == "X":
                best, alpha = max(best, v), max(alpha, v)
            else:
                best, beta = min(best, v), min(beta, v)
            if prune and alpha >= beta:
                break                            # the other player will never allow this
    return best

for prune in (False, True):
    visits = 0
    v = value("." * 9, "X", -2, 2, prune)
    print(f"pruning {'on' if prune else 'off':<3}  value {v}  positions visited {visits}")
pruning off  value 0  positions visited 549946
pruning on   value 0  positions visited 18297

The value is 0, so perfect tic-tac-toe is a draw. Plain minimax visits the whole game tree, 549,946 positions. Alpha-beta gives the same value after 18,297 positions, 30 times fewer. Knuth and Moore showed in 1975 that with perfect move order, alpha-beta looks at about b^{d/2} positions instead of b^d. So in the same time it searches about twice as deep.

Chess has far too many positions to search to the end. Real engines stop at a depth limit and use an evaluation function, such as a weighted count of pieces. IBM's Deep Blue used deep alpha-beta search and beat the world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.

Monte Carlo tree search

Go has about 250 moves per position, and a good evaluation function was hard to write. Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) does not need one. It plays many fast games to the end and learns which moves win often.

Selection

Start at the root. Walk down the tree. At each node pick the child with the highest UCB1 score.

Expansion

At the edge of the tree, add one new child node for an untried move.

Simulation

From the new node, play the game to the end with quick, simple moves. Note who won.

Backpropagation

Walk back up to the root. Add one visit, and the win if there was one, to every node on the path.

Choose a move

After many rounds, play the root move with the most visits.

A child j has won w_j of its n_j visits, and its parent has N visits. Select the child with the largest

\frac{w_j}{n_j} + c \sqrt{\frac{\ln N}{n_j}}

The first term rewards moves that win. The second term rewards moves with few visits. A common choice is c = \sqrt{2}.

  1. Move A won 6 of 10 visits. Move B won 3 of 4. The parent has N = 14, so \ln 14 \approx 2.639.
  2. A: 0.6 + 1.414 \sqrt{2.639 / 10} \approx 0.6 + 0.727 = 1.327.
  3. B: 0.75 + 1.414 \sqrt{2.639 / 4} \approx 0.75 + 1.149 = 1.899.
  4. B wins the selection. It has a good rate and few visits, so we want to learn more about it.

Kocsis and Szepesvári called this UCT in 2006. DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4 to 1 in March 2016. It guided MCTS with two neural networks: a policy network to suggest moves and a value network to judge positions. Its successor AlphaZero learned chess, shogi and Go by playing against itself.

Stopping a depth-limited search in the middle of a fight. If a queen is about to be taken one move after the limit, the evaluation function cannot see it. This is the horizon effect. Engines search further in "noisy" positions until things are quiet.

Constraint satisfaction

A conference has five talks, A to E, and three time slots. Some talks share a speaker, so they need different slots. The conflicts are A–B, A–C, B–C, B–D, C–D and D–E.

A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) has variables, a domain of allowed values for each variable, and constraints that say which value combinations are allowed. A solution gives every variable a value and breaks no constraint.

The basic method is backtracking: give a value to one variable at a time, and go back when a constraint breaks. Three tricks make it fast:

  • MRV. Choose the variable with the fewest values left. Break ties by the most constraints.
  • Forward checking. After each choice, remove the clashing values from the neighbours.
  • Least constraining value. Try first the value that removes the fewest options from neighbours.
  1. All domains are {1, 2, 3}. B, C and D have the most constraints. Choose the first, B, and give it slot 1.
  2. Forward checking: A, C and D lose slot 1. They now have {2, 3}.
  3. MRV ties A, C and D. C and D have the most open neighbours. Choose C and give it slot 2. Now A and D have only {3}.
  4. A = 3 and D = 3. They are not connected, so this is allowed.
  5. E clashes only with D. Give E slot 1. Done: A3, B1, C2, D3, E1, with no backtracking.

A stronger check is arc consistency. The arc from X to Y is consistent if every value left for X has some allowed value in Y. The AC-3 algorithm keeps a queue of arcs and removes values until all arcs are consistent. For c constraints and domains of size d, it takes at most O(c d^3) time.

Colouring a graph with three colours is NP-complete, so no method is fast on every input. See Complexity theory. In practice, MRV and propagation solve large real problems. Modern SAT solvers use the same ideas, as Logic and formal methods shows.

Taking the variables in a fixed order, such as alphabetical. A hard variable found late causes deep, slow backtracking. Let MRV choose. It finds dead ends early, when they are cheap to undo.

Planning

A robot must bring a parcel from room B to room C. It starts in room A. A planner describes the world with facts and each action with three lists.

Move(r, from, to)
  pre:  At(r, from), Door(from, to)
  add:  At(r, to)
  del:  At(r, from)

Pick(r, p, room)
  pre:  At(r, room), ParcelAt(p, room), HandEmpty(r)
  add:  Holding(r, p)
  del:  ParcelAt(p, room), HandEmpty(r)

Drop(r, p, room)
  pre:  At(r, room), Holding(r, p)
  add:  ParcelAt(p, room), HandEmpty(r)
  del:  Holding(r, p)

A state is a set of true facts. An action has preconditions, an add list and a delete list. It can run when all preconditions are in the state. The new state is the old state minus the delete list plus the add list. A plan is a list of actions that turns the start state into a state where the goal facts are true.

From At(R, A), Door(A, B), Door(B, C) and ParcelAt(P, B), a planner finds: Move(R, A, B), Pick(R, P, B), Move(R, B, C), Drop(R, P, C). STRIPS comes from Fikes and Nilsson (1971). The standard language today is PDDL, first defined in 1998 for planning competitions.

How does a planner search? It runs A* over states. The heuristic comes from a relaxed problem again: ignore the delete lists. Then facts are never lost, and a plan for the relaxed problem is easy to find. Its length is a good guess. The FF planner by Hoffmann and Nebel (2001) made this idea famous. It is a good example of one method, A* with relaxation, serving many problems.

LLM agents plan too, as the chapter Large language models and agents shows. A language model is good at writing a plan in words. A classical planner is good at checking that every precondition holds. Some systems use both: the model writes the plan, and code checks each step before it runs.

Forgetting the delete list. If Move does not delete At(r, from), the robot is in two rooms at once, and the planner finds impossible plans. Every action must say what stops being true.

Bayesian networks and hidden Markov models

An alert fires in your monitoring system. Was there a bad deploy? A Bayesian network answers this with probabilities. Each arrow points from a cause to an effect.

The numbers: P(Deploy) = 0.1 and P(Traffic) = 0.2. An error spike has probability 0.9 with both causes, 0.7 with only a deploy, 0.3 with only traffic and 0.05 with neither. The alert fires with probability 0.95 after a spike and 0.02 without one.

A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph. Each variable has a table P(X_i \mid \text{parents}(X_i)). The joint probability is the product

P(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i \mid \text{parents}(x_i))

The full joint table of four yes-or-no variables needs 15 numbers. The network needs 1 + 1 + 4 + 2 = 8. With 30 variables, the gap is huge.

  1. Chance of a spike: 0.02 \cdot 0.9 + 0.08 \cdot 0.7 + 0.18 \cdot 0.3 + 0.72 \cdot 0.05 = 0.164.
  2. Chance of an alert: 0.164 \cdot 0.95 + 0.836 \cdot 0.02 = 0.17252.
  3. With a deploy, a spike has chance 0.2 \cdot 0.9 + 0.8 \cdot 0.7 = 0.74. So P(\text{Alert} \mid \text{Deploy}) = 0.74 \cdot 0.95 + 0.26 \cdot 0.02 = 0.7082.
  4. Bayes' rule: P(\text{Deploy} \mid \text{Alert}) = 0.1 \cdot 0.7082 / 0.17252 \approx 0.41.
  5. Now we also learn there was a traffic peak. The same method gives P(\text{Deploy} \mid \text{Alert}, \text{Traffic}) \approx 0.24.

The last step is called explaining away. The traffic peak explains the alert, so a deploy is less likely. Rules like "if alert then deploy" cannot do this. Exact inference in a general network is NP-hard. Real tools use the graph structure or sampling.

Hidden Markov models

Now add time. A server is Healthy or Degraded, but you cannot see this. You only see the latency of each minute: Fast or Slow. A hidden Markov model (HMM) links the two:

  • Start: Healthy 0.8, Degraded 0.2.
  • Change each minute: Healthy stays Healthy with 0.9. Degraded stays Degraded with 0.7.
  • Signals: a Healthy server is Fast with 0.9. A Degraded server is Slow with 0.7.
  1. Minute 1, Fast: f_1(H) = 0.8 \cdot 0.9 = 0.72 and f_1(D) = 0.2 \cdot 0.3 = 0.06.
  2. Minute 2, Slow: f_2(H) = (0.72 \cdot 0.9 + 0.06 \cdot 0.3) \cdot 0.1 = 0.0666 and f_2(D) = (0.72 \cdot 0.1 + 0.06 \cdot 0.7) \cdot 0.7 = 0.0798.
  3. Minute 3, Slow: f_3(H) = 0.008388 and f_3(D) = 0.043764.
  4. Normalise: P(\text{Degraded now}) = 0.043764 / 0.052152 \approx 0.84.
  5. Viterbi keeps the best path instead of the sum. The most likely story is Healthy, Degraded, Degraded.

The first four steps are the forward algorithm. The last step is the Viterbi algorithm, from 1967. Both cost O(T \cdot S^2) for T steps and S states, not S^T. They are dynamic programming, like the methods in Dynamic programming and greedy algorithms.

Mixing up P(\text{Alert} \mid \text{Deploy}) and P(\text{Deploy} \mid \text{Alert}). The first is 0.71 here. The second is only 0.41. Deploys are rare, so most alerts have other causes. Always include the base rate.

Markov decision processes and value iteration

A warehouse robot lives on a 3 × 4 grid. It starts at S in the bottom-left corner. The charger C in the bottom-right gives +10 and ends the trip. A hole H in the top row gives −10 and also ends it. Every other move costs 1. The floor is slippery: a move goes the planned way with 0.8, and slips to each side with 0.1.

A Markov decision process (MDP) has states S, actions A, transition probabilities P(s' \mid s, a), rewards R(s, a, s') and a discount factor \gamma. A policy \pi chooses an action in each state. Its value V^\pi(s) is the expected sum of discounted rewards r_1 + \gamma r_2 + \gamma^2 r_3 + \dots from s.

"Markov" means the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the past. The best values obey one equation.

The optimal value function V^* satisfies, for every state s,

V^*(s) = \max_{a} \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V^*(s') \big]

In the same way, the optimal action values satisfy Q^*(s, a) = \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \big]. For \gamma \lt 1 and bounded rewards, V^* is the only solution.

Proof idea

Split the return into the first reward and the rest: G = r_1 + \gamma G'. By Bellman's principle of optimality, after the first step an optimal policy must act optimally from s', so the rest is worth V^*(s'). By linearity of expectation, the expected return of action a is the sum over s' in the formula. The best action takes the maximum.

Uniqueness: call the right side T V. For any two value functions, \max_s |TV(s) - TU(s)| \le \gamma \max_s |V(s) - U(s)|. So T is a contraction. A contraction has exactly one fixed point, by Banach's fixed-point theorem.

In simple words: the value of a state is the best "reward now plus discounted value next". With \gamma = 0.5 and a reward of 1 on every step forever, V = 1 + 0.5 V, so V = 2.

Value iteration turns the equation into an algorithm. Start with all values 0. Replace each value by the right side of the equation. Repeat. The code is in three parts. Part 1 is the world. Part 2 is value iteration. Part 3, in the next section, is Q-learning.

// A 3 x 4 warehouse. S start, # wall, H hole (-10, ends), C charger (+10, ends).
const GRID: [&[u8; 4]; 3] = [b"..H.", b".#..", b"S..C"];
const MOVES: [(i32, i32); 4] = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]; // up, right, down, left
const GAMMA: f64 = 0.9;
type S = (usize, usize);

fn cell(s: S) -> u8 { GRID[s.0][s.1] }
fn end(s: S) -> bool { cell(s) == b'H' || cell(s) == b'C' }
fn reward(s: S) -> f64 { match cell(s) { b'H' => -10.0, b'C' => 10.0, _ => -1.0 } }

fn go(s: S, a: usize) -> S { // one move; walls and edges block it
    let (r, c) = (s.0 as i32 + MOVES[a].0, s.1 as i32 + MOVES[a].1);
    let ok = (0..3).contains(&r) && (0..4).contains(&c) && GRID[r as usize][c as usize] != b'#';
    if ok { (r as usize, c as usize) } else { s }
}

fn outcomes(s: S, a: usize) -> [(f64, S); 3] { // 80% as planned, 10% slip to each side
    [(0.8, go(s, a)), (0.1, go(s, (a + 1) % 4)), (0.1, go(s, (a + 3) % 4))]
}

fn q_value(v: &[[f64; 4]; 3], s: S, a: usize) -> f64 { // right side of the Bellman equation
    outcomes(s, a).iter().map(|&(p, t)| p * (reward(t) + GAMMA * v[t.0][t.1])).sum()
}

fn argmax(f: impl Fn(usize) -> f64) -> usize { // first best action on a tie
    (1..4).fold(0, |best, a| if f(a) > f(best) { a } else { best })
}

fn show(v: &[[f64; 4]; 3], best: impl Fn(S) -> usize) { // values and arrows, row by row
    for r in 0..3 {
        let (mut nums, mut arrows) = (Vec::new(), String::new());
        for c in 0..4 {
            let ch = cell((r, c));
            nums.push(if ch == b'#' { "   #  ".to_string() } else { format!("{:6.2}", v[r][c]) });
            arrows.push(if b"#HC".contains(&ch) { ch as char } else { b"^>v<"[best((r, c))] as char });
        }
        println!("{}    {}", nums.join(" "), arrows);
    }
}
# A 3 x 4 warehouse. S start, # wall, H hole (-10, ends), C charger (+10, ends).
GRID = ["..H.",
        ".#..",
        "S..C"]
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]       # up, right, down, left
GAMMA = 0.9
CELLS = [(r, c) for r in range(3) for c in range(4) if GRID[r][c] != "#"]

def end(s): return GRID[s[0]][s[1]] in "HC"
def reward(s): return {"H": -10.0, "C": 10.0}.get(GRID[s[0]][s[1]], -1.0)

def go(s, a):                                    # one move; walls and edges block it
    r, c = s[0] + MOVES[a][0], s[1] + MOVES[a][1]
    return (r, c) if 0 <= r < 3 and 0 <= c < 4 and GRID[r][c] != "#" else s

def outcomes(s, a):                              # 80% as planned, 10% slip to each side
    return [(0.8, go(s, a)), (0.1, go(s, (a + 1) % 4)), (0.1, go(s, (a + 3) % 4))]

def q_value(V, s, a):                            # the right side of the Bellman equation
    return sum(p * (reward(t) + GAMMA * V[t]) for p, t in outcomes(s, a))

def show(values, best_action):                   # print values and arrows, row by row
    for r in range(3):
        nums = ["   #  " if GRID[r][c] == "#" else f"{values[(r, c)]:6.2f}" for c in range(4)]
        arrows = [GRID[r][c] if GRID[r][c] in "#HC" else "^>v<"[best_action((r, c))]
                  for c in range(4)]
        print(" ".join(nums), "  ", "".join(arrows))
fn value_iteration() -> [[f64; 4]; 3] {
    let mut v = [[0.0; 4]; 3];
    for sweep in 1..1000 {
        let mut new = [[0.0; 4]; 3];
        let mut change: f64 = 0.0;
        for r in 0..3 {
            for c in 0..4 {
                if cell((r, c)) == b'#' || end((r, c)) { continue; }
                new[r][c] = q_value(&v, (r, c), argmax(|a| q_value(&v, (r, c), a)));
                change = change.max((new[r][c] - v[r][c]).abs());
            }
        }
        v = new;
        if change < 1e-6 {
            println!("value iteration: {sweep} sweeps");
            break;
        }
    }
    v
}
V = {s: 0.0 for s in CELLS}
for sweep in range(1, 1000):                     # value iteration
    new = {s: 0.0 if end(s) else max(q_value(V, s, a) for a in range(4)) for s in CELLS}
    change = max(abs(new[s] - V[s]) for s in CELLS)
    V = new
    if change < 1e-6:
        break
print(f"value iteration: {sweep} sweeps")
show(V, lambda s: max(range(4), key=lambda a: q_value(V, s, a)))
value iteration: 26 sweeps
  1.16  -0.20   0.00   5.25    v<Hv
  2.88    #     7.16   9.28    v#vv
  4.67   6.93   9.28   0.00    >>>C

Read the arrows on the right. From the start, the robot goes right along the bottom row to the charger. The cell left of the hole points further left, away from both the hole and the charger. Going right would risk the hole, and down is a wall. A slip into the hole costs 10, so the robot takes the long, safe road. The start is worth 4.67.

How fast does it converge? Each sweep shrinks the error by at least the factor \gamma. After k sweeps the error is at most \gamma^k times the first error. With \gamma = 0.9, 100 sweeps shrink it below 3 \times 10^{-5}. With \gamma = 0.99, 100 sweeps shrink it only to about 0.37.

Policy iteration is the other classic method. It evaluates one policy exactly, then makes it greedy, and repeats. It often needs very few rounds.

A badly chosen reward. If every move gave +1 instead of −1, the best policy would be to walk around forever and never reach the charger. The agent does what the reward says, not what you meant. In language models this is reward hacking, as Large language models and agents explains.

Q-learning: learning without a model

Value iteration needs the transition probabilities. A real robot does not know that it slips 10% of the time. It can only try moves and see what happens. Reinforcement learning learns from this experience.

Q-learning learns the action values Q(s, a) directly. After every step it sees a state s, an action a, a reward r and a next state s'.

With a learning rate \alpha:

Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \Big[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \Big]

The part in brackets is the temporal-difference error. If s' ends the episode, the target is just r.

The agent must also explore. With epsilon-greedy choice, it picks a random action with probability \varepsilon and its best action otherwise. Part 3 runs 20,000 trips with \alpha = 0.1 and \varepsilon = 0.1. A tiny random number generator, the same in both languages, makes the runs repeatable.

struct Rng(u64); // a tiny random generator (xorshift)
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> f64 {
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13;
        self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7;
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 17;
        (self.0 >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64 // a number in [0, 1)
    }
}

fn step(rng: &mut Rng, s: S, a: usize) -> (S, f64) { // the learner cannot see inside
    let u = rng.next();
    let t = go(s, if u < 0.8 { a } else if u < 0.9 { (a + 1) % 4 } else { (a + 3) % 4 });
    (t, reward(t))
}

fn main() {
    let v = value_iteration();
    show(&v, |s| argmax(|a| q_value(&v, s, a)));
    let (alpha, epsilon, mut rng) = (0.1, 0.1, Rng(2026));
    let mut q = [[[0.0f64; 4]; 4]; 3];
    for _episode in 0..20000 {
        let mut s: S = (2, 0);
        for _ in 0..100 {
            let explore = rng.next() < epsilon; // explore or exploit
            let a = if explore { (rng.next() * 4.0) as usize }
                    else { argmax(|b| q[s.0][s.1][b]) };
            let (t, r) = step(&mut rng, s, a);
            let best_next = q[t.0][t.1].iter().cloned().fold(f64::MIN, f64::max);
            let target = if end(t) { r } else { r + GAMMA * best_next };
            q[s.0][s.1][a] += alpha * (target - q[s.0][s.1][a]); // the Q-learning update
            s = t;
            if end(s) { break; }
        }
    }
    println!("Q-learning: 20000 episodes");
    let best = q.map(|row| row.map(|qa| qa.iter().cloned().fold(f64::MIN, f64::max)));
    show(&best, |s| argmax(|b| q[s.0][s.1][b]));
}
x = 2026                                         # a tiny random generator (xorshift)
def rand() -> float:
    global x
    x ^= (x << 13) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
    x ^= x >> 7
    x ^= (x << 17) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
    return (x >> 11) / 2**53                     # a number in [0, 1)

def step(s, a):                                  # the world; the learner cannot see inside
    u = rand()
    t = go(s, a if u < 0.8 else (a + 1) % 4 if u < 0.9 else (a + 3) % 4)
    return t, reward(t)

Q = {(s, a): 0.0 for s in CELLS for a in range(4)}
ALPHA, EPSILON = 0.1, 0.1
greedy = lambda s: max(range(4), key=lambda a: Q[(s, a)])
for episode in range(20000):
    s = (2, 0)
    for _ in range(100):
        a = int(rand() * 4) if rand() < EPSILON else greedy(s)   # explore or exploit
        t, r = step(s, a)
        target = r if end(t) else r + GAMMA * max(Q[(t, b)] for b in range(4))
        Q[(s, a)] += ALPHA * (target - Q[(s, a)])               # the Q-learning update
        s = t
        if end(s):
            break
print("Q-learning: 20000 episodes")
show({s: max(Q[(s, a)] for a in range(4)) for s in CELLS}, greedy)
value iteration: 26 sweeps
  1.16  -0.20   0.00   5.25    v<Hv
  2.88    #     7.16   9.28    v#vv
  4.67   6.93   9.28   0.00    >>>C
Q-learning: 20000 episodes
  1.08  -0.83   0.00   5.28    v<Hv
  2.58    #     6.87   9.61    v#vv
  4.57   6.94   9.26   0.00    >>>C

Compare the two grids. Q-learning never saw the slip probabilities, yet it found exactly the same arrows. Its values are close but noisy, for example 4.57 against 4.67 at the start. Cells near the hole are visited rarely, so their values are the least accurate.

Watkins introduced Q-learning in 1989. Watkins and Dayan proved in 1992 that it converges to the optimal action values with probability 1. The conditions: every action is tried in every state again and again, the values are kept in a table, and the learning rate shrinks in the right way. Our fixed \alpha = 0.1 breaks the last condition a little. That is one reason for the noise.

Q-learning is off-policy. It explores with random moves, but it learns the values of the greedy policy, because the target uses the max. In 2015 DeepMind replaced the table with a neural network, the Deep Q-Network, and learned to play many Atari games from the screen pixels.

Setting \varepsilon = 0 from the start. The agent tries one path, finds it "good enough" and never tests the others. Explore early, then lower \varepsilon slowly. A second classic bug: adding \gamma \max Q(s') after a final state. A final state has no future.

Policy gradients

A machine has three buttons. Each button pays 1 with a hidden probability: 0.2, 0.5 or 0.8. Our policy is a softmax over three numbers \theta. Instead of learning values, we change \theta to make good buttons more likely. This is a policy gradient method.

Let \pi_\theta(a \mid s) be a policy that is differentiable in \theta, and let J(\theta) be its expected return. For an episode s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, \dots with returns G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \dots,

\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta} \Big[ \sum_{t} \gamma^t \, G_t \, \nabla_\theta \ln \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \Big]

Subtracting a baseline b(s_t) from G_t does not change this expectation.

Proof idea

Write J = \sum_\tau P_\theta(\tau) R(\tau) over whole episodes \tau. The log-derivative trick gives \nabla P_\theta(\tau) = P_\theta(\tau) \nabla \ln P_\theta(\tau). So \nabla J = \mathbb{E}[R(\tau) \nabla \ln P_\theta(\tau)].

P_\theta(\tau) is a product of policy terms and environment terms. The environment terms do not depend on \theta. So \nabla \ln P_\theta(\tau) = \sum_t \nabla \ln \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t). An action cannot change rewards that came before it, so those rewards add zero on average. That leaves G_t. For the baseline: \mathbb{E}[\nabla \ln \pi] = \sum_a \nabla \pi(a) = \nabla 1 = 0.

In simple words: push up the log-probability of each action you took, more strongly when the return was good. Sutton, McAllester, Singh and Mansour proved the general form in 1999. The sample version is called REINFORCE, from Williams (1992). For a softmax policy, \partial \ln \pi(a) / \partial \theta_k is 1 - \pi_k when k = a and -\pi_k otherwise.

struct Rng(u64); // the same xorshift generator as before
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> f64 {
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13;
        self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7;
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 17;
        (self.0 >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64
    }
}

fn policy(theta: &[f64; 3]) -> [f64; 3] { // softmax over the preferences
    let es = theta.map(f64::exp);
    let total: f64 = es.iter().sum();
    es.map(|e| e / total)
}

fn main() {
    let win = [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]; // chance that each button gives reward 1 (hidden)
    let mut theta = [0.0f64; 3]; // the policy's parameters: one preference per button
    let (lr, mut baseline, mut rng) = (0.1, 0.0, Rng(7));
    for step in 1..=3000 {
        let pi = policy(&theta);
        let (u, mut a) = (rng.next(), 0);
        while a < 2 && u >= pi[..=a].iter().sum::<f64>() { // sample a button from pi
            a += 1;
        }
        let r = if rng.next() < win[a] { 1.0 } else { 0.0 };
        baseline += (r - baseline) / step as f64; // average reward so far
        for k in 0..3 { // grad of ln pi(a) is 1[k == a] - pi[k]
            theta[k] += lr * (r - baseline) * (if k == a { 1.0 } else { 0.0 } - pi[k]);
        }
        if [10, 100, 1000, 3000].contains(&step) {
            let p: Vec<String> = policy(&theta).iter().map(|p| format!("{p:.3}")).collect();
            println!("step {step:4}: {}", p.join("  "));
        }
    }
}
from math import exp

x = 7                                            # the same xorshift generator as before
def rand() -> float:
    global x
    x ^= (x << 13) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
    x ^= x >> 7
    x ^= (x << 17) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
    return (x >> 11) / 2**53

WIN = [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]           # chance that each button gives reward 1 (hidden)
theta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]         # the policy's parameters: one preference per button
LR, baseline = 0.1, 0.0

def policy():                                    # softmax over the preferences
    es = [exp(t) for t in theta]
    return [e / sum(es) for e in es]

for step in range(1, 3001):
    pi = policy()
    u, a = rand(), 0
    while a < 2 and u >= sum(pi[:a + 1]):        # sample a button from pi
        a += 1
    r = 1.0 if rand() < WIN[a] else 0.0
    baseline += (r - baseline) / step            # average reward so far
    for k in range(3):                           # grad of ln pi(a) is 1[k == a] - pi[k]
        theta[k] += LR * (r - baseline) * ((1.0 if k == a else 0.0) - pi[k])
    if step in (10, 100, 1000, 3000):
        print(f"step {step:4}: " + "  ".join(f"{p:.3f}" for p in policy()))
step   10: 0.325  0.315  0.359
step  100: 0.088  0.148  0.764
step 1000: 0.007  0.019  0.973
step 3000: 0.002  0.005  0.993

The policy starts at one third for each button. After 100 pulls it already prefers the best button. After 3,000 pulls it chooses it 99.3% of the time. The baseline is the average reward so far. A reward above average pushes the chosen button up. A reward below average pushes it down.

Why use policy gradients at all, when Q-learning works? They handle huge or continuous action spaces, such as robot joint angles or the next token of a language model. They can learn random policies. And they plug straight into neural networks. The price is noise: estimates from samples vary a lot. A baseline lowers the noise. Actor-critic methods learn a value function to act as the baseline.

PPO, from Schulman and others (2017), limits how far one update can move the policy. InstructGPT used PPO for RLHF. So the theorem in this section is a direct ancestor of how chat models learn from feedback. See Large language models and agents.

  1. 1957 Bellman. Dynamic programming and the Bellman equation.
  2. 1968 A*. Hart, Nilsson and Raphael publish heuristic search.
  3. 1989 Q-learning. Watkins learns action values from experience.
  4. 1997 Deep Blue. Alpha-beta search beats the chess world champion.
  5. 2016 AlphaGo. MCTS with neural networks wins at Go.
  6. 2022 RLHF for chat. Policy gradients align language models with human preferences.

A learning rate that is too high. One lucky reward can push one action to probability near 1. Then the agent stops trying the others and never recovers. Use a small learning rate, a baseline and, for big models, a limit on each update as in PPO.

Three questions come up again and again. Why is A* optimal? Use the admissibility argument with f(n) \le C^* \lt f(G_2). What does alpha-beta save? About b^{d/2} instead of b^d with perfect move order. Why does value iteration converge? The Bellman update is a \gamma-contraction.

Patterns to remember
