Vector search and vector databases

An AI system turns text into lists of numbers. Then it must find the lists that are closest to a question. This chapter shows how that search works, from a simple loop to graph indexes inside PostgreSQL. Every trick has a theorem under it, and we test each one with real numbers.

  • Compute L2, inner product and cosine distance by hand, and choose the right one.
  • Explain why exact search gets slow and why high dimensions make search hard.
  • Describe IVF and HNSW step by step, and tune lists, probes, m and ef_search.
  • Use pgvector: types, operators, both index kinds, filters, iterative scans and quantisation.
  • Decide when PostgreSQL is enough and when a dedicated vector database is the better tool.

Embeddings are points

Look at five short notes. A model gives each note three numbers. "Postgres stores rows in pages" becomes [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]. "Embeddings map text to points" becomes [0.1, 0.9, 0.2]. Notes about the same topic get similar numbers.

An embedding is such a list. Each number is one dimension. You can draw an embedding as a point in space. Similar meanings land close together. Real models use 384, 768, 1536 or more dimensions, but the idea is the same.

The search problem has a name. k-nearest-neighbour search (kNN) asks for the k points closest to the query. A vector database is a store that answers kNN questions fast. It also keeps the text and other data next to each vector.

Do not mix embeddings from two models. Model A and model B use different spaces. A distance between an A point and a B point means nothing. When you change the model, embed every row again.

Measuring distance

Take a = [1, 2, 3] and b = [4, 6, 3]. Here are four common measures, with the values pgvector printed for these two vectors.

Four ways to compare a = [1, 2, 3] and b = [4, 6, 3]
MeasureFormulaValuepgvector operator
L2 (straight line)\sqrt{\sum (a_i - b_i)^2}\sqrt{9+16+0} = 5<->
Inner product\sum a_i b_i4+12+9 = 25<#> gives −25
Cosine similarity\frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a\rVert \lVert b\rVert}\frac{25}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{61}} \approx 0.8555<=> gives 1 − 0.8555
L1 (city blocks)\sum \lvert a_i - b_i\rvert3+4+0 = 7<+>

Norm means length. The inner product grows with length and with direction. Cosine similarity looks only at direction. For bits there are two more measures. Hamming distance counts different bits. Jaccard distance compares the sets of 1 bits.

For any two vectors a and b: \lvert a \cdot b \rvert \le \lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert. So cosine similarity always lies between −1 and 1.

In simple words: the inner product can never beat the product of the two lengths. Check it with our numbers. 25 \le \sqrt{14}\sqrt{61} \approx 29.22. So the cosine is 0.8555, which is inside [−1, 1].

Proof idea

Look at f(t) = \lVert a - t b \rVert^2 \ge 0 for every real t. Expand it: \lVert a\rVert^2 - 2t(a\cdot b) + t^2 \lVert b\rVert^2. A quadratic that is never negative has at most one root. So its discriminant is not positive: 4(a\cdot b)^2 - 4\lVert a\rVert^2\lVert b\rVert^2 \le 0. That is the inequality.

One more useful fact follows. If both vectors have length 1, then \lVert a-b \rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos(a,b). So L2, cosine and inner product give the same ranking for unit vectors. The pgvector README uses this: for normalised embeddings, inner product is the fastest choice.

Some indexes skip work with a rule about three points. This rule only holds for a true metric.

In a metric, d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points. Consequence (Elkan's skip rule): if a point x has its centre c, and another centre c' has d(c, c') \ge 2\, d(x, c), then d(x, c') \ge d(x, c). So you never need to compute d(x, c').

Proof of the skip rule

The triangle inequality gives d(c, c') \le d(c, x) + d(x, c'). So d(x, c') \ge d(c, c') - d(x, c) \ge 2d(x,c) - d(x,c) = d(x, c). For L2 the triangle inequality itself comes from Cauchy-Schwarz: expand \lVert u+v\rVert^2 and bound the middle term.

  1. A point x is 3 away from its centre c.
  2. Another centre c' is 10 away from c. We know this from a small table of centre distances.
  3. Check: 10 \ge 2 \cdot 3. The rule says c' cannot be closer than c.
  4. We skip one full distance computation. With 1536 dimensions, that saves 1536 multiplications.

Cosine distance (1 − cosine) is not a metric. Take a = (1, 0), b = (0.707, 0.707) and c = (0, 1). Then d(a, b) and d(b, c) are both 0.293, but d(a, c) is 1. And 0.293 + 0.293 is less than 1. Squared L2 also breaks the rule. This is why pgvector's k-means code uses plain L2, or the angle itself, when it needs the triangle inequality.

Exact search and the curse of dimensionality

The simplest search compares the query with every stored vector. Then it keeps the best k. Here it is in Rust and in Python, with the five notes from the first section.

// Exact search: compare the query with every vector, keep the best k.
fn dot(a: &[f64], b: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    a.iter().zip(b).map(|(x, y)| x * y).sum()
}

fn cosine_distance(a: &[f64], b: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    1.0 - dot(a, b) / (dot(a, a).sqrt() * dot(b, b).sqrt())
}

fn main() {
    let notes = [
        ("Postgres stores rows in pages", [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]),
        ("An index speeds up search", [0.8, 0.3, 0.1]),
        ("Embeddings map text to points", [0.1, 0.9, 0.2]),
        ("Agents call tools in a loop", [0.0, 0.7, 0.6]),
        ("Backups protect the data", [0.6, 0.0, 0.7]),
    ];
    let query = [0.2, 0.8, 0.1];
    // n distance computations: this is the cost of exact search
    let mut scored: Vec<(f64, &str)> = notes
        .iter()
        .map(|(text, v)| (cosine_distance(v, &query), *text))
        .collect();
    scored.sort_by(|a, b| a.0.total_cmp(&b.0));
    for (d, text) in scored.iter().take(3) {
        println!("{d:.4}  {text}");
    }
}
# Exact search: compare the query with every vector, keep the best k.
import heapq, math

def cosine_distance(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    return 1 - dot / (math.hypot(*a) * math.hypot(*b))

notes = [
    ("Postgres stores rows in pages", [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]),
    ("An index speeds up search", [0.8, 0.3, 0.1]),
    ("Embeddings map text to points", [0.1, 0.9, 0.2]),
    ("Agents call tools in a loop", [0.0, 0.7, 0.6]),
    ("Backups protect the data", [0.6, 0.0, 0.7]),
]
query = [0.2, 0.8, 0.1]
# n distance computations; a heap keeps only the best k
best = heapq.nsmallest(3, ((cosine_distance(v, query), t) for t, v in notes))
for d, text in best:
    print(f"{d:.4f}  {text}")
0.0134  Embeddings map text to points
0.1904  Agents call tools in a loop
0.4262  An index speeds up search

Both programs print the same lines. The cost is clear: n vectors times d numbers. For one million vectors with 1536 dimensions, that is about 1.5 billion multiplications for each query. In my PostgreSQL test, a full scan of 20,000 vectors with 128 dimensions took 5 to 11 ms per query. Exact search has perfect recall. It is just slow at scale.

Can a clever tree fix this, like a B-tree for numbers? In two or three dimensions, yes. In hundreds of dimensions, no. The next experiment shows why. We place 1,000 random points and one random query in a cube. Then we compare the nearest and the farthest distance.

// How far is the nearest point compared with the farthest one?
struct Rng(u64);
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> f64 {
        // xorshift64: a tiny random number generator
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13;
        self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7;
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 17;
        (self.0 >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64 // a number in [0, 1)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng = Rng(42);
    for d in [2, 10, 100, 1000] {
        let q: Vec<f64> = (0..d).map(|_| rng.next()).collect();
        let (mut lo, mut hi) = (f64::MAX, 0.0f64);
        for _ in 0..1000 {
            let s: f64 = q.iter().map(|x| { let t = x - rng.next(); t * t }).sum();
            lo = lo.min(s.sqrt());
            hi = hi.max(s.sqrt());
        }
        println!("d={d:<5} nearest={lo:7.3} farthest={hi:7.3} contrast={:.3}", (hi - lo) / lo);
    }
}
# How far is the nearest point compared with the farthest one?
import math

class Rng:
    def __init__(self, seed):
        self.s = seed
    def next(self):
        # xorshift64: a tiny random number generator
        m = (1 << 64) - 1
        self.s ^= (self.s << 13) & m
        self.s ^= self.s >> 7
        self.s ^= (self.s << 17) & m
        return (self.s >> 11) / (1 << 53)   # a number in [0, 1)

rng = Rng(42)
for d in [2, 10, 100, 1000]:
    q = [rng.next() for _ in range(d)]
    lo, hi = math.inf, 0.0
    for _ in range(1000):
        dist = math.sqrt(sum((x - rng.next()) ** 2 for x in q))
        lo, hi = min(lo, dist), max(hi, dist)
    print(f"d={d:<5} nearest={lo:7.3f} farthest={hi:7.3f} contrast={(hi - lo) / lo:.3f}")
d=2     nearest=  0.026 farthest=  1.142 contrast=43.408
d=10    nearest=  0.551 farthest=  2.148 contrast=2.901
d=100   nearest=  3.188 farthest=  4.683 contrast=0.469
d=1000  nearest= 11.978 farthest= 13.565 contrast=0.133

Both languages use the same small random generator, so they print the same numbers. In 2 dimensions the farthest point is about 44 times as far away as the nearest. In 1000 dimensions the farthest point is only 13% farther. Everything is almost the same distance away.

(Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft, 1999.) Let the data and the query be random, with dimension d growing. If the spread of the distance becomes small compared with its mean, then for every \varepsilon \gt 0: P\left[ D_{\max} \le (1+\varepsilon) D_{\min} \right] \to 1. The farthest point is barely farther than the nearest one.

Proof idea

A squared distance is a sum of d independent parts. Its mean grows like d. Its standard deviation grows only like \sqrt{d}. So the relative spread shrinks like 1/\sqrt{d}. By Chebyshev's inequality, almost all distances fall in a thin shell. Our run agrees. From 100 to 1000 dimensions, the contrast fell from 0.47 to 0.13, a factor of about 0.28. The theory predicts about 1/\sqrt{10} \approx 0.32 for large d.

This is the curse of dimensionality. Tree indexes cut space into boxes. They work because far boxes can be skipped. When all points are nearly equally far, almost no box can be skipped. Real embeddings are not uniform random points, so search still works. But we must accept approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search.

One more theorem gives hope. You can often throw away many dimensions and keep the distances.

Take N points in any dimension and 0 \lt \varepsilon \lt 1. If k \gt 8 \ln N / \varepsilon^2, there is a linear map f into k dimensions with (1-\varepsilon)\lVert u-v\rVert^2 \le \lVert f(u)-f(v)\rVert^2 \le (1+\varepsilon)\lVert u-v\rVert^2 for every pair of points. A random projection works with high probability.

The surprise: k depends on the number of points, not on the old dimension. Try one million points: \ln N \approx 13.8. With \varepsilon = 0.5 you need k \gt 8 \cdot 13.8 / 0.25 \approx 442. With \varepsilon = 0.1 you need about 11,052, which is more than most models use. So the worst-case bound is loose. In practice, embeddings have structure, and quantisation (later in this chapter) does better than the bound.

Proof idea

Project with a random Gaussian matrix and scale by 1/\sqrt{k}. For one fixed pair, the squared length after projection is a sum of k random squares. It concentrates around the true value, with a failure chance like e^{-c k \varepsilon^2}. There are fewer than N^2 pairs. Choose k so that N^2 e^{-ck\varepsilon^2} \lt 1. This gives k of order \ln N / \varepsilon^2.

IVF: cut the space into cells

Here is the first ANN idea. Before any query, group the vectors into clusters. At query time, look only inside the few clusters closest to the query.

The clusters come from k-means. Each centre owns the points that are closer to it than to any other centre. Such a region is a Voronoi cell. An IVF index stores one list of vectors per cell. In pgvector the number of cells is lists, and the number of cells searched is ivfflat.probes.

Sample and train

Take a sample of the rows. Run k-means to find lists centres. pgvector starts with k-means++ seeding, then runs Elkan's version of k-means.

Assign

Put every row into the list of its nearest centre. Store each list on its own pages.

Rank the centres

Compare the query with every centre. With 100 lists, that is only 100 distances.

Open a few lists

Open the probes closest lists. Compare the query with every vector inside them.

Return the best k

Keep a heap of the best k. A true neighbour in an unopened list is lost. This is where recall drops.

The cost is about lists + probes × (n / lists) distances. With n = 20,000, lists = 100 and probes = 3, that is 100 + 600 = 700 distances instead of 20,000. Elkan's k-means makes the build faster with the triangle inequality. Its code says so in a comment. It keeps half the distance between every pair of centres, and skips a centre when the skip rule above allows.

The pgvector README gives starting values. Use lists = rows / 1000 for up to one million rows, and \sqrt{\text{rows}} above that. Start with probes = \sqrt{\text{lists}}. Build the index after the table has data, because k-means needs real rows.

An IVF index built on an empty or tiny table has poor centres. Recall stays low forever. Rebuild the index after loading most of the data. This does not apply to HNSW, which has no training step.

HNSW: walk a graph of shortcuts

Think of finding a house in a new city. You first take a highway to the right district. Then you take main roads. Then you walk the small streets. Each stage needs only a few moves. HNSW searches vectors the same way.

A small-world graph has many short links and a few long links. HNSW builds several layers of such graphs. Layer 0 holds every vector. Each higher layer holds a random, much smaller subset. Search starts at the top and moves greedily toward the query.

Enter at the top

Start at the entry point, the one node on the highest layer.

Greedy moves

Look at the neighbours of the current node. Move to the one closest to the query. Repeat until no neighbour is closer.

Go down

Drop to the same node on the next layer. Its links there are shorter. Do greedy moves again.

Wide search on layer 0

On layer 0, keep a list of the best ef_search candidates, not just one. Explore their neighbours. Stop when no candidate can improve the list.

Return k

Return the best k from the candidate list. A bigger list finds more true neighbours but costs more distances.

How does a node get its layer? pgvector draws a random number U in (0, 1). The layer is \lfloor -\ln(U) \cdot m_L \rfloor with m_L = 1/\ln m. With the default m = 16, the chance to reach layer 1 or higher is 1/16. Layer 2 or higher has a chance of 1/256. So each layer has about 16 times fewer nodes. This is the same trick as a skip list. For one million rows, the top layer is about 13.8 \times 0.36 \approx 5.

The three HNSW settings in pgvector (defaults and limits from the source code)
SettingMeaningDefaultBigger value gives
mlinks per node on each layer (layer 0 gets 2m)16 (2 to 100)better recall, bigger index
ef_constructioncandidate list size while building64 (4 to 1000)better graph, slower build
hnsw.ef_searchcandidate list size while searching40 (1 to 1000)better recall, slower query

Why do so few steps reach the goal? Greedy search can only work if the graph is navigable. Jon Kleinberg proved when that happens.

(Kleinberg, 2000.) Take an L \times L grid. Each node links to its 4 grid neighbours and to one far node, chosen with probability proportional to r^{-2}, where r is the grid distance. Then greedy routing between any two nodes takes O(\log^2 n) steps on average, where n is the number of nodes. With any other exponent, every local routing method needs a number of steps that grows like a power of L.

In simple words: the long links must exist at every scale, with the right mix. Then each greedy step has a fair chance to halve the remaining distance. Halving many times is the logarithm. HNSW makes the scales explicit with layers. Its authors report logarithmic scaling in their tests, but HNSW itself has no formal worst-case proof. Let us test Kleinberg's theorem. We route between 300 random pairs and count greedy steps.

// Greedy routing on an L x L grid (with wrap) plus one long link per node.
struct Rng(u64);
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> f64 { // xorshift64, a number in [0, 1)
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13; self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7; self.0 ^= self.0 << 17;
        (self.0 >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64
    }
    fn cell(&mut self, l: i64) -> (i64, i64) { ((self.next() * l as f64) as i64, (self.next() * l as f64) as i64) }
}
fn route(l: i64, harmonic: bool, rng: &mut Rng, cdf: &[f64]) -> u64 {
    let d1 = |p: i64, q: i64| (p - q).abs().min(l - (p - q).abs());
    let dist = |a: (i64, i64), b: (i64, i64)| d1(a.0, b.0) + d1(a.1, b.1);
    let (mut cur, goal, mut steps) = (rng.cell(l), rng.cell(l), 0);
    while cur != goal {
        let (x, y) = cur;
        let far = if harmonic { // P(length r) ~ 1/r, so P(one node) ~ 1/r^2
            let v = rng.next() * cdf[cdf.len() - 1];
            let r = cdf.partition_point(|&c| c < v) as i64 + 1;
            let k = (rng.next() * 4.0 * r as f64) as i64; let t = k % r;
            let (dx, dy) = [(r - t, t), (-t, r - t), (t - r, -t), (t, t - r)][(k / r) as usize];
            ((x + dx).rem_euclid(l), (y + dy).rem_euclid(l))
        } else { rng.cell(l) }; // long link to any node, all equally likely
        let w = |a: i64| a.rem_euclid(l);
        let near = [(w(x + 1), y), (w(x - 1), y), (x, w(y + 1)), (x, w(y - 1))];
        cur = near[1..].iter().copied().chain([far]) // greedy: go to the closest of 5 links
            .fold(near[0], |best, v| if dist(v, goal) < dist(best, goal) { v } else { best });
        steps += 1;
    }
    steps
}
fn main() {
    let mut rng = Rng(7);
    for l in [64i64, 256, 1024, 4096] {
        let mut s = 0.0; let cdf: Vec<f64> = (1..=l / 2).map(|r| { s += 1.0 / r as f64; s }).collect();
        let a: u64 = (0..300).map(|_| route(l, true, &mut rng, &cdf)).sum();
        let b: u64 = (0..300).map(|_| route(l, false, &mut rng, &cdf)).sum();
        println!("nodes={:>9}  harmonic={:6.1}  uniform={:7.1}", l * l, a as f64 / 300.0, b as f64 / 300.0);
    }
}
# Greedy routing on an L x L grid (with wrap) plus one long link per node.
import bisect

class Rng:
    def __init__(self, seed): self.s = seed
    def next(self):  # xorshift64, a number in [0, 1)
        m = (1 << 64) - 1
        self.s ^= (self.s << 13) & m; self.s ^= self.s >> 7; self.s ^= (self.s << 17) & m
        return (self.s >> 11) / (1 << 53)

def route(L, harmonic, rng, cdf):
    dist = lambda a, b: sum(min(abs(p - q), L - abs(p - q)) for p, q in zip(a, b))
    cur = (int(rng.next() * L), int(rng.next() * L))
    goal = (int(rng.next() * L), int(rng.next() * L))
    steps = 0
    while cur != goal:
        x, y = cur
        if harmonic:  # long link: P(length r) ~ 1/r, so P(one node) ~ 1/r^2
            r = bisect.bisect_left(cdf, rng.next() * cdf[-1]) + 1
            k = int(rng.next() * 4 * r); t = k % r
            dx, dy = [(r - t, t), (-t, r - t), (t - r, -t), (t, t - r)][k // r]
            far = ((x + dx) % L, (y + dy) % L)
        else:         # long link to any node, all equally likely
            far = (int(rng.next() * L), int(rng.next() * L))
        near = [((x + 1) % L, y), ((x - 1) % L, y), (x, (y + 1) % L), (x, (y - 1) % L)]
        cur = min(near + [far], key=lambda v: dist(v, goal))  # greedy step
        steps += 1
    return steps

rng = Rng(7)
for L in [64, 256, 1024, 4096]:
    cdf, s = [], 0.0
    for r in range(1, L // 2 + 1):
        s += 1.0 / r; cdf.append(s)
    a = sum(route(L, True, rng, cdf) for _ in range(300)) / 300
    b = sum(route(L, False, rng, cdf) for _ in range(300)) / 300
    print(f"nodes={L*L:>9}  harmonic={a:6.1f}  uniform={b:7.1f}")
nodes=     4096  harmonic=  17.6  uniform=   15.6
nodes=    65536  harmonic=  38.7  uniform=   40.3
nodes=  1048576  harmonic=  68.7  uniform=  101.7
nodes= 16777216  harmonic= 103.5  uniform=  261.3

Read the numbers. Each row has 16 times more nodes. With the r^{-2} links, steps grow by 2.2, then 1.8, then 1.5 times. The growth slows down, as \log^2 n predicts. With uniform long links, steps grow by about 2.5 times every row. That is 4^{2/3} \approx 2.52, the power law from Kleinberg's lower bound. At 16 million nodes, the right mix of links is 2.5 times faster.

Graph indexes also prune links when they build. pgvector keeps a candidate as a link only if the candidate is closer to the new node than to every link chosen before. This is Algorithm 4 of the HNSW paper. It spreads the links in different directions and keeps some long ones, which helps on clustered data.

Quantisation: store fewer bits

A 1536-dimension embedding in 32-bit floats needs about 6 KB. Ten million of them need about 61 GB, before any index. Graph search jumps around in memory, so the index should fit in RAM. The answer is quantisation.

Bytes for one 1536-dimension vector (data only)
FormBits per numberBytesSmaller by
float32 (vector)326,1441×
float16 (halfvec)163,0722×
product quantisation, 96 groups of 16 numbers0.59664×
binary (bit, sign of each number)119232×
  • Half precision keeps each number with 16 bits. The ranking almost never changes.
  • Product quantisation (PQ) cuts the vector into groups. It runs k-means inside each group with 256 centres. Then it stores one byte per group: the number of the nearest centre.
  • Binary quantisation keeps only the sign of each number. Hamming distance on bits is very fast. But it loses much detail.

Less storage always means more error. Shannon's rate-distortion theory makes this exact. For a Gaussian source, each extra bit per number cuts the mean squared error by 4 times. So there is no free lunch. The practical fix is re-ranking. Search with small codes to get many candidates. Then sort those candidates with the full vectors.

The rate-distortion idea and the bit counts come from the information and coding theory chapter. Here we test it. These are my results on 20,000 vectors with 128 dimensions in PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector 0.8.7.

Recall@10 against index size (my run, one machine)
IndexSizeRecall@10
HNSW on vector16 MB0.994 (ef_search 100)
HNSW on halfvec11 MB0.994
HNSW on bits, no re-rank6.1 MB0.205
bits, then re-rank top 1006.1 MB0.692
bits, then re-rank top 4006.1 MB0.989

Half precision lost nothing here. Bits alone were poor, because 128 bits is little information. Re-ranking 400 candidates brought recall back to 0.989.

Disk-based graphs in brief. When even compressed vectors do not fit in RAM, put the graph on an SSD. DiskANN (Microsoft Research, NeurIPS 2019) keeps PQ codes in RAM and the graph and full vectors on SSD. Its graph, Vamana, has a small diameter, so a search needs few disk reads. The authors report one billion points on one machine with 64 GB RAM. They measured over 5,000 queries per second and 95% recall at under 3 ms mean latency. These are the authors' numbers on the SIFT1B data set. In PostgreSQL, the separate pgvectorscale extension offers a DiskANN-style index called StreamingDiskANN.

Binary quantisation without re-ranking. You save memory but lose most of the recall. Always fetch more candidates than you need, then re-rank with the full vectors.

Case study: pgvector

The problem. Many teams already keep their data in PostgreSQL. They want vector search without a second database to sync, back up and secure.

How it works. pgvector is an extension written in C. It adds four types, six distance operators and two index kinds. The planner treats an ORDER BY distance LIMIT k query like any other query. If an index fits, it does an index scan. All writes go through the WAL, so replicas and point-in-time recovery work. I read the README, the changelog and the C source on 2026-11-15. The newest release was 0.8.7 (2026-10-01). Version 0.9.0 was not released yet. The licence is the PostgreSQL License.

A real example. I ran this SQL in PostgreSQL 18.3 with pgvector 0.8.7. The output is real.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE notes (
  id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  topic     text,
  body      text,
  embedding vector(3)          -- 3 dimensions; real models use hundreds
);

INSERT INTO notes (topic, body, embedding) VALUES
  ('db',  'Postgres stores rows in pages', '[0.9, 0.1, 0.0]'),
  ('db',  'An index speeds up search',     '[0.8, 0.3, 0.1]'),
  ('ai',  'Embeddings map text to points', '[0.1, 0.9, 0.2]'),
  ('ai',  'Agents call tools in a loop',   '[0.0, 0.7, 0.6]'),
  ('ops', 'Backups protect the data',      '[0.6, 0.0, 0.7]');

-- the three nearest notes by cosine distance
SELECT id, body, round((embedding <=> '[0.2, 0.8, 0.1]')::numeric, 4) AS cos_dist
FROM notes ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.2, 0.8, 0.1]' LIMIT 3;

-- other types and helper functions
SELECT binary_quantize('[0.4, -0.2, 0.9, -0.7]'::vector) AS bits,
       l2_normalize('[3, 4]'::vector) AS unit,
       '[1,2,3]'::vector(3)::halfvec(3) AS half,
       '{1:1.5,3:2}/5'::sparsevec AS sparse;
 id | body                          | cos_dist
----+-------------------------------+----------
 3  | Embeddings map text to points | 0.0134
 4  | Agents call tools in a loop   | 0.1904
 2  | An index speeds up search     | 0.4262
(3 rows)

 bits | unit      | half    | sparse
------+-----------+---------+---------------
 1010 | [0.6,0.8] | [1,2,3] | {1:1.5,3:2}/5
(1 row)

The cosine distances match the Rust and Python programs. binary_quantize keeps 1 for each positive number. A sparsevec stores only the non-zero positions, as {position:value}/dimensions.

pgvector types (README, version 0.8.7)
TypeStoresIndex limitIndex operator classes
vector32-bit floats2,000 dimensionsvector_l2_ops, vector_ip_ops, vector_cosine_ops, vector_l1_ops
halfvec16-bit floats4,000 dimensionshalfvec_l2_ops and so on
bitbits64,000 dimensionsbit_hamming_ops, bit_jaccard_ops
sparsevecnon-zero entries only1,000 non-zero entries (HNSW)sparsevec_l2_ops and so on

Next I loaded 20,000 vectors with 128 dimensions and 100 test queries. I measured recall against exact search. The index commands come straight from the README.

CREATE INDEX items_hnsw ON items
  USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);
SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;           -- candidate list size at query time

CREATE INDEX items_ivf ON items
  USING ivfflat (embedding vector_l2_ops) WITH (lists = 100);
SET ivfflat.probes = 3;             -- how many lists to open

-- half-precision index and binary quantisation with re-ranking
CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(128)) halfvec_l2_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw ((binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(128)) bit_hamming_ops);
SELECT id FROM (                    -- $1 is the query vector
  SELECT id, embedding FROM items
  ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(128) <~> binary_quantize($1) LIMIT 400
) c ORDER BY c.embedding <-> $1 LIMIT 10;

A second build gave slightly different recall, for example 0.948 instead of 0.938. Both index builds use random choices. Timings also moved with the load on my machine. The pattern stayed the same. Recall rises fast at first, then flattens, while time keeps growing.

The theory under it. HNSW is fast because of greedy routing in a navigable small world, the theorem above. IVFFlat builds faster because Elkan's k-means skips distances with the triangle inequality. Re-ranking works because quantisation error is small for most points, as rate-distortion theory predicts.

The trade-off. In my run the HNSW index (16 MB) was bigger than the table (12 MB). The IVF index was 11 MB. HNSW builds slower and uses more memory, but gives better recall per millisecond. IVFFlat needs data before you build it. Both are approximate, so the same query can return different rows after you add an index.

Know the four knobs and their direction. lists and probes for IVFFlat. m, ef_construction and ef_search for HNSW. Every knob trades recall for time or memory. Also know that <#> returns the negative inner product, so smaller is better for every operator.

Filters, iterative scans and choosing a database

Real queries have conditions. "Find the nearest notes, but only from tenant 7." Here is the trap. I gave 1% of my 20,000 rows the category 7. Then I asked for the 10 nearest rows with category 7.

SET hnsw.ef_search = 40;
SELECT count(*) AS rows_back FROM (
  SELECT id FROM items WHERE category = 7
  ORDER BY embedding <-> (SELECT v FROM q WHERE qid = 1) LIMIT 10
) s;

SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order;   -- new in 0.8.0
-- (the same query again)
 rows_back
-----------
 0
(1 row)

 rows_back
-----------
 10
(1 row)

The first query returned zero rows. The index found its 40 best candidates, then the filter removed them all. With 1% matching rows, 40 candidates give 0.4 matches on average. The README gives the same sum for 10%: about 4 rows. An iterative index scan fixes this. It keeps scanning until enough rows pass the filter. It stops at hnsw.max_scan_tuples (default 20,000).

  • Few matching rows: a normal B-tree index on the filter column, then exact search, is often best.
  • A few fixed values: a partial index per value, for example WHERE (category_id = 123).
  • Many tenants: list partitioning or separate tables. One shared index lets tenants hurt each other's recall.
  • Keywords too: combine full-text search and vector search, then merge the two lists. Reciprocal rank fusion, from the agent memory chapter, is a common way to merge.

When is PostgreSQL enough? pgvector is a good default when the vectors fit on one strong machine and you want joins, transactions and one backup story. Its README describes scaling up with replicas and with sharding tools such as Citus. A dedicated vector database earns its place in other cases.

Stay with pgvector when

  • vectors fit in one server's RAM, maybe after halfvec or bits
  • you need joins, foreign keys and ACID with the vectors
  • the team already runs PostgreSQL well
  • updates and deletes must be visible at once

Consider a dedicated store when

  • you have billions of vectors across many machines
  • you need very high query rates with heavy filtering
  • you want built-in features such as many vectors per item or GPU indexes
  • vector search is a separate service with its own team

Choosing a store by a benchmark from its vendor. Measure on your own data with your own filters. Report recall and latency together, because one number alone hides the trade-off.

Patterns to remember

Vector search patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
Normalise, then inner productFastest exact ranking for unit vectorsORDER BY embedding <#> $1 LIMIT 10<#> is negative: smaller is closer.

IVF: lists ≈ rows / 1000, probes ≈ \sqrt{\text{lists}}Cheap index with fast buildWITH (lists = 100), SET ivfflat.probes = 10Build after loading data.

One index per operatorLet the planner use the indexvector_cosine_ops for <=>A cosine index does not serve <->.

Practice

The L2 distance between [0, 0] and [3, 4] is ?.

The inner product of [1, 2] and [3, 4] is ?.

With m = 16, the chance that a new HNSW node reaches layer 2 or higher is 1 in ?.

Your filter matches 5% of rows. HNSW uses ef_search = 40. How many rows do you expect back without iterative scans?

  • 40
  • 10
  • about 2
  • always 0

The filter runs after the index. 5% of 40 candidates is 2 rows on average.

Which distance can you safely use with Elkan's triangle-inequality skip rule?

  • Cosine distance, 1 − cos
  • Plain L2 distance
  • Squared L2 distance

Only a metric obeys the triangle inequality. Cosine distance and squared L2 break it. pgvector uses plain L2 or the angle for k-means.

You add an HNSW index. A query now returns a different 10th row. What happened?

  • The index is broken.
  • HNSW is approximate, so it can miss a true neighbour.
  • PostgreSQL sorts randomly.

The README warns about this. Raise ef_search to raise recall.

  1. Show with numbers that cosine distance breaks the triangle inequality. Use a = (1, 0), b = (0.6, 0.8), c = (0, 1).
    Answer

    cos(a, b) = 0.6, so d(a, b) = 0.4. cos(b, c) = 0.8, so d(b, c) = 0.2. cos(a, c) = 0, so d(a, c) = 1. But 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 is less than 1. The rule fails.

  2. A table has 4 million rows. Suggest lists and probes for IVFFlat. Estimate the distances per query.
    Answer

    Above one million rows, use \sqrt{4{,}000{,}000} = 2000 lists. Start with probes = \sqrt{2000} \approx 45. Each list holds about 2,000 rows. Distances: 2,000 centres + 45 × 2,000 = 92,000. That is about 43 times fewer than 4 million.

  3. Use the Johnson-Lindenstrauss bound. How many dimensions keep all distances within ±20% for 10,000 points?
    Answer

    Here \ln 10{,}000 \approx 9.21 and \varepsilon = 0.2. So k \gt 8 \cdot 9.21 / 0.04 \approx 1842. The bound is a worst case. Real data often needs far fewer.

  4. Your 50 million vectors have 1024 dimensions. RAM is 128 GB. Plan the storage and index.
    Answer

    float32 needs 50M × 4 KB = 205 GB, too much. halfvec needs about 102 GB, which is tight with an index. A binary index needs 50M × 128 bytes = 6.4 GB and fits easily. Keep the table in halfvec on disk. Search the bit index for the top few hundred, then re-rank them with the halfvec values. Measure recall against exact search on a sample. If you outgrow one machine, consider sharding or a dedicated store.

  5. Explain in three sentences why HNSW search needs about log n steps, and name the theorem.
    Answer

    Each layer has about m times fewer nodes, so there are about \log_m n layers. On each layer the greedy walk takes only a few steps, because links at that scale cross the space quickly. Kleinberg's theorem explains why links at every distance scale make greedy routing short: O(\log^2 n) on his grid, while HNSW reports log-like scaling in tests.

Key takeaways

  • An embedding is a point. Search means finding the k nearest points to a query.
  • Cauchy-Schwarz keeps cosine in [−1, 1]. For unit vectors, L2, cosine and inner product rank the same.
  • Exact search costs n × d per query. In high dimensions distances concentrate, so tree indexes stop working.
  • IVF searches a few k-means cells. HNSW walks a layered small-world graph. Both trade recall for speed.
  • The triangle inequality lets pgvector's k-means skip distances. Kleinberg's theorem explains short greedy walks.
  • Quantisation shrinks memory 2 to 64 times. Re-ranking with full vectors wins back recall.
  • With pgvector, filters run after the index. Use iterative scans, partial indexes or partitions.

Sources

  • pgvector on GitHub. README, CHANGELOG and C source (hnsw.h, hnswutils.c, ivfkmeans.c), read on 2026-11-15, release 0.8.7.
  • Malkov and Yashunin: HNSW paper. Layers, random levels, the neighbour heuristic and log scaling.
  • DiskANN, NeurIPS 2019. Billion-point search on one machine with an SSD (authors' numbers).
  • Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma. Statement and the bound k \gt 8 \ln N / \varepsilon^2.
  • Beyer et al.: When is nearest neighbor meaningful? (ICDT 1999). The distance concentration result.
  • pgvectorscale on GitHub. A DiskANN-style index (StreamingDiskANN) for PostgreSQL.

Memory systems for agents

A language model forgets everything when a session ends. A memory system decides what to keep, how to store it and what to bring back later. This chapter opens three real open-source memory systems and shows the theorems that make them fast, small and reliable.

  • Name the five kinds of agent memory and say where each one lives.
  • Draw the write path and the read path of a memory system.
  • Explain how Mem0, Graphiti and Hindsight store and recall memories, from their own code and documents.
  • Compute reciprocal rank fusion, a bi-temporal query and cache hit rates with real numbers.
  • Estimate the tokens and money that a memory layer saves, and choose what to forget.

Why agents need memory

Monday: you tell an assistant, "My dog is called Max." Friday: you ask, "What food is good for my dog?" A plain model has no idea who Max is. The Monday chat is gone. Only the text inside the current request reaches the model.

That text is the context window. It is large but limited, and every token costs time and money. A memory system keeps useful facts outside the window. Before each answer, it puts the few right facts back in. The large language models and agents chapter explains tokens and the agent loop.

Five kinds of memory, with an example from the dog story
KindWhat it holdsExampleWhere it lives
Context windowthis request only"What food is good for my dog?"the prompt
Working notesa plan or scratchpad for this task"Step 2: check allergies"a file or state object
Episodicevents with a time"On Monday the user said the dog is Max."a log, episodes
Semanticfacts without the story"User has a dog named Max."facts, a graph
Proceduralhow to do things"Always answer this user in short lists."instructions, skills

Putting the whole chat history in every prompt. It works for a week. Then the history passes the window size, the cost grows every turn, and the model starts to miss facts in the middle. Store facts, not transcripts.

The write path and the read path

Every memory system has two jobs. The write path runs after a conversation turn. The read path runs before the next answer. The picture shows both. The three systems in this chapter all follow it, with different choices in each box.

  • Extract. An LLM reads the new messages and writes short facts. "I just adopted a puppy called Max" becomes "User has a dog named Max."
  • Remove duplicates. If the fact is already stored, do not store it again.
  • Store and index. Save the fact with its time, its source and an embedding. Index it for meaning, for words and for links.
  • Search in parallel. Meaning search finds paraphrases. Keyword search finds exact names. Graph search finds connected facts.
  • Fuse and budget. Merge the ranked lists into one. Add facts from the top until the token budget is full.

Writing is slow and careful, like a librarian who files each new book. Reading must be fast, like finding a book on the shelf. Good systems do the hard work at write time, so reading is quick.

Case study: Mem0

The problem. Developers want a drop-in memory layer for chat apps and agents. It should remember user facts across sessions without sending the whole history every time.

What I looked at. The mem0ai/mem0 repository on 2026-11-15: the README, the migration guide and the Python source (mem0/memory/main.py, the prompts and the scoring code). The package version was 2.2.1 (PyPI, 2026-09-25). The licence is Apache-2.0.

Two versions of the algorithm. The 2025 Mem0 paper described a compare-and-edit loop. The LLM extracted facts, looked at similar old memories, and chose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NONE for each one. In April 2026 the team changed this. The README and migration guide now describe single-pass, ADD-only extraction. One LLM call writes new facts. Nothing is overwritten, and memories accumulate. The old update prompt is still in the prompts file, but the new add() returns only ADD events.

Gather context

Load the last 10 messages of this session from the history database.

Find related memories

Embed the new messages. Search the vector store for the 10 most similar existing memories. Replace their long IDs with small numbers, so the LLM cannot invent IDs.

One LLM call

Send the old memories, the recent messages and the new messages. The LLM returns new facts as JSON.

Embed in a batch

Embed all new facts in one call.

Hash and skip duplicates

Compute an MD5 hash of each fact text. Skip it if the same hash is in the old memories or earlier in this batch.

Store

Insert the vectors and payloads. Write one ADD row per fact to the history table.

Link entities

Find names with spaCy. Embed each entity once. Link it to the memories that mention it.

The read path. search() runs three signals. First, a vector search fetches max(4 × top_k, 60) candidates. Second, a keyword search gives BM25 scores. Third, an entity search gives a boost of up to 0.5 to memories that share a name with the question. The code then adds the three numbers and divides by the largest possible sum.

\text{score} = \min\left(1, \dfrac{s_{\text{sem}} + \sigma(\text{bm25}) + b_{\text{entity}}}{1 + 1 + 0.5}\right), where \sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-a(x - m)}). The midpoint m and steepness a depend on the query length. For queries of 1 to 3 terms, m = 5 and a = 0.7.

A worked example. A memory has semantic score 0.62. Its raw BM25 score is 8, so \sigma(8) = 1/(1 + e^{-0.7 \cdot 3}) \approx 0.89. Its entity boost is 0.5. The score is (0.62 + 0.89 + 0.5) / 2.5 \approx 0.80. A memory below the semantic threshold of 0.1 is dropped before any boost.

A real example. This is the call shape from the README for version 2.2.1. I could not run it: it needs an LLM API key and a vector store. Note that user IDs now go inside filters for search().

from mem0 import Memory

memory = Memory()   # defaults: an OpenAI LLM and embedder, a local Qdrant store

# write path: one LLM call extracts facts; returns only ADD events
result = memory.add("I just adopted a puppy called Max.", user_id="ana")
for item in result["results"]:
    print(item["event"], item["memory"])

# read path: semantic + BM25 + entity signals, fused into one score
hits = memory.search("What is my dog's name?",
                     filters={"user_id": "ana"}, top_k=3)
for h in hits["results"]:
    print(round(h["score"], 2), h["memory"])

The theory under it. The hash check is exact deduplication. Equal strings give equal MD5 hashes, so a set lookup finds them in constant expected time. But "User has a dog named Max" and "User's dog is Max" have different hashes. Near-duplicates need embeddings or fuzzy matching. You will see both later in this chapter.

The trade-off. ADD-only extraction is one LLM call instead of two, and it never loses an old fact by mistake. The cost is growth. When a fact changes, both versions stay, and the read path must pick the right one. The README says the platform adds time-aware ranking for this. Graph memory is also gone from the open-source Memory class. The migration guide says it moved to the paid platform. Some older files in the repository still mention graph providers.

The README reports 92.5 on LoCoMo and 94.4 on LongMemEval for the new algorithm, at about 7,000 tokens per query. These are the authors' numbers on their managed platform. The README says open-source users should expect similar gains, not identical numbers. The 2025 paper reported over 90% token savings against putting the full history in the prompt.

Case study: Graphiti and Zep

The problem. Facts change. Alice worked at Acme. In May she moved to Globex. An agent must answer "Where does Alice work?" and also "Where did she work last year?" A flat list of facts cannot tell old from new.

What I looked at. The getzep/graphiti repository on 2026-11-15: the README, the quickstart and the core source files. The package version was graphiti-core 0.31.2 (PyPI, 2026-10-20). The licence is Apache-2.0. Zep is the company's commercial context platform, and Graphiti is the open-source graph engine inside it. The Zep paper (arXiv, January 2025) describes the design.

How it works. Graphiti calls its graph a context graph. It has three main parts.

  • Episodes: the raw input, kept as the source of truth. Every derived fact points back to its episodes.
  • Entities: nodes such as people, products and places, each with a summary that changes over time.
  • Facts: edges between two entities, such as "Alice works at Acme". Each edge has a text, an embedding and four timestamps.
The four timestamps on a Graphiti edge (fields of EntityEdge)
FieldKind of timeMeaning
valid_atvalid timewhen the fact became true in the world
invalid_atvalid timewhen the fact stopped being true
created_atsystem timewhen Graphiti stored the edge
expired_atsystem timewhen Graphiti marked the edge as replaced

Bi-temporal data stores two time periods for each fact. Valid time says when the fact is true in the world. System time (also called transaction time) says when the database believed it. Old rows are closed, never deleted, so you can ask what was true at any time, as known at any time.

When a new edge contradicts an old one, Graphiti does not delete the old edge. The code in edge_operations.py sets the old edge's invalid_at to the new edge's valid_at. It also sets expired_at to the current time. Here is the same idea as a plain PostgreSQL table, with two range columns. I ran it in PostgreSQL 18.3.

CREATE TABLE works_at (
  person   text,
  company  text,
  valid    daterange,   -- when it is true in the world
  recorded tstzrange    -- when the database believed it
);
INSERT INTO works_at VALUES                  -- learned on 2026-01-10
  ('Alice', 'Acme', '[2024-03-01,)', '[2026-01-10 00:00+00,)');

-- 2026-06-02: we learn Alice moved on 2026-05-15. Close the old belief...
UPDATE works_at SET recorded = tstzrange(lower(recorded), '2026-06-02 00:00+00')
WHERE person = 'Alice' AND upper_inf(recorded);
INSERT INTO works_at VALUES                  -- ...and record the new beliefs
  ('Alice', 'Acme',   '[2024-03-01,2026-05-15)', '[2026-06-02 00:00+00,)'),
  ('Alice', 'Globex', '[2026-05-15,)',           '[2026-06-02 00:00+00,)');

SELECT q.question, w.company
FROM (VALUES
  ('today, about today',         date '2026-11-15', timestamptz '2026-11-15 00:00+00'),
  ('today, about 2025-12-01',    date '2025-12-01', timestamptz '2026-11-15 00:00+00'),
  ('on 2026-03-01, about 05-20', date '2026-05-20', timestamptz '2026-03-01 00:00+00'),
  ('today, about 2026-05-20',    date '2026-05-20', timestamptz '2026-11-15 00:00+00')
) AS q(question, world_day, belief_time)
JOIN works_at w ON w.valid @> q.world_day AND w.recorded @> q.belief_time
ORDER BY q.question;
 question                   | company
----------------------------+---------
 on 2026-03-01, about 05-20 | Acme
 today, about 2025-12-01    | Acme
 today, about 2026-05-20    | Globex
 today, about today         | Globex
(4 rows)

The table kept all 3 rows. That is the price of bi-temporal data: more rows. The gain is a full audit trail. You can explain why the agent said "Acme" in March.

The read path. Graphiti's search() runs cosine similarity, BM25 and breadth-first search over the graph in parallel. Each method fetches twice the result limit. A reranker then merges the lists. The default is reciprocal rank fusion. Other options are MMR, distance in the graph from a centre node, the number of episode mentions, and a cross-encoder.

A real example. This follows the repository quickstart. I could not run it: it needs Neo4j or FalkorDB and an LLM key. The method names and parameters match graphiti.py on the main branch.

import asyncio
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.nodes import EpisodeType

async def main():
    g = Graphiti("bolt://localhost:7687", "neo4j", "password")
    await g.add_episode(                       # write path: one episode
        name="chat-2026-06-02",
        episode_body="Alice: I left Acme. I joined Globex on May 15.",
        source=EpisodeType.message,
        source_description="support chat",
        reference_time=datetime(2026, 6, 2, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
    )
    edges = await g.search("Where does Alice work?")   # hybrid search + RRF
    for e in edges:
        print(e.fact, e.valid_at, e.invalid_at)
    await g.close()

asyncio.run(main())

The theory under it. Two ideas carry Graphiti. Bi-temporal data gives correct answers about change. And duplicate entities are found cheaply with information theory and hashing. The file dedup_helpers.py does three checks before it asks the LLM.

  1. It computes the Shannon entropy of the name's letters. Short or repetitive names, below 1.5 bits, are not trusted for fuzzy matching.
  2. It cuts each name into 3-letter pieces called shingles. It builds a MinHash signature with 32 hashes, in 8 bands of 4.
  3. Names that share a band become candidates. It merges a pair only if the Jaccard similarity of the shingles is at least 0.9.

The MinHash trick rests on one fact. For a random hash function, the chance that two sets have the same smallest hash equals their Jaccard similarity. With 8 bands of 4, a pair with similarity s becomes a candidate with chance 1 - (1 - s^4)^8. Here are the checks in code.

// Graphiti-style name checks: entropy gate, 3-gram Jaccard, LSH chance.
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};

fn entropy(name: &str) -> f64 { // Shannon entropy over characters, in bits
    let mut counts: HashMap<char, f64> = HashMap::new();
    for c in name.chars().filter(|c| *c != ' ') { *counts.entry(c).or_insert(0.0) += 1.0; }
    let total: f64 = counts.values().sum();
    counts.values().map(|c| -(c / total) * (c / total).log2()).sum()
}

fn shingles(name: &str) -> HashSet<String> { // all 3-letter pieces, spaces removed
    let s: Vec<char> = name.chars().filter(|c| *c != ' ').collect();
    s.windows(3).map(|w| w.iter().collect()).collect()
}

fn main() {
    for (a, b) in [("northwind trading partner", "northwind trading partners"), ("alice chen", "alice chan"), ("bob", "rob")] {
        let trusted = (a.len() >= 6 || a.split_whitespace().count() >= 2) && entropy(a) >= 1.5;
        let (sa, sb) = (shingles(a), shingles(b));
        let j = sa.intersection(&sb).count() as f64 / sa.union(&sb).count() as f64;
        let lsh = 1.0 - (1.0 - j.powi(4)).powi(8); // 32 hashes in 8 bands of 4
        println!("{:27} H={:.3} trusted={:5} J={j:.3} P(candidate)={lsh:.3}", format!("{a:?}"), entropy(a), trusted.to_string());
    }
}
# Graphiti-style name checks: entropy gate, 3-gram Jaccard, LSH chance.
import math
from collections import Counter

def entropy(name):                   # Shannon entropy over characters, in bits
    counts = Counter(name.replace(" ", ""))
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return -sum(c / total * math.log2(c / total) for c in counts.values())

def shingles(name):                  # all 3-letter pieces, spaces removed
    s = name.replace(" ", "")
    return {s[i:i + 3] for i in range(len(s) - 2)}

def jaccard(a, b):
    return len(a & b) / len(a | b)

for a, b in [("northwind trading partner", "northwind trading partners"), ("alice chen", "alice chan"), ("bob", "rob")]:
    trusted = (len(a) >= 6 or len(a.split()) >= 2) and entropy(a) >= 1.5
    j = jaccard(shingles(a), shingles(b))
    lsh = 1 - (1 - j ** 4) ** 8      # 32 hashes in 8 bands of 4
    print(f"{chr(34) + a + chr(34):27} H={entropy(a):.3f} trusted={str(trusted).lower():5} J={j:.3f} P(candidate)={lsh:.3f}")
"northwind trading partner" H=3.360 trusted=true  J=0.955 P(candidate)=1.000
"alice chen"                H=2.725 trusted=true  J=0.556 P(candidate)=0.551
"bob"                       H=0.918 trusted=false J=0.000 P(candidate)=0.000

Read the three rows. The plural pair has Jaccard 0.955, so it merges without any LLM call. "alice chen" and "alice chan" differ by one letter, but share only 56% of their shingles. They are not merged by the fuzzy check, so the LLM decides. "bob" fails the entropy gate. Three letters carry too little information to trust a fuzzy match.

The trade-off. Every episode costs several LLM calls: extract entities, extract edges, resolve duplicates and date the edges. The README warns about rate limits and sets low concurrency by default. In return, reads need no LLM and can be fast. The graph also needs a graph database to run and back up.

Case study: Hindsight

The problem. Most memory systems only recall. Hindsight wants agents that also learn: they should form beliefs from many facts and update them when evidence changes.

What I looked at. The vectorize-io/hindsight repository on 2026-11-15: the README, the documentation pages on retain, retrieval, observations, mental models, storage and performance, and the Python client. The server and client packages were version 1.2.1 (PyPI, 2026-11-10). The licence is MIT. The authors also link a paper on arXiv (2512.12818).

How it works. Memories live in banks. There are three operations and four memory kinds.

Three operations

  • retain: an LLM extracts facts, entities, times and relations, then indexes them
  • recall: four searches in parallel, fused and reranked, cut to a token budget
  • reflect: an agent loop that reasons over memories to answer deeper questions

Four memory kinds

  • world facts: facts about the world
  • experiences: what the agent itself did
  • observations: beliefs consolidated from many facts, with their evidence
  • mental models: standing answers to fixed questions, rewritten in the background

Storage is one PostgreSQL database. The storage page lists pgvector with HNSW indexes for vectors, tsvector with GIN indexes for text, JSONB for documents, and recursive CTEs for graph queries. The performance page says the design favours reads. The heavy LLM work happens in retain, so recall can stay under a second.

The read path in three stages. The retrieval page explains it in detail.

  1. Run semantic, keyword (BM25), graph and temporal search in parallel.
  2. Merge the four lists with reciprocal rank fusion, k = 60. Every strategy has equal weight.
  3. Keep the top 300 and rerank them with a cross-encoder, a model that reads the question and the memory together.
  4. Multiply by small boosts for recency (±10%), time match (±10%) and evidence count (±5%).
  5. Add memories from the top until max_tokens (default 4,096) is used up.

Why fuse by rank and not by score? A cosine score of 0.8 and a BM25 score of 12.5 live on different scales. Adding them is like adding metres and kilograms. Ranks are always comparable.

(Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009.) Given ranked lists R_1, \dots, R_m, score each item d by \text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \dfrac{1}{k + r_i(d)}, where r_i(d) is its rank in list i, starting at 1. Items missing from a list get nothing from it. Sort by the score. The paper used k = 60.

// Reciprocal rank fusion: merge ranked lists by position, not by score.
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn rrf<'a>(lists: &[Vec<&'a str>], k: f64) -> Vec<(&'a str, f64)> {
    let mut score: HashMap<&str, f64> = HashMap::new();
    for list in lists {
        for (i, id) in list.iter().enumerate() {
            let rank = (i + 1) as f64; // ranks start at 1
            *score.entry(id).or_insert(0.0) += 1.0 / (k + rank);
        }
    }
    let mut out: Vec<(&str, f64)> = score.into_iter().collect();
    out.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.total_cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0))); // ties: by id
    out
}

fn main() {
    let semantic = vec!["m3", "m1", "m7", "m2"];
    let keyword = vec!["m1", "m5", "m3"];
    let graph = vec!["m7", "m3", "m9"];
    let lists = [semantic, keyword, graph];
    for k in [60.0, 0.0] {
        let top: Vec<String> = rrf(&lists, k).iter().take(4)
            .map(|(id, s)| format!("{id}={s:.4}")).collect();
        println!("k={k:<3} {}", top.join("  "));
    }
}
# Reciprocal rank fusion: merge ranked lists by position, not by score.
from collections import defaultdict

def rrf(lists, k):
    score = defaultdict(float)
    for ranked in lists:
        for rank, mem_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):  # ranks start at 1
            score[mem_id] += 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(score.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))  # ties: by id

semantic = ["m3", "m1", "m7", "m2"]
keyword = ["m1", "m5", "m3"]
graph = ["m7", "m3", "m9"]
for k in [60, 0]:
    top = rrf([semantic, keyword, graph], k)[:4]
    print(f"k={k:<3}", "  ".join(f"{m}={s:.4f}" for m, s in top))
k=60  m3=0.0484  m1=0.0325  m7=0.0323  m5=0.0161
k=0   m3=1.8333  m1=1.5000  m7=1.3333  m5=0.5000

Memory m3 wins: it is in all three lists. Check one value by hand: 1/61 + 1/63 + 1/62 \approx 0.0484. Now see what k does. Take item A, ranked first in one list only, and item B, ranked third in two lists. With k = 60, A gets 1/61 ≈ 0.016 and B gets 2/63 ≈ 0.032, so B wins. With k = 0, A gets 1 and B gets 0.67, so A wins. A large k rewards agreement. A small k trusts a single top hit. Hindsight uses k = 60. Graphiti's code adds 1/(i + 1) for a 0-based position i, which is k = 0 in this formula.

For a query with terms q_i and a memory D of length |D|: \text{BM25}(D) = \sum_i \text{IDF}(q_i) \cdot \dfrac{f(q_i, D)(k_1 + 1)}{f(q_i, D) + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,|D|/\text{avgdl}\right)}. Here f is the term count, avgdl the average length, and usually k_1 \approx 1.2 and b = 0.75.

BM25 rewards rare words, gives less for each extra repeat, and is fair to short texts. It finds "Globex" when the embedding does not. The data science and information retrieval chapter derives it. One honest detail from Hindsight's docs: its default "native" backend uses PostgreSQL's ts_rank_cd, which is TF-IDF style, not true BM25. Other backends give true BM25.

A real example. These calls match the Python client (hindsight_client, version 1.2.1). I could not run them: they need a running Hindsight server with an LLM key.

from hindsight_client import Hindsight

client = Hindsight(base_url="http://localhost:8888")

# retain: the server extracts facts, entities, time and relations
client.retain(bank_id="ana", content="I just adopted a puppy called Max.",
              context="chat", timestamp="2026-11-09T10:00:00Z")

# recall: 4 searches, RRF (k = 60), cross-encoder, then a token budget
result = client.recall(bank_id="ana", query="What is my dog's name?",
                       max_tokens=1024, budget="low")

# reflect: an agent loop over the memories for a deeper question
answer = client.reflect(bank_id="ana", query="What should I know before suggesting dog food?")

The theory under it. Rank fusion is robust because it ignores scales. The multiplicative boosts keep relevance first. A boost of ±10% can reorder close results, but it cannot lift an unrelated memory above a strongly relevant one. Observations are a form of compression: many facts become one belief, which keeps a list of its evidence.

The trade-off. Retain is the slow part. The performance page lists 500 to 2,000 ms per batch, mostly LLM extraction, against 100 to 600 ms for recall. Consolidation also uses LLM calls in the background. The docs say a small decision model can settle easy cases and cut those calls by about 40% on their own evaluation.

When asked to compare memory systems, compare the write path, the data model and the fusion method. Benchmark scores in READMEs are the authors' own numbers. Say so, and say on which product they were measured.

Memory efficiency: tokens, duplicates and forgetting

Here is a worked example with assumed numbers. A user talks to an agent for six months: 300 sessions of 2,000 tokens. That is 600,000 tokens of history. Assume input tokens cost $3 per million.

Full history against a memory layer (assumed prices and sizes)
ApproachTokens per answerCost per answerNote
Full history in the prompt600,000$1.80too big for most windows
Last 10 sessions only20,000$0.06forgets older facts
Memory: 20 facts of 25 tokens500$0.0015plus one extraction call per turn

The memory layer reads 1,200 times fewer tokens than the full history. It pays this back at write time: one extraction call of maybe 2,000 tokens per turn. Reads usually outnumber writes, so the trade is good. Hindsight's performance page assumes 10 reads per write or more.

Compression has a floor

Can we keep everything and just compress it well? Shannon's theorem says there is a hard limit.

For a source of independent symbols with entropy H = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x) bits, no lossless code has an average length below H bits per symbol. A code with average length below H + 1 always exists. Coding long blocks gets as close to H as you want.

An example. An agent logs four event types with chances 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8. Then H = 0.5 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 0.125 \cdot 3 = 1.75 bits. A fixed code needs 2 bits per event. A Huffman code reaches exactly 1.75. Nothing lossless can do better. So to save more tokens, a memory system must drop information: keep facts, drop chatter. Mem0's extraction, Graphiti's facts and Hindsight's observations are all lossy compression. The skill is to drop the right things. The information and coding theory chapter proves the theorem.

Proof idea

Lower bound: the code word lengths \ell(x) of a prefix code obey Kraft's inequality \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1. Minimising \sum_x p(x)\ell(x) under this limit gives \ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x), whose average is H. Upper bound: round each length up, \ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil. Kraft still holds, and the average grows by less than 1 bit.

Remove duplicates at three strengths

  • Exact (Mem0): a hash of the text. Cheap, but "dog named Max" and "dog is Max" both stay.
  • Fuzzy (Graphiti): shingles, MinHash and Jaccard. Catches spelling variants of names.
  • Semantic (Hindsight): embeddings with cosine ≥ 0.97 for observations. Catches the same idea in new words.

Forget on purpose

Human recall fades over time. Ebbinghaus measured a forgetting curve, often modelled as R = e^{-t/S} with strength S. Agent memories need a softer rule, because old facts may still be true. The three systems choose differently.

  • Mem0 can give a memory an expiration_date. Expired memories are hidden from search unless you ask for them.
  • Graphiti never forgets an edge. It marks the edge invalid, with times.
  • Hindsight lowers old memories a little. Recency is \max(0.1, 1 - \text{days}/365), and the boost is 1 + 0.2(\text{recency} - 0.5). A memory from today gets ×1.10. One older than a year gets ×0.92.

Cache what you read often

A memory server reads the same embeddings, facts and mental models again and again. A cache keeps some of them in fast memory. When the cache is full, which item should go?

(Belady, 1966.) For a cache of fixed size and a known future request sequence, this rule has the fewest misses: when you must evict, evict the item whose next request is farthest in the future.

Proof idea

Take any optimal schedule. Find the first eviction where it differs from Belady's choice. Swap the two evicted items from that point on. The item Belady keeps is needed sooner, so the swap never adds a miss. Repeat until the schedules match.

Belady needs the future, so real systems cannot use it. It is the yardstick. The best-known practical rule is LRU.

(Sleator and Tarjan, 1985.) For every request sequence, LRU with a cache of size k has at most k times as many misses as Belady's optimal rule with the same cache, plus a constant. No deterministic online rule has a better worst-case ratio than k.

The worst case is rare in practice. Requests to memories are skewed: a few facts are asked again and again, which is roughly Zipf's law. The next program builds such a trace. It has 1,000 facts and 20,000 requests, and fact i is asked with weight 1/i. Then it measures both rules.

// Hit rates of LRU and Belady's optimal rule on a Zipf-like request trace.
use std::collections::HashMap;
struct Rng(u64);
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> f64 { // xorshift64, a number in [0, 1)
        self.0 ^= self.0 << 13; self.0 ^= self.0 >> 7; self.0 ^= self.0 << 17;
        (self.0 >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64
    }
}
fn hits(trace: &[usize], nxt: &[usize], k: usize, belady: bool) -> f64 {
    let mut cache: HashMap<usize, usize> = HashMap::new(); // item -> next use or last use
    let mut h = 0;
    for (t, &x) in trace.iter().enumerate() {
        if cache.contains_key(&x) { h += 1; }
        else if cache.len() == k { // full: evict one item
            let keys = cache.iter().map(|(&y, &v)| (v, y));
            let (_, victim) = if belady { keys.max().unwrap() } else { keys.min().unwrap() };
            cache.remove(&victim);
        }
        cache.insert(x, if belady { nxt[t] } else { t });
    }
    h as f64 / trace.len() as f64
}
fn main() {
    let (mut rng, mut s) = (Rng(2026), 0.0);
    // 1,000 facts; fact i is asked with weight 1/i
    let cdf: Vec<f64> = (1..=1000).map(|i| { s += 1.0 / i as f64; s }).collect();
    let trace: Vec<usize> = (0..20000).map(|_| { let v = rng.next() * s; cdf.partition_point(|&c| c < v) }).collect();
    let (mut nxt, mut seen) = (vec![0; trace.len()], HashMap::new()); // when is trace[t] asked again?
    for t in (0..trace.len()).rev() {
        nxt[t] = *seen.get(&trace[t]).unwrap_or(&trace.len());
        seen.insert(trace[t], t);
    }
    for k in [10, 50, 100] {
        println!("k={k:<4} LRU={:.3}  Belady={:.3}", hits(&trace, &nxt, k, false), hits(&trace, &nxt, k, true));
    }
}
# Hit rates of LRU and Belady's optimal rule on a Zipf-like request trace.
import bisect

class Rng:  # xorshift64, a number in [0, 1)
    def __init__(self, seed): self.s = seed
    def next(self):
        m = (1 << 64) - 1
        self.s ^= (self.s << 13) & m; self.s ^= self.s >> 7; self.s ^= (self.s << 17) & m
        return (self.s >> 11) / (1 << 53)

rng, cdf, s = Rng(2026), [], 0.0
for i in range(1, 1001):            # 1,000 facts; fact i is asked with weight 1/i
    s += 1.0 / i; cdf.append(s)
trace = [bisect.bisect_left(cdf, rng.next() * s) for _ in range(20000)]

nxt, seen = [0] * len(trace), {}      # nxt[t]: when is trace[t] asked again?
for t in range(len(trace) - 1, -1, -1):
    nxt[t] = seen.get(trace[t], len(trace)); seen[trace[t]] = t

def hits(k, belady):
    cache, h = {}, 0                  # item -> next use (Belady) or last use (LRU)
    for t, x in enumerate(trace):
        if x in cache: h += 1
        elif len(cache) == k:         # full: evict one item
            pick = max if belady else min
            del cache[pick(cache, key=lambda y: (cache[y], y))]
        cache[x] = nxt[t] if belady else t
    return h / len(trace)

for k in [10, 50, 100]:
    print(f"k={k:<4} LRU={hits(k, False):.3f}  Belady={hits(k, True):.3f}")
k=10   LRU=0.207  Belady=0.431
k=50   LRU=0.457  Belady=0.659
k=100  LRU=0.575  Belady=0.750

Two lessons. First, a small cache helps a lot with skewed requests: 10% of the facts serve 57.5% of requests. Second, LRU is far from its worst case of k times Belady. Here it gets 77% of Belady's hits at k = 100. The same thinking applies to prompt caching and to Hindsight's mental models, which turn a whole retrieval into one database read.

Caching answers that depend on time. "Where does Alice work?" has a different answer after May. Put the memory version or a time window in the cache key, or clear the entry when a related fact changes.

Practice

The RRF score with k = 60 of an item ranked 1st in one list and 2nd in another is 1/61 + 1/?.

The entropy of a source with four equally likely symbols is ? bits.

In Graphiti, the field that says when a fact stopped being true in the world is ?.

Mem0 version 2.2.1 learns that the user moved from Tokyo to Osaka. What does its write path do?

  • It updates the old Tokyo memory in place.
  • It deletes the Tokyo memory.
  • It adds a new memory. The old one stays.

Since April 2026, Mem0 extraction is ADD-only. The read path must rank the right version.

Why does Hindsight fuse its four searches with RRF instead of adding their scores?

  • RRF is more accurate in every case.
  • The scores use different scales, but ranks are comparable.
  • Adding scores is too slow.

Cosine, BM25 and graph scores cannot be added directly. RRF uses only positions.

A cache holds 3 items: A, B and C. A request for D arrives now, so one item must go. After D, the requests are B, A, B, C. Which item does Belady evict?

  • A
  • B
  • C

C is requested last of the three, so it is needed farthest in the future.

  1. Compute Mem0's combined score for a memory with semantic score 0.40, no BM25 match and an entity boost of 0.5, when all three signals are active.
    Answer

    The sum is 0.40 + 0 + 0.5 = 0.90. The divisor is 2.5 because all three signals are active. The score is 0.90 / 2.5 = 0.36.

  2. Write the rows of a bi-temporal table after this story. On 2026-02-01 you store "Bo lives in Kyoto since 2020". On 2026-04-01 you learn he moved to Nara on 2026-03-10.
    Answer

    Row 1: Kyoto, valid [2020, ∞), recorded [2026-02-01, 2026-04-01). Row 2: Kyoto, valid [2020, 2026-03-10), recorded [2026-04-01, ∞). Row 3: Nara, valid [2026-03-10, ∞), recorded [2026-04-01, ∞). No row is deleted.

  3. With Graphiti's 8 bands of 4 hashes, what is the chance that two names with Jaccard similarity 0.5 become candidates? And with 0.9?
    Answer

    For 0.5: 0.5^4 = 0.0625, and 1 - 0.9375^8 \approx 0.40. For 0.9: 0.9^4 = 0.656, and 1 - 0.344^8 \approx 0.9998. Similar names almost always meet. Different names usually do not.

  4. Your agent has 50,000 users. Each user's memory is read 8 times per day and written 2 times. Extraction costs 2,000 tokens and a read costs 600 tokens. How many tokens per day go to writes and to reads? Where would you optimise first?
    Answer

    Writes: 50,000 × 2 × 2,000 = 200 million tokens. Reads: 50,000 × 8 × 600 = 240 million tokens. They are similar in size. Writes use LLM generation, which usually costs more per token. So optimise writes first: skip chatter with a small decision model, batch extraction, and skip duplicates before the LLM call.

  5. Explain with the source coding theorem why a memory system cannot keep every detail and still use very few tokens.
    Answer

    Lossless compression cannot go below the entropy of the history. A long, varied history has high entropy, so its compressed size stays large. To use far fewer tokens, the system must drop information. That is lossy compression, so the design question is which details to drop.

Key takeaways

  • Agent memory has five kinds: context window, working notes, episodic, semantic and procedural.
  • Every system has a write path (extract, dedupe, store, index) and a read path (search, fuse, rerank, budget).
  • Mem0 2.2.1 uses one ADD-only extraction call, hash dedup and an additive hybrid score. Graph memory left the open-source class.
  • Graphiti keeps bi-temporal edges and never deletes facts. It finds duplicate names with entropy, MinHash and Jaccard.
  • Hindsight runs four searches, fuses them with RRF (k = 60), reranks, boosts and fills a token budget.
  • Lossless compression stops at the entropy. Real token savings come from dropping information on purpose.
  • Belady is the best possible cache. LRU is k-competitive in theory and much better on skewed real traffic.
