Context graphs and GraphRAG

Some questions need several steps: from an incident to a service, from the service to a team, from the team to a person. Vector search finds similar text, but it cannot follow links. This chapter shows how graphs give an agent connected context, and which theorems keep graph search fast and correct.

  • Tell a knowledge graph, a memory graph and a context graph apart by what they store.
  • Explain why plain vector search misses multi-step questions, with k-hop numbers.
  • Describe GraphRAG: entity extraction, communities, community summaries, local and global search.
  • Explain what Graphify, Graphiti, Omnigraph and pgGraph really do, from their repositories.
  • Write recursive graph queries in PostgreSQL and prove why they stop, then compute PageRank and modularity.

Three kinds of graph

A support agent gets a message: "Checkout is broken again." To help, it needs more than the words. It needs to know which service failed, who owns it, what was decided last time, and why. Those are things and the links between them.

A graph stores exactly that. Nodes are things. Edges are relations, such as "owned by". Three kinds of graph are common in AI systems. They differ in what they store.

Three kinds of graph for agents
KindStoresExample edgeChanges
Knowledge graphgeneral facts about a domainpayments-api → owned by → Team Falconslowly, by curation
Memory graphwhat one agent learned from its sessionsuser → has pet → Maxevery conversation
Context graphentities, decisions, reasons and time, with sourcesdecision 17 → rolled back → deploy 9, because error rate 8%at every decision, never deleted

The term "context graph" spread widely after a December 2025 essay by Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg of Foundation Capital. Their point: rules say what should usually happen, but decision traces say what happened in one case and why. Graphiti's README uses the term for a graph whose facts carry time windows. The idea is not new. It joins old ideas: knowledge graphs, audit logs and temporal databases.

Calling any graph a context graph. If it has no time, no source and no decisions, it is a knowledge graph. That is fine, but it cannot answer "why did we do this last time?"

Why vector search misses multi-step questions

The question is: "Who should I page about incident 42?" The documents hold three useful chunks.

  1. "Incident 42: checkout errors after the payments-api deploy at 02:10."
  2. "payments-api is owned by Team Falcon."
  3. "Team Falcon on-call this week: Dana."

Vector search embeds the question and finds similar chunks. Chunk 1 is similar: it says "incident 42". Chunks 2 and 3 share almost no words or meaning with the question. They rank below other incident reports. The answer, Dana, needs three hops: incident to service, service to team, team to person. Each hop needs the result of the hop before. Similarity to the question cannot see that chain.

In a graph the chain is a path. Here is the same data as an edge table in PostgreSQL 18.3. A three-way join follows the three hops. The output is real.

CREATE TABLE edge (src text, rel text, dst text);
INSERT INTO edge VALUES
  ('incident-42',   'affects',     'payments-api'),
  ('incident-42',   'reported_by', 'acme-corp'),
  ('payments-api',  'owned_by',    'team-falcon'),
  ('payments-api',  'depends_on',  'postgres-main'),
  ('postgres-main', 'owned_by',    'team-otter'),
  ('team-falcon',   'on_call',     'dana'),
  ('team-otter',    'on_call',     'eli'),
  ('dana',          'member_of',   'team-falcon');   -- a cycle: dana <-> team-falcon

SELECT e3.dst AS page_this_person
FROM edge e1
JOIN edge e2 ON e2.src = e1.dst AND e2.rel = 'owned_by'
JOIN edge e3 ON e3.src = e2.dst AND e3.rel = 'on_call'
WHERE e1.src = 'incident-42' AND e1.rel = 'affects';
 page_this_person
------------------
 dana
(1 row)

Graphs bring a new danger: the number of nodes grows fast with each hop. If each node has about d neighbours, k hops reach up to d^k nodes. That is k-hop growth.

So graph retrieval needs limits. Graphify's query code does three things. It walks with breadth-first search to depth 2 by default. It does not walk through hubs: nodes whose degree is at least max(50, the 99th percentile). And it cuts the text at a budget of 2,000 tokens, counted as about 3 characters per token. One hub with 5,000 links would otherwise flood the context.

Breadth-first search from a start node visits every reachable node exactly once. It finds the fewest hops to each one. It runs in O(V + E) time for V nodes and E edges. See the graph algorithms chapter for the proof.

Mix both tools. Use vector search to find the entry nodes ("incident 42"). Then use the graph to walk a few hops from them. Most GraphRAG systems work this way.

GraphRAG: communities and summaries

Some questions are not about one entity at all. "What are the main risks in all our incident reports this year?" No single chunk holds the answer. Vector search returns ten similar chunks and misses the big picture. Microsoft Research's GraphRAG paper (Edge and others, 2024) calls these global questions.

Cut into text units

Split the documents into small pieces. Each answer can point back to them.

Extract entities and relations

An LLM reads each piece and writes entities, relations and key claims. This builds the graph.

Find communities

Run the Leiden algorithm to group densely linked entities. Run it again inside each group. This gives a hierarchy of communities.

Summarise each community

An LLM writes a report for each community, from the bottom level up.

Answer

Global search: each community report gives a partial answer, then the partial answers are combined. Local search: start at entities in the question and fan out to their neighbours.

The GraphRAG documentation lists four query modes: global, local, DRIFT (local search plus community information) and basic vector search. The paper reports clearly more complete and more varied answers than plain RAG for global questions, on data sets of about one million tokens. Those are the authors' results. The price is high: the LLM must read the whole corpus once to build the graph and the reports.

How do we know a grouping is good? A good community has many edges inside and few edges to the outside, more than chance would give.

(Newman and Girvan, 2004.) For a graph with m edges and a split into communities, Q = \sum_{c} \left[ \dfrac{L_c}{m} - \left(\dfrac{d_c}{2m}\right)^2 \right]. Here L_c is the number of edges inside community c and d_c is the sum of degrees of its nodes. The first term is the real share of inside edges. The second is the share you would expect if edges were placed at random with the same degrees.

  1. Nodes 0, 1, 2 form a triangle. Nodes 3, 4, 5 form another. Edge 2–3 joins them. So m = 7.
  2. Split into {0,1,2} and {3,4,5}. Each side has L_c = 3 inside edges and degree sum d_c = 2+2+3 = 7.
  3. Each side gives 3/7 - (7/14)^2 = 0.4286 - 0.25 = 0.1786.
  4. Total: Q = 2 \times 0.1786 \approx 0.357. Putting all nodes in one group gives Q = 1 - 1 = 0.

The Louvain method raises Q greedily. It moves one node at a time to the neighbour community that raises Q most, then merges each community into one node and repeats. Leiden (Traag, Waltman and van Eck, 2019) adds a refine step. It guarantees that every community is connected, which Louvain does not. Here is the first Louvain phase, local moving, on the triangle example.

// Modularity Q, and Louvain-style local moving on two triangles and a bridge.
use std::collections::BTreeSet;
const EDGES: [(usize, usize); 7] = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (3, 5), (4, 5)];
const N: usize = 6;

fn q(comm: &[usize], deg: &[f64]) -> f64 { // Q = sum over communities of L_c/m - (d_c/2m)^2
    let m = EDGES.len() as f64;
    let groups: BTreeSet<usize> = comm.iter().copied().collect();
    groups.iter().map(|&c| {
        let inside = EDGES.iter().filter(|&&(a, b)| comm[a] == c && comm[b] == c).count() as f64;
        let d: f64 = (0..N).filter(|&v| comm[v] == c).map(|v| deg[v]).sum();
        inside / m - (d / (2.0 * m)).powi(2)
    }).sum()
}

fn main() {
    let deg: Vec<f64> = (0..N).map(|v| EDGES.iter().filter(|e| e.0 == v || e.1 == v).count() as f64).collect();
    println!("one big group  Q={:.4}", q(&[0; N], &deg));
    println!("all alone      Q={:.4}", q(&(0..N).collect::<Vec<_>>(), &deg));

    let mut comm: Vec<usize> = (0..N).collect(); // start: every node alone
    let mut moved = true;
    while moved { // move nodes while Q improves
        moved = false;
        for v in 0..N {
            let near: BTreeSet<usize> = EDGES.iter()
                .filter_map(|&(a, b)| if a == v { Some(comm[b]) } else if b == v { Some(comm[a]) } else { None })
                .collect();
            for c in near {
                let mut trial = comm.clone();
                trial[v] = c;
                if q(&trial, &deg) > q(&comm, &deg) + 1e-12 { comm = trial; moved = true; }
            }
        }
    }
    println!("local moving   Q={:.4} groups={:?}", q(&comm, &deg), comm);
}
# Modularity Q, and Louvain-style local moving on two triangles and a bridge.
edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (3, 5), (4, 5)]
n, m = 6, len(edges)
deg = [sum(v in e for e in edges) for v in range(n)]

def q(comm):  # Q = sum over communities of L_c/m - (d_c/2m)^2
    total = 0.0
    for c in set(comm):
        inside = sum(1 for a, b in edges if comm[a] == c and comm[b] == c)
        d = sum(deg[v] for v in range(n) if comm[v] == c)
        total += inside / m - (d / (2 * m)) ** 2
    return total

print(f"one big group  Q={q([0] * n):.4f}")
print(f"all alone      Q={q(list(range(n))):.4f}")

comm = list(range(n))                      # start: every node alone
moved = True
while moved:                               # move nodes while Q improves
    moved = False
    for v in range(n):
        for c in sorted({comm[b] for a, b in edges if a == v} | {comm[a] for a, b in edges if b == v}):
            trial = comm[:v] + [c] + comm[v + 1:]
            if q(trial) > q(comm) + 1e-12:
                comm, moved = trial, True
print(f"local moving   Q={q(comm):.4f} groups={comm}")
one big group  Q=0.0000
all alone      Q=-0.1735
local moving   Q=0.3571 groups=[1, 1, 1, 5, 5, 5]

The greedy moves found the two triangles, with Q = 0.3571, as computed by hand. The group names 1 and 5 do not matter. Only who is together matters.

Trusting the biggest Q blindly. Modularity has a resolution limit (Fortunato and Barthélemy, 2007). In a large graph, the best Q can merge small real communities into one. That is why tools offer a resolution setting, and why Graphify splits very large communities again.

Case study: Graphify

The problem. A coding agent wastes tokens when it reads many files to understand a codebase. Graphify turns code, docs, schemas and PDFs into a graph that the agent can query instead.

What I looked at. The Graphify-Labs/graphify repository on 2026-11-15: the README, ARCHITECTURE.md, the how-it-works page and the clustering, analysis and query source. The package on PyPI is named graphifyy, version 0.9.108 (2026-11-12). The repository shows both an Apache-2.0 and an MIT licence file, and the package metadata says Apache-2.0.

How it works. Pass 1 parses code with tree-sitter: classes, functions, imports and calls. The docs say about 40 languages are supported. Pass 2 transcribes audio and video locally. Pass 3 sends documents and images to LLM subagents in parallel. Each edge carries a tag. EXTRACTED means found directly in the source. INFERRED comes with a confidence score from 0.55 to 0.95. AMBIGUOUS is flagged for review. A SHA-256 hash of each file lets re-runs skip unchanged files. Communities come from Leiden through the graspologic library, with a fixed seed of 42. If that library is missing, it falls back to NetworkX's Louvain.

A real example. These commands come from the README. I did not run them, because installing the tool was outside what I could do here.

graphify install                           # register the /graphify skill for your assistant
graphify extract .                         # build the graph from the command line
graphify update .                          # re-extract only changed files
graphify query "what connects auth to the database?" --budget 2000 --depth 2
graphify path "UserService" "DatabasePool" # shortest path between two names
graphify explain "RateLimiter"             # one node and its neighbours

The theory under it. Three graph ideas carry the design. Leiden maximises modularity, so each community is a dense area of the code. A community bigger than 25% of the graph is split again, which works around the resolution limit. The "god nodes" in the report are simply the nodes of highest degree. The query walks with bounded breadth-first search, so its cost is limited by depth, hub blocking and the token budget, not by the size of the repository.

The trade-off. The authors report 71.5 times fewer tokens per query on a mixed corpus of 52 files, and about 1 times on a 6-file library. Those are their numbers. Small projects fit in the context window anyway. Inferred edges from LLMs can be wrong, so the tags matter. And the graph is a snapshot: it must be updated when code changes.

Case study: Graphiti as a context graph with time

The problem. An agent's world changes every day. The graph must take new facts at once, keep old facts with their time, and answer fast without an LLM at read time. The agent memory chapter covers Graphiti's write path and its four timestamps. Here we look at its graph side.

How it works. Episodes are nodes too, linked to every entity they mention. So each fact can be traced to its source. Search runs cosine similarity, BM25 and breadth-first search, then fuses them. One reranker, node distance, gives a higher score to results that link directly to a chosen centre node, such as the user. Communities come from label propagation, not Leiden. In Graphiti's code, every node takes the label with the most edge weight among its neighbours. Ties go to the larger label number. This repeats until no label changes. Each round costs O(V + E).

A real example. The method names match graphiti.py (version 0.31.2). Not run: it needs a graph database and an LLM key.

from graphiti_core import Graphiti

async def explore(g: Graphiti, user_node_uuid: str):
    await g.build_communities()                  # label propagation + LLM summaries
    # rerank by graph distance from the user's node instead of plain RRF
    edges = await g.search("What did we decide about the payments deploy?",
                           center_node_uuid=user_node_uuid, num_results=5)
    for e in edges:
        print(e.fact, "| valid from", e.valid_at, "| until", e.invalid_at)

The theory under it. Breadth-first search gives the fewest hops from the seeds, and its cost is linear in the part of the graph it visits. Label propagation is near-linear per round, so communities stay cheap to rebuild. But it does not maximise modularity, and on some graphs it can produce one giant group.

The trade-off. Graphiti does the LLM work at write time, so reads can be fast, but writes are slow and use many LLM calls. You also run a graph database: Neo4j, FalkorDB or Amazon Neptune. Kuzu support is marked deprecated.

Case studies: Omnigraph and pgGraph

The brief for this chapter only guessed what these two projects are. Here is what their repositories show on 2026-11-15.

Omnigraph

The problem. Many agents must share one typed model of their world, read it, and propose changes safely. Omnigraph describes itself as an object-storage native graph database with branching and a typed schema.

What I looked at. The ModernRelay/omnigraph repository: the README, the quickstart, the search and branching docs, and the Cargo workspace. It is written in Rust, edition 2024, with about 20 crates. The licence is MIT. The release notes describe version 0.14.0, released 2026-10-22. A cloud service is in private preview.

A real example. This is the shape of the quickstart: a schema, one query and the CLI calls. Not run: I did not install the binary.

node Source { slug: String @key  title: String }
node Claim  { slug: String @key  statement: String }
edge Supports: Source -> Claim

query sources_for_claim($claim: String) {
  match {
    $source: Source
    $claim_node: Claim { slug: $claim }
    $source supports $claim_node
  }
  return { $source.title as source }
  order { source asc }
}
omnigraph init --schema schema.pg graph.omni
omnigraph load --data evidence.jsonl --mode overwrite --target ./graph.omni
omnigraph branch create review/add-benchmark --target ./graph.omni
omnigraph branch merge review/add-benchmark --into main --target ./graph.omni

The theory under it. A branch with a three-way merge works like Git. Both sides are compared with their common ancestor, so a change made on only one side is safe to apply. The docs say a load or a merge publishes as one atomic commit. Search has nearest() by L2 distance, bm25() and rrf() with a default k of 60, the same fusion formula as in the agent memory chapter.

The trade-off. Object storage is cheap and scales, but each read has higher latency than local memory. The docs explain limits: for example, a vector arm inside rrf() is only a top-k window, so a traversal can shorten the fused answer. It is a young project, at version 0.14.

pgGraph

The problem. Teams keep their data in PostgreSQL tables. They want graph questions, such as "everything within 2 hops of Alice" or "the shortest path from this person to that company", without a second database.

What I looked at. The evokoa/pggraph repository: the README, the quickstart and META.json. pgGraph is a PostgreSQL extension written in Rust with pgrx. Version 1.2.1 supports PostgreSQL 14 to 18. The licence is Apache-2.0. Your tables stay the source of truth. pgGraph builds a derived graph index and offers SQL functions in a graph schema.

How it works. The default projection mode is csr_readonly. CSR is a classic graph layout. One array holds every node's neighbours, one list after another. A second array says where each node's list starts.

This is the idea behind index-free adjacency. A plain edge table needs a B-tree lookup for each hop, about \log_2 E steps. With a million edges that is about 20 steps per hop. CSR needs one. The cost is memory: V + 1 offsets plus E targets, and the projection must be rebuilt or patched when tables change.

A real example. This is shortened from the pgGraph quickstart (version 1.2.1). I did not run it: the extension is not installed on my test server.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS graph;
CREATE TABLE companies (id text PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE people (id text PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL,
                     company_id text REFERENCES companies(id));
-- ... insert rows ...
SELECT * FROM graph.auto_discover('public');   -- tables + foreign keys -> graph
SELECT depth, node_table_name, node_id, edge_path
FROM graph.traverse('public.people'::regclass, 'p1', 2, hydrate := false);
SELECT step, node_table_name, node_id, edge_label
FROM graph.shortest_path('public.people'::regclass, 'p1',
                         'public.companies'::regclass, 'c1', hydrate := false);

The theory under it. Foreign keys already are edges. Auto-discovery turns them into a graph. Traversal and shortest paths on an unweighted graph are breadth-first search, which CSR makes fast. The docs also list weighted shortest paths and connected components.

The trade-off. The projection is a second copy of the links, so it costs memory and needs syncing with the tables. The quickstart notes a scheduled maintenance job for this. It is a derived index, not the source of truth.

Graphs inside PostgreSQL

You can do a lot of graph work in plain SQL. The tool is the recursive CTE. Here are two queries on the edge table from before, run in PostgreSQL 18.3.

-- every node reachable from incident-42 (UNION removes repeats)
WITH RECURSIVE reach(node) AS (
    SELECT 'incident-42'::text
  UNION
    SELECT e.dst FROM reach r JOIN edge e ON e.src = r.node
)
SELECT count(*) AS reachable_nodes FROM reach;

-- nodes by hop count; the CYCLE clause stops at dana <-> team-falcon
WITH RECURSIVE walk(node, depth) AS (
    SELECT 'incident-42'::text, 0
  UNION ALL
    SELECT e.dst, w.depth + 1 FROM walk w JOIN edge e ON e.src = w.node
) CYCLE node SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT depth, count(DISTINCT node) AS nodes_at_depth, string_agg(DISTINCT node, ', ') AS nodes
FROM walk WHERE NOT is_cycle
GROUP BY depth ORDER BY depth;
 reachable_nodes
-----------------
 8
(1 row)

 depth | nodes_at_depth | nodes
-------+----------------+----------------------------
 0     | 1              | incident-42
 1     | 2              | acme-corp, payments-api
 2     | 2              | postgres-main, team-falcon
 3     | 2              | dana, team-otter
 4     | 1              | eli
(5 rows)

The graph has a cycle: dana is a member of team-falcon, and team-falcon has dana on call. Why did the first query stop anyway? PostgreSQL evaluates a recursive CTE as a loop. Each round joins only the new rows from the last round. With UNION, rows already seen are thrown away. When a round adds nothing new, the loop stops. The theorem below says this always happens, with one smallest answer.

(Knaster and Tarski.) Let L be a complete lattice and f: L \to L a monotone function: x \le y implies f(x) \le f(y). Then the fixed points of f form a complete lattice. In particular f has a least fixed point, \text{lfp}(f) = \bigwedge \{ x : f(x) \le x \}. If L is finite, the chain \bot \le f(\bot) \le f(f(\bot)) \le \dots reaches \text{lfp}(f) in finitely many steps.

In simple words: a fixed point is a set that one more round does not change. For reachability, the lattice is all subsets of nodes, ordered by ⊆. The round is T(R) = \{\text{start}\} \cup \{ y : x \in R,\ (x, y) \in E \}. Adding nodes to R can only add nodes to T(R), so T is monotone. Start from the empty set and apply T: {incident-42}, then 3 nodes, then 5, then 7, then 8, then 8 again. That last set is the least fixed point. With 8 nodes, there can never be more than 9 rounds.

Proof idea for the finite case

Start at \bot. Since \bot \le f(\bot) and f is monotone, applying f again keeps the order, so the chain only grows. A finite lattice has no infinite strictly growing chain, so the chain stops at some x with f(x) = x. If y is any other fixed point, then \bot \le y, so f^i(\bot) \le f^i(y) = y for every i. So x \le y, and x is the least.

Using UNION ALL on a graph with a cycle and no guard. Duplicates are kept, so every round finds new rows and the loop never stops. I checked: with UNION ALL from team-falcon, an outer LIMIT 1000 returned 1,000 rows from a 2-node cycle. Use UNION, the CYCLE clause (PostgreSQL 14 and later), or a depth limit.

Other ways to do graphs in PostgreSQL.

  • Extensions. Apache AGE adds openCypher queries to PostgreSQL. pgGraph, above, adds a CSR projection and graph functions over normal tables.
  • SQL/PGQ. The SQL:2023 standard added Part 16, property graph queries, with GRAPH_TABLE and MATCH. A PostgreSQL implementation was committed for version 19 and then reverted. pgGraph's README says this happened on the release branch on 2026-09-07. I confirmed that the revert commit, "Revert SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ)", exists. I could not see its date myself. Check the PostgreSQL release notes: this can change.

Union-find: grouping duplicate entities

Entity extraction produces many names for one thing: "Alice Chen", "A. Chen", "alice@acme.com". A matcher says which pairs are the same. Then we need the groups. The pairs form a graph, and the groups are its connected components. Union-find builds them as the pairs arrive.

// Union-find: merge entity mentions that a matcher says are the same thing.
struct Dsu { parent: Vec<usize>, size: Vec<usize> }

impl Dsu {
    fn find(&mut self, mut x: usize) -> usize {
        while self.parent[x] != x {
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]; // path halving: skip a level
            x = self.parent[x];
        }
        x
    }
    fn union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) {
        let (mut ra, mut rb) = (self.find(a), self.find(b));
        if ra == rb { return; }
        if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb] { std::mem::swap(&mut ra, &mut rb); } // smaller under bigger
        self.parent[rb] = ra;
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb];
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mentions = ["Alice Chen", "A. Chen", "alice@acme.com", "Bob Ito", "B. Ito", "Acme Corp", "ACME"];
    let n = mentions.len();
    let mut d = Dsu { parent: (0..n).collect(), size: vec![1; n] };
    for (a, b) in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6), (2, 0)] { d.union(a, b); } // matcher output
    let mut groups: Vec<(usize, Vec<&str>)> = Vec::new(); // keep first-seen order
    for (i, name) in mentions.iter().enumerate() {
        let root = d.find(i);
        match groups.iter_mut().find(|g| g.0 == root) {
            Some(g) => g.1.push(name),
            None => groups.push((root, vec![name])),
        }
    }
    for (_, g) in groups { println!("{g:?}"); }
}
# Union-find: merge entity mentions that a matcher says are the same thing.
mentions = ["Alice Chen", "A. Chen", "alice@acme.com", "Bob Ito", "B. Ito", "Acme Corp", "ACME"]
parent = list(range(len(mentions)))
size = [1] * len(mentions)

def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]      # path halving: skip a level
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def union(a, b):
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra == rb:
        return
    if size[ra] < size[rb]:
        ra, rb = rb, ra                    # hang the smaller tree under the bigger
    parent[rb] = ra
    size[ra] += size[rb]

for a, b in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6), (2, 0)]:   # matcher output
    union(a, b)

groups = {}
for i, name in enumerate(mentions):
    groups.setdefault(find(i), []).append(name)
for g in groups.values():
    print(g)
["Alice Chen", "A. Chen", "alice@acme.com"]
["Bob Ito", "B. Ito"]
["Acme Corp", "ACME"]

Python prints the same groups with single quotes. With union by size and path halving, m operations on n items cost O(m\,\alpha(n)) in total (Tarjan, 1975). Here \alpha is the inverse Ackermann function. It is at most 4 for any input that fits in our universe, so each operation is nearly constant time. The pair (2, 0) changed nothing: they were already in one group.

Ranking nodes: PageRank

A graph walk returns many nodes. Which ones matter most? PageRank imagines a walker. With chance \alpha = 0.85 it follows a random outgoing edge. Otherwise it jumps to a random node. A node's score is the share of time the walker spends there. HippoRAG (NeurIPS 2024) uses a personalised version, where the walker always jumps back to entities from the question. It reports good multi-hop retrieval in a single step. Those are the authors' results.

// PageRank by power iteration on a small context graph.
fn main() {
    let names = ["incident", "payments", "postgres", "falcon", "dana", "runbook"];
    let edges = [(0, 1), (0, 5), (5, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 1), (3, 4), (4, 0)];
    let (n, alpha) = (names.len(), 0.85); // alpha: chance to follow a link
    let out: Vec<f64> = (0..n).map(|v| edges.iter().filter(|e| e.0 == v).count() as f64).collect();

    let mut r = vec![1.0 / n as f64; n]; // start: every node equal
    for t in 1..=60 {
        let mut new = vec![(1.0 - alpha) / n as f64; n]; // teleport share
        for &(a, b) in &edges {
            new[b] += alpha * r[a] / out[a]; // follow a link
        }
        let change: f64 = new.iter().zip(&r).map(|(x, y)| (x - y).abs()).sum();
        r = new;
        if [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60].contains(&t) {
            println!("t={t:<3} change={change:.2e}");
        }
    }
    let mut ranked: Vec<(&str, f64)> = names.iter().copied().zip(r).collect();
    ranked.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.total_cmp(&a.1)); // stable: ties keep their order
    for (name, score) in ranked {
        println!("{name:9} {score:.4}");
    }
}
# PageRank by power iteration on a small context graph.
names = ["incident", "payments", "postgres", "falcon", "dana", "runbook"]
edges = [(0, 1), (0, 5), (5, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 1), (3, 4), (4, 0)]
n, alpha = len(names), 0.85               # alpha: chance to follow a link
out = [sum(1 for a, _ in edges if a == v) for v in range(n)]

r = [1.0 / n] * n                          # start: every node equal
for t in range(1, 61):
    new = [(1 - alpha) / n] * n            # teleport share
    for a, b in edges:
        new[b] += alpha * r[a] / out[a]    # follow a link
    change = sum(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(new, r))
    r = new
    if t in (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60):
        print(f"t={t:<3} change={change:.2e}")

for name, score in sorted(zip(names, r), key=lambda p: -p[1]):
    print(f"{name:9} {score:.4f}")
t=1   change=4.25e-1
t=2   change=3.61e-1
t=5   change=1.85e-1
t=10  change=8.20e-3
t=20  change=8.83e-5
t=40  change=2.87e-9
t=60  change=3.62e-14
payments  0.2972
incident  0.1556
dana      0.1536
postgres  0.1513
falcon    0.1513
runbook   0.0911

This is the Rust output. Python writes the exponents with two digits, such as 4.25e-01. The numbers are the same. The service payments-api wins: three nodes point to it. The change between rounds shrinks quickly, and the scores settle. Why must they settle?

Let P be the column-stochastic link matrix of a graph (every node has an outgoing edge) and 0 \lt \alpha \lt 1. The Google matrix G = \alpha P + \frac{1-\alpha}{n} \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} has all entries positive. By the Perron-Frobenius theorem, it has exactly one probability vector r with Gr = r. Power iteration r_{t+1} = G r_t reaches it from any start, with \lVert r_t - r \rVert_1 \le \alpha^t \lVert r_0 - r \rVert_1.

Proof idea

Take two probability vectors x and y. Their difference z = x - y sums to 0, so the jump part gives \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} z = 0. Then \lVert Gz \rVert_1 = \alpha \lVert Pz \rVert_1 \le \alpha \lVert z \rVert_1, because a stochastic matrix never makes the L1 norm larger. So G is a contraction with factor \alpha. By the Banach fixed-point theorem, it has one fixed point, and the error shrinks by \alpha or better every round.

Check with numbers. The bound says the error after 60 rounds is at most 0.85^{60} \approx 5.8 \times 10^{-5} times the start error. Our real change was 3.6 \times 10^{-14}, much smaller. The true speed is set by the second-largest eigenvalue of G, which here is much smaller than 0.85. The damping factor also gives a practical rule. To shrink the error 1,000 times, you need at most \ln 1000 / \ln(1/0.85) \approx 43 rounds, whatever the size of the graph.

Know why the jump term matters. Without it, a graph can have nodes with no way out, or two separate parts. Then the stationary vector may not be unique, and power iteration may not converge. The jump makes every entry positive, so Perron-Frobenius applies.

Patterns to remember

Graph and GraphRAG patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
Vector search for entry, graph for hopsAnswer multi-step questionsembed "incident 42", then walk 3 hopsSimilarity cannot follow a chain.
Bounded BFS (Graphify)Keep context smalldepth 2, budget 2,000 tokensDo not expand through hubs.
Communities, then summaries (GraphRAG)Answer global questionsLeiden levels, one report eachIndexing reads the whole corpus.
Check modularityJudge a groupingQ = \sum L_c/m - (d_c/2m)^2Beware the resolution limit.
Tag every edge with its originTrust what was read, check what was guessedEXTRACTED or INFERRED 0.75LLM edges can be wrong.
Facts with time windows (Graphiti)Answer "now" and "then"valid_at, invalid_at on each edgeInvalidate, never delete.
Branch, review, merge (Omnigraph)Safe writes by many agentsbranch merge review/x --into mainThree-way merge needs a common ancestor.
Graph index over tables (pgGraph)Graph queries without a second databasegraph.traverse(..., 'p1', 2)The CSR copy must stay in sync.
Recursive CTE with UNION or CYCLEReachability in plain SQLWITH RECURSIVE reach(node) AS (...)UNION ALL on a cycle never stops.
Union-find for entity groupsMerge duplicate mentionsunion("A. Chen", "Alice Chen")Use union by size and path halving.
PageRank to rank a subgraphShow the most central nodes firstα = 0.85, about 40 roundsKeep the jump term.

Practice

If every node has 5 neighbours, three hops can reach up to ? nodes.

In CSR with offsets [0, 2, 3, 5, 5], node 2's neighbours start at position 3 and stop before position ?.

The modularity of putting every node in one single community is ?.

Which question needs GraphRAG's global search most?

  • Who owns payments-api?
  • What are the main themes across all incident reports this year?
  • When did incident 42 start?

A theme question is about the whole collection. Community summaries cover it. The others are local lookups.

Why does a recursive CTE with UNION stop on a graph with cycles?

  • PostgreSQL has a fixed limit of 100 rounds.
  • Repeated rows are dropped, the set can only grow, and a finite set cannot grow forever.
  • Cycles are removed from the table first.

This is the least fixed point from Knaster-Tarski on a finite lattice.

What does pgGraph keep as the source of truth?

  • Its CSR projection
  • The ordinary PostgreSQL tables
  • A separate graph database

The README says your tables stay the source of truth. The graph is a derived index.

  1. Compute the modularity of the split {0, 1, 2, 3} and {4, 5} for the two-triangle graph.
    Answer

    Inside {0,1,2,3}: edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–2, 2–3, so L = 4. Degrees 2+2+3+3 = 10. Inside {4,5}: edge 4–5, so L = 1, degrees 2+2 = 4. Q = (4/7 - (10/14)^2) + (1/7 - (4/14)^2) = (0.571 - 0.510) + (0.143 - 0.082) \approx 0.122. Lower than 0.357, so it is a worse split.

  2. Write the rounds of T for reachability from incident-42 in the edge table, as sets of node counts. Why can there be no more than 9 rounds?
    Answer

    Start with the empty set. Then 1 node, 3, 5, 7, 8, and 8 again. Each round before the end adds at least one node. There are only 8 nodes, so after at most 8 growing rounds and 1 final check, the set must stop changing.

  3. With α = 0.85, how many PageRank rounds guarantee that the error falls below one millionth of the start error?
    Answer

    We need 0.85^t \le 10^{-6}. So t \ge \ln(10^6) / \ln(1/0.85) = 13.82 / 0.1625 \approx 85 rounds. The real number is often smaller, as our run showed.

  4. Your graph has 10 million edges in a plain table with a B-tree index. Estimate the index steps for a 3-hop walk from one node that visits 1,000 nodes. Compare with CSR.
    Answer

    One B-tree lookup takes about \log_2 10^7 \approx 23 steps. Visiting 1,000 nodes needs about 1,000 lookups, so about 23,000 steps, plus reading the edges. CSR needs about 1 step per node to find each list, so about 1,000 steps plus the edges. B-tree pages are wide, so the real gap is smaller, but CSR still wins for deep walks.

  5. Design retrieval for "Who approved the last rollback of payments-api, and why?" in a context graph. Name the steps and one theorem behind each.
    Answer

    1. Find entry nodes with vector search plus BM25 ("payments-api", "rollback"), fused with RRF. 2. Walk a bounded BFS from them along "rolled back", "made by" and "because" edges. BFS gives the fewest hops. 3. Keep only edges valid at the time asked, using bi-temporal fields. 4. Rank the subgraph with personalised PageRank from the entry nodes, which converges by Perron-Frobenius. 5. Render the top nodes and their sources within a token budget.

Key takeaways

  • Knowledge graphs store facts, memory graphs store what an agent learned, and context graphs add decisions, reasons, time and sources.
  • Vector search finds similar text. It cannot follow a chain of hops. Use it to find entry nodes, then walk the graph.
  • k-hop growth is d^k, so graph retrieval needs depth limits, hub blocking and a token budget.
  • GraphRAG builds communities with Leiden and summarises them, so global questions can be answered. Modularity measures community quality.
  • Graphify parses code locally and clusters with Leiden. Graphiti keeps time on every fact. Omnigraph adds typed schemas and branches. pgGraph adds a CSR graph index over normal PostgreSQL tables.
  • Recursive CTEs with UNION stop at a least fixed point (Knaster-Tarski). PageRank converges because the Google matrix is a positive contraction (Perron-Frobenius).

Sources

  • Edge et al.: From Local to Global, a Graph RAG approach. The GraphRAG paper (2024, revised 2025).
  • Graphify-Labs/graphify on GitHub. README, docs and source, read on 2026-11-15 (graphifyy 0.9.108).
  • getzep/graphiti on GitHub. Search, communities and temporal edges (version 0.31.2).
  • ModernRelay/omnigraph on GitHub. README, quickstart, search and branching docs (version 0.14.0).
  • evokoa/pggraph on GitHub. README and quickstart (version 1.2.1), with the note on SQL/PGQ.
  • PostgreSQL 18 documentation: WITH queries. How recursive queries run, and the CYCLE and SEARCH clauses.

Making AI systems fast and reliable

An AI demo works once. A product must work ten thousand times a day, fast and at a known cost. This chapter shows where the time and money go, and which practices fix each problem. Every practice comes with the theorem that explains it and an open-source project that uses it.

  • Find the main costs of an agent run: tokens, round trips and retrieval.
  • Use caching, batching, retries with jitter and idempotency keys correctly.
  • Explain durable execution with checkpoints, using the idea of a consistent snapshot.
  • Size a system with Little's law, a queueing model and Amdahl's law.
  • Design, test and guard a multi-agent research system, with numbers.

Where time and money go

Look at one run of a research agent. It makes 20 model calls. Each call sends about 32,000 tokens and gets 800 tokens back. Between calls it runs tools: web search, a vector search and a database query.

The four big costs of an agent run
CostWhy it is bigMain fix
Input tokensThe whole history is sent again on every callPrompt caching, shorter context
Output tokensMade one by one, so slow, and often priced higherShort answers, structured output
Round tripsEach tool call means one more model call and one more waitParallel tool calls, fewer steps
RetrievalEmbedding, vector search, graph search, rerankingGood indexes, result caches

Input tokens are cheap per token but there are very many. A model reads input in parallel. This phase is called prefill. It writes output one token at a time. That phase is called decode. So 800 output tokens at, say, 60 tokens per second take more than 13 seconds. Long answers are slow answers.

Do not guess where the time goes. Measure it. Put a timer and a token counter around every model call and every tool call. Most teams find one surprise, such as a tool that returns 20,000 tokens of raw HTML.

Caching, batching and streaming

Prompt caching

Most of each call is the same: the system prompt, the tool list and the documents. Only the last part is new. A cache can keep the model's work on that same start, the prefix.

Anthropic's docs give the rules for its API. The cache matches only an exact prefix, in the order tools, then system, then messages. One changed character early in the prompt breaks the cache for everything after it. For many models a cache read costs 10% of the normal input price. A cache write costs 1.25 times the price for a 5-minute cache, or 2 times for a 1-hour cache. Prices and rules change, so check the price page.

// Cost of one agent run: 20 model calls that share a 30,000-token prefix.
const PRICE_IN: f64 = 2.00; // example dollars per million tokens
const PRICE_OUT: f64 = 10.00;
const WRITE: f64 = 1.25; // cache write, times the input price
const READ: f64 = 0.10; // cache read, times the input price
const CALLS: f64 = 20.0;
const PREFIX: f64 = 30_000.0;
const FRESH: f64 = 2_000.0;
const OUT: f64 = 800.0;

fn dollars(tokens: f64, price: f64) -> f64 {
    tokens * price / 1_000_000.0
}

fn main() {
    let plain = dollars(CALLS * (PREFIX + FRESH), PRICE_IN);
    // call 1 writes the prefix to the cache, calls 2..20 read it
    let cached = dollars(PREFIX * WRITE + (CALLS - 1.0) * PREFIX * READ + CALLS * FRESH, PRICE_IN);
    let out = dollars(CALLS * OUT, PRICE_OUT);
    println!("no cache:   input ${plain:.3} + output ${out:.3} = ${:.3}", plain + out);
    println!("with cache: input ${cached:.3} + output ${out:.3} = ${:.3}", cached + out);
    println!("saving: {:.0}%", (1.0 - (cached + out) / (plain + out)) * 100.0);
}
# Cost of one agent run: 20 model calls that share a 30,000-token prefix.
PRICE_IN, PRICE_OUT = 2.00, 10.00      # example dollars per million tokens
WRITE, READ = 1.25, 0.10               # cache write and read, times the input price
CALLS, PREFIX, FRESH, OUT = 20, 30_000, 2_000, 800


def dollars(tokens: float, price: float) -> float:
    return tokens * price / 1_000_000


plain = dollars(CALLS * (PREFIX + FRESH), PRICE_IN)
# call 1 writes the prefix to the cache, calls 2..20 read it
cached = dollars(PREFIX * WRITE + (CALLS - 1) * PREFIX * READ + CALLS * FRESH, PRICE_IN)
out = dollars(CALLS * OUT, PRICE_OUT)
print(f"no cache:   input ${plain:.3f} + output ${out:.3f} = ${plain + out:.3f}")
print(f"with cache: input ${cached:.3f} + output ${out:.3f} = ${cached + out:.3f}")
print(f"saving: {1 - (cached + out) / (plain + out):.0%}")
no cache:   input $1.280 + output $0.160 = $1.440
with cache: input $0.269 + output $0.160 = $0.429
saving: 70%

The prices in the code are examples, not real prices. The shape of the result is what matters. When most of each call is a shared prefix, caching removes most of the input cost.

The open-source server vLLM does the same inside the model server. Its design docs describe automatic prefix caching. The server splits the prompt's saved model state into blocks. Each block gets a hash made from its parent block's hash and its own tokens. So two prompts with the same start get the same chain of hashes and share blocks. When memory is full, vLLM drops the LRU block first. The chapter Randomised, approximate, streaming and string algorithms shows why LRU is a good rule: it is at most k times worse than a perfect rule that knows the future.

Putting the date and time at the top of the system prompt. Now the prefix changes every second, and the cache never hits. Put things that change at the end. Keep the tool list in a fixed order. The MCP spec asks servers to return tools in a fixed order for exactly this reason.

Result caching

A second kind of cache saves whole answers. The key is a hash of the model, the prompt and the settings. It works well for repeated, fixed questions, like "classify this ticket". Give each entry a TTL. Do not use it when the answer must be fresh or must change from run to run.

Batching

Some work has no user waiting: nightly evaluations, tagging a million documents. Send it as a batch. Anthropic's batch docs promise a 50% lower price and say most batches finish in under an hour. Inside a model server, batching also helps. The server runs many requests through the GPU together, so it does more work per second.

Streaming

Streaming sends tokens to the user as soon as the model makes them. The total time stays the same. But the first words appear in under a second instead of after 13 seconds. The user feels the system is fast, and can stop a bad answer early.

Retries, timeouts and idempotency

An agent asks a payment tool to charge an order. The network times out. Did the charge happen? The agent cannot know. Maybe the request never arrived. Maybe the charge happened and only the reply was lost.

Two parties talk over a channel that can lose any message. No protocol with a finite number of messages can make both parties sure that they agree. So a sender can never be sure that its last message arrived.

Proof idea

Take the shortest protocol that works. Its last message can be lost. The sender of that last message acts the same either way, because it cannot see the loss. So the protocol must also work without the last message. Then a shorter protocol works, which contradicts "shortest". Repeat until zero messages are left, and with zero messages no agreement is possible.

The theorem says we cannot have "exactly once" over a lossy network. The practical answer has two parts:

  1. At-least-once delivery. Retry until you get a reply. The request may arrive more than once.
  2. An idempotent receiver. Idempotent means a repeat changes nothing. The sender adds an idempotency key. The receiver saves the key with the result. A repeat with the same key gets the old result back.

Together they give "effectively once". Retries need one more idea: wait a random time between tries. If 1,000 clients fail at the same moment and all retry after exactly 1 second, they hit the server together again. Marc Brooker's AWS article from 2015 compares ways to add randomness, called jitter. "Full jitter" picks a wait between 0 and a ceiling. The ceiling doubles after each failure, up to a cap.

// Retries with full jitter, with and without an idempotency key.
use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Lcg(u64); // tiny LCG so Rust and Python match
impl Lcg {
    fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_mul(6364136223846793005).wrapping_add(1442695040888963407);
        self.0 >> 33
    }
    fn full_jitter(&mut self, attempt: u32) -> u64 {
        let ceiling = (100u64 * 2u64.pow(attempt)).min(2000); // exponential, with a cap
        self.next_u32() % (ceiling + 1) // random from 0 to ceiling
    }
}

fn run(use_key: bool, rng: &mut Lcg) {
    let script = ["down", "lost", "ok"]; // what the network does each time
    let (mut charges, mut seen) = (0, HashMap::new());
    for (i, event) in script.iter().enumerate() {
        let attempt = i as u32 + 1;
        let key = if use_key { Some("charge:order-7") } else { None };
        if *event == "down" {
            print!("  attempt {attempt}: 503, nothing done");
        } else if key.is_some_and(|k| seen.contains_key(k)) {
            print!("  attempt {attempt}: key seen, old result returned");
        } else {
            charges += 1; // the side effect happens
            if let Some(k) = key {
                seen.insert(k, "receipt-1");
            }
            let lost = if *event == "lost" { ", reply lost" } else { "" };
            print!("  attempt {attempt}: charged{lost}");
        }
        if *event == "ok" {
            println!();
            break;
        }
        println!(", sleep {} ms", rng.full_jitter(attempt));
    }
    println!("  total charges: {charges}");
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng = Lcg(42);
    for use_key in [true, false] {
        println!("{}", if use_key { "with key:" } else { "without key:" });
        run(use_key, &mut rng);
    }
}
# Retries with full jitter, with and without an idempotency key.
MASK = (1 << 64) - 1
seed = 42


def rand_u32() -> int:                    # tiny LCG so Rust and Python match
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 6364136223846793005 + 1442695040888963407) & MASK
    return seed >> 33


def full_jitter(attempt: int, base: int = 100, cap: int = 2000) -> int:
    ceiling = min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)        # exponential, with a cap
    return rand_u32() % (ceiling + 1)              # random from 0 to ceiling


def run(use_key: bool) -> None:
    script = ["down", "lost", "ok"]                # what the network does each time
    charges, seen = 0, {}
    for attempt, event in enumerate(script, start=1):
        key = "charge:order-7" if use_key else None
        if event == "down":
            print(f"  attempt {attempt}: 503, nothing done", end="")
        elif key in seen:
            print(f"  attempt {attempt}: key seen, old result returned", end="")
        else:
            charges += 1                           # the side effect happens
            if key:
                seen[key] = "receipt-1"
            lost = event == "lost"
            print(f"  attempt {attempt}: charged" + (", reply lost" if lost else ""), end="")
        if event == "ok":
            print()
            break
        print(f", sleep {full_jitter(attempt)} ms")
    print(f"  total charges: {charges}")


for use_key in (True, False):
    print("with key:" if use_key else "without key:")
    run(use_key)
with key:
  attempt 1: 503, nothing done, sleep 163 ms
  attempt 2: charged, reply lost, sleep 398 ms
  attempt 3: key seen, old result returned
  total charges: 1
without key:
  attempt 1: 503, nothing done, sleep 175 ms
  attempt 2: charged, reply lost, sleep 320 ms
  attempt 3: charged
  total charges: 2

Attempt 2 is the two generals case. The charge happened, but the reply was lost. With a key, the third attempt is safe. Without a key, the customer pays twice.

Real projects follow these rules:

  • LangGraph. Its RetryPolicy defaults are 3 attempts, a first wait of 0.5 seconds, a factor of 2, a cap of 128 seconds and jitter on. Its docs say retries give at-least-once execution of a node. They also warn: make the key from state that is already saved. A key made inside the failing node is lost with the node.
  • MCP. In revision 2026-07-28, a broken response stream loses the request. The client must send it again as a new request. So a tool that changes things should accept a key.
  • Paperclip. A checkout that returns 409 must never be retried. A 409 is not a passing network error. It is a real answer: someone else owns the task.

Retrying every error. Retry only errors that can pass: timeouts, 429 "too many requests", 5xx server errors. Do not retry 400 "bad request" or 409 "conflict". They will fail the same way again. And always set a timeout. A call with no timeout can hang a worker forever.

Durable execution: checkpoints and replay

A research run has done 40 steps in 12 minutes. Then the server restarts for a deploy. Without saved progress, all 40 steps are lost. Durable execution saves progress so the run continues where it stopped.

A checkpoint must be consistent. Think of a bank with two accounts, A and B, each with 500 dollars. A sends 100 to B. If we save A after the send and B before the money arrives, the saved total is 900. One hundred dollars have vanished from the record. The missing money is still "on the wire".

Take processes joined by reliable first-in first-out channels. One process records its state and sends a marker on every outgoing channel. When a process first gets a marker, it records its own state and sends markers on. For each incoming channel it also records the messages that arrive before that channel's marker. The recorded states and channel messages form a consistent global state: one that the system could really have been in.

Proof idea

A cut is inconsistent only if it records a message as received but not as sent. Suppose B receives a message from A before B records its state. Could A have sent it after A recorded? Then A's marker went first on that channel. The channel is first in, first out, so B would get the marker first and record before the message. That is a contradiction. So A sent the message before it recorded, and the send is inside A's snapshot too. Messages sent before the cut and received after it are exactly the recorded channel messages. Chandy and Lamport published this in 1985.

LangGraph does not run the marker algorithm. It does not need to. Its runtime uses BSP super-steps, and at the barrier no writes are in flight. So the state at a super-step boundary is consistent by design. There is one more detail. When some nodes in a step finish and another fails, LangGraph saves the finished nodes' writes as pending writes. On resume, those nodes do not run again. Pending writes play the role of the recorded channel messages. This link is our own reading of the LangGraph docs.

The docs give three durability modes:

LangGraph durability modes
ModeWhen the checkpoint is writtenRisk
"exit"Only when the run ends or pausesA crash loses the whole run
"async"In the background while the next step runsA crash can lose the latest checkpoint
"sync"Before the next step startsSlowest, but every step is safe

Run

Steps 0 to 5 finish. Each step boundary is saved under the thread id in PostgreSQL.

Partial step

In step 6, three searches run. Two finish and their writes are saved as pending writes. The third is still running.

Crash

The process dies. The third search's work is lost. Its side effects, if any, may have happened.

Resume

A new process loads the step 5 checkpoint and the two pending writes. Only the third search runs again.

Continue

The barrier merges all three results. The run goes on to step 7 as if nothing happened.

"We have checkpoints, so side effects happen once." No. A node that crashed runs again from its first line. An email sent inside it is sent again. Checkpoints protect the state in the graph. Idempotency keys protect the world outside it.

Parallel work, queues and capacity

Amdahl's law

The chapter Orchestrators and coordinators for agents used parallel subagents to cut a run from 350 to 110 seconds. Here is the law behind that.

A job has a part f that can run in parallel and a part 1 - f that must run in order. With n workers the speed-up is

S(n) = \frac{1}{(1 - f) + f / n} \le \frac{1}{1 - f}
Proof

Let one worker take time T. The serial part takes (1-f)T and cannot get faster. The parallel part takes fT and at best splits evenly, so it takes fT/n. The new time is (1-f)T + fT/n. Divide T by it. As n grows, f/n goes to 0, so S(n) never passes 1/(1-f).

Parallel agents have one more enemy. The gather step waits for the slowest worker. Say each call is slow 1% of the time. A step with 20 calls in parallel is slow with probability 1 - 0.99^{20} \approx 18\%. The chapter Cloud and system design calls this the tail at scale. Two fixes help: a deadline on the gather step, and accepting k of n results. With 4 subagents that each succeed with probability 0.97, "all 4" happens with probability 0.885. "At least 3 of 4" happens with probability 0.995.

Little's law

How many runs are inside the system at once? You need this number for memory, connections and rate limits.

In a stable system, the average number of items inside, L, equals the average arrival rate, \lambda, times the average time each item stays, W:

L = \lambda W
Proof idea

Draw the number of items inside over a long time T. The area under that curve is the total time that all items spent inside. Count the area another way: about \lambda T items came, and each stayed W on average. So the area is \lambda T W. The average height of the curve is the area divided by T, which is \lambda W. John Little proved it in full in 1961. It needs no assumption about the kind of arrivals.

Little's law gives the average. A queueing model gives the waiting. In the M/M/1 model, a server handles \mu requests per second and requests arrive at rate \lambda. The utilisation is \rho = \lambda / \mu. The mean time in the system is W = 1/(\mu - \lambda). It explodes as \rho gets close to 1.

// Little's law for the whole system, then M/M/1 for one tool server.
fn main() {
    let (lam, w) = (6.0 / 60.0, 42.0); // 6 runs per minute, 42 s per run
    println!("runs in flight L = {:.1}", lam * w);
    let tokens_per_run = 25 * 12_600; // 25 model calls, 12,600 tokens each
    let per_min = (6 * tokens_per_run).to_string();
    let with_commas: Vec<String> = per_min.as_bytes().rchunks(3).rev()
        .map(|c| String::from_utf8(c.to_vec()).unwrap()).collect();
    println!("tokens per minute = {}", with_commas.join(","));

    let mu = 10.0; // the tool server can serve 10 requests/s
    println!("arrivals/s  busy  time in system  requests inside");
    for lam in [5.0, 8.0, 9.0, 9.5] {
        let rho: f64 = lam / mu; // utilisation
        let w = 1.0 / (mu - lam); // M/M/1 mean time in system
        println!("{lam:10.1}  {:3.0}%  {:11.0} ms  {:15.1}", rho * 100.0, w * 1000.0, lam * w);
    }
}
# Little's law for the whole system, then M/M/1 for one tool server.
lam, w = 6 / 60, 42.0                  # 6 runs per minute, 42 s per run
print(f"runs in flight L = {lam * w:.1f}")
tokens_per_run = 25 * 12_600           # 25 model calls, 12,600 tokens each
print(f"tokens per minute = {6 * tokens_per_run:,}")

mu = 10.0                              # the tool server can serve 10 requests/s
print("arrivals/s  busy  time in system  requests inside")
for lam in (5.0, 8.0, 9.0, 9.5):
    rho = lam / mu                     # utilisation
    w = 1 / (mu - lam)                 # M/M/1 mean time in system
    print(f"{lam:10.1f}  {rho:4.0%}  {w * 1000:11.0f} ms  {lam * w:15.1f}")
runs in flight L = 4.2
tokens per minute = 1,890,000
arrivals/s  busy  time in system  requests inside
       5.0   50%          200 ms              1.0
       8.0   80%          500 ms              4.0
       9.0   90%         1000 ms              9.0
       9.5   95%         2000 ms             19.0

The last column checks Little's law: L = \lambda W, for example 9 \times 1.0 = 9. The rule of thumb: keep each shared server below about 70 to 80% busy. Use a queue with a size limit in front of it, and say "try later" when the queue is full. That is back-pressure.

Sizing for the average. Model APIs have limits in requests per minute and tokens per minute. Bursts hit those limits long before the average does. Size for the busy hour, and handle 429 errors with backoff and jitter.

Evaluation, tracing and guardrails

Evaluation sets and regression tests

You change a prompt. Is the agent better or worse? You need an evaluation set. Anthropic's research team wrote that they started with about 20 real questions. Early changes had big effects, so 20 were enough to see them. They used a model as a judge with a clear rubric, and people checked the edge cases.

Small sets have a limit. They see only big changes. This code shows the noise in a pass rate.

const Z: f64 = 1.96; // 95% confidence

fn half_width(p: f64, n: f64) -> f64 {
    Z * (p * (1.0 - p) / n).sqrt() // normal approximation
}

fn main() {
    println!("cases  pass rate 0.80 +/-");
    for n in [20.0, 100.0, 400.0] {
        println!("{n:5}  {:5.1} points", half_width(0.8, n) * 100.0);
    }
    let (old, new): (f64, f64) = (0.80, 0.86); // pass rates of two versions
    for n in [20.0, 400.0] {
        let se = (old * (1.0 - old) / n + new * (1.0 - new) / n).sqrt();
        let diff = new - old;
        let verdict = if diff > Z * se { "real gain" } else { "could be noise" };
        println!("n={n}: gain {:.0} points, needs > {:.1}: {verdict}", diff * 100.0, Z * se * 100.0);
    }
}
from math import sqrt

Z = 1.96                                   # 95% confidence


def half_width(p: float, n: int) -> float:  # normal approximation
    return Z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)


print("cases  pass rate 0.80 +/-")
for n in (20, 100, 400):
    print(f"{n:5}  {half_width(0.8, n) * 100:5.1f} points")

old, new = 0.80, 0.86                      # pass rates of two versions
for n in (20, 400):
    se = sqrt(old * (1 - old) / n + new * (1 - new) / n)
    diff = new - old
    verdict = "real gain" if diff > Z * se else "could be noise"
    print(f"n={n}: gain {diff * 100:.0f} points, needs > {Z * se * 100:.1f}: {verdict}")
cases  pass rate 0.80 +/-
   20   17.5 points
  100    7.8 points
  400    3.9 points
n=20: gain 6 points, needs > 23.2: could be noise
n=400: gain 6 points, needs > 5.2: real gain

A gain of 6 points means nothing with 20 cases. With 400 cases it is real. Grow the set as the system gets better. Add every bug from production as a new case. Then the set works as a regression test in CI.

Tracing

A trace records every step of one run: each model call, each tool call, the tokens and the time. A trace is made of spans. OpenTelemetry keeps semantic conventions for generative AI in their own repository. They cover spans, metrics and events for model clients and for MCP. On 2026-11-15 that repository shows no release yet, so check the names before you use them. The MCP spec also says how to pass the trace context, traceparent, in a request's _meta field. Then one trace can follow a run across agents and tool servers.

Guardrails and permission design

Guardrails are limits that hold even when the model makes a mistake. Build them in layers:

  • Least privilege. Each agent gets only the tools and scopes it needs. See Agent standards.
  • Hard limits. A step limit, a token limit per run and a money limit per agent. Paperclip warns at 80% of a budget and pauses the agent at 100%.
  • Human approval. Risky actions pause for a person. In LangGraph that is interrupt(). In Paperclip it is a board approval.
  • Checks on output. Schemas for structured output, tests for code, link checks for citations.
  • Logs. An audit trail of who did what, when and why.

Using a model as the only guardrail. A second model that "checks for danger" can be tricked by the same text. Put the hard limits in code and in permissions. Use model checks as an extra layer, never as the only one.

A worked design: a multi-agent research system

Now we put it all together. The task: answer research questions for a team of analysts, with sources. The system remembers past work, searches internal documents and keeps a graph of people, projects and decisions.

The numbers below are assumptions for the exercise, not measurements of these projects. Change them to your own measured numbers.

  1. Load. At the busy hour, 6 questions arrive per minute: \lambda = 0.1 per second.
  2. Time per run. The lead plans for 6 s. Four subagents search in parallel. Each makes 5 model calls and takes 25 s. The writer takes 8 s and the evaluator 3 s. So W = 6 + 25 + 8 + 3 = 42 s.
  3. Amdahl. In order, the run would take 6 + 4 \cdot 25 + 8 + 3 = 117 s. The parallel part is f = 100/117 \approx 0.85. The speed-up is 117/42 \approx 2.8. The limit is 1/(1-f) \approx 6.9. To go faster, shorten plan, write and check.
  4. Little. Runs in flight: L = \lambda W = 0.1 \cdot 42 = 4.2. With peaks, plan for about 10 parallel runs and 40 parallel subagents.
  5. Tokens. Each run makes 2 + 4 \cdot 5 + 2 + 1 = 25 calls of about 12,000 tokens in and 600 out. That is 1.89 million tokens per minute. Check this against the provider's rate limit.
  6. Money. With the example prices from the cost code, one run costs about 0.75 dollars without caching. If 8,000 tokens of each call are a cached prefix, it costs about 0.41 dollars. At the busy hour that is about 147 dollars per hour instead of 270.
  7. Reliability. Each subagent succeeds with 0.97. Waiting for all 4 gives 0.885. Accepting 3 of 4, with a 40-second deadline, gives 0.995 and cuts the slow tail.

The reliability rules for this design:

  • Checkpoint every step in PostgreSQL. Use "sync" durability around steps with side effects, and "async" elsewhere.
  • Retry model and tool calls on timeouts, 429 and 5xx, with full jitter, at most 3 attempts.
  • Every write tool takes an idempotency key made from saved state, for example run_id + step + item.
  • Subagents get read-only tools. Only the writer can save a report. Publishing pauses for a human.
  • A run stops at 30 steps, 500,000 tokens or 2 dollars, whichever comes first.
  • An evaluation set of 200 questions runs in CI with a batch request. A drop larger than the noise blocks the deploy.

The checklist

Cost

Count tokens per call and per run. Keep a stable prefix at the start of every prompt. Cache it. Put changing text last. Cut raw tool output before it reaches the model. Use batches for work with no waiting user.

Speed

Stream the answer. Run independent tool calls and subagents in parallel. Keep the serial parts short, because Amdahl's law limits the rest. Put a deadline on every gather step and accept k of n results.

Failures

Set a timeout on every call. Retry only passing errors, with backoff and full jitter. Give every side effect an idempotency key from saved state. Treat a missing reply as "unknown" and ask the other side.

Durability

Checkpoint at step boundaries in a real database. Choose the durability mode per step. Test a crash on purpose: kill the process in the middle of a run and resume it.

Capacity

Use Little's law to find how many runs are in flight. Keep shared servers below about 80% busy. Put a bounded queue in front and push back when it is full. Size for the busy hour and the rate limits.

Quality

Keep an evaluation set and grow it with every production bug. Report pass rates with their noise. Trace every run with spans for model and tool calls. Read real traces every week.

Safety

Least privilege for every agent. Hard limits on steps, tokens and money. Human approval for risky actions. Never give one agent private data, untrusted input and a way out at the same time. Keep an audit log.
