Practice

A client times out while charging a card. What is the safest next step?

  • Charge again with a new request id
  • Retry with the same idempotency key
  • Assume the charge failed and tell the user

The charge may have happened. The same key lets the server return the old result instead of charging twice.

Which prompt layout gets the most prompt-cache hits?

  • Current time, then system prompt, then tools, then question
  • Tools, then system prompt, then documents, then the new question
  • Question first, then everything else

The cache matches an exact prefix. Things that never change go first. The new part goes last.

A tool server handles 20 requests per second. Requests arrive at 19 per second. In the M/M/1 model, what is the mean time in the system?

  • 50 ms
  • 100 ms
  • 1 second

W = 1/(\mu - \lambda) = 1/(20 - 19) = 1 second. At 95% busy, waiting is 20 times the service time.

Little's law: 3 requests arrive per second and each stays 2 seconds. On average there are ? requests inside.

A job is 90% parallel. Amdahl's law says the speed-up can never pass ?.

Doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. Such an operation is called ?.

  1. Why can no protocol give "exactly once" delivery over a network that loses messages? What do real systems do instead?
    Answer

    By the two generals problem, the sender of the last message can never know it arrived. So real systems retry until they get a reply (at-least-once) and make the receiver idempotent with keys. The result is effectively once.

  2. A LangGraph node creates a random key with uuid4() and then calls a payment API in the same node. What can go wrong, and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    If the process dies after the charge but before the node returns, the key was never saved. The retry makes a new key and charges again. Make the key from saved state, such as the order id. Or create the key in its own node before the payment node, with sync durability.

  3. Your evaluation set has 25 questions. Version B passes 21 and version A passes 19. Should you ship B because it is better?
    Answer

    Not on this evidence. The pass rates are 0.84 and 0.76. With 25 cases the noise is about 14 to 17 points each way, so an 8-point gain could be chance. Run more cases, or check the failing cases by hand.

  4. In the worked design, the lead's planning step grows from 6 to 20 seconds. Find the new run time and the new runs in flight.
    Answer

    W = 20 + 25 + 8 + 3 = 56 seconds. L = 0.1 \times 56 = 5.6 runs in flight. The serial part is now 31 of 131 seconds when run in order, so the best possible speed-up falls to about 4.2.

  5. Design guardrails for an agent that can read the company wiki, browse the web and send email. Name at least four layers.
    Answer

    Least privilege: split it into a reader agent and a sender agent. Cut one leg of the lethal trifecta: the agent that browses the web cannot send email by itself. Human approval for every email. Hard limits on steps and tokens. Output checks on recipients against an allow list. An audit log of every tool call.

Key takeaways

  • Agent runs spend time and money on input tokens, slow output tokens, round trips and retrieval. Measure them first.
  • Keep a stable prefix and cache it. Batch offline work. Stream answers to users.
  • The two generals problem rules out exactly-once delivery. Use at-least-once retries with full jitter plus idempotency keys.
  • Durable execution saves consistent checkpoints. A BSP barrier makes the cut consistent, and pending writes save finished work.
  • Amdahl's law limits parallel speed-up. Deadlines and k of n results cut the slow tail.
  • Little's law, L = \lambda W, sizes the system. Waiting explodes as a server nears 100% busy.
  • Grow an evaluation set, trace every run, and put hard limits in code and permissions.

Sources

  • LangGraph fault tolerance. Retry policy defaults, at-least-once nodes and idempotency keys.
  • LangGraph checkpointers. Durability modes, pending writes and resume.
  • Prompt caching (Claude docs). Prefix rules, cache lifetime and price multipliers.
  • vLLM automatic prefix caching. Block hashing with parent hashes and LRU eviction.
  • Exponential backoff and jitter. Marc Brooker's comparison of jitter methods (AWS, 2015).
  • How we built our multi-agent research system. Anthropic's lessons on evaluation, checkpoints and parallel subagents.

Data science and information retrieval

Data science turns raw data into answers you can trust. Information retrieval finds the few useful documents in a huge pile. Both start with messy data and end with a number. This chapter shows how that number is made, how it can lie, and how to check it.

  • Clean and explore a small data set, and spot missing values, duplicates and outliers.
  • Explain sampling bias and run a correct A/B test with a sample size plan.
  • Build an inverted index and rank documents with TF-IDF and BM25.
  • Measure a search system with precision, recall and nDCG, and rank pages with PageRank.
  • Describe how recommender systems and big-data engines such as MapReduce work.

Cleaning and exploring data

Here is a small log from an AI service. Each row is one request. Look at it before you read the code. Can you see four problems?

id,model,latency_ms,tokens,country
1,small,120,300,US
2, Small ,130,310,us
2, Small ,130,310,us
3,large,,900,DE
4,large,98000,950,DE
5,large,450,n/a,de
6,small,115,290,US
7,large,480,920,DE

Row 2 appears twice. The name " Small " has spaces and a capital letter. Row 3 has no latency, and row 5 has the text "n/a" as a number. Row 4 took 98 seconds, maybe a timeout. This work of finding and fixing problems is data cleaning. The Python library pandas is the usual tool.

import io
import pandas as pd

raw = io.StringIO("""id,model,latency_ms,tokens,country
1,small,120,300,US
2, Small ,130,310,us
2, Small ,130,310,us
3,large,,900,DE
4,large,98000,950,DE
5,large,450,n/a,de
6,small,115,290,US
7,large,480,920,DE
""")
df = pd.read_csv(raw)
print(len(df), "rows read")
df = df.drop_duplicates()                                  # row 2 was sent twice
df["model"] = df["model"].str.strip().str.lower()          # " Small " -> "small"
df["country"] = df["country"].str.upper()
df["tokens"] = pd.to_numeric(df["tokens"], errors="coerce")  # "n/a" -> NaN
print(df.isna().sum()[lambda s: s > 0].to_dict())            # missing per column

q1, q3 = df["latency_ms"].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
fence = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)                               # Tukey's outlier fence
df["outlier"] = df["latency_ms"] > fence
print("fence:", fence, "outliers:", df.loc[df["outlier"], "id"].tolist())
print(df.groupby("model")["latency_ms"].agg(["count", "mean", "median"]).round(1))
8 rows read
{'latency_ms': 1, 'tokens': 1}
fence: 997.5 outliers: [4]
       count     mean  median
model
large      3  32976.7   480.0
small      3    121.7   120.0

Look at the last two lines. The mean latency of the large model is 33 seconds. The median is 480 milliseconds. One bad row moved the mean 68 times. An outlier pulls the mean but not the median.

The rules

  • Keep the data tidy. One row is one observation. One column is one variable. Hadley Wickham called this tidy data.
  • Count before you fix. Print the number of rows, the missing values and the types first.
  • Flag, do not delete. Add an outlier column. Then decide with the owner of the data.
  • Look at pictures. Exploratory data analysis means summaries plus plots. Anscombe's quartet (1973) has four data sets with the same mean, variance and correlation. Their plots look completely different.

Tukey's fence uses quartiles. Here Q1 is 122.5 and Q3 is 472.5. The fence is 472.5 + 1.5 \times 350 = 997.5. Only the 98-second request is above it.

Missing values also have a cause. Values can be missing at random, like a lost network packet. Or the missing part can depend on the value itself. A slow request may time out and log no latency at all. Then the missing rows are exactly the slow ones. Filling them with the mean hides your worst cases.

Filling missing numbers with 0. A missing latency is not a latency of 0 ms. It makes the service look faster. Use NaN, count the gaps, and report them. Fill a gap only with a clear rule, and write the rule down. This filling is called imputation.

Sampling and bias

In 1936 the magazine Literary Digest sent about 10 million voting cards. About 2.4 million came back. The answers said Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with about 61% of the vote. George Gallup asked only about 50,000 people and predicted the right winner. How can a huge sample lose to a small one?

The Digest took its addresses from phone books, car lists and club lists. In 1936 those people were richer than average. Also, only a quarter of them answered. A sample should look like the population. This one did not.

Random error comes from bad luck in who you picked. It shrinks when the sample grows. For a share p and a sample of n, the standard error is \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}.

Bias comes from the method. It does not shrink when the sample grows. Ten million biased answers give the wrong result with great confidence.

A number example. With p = 0.5 and n = 1{,}000, the standard error is \sqrt{0.25/1000} \approx 0.0158. The 95% margin is about 1.96 \times 0.0158 \approx 3.1 points. With n = 2.4 million the margin is about 0.06 points. But the Digest was wrong by about 18 points. Bias, not chance, made that error.

Kinds of bias

  • Selection bias: the sampling frame misses people. Example: you survey users of your app, not people who left it.
  • Non-response bias: only some people answer. Angry or very happy users answer more.
  • Survivorship bias: you only see the winners. You study successful startups and copy habits that failed startups had too.
  • Response bias: people answer wrongly, maybe because of how the question is worded.

Good ways to sample

In a simple random sample every member has the same chance. In a stratified sample you split the population into groups first. Then you sample inside each group, in proportion. For a stream of unknown length, use reservoir sampling from the advanced algorithms chapter.

Groups can also flip a result. This surprise is called Simpson's paradox. Look at two search models on easy and hard queries.

ModelEasy queriesHard queriesAll queries
A95 / 100 = 95%150 / 300 = 50%245 / 400 = 61%
B280 / 300 = 93%45 / 100 = 45%325 / 400 = 81%

Model A wins on easy queries and on hard queries. Model B wins on all queries together. Why? Model B got mostly easy queries. The mix of queries, not the model, made B look better. Compare models on the same mix.

A/B tests

Your team changes the sign-up button. With the old button, 5.0% of visitors sign up. With the new one, 5.6% sign up. That is 12% more sign-ups. Is the new button really better?

// Normal CDF by Simpson's rule: Rust's standard library has no erf.
fn normal_cdf(z: f64) -> f64 {
    let pdf = |x: f64| (-x * x / 2.0).exp() / (2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI).sqrt();
    let (n, h) = (2000, z.abs() / 2000.0);
    let mut s = pdf(0.0) + pdf(z.abs());
    for i in 1..n {
        s += pdf(i as f64 * h) * if i % 2 == 1 { 4.0 } else { 2.0 };
    }
    let area = s * h / 3.0; // area from 0 to |z|
    if z >= 0.0 { 0.5 + area } else { 0.5 - area }
}

fn ab_test(n_a: f64, conv_a: f64, n_b: f64, conv_b: f64) -> (f64, f64, f64, f64) {
    let (p_a, p_b) = (conv_a / n_a, conv_b / n_b);
    let p = (conv_a + conv_b) / (n_a + n_b); // pooled rate under H0
    let se = (p * (1.0 - p) * (1.0 / n_a + 1.0 / n_b)).sqrt(); // standard error
    let z = (p_b - p_a) / se;
    (p_a, p_b, z, 2.0 * (1.0 - normal_cdf(z.abs()))) // two-sided p-value
}

fn users_per_group(p: f64, delta: f64) -> f64 {
    (16.0 * p * (1.0 - p) / (delta * delta)).round() // alpha 0.05, power 0.8
}

fn main() {
    for n in [10_000u32, 25_000] {
        let (conv_a, conv_b) = (n * 5 / 100, n * 56 / 1000); // 5.0% and 5.6%
        let (p_a, p_b, z, pv) = ab_test(n as f64, conv_a as f64, n as f64, conv_b as f64);
        println!("n={n} A={p_a:.3} B={p_b:.3} z={z:.2} p={pv:.3}");
    }
    println!("users needed per group: {}", users_per_group(0.05, 0.006));
}
from math import sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

def ab_test(n_a, conv_a, n_b, conv_b):
    p_a, p_b = conv_a / n_a, conv_b / n_b
    p = (conv_a + conv_b) / (n_a + n_b)               # pooled rate under H0
    se = sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / n_a + 1 / n_b))      # standard error
    z = (p_b - p_a) / se
    p_value = 2 * (1 - NormalDist().cdf(abs(z)))      # two-sided
    return p_a, p_b, z, p_value

def users_per_group(p, delta):
    return round(16 * p * (1 - p) / delta ** 2)       # alpha 0.05, power 0.8

for n in (10_000, 25_000):
    conv_a, conv_b = n * 5 // 100, n * 56 // 1000     # 5.0% and 5.6%
    p_a, p_b, z, pv = ab_test(n, conv_a, n, conv_b)
    print(f"n={n} A={p_a:.3f} B={p_b:.3f} z={z:.2f} p={pv:.3f}")
print("users needed per group:", users_per_group(0.05, 0.006))
n=10000 A=0.050 B=0.056 z=1.89 p=0.058
n=25000 A=0.050 B=0.056 z=2.99 p=0.003
users needed per group: 21111

With 10,000 users per group, the p-value is 0.058. That is above 0.05, so the test cannot call a winner. With 25,000 users per group, the same rates give p = 0.003. The rule of thumb says we needed about 21,000 users per group. The first test was too small.

An A/B test (also called a controlled experiment) shows version A to one random group and version B to another. Random assignment is the key. It makes the two groups alike in every way except the change. So a difference in the result comes from the change or from chance. The null hypothesis says the change does nothing.

The p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true. The significance level \alpha (often 0.05) is the false-alarm rate you accept. Power is the chance to detect a real effect of a given size. Teams often want 80%.

For two equal groups, \alpha = 0.05 (two-sided) and 80% power, each group needs about n \approx 16\,\sigma^2 / \delta^2 users. Here \sigma^2 is the variance of the metric and \delta is the smallest change you care about. For a conversion rate p, \sigma^2 = p(1-p).

Where does 16 come from? The exact formula is n = 2\sigma^2 (z_{0.975} + z_{0.8})^2 / \delta^2. With z_{0.975} = 1.96 and z_{0.8} = 0.84, we get 2 \times 2.8^2 = 15.7 \approx 16. Our numbers: 16 \times 0.05 \times 0.95 / 0.006^2 \approx 21{,}111. Halve the effect you want to see, and you need four times as many users.

Write the hypothesis

"The new button raises sign-ups." Name one main metric before you start.

Add guardrails

Pick metrics that must not get worse, such as page speed or errors.

Plan the size

Choose the smallest useful effect. Compute users per group. Turn that into days of traffic.

Randomise by user

Hash the user id to pick A or B. The same user always sees the same version.

Run an A/A test

Show both groups the same page. About 5% of A/A tests should look "significant" at 0.05. Many more means the system is broken.

Run the full time

Run whole weeks. Weekend users behave differently from weekday users.

Check the split

You planned 50/50 but got 52/48 with large numbers? That is a sample ratio mismatch. Find the bug before you trust anything.

Analyse once and decide

Look at the main metric at the planned end. Check the guardrails. Ship, stop or test again.

You check the p-value every day and stop when it drops below 0.05. This raises the false-alarm rate far above 5%. The p-value moves up and down by chance, and you stop on a lucky dip. Fix the sample size first, or use a sequential test that is designed for repeated looks.

A p-value of 0.03 does not mean "a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true". It means: if the change did nothing, data this extreme would appear 3% of the time. Testing 20 metrics at 0.05 gives about one false winner by chance alone.

Inverted indexes and Zipf's law

Take six short documents. Number them 0 to 5.

  1. Rust gives memory safety without a garbage collector
  2. Python is easy to learn and has a garbage collector
  3. The borrow checker in Rust checks memory rules at compile time
  4. A memory leak means memory that is never freed
  5. A vector database stores embeddings for search
  6. Search engines use an inverted index to find documents fast

Which documents contain "memory"? Reading all six is fine. Reading ten billion web pages for every query is not. So a search engine turns the table around. For each word it stores the list of documents that contain it.

This structure is an inverted index. The word list is the dictionary. Each list is a postings list. The number of documents in a list is the document frequency. Here is the code that builds it.

use std::collections::{BTreeMap, HashMap};

const DOCS: [&str; 6] = [
    "Rust gives memory safety without a garbage collector",
    "Python is easy to learn and has a garbage collector",
    "The borrow checker in Rust checks memory rules at compile time",
    "A memory leak means memory that is never freed",
    "A vector database stores embeddings for search",
    "Search engines use an inverted index to find documents fast",
];

fn tokens(text: &str) -> Vec<String> {
    text.to_lowercase()
        .split(|c: char| !c.is_ascii_alphanumeric()) // split on the rest
        .filter(|w| !w.is_empty())
        .map(String::from)
        .collect()
}

struct Index { post: HashMap<String, Vec<(usize, u32)>>, len: Vec<f64>, avgdl: f64 }

fn build(docs: &[&str]) -> Index {
    let (mut post, mut len) = (HashMap::new(), Vec::new());
    for (d, text) in docs.iter().enumerate() {
        let toks = tokens(text);
        len.push(toks.len() as f64);
        let mut counts: BTreeMap<String, u32> = BTreeMap::new();
        for t in toks {
            *counts.entry(t).or_insert(0) += 1;
        }
        for (t, c) in counts {
            post.entry(t).or_insert_with(Vec::new).push((d, c)); // ids arrive in order
        }
    }
    let avgdl = len.iter().sum::<f64>() / len.len() as f64;
    Index { post, len, avgdl }
}
import math, re
from collections import defaultdict

DOCS = [
    "Rust gives memory safety without a garbage collector",
    "Python is easy to learn and has a garbage collector",
    "The borrow checker in Rust checks memory rules at compile time",
    "A memory leak means memory that is never freed",
    "A vector database stores embeddings for search",
    "Search engines use an inverted index to find documents fast",
]

def tokens(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())   # lower case, split on the rest

def build(docs):
    post, lengths = defaultdict(list), []           # term -> [(doc id, count)]
    for d, text in enumerate(docs):
        toks = tokens(text)
        lengths.append(len(toks))
        counts = defaultdict(int)
        for t in toks:
            counts[t] += 1
        for t, c in sorted(counts.items()):
            post[t].append((d, c))                   # ids arrive in order
    return post, lengths, sum(lengths) / len(lengths)

Answering a query

The query rust AND memory needs documents in both lists. The lists are sorted by document id. So two pointers walk them side by side, like the merge step of merge sort. The cost is O(m + n) for lists of length m and n. Start with the shortest list, because the result can never be longer.

Real engines store more and squeeze it hard:

  • Gaps, not ids. The ids 1000, 1004, 1009 become 1000, 4, 5. Small numbers need fewer bytes. A variable-byte code uses one byte for each gap below 128.
  • Positions. To answer the phrase "garbage collector", store where each word sits. Then check that "collector" comes right after "garbage".
  • Normalisation. Lower case, accents, and stemming. Then "checks" and "checker" can match "check".
  • Segments. Apache Lucene writes the index in small unchanging parts called segments. It merges them in the background. New documents go into new segments.

Why some lists are huge: Zipf's law

We counted every word in 29 finished chapters of this book. There are 144,291 words and 6,160 different ones. Here are the most common.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let path = std::env::args().nth(1).expect("give a text file");
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path).unwrap().to_lowercase();
    let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u64> = HashMap::new();
    for w in text.split(|c: char| !c.is_ascii_lowercase()).filter(|w| !w.is_empty()) {
        *counts.entry(w).or_insert(0) += 1; // words are runs of letters
    }
    let total: u64 = counts.values().sum();
    let mut top: Vec<(&str, u64)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
    top.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0))); // ties: a to z
    println!("{total} words, {} different", top.len());
    for (i, (w, f)) in top.iter().take(8).enumerate() {
        let r = i + 1;
        println!("{r:>3} {w:<6} f={f:<6} r*f/total={:.3}", (r as u64 * f) as f64 / total as f64);
    }
    // Fit log f = c - s log r on ranks 1..1000 with least squares.
    let pts: Vec<(f64, f64)> = top.iter().take(1000).enumerate()
        .map(|(i, (_, f))| (((i + 1) as f64).ln(), (*f as f64).ln()))
        .collect();
    let n = pts.len() as f64;
    let mx = pts.iter().map(|p| p.0).sum::<f64>() / n;
    let my = pts.iter().map(|p| p.1).sum::<f64>() / n;
    let num: f64 = pts.iter().map(|(x, y)| (x - mx) * (y - my)).sum();
    let den: f64 = pts.iter().map(|(x, _)| (x - mx).powi(2)).sum();
    println!("fitted exponent s = {:.2}", -num / den);
}
import math, re, sys
from collections import Counter

text = open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8").read().lower()
counts = Counter(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text))   # words are runs of letters
total = sum(counts.values())
top = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))  # ties: a to z
print(f"{total} words, {len(counts)} different")
for r, (w, f) in enumerate(top[:8], start=1):
    print(f"{r:>3} {w:<6} f={f:<6} r*f/total={r * f / total:.3f}")

# Fit log f = c - s log r on ranks 1..1000 with least squares.
pts = [(math.log(r), math.log(f)) for r, (_, f) in enumerate(top[:1000], 1)]
mx = sum(x for x, _ in pts) / len(pts)
my = sum(y for _, y in pts) / len(pts)
slope = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in pts) / sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x, _ in pts)
print(f"fitted exponent s = {-slope:.2f}")
144291 words, 6160 different
  1 the    f=9017   r*f/total=0.062
  2 a      f=6046   r*f/total=0.084
  3 and    f=3773   r*f/total=0.078
  4 is     f=3714   r*f/total=0.103
  5 in     f=2000   r*f/total=0.069
  6 it     f=1995   r*f/total=0.083
  7 of     f=1838   r*f/total=0.089
  8 with   f=1505   r*f/total=0.083
fitted exponent s = 0.91

Run it on any text file you like, for example python3.14 zipf.py book.txt. Our counts are from 15 November 2026. Your numbers will differ, but the shape will be the same.

Sort the words of a large text by how often they appear. Let f(r) be the count of the word with rank r. Then, roughly, f(r) \approx \frac{C}{r^{s}} with s close to 1 for many languages. So r \cdot f(r) stays roughly constant. This is an empirical law: it describes data. It is not a mathematical theorem.

Why there is no proof

There is nothing to prove from axioms. Zipf's law is a pattern in measured data. Many simple models produce it. Zipf thought speakers save effort. Herbert Simon showed that "rich get richer" growth gives the same shape. George Miller showed that even random typing, with a space key, gives a Zipf-like curve.

Piantadosi's 2014 review makes the key point. So many models fit the law that a good fit proves none of them. The law also bends at the very top and in the long tail. A common refinement is f(r) \approx C / (r + \beta)^{s}. Treat Zipf's law as a strong rule of thumb, not as an exact truth.

What does it mean for search? A few words such as "the" and "a" fill huge postings lists. They carry almost no meaning. At the other end is a long tail: 1,775 of our 6,160 words appear only once. That is 29% of the dictionary. So most postings lists are tiny, and a few are giant. Rare words are the ones that tell documents apart. TF-IDF and BM25 use exactly this fact.

Deleting all common words as "stop words". The query "to be or not to be" is made only of stop words. Modern engines usually keep all words and let the ranking formula give common words a low weight.

Ranking: TF-IDF and BM25

A query such as "rust memory" matches three documents. Which comes first? Two ideas help. A word that appears more often in a document counts more. A word that appears in fewer documents counts more too. Here are both ideas in code. Paste the blocks of one language after block 1, in order, and run them.

// Sort by score, best first. Ties go to the smaller doc id.
fn ranked(scores: BTreeMap<usize, f64>) -> Vec<(usize, f64)> {
    let mut v: Vec<(usize, f64)> = scores.into_iter().collect();
    v.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.total_cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(&b.0)));
    v
}

fn bm25(ix: &Index, query: &str, k1: f64, b: f64) -> Vec<(usize, f64)> {
    let n_docs = ix.len.len() as f64;
    let mut scores = BTreeMap::new();
    for t in tokens(query) {
        let Some(postings) = ix.post.get(&t) else { continue };
        let n = postings.len() as f64; // document frequency
        let idf = (1.0 + (n_docs - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)).ln();
        for &(d, f) in postings {
            let f = f as f64;
            let norm = k1 * (1.0 - b + b * ix.len[d] / ix.avgdl);
            *scores.entry(d).or_insert(0.0) += idf * f * (k1 + 1.0) / (f + norm);
        }
    }
    ranked(scores)
}

fn tfidf(ix: &Index, query: &str) -> Vec<(usize, f64)> {
    let n_docs = ix.len.len() as f64;
    let mut scores = BTreeMap::new();
    for t in tokens(query) {
        let Some(postings) = ix.post.get(&t) else { continue };
        let idf = (n_docs / postings.len() as f64).ln();
        for &(d, f) in postings {
            *scores.entry(d).or_insert(0.0) += (1.0 + (f as f64).ln()) * idf;
        }
    }
    ranked(scores)
}
# Sort by score, best first. Ties go to the smaller doc id.
def ranked(scores):
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))

def bm25(ix, query, k1=1.2, b=0.75):
    post, lengths, avgdl = ix
    n_docs, scores = len(lengths), defaultdict(float)
    for t in tokens(query):
        postings = post.get(t, [])
        n = len(postings)                            # document frequency
        idf = math.log(1 + (n_docs - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5))
        for d, f in postings:
            norm = k1 * (1 - b + b * lengths[d] / avgdl)
            scores[d] += idf * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + norm)
    return ranked(scores)

def tfidf(ix, query):
    post, lengths, _ = ix
    scores = defaultdict(float)
    for t in tokens(query):
        postings = post.get(t, [])
        for d, f in postings:
            scores[d] += (1 + math.log(f)) * math.log(len(lengths) / len(postings))
    return ranked(scores)
fn show(v: Vec<(usize, f64)>) -> String {
    let parts: Vec<String> = v.iter().map(|(d, s)| format!("({d}, {s:.3})")).collect();
    format!("[{}]", parts.join(", "))
}

fn main() {
    let ix = build(&DOCS);
    for t in ["memory", "rust", "garbage"] {
        println!("{t} {:?}", ix.post[t]);
    }
    println!("N={} avgdl={:.3}", DOCS.len(), ix.avgdl);
    for q in ["rust memory", "memory"] {
        println!("query: {q}\n  tf-idf: {}", show(tfidf(&ix, q)));
        println!("  bm25:   {}", show(bm25(&ix, q, 1.2, 0.75)));
    }
}
def show(pairs):
    return "[" + ", ".join(f"({d}, {s:.3f})" for d, s in pairs) + "]"

ix = build(DOCS)
for t in ["memory", "rust", "garbage"]:
    print(t, ix[0][t])
print(f"N={len(DOCS)} avgdl={ix[2]:.3f}")
for q in ["rust memory", "memory"]:
    print(f"query: {q}\n  tf-idf: {show(tfidf(ix, q))}")
    print(f"  bm25:   {show(bm25(ix, q))}")
memory [(0, 1), (2, 1), (3, 2)]
rust [(0, 1), (2, 1)]
garbage [(0, 1), (1, 1)]
N=6 avgdl=9.167
query: rust memory
  tf-idf: [(0, 1.792), (2, 1.792), (3, 1.174)]
  bm25:   [(0, 1.817), (2, 1.592), (3, 0.958)]
query: memory
  tf-idf: [(3, 1.174), (0, 0.693), (2, 0.693)]
  bm25:   [(3, 0.958), (0, 0.731), (2, 0.641)]

TF-IDF gives documents 0 and 2 the same score. Both contain each query word once. BM25 puts document 0 first. Document 0 has 8 words and document 2 has 11. The same match in a shorter text is stronger evidence.

TF-IDF

Term frequency (tf) counts a word inside one document. Inverse document frequency (idf) is \ln(N / n), where N is the number of documents and n the document frequency. The word "memory" is in 3 of 6 documents, so its idf is \ln 2 \approx 0.693. We use 1 + \ln(\text{tf}) instead of raw tf. Ten copies of a word should not count ten times as much.

BM25

For a query with terms q_1, \dots, q_m and a document D with |D| words: \text{BM25}(D) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \text{IDF}(q_i) \cdot \frac{f(q_i, D)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(q_i, D) + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|D|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)} \text{IDF}(q) = \ln\left(1 + \frac{N - n(q) + 0.5}{n(q) + 0.5}\right) Here f(q, D) is the count of q in D, N is the number of documents, n(q) is the document frequency and avgdl is the average document length. Apache Lucene and Elasticsearch use k_1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75 by default.

Where the formula comes from

BM25 comes from the probabilistic relevance framework of Robertson and his colleagues. The starting idea: rank documents by the chance that they are relevant. If you model only "word present or absent", the weight of a word becomes \ln \frac{N - n + 0.5}{n + 0.5}. That is the idf part.

Next, model word counts. A document is either "about" the word or not, and each kind has its own count pattern. This model gives a curve that grows fast and then flattens. The simple function f / (f + k_1) has the same shape, so BM25 uses it. Last, a long document has more words by chance. So BM25 scales k_1 by the document length, and b says how much.

The original idf is negative for words in more than half the documents. Lucene adds 1 inside the logarithm, so the weight stays positive. Since Lucene 8, its code also leaves out the constant factor (k_1 + 1). Every score shrinks by the same factor, so the order of results does not change.

  1. Count: N = 6, n = 3, f = 2, |D| = 9, avgdl = 55/6 \approx 9.167.
  2. IDF: \ln\left(1 + \frac{6 - 3 + 0.5}{3 + 0.5}\right) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693.
  3. Length part: 1.2 \times (0.25 + 0.75 \times 9 / 9.167) \approx 1.184.
  4. Count part: \frac{2 \times 2.2}{2 + 1.184} \approx 1.382.
  5. Score: 0.693 \times 1.382 \approx 0.958. This matches the program.

The two settings have clear jobs. k_1 controls how fast repeats stop helping. With k_1 = 0, only presence counts. A large k_1 acts more like raw counts. b controls length. With b = 0 length is ignored. With b = 1 the count is fully divided by relative length.

BM25 is the keyword half of most hybrid search today. Vector search finds meaning, and BM25 finds exact names and codes. The agent memory systems chapter uses this same formula. It fuses BM25 and vector results with reciprocal rank fusion. The vector search chapter covers the other half. A neural reranker can then reorder the top 50 or 100 results.

Comparing raw BM25 scores across queries, or adding them to cosine scores. A BM25 score of 9 is not "better" than 4 from another query. The scale depends on the words and the collection. Compare ranks, or normalise first.

Evaluating search: precision, recall and nDCG

A search system returns ten documents for a query. People have judged the documents with grades: 3 is perfect, 2 is good, 1 is fair, 0 is useless. Five documents have a grade above 0. One of them, d11, was not returned at all.

ranking: d3 d7 d1 d9 d2 d5 d8 d4 d6 d10
grades:  d1=3  d7=2  d11=2  d2=1  d4=1  (all others 0)
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn dcg(gains: &[f64], k: usize) -> f64 {
    gains.iter().take(k).enumerate()
        .map(|(i, g)| g / ((i + 2) as f64).log2()) // position i+1 gets log2(i+2)
        .sum()
}

fn main() {
    let ranking = ["d3", "d7", "d1", "d9", "d2", "d5", "d8", "d4", "d6", "d10"];
    let grade: HashMap<&str, f64> =
        [("d1", 3.0), ("d7", 2.0), ("d11", 2.0), ("d2", 1.0), ("d4", 1.0)].into();
    let g = |d: &str| *grade.get(d).unwrap_or(&0.0); // 0 for all others
    let n_rel = grade.len() as f64;

    let gains: Vec<f64> = ranking.iter().map(|d| g(d)).collect();
    let mut ideal: Vec<f64> = grade.values().copied().collect();
    ideal.sort_by(|a, b| b.total_cmp(a));

    for k in [3, 5, 10] {
        let hits = gains[..k].iter().filter(|&&x| x > 0.0).count() as f64;
        let ndcg = dcg(&gains, k) / dcg(&ideal, k);
        println!("k={k:<2} P@k={:.3} R@k={:.3} nDCG@k={ndcg:.3}", hits / k as f64, hits / n_rel);
    }
    let (mut hits, mut total) = (0.0, 0.0);
    for (i, x) in gains.iter().enumerate() {
        if *x > 0.0 {
            hits += 1.0;
            total += hits / (i + 1) as f64; // precision at each hit
        }
    }
    println!("AP={:.3}", total / n_rel); // missed items count as 0
}
import math

ranking = ["d3", "d7", "d1", "d9", "d2", "d5", "d8", "d4", "d6", "d10"]
grade = {"d1": 3, "d7": 2, "d11": 2, "d2": 1, "d4": 1}   # 0 for all others

def precision_recall(k):
    hits = sum(1 for d in ranking[:k] if grade.get(d, 0) > 0)
    return hits / k, hits / len(grade)

def average_precision():
    hits, total = 0, 0.0
    for i, d in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
        if grade.get(d, 0) > 0:
            hits += 1
            total += hits / i                  # precision at each hit
    return total / len(grade)                  # missed items count as 0

def dcg(gains, k):
    return sum(g / math.log2(i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(gains[:k], start=1))

def ndcg(k):
    gains = [grade.get(d, 0) for d in ranking]
    ideal = sorted(grade.values(), reverse=True)
    return dcg(gains, k) / dcg(ideal, k)

for k in (3, 5, 10):
    p, r = precision_recall(k)
    print(f"k={k:<2} P@k={p:.3f} R@k={r:.3f} nDCG@k={ndcg(k):.3f}")
print(f"AP={average_precision():.3f}")
k=3  P@k=0.667 R@k=0.400 nDCG@k=0.525
k=5  P@k=0.600 R@k=0.600 nDCG@k=0.518
k=10 P@k=0.400 R@k=0.800 nDCG@k=0.570
AP=0.453

We checked the nDCG numbers against sklearn.metrics.ndcg_score. It gave 0.525, 0.518 and 0.57.

  • Precision asks: of what I returned, how much is good? P@k looks only at the top k.
  • Recall asks: of all the good documents, how many did I return? R@k also looks at the top k.
  • Average precision (AP) takes the precision at each hit and averages over all relevant documents. Here: (1/2 + 2/3 + 3/5 + 4/8) / 5 \approx 0.453. The mean over many queries is MAP.

Precision and recall ignore order inside the top k and ignore grades. Users read from the top, and a perfect document matters more than a fair one. nDCG handles both.

With grade g_i at position i: \text{DCG@}k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{g_i}{\log_2(i + 1)}, \qquad \text{nDCG@}k = \frac{\text{DCG@}k}{\text{IDCG@}k} IDCG is the DCG of the best possible order. So nDCG lies between 0 and 1 (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002). Some systems use the gain 2^{g_i} - 1 instead of g_i. It rewards top grades more. Always say which gain you use.

By hand for k = 3: the top three grades are 0, 2, 3. DCG = 0 + 2/\log_2 3 + 3/\log_2 4 = 1.262 + 1.5 = 2.762. The best order is 3, 2, 2, so IDCG = 3 + 1.262 + 1 = 5.262. nDCG@3 = 2.762 / 5.262 \approx 0.525.

Two more measures are common. MRR uses only the first good result: 1 at rank 1, 0.5 at rank 2. It suits question answering. Recall@k is the main measure for the first stage of a RAG system. A document that is not retrieved can never reach the model.

Offline tests use judged documents, as in the TREC conferences. Judges cannot read millions of documents. So TREC judges only a pool: the top results from many systems. Online tests use real users. They use A/B tests or interleaving, which mixes two rankings in one list and counts clicks. Clicks are noisy and biased towards the top position.

Reporting recall without saying how you found "all" relevant documents. In a big collection you never know them all. Your recall is recall against your judgements. Also, compute IDCG from all known relevant documents, including ones the system missed, like d11.

PageRank: ranking by links

Text scores say a page is about your words. They do not say if the page is trusted. In 1998 Sergey Brin and Larry Page used the links between pages for that. A link is a vote. A vote from an important page counts more.

Imagine a random surfer. With chance \alpha = 0.85 the surfer clicks a random link on the page. Otherwise the surfer jumps to a random page. PageRank is the share of time the surfer spends on each page in the long run. For n pages:

\text{PR}(v) = \frac{1 - \alpha}{n} + \alpha \sum_{u \to v} \frac{\text{PR}(u)}{\text{out}(u)}

Start with every page at 1/4 = 0.25. One round for page C: 0.0375 + 0.85 \times (0.25/2 + 0.25/1 + 0.25/1) = 0.569. Page D has no incoming links. It only gets the jump share, 0.15 / 4 = 0.0375. After many rounds C has 0.394 and A has 0.373. A has only one incoming link. But that link comes from C, the strongest page.

Why do the rounds settle on one answer? The jump term makes every entry of the Google matrix positive. The Perron-Frobenius theorem then gives one stationary vector. The context graphs chapter proves this and gives tested code. Same α, same formula.

  • Dangling pages have no outgoing links. Their score would leak away. The usual fix: spread their score evenly over all pages.
  • Personalised PageRank always jumps back to a chosen set of pages. It ranks pages near those pages. Graph RAG systems use it to rank nodes near the question.
  • One signal among many. A real search engine mixes link scores, text scores, freshness and much more. Link farms try to fake votes, so engines also fight spam.

Dropping the jump term "to be exact". Without it, a page with no way out traps the surfer. Two separate groups of pages give more than one answer. The jump is what makes PageRank well defined.

Recommender systems

Five learners rate five courses from 1 to 5. A 0 means "not rated yet". Eva has not rated the Go course or the ML course. Which one should we suggest to her?

        rust  go  ml  stats  sql
ana       5    4   0    1     2
ben       4    5   1    0     1
cai       1    0   5    4     4
dev       0    1   4    5     5
eva       5    0   0    2     1
const ITEMS: [&str; 5] = ["rust", "go", "ml", "stats", "sql"];
const R: [(&str, [f64; 5]); 5] = [ // 0 means "not rated yet"
    ("ana", [5.0, 4.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]),
    ("ben", [4.0, 5.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0]),
    ("cai", [1.0, 0.0, 5.0, 4.0, 4.0]),
    ("dev", [0.0, 1.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0]),
    ("eva", [5.0, 0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0]),
];

fn sim(i: usize, j: usize) -> f64 { // cosine over users who rated both items
    let pairs: Vec<(f64, f64)> = R.iter()
        .filter(|(_, r)| r[i] > 0.0 && r[j] > 0.0)
        .map(|(_, r)| (r[i], r[j]))
        .collect();
    if pairs.is_empty() { return 0.0; }
    let dot: f64 = pairs.iter().map(|(a, b)| a * b).sum();
    let na = pairs.iter().map(|(a, _)| a * a).sum::<f64>().sqrt();
    let nb = pairs.iter().map(|(_, b)| b * b).sum::<f64>().sqrt();
    dot / (na * nb)
}

fn predict(user: usize, i: usize) -> f64 { // weighted mean of the user's own ratings
    let r = &R[user].1;
    let rated = (0..ITEMS.len()).filter(|&j| r[j] > 0.0);
    let num: f64 = rated.clone().map(|j| sim(i, j) * r[j]).sum();
    let den: f64 = rated.map(|j| sim(i, j)).sum();
    num / den
}

fn main() {
    println!("sim(rust, go) = {:.3}  sim(rust, ml) = {:.3}", sim(0, 1), sim(0, 2));
    for i in [1, 2] {
        println!("{}, {}: {:.2}", R[4].0, ITEMS[i], predict(4, i));
    }
}
from math import sqrt

items = ["rust", "go", "ml", "stats", "sql"]
R = {                      # 0 means "not rated yet"
    "ana": [5, 4, 0, 1, 2],
    "ben": [4, 5, 1, 0, 1],
    "cai": [1, 0, 5, 4, 4],
    "dev": [0, 1, 4, 5, 5],
    "eva": [5, 0, 0, 2, 1],
}

def sim(i, j):             # cosine over users who rated both items
    pairs = [(r[i], r[j]) for r in R.values() if r[i] and r[j]]
    dot = sum(a * b for a, b in pairs)
    na = sqrt(sum(a * a for a, _ in pairs))
    nb = sqrt(sum(b * b for _, b in pairs))
    return dot / (na * nb) if pairs else 0.0

def predict(user, i):      # weighted mean of the user's own ratings
    r = R[user]
    num = sum(sim(i, j) * r[j] for j in range(len(items)) if r[j])
    den = sum(sim(i, j) for j in range(len(items)) if r[j])
    return num / den

print("sim(rust, go) =", f"{sim(0, 1):.3f}", " sim(rust, ml) =", f"{sim(0, 2):.3f}")
for i in (1, 2):
    print(f"eva, {items[i]}: {predict('eva', i):.2f}")
sim(rust, go) = 0.976  sim(rust, ml) = 0.428
eva, go: 3.27
eva, ml: 2.13

People who liked Rust also liked Go. Eva gave Rust a 5. So the model predicts 3.27 for Go and only 2.13 for ML. We suggest Go. This is item-based collaborative filtering. Collaborative filtering means we use other people's ratings, not the course descriptions.

For user u and an unrated item i: \hat{r}_{ui} = \dfrac{\sum_{j} \text{sim}(i, j)\, r_{uj}}{\sum_{j} \lvert \text{sim}(i, j) \rvert}, where j runs over the items that u has rated. Amazon described item-to-item filtering in 2003. Item similarities change slowly, so they can be computed offline.

Matrix factorisation

The rating table is mostly empty. Matrix factorisation gives each user a short vector p_u and each item a short vector q_i, maybe 50 numbers each. The guess is their dot product plus some biases:

\hat{r}_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i + p_u^{\top} q_i

Here \mu is the global mean, and b_u and b_i say that some users and items are above average. Training minimises the squared error on known ratings plus a penalty \lambda(\lVert p_u \rVert^2 + \lVert q_i \rVert^2). The penalty stops overfitting. Koren, Bell and Volinsky described this method in 2009. That year their team, BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos, won the Netflix Prize. Its error was 10.06% lower than that of Netflix's own system.

Modern systems work in stages. A two-tower model turns users and items into vectors. A vector index finds a few hundred candidates in milliseconds. Then a heavier model ranks them. This is the same shape as search: retrieve, then rerank.

Raw cosine on ratings. All ratings are positive, so all items look similar. Rust and ML still get 0.428, although their fans disagree. Subtract each user's mean rating first.

Cold start. A new item has no ratings, so collaborative filtering cannot see it. Use content features until ratings arrive.

Random test splits. Split by time instead. Otherwise you train on the future to predict the past.

Big-data processing models

Count the words in a petabyte of web pages. One machine would take months. In 2004 Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat of Google described MapReduce. You write two small functions. The system runs them on thousands of machines and handles failures.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn mapper(text: &str) -> Vec<(&str, u32)> { // map: emit (word, 1) pairs
    text.split_whitespace().map(|w| (w, 1)).collect()
}

fn partition(key: &str, r: usize) -> usize { // same key -> same reducer
    key.bytes().map(|b| b as usize).sum::<usize>() % r
}

fn main() {
    let splits = ["the cat sat", "the dog sat down", "a cat ran"]; // one per mapper
    let r = 2; // number of reducers
    // Shuffle: every pair goes to its reducer, grouped by key.
    let mut groups: Vec<BTreeMap<&str, Vec<u32>>> = vec![BTreeMap::new(); r];
    for s in splits {
        for (k, v) in mapper(s) {
            groups[partition(k, r)].entry(k).or_default().push(v);
        }
    }
    for (i, g) in groups.iter().enumerate() { // reduce: add the values of each key
        let out: Vec<String> = g.iter()
            .map(|(k, vs)| format!("'{k}': {}", vs.iter().sum::<u32>()))
            .collect();
        println!("reducer {i}: {{{}}}", out.join(", "));
    }
}
from collections import defaultdict

splits = ["the cat sat", "the dog sat down", "a cat ran"]   # one per mapper
R = 2                                                       # number of reducers

def mapper(text):                    # map: emit (word, 1) pairs
    return [(w, 1) for w in text.split()]

def partition(key):                  # same key -> same reducer, every time
    return sum(key.encode()) % R

# Shuffle: every pair goes to its reducer, grouped by key.
groups = [defaultdict(list) for _ in range(R)]
for s in splits:
    for k, v in mapper(s):
        groups[partition(k)][k].append(v)

for r in range(R):                   # reduce: add the values of each key
    print(f"reducer {r}:", {k: sum(vs) for k, vs in sorted(groups[r].items())})
reducer 0: {'cat': 2, 'dog': 1, 'down': 1, 'sat': 2}
reducer 1: {'a': 1, 'ran': 1, 'the': 2}

There are three phases. Map turns each input split into key and value pairs. Shuffle sends every pair with the same key to the same reducer. Reduce combines the values of each key. The shuffle is the expensive part, because the data crosses the network. A combiner adds counts on each mapper first, so less data moves. If a machine dies, the system simply runs its task again. That only works because map and reduce have no side effects.

All values of one key go to one reducer. By Zipf's law, a few keys hold a large share of all values. In our book corpus, "the" alone is 6% of all words. The job finishes only when the slowest reducer finishes. Combiners, salting a hot key into several keys, or special handling for the top keys fix this.

After MapReduce

  1. 2004 MapReduce. Batch jobs on disk. Every step writes its result to files.
  2. 2012 Spark and RDDs. Data stays in memory between steps. A lost part is rebuilt from its lineage, the recipe of steps that made it.
  3. 2015 The Dataflow model. One model for batch and streams. It separates event time from processing time and uses windows and watermarks. Apache Beam implements it.
  4. Today Columns and lakehouses. Columnar files such as Parquet, table formats on object storage, and fast single-machine engines such as DuckDB and Polars.

A stream never ends, so "count per hour" needs a window. Events also arrive late. A phone may send a click from the train an hour later. A watermark says "I think all events up to 10:00 are here". Then the 9:00 to 10:00 window can close. The distributed systems chapter explains MapReduce and dataflow from the systems side. The modern data systems chapter covers Kafka and lakehouses.

Try one machine first. A laptop can scan many gigabytes of Parquet in seconds with DuckDB or Polars. Move to a cluster when one machine is really too small. A cluster adds network costs, failures and harder debugging.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for data science and information retrieval
PatternPurposeModelNote
Count, then clean, then flagClean a data set safely8 rows, 1 duplicate, 1 outlier flaggedNever fill missing values with 0.
Median and quartilesSummarise skewed datamean 32,977 ms, median 480 msOne outlier can wreck the mean.
Random beats bigSample without biasGallup 50,000 beat Digest 2.4 millionBias does not shrink with n.
Compare on the same mixAvoid Simpson's paradoxA wins each group, B wins overallCheck the groups before you trust a total.
n \approx 16\sigma^2/\delta^2 per groupPlan an A/B test5.0% vs 5.6% needs 21,111 per groupDo not peek and stop early.
Term to sorted postingsFind documents fastmemory: 0, 2, 3Store gaps, intersect from the shortest list.
r \cdot f(r) \approx constantExpect skew in text"the" is 6% of all wordsAn empirical law, not a theorem.
idf times saturated tfRank with BM25k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75Scores are not comparable across queries.
P@k, R@k, nDCG@kMeasure rankingnDCG@3 = 0.525IDCG includes the missed documents.
