Practice

A survey of 3 million app users finds 90% are happy. Why might this be wrong?

  • 3 million is too small a sample
  • Unhappy people may have left the app or not answered
  • The standard error is too large

This is selection and non-response bias. A big sample has a tiny standard error, but bias does not shrink.

Your A/B test shows p = 0.04 after 3 days. You planned 14 days. What should you do?

  • Stop now and ship B
  • Keep running to the planned end, then analyse
  • Restart the test with a new p-value

Stopping on an early dip is peeking. It raises the false-alarm rate well above 5%.

In BM25, what happens to the count part when k_1 = 0?

  • Long documents win
  • Only presence counts: one copy scores the same as ten
  • The score becomes negative

With k_1 = 0 the part becomes f / f = 1 for any f \gt 0.

The term "memory" is in 3 of 6 documents. Its BM25 idf is \ln(1 + 3.5/3.5) = \ln ?.

A list of 8 results has 2 relevant documents. Precision@8 is ?.

With α = 0.85 and 4 pages, a page with no incoming links has PageRank ?.

  1. A metric has standard deviation 2.0. You want to detect a change of 0.1. How many users per group do you need?
    Answer

    16 \times 2.0^2 / 0.1^2 = 16 \times 4 / 0.01 = 6{,}400 users per group. To detect 0.05 instead, you need four times as many: 25,600.

  2. Intersect the postings lists 2, 5, 9, 14, 30 and 5, 6, 14, 15, 40 step by step. How many comparisons do you need?
    Answer

    Compare 2 and 5: move the first pointer. 5 and 5: match, keep 5. 9 and 6: move the second. 9 and 14: move the first. 14 and 14: match, keep 14. 30 and 15: move the second. 30 and 40: move the first, list ended. Result: 5 and 14, after 7 comparisons. The work is at most m + n steps.

  3. Compute nDCG@3 for the grades 3, 0, 2 (in result order), when the known relevant grades are 3, 2, 1.
    Answer

    DCG = 3/1 + 0 + 2/\log_2 4 = 3 + 1 = 4. IDCG = 3 + 2/\log_2 3 + 1/2 = 3 + 1.262 + 0.5 = 4.762. nDCG@3 = 4 / 4.762 \approx 0.84.

  4. The original BM25 idf is \ln \frac{N - n + 0.5}{n + 0.5}. Compute it for N = 6, n = 4. What is wrong, and how does Lucene fix it?
    Answer

    \ln(2.5 / 4.5) = \ln 0.556 \approx -0.588. A negative weight means a matching word lowers the score. Lucene uses \ln(1 + 0.556) \approx 0.442, which is always positive.

  5. A word-count MapReduce job has 100 reducers. 99 finish in 1 minute, and one takes 40 minutes. What is the likely cause, and what are two fixes?
    Answer

    A hot key such as "the" sends a large share of the pairs to one reducer, as Zipf's law predicts. Fixes: a combiner adds counts on the mappers first. Salting splits the hot key into keys like "the#1" to "the#10", then a second small step adds those up.

  6. Expert: design the evaluation of a RAG search stage for a company wiki. Which metrics, which data, and which traps?
    Answer

    Build a set of real questions with judged passages, graded 0 to 3. Measure Recall@k (for example k = 20) for the retriever, because a missed passage can never reach the model. Measure nDCG@10 or MRR for the order after reranking. Split questions by time and team so the test is not easier than real use. Pool results from several retrievers (BM25, vectors, hybrid) before judging, so recall is fair to all. Then confirm with an online A/B test on answer quality or user success. Traps: judging only one system's results, leaking test questions into tuning, and reading tiny differences without a significance test.

Key takeaways

  • Clean data by counting first, fixing with written rules, and flagging outliers. Use the median for skewed data.
  • Random error shrinks with sample size. Bias does not. Simpson's paradox can reverse a result when groups mix.
  • An A/B test needs random assignment by user, a sample size plan (about 16\sigma^2/\delta^2 per group) and no peeking.
  • An inverted index maps each term to a sorted postings list. Intersection walks two lists in linear time.
  • Zipf's law is an empirical law: a few words are very common, most are rare. It explains stop words, idf and skew.
  • BM25 multiplies idf by a saturating, length-normalised term count. Defaults are k_1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75.
  • Precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG each answer a different question. Say which one, at which k, with which gain.
  • PageRank is a random surfer with jumps. Recommenders use similar items or learned vectors. MapReduce and its successors split work into map, shuffle and reduce.

Sources

  • Apache Lucene: BM25Similarity. The default k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75 and the idf formula with the added 1.
  • Elasticsearch: similarity module. BM25 as the default similarity and what k1 and b control.
  • UC Berkeley Data 100: Sampling. Kinds of bias and the 1936 Literary Digest poll.
  • Zhou, Lu and Shallah (2023): All about sample-size calculations for A/B testing. The 16σ²/δ² rule for α = 0.05 and 80% power.
  • Piantadosi (2014): Zipf's word frequency law in natural language. A critical review of the evidence and the models.
  • Dean and Ghemawat (2004): MapReduce. The original paper from OSDI 2004.

Software engineering

Programming is making code work today. Software engineering is keeping it working for years, with a team, while everything changes. This chapter covers the habits that make that possible: clear requirements, good design, tests, review, automation, honest estimates and good use of AI coding tools.

  • Write requirements that a test can check, and split code into modules with low coupling and high cohesion.
  • Explain SOLID in simple words, compare architecture styles, and use Conway's law.
  • Design tests with equivalence classes, boundary values and properties, at the right level.
  • Run a short-lived branch flow with code review, CI and CD, and read the DORA metrics.
  • Estimate with ranges, explain Brooks's law, manage technical debt, and use AI coding tools with care.

Requirements

A manager says: "Make search faster." Is that a requirement? Look at two versions.

Search must be fast and user-friendly.

When a user submits a search, the system shall show the first 20 results within 300 ms for 95% of requests.

Nobody can test "fast". Everybody can test "300 ms for 95% of requests". A requirement is useful only when you can check it. So write it with a trigger, a system and a measurable response.

  • A functional requirement says what the system does: "The system shall email a receipt after payment."
  • A quality requirement says how well it works: speed, security, reliability. People also call these non-functional requirements. The ISO/IEC 25010:2023 model lists nine quality characteristics. Examples are performance efficiency, reliability, security and maintainability.

Shapes that help

The EARS style (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) gives fixed sentence shapes. They are also good English patterns.

  • Always: "The API shall return JSON."
  • Event: "When a payment fails, the system shall retry once after 2 seconds."
  • State: "While the user is offline, the app shall queue new messages."
  • Unwanted case: "If the token has expired, then the API shall return status 401."

Agile teams often write a user story: "As a learner, I want to search my notes, so that I can find old answers." Each story needs acceptance criteria. The Given, When, Then form works well:

Given I have 3 notes that contain "BM25"
When I search for "bm25"
Then I see those 3 notes, newest first
And the search takes less than 300 ms

You cannot build everything at once. MoSCoW sorts requirements into Must, Should, Could and Won't (this time). The "Won't" list is important. It tells everyone what is out of scope.

Putting a solution into a requirement. "Use Redis to cache searches" is a design choice, not a need. The need is "95% of searches finish within 300 ms". Maybe a better index solves it without any cache. Keep the "what" in the requirement and the "how" in the design.

Design principles: coupling, cohesion and SOLID

A service must send a welcome email to a new user. Look at how the business rule below knows nothing about databases or email servers. It only knows two small interfaces.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// Two small interfaces. The business rule depends only on these.
trait UserStore { fn email(&self, id: u32) -> Option<String>; }
trait Mailer { fn send(&mut self, to: &str, body: &str); }

fn send_welcome(store: &dyn UserStore, mailer: &mut dyn Mailer, id: u32) -> Result<(), String> {
    let email = store.email(id).ok_or(format!("no user {id}"))?;
    mailer.send(&email, "Welcome to the course!");
    Ok(())
}

// Fakes for tests. A real app would plug in PostgreSQL and SMTP here.
struct MemStore(HashMap<u32, String>);
impl UserStore for MemStore {
    fn email(&self, id: u32) -> Option<String> { self.0.get(&id).cloned() }
}
struct FakeMailer { sent: Vec<(String, String)> }
impl Mailer for FakeMailer {
    fn send(&mut self, to: &str, body: &str) { self.sent.push((to.into(), body.into())); }
}

fn main() {
    let store = MemStore(HashMap::from([(7, "ana@example.com".to_string())]));
    let mut mailer = FakeMailer { sent: vec![] };
    println!("{:?}", send_welcome(&store, &mut mailer, 7));
    println!("{:?}", send_welcome(&store, &mut mailer, 8));
    println!("sent: {:?}", mailer.sent);
}
from typing import Protocol

# Two small interfaces. The business rule depends only on these.
class UserStore(Protocol):
    def email(self, user_id: int) -> str | None: ...

class Mailer(Protocol):
    def send(self, to: str, body: str) -> None: ...

def send_welcome(store: UserStore, mailer: Mailer, user_id: int) -> None:
    email = store.email(user_id)
    if email is None:
        raise LookupError(f"no user {user_id}")
    mailer.send(email, "Welcome to the course!")

# Fakes for tests. A real app would plug in PostgreSQL and SMTP here.
class MemStore:
    def __init__(self, rows): self.rows = rows
    def email(self, user_id): return self.rows.get(user_id)

class FakeMailer:
    def __init__(self): self.sent = []
    def send(self, to, body): self.sent.append((to, body))

store, mailer = MemStore({7: "ana@example.com"}), FakeMailer()
send_welcome(store, mailer, 7)
try:
    send_welcome(store, mailer, 8)
except LookupError as e:
    print("error:", e)
print("sent:", mailer.sent)
Ok(())
Err("no user 8")
sent: [("ana@example.com", "Welcome to the course!")]
error: no user 8
sent: [('ana@example.com', 'Welcome to the course!')]

The test needs no database and no network. We can swap PostgreSQL for another store, and send_welcome does not change. Two ideas explain why this design is good.

  • Coupling is how much one module depends on another. Low coupling is good. A change in one place then stays in one place.
  • Cohesion is how well the parts of one module belong together. High cohesion is good. A module about billing should not also resize images.

Larry Constantine and his colleagues named these ideas in 1974. David Parnas added information hiding in 1972. Each module hides one decision that may change, such as the database or a file format.

SOLID in simple words

Robert C. Martin collected five design principles. Their first letters spell SOLID.

Single responsibility

A module should have one reason to change. Example: a report class should not also send emails. The finance team and the email team would both edit it.

Open and closed

Add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing old code. Example: a new payment type is a new struct that implements the Payment trait. The old code stays the same.

Liskov substitution

A subtype must work everywhere its parent type works. Example: a read-only list that throws an error on add breaks code that expects a normal list. Barbara Liskov described this rule.

Interface segregation

Prefer several small interfaces to one big one. Example: UserStore and Mailer above, not one giant Services interface.

Dependency inversion

Business rules depend on abstractions, and details plug into them. Example: send_welcome depends on the Mailer trait, not on an SMTP library.

An interface for everything. If a type has one implementation and no test needs a fake, an interface only adds a file to read. Add the abstraction when a second need appears. Removing a wrong abstraction later costs more than adding a right one.

Architecture styles and Conway's law

Three teams build a shop. One team does the web pages, one does payments, one does stock. A year later the software has three big parts: a web app, a payment service and a stock service. The borders between the parts are the borders between the teams. This is not an accident.

An organisation that designs a system will produce a design whose structure copies the organisation's communication structure (Melvin Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, 1968). Fred Brooks later gave it the name Conway's law.

Why it holds (Conway's argument)

A system is made of parts, and the parts meet at interfaces. To agree on an interface, the people who build the two parts must talk. So every interface in the system needs a line of communication in the organisation. Conway described this as a structure-preserving map from the system's graph to the organisation's graph.

If two groups rarely talk, a clean, rich interface between their parts is unlikely. If one group builds everything, its parts can be tightly mixed. This is an observation about people, not a mathematical proof. Empirical studies of open-source and company code found support for it, but it is a tendency, not a rule of nature.

The law also works backwards. Do you want two independent services? Then give them two teams with a clear contract between them. People call this the inverse Conway manoeuvre. Change the team map first, and the system map follows.

Common styles

StyleThe ideaGood forCost
LayeredUI, then business logic, then data. Each layer calls only the one below.Simple business appsChanges often cut through every layer.
Modular monolithOne program and one deployment, with strict module borders inside.Most new products and small teamsBorders need discipline, because nothing enforces them at run time.
MicroservicesMany small services, each with its own data, talking over the network.Many teams that must deploy on their ownNetwork failures, distributed data, hard debugging.
Event-drivenParts publish events such as "order paid". Others react.Loose coupling, many consumersThe flow is hard to follow. Events can arrive twice or late.
Hexagonal (ports and adapters)Business core in the middle. Databases and APIs plug in through interfaces.Testable core logicMore interfaces and files.
Pipes and filtersEach step reads input, transforms it and passes it on.Compilers, data pipelines, Unix toolsHard when steps need shared state.

The send_welcome example above is hexagonal in small: the core uses ports (traits), and the adapters are the store and the mailer. The compilers chapter is pipes and filters. The distributed systems chapter explains what the network does to microservices.

Microservices for a team of four. Every function call becomes a network call that can fail. Every join becomes a distributed query. Conway's law says one team tends to build one system. Start with a modular monolith, and split a module out when a separate team really needs it.

Testing: levels and test design

A cinema sells tickets. Children from 0 to 11 pay 5 euros. Adults from 12 to 64 pay 10. Seniors from 65 to 130 pay 6. Other ages are errors. Which ages should a test try? Not all of them. Pick a few that find the most bugs.

/// Ticket price in euros. Children 0-11 pay 5, adults 12-64 pay 10, seniors 65-130 pay 6.
pub fn price(age: i32) -> Result<u32, String> {
    match age {
        0..=11 => Ok(5),
        12..=64 => Ok(10),
        65..=130 => Ok(6),
        _ => Err(format!("invalid age {age}")),
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::price;

    #[test]
    fn boundaries() {
        // One value on each side of every edge between classes.
        let cases = [(0, 5), (11, 5), (12, 10), (64, 10), (65, 6), (130, 6)];
        for (age, want) in cases {
            assert_eq!(price(age), Ok(want), "age {age}");
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn invalid_ages() {
        for age in [-1, 131, i32::MIN, i32::MAX] {
            assert!(price(age).is_err(), "age {age}");
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn property_never_above_adult_price() {
        // A property: for every valid age, the price is at most 10.
        for age in 0..=130 {
            assert!(price(age).unwrap() <= 10);
        }
    }
}
import pytest
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

def price(age: int) -> int:
    """Children 0-11 pay 5, adults 12-64 pay 10, seniors 65-130 pay 6."""
    if 0 <= age <= 11:
        return 5
    if 12 <= age <= 64:
        return 10
    if 65 <= age <= 130:
        return 6
    raise ValueError(f"invalid age {age}")

# One value on each side of every edge between classes.
@pytest.mark.parametrize("age, want", [(0, 5), (11, 5), (12, 10), (64, 10), (65, 6), (130, 6)])
def test_boundaries(age, want):
    assert price(age) == want

@pytest.mark.parametrize("age", [-1, 131, -10**9, 10**9])
def test_invalid_ages(age):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        price(age)

# A property: for every valid age, the price is at most 10.
@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=130))
def test_never_above_adult_price(age):
    assert price(age) <= 10
running 3 tests
test tests::boundaries ... ok
test tests::property_never_above_adult_price ... ok
test tests::invalid_ages ... ok

test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s
...........                                                              [100%]
11 passed in 0.39s

We ran Python with pytest 9.2 and Hypothesis 6.170. Rust runs tests in parallel, so the order of the lines can change.

Test design techniques

  • Equivalence partitioning: the ages fall into five classes: too low, child, adult, senior, too high. One value from each class is enough to start.
  • Boundary value analysis: bugs live at the edges. Test 11 and 12, 64 and 65, 130 and 131, -1 and 0.
  • Decision tables: when several conditions combine, list every combination in a table. One row becomes one test.
  • Property-based testing: state a rule that is always true, and let a tool generate inputs. Hypothesis does this in Python. The proptest crate does it in Rust.

How good are our tests? Change the code on purpose and see if a test fails. We changed 0..=11 to 0..=10 and 12..=64 to 11..=64. The boundary test caught it:

test tests::boundaries ... FAILED
assertion `left == right` failed: age 11
  left: Ok(10)
 right: Ok(5)

This is mutation testing. Tools such as cargo-mutants and mutmut do it automatically. A change that no test notices shows a weak spot.

Test levels

  • A unit test checks one function alone, like price. It runs in milliseconds.
  • An integration test checks parts together, such as your code with a real PostgreSQL in a container.
  • An end-to-end test drives the whole system like a user, maybe through a browser.
  • An acceptance test checks the Given, When, Then criteria from the requirements.

In test-driven development (TDD) you write a failing test first. Then you write the simplest code that passes. Then you clean up. People call this loop red, green, refactor.

Trusting coverage numbers. 100% line coverage means every line ran, not that every line was checked. A test with no assertion covers code and proves nothing. Use coverage to find untested code, and mutation testing to judge the tests. Also fix flaky tests at once. A team that learns to ignore red builds will miss a real failure.

Version control and code review

Here is one small change, from start to finish, in a trunk-based team.

git switch main && git pull                 # start from the newest main
git switch -c fix/ticket-age-boundary       # a branch for one small change
# ... edit code and tests ...
git add -p                                  # stage only the parts you mean
git commit -m "fix: charge adult price from age 12"
git push -u origin fix/ticket-age-boundary  # then open a pull request
# after review and green CI: merge, delete the branch, deploy

The branch lives for hours or a day, not weeks. Small branches merge without pain. A team can work in a few common ways.

  • Trunk-based development: everyone merges into main at least daily. Unfinished features hide behind feature flags.
  • GitHub flow: a short branch per change, a pull request, review, merge, deploy.
  • Git flow: long-lived develop and release branches. Its author, Vincent Driessen, added a note in 2020. For web apps with continuous delivery, he now suggests a simpler flow such as GitHub flow. Git flow can still fit software with several versions in use.

A good commit message has a short subject line and a body that says why. The Conventional Commits style adds a type: feat:, fix:, docs:, refactor:. Tools can then build change logs from the history.

Code review

In a code review, another engineer reads the change before it merges. Google's public review guide gives one main standard. Approve a change once it clearly improves the overall health of the code, even if it is not perfect. Look for these things, in this order:

  1. Design. Does the change belong here? Is it the right size?
  2. Correctness. Edge cases, errors, concurrency, security.
  3. Tests. Do they fail when the code is wrong?
  4. Clarity. Names, comments that explain why, no dead code.
  5. Style. Let the formatter and the linter handle it, not people.

Ana: Could you look at my pull request for the ticket price? It is about 40 lines.

Ben: Sure. One question on line 12: what happens at age 131?

Ana: Good catch. It returns an error. I will add a test for it.

Ben: Thanks. Nit: maybe call it price_eur. Not blocking. Approved after the test.

Review comments are about the code, not the person. Ask questions. Mark small style points as "nit" so the author knows they are optional. Keep changes small. A 40-line change gets a careful review. A 2,000-line change gets a quick "looks good".

Long-lived branches. After three weeks apart, two branches have changed the same files. The merge is large and risky, and the review is useless because nobody can read it all. Merge small changes often instead.

CI and CD

Every push to the repository starts a pipeline like this one. It is a GitHub Actions workflow for a repository with Rust and Python code.

name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7          # get the code
      - name: Format and lint (Rust)
        run: |
          cargo fmt --check
          cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
      - name: Unit and integration tests (Rust)
        run: cargo test --all-targets
      - name: Tests (Python)
        run: |
          python3 -m venv .venv
          .venv/bin/pip install pytest hypothesis
          .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q

We checked that this file is valid YAML. We did not run it, because it runs on GitHub's servers. Check the latest major version of actions/checkout before you copy it. It was v7 in November 2026.

  • Continuous integration (CI): everyone merges into main often, and every merge is built and tested by a machine. A red build is fixed first.
  • Continuous delivery: every green build is ready to release. A person presses the button.
  • Continuous deployment: every green build goes to production with no button at all.

Safe releases use small steps. A canary release sends the new version to 1% of users first. If error rates stay normal, it goes to 10%, then 100%. A feature flag lets you turn off a broken feature in seconds, without a new deploy.

Measuring delivery: the DORA metrics

The DORA research program measures software delivery with five metrics in two groups.

GroupMetricQuestion
ThroughputChange lead timeHow long from commit to running in production?
ThroughputDeployment frequencyHow often do we deploy?
ThroughputFailed deployment recovery timeHow fast do we recover from a bad deploy?
InstabilityChange fail rateWhat share of deploys need a rollback or hotfix?
InstabilityDeployment rework rateWhat share of deploys are unplanned fixes for incidents?

DORA's research finds that speed and stability go together. The best teams deploy often and break things rarely. Small changes are the reason. A small change is easy to test, easy to review and easy to roll back.

Turning a metric into a target for individuals. If people are judged by deployment frequency, they will split one change into ten deploys. Use the metrics to find bottlenecks in the system, not to rank people.

Estimation and Brooks's law

Your team must build a feature with five tasks. For each task you give three numbers of days: the best case, the most likely case and the worst case. The most likely values add up to 18 days. Is "18 days" a good answer to give your manager? Let a simulation decide.

// (name, optimistic, likely, pessimistic) in days
const TASKS: [(&str, f64, f64, f64); 5] = [("design", 2.0, 3.0, 6.0), ("backend", 4.0, 6.0, 12.0),
    ("frontend", 3.0, 5.0, 10.0), ("tests", 2.0, 3.0, 5.0), ("deploy", 1.0, 1.0, 4.0)];

fn splitmix64(state: &mut u64) -> u64 { // small, repeatable random numbers
    *state = state.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
    let mut z = *state;
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
    (z ^ (z >> 31)) >> 11 // keep 53 random bits
}

fn triangular(u: f64, a: f64, m: f64, b: f64) -> f64 { // inverse CDF of a triangle
    if u < (m - a) / (b - a) {
        a + (u * (b - a) * (m - a)).sqrt()
    } else {
        b - ((1.0 - u) * (b - a) * (b - m)).sqrt()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let likely: f64 = TASKS.iter().map(|t| t.2).sum();
    let (mut state, mut totals) = (42u64, Vec::new());
    for _ in 0..10_000 {
        let mut total = 0.0;
        for &(_, a, m, b) in &TASKS {
            let bits = splitmix64(&mut state);
            total += triangular(bits as f64 / 2f64.powi(53), a, m, b);
        }
        totals.push(total);
    }
    totals.sort_by(f64::total_cmp);
    let mean = totals.iter().sum::<f64>() / totals.len() as f64;
    let within = totals.iter().filter(|&&t| t <= likely).count() as f64 / 100.0;
    println!("sum of likely values: {likely} days");
    println!("simulated mean:       {mean:.1} days");
    println!("simulated P50: {:.1}  P85: {:.1}  P95: {:.1}", totals[5000], totals[8500], totals[9500]);
    println!("chance to finish in {likely} days: {within:.1}%");
}
import math

TASKS = [("design", 2, 3, 6), ("backend", 4, 6, 12), ("frontend", 3, 5, 10),
         ("tests", 2, 3, 5), ("deploy", 1, 1, 4)]     # optimistic, likely, pessimistic
M = 2**64 - 1

def splitmix64(state):                                # small, repeatable random numbers
    state = (state + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M
    z = state
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M
    return state, (z ^ (z >> 31)) >> 11              # keep 53 random bits

def triangular(u, a, m, b):                           # inverse CDF of a triangle
    if u < (m - a) / (b - a):
        return a + math.sqrt(u * (b - a) * (m - a))
    return b - math.sqrt((1 - u) * (b - a) * (b - m))

likely = sum(m for _, _, m, _ in TASKS)
state, totals = 42, []
for _ in range(10_000):
    total = 0.0
    for _, a, m, b in TASKS:
        state, bits = splitmix64(state)
        total += triangular(bits / 2**53, a, m, b)
    totals.append(total)
totals.sort()
print(f"sum of likely values: {likely} days")
print(f"simulated mean:       {sum(totals) / len(totals):.1f} days")
print(f"simulated P50: {totals[5000]:.1f}  P85: {totals[8500]:.1f}  P95: {totals[9500]:.1f}")
print(f"chance to finish in {likely} days: {sum(t <= likely for t in totals) / 100:.1f}%")
sum of likely values: 18 days
simulated mean:       22.3 days
simulated P50: 22.2  P85: 25.1  P95: 26.7
chance to finish in 18 days: 3.6%

"18 days" has a 3.6% chance. Why? Each task can be late by much more than it can be early. The backend can take 2 days less than likely, or 6 days more. When you add five skewed tasks, the delays add up. A better answer: "about 22 days, and 25 days if you need 85% confidence."

Rules for estimates

  • Give ranges, not points. Say "P50 22 days, P85 25 days".
  • Break the work down into tasks of a few days. Big tasks hide big surprises.
  • Use history. How long did similar work take last time? This is reference class forecasting.
  • Expect early estimates to be wide. In Steve McConnell's cone of uncertainty, estimates at the idea stage can be 4 times too high or 4 times too low. The range narrows as you learn.
  • Re-estimate when you learn something new. An estimate is not a promise.

The classic three-point formula from PERT is E = (a + 4m + b) / 6, with best case a, most likely m and worst case b. For the backend: (4 + 24 + 12)/6 \approx 6.7 days. It is above the most likely 6 days for the same reason: the long tail.

Adding people to a late project

The project is late. Can we add four more engineers? Fred Brooks studied this at IBM and wrote The Mythical Man-Month (1975).

Adding people to a late software project makes it later. Three costs cause this. New people need training from the people who know the system. Not all work can be split into parallel parts. And the number of communication paths in a team of n people is \binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}, which grows with the square of the team size.

Why it holds (an argument, not a proof)

Count the pairs. Each pair of people may need to talk, so n people have n(n-1)/2 paths. 5 people have 10 paths. 9 people have 36. The useful work grows at most linearly with n, but the talking grows like n^2. So at some team size, more people means less output per day.

Next, the work that cannot be split. Like the serial part in Amdahl's law, it sets a limit on speed-up. Nine people cannot make one design decision nine times faster. Last, training: the experts slow down while they teach. Brooks himself later called the law an "outrageous oversimplification". It is a strong warning, not an exact rule. Adding people early, to work that splits well, can help.

Treating an estimate as a promise, then "fixing" the date by adding people. Better options are to cut scope (move features to "Won't"), to move the date, or to remove blockers for the people you already have.

Technical debt and documentation

A developer must ship a tax feature by Friday. She writes the tax rate, 0.10, in five different files. It works. Later the rate changes to 0.08 in one country only. Now every change means a search through five files and a risk of missing one. The quick shortcut keeps costing time.

Ward Cunningham called this technical debt in 1992. A shortcut is like a loan. You get speed now. You pay interest later, as extra time on every change near the shortcut. Paying back the loan means refactoring: here, one function tax_rate(country) used everywhere.

Deliberate and prudent. "We must ship now. We will clean this up next sprint." This can be a good business choice.

Deliberate and reckless. "We have no time for design." This debt grows fast.

Inadvertent and prudent. "Now we know how we should have built it." Learning creates this debt. It is normal.

Inadvertent and reckless. "What is layering?" The team lacks the skills.

This grid is Martin Fowler's technical debt quadrant. Not all debt is bad. Debt you do not know about, and debt you never pay, is bad.

  • Make it visible. Keep debt items in the issue tracker with the interest you pay: "every tax change takes 2 extra hours".
  • Pay where you work. Clean up the code you are already changing. Leave it a bit better than you found it.
  • Pay the expensive debt first. Debt in code that never changes costs almost nothing.

Documentation

Good documentation answers the question the reader has right now. The Diátaxis framework by Daniele Procida names four kinds:

KindThe reader wants toExample
Tutoriallearn by doing"Build your first search index in 15 minutes"
How-to guidefinish a real task"How to rotate the API key"
Referencelook up a factThe list of every config option
Explanationunderstand why"Why we use BM25 and vectors together"

For design choices, many teams write an architecture decision record (ADR). Michael Nygard proposed this short format in 2011. One decision goes in one file. You never edit an old ADR. You write a new one that replaces it.

# 7. Start as a modular monolith

Status: accepted (2026-11-15)

Context: 4 engineers, one product, frequent changes across modules.
Decision: one deployable service with strict module borders.
          Modules talk only through public interfaces.
Consequences: simple deploys and debugging. We must check borders in
              review. We may split "payments" out when a second team forms.

Comments that repeat the code: i += 1 # add one to i. The code already says what. A good comment says why: # the API counts pages from 1, not 0. Keep docs next to the code in the same repository, and review them in the same pull request.

Working with AI coding tools

A developer types into a coding agent: "Make the client better." The agent edits 14 files, adds a new library and rewrites the tests. Some changes are good. The developer cannot tell which. Now compare a better request.

Make the client better.

In src/http/client.rs, add retries for status 503 only: at most 3 tries, exponential backoff with jitter, starting at 200 ms. Do not add new crates. First write a failing test that uses the fake server in tests/support. Then run cargo test and cargo clippy, and show me the diff.

The strong request names the file, the exact behaviour, the limits and a check. It looks like a good requirement. That is no accident. An AI coding tool is a fast new colleague who has not read your project. Every skill in this chapter helps you guide it.

What the research says, honestly

Studies disagree, because they measure different tasks, people and tools. Here are careful results with their limits.

StudySettingResult
Peng and others, 2023 (GitHub, Microsoft, MIT)95 developers, one new task: write an HTTP server in JavaScript, 2022 CopilotThe Copilot group needed 55.8% less time. The confidence interval was wide (21% to 89%).
METR, July 202516 experienced developers, 246 real issues in their own large open-source projects, early-2025 toolsWith AI they took 19% longer. They expected a 24% speed-up and afterwards believed they had been 20% faster.
METR, February 2026 update57 developers, more than 800 tasks, late-2025 toolsThe new estimates have wide confidence intervals that include zero. METR calls the data unreliable, because many developers refused to work without AI. It believes AI speeds developers up more than in early 2025, but calls its own evidence for this very weak.
DORA report, 2025Survey of nearly 5,000 technology professionals90% use AI at work. More than 80% believe it made them more productive. 30% have little or no trust in AI-generated code. AI use was linked to higher throughput but also to more delivery instability.
Perry and others, CCS 2023User study on security tasksPeople with an AI assistant wrote less secure code, and were more confident that it was secure.
Spracklen and others, USENIX Security 2025576,000 code samples from 16 modelsCode often imported packages that do not exist: at least 5.2% on average for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models.

Three lessons follow. First, people's feeling of speed is not a measurement. Measure your own team with the DORA metrics or a careful trial. Second, the effect depends on the task. A new small program is not the same as a large, old codebase. Third, AI can make quality and security worse unless your checks are strong.

Attackers can register a package name that models often invent. Then a developer who installs it runs the attacker's code. People call this slopsquatting. Before you add a dependency, check that it exists, who maintains it and how many people use it. The systems and software security chapter covers supply-chain attacks.

A workflow that works

Give context

Write the build commands, test commands, style rules and "never do" rules in a file the tool reads, such as AGENTS.md. The agent standards chapter describes this format.

Ask for a plan first

Let the tool read the code and propose a plan. Fix the plan before any code is written. A wrong plan is cheap to change.

Small steps

One small change per request. A 40-line diff can be reviewed. A 2,000-line diff cannot.

Give it a check

Tests, a type checker, a linter. The tool should run them and show the result. Without a check, "done" only means "the model stopped".

Review every diff

Read it as you would read a pull request from a new colleague. You own the commit, not the tool.

Verify facts

Check that packages, functions and flags really exist in the version you use.

Limit permissions

Run agents in a sandbox or container. Give them no production secrets. Ask before commands that delete, deploy or send.

# Notes for coding agents

Build: cargo build
Test: cargo test && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q
Lint: cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings

Rules:
- Keep changes small. One topic per pull request.
- Write or update a test for every behaviour change.
- Do not add dependencies without asking.
- Never read or print files in secrets/ or any .env file.
- Database migrations go in migrations/ and need human review.

If each step of a long task succeeds with probability p, a chain of n unchecked steps succeeds with probability p^n. With p = 0.95 and n = 20, that is only 0.95^{20} \approx 0.36. A test after each step catches most errors while they are small and cheap to fix. So split agent work into small steps, and check each one.

Give an agent only the files, commands and network access its task needs. A prompt injection hidden in a web page or an issue can then do little harm. Ask a person to confirm actions that cannot be undone.

Letting the tool grade its own homework. An agent can write code with a bug, then write tests that expect the bug. The tests pass, and everything looks green. Write or review the tests yourself, especially for boundaries and error cases. And never merge code you cannot explain.

A common question is "How do you use AI tools at work?" A strong answer names a workflow (context, plan, small steps, tests, review), one limit you watch for (such as invented packages), and how you measure the result.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for software engineering
PatternPurposeModelNote
When [trigger], the [system] shall [response]Write a testable requirementWhen a payment fails, the system shall retry once after 2 seconds.Use a number, not "fast".
Given, When, ThenWrite acceptance criteriaGiven 3 notes, when I search "bm25", then I see 3 results.One behaviour per scenario.
Depend on a small interfaceLower coupling, easy testssend_welcome(store, mailer, id)No interface for a type with one use and no fake.
