Real ray tracers add more rays. A shadow ray checks if anything blocks the light. Mirrors send a new reflected ray. Turner Whitted described this recursive method in 1980. Path tracing follows many random bounces and averages them. It solves Kajiya's rendering equation of 1986, and it gives soft shadows and indirect light. Films use it. To find the nearest hit fast, scenes use a BVH, a tree of boxes. A ray then tests about \log n boxes, not all n objects.

Rasterisation and ray tracing side by side
QuestionRasterisationRay tracing
Outer loopOver trianglesOver pixels (rays)
Hidden surfacesDepth bufferNearest hit along the ray
Shadows, reflectionsTricks such as shadow mapsNatural: just send more rays
SpeedVery fast on every GPUCostly. Needs a BVH, hardware help and denoising
Typical useGames, user interfaces, mapsFilms, product images, and more and more in games

Modern games mix both. They rasterise the main image and trace rays for shadows and reflections. GPUs have had ray tracing hardware since 2018, starting with NVIDIA's RTX cards. A newer idea, 3D Gaussian splatting (2023), rasterises millions of soft blobs learned from photos. It renders captured real places in real time.

Testing pixel corners instead of pixel centres, or drawing shared edges twice. Two triangles that share an edge then leave gaps or overlap. GPUs follow a strict fill rule, such as the "top-left rule", so each pixel on a shared edge belongs to exactly one triangle.

Qubits, gates, superposition and entanglement

A normal bit is 0 or 1. A qubit is described by two numbers called amplitudes: \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle, with |\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1. When you measure it, you get 0 with chance |\alpha|^2 and 1 with chance |\beta|^2. After that, the qubit is just that result.

Example: \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|1\rangle gives 0 or 1 with chance 1/2 each. A state with both amplitudes non-zero is a superposition. So far it looks like a coin flip. The difference: amplitudes can be negative, or even complex. Positive and negative amplitudes can cancel. This is interference, and every quantum algorithm uses it.

Gates change the amplitudes. Each gate is a unitary matrix, so every gate can be undone.

X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad H = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}.

X is NOT. Z flips the sign of |1\rangle. The Hadamard gate H turns |0\rangle into (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt2. Apply H twice and you are back at |0\rangle. The two paths to |1\rangle cancel. That is interference in one line.

With n qubits there are 2^n amplitudes, one for every bit string. A normal computer needs memory for all of them. 50 qubits need 2^{50} complex numbers. At 16 bytes each, that is 16 PiB. This is why we think quantum computers can do some things that normal computers cannot.

The CNOT gate acts on two qubits. It flips the second qubit when the first is 1. Together with H it makes entanglement.

  1. Start with both qubits at 0: |00\rangle.
  2. Apply H to the first qubit: (|00\rangle + |10\rangle)/\sqrt2.
  3. Apply CNOT. It flips the second qubit only in the part where the first is 1: (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt2.
  4. Measure. You get 00 or 11, each with chance 1/2. Never 01 or 10.
  5. Try to write it as (state of q0) times (state of q1). You cannot. That is what "entangled" means.

In simple words: the two qubits have one shared state, not two separate ones. Measuring one tells you the other. But each person alone sees a fair random bit. So entanglement cannot send a message faster than light.

Can we copy a qubit to make a backup? No.

No quantum operation copies every unknown state. There is no unitary U with U\,|\psi\rangle|0\rangle = |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle for all states |\psi\rangle.

Proof

Say U copies |0\rangle and |1\rangle: U|0\rangle|0\rangle = |00\rangle and U|1\rangle|0\rangle = |11\rangle. Take |\psi\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt2. U is linear, so U|\psi\rangle|0\rangle = (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt2. A true copy would be |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle = (|00\rangle + |01\rangle + |10\rangle + |11\rangle)/2. These are different. So U fails on |\psi\rangle. Wootters and Zurek, and Dieks, proved this in 1982.

This has two big effects. First, quantum error correction cannot just keep copies, as the repetition code in Information and coding theory does. It spreads one logical qubit over many physical qubits and measures only parity checks. Second, an eavesdropper cannot copy qubits in quantum key distribution without leaving traces.

"A quantum computer tries all answers at once and picks the right one." Measurement gives one random result, not the best one. The art is to arrange interference so that wrong answers cancel and right answers grow. Only some problems have such a structure.

Quantum algorithms: Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover and Shor

Quantum algorithms are often compared by queries. A function f is hidden in a box, called an oracle. How many times must we ask it? A quantum oracle flips the sign of the amplitude of |x\rangle when f(x) = 1.

Deutsch-Jozsa (1992). We are promised that f on n bits is either constant or balanced. A sure classical answer may need 2^{n-1} + 1 queries. The quantum algorithm needs one. Apply H to all qubits, query once, apply H again, and measure. The amplitude of |0\dots0\rangle is the average of (-1)^{f(x)}. It is \pm 1 if f is constant and 0 if f is balanced.

Grover (1996). One item among N is marked, and nothing else is known. A classical search checks about N/2 items on average. Grover repeats two reflections. The oracle flips the sign of the marked item. The diffusion step reflects every amplitude about the mean. Each round moves amplitude to the marked item.

// A tiny state-vector simulator: Deutsch-Jozsa and Grover on 3 qubits.
const N_QUBITS: usize = 3;
const N: usize = 1 << N_QUBITS; // 8 basis states |000> .. |111>

fn hadamard_all(s: &mut [f64]) {
    let r = 1.0 / 2f64.sqrt();
    for q in 0..N_QUBITS {
        for i in 0..N {
            if i & (1 << q) == 0 { // pair state i with the state where qubit q is 1
                let (a, b) = (s[i], s[i | 1 << q]);
                (s[i], s[i | 1 << q]) = (r * (a + b), r * (a - b));
            }
        }
    }
}

fn deutsch_jozsa(f: impl Fn(usize) -> u8) -> f64 {
    let mut s = vec![0.0; N];
    s[0] = 1.0; // start in |000>
    hadamard_all(&mut s);
    for x in 0..N { if f(x) == 1 { s[x] = -s[x]; } } // the oracle flips signs: one call
    hadamard_all(&mut s);
    s[0] * s[0] // chance to measure |000>
}

fn main() {
    println!("constant f: P(000) = {:.3}", deutsch_jozsa(|_| 1));
    println!("balanced f: P(000) = {:.3}", deutsch_jozsa(|x| (x.count_ones() % 2) as u8));
    let marked = 5; // Grover looks for x = 5 = |101>
    let mut s = vec![1.0 / (N as f64).sqrt(); N]; // equal superposition
    for k in 0..=4 {
        println!("after {k} Grover steps: P(marked) = {:.3}", s[marked] * s[marked]);
        s[marked] = -s[marked]; // oracle: flip the sign of the answer
        let mean = s.iter().sum::<f64>() / N as f64;
        for a in s.iter_mut() { *a = 2.0 * mean - *a; } // diffusion: reflect about the mean
    }
}
# A tiny state-vector simulator: Deutsch-Jozsa and Grover on 3 qubits.
from math import sqrt

N_QUBITS = 3
N = 1 << N_QUBITS  # 8 basis states |000> .. |111>


def hadamard_all(s: list[float]) -> None:
    r = 1 / sqrt(2)
    for q in range(N_QUBITS):
        for i in range(N):
            if i & (1 << q) == 0:  # pair state i with the state where qubit q is 1
                j = i | 1 << q
                s[i], s[j] = r * (s[i] + s[j]), r * (s[i] - s[j])


def deutsch_jozsa(f) -> float:
    s = [0.0] * N
    s[0] = 1.0  # start in |000>
    hadamard_all(s)
    s = [-a if f(x) == 1 else a for x, a in enumerate(s)]  # the oracle flips signs: one call
    hadamard_all(s)
    return s[0] ** 2  # chance to measure |000>


print(f"constant f: P(000) = {deutsch_jozsa(lambda x: 1):.3f}")
print(f"balanced f: P(000) = {deutsch_jozsa(lambda x: bin(x).count('1') % 2):.3f}")
marked = 5  # Grover looks for x = 5 = |101>
s = [1 / sqrt(N)] * N  # equal superposition
for k in range(5):
    print(f"after {k} Grover steps: P(marked) = {s[marked] ** 2:.3f}")
    s[marked] = -s[marked]  # oracle: flip the sign of the answer
    mean = sum(s) / N
    s = [2 * mean - a for a in s]  # diffusion: reflect about the mean
constant f: P(000) = 1.000
balanced f: P(000) = 0.000
after 0 Grover steps: P(marked) = 0.125
after 1 Grover steps: P(marked) = 0.781
after 2 Grover steps: P(marked) = 0.945
after 3 Grover steps: P(marked) = 0.330
after 4 Grover steps: P(marked) = 0.012

Look at step 3. The chance falls again. Grover is a rotation, and too many rounds turn past the answer.

With one marked item among N, Grover's algorithm finds it with high probability after about \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N} oracle queries. No quantum algorithm can do it with fewer than order \sqrt{N} queries (Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani, 1997).

Proof idea

The state stays in a flat plane spanned by two vectors: the marked item, and the even mix of all the others. The start state makes a small angle \theta with the "others" axis, where \sin\theta = 1/\sqrt{N}. Two reflections make one rotation by 2\theta. After k rounds the angle is (2k+1)\theta, and the chance of success is \sin^2((2k+1)\theta). It reaches about 1 when (2k+1)\theta \approx \pi/2, so k \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N}. The lower bound shows each query can move the state only a little.

For N = 8, \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{8} \approx 2.2, so 2 rounds. The code gave 94.5%. For a million items, about 785 rounds instead of about 500,000 checks. That is a square-root speed-up, not an exponential one. It also halves the bits of security of symmetric keys, which is why long-term systems choose AES-256. See Cryptography.

Shor (1994). Factoring N reduces to finding a period. Pick a and find the smallest r with a^r \equiv 1 \pmod N. The quantum part finds r with the quantum Fourier transform. A normal computer does the rest.

  1. Powers of 7 modulo 15: 7, 4, 13, 1. So the period is r = 4. (A quantum computer finds this step.)
  2. r is even, so compute 7^{r/2} = 7^2 = 49.
  3. \gcd(49 - 1, 15) = \gcd(48, 15) = 3.
  4. \gcd(49 + 1, 15) = \gcd(50, 15) = 5.
  5. 15 = 3 \times 5. If r is odd, or a^{r/2} \equiv -1, pick another a.

Shor needs a number of steps that grows only like a polynomial in the number of digits. The best known classical methods are much slower for large numbers. The same idea breaks discrete logarithms and elliptic curves. So a large quantum computer would break RSA, Diffie-Hellman and today's elliptic-curve cryptography. In complexity terms, factoring is in BQP. Most researchers do not believe that NP-complete problems are in BQP. See Complexity theory.

"Deutsch-Jozsa shows an exponential speed-up in practice." Only against sure, deterministic classical answers. A random classical test of 21 inputs is wrong with chance below one in a million. The algorithm is a teaching example. Grover and Shor are the ones with real targets.

Where quantum computing really is today (November 2026)

News about quantum computers is loud. Read it like an engineer. Ask three questions. Is it peer-reviewed, a preprint, or a company announcement? Is it about physical qubits or logical qubits? Does it solve a useful problem, or a task made to be hard for classical computers?

The key idea is the error-correction threshold. Physical qubits make an error every few hundred to few thousand operations. Useful algorithms need billions of operations. A code such as the surface code makes one logical qubit from many physical ones. If the hardware is good enough, a bigger code gives fewer errors. If not, a bigger code makes things worse.

The state of the field, as of 15 November 2026 (check the links: this changes fast)
WhoWhat they reportedKind of claim

Microsoft disagrees.Vendor claim (Microsoft, 2 June 2026), contested (University of St Andrews, 24 June 2026)

So where are we? Error correction works on small codes. Logical qubits are starting to beat physical ones. Several companies name 2029 for the first fault-tolerant machines, but those are targets, not results. Advantage has been claimed for narrow tasks. Classical methods later caught up with some earlier claims, such as Google's claim from 2019. No machine today runs Shor on a number that matters. Experiments have factored only tiny numbers such as 15 and 21, and they used shortcuts that rely on knowing the answer.

  1. 1982 No-cloning. Wootters and Zurek, and Dieks. Feynman suggests quantum simulation.
  2. 1992 Deutsch-Jozsa. The first clear query separation.
  3. 1994 Shor. Factoring and discrete logarithms in polynomial time.
  4. 1996 Grover. Search in about \sqrt{N} queries.
  5. 2001 15 = 3 × 5. A tiny Shor run on a nuclear magnetic resonance machine.
  6. 2019 Advantage claim. Google's Sycamore on random circuits. Classical methods later caught up.
  7. 2024 Below threshold. Google's Willow: bigger codes give fewer errors.
  8. 2025 Many claims. Topological qubits (contested), large atom arrays, Helios logical qubits.
  9. 2026 Advantage debate. IBM's verifiable advantage preprints and magic state cultivation.
  10. 2029 Targets. IBM and Microsoft name 2029 for fault-tolerant machines. Not yet results.

What should an engineer do now? Plan the move to post-quantum cryptography, because data recorded today may be decrypted later. NIST published the ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA standards in 2024. You can learn quantum programming with simulators and cloud machines. But do not expect a quantum speed-up for normal business software soon.

Comparing qubit counts across companies. 1,000 noisy physical qubits may do less than 50 good ones. Ask for logical qubits, logical error rates, and the number of operations a machine can run before it fails.

Typical questions: compute a Fitts ID, order two matrix products, decide if a pixel is inside a triangle, write the Bell state, give Grover's number of rounds, and do Shor's classical step for a small N. Keep \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N} and \gcd(a^{r/2} \pm 1, N) in memory.

Practice

A web form shows no message after "Submit", so users click many times. Which heuristic does it break first?

  • Aesthetic and minimalist design
  • Visibility of system status
  • Help and documentation

The user cannot see that the system is working. Show progress and a clear result.

Which change makes a target easier to hit, by Fitts's law?

  • Move it twice as far and make it half as wide
  • Keep the distance and make it twice as wide
  • Change its colour to red

ID depends on D/W. A wider target gives a smaller ratio and a smaller ID.

A vertex shader computes T R \mathbf{p}. What happens first to the point?

  • It is translated by T.
  • It is rotated by R.
  • Both at the same time.

Matrices act from right to left. R touches the point first.

You measure the first qubit of (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt2 and get 1. What will the second qubit show?

  • 0 or 1 with chance 1/2 each
  • 1 for sure
  • 0 for sure

Only 00 and 11 have non-zero amplitudes. After the first result is 1, only 11 is left.

A target is 300 px away and 20 px wide. Its index of difficulty is \log_2 of ?, which is 4 bits.

WCAG 2.2 level AA asks for a contrast of at least ? for normal text.

Grover on N = 10{,}000 items needs about ? rounds.

  1. Compute H H |0\rangle step by step and explain why the result is |0\rangle.
    Answer

    H|0\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt2. Apply H to each part. H|0\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt2 and H|1\rangle = (|0\rangle - |1\rangle)/\sqrt2. Add them and divide by \sqrt2: \tfrac12(|0\rangle + |1\rangle + |0\rangle - |1\rangle) = |0\rangle. The two paths to |1\rangle cancel. That is interference.

  2. Do Shor's classical step for N = 21 with a = 2.
    Answer

    Powers of 2 mod 21: 2, 4, 8, 16, 11, 1. So r = 6, which is even. 2^3 = 8. \gcd(7, 21) = 7 and \gcd(9, 21) = 3. So 21 = 3 \times 7.

  3. For the triangle a = (0, 0), b = (4, 0), c = (0, 4), compute the three edge functions at p = (1, 1) and at q = (3, 3). Which point is inside?
    Answer

    At p: E_{ab} = 4 \cdot 1 - 0 = 4. E_{bc} = (-4)(1 - 0) - (4)(1 - 4) = -4 + 12 = 8. E_{ca} = (0)(1 - 4) - (-4)(1 - 0) = 4. All positive, so p is inside. At q: E_{ab} = 12, E_{bc} = -12 - 4 \cdot (-1) = -8, E_{ca} = 12. The signs differ, so q is outside. It is beyond the long edge from b to c.

  4. A deterministic classical algorithm must decide Deutsch-Jozsa for n = 3 for sure. How many queries does it need in the worst case, and why?
    Answer

    2^{n-1} + 1 = 5. After 4 equal answers, the function could still be constant or balanced (the other 4 inputs might all differ). The fifth answer decides it. The quantum algorithm needs 1 query.

  5. Plan a usability test for a new "invite a teammate" flow. Give the tasks, the measures, the number of users and one ethical rule.
    Answer

    One possible plan: 5 users who match the real audience. Task 1: "Invite Bo as an editor." Task 2: "Change Bo to a viewer." Use think-aloud. Measure success, time on task, wrong clicks and a SUS score at the end. Fix the problems, then test 5 more users. Ethics: get informed consent, say what you record, and let people stop at any time.

  6. A startup says: "Our chip has 1,200 qubits, so it will break RSA next year." What questions do you ask, and what does the public evidence say?
    Answer

    Ask: are these physical or logical qubits? What are the two-qubit error rates? How many operations can it run before failing? Is the result peer-reviewed? The best public estimate (Gidney, 2025) needs close to a million physical qubits at 0.1% error running for days, with full error correction. No public machine is near that. The claim is not believable as stated. Still, plan the move to post-quantum cryptography now.

Name three of Nielsen's heuristics.

For example: visibility of system status, error prevention, recognition rather than recall.

State Fitts's law.

MT = a + b \log_2(D/W + 1). Far and small targets take longer.

Why do graphics use 4x4 matrices for 3D points?

With homogeneous coordinates (x, y, z, 1), translation and projection also become matrix products.

Rasterisation or ray tracing: which loops over pixels?

Ray tracing. Rasterisation loops over triangles.

What does the no-cloning theorem say?

No quantum operation can copy an unknown quantum state.

How fast is Grover, and is that optimal?

About \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N} queries, and order \sqrt{N} is optimal.

Key takeaways

  • Usability is measured with real users: tasks, success, time, errors and satisfaction. Heuristics find problems cheaply.
  • Fitts's law: pointing time grows with \log_2(D/W + 1). Make frequent targets big and close.
  • WCAG 2.2 AA is the usual bar: 4.5:1 contrast, full keyboard use, labels, alt text, and 24 by 24 px targets.
  • The pipeline transforms vertices with matrices, rasterises triangles with edge functions, and shades fragments.
  • Ray tracing follows rays per pixel. It gives shadows and reflections naturally, at a higher cost.
  • Qubits hold amplitudes. Interference and entanglement are the tools. Unknown states cannot be copied.
  • Grover gives a square-root speed-up. Shor breaks RSA and elliptic curves once large fault-tolerant machines exist.
  • In November 2026, error correction works on small scales, advantage claims are debated, and 2029 is a vendor target.

Sources

  • 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design. Nielsen Norman Group: the ten heuristics, first published 1994, wording refined in 2020.
  • Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2. W3C Recommendation, edition of 12 December 2024: contrast, target size and the luminance formula.
  • Fitts' Law. I. Scott MacKenzie: Fitts's 1954 form, the Shannon form, throughput and ISO 9241-411.
  • WebGPU is now supported in major browsers. web.dev, November 2025: browser versions and platforms.
  • Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold. Google Quantum AI in Nature: the Willow below-threshold result.
  • IBM's verifiable quantum advantage claims. IEEE Spectrum, July 2026: the three preprints and what outside experts said.

Research methods and the thesis

Research turns a question into checked evidence and a clear claim. A Master's thesis is your first full research project. This chapter shows the whole path: read papers fast, find a good question, test it fairly, report the numbers honestly, and plan the months of work.

  • Read a research paper in three passes and decide quickly if it matters to you.
  • Find related work, and turn a vague topic into a question and a testable hypothesis.
  • Design an experiment with strong baselines, and report results with intervals and fair tests.
  • Write a paper or thesis with a clear structure, and answer reviews well.
  • Name 30 classic papers, follow the rules of ethics and reproducibility, and plan a thesis week by week.

What research is

Start with an example. Your team runs a search system for an AI assistant. Someone says, "A reranker will make answers better." Is that true? By how much? On which questions? Research is the work that answers those questions with evidence.

A research question says what you want to know. A hypothesis is a precise guess you can test. Evidence comes from experiments, proofs or careful observation. A contribution is what your work adds to the field.

Computer science has several kinds of research. Each kind gives evidence in its own way.

Kinds of research in computer science
KindEvidenceExample question
TheoryA proofIs there a faster algorithm for this problem?
SystemsA built system and measurementsDoes this cache design cut tail latency?
Empirical or machine learningExperiments on datasetsDoes this model beat the baseline on held-out data?
Human-centredUser studies, interviewsDo developers find bugs faster with this tool?
MeasurementData from real systemsHow many websites still use TLS 1.2?

"I built a cool tool, so I did research." A tool alone is engineering. It becomes research when you ask a question, test the tool fairly against something else, and show what we learn.

Reading a paper in three passes

A new student often reads a paper from the first word to the last. After three hours, they still cannot say what it adds. S. Keshav described a better way in 2007. You read the paper in up to three passes. Each pass has one goal.

The bird's-eye view: 5 to 10 minutes

Read the title, the abstract and the introduction carefully. Read only the headings. Read the conclusions. Glance at the references and tick the ones you know.

Answer the five Cs

Category: what kind of paper is it? Context: which work is it close to? Correctness: do the assumptions look valid? Contributions: what is new? Clarity: is it well written?

The content: up to one hour

Read with care, but skip the proofs. Study every figure and graph. Check the axes and the error bars. Mark the references you have not read. Write notes in the margin.

Tell it to a friend

You can now explain the main point and its evidence to someone else. For many papers, you stop here.

Rebuild the paper: hours

Re-create the work in your head with the same assumptions. Challenge every claim. Keshav says this takes four or five hours for a beginner and about one hour for an expert.

Find hidden problems

You can rebuild the paper's structure from memory. You see hidden assumptions, missing citations and weak experiments. You also collect ideas for future work.

The first pass is enough for papers outside your area. The third pass is for papers you will build on or review. Keshav also gives a tip for writers. Most reviewers read your paper only once. So clear headings and a strong abstract matter a lot.

Keep a reading log. For each paper write one line for each of the five Cs, plus one open question. After 40 papers, this log becomes your related work section.

Trusting the abstract alone. Abstracts sell the best result. Always look at the evaluation figures before you cite a claim.

Finding related work

Related work is the earlier research close to yours. You need it for two reasons. It shows your idea is new. It also gives you baselines to compare against.

  1. Search with good keywords in Google Scholar, DBLP, Semantic Scholar, arXiv or the ACM Digital Library. Pick three to five recent papers.
  2. Do one pass on each. Read their related work sections. Look for a recent survey paper. If you find one, read it first.
  3. Look for references that many papers share, and names that appear again and again. These are the key papers and key researchers.
  4. Visit the pages of the key researchers. See where they publish. Those venues are the top ones for this area.
  5. Scan the last few years of those venues. Add the strong papers to your list. Repeat when a new key paper appears.

Two moves help a lot. Backward snowballing means you follow a paper's references to older work. Forward snowballing means you find newer papers that cite it. Claes Wohlin wrote guidelines for this method in 2014. For a very careful review, software engineering uses a systematic literature review with written search rules.

Where to search
ToolGood forWatch out
DBLPExact author lists, venues and years in computer scienceNo full text, no citation counts
Google ScholarWide search and "cited by" lists for forward snowballingMixes versions, includes weak sources
Semantic ScholarCitation graphs and short summariesSummaries are machine-made
arXivThe newest preprints, especially in machine learningNot peer reviewed
ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, ACL AnthologyThe published versions of recordSome full texts need a library login

Citing a paper you only know from someone else's citation. Errors copy themselves this way. If you cite it, open it and check that it really says what you claim.

From a topic to a question and a hypothesis

A topic is too wide to test. "Retrieval for AI" is a topic. You must narrow it in steps until you can design one experiment.

  1. Topic: retrieval for AI assistants.
  2. Problem: answers miss facts that are spread over two documents.
  3. Question: does a cross-encoder reranker help on multi-document questions?
  4. Hypothesis: on our 400-question test set, adding the reranker raises nDCG@10 by at least 3 points over BM25 alone.
  5. Plan: run both systems on the same questions, compare per question, report a 95% interval.

A good hypothesis is falsifiable. Some result could prove it wrong. "The reranker is better in some way" is not falsifiable. "At least 3 points on this test set" is. In statistics, we write a null hypothesis H_0, for example "no difference". The alternative hypothesis H_1 says there is a difference.

Can large language models help programmers?

Is Rust better than C?

How can we make databases faster?

Does an LLM code reviewer find more injected bugs than a linter, on 200 real pull requests?

Does a Rust port of this parser remove the memory bugs found by fuzzing, with less than 10% slowdown?

Does a learned index beat a B+ tree on point lookups for this key distribution?

Before you start, test your idea with the Heilmeier catechism. George Heilmeier led DARPA from 1975 to 1977. DARPA still lists his questions for new projects.

  • What are you trying to do? Say it with no jargon.
  • How is it done today, and what are the limits?
  • What is new in your approach, and why do you think it will work?
  • Who cares? If you succeed, what changes?
  • What are the risks?
  • How much will it cost, and how long will it take?
  • What are the mid-term and final checks of success?

Choosing the hypothesis after you see the results. This is called HARKing (hypothesising after the results are known). Write your hypothesis and your main metric down before the main experiment.

Experiments and baselines

An experiment changes one thing and measures the effect. The thing you change is the independent variable. The thing you measure is the dependent variable. Everything else should stay the same. Those are the controlled variables.

A baseline is the method you compare against. Use a simple baseline and a strong one. The simple baseline shows the problem is not trivial. The strong baseline is the best known method, tuned as carefully as yours. An ablation study removes one part of your method at a time. It shows which part gives the gain.

Four threats to validity
ThreatQuestionExample problem
Internal validityDid my change cause the effect?The new system also had a bigger GPU.
External validityDoes it hold elsewhere?Tested only on English questions.
Construct validityDoes my metric measure what I mean?"Answer quality" measured only by length.
Conclusion validityIs the statistics sound?Three runs, no error bars, one lucky seed.

Machine learning has special dangers. Data leakage happens when test data affects training or tuning. If you tune on the test set, your test score is too high. Large language models add contamination: the model may have seen the benchmark during pre-training. Use a fresh, private test set when you can. See Machine learning for train, validation and test splits.

Systems research has its own rules. Warm up caches before you measure. Run each test many times. Report the median and the 99th percentile, not only the mean. Pin the hardware, the software versions and the settings. The chapter Cloud and system design shows why tail latency matters.

A weak baseline. Comparing your tuned model with an untuned old one makes any idea look good. Reviewers notice this first. Give the baseline the same tuning budget as your method.

Statistics for results

Back to our reranker. We run both systems on 20 questions and get one nDCG@10 score per question. The data below is invented for teaching. Each question gives a paired difference: new score minus old score. Pairing removes the effect of easy and hard questions.

// Paired comparison: bootstrap interval and permutation test.
const BASE: [f64; 20] = [0.42, 0.55, 0.31, 0.60, 0.48, 0.39, 0.70, 0.52, 0.45, 0.58,
                         0.33, 0.61, 0.47, 0.50, 0.44, 0.66, 0.38, 0.57, 0.49, 0.53];
const NEW: [f64; 20] = [0.47, 0.58, 0.30, 0.66, 0.55, 0.41, 0.72, 0.60, 0.44, 0.63,
                        0.40, 0.62, 0.52, 0.49, 0.50, 0.69, 0.45, 0.58, 0.55, 0.57];

struct Rng(u64);
impl Rng {
    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 { // splitmix64: a small, well-known random generator
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_add(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15);
        let mut z = self.0;
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9);
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D049BB133111EB);
        z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let d: Vec<f64> = BASE.iter().zip(NEW).map(|(a, b)| b - a).collect(); // one difference per query
    let n = d.len();
    let mean = d.iter().sum::<f64>() / n as f64;
    let sd = (d.iter().map(|x| (x - mean).powi(2)).sum::<f64>() / (n - 1) as f64).sqrt();
    let se = sd / (n as f64).sqrt();
    println!("mean diff = {mean:.4}, sd = {sd:.4}, se = {se:.4}");
    println!("t-interval: [{:.4}, {:.4}]", mean - 2.093 * se, mean + 2.093 * se);
    let mut rng = Rng(42);
    let b = 10000; // bootstrap: resample the 20 differences with replacement
    let mut means: Vec<f64> = (0..b)
        .map(|_| (0..n).map(|_| d[(rng.next() % n as u64) as usize]).sum::<f64>() / n as f64)
        .collect();
    means.sort_by(|x, y| x.partial_cmp(y).unwrap());
    println!("bootstrap 95%: [{:.4}, {:.4}]", means[250], means[9749]);
    let mut hits = 0; // permutation test: flip the sign of each difference at random
    for _ in 0..b {
        let m = d.iter().map(|&x| if rng.next() & 1 == 1 { x } else { -x }).sum::<f64>() / n as f64;
        if m.abs() >= mean.abs() { hits += 1; }
    }
    println!("permutation p = {:.4}", (hits + 1) as f64 / (b + 1) as f64);
}
# Paired comparison: bootstrap interval and permutation test.
base = [0.42, 0.55, 0.31, 0.60, 0.48, 0.39, 0.70, 0.52, 0.45, 0.58,
        0.33, 0.61, 0.47, 0.50, 0.44, 0.66, 0.38, 0.57, 0.49, 0.53]
new = [0.47, 0.58, 0.30, 0.66, 0.55, 0.41, 0.72, 0.60, 0.44, 0.63,
       0.40, 0.62, 0.52, 0.49, 0.50, 0.69, 0.45, 0.58, 0.55, 0.57]
M = (1 << 64) - 1
state = 42


def rand() -> int:  # splitmix64: a small, well-known random generator
    global state
    state = (state + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & M
    z = state
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & M
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & M
    return z ^ (z >> 31)


d = [b - a for a, b in zip(base, new)]  # one difference per query
n = len(d)
mean = sum(d) / n
sd = (sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in d) / (n - 1)) ** 0.5
se = sd / n ** 0.5
print(f"mean diff = {mean:.4f}, sd = {sd:.4f}, se = {se:.4f}")
print(f"t-interval: [{mean - 2.093 * se:.4f}, {mean + 2.093 * se:.4f}]")

B = 10000  # bootstrap: resample the 20 differences with replacement
means = sorted(sum(d[rand() % n] for _ in range(n)) / n for _ in range(B))
print(f"bootstrap 95%: [{means[250]:.4f}, {means[9749]:.4f}]")

hits = 0  # permutation test: flip the sign of each difference at random
for _ in range(B):
    m = sum(x if rand() & 1 else -x for x in d) / n
    hits += abs(m) >= abs(mean)
print(f"permutation p = {(hits + 1) / (B + 1):.4f}")
mean diff = 0.0375, sd = 0.0290, se = 0.0065
t-interval: [0.0239, 0.0511]
bootstrap 95%: [0.0250, 0.0495]
permutation p = 0.0002

Both programs use the same random generator, so they print the same numbers. The reranker adds 3.75 points on average. Three methods agree that the true gain is roughly between 2.4 and 5 points. A standard paired t-test from SciPy gives t = 5.78 with 19 degrees of freedom and p \approx 0.00001.

Now the rules behind these numbers. The standard deviation s measures spread. The standard error measures how much the mean itself would move in a new sample.

For n independent values with sample standard deviation s: \mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} An approximate 95% confidence interval for the true mean is \bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1} \cdot \mathrm{SE}.

In our data s = 0.0290 and n = 20. So \mathrm{SE} = 0.0290 / 4.47 = 0.0065. The t value for 19 degrees of freedom is 2.093. The interval is 0.0375 \pm 0.0136. Four times more data halves the standard error.

Take n independent values from one distribution with mean \mu and finite variance \sigma^2. As n grows, the distribution of the sample mean gets close to a normal distribution with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma / \sqrt{n}.

Proof idea

Standardise each value so it has mean 0 and variance 1. Look at the characteristic function (a Fourier transform of the distribution) of the scaled sum. A Taylor expansion shows it tends to e^{-t^2/2}, which is the characteristic function of the standard normal. A continuity theorem turns this into convergence of distributions. In simple words: many small independent errors add up to a bell curve.

The theorem explains why the t-interval works even when single scores are not normal. With very few values, use the bootstrap. It resamples your own data thousands of times and reads the interval from the results.

A p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if H_0 were true. Our permutation test asks: if the reranker did nothing, each sign would be random. How often do random signs give a mean as big as 0.0375? Almost never, so p is small.

In 2016 the American Statistical Association published six principles on p-values. A p-value does not give the chance that your hypothesis is true. It does not measure the size or importance of an effect. Decisions should not rest only on p \lt 0.05. Report everything you tested.

An effect size says how big the gain is. Always report it with an interval: "+3.75 nDCG points, 95% CI [2.4, 5.1]". A tiny gain can have a tiny p-value with a huge test set. That does not make it useful.

Testing many things creates false alarms. Suppose you test 20 settings with no real effect, each at the 5% level. The chance of at least one "significant" result is 1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 64\%.

If you run m tests and use the level \alpha / m for each one, the chance of one or more false positives is at most \alpha.

Proof

Let A_i be the event "test i gives a false positive". Each has probability at most \alpha / m. By the union bound from Discrete maths for computer science, P(A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_m) \le m \cdot \alpha / m = \alpha.

For 20 tests at \alpha = 0.05, each test needs p \lt 0.0025. The rule is safe but strict. Statistical power is the chance that your study finds a real effect. Small test sets have low power. Plan the size before you start.

"p = 0.03, so there is a 97% chance my method is better." This is wrong. The p-value assumes H_0 is true. It is not the probability of H_0. Also wrong: running seeds until one gives p \lt 0.05. That is called p-hacking.

Writing the paper and the review process

Most computer science papers follow one shape. Readers know it, so they find things fast.

The usual structure of a computer science paper
PartJobSize
AbstractProblem, gap, idea, main number, meaning150 to 250 words
IntroductionWhy it matters, what is missing, a numbered list of contributions1 to 1.5 pages
BackgroundOnly what the reader needsShort
Design or methodThe idea, with one running exampleThe core
EvaluationQuestions, setup, results, ablations, threats to validityThe core
Related workHow others differ, said fairlyAbout 1 page
ConclusionWhat we learned, limits, future workShort

Simon Peyton Jones gives seven pieces of advice in his talk "How to write a great research paper". Start writing early, because writing helps you think. Find your one key idea. Tell it as a story. State your contributions clearly and back each one with evidence. Put related work later. Write for the reader, not as a diary of your work. Ask readers for feedback.

A contribution list is the heart of the introduction. Each item must be a claim that the paper proves.

We study rerankers for retrieval and present some interesting results.

We show that a small cross-encoder reranker raises nDCG@10 by 3.8 points on multi-document questions (Section 5.2), and that half of the gain comes from the first 20 candidates (Section 5.4).

Peer review decides if a paper is published. In computer science, top conferences are as important as journals. A typical conference round works like this.

  1. You submit before a fixed deadline. Many venues are double-blind, so you hide your name.
  2. The programme committee bids on papers. Each paper gets about three reviews.
  3. Each review gives a summary, strengths, weaknesses, questions, a score and a confidence level.
  4. Many venues allow a short author response, often called a rebuttal.
  5. Reviewers discuss. The chairs decide: accept, reject, or sometimes revise.
  6. An accepted paper gets a final "camera-ready" version. Journals use rounds of revision instead.

A good rebuttal is calm and short. Thank the reviewers. Answer the biggest concern first, with facts and new numbers if allowed. Do not argue about taste. When you review others, judge the work, not the authors. Name the main problem and say how to fix it.

Hiding the limits. Reviewers find them anyway, and then they trust nothing else. A clear "Limitations" paragraph makes the paper stronger.

Ethics and reproducibility

Research needs trust. Readers cannot check every step. So the rules of honest work are strict, and breaking them can end a career.

  • Never fabricate or falsify. Fabrication invents data. Falsification changes or hides it.
  • Never plagiarise. Plagiarism is using others' words or ideas without credit. Reusing your own old text without saying so is also a problem.
  • Fair authorship. Authors are people who did real intellectual work and can defend the paper. The ACM policy says AI tools cannot be authors. Rules for disclosing AI help differ by venue and change often. Check the call for papers.
  • People and data. Studies with people need approval from an ethics board, often called an IRB in the United States. Get informed consent. Protect personal data and follow data laws.
  • Licences. Check that you may use each dataset, model and code base. Respect their licences when you share.
  • Harm. Think about misuse of your work. In security research, tell the vendor about a bug before you publish it. This is called coordinated disclosure.

Now reproducibility. ACM uses three words in version 1.1 of its badging policy. Check the official page, because these terms changed in 2020.

Three levels of repeating work (ACM terms)
WordWhoSetup
RepeatabilitySame teamSame setup
ReproducibilityDifferent teamSame setup, your artifacts
ReplicabilityDifferent teamDifferent setup, built on their own

Many systems conferences run artifact evaluation. Volunteers try your code and award badges. For example, SOSP 2025 used the ACM badges Available, Functional and Reproduced. NeurIPS asks every paper for a checklist. It covers claims, limits, reproducibility, code and data, error bars, compute, ethics and licences. A paper without the checklist is rejected without review.

A reproducible project has: a public repository with a tag, a lock file for packages, a container or setup script, fixed seeds, one script per figure, the raw results, and a README that says how long each step takes.

"The code is available on request." Requests often fail years later. Put code and data in a public archive with a permanent link when the licence allows it.

Thirty classic papers

These 30 papers shaped the topics of this book. Each title links to the publisher's page. We checked authors and years against the publishers' records on 2026-11-15. Read the first pass of each. Choose the third pass for the five closest to your thesis.

Thirty classic papers, oldest first

  1. 1936-1959 Foundations. What can be computed, how much information a channel carries, the first graph algorithms.
  2. 1969-1978 The golden decade. Proofs of programs, relational data, NP-completeness, UNIX, TCP/IP, public keys and logical time.
  3. 1982-1988 Distributed and learning theory. Byzantine faults, FLP, end-to-end design, PAC learning, backpropagation, congestion control.
  4. 1998-2007 Web scale. PageRank, MapReduce and Dynamo show how to run on thousands of cheap machines.
  5. 2012-2020 Deep learning. CNNs on GPUs, Raft, the transformer and retrieval-augmented generation.

Turing's paper was received in May 1936 and printed in late 1936. The journal volume carries the dates 1936-37, so some lists say 1937. MapReduce first appeared at OSDI 2004. A later version came out in Communications of the ACM in 2008.

Planning a thesis

A Master's thesis is a small research project with a fixed end date. Programs differ a lot. Some give six months full-time. Others spread the thesis over a year next to courses. Read your school's rules on length, format and the defence first.

  1. Weeks 1 to 4: read 30 to 50 papers with the three-pass method. Write a two-page proposal with the question, the hypothesis, the baselines and the main metric.
  2. Weeks 5 to 10: build the system. Run a small pilot study. Fix the evaluation pipeline before you scale up.
  3. Weeks 11 to 16: run the main experiments and the ablations. Keep a lab notebook with every run, its settings and its result.
  4. Weeks 17 to 21: write the full draft. Make every figure with a script.
  5. Weeks 22 to 24: get feedback, revise, prepare the talk and the defence.

Meet your supervisor at a fixed rhythm, for example every week for 30 minutes. Bring a one-page update: what you did, what you found, what blocks you and the next step. Plan for risk. Ask early, "What if the main idea fails?" A careful negative result can still make a good thesis if the question was good.

Examiners often ask four things. What is your contribution in one sentence? Why is your baseline fair? What are the limits? What would you do next? Prepare a short answer for each.

Planning the writing for the last month. Then the experiments run late, and the writing gets two weeks. Write the method and setup sections while you build. Draft results as soon as each experiment ends.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for research writing and work
PatternPurposeModelNote
Gap sentence: "X works well for A, but not for B."Show what is missingVector search works well for single facts, but not for multi-step questions.Give evidence for the gap, with a citation or a number.
Contribution: "We show that X does Y by Z (Section N)."State a claim you proveWe show that the reranker adds 3.8 points of nDCG@10 (Section 5.2).Every item needs a section that proves it.
Hypothesis: "On D, method M improves metric K by at least T."Make a testable guessOn our 400 questions, the reranker improves nDCG@10 by 3 points or more.Fix D, M, K and T before the main run.
Result with interval: "+E (95% CI [L, H])"Report size and certainty+3.75 points (95% CI [2.4, 5.1]), n = 20 paired queries.Never report a mean with no spread.
Hedge: "This suggests..." / "In our setting..."Claim only what the data showsThis suggests the gain comes from early candidates.Do not hedge a result you proved. Hedge only real doubt.
Limitation: "Our study is limited to X. Results may differ for Y."Show the honest scopeWe test only English questions. Results may differ for other languages.Name the limit before a reviewer does.
Related work contrast: "Unlike A, which does P, we do Q."Show how you differUnlike GraphRAG, which builds communities, we rerank passages only.Be fair. Describe others as they would describe themselves.
Review: "The main weakness is X. It could be fixed by Y."Give useful criticismThe main weakness is the untuned baseline. Tuning BM25 parameters would fix it.Judge the work, never the people.
Rebuttal: "We thank R2. On concern C, new results show..."Answer a reviewOn the baseline concern, the tuned BM25 gives 0.49. Our gain stays at 3.5 points.Answer the biggest concern first. Stay calm and short.
Three-pass readingRead many papers fast10 minutes, then 1 hour, then a full rebuildStop after pass one for most papers.
Ablation tableShow which part helpsFull system 0.55, without reranker 0.51, without query rewrite 0.54Remove one part at a time.
Reproducibility kitLet others rerun your workTagged repo, lock file, container, seeds, one script per figureTest it on a clean machine before you publish.

Practice

You have 10 minutes for a paper outside your area. What should you read?

  • The introduction and the first half of the method
  • The title, abstract, introduction, headings and conclusions
  • The proofs, because they show if the paper is correct

That is Keshav's first pass. It takes five to ten minutes and lets you answer the five Cs.

Which hypothesis is falsifiable?

  • Our cache design is better in many ways.
  • On the YCSB-B workload, our cache cuts p99 latency by at least 20% against LRU.
  • Caching is important for modern systems.

Only the second one names a workload, a metric, a baseline and a threshold. A result could prove it wrong.

A paper reports p = 0.01. What does this mean?

  • There is a 99% chance the new method is better.
  • The effect is large.
  • If there were no real effect, a result this extreme would happen about 1% of the time.

A p-value is computed assuming H_0 is true. It says nothing direct about the chance that H_1 is true, and nothing about effect size.

Another team downloads your code and data and gets your numbers. In ACM version 1.1 terms, this is:

  • Repeatability
  • Reproducibility
  • Replicability

Different team, same setup with your artifacts. Replicability would mean they built their own artifacts.

Your sample has s = 0.08 and n = 16. The standard error is ?.

You run 10 tests and want a total false-positive risk of 5%. With Bonferroni, each test needs p \lt ?.

Finding newer papers that cite a known paper is called ? snowballing.

  1. Turn the topic "LLM agents for testing" into a question and a falsifiable hypothesis.
    Answer

    One good answer. Question: can an LLM agent write unit tests that raise branch coverage beyond a search-based tool? Hypothesis: on 50 Python packages, the agent reaches at least 5 points more branch coverage than Pynguin with the same time budget. It names the data, the baseline, the metric and the threshold.

  2. A student reports "our model gets 81.2% accuracy, the baseline gets 80.9%". They ran each model once. What is missing?
    Answer

    Several runs with different seeds, a spread or interval for each model, and a paired test on the same test items. A 0.3-point gap can easily come from a lucky seed. They should also say whether the baseline got the same tuning budget.

  3. The bootstrap in this chapter gave [0.0250, 0.0495]. Why is it close to, but not the same as, the t-interval [0.0239, 0.0511]?
    Answer

    Both estimate the same uncertainty in different ways. The t-interval assumes the mean is roughly normal. The bootstrap uses the shape of the 20 real differences. The bootstrap interval is often a bit narrow for small samples, because 20 values cannot show the full spread. The two agree on the main point: the gain is clearly above zero.

  4. Your test set has 20 settings, and one gives p = 0.03. Your adviser says it is not significant. Explain why.
    Answer

    With 20 tests and no real effect, the chance of at least one p \lt 0.05 is about 64%. With a Bonferroni correction, each test needs p \lt 0.0025. So 0.03 is weak evidence after the correction. A fresh test of that one setting on new data would be better evidence.

  5. Write a calm rebuttal sentence for this review: "The baseline is not tuned, so the gain is unclear."
    Answer

    "We thank the reviewer. We tuned BM25 with a grid over k1 and b on the validation set. The tuned baseline reaches 0.49 nDCG@10, and our gain stays at 3.5 points (95% CI [2.2, 4.8]). We will add this table to Section 5."

  6. Pick three classic papers from the table that connect to distributed systems. Say in one line each what they contribute.
    Answer

    Lamport 1978: happens-before and logical clocks order events without real time. Fischer, Lynch and Paterson 1985: in a fully asynchronous system, one crash can block deterministic consensus. Ongaro and Ousterhout 2014: Raft, a consensus algorithm designed to be understandable. Lamport, Shostak and Pease 1982 or Dynamo 2007 are also good answers.

  7. Your main experiment failed: the idea gives no gain. You have eight weeks left. What do you do?
    Answer

    Tell the supervisor at once. Check the pipeline for bugs with a small known case. If the result holds, turn it into a careful negative result. Explain why the idea should have worked, show strong evidence that it does not, and analyse why. Add an ablation or a study of when it helps. Start writing now, because a clear negative result is still a valid thesis in many programs.

What are the five Cs of the first pass?

Category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity.

What is an ablation study?

Removing one part of your method at a time to see how much each part helps.

What is the standard error of a mean?

s / \sqrt{n}. It shrinks with more data.

What does the Bonferroni correction do?

It tests each of m hypotheses at level α/m, so the total false-positive risk stays below α.

Repeatability, reproducibility, replicability?

Same team same setup. Different team same setup. Different team different setup.

Who wrote the first consensus paper designed to be understandable?

Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, Raft, USENIX ATC 2014.

Key takeaways

  • Research turns a question into evidence and a claim. A tool becomes research when you test it fairly and show what we learn.
  • Read in three passes: 10 minutes, then an hour, then a full rebuild for the few papers that matter most.
  • Find related work with search, survey papers and snowballing. Open every paper you cite.
  • Narrow a topic into a falsifiable hypothesis. Fix the data, metric, baseline and threshold before the main run.
  • Use strong, tuned baselines and ablations. Watch for leakage, contamination and the four threats to validity.
  • Report effect sizes with intervals. A p-value is not the chance your idea is right. Correct for many tests.
  • Write a clear contribution list, show your limits, answer reviews calmly, and share artifacts so others can reproduce your work.
  • Plan the thesis in phases, meet your supervisor often, and write from the first week.

Sources

  • How to Read a Paper. S. Keshav, ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 37(3), July 2007: the three-pass method and the literature survey steps.
  • How to Write a Great Research Paper. Simon Peyton Jones's slides at Microsoft Research: the seven suggestions for writing.
  • The ASA Statement on p-Values. American Statistical Association, 2016: six principles on what p-values mean and do not mean.
  • The Heilmeier Catechism. DARPA's page with the questions for judging a research proposal.
  • NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines. The required checklist on claims, limits, reproducibility, error bars, compute and ethics.
  • SOSP 2025 artifact badges. How a systems conference awards the ACM Available, Functional and Reproduced badges.

Master's exam preparation

This is the last chapter of the book. It turns everything you studied into exam skill. You get a checklist of every topic, a clear picture of how exams ask questions, a 12-week plan, a sheet of every formula and theorem, and 100 original questions with worked answers.

  • Check your knowledge of every chapter against one list, and find your weak parts.
  • Describe how entrance, comprehensive and qualifying exams ask questions, using only public facts.
  • Answer numeric, multiple-choice, proof and design questions with a fixed method.
  • Follow a 12-week revision plan with timed mock exams.
  • Use the formula and theorem sheet, and solve 100 exam-style questions from all parts of the book.

How exams ask questions

Start with one real-style question. "A direct-mapped cache holds 32 KiB in blocks of 64 bytes. Addresses have 32 bits. How many bits are in the tag?" You type one number. There is no menu of answers. Can you do it in two minutes?

Here is the work. The offset needs \log_2 64 = 6 bits. The cache has 32768 / 64 = 512 lines, so the index needs 9 bits. The tag is the rest: 32 - 6 - 9 = 17 bits. This is a numerical answer question. Many exams love it, because guessing does not help.

Exams use a small set of question styles. Learn to spot the style first. The style tells you how to answer.

Question styles and how to answer them
StyleWhat you doWhere you meet it
Multiple choice (MCQ)Pick one option. Remove wrong ones first.Entrance exams, course exams
Multiple select (MSQ)Check every option on its own.GATE, some course exams
Numerical answer (NAT)Compute a number. Check units and rounding.GATE, course exams
ProofState the claim, give the idea, then the steps.Theory courses, written qualifying exams
DesignAsk for numbers, draw parts, name trade-offs.Systems exams, interviews
OralExplain, then defend under questions.Qualifying exams, thesis defences

Three kinds of exam

An entrance exam decides who joins a Master's program. A comprehensive exam checks the whole degree at the end. Some Master's programs offer it as an option instead of a thesis. A qualifying exam decides if a PhD student may go on to research. The rules differ by school, so always read your own school's page.

GATE CS: the public facts

GATE is a large entrance exam in India. IISc and the IITs run it together. Its scores are used for Master's and PhD admission, for study grants, and by some public-sector employers in hiring. The facts below come from the official GATE 2027 site, checked on 2026-11-15. Check the official page: this can change.

Qualifying exams: two public examples

PhD qualifying exams look very different from school to school. Two public pages show the range.

Project style. The University of Wisconsin-Madison graduate handbook (2025-26) says every Computer Sciences area except Optimization uses a project-based qualifying exam. A committee of at least three faculty judges the project. Students also take breadth courses, and finish both within three years.

Oral style. The Systems and Networking area at the University of Illinois uses an oral exam. The student presents two assigned papers, about 20 minutes each, and answers questions on them. The committee also asks about a published reading list.

Old exams are the best guide to style. Many departments post past papers and reading lists. Use them to learn the style, then write your own questions. Do not just memorise old answers.

Studying only from an exam syllabus. A syllabus lists topics. It does not show depth. Do practice questions early, so you learn how deep each topic goes.

Marking a topic green because the chapter "feels familiar". Familiar is not the same as able. Mark it green only after you solve its questions with no notes.

How to answer: one method per question type

Under time pressure, people skip steps and make small errors. A fixed method protects you. Here is one method for each style.

  1. Underline every number and its unit. Write what is asked, with its unit.
  2. Name the formula or theorem. Write it down before you use it.
  3. Put in the numbers. Keep fractions or powers of two as long as you can.
  4. Check the size. Is the answer in a sensible range? A cache miss rate above 100% is wrong.
  5. Check the rounding rule in the question. Type the answer.
  1. Write the claim in symbols. Say which proof method you use: direct, contradiction, induction or reduction.
  2. Give the idea in one or two sentences. Examiners give marks for a correct idea.
  3. Write the steps. Name each theorem you use.
  4. End by saying what you proved.
  1. Ask or state the requirements and the numbers: users, requests per second, data size.
  2. Do the capacity maths with Little's law and simple products.
  3. Draw the parts and the data flow.
  4. Name two trade-offs and one failure case. Say how you would measure success.

Negative marks: when to guess

Suppose a 1-mark MCQ has four choices and a wrong answer costs 1/3 mark. Is a blind guess worth it? Use linearity of expectation.

A blind guess is right with probability 1/4. The expected score is \tfrac14 \cdot 1 - \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac13 = 0. So a blind guess gains nothing on average. Now remove one choice you know is wrong. The expected score becomes \tfrac13 \cdot 1 - \tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac13 = \tfrac19 \approx 0.11. That is positive. The same maths holds for 2-mark MCQs, because the penalty doubles with the mark.

MSQ and NAT questions have no negative marks in GATE. So never leave them empty. Plan your time too. Three hours for 65 questions is under three minutes each. Do a first pass for questions you can solve fast. Mark the others and come back.

Check numeric answers with code

When you study, check your hand answers with a tiny program. This program recomputes eight answers from the question bank below.

// Recompute eight answers from the question bank.
fn amdahl(p: f64, n: f64) -> f64 {
    1.0 / ((1.0 - p) + p / n)
}

fn pow_mod(mut b: u64, mut e: u64, m: u64) -> u64 {
    let mut r = 1; // square-and-multiply
    b %= m;
    while e > 0 {
        if e & 1 == 1 { r = r * b % m; }
        b = b * b % m;
        e >>= 1;
    }
    r
}

fn main() {
    println!("Q1  0b11010110 as i8 = {}", 0b1101_0110u8 as i8); // top bit counts as -128
    let fact5 = (1..=5u64).product::<u64>() as f64;
    println!("Q20 comparisons for 5 keys = {}", fact5.log2().ceil());
    println!("Q48 Amdahl p=0.9 n=10 = {:.2}", amdahl(0.9, 10.0));
    println!("Q61 hosts in a /26 = {}", 2u32.pow(32 - 26) - 2); // minus network and broadcast
    println!("Q73 fan-out 100, p=1% -> {:.3}", 1.0 - 0.99f64.powi(100));
    println!("Q81 RSA 7^3 mod 55 = {} and back: {}", pow_mod(7, 3, 55), pow_mod(13, 27, 55));
    println!("Q90 chain 0.95^10 = {:.3}", 0.95f64.powi(10));
    println!("Q91 RRF ranks (1,3) = {:.5}, ranks (2,2) = {:.5}", 1.0 / 61.0 + 1.0 / 63.0, 2.0 / 62.0);
}
# Recompute eight answers from the question bank.
import math


def amdahl(p: float, n: float) -> float:
    return 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)


print("Q1  0b11010110 as i8 =", 0b11010110 - 256)  # top bit counts as -128
print("Q20 comparisons for 5 keys =", math.ceil(math.log2(math.factorial(5))))
print(f"Q48 Amdahl p=0.9 n=10 = {amdahl(0.9, 10):.2f}")
print("Q61 hosts in a /26 =", 2 ** (32 - 26) - 2)  # minus network and broadcast
print(f"Q73 fan-out 100, p=1% -> {1 - 0.99 ** 100:.3f}")
print("Q81 RSA 7^3 mod 55 =", pow(7, 3, 55), "and back:", pow(13, 27, 55))
print(f"Q90 chain 0.95^10 = {0.95 ** 10:.3f}")
print(f"Q91 RRF ranks (1,3) = {1/61 + 1/63:.5f}, ranks (2,2) = {2/62:.5f}")

Spending ten minutes on one hard 1-mark question. It costs you three easy questions later. Set a limit, for example four minutes. When time is up, mark it and move on.

A 12-week revision plan

This plan assumes about 15 hours a week. Each week has new topics, old topics and timed practice. Old topics come back again and again, because active recall and spaced review make memory last.

Find your weak spots

Do 30 mixed questions from the bank in 90 minutes. Mark the checklist. Then review How computers compute, Programming foundations and Discrete maths.

Data structures and sorting

Write the cost table from memory. Prove the sorting lower bound. Solve Q4, Q11 to Q13, Q20 and Q21.

Graphs, DP and greedy

Trace Dijkstra and Kruskal on paper. Fill one DP table each day. Solve Q14 to Q17 and Q22 to Q25.

Flow, LP and randomised algorithms

Run one augmenting path search by hand. Write one dual LP. At the end, take a 90-minute half mock.

Automata and computability

Build five DFAs. Write the halting proof from memory. Solve Q29 to Q31 and Q36 to Q39.

Complexity and logic

Draw the reduction map. Write two loop invariants. Solve Q32 to Q35, Q40 and Q41.

Architecture and operating systems

Do ten cache and paging calculations. Simulate FIFO, LRU and OPT. Solve Q42 to Q45 and Q48 to Q52.

Concurrency, compilers and types

Explain ABA and SSA aloud. Reduce three lambda terms. Take a second half mock.

Networks and databases

Do subnet and window maths. Find keys and normal forms. Solve Q58, Q61 to Q65, Q68 and Q69.

Distributed systems, design and security

Size quorums. Do one full design with numbers. Run toy RSA. Solve Q66, Q67, Q70 to Q76, Q81 and Q82.

AI, AI systems and electives

Backpropagate one network by hand. Solve Q77 to Q80, Q83 to Q100.

Full mocks and rest

Take two full 3-hour mocks. Study your error log and the formula sheet. Sleep well the night before the exam.

Every day follows the same rhythm.

  1. Ten minutes: write five formulas from the sheet from memory, then check them.
  2. Sixty minutes: study the new topic of the week.
  3. Thirty minutes: solve questions with a timer.
  4. Ten minutes: write each mistake in an error log, with its cause and the right idea.

Sort your error log by cause, not by topic. Common causes are "misread the question", "wrong formula", "arithmetic slip" and "did not know". Each cause has its own fix.

Reading chapters again and again. Re-reading feels good but builds little memory. Close the book and write the answer first. Then check.
